entries.n: Basic planning rules for JOA road/airfield engineering
entries.desc: Eight planning guidelines for military engineers in the JOA
entries.use: Guide every design decision in a joint operations area where time and risk are high
entries.how: Keep designs simple; use local materials; use existing facilities; reduce safety factors for time/war risk; design for initial (up to 6 months) or temporary (up to 2 years) life; phase construction for early use; avoid dense brush, timber and rolling terrain needing heavy clearing/grading; protect natural drainage, culverts and roads
entries.dim: Initial design life: up to 6 months; temporary design life: up to 2 years
entries.wn: Safety factors in design are drastically reduced in the JOA because of time constraints and risks of war

entries.desc: List of engineer construction unit responsibilities
entries.use: Know what engineer units do for route traffic
entries.how: Reconnoiter roads and bridges; recommend traffic-control procedures; construct/install signs and route markers; regulate traffic where engineer work is going on; help keep traffic moving on main supply routes regardless of weather or enemy

entries.n: Select a site: location factors checklist
entries.desc: 18 factors used to locate and lay out construction projects
entries.use: Choose the best location for a road or airfield before construction
entries.how: Evaluate mission, existing facilities, soils, drainage, geology, topography, earthwork, alignment, obstacle crossings, bridge approaches, ground cover, required area, material/utility access, marginal material, flight-way obstructions, sunlit slopes, tactical considerations, future expansion

entries.n: Locate roads and airfields for drainage, soils and terrain
entries.desc: Siting rules for soils, drainage, geology, topography and alignment
entries.use: Reduce construction effort by siting on good ground
entries.how: Put roads where drainage is easy and structures few; drainage is more critical for airfields (divert water completely around). Avoid valley low points, depressions, unprotected floodplains and alluvial fans, and high water table areas (if unavoidable, lower the water table during construction). Alluvial terraces are often ideal for airfields. Run route along the side of a steep hill rather than over it. Keep curves and grades to a minimum; make tangents long. Align runways with prevailing wind
entries.wn: Avoid rock-heavy areas: rock removal needs special equipment and training. Take borings or test pits to find rock where cutting is required

entries.desc: Rock-cut orientation rule
entries.use: Lay out road cuts in rock
entries.how: Align road cuts perpendicular to the strike in sedimentary rocks; if not possible, use safe-slope ratios (Figure 2-1)

entries.desc: Glide-angle clearance criteria
entries.use: Check that obstacles do not penetrate approach surfaces at a proposed airfield or heliport
entries.how: Most heliports need an approach zone with 10:1 glide angle (8:1 for short-duration operations); heavy-cargo aircraft in the support area need a glide angle as flat as 50:1. Clear a similar width on runway sides and grade to specification
entries.dim: Heliport approach 10:1 (8:1 short duration); heavy cargo up to 50:1
entries.wn: Avoid locations needing extensive work to achieve the glide angle

entries.n: Siting roads for sun, wind and tactical cover
entries.desc: Sunlit slope and tactical siting rules
entries.use: Locate roads so surface dries fast or is concealed
entries.how: If concealment is not needed, put roads on sunny exposed sides of valleys/hills (surface dries, less ice). Consider prevailing wind for snow/sand; orient snow or sand fences for wind. Tactically: use defilade on reverse side of hill/ravine, use natural camouflage, disperse airfield facilities

entries.desc: Typical airfield ground-reconnaissance party and suggested equipment
entries.use: Organize a ground reconnaissance team
entries.how: Typical party (Table 2-1): officer in charge, senior NCO, technical engineer, plane-table man, terrain intelligence analyst, geospatial engineer, 2 driver/RTOs (8 personnel). Equipment per Table 2-2
entries.dim: 8-person party
entries.eq: See Table 2-2 (trucks, binoculars, clinometer, measuring tapes, lensatic compasses, radio, camera, etc.)

entries.desc: Route/road/location reconnaissance types and forms
entries.use: Gather route data for movement or classification
entries.how: Hasty route recon: immediate trafficability, critical terrain data, map overlay/sketch. Deliberate route recon: detailed analysis and classification of significant features, repair/demolition procedures, overlay plus enclosed reconnaissance reports. Road recon uses DA Form 1248; engineer recon uses DA Form 1711
entries.eq: DA Form 1248 (Road Reconnaissance Report); DA Form 1711 (Engineer Reconnaissance Report)

entries.desc: Ford site selection and measurements
entries.use: Decide whether a stream can be forded
entries.how: Look for slow current (usually under 2 mph), low sloping banks, good approaches, uniformly increasing bottom depth and firm bottom. Locate between bends (reach). Normal stream velocity at fording site should not exceed 3 ft/s. Check base flow, high-water flow, flood flow (use bank erosion cuts; note highest flood level within a 2-year period). Make a cross section with bank slopes, bottom slopes, bottom variations, depth, average velocity from measurements at equal intervals, streambed character (for Manning's n)
entries.dim: Current < 2 mph typical; velocity <= 3 ft/s; max depth 2 ft for trucks; see Table 2-3
entries.eq: Measuring tape, improvised depth measuring means
entries.wn: Increased water depth can close a ford; mountain and desert streams change depth suddenly

entries.desc: Ford approach, bottom, marking and maintenance steps
entries.use: Prepare a ford crossing
entries.how: Approach: use max slopes in Table 2-3; place bank cut material off to side, not in stream; protect surface. Bottom: fill short deep gaps with rock or gravel (preferably retained by wire mesh); soft mud bottoms: cover with willow, brush mattresses or timbers, then metal planking, rock or coarse gravel. Mark posts at each end and intermediate points with depth index at each end; place warning notices. After each flood: inspect, repair scour with riprap, remove boulders/debris
entries.dim: Approach slopes per Table 2-3 (trucks 3:1; tanks 2:1; infantry 1:1)
entries.eq: Willow, brush mattress, timber, metal planking, rock, coarse gravel, wire mesh, riprap, marking posts
entries.wn: Raising the ford bottom increases upstream depth and flow velocity over ford, making vehicles harder to control

entries.desc: Dip location and construction rules
entries.use: Cross dry, wide, shallow arroyos subject to flash floods
entries.how: Site in straight run of arroyo, not in a bend. Subgrade of erosion-resistant material or rock-compacted base, set between cutoff retaining walls. Pavement of concrete or compacted macadam. Set structure at right angles to flow and at true dry-streambed level (never above). Mark like fords. Examine after each flood; riprap scour; stockpile rock for macadam hole repair
entries.dim: Structure at true dry-streambed level
entries.wn: Never set the structure above dry-streambed level (scour/silting)

entries.desc: Causeway design elements
entries.use: Keep a road open in medium-intensity floods
entries.how: Provide enough waterway at streambed level to pass design flow before flood reaches top; set culvert inverts at streambed level; provide enough cover over culverts for traffic loads; protect upstream/downstream faces from scour (concrete or rock-gabion facing, carried below streambed with aprons); anchor ends into banks; provide replaceable guardrails. Inspect after each partial submergence/overtopping and repair immediately
entries.eq: Culverts/CMP, concrete or rock-gabion facing, guardrails, heavy rock and gabions stockpile
entries.wn: Repair scour damage immediately or the next heavy flow could destroy the structure

entries.desc: Bridge siting and abutment drainage
entries.use: Locate a bridge and relieve abutment pressure
entries.how: Locate in a straight reach away from bends. High-level bridge if flood high-water mark is above banks; low-level if below. Abutments at Points 1A/1B (high dry ground, longer bridge) or 2A/2B (fewer piers but reduced waterway). With concrete abutments relieve saturated soil pressure with weep holes with bagged gravel backing, or gravel backing on lower abutment with perforated pipe at footing elevation draining to the sides. Approaches need gentle slope
entries.eq: Weep holes, bagged gravel, perforated pipe

entries.n: Select and survey an airfield runway site
entries.desc: Airfield siting steps
entries.use: Choose runway location and run ground survey
entries.how: Draw 5-mile diameter circle around existing airfields and shade a 2-mile wide strip centered on high-tension lines; search unshaded map areas. Use siting template for glide-angle check (example: hill >160 ft above runway end at 8,000 ft from overrun end lies in a 50:1 glide angle, so site unsuitable). Air recon passes: first circuit about 300 ft altitude; low pass about 50 yd to one side of centerline then opposite side at constant airspeed (length = airspeed x average time; average opposite passes); final circuit about 200 ft. Ground: pace lengths, measure slopes with clinometer, compass directions; stake runway ends; centerline and shoulder profile levels at 500-ft intervals (up to 1,000 ft in flat area). Preliminary runway check about 15 minutes in open country; designated site recon in one day; expedient soil evaluation 1 to 2 hours
entries.dim: 5-mile circle; 2-mile strip; 50:1 glide; levels 500 ft (max 1,000 ft flat)
entries.eq: Clinometer, compass, siting template (acetate), GPS, dynamic cone penetrometer
entries.tm: Preliminary runway check 15 min; soil eval 1-2 hr; recon of site in 1 day

entries.n: Four construction survey phases and control points
entries.desc: Survey sequence and control
entries.use: Know which survey to do and what control to set
entries.how: Reconnaissance and preliminary surveys pick location; final location survey sets permanent benchmarks (vertical) and hubs (horizontal); construction layout is last pre-construction operation (centerline, curves, stakes, grades, shoulders, structures, culvert sites). On airfields place control points beyond the clear zone; set target boards at each runway end. Tie grid to military grid if available. Datum from known benchmark, barometer reading or assumed elevation
entries.dim: Hub stake 2 in x 2 in; guard stake about 3/4 in x 3 in
entries.eq: Total station/GPS or manual survey gear

entries.n: Construction stake types, sizes and crew
entries.desc: Stake sizes and the three-point system
entries.use: Make and set stakes to guide earthwork
entries.how: General stakes about 1 in x 3 in x 2 ft (finished lumber, or blazed small trees/branches cut to length). Finished grade stakes and temporary benchmarks 2 in x 2 in x 12 in. Reference stakes about 2 in x 2 in x 18 in. Use a 3- to 5-person crew with survey gear or RTK GPS, ax, sledgehammer, machete. Mark with colored crayons using a uniform system. Standard three-point system: centerline stake plus two slope stakes at cut/fill limits at right angles to the centerline
entries.dim: General 1x3x2 ft; finish-grade/TBM 2x2x12 in; reference 2x2x18 in
entries.eq: Ax, sledgehammer, machete, crayons, survey equipment

entries.desc: Centerline stake spacing and marking
entries.use: Mark alignment and cut/fill at each station
entries.how: Place at 100-ft intervals (closer on rough ground or sharp horizontal/vertical curves); stake PC, PI, PT on horizontal curves and PVC, PVI, PVT and low/high point on vertical curves. Broad side perpendicular to centerline; front faces start point and shows station (6+5422 means 654.22 ft); back shows cut (C) or fill (F) amount; write decimal parts of a foot smaller, raised and underlined
entries.dim: 100-ft spacing

entries.desc: Slope stake placement and marking
entries.use: Define limits of grading and clearing width
entries.how: Set one each side on a line perpendicular to the centerline where cut or fill slope meets natural ground. Slope stakes outward (so equipment can work up to stake). Spacing 100 ft on tangents, 50 ft on horizontal/vertical curves; stake sharp breaks in ground profile. Front (faces centerline): elevation difference ground vs finished shoulder grade, then horizontal distance from centerline; back: station number and slope ratio. Clear area usually extends 6 ft beyond slope stakes
entries.dim: 100 ft tangent / 50 ft curve spacing; clear 6 ft beyond slope stakes

entries.n: Offset, finish-grade, reference, culvert stakes and benchmarks
entries.desc: Support stakes and benchmarks
entries.use: Preserve control and set final grade
entries.how: Offset stakes: beyond construction limits on line at right angles to centerline; carry slope stake data plus offset distance (circled) and elevation difference; relocate centerline by measuring slope-stake horizontal distance back toward centerline. Finish-grade (blue/red top) stakes 2x2 in, color-top only, used when within inches of final grade; not used in combat road construction except steep slopes; use string and graduated stick to check grade. Reference: witness points to objects, fix by two tapes with distances under 100 ft with arcs crossing near right angles, outside construction limits. Culvert stakes: on line parallel to and a few feet from centerline, with distance to centerline, vertical distance to invert, station; use batter boards. Temporary benchmarks every 500-1,000 ft off construction limits, set before centerline stakes
entries.dim: TBM spacing 500-1,000 ft; reference stakes < 100 ft from point; finish-grade stake 2x2 in
entries.eq: Tapes, string, graduated rod/stick, batter boards

entries.n: Compute cross-section end area (trapezoidal, stripper, double-meridian)
entries.desc: Three end-area methods
entries.use: Find end areas of cut/fill cross sections
entries.how: Trapezoidal: split section with verticals into triangles A=0.5bh and trapezoids A=0.5(b1+b2)h; bases are vertical (elevation differences), altitudes horizontal; field notes are elevation over distance from centerline. Stripper: verticals at constant spacing w, A = w x (sum of vertical lengths), measure on strip of paper (example 21.7 ft x 10 ft = 217 sq ft); closer spacing in rough ground. Double-meridian: for each adjacent point pair multiply elevation difference by sum of distances from centerline, plus for low-to-high, minus high-to-low, sum algebraically, divide by 2 (example 385.0/2 = 192.5 sq ft). Treat cut and fill separately
entries.eq: Plotted cross sections, subgrade template, strip of paper, planimeter or CAD
entries.wn: Stripper method loses accuracy when areas are curved or a triangle/trapezoid falls within the width

entries.n: Compute earthwork volume: average end area and prismoidal
entries.desc: Volume formulas
entries.use: Convert end areas to cubic yards of cut/fill
entries.how: Average end area: V (cu yd) = (A1+A2)/2 x L/27, with L in feet; at 100-ft stations V = 1.85(A1+A2). Accurate only if A1 and A2 are similar in shape. Prismoidal (for widely differing end areas): V = (1/6)(A1+4Am+A2)(L/27); get Am by averaging corresponding linear dimensions of A1 and A2, not their areas. 1 cu yd = 27 cu ft
entries.dim: 1 cu yd = 27 cu ft; 100-ft stations V=1.85(A1+A2)

entries.n: Estimate earthwork with Table 3-1 (average depth of cut or fill)
entries.desc: Table 3-1 procedure
entries.use: Quick earthwork estimate when time is short
entries.how: Find average cut/fill depth (col 1); move right to base width of cut (including ditches) or top width of fill, in 2-ft steps 26-44 ft (col 2); add column 3 per extra foot of width for odd widths; add column 4 if side slopes are 1.5:1 or 2:1 (col 2 assumes 1:1); result is cu yd for 100-ft section, scale proportionally for other lengths (85 ft x 0.85). Good for roads; for airfields use cross sections where possible since centerline profile may mislead
entries.dim: Widths 26-44 ft; depth 1-15 ft; slope 1:1, 1.5:1, 2:1
entries.wn: Centerline profile may mislead on wide airfield sections

entries.n: Borrow pit volume by grid method
entries.desc: Grid-method borrow computation
entries.use: Compute borrow volume available or taken
entries.how: Stake the pit as squares, size dependent on roughness (rougher = smaller), referenced outside limits; label lines with numbers and letters (C3). Take elevations before and after excavation. Single square: V = (A/27)(sum of four corner heights)/4. Whole grid: V = A(h1+2h2+3h3+4h4)/(4x27) where hn is corner heights common to n squares. Example: 50-ft squares, total corner cuts 123 ft over 25 squares, average 4.92 ft, V = 4.92 x 250 x 250/(4x27)... = 11,388 cu yd. Add wedge-shaped edge volumes using proportional areas
entries.dim: Example squares 50 ft x 50 ft

entries.n: Allow for shrinkage, swell and net volume (Table 3-2)
entries.desc: Volume change factors
entries.use: Make cut and fill volumes comparable
entries.how: Shrinkage: small in sand/gravel, large in silt, loam, clay; common allowance 10 to 30 percent for ordinary earth; can reach about 70 percent for humus stripping (shallow cuts usually 4 to 8 in). Swell: 10 to 40 percent. Allowances may prove 5 percent or more in error. Use Table 3-2 factors to convert between in-place, loose and compacted volumes. Typical: 1 cu yd in place becomes about 1.25 loose and about 0.9 compacted
entries.dim: Shrinkage 10-30%; swell 10-40%; stripping 4-8 in (humus layer 4-6 in on volume sheet)
entries.wn: Settlement of embankment can occur under traffic and foundation flow

entries.desc: Column-by-column procedure
entries.use: Tabulate cut/fill to feed the mass diagram
entries.how: 12 columns: station; end area cut; end area fill; volume of cut (in-place BCY); volume of fill (compacted); stripping fill-cut; stripping fill; net cut (col4 - col6); adjusted cut (col8 x conversion, e.g., 0.9); total fill (col5 + col7 + replacement); algebraic sum (col10 vs col9, sign per sheet); mass ordinate (running total from Station 0+00)
entries.dim: Stripping layer usually 4 to 6 in; 1 cu yd in place = 1.25 loose = 0.9 compacted

entries.n: Plot and read a mass diagram
entries.desc: Mass diagram properties
entries.use: Plan earthmoving, haul distances and equipment
entries.how: Plot stations horizontally, mass ordinate (col 12) vertically; positives above, negatives below datum. Ascending curve = cut; descending = fill; peak/valley = transition point (grade line crosses ground line); crossing the zero datum = balanced; segment between crossings = node. Ending above datum = waste; below = borrow. Area between mass line and balance line = work; if curve is above balance line haul is left to right
entries.wn: Assumes cut material is usable as fill; best for elongated projects; invalid when project is wide relative to length; handles one phase at a time

entries.n: Place balance lines for equipment haul limits
entries.desc: Balance line rules
entries.use: Assign dozers, scrapers and trucks to haul segments
entries.how: Draw horizontal balance lines cutting the mass curve twice; line length equals max haul distance: dozer up to 300 ft; scraper 301 to 5,000 ft; dump truck 5,001 ft to several miles. Start each node with dozer, then scraper, then truck. Quantity balanced is vertical distance; average haul distance is the horizontal bisector midway between balance line and transition point. Two adjacent nodes: use equal balance lines. Even number of nodes: one continuous line with AB+CD+EF = BC+DE+FG. Odd number: AB+CD+EF-(BC+DE) about 1,000 ft efficient haul. Material outside balance lines: rising portion = waste, falling = borrow; concentrate borrow and waste in one area
entries.dim: Dozer <=300 ft; scraper 301-5,000 ft; truck 5,001 ft+; odd-node limit approx 1,000 ft

entries.n: Average grade for earthmoving from the mass diagram
entries.desc: Average grade method
entries.use: Find the grade equipment works for scheduling
entries.how: Draw a horizontal line roughly halving the work area; extend verticals from ends of average haul line through the profile; connect intersections; average grade % = (average change in elevation / average haul distance) x 100. Example: 18 ft / 103 ft x 100 = -8.87% (downhill negative, uphill positive)
entries.dim: Example 18 ft / 103 ft = -8.87%

entries.n: Plan clearing, grubbing and stripping (recon, timber cruise)
entries.desc: Clearing planning and timber cruising
entries.use: Size the clearing job and pick equipment before committing troops
entries.how: Verify tree/soil/terrain from maps and recon, estimate quantity of work, select equipment, determine personnel, plan sequence. Timber cruise: cruise a sample (usually 10 percent of forested area; 100 percent on small areas) recording species, number, and diameter at breast height (4 1/2 ft above ground). Decisive factors: equipment type/amount and time available
entries.dim: Cruise sample 10% (100% small areas); DBH measured at 4 1/2 ft

entries.n: Clearing considerations: safety, camouflage, salvage, drainage
entries.desc: Clearing support considerations
entries.use: Avoid problems during clearing
entries.how: Use protective tractor-mounted cabs; fit heavy steel plating on undercarriages. Do not remove trees/brush outside the designated cleared area (camouflage); control tree fall. Trim and stockpile useful timber (logs, piles, lumber). Build drainage early: use original features, slope ditches downhill, fill stump holes with acceptable soil and compact, slope ground to ditches, backfill existing ditches as late as possible
entries.eq: Dozers, graders for stump hole fill
entries.wn: Clearing ground cover over near-freezing permafrost can cause thaw and considerable subsidence. Falling trees, uprooted stumps, stump holes are hazards

entries.n: Dispose of cleared material (waste, dump, burn)
entries.desc: Debris disposal options
entries.use: Get rid of debris quickly without hindering operations
entries.how: Push/skid debris into surrounding timber or pile adjacent to work area in forward areas; clear off-site disposal as close as possible if needed. Waste must not obstruct air traffic (consider approach/takeoff slopes). Cleared material may be used as fill in revetments around hardstands. Burn only if equipment/personnel unavailable: keep fires hot to limit smoke, no night fires without HQ approval, strip a firebreak around the debris (firebreaks each side for large areas), keep a fire guard and hand shovels/water buckets. Best burning: dozer-dug burn pit/trench (start with limbs and brush for coal bed, minimize dirt, not in swampy ground); or loosely piled logs. Wet logs: fuel oil/diesel via drilled pipe to center, remove pipe once burning, avoid ground contamination. Stumps: knock off dirt, dry roots in sun/wind, pile tightly with trunks toward center
entries.eq: Dozer, scraper, pipe for fuel oil, shovels, water buckets
entries.wn: Gusty winds and big debris piles can make fires uncontrollable

entries.n: Clear airfield approach zones and remove structures
entries.desc: Approach-zone and structure removal
entries.use: Meet glide angle and remove site obstructions
entries.how: Remove obstructions above the glide angle; best to fell or uproot rather than top trees; demolished material may stay if conditions allow. Power lines: remove, or relocate around nearest runway end if they cross, underground armored cable/conduit as last resort, or mark with warning lights in support area if outside glide angle. Do not destroy paved highways/railroads. Buildings: demolish or dismantle to salvage

entries.desc: Dozer clearing methods
entries.use: Clear trees and stumps with a dozer
entries.how: Dozer is primary clearing unit; best on brush, trees, stumps up to 6 in; can remove trees up to 30 in with more time if no clearing unit/saws. Start at disposal area and work away; one or two dozers for small trees and brush, another pair for larger trees/stumps, extra dozers for a third pass. Small (6 in or less): blade straight, digging slightly, windrow or push aside. Medium (6-12 in): blade as high as possible, push over, back up fast, lower blade, go forward and lift to dig roots. Large (12 in or more): probe for dead limbs, blade high and centered, push in direction of lean; with deep roots, cut V ditch on side opposite fall, cut sides two and three, build earth ramp on original side, push over, reverse quickly; fill stump hole. Spoil area: shortest haul, downgrade, camouflaged, accessible
entries.dim: Small <=6 in; medium 6-12 in; large >=12 in; dozer capable to 30 in
entries.wn: Maneuverability limited in mud/swamp and dense growth. Reverse quickly as root mass rises

entries.desc: Tree-dozer methods
entries.use: Shear trees at ground level over large areas
entries.how: Rate about 1 to 2 acres per hour depending on density and size. Check that soil supports tractor; not for heavy swamp. Counterclockwise: lay out strips 200-400 ft wide, cut outside toward center, windrows lengthwise on borders. Clockwise: 200-400 ft strips cut center toward sides, windrow at center; keep blade on ground pushing and raise when backing. Steep slope: semicircular pattern left to right, windrows on contour, work from uphill, push downhill. Level terrain with dense small vegetation: cut and windrow together at 90 degrees to windrow; deposit when moldboard full; teams abreast speed piling
entries.dim: Strip width 200-400 ft; 1-2 acres/hr
entries.eq: Tree-dozer (tractor with shear blade, steel canopy, guide bar)
entries.tm: 1 to 2 acres per hour per tractor

entries.n: Winches, felling, ripper and grader in clearing
entries.desc: Equipment limits in clearing
entries.use: Select supporting equipment
entries.how: Tractor winch uproots trees/stumps up to 24 in (line pull about half of a standard tree-and-stump unit); truck winch up to 6 in, expedient, good for skidding. Chain saws: controlled felling of nearly unlimited diameters; pneumatic saws dangerous on steep rugged ground. Hand tools (axes, two-man saws, pick-mattocks, machetes) slow, use when labor plentiful. Ripper breaks shallow roots and loosens frozen soil/organic material before stripping. Grader cuts grass, small brush on level boulder-free ground
entries.dim: Tractor winch to 24 in; truck winch to 6 in; dozer to 6 in (30 in slower)

entries.desc: Blasting guidance
entries.use: Remove stumps or boulders where equipment cannot work
entries.how: Charge size depends on explosive strength, tree/stump size, species, age and soil. Drill with pinch bars, earth augers, spoons (wood augers for taproots). Load and tamp with smooth wooden pole about 5 ft long by 1 1/2 in diameter; tamp holes firmly with earth. Boulders: mud-capping, blockholing or snakeholing. See FM 3-34.214 for charges
entries.dim: Tamping pole about 5 ft x 1 1/2 in
entries.eq: Explosives, augers, pinch bars, tamping pole
entries.wn: Sound carries far; loose soil may need second charge; taproots may only break; large craters need borrow and compaction to backfill

entries.n: Strip topsoil and remove surface rock
entries.desc: Stripping and rock removal
entries.use: Remove unsuitable topsoil, sod and rocks before earthwork
entries.how: Strip organic soil, humus, peat, muck, sod to a depth where compaction and thickness requirements are met, concurrent with clearing, using dozers, graders, scrapers, sometimes shovels. Stockpile good topsoil/sod for dust control, erosion control, camouflage. Surface rock: by hand (expedient), by bulldozer (windrow or push to fill/disposal, most common), or crane/scoop loader after dozers pile them
entries.dim: Stripping layer usually 4-8 in (earthwork sheet uses 4-6 in)

entries.n: Locate and clear buried explosives before construction
entries.desc: Mine/UXO clearing before construction
entries.use: Make the site safe for equipment and crews
entries.how: Check reports, set boundaries, visually search likely places (near structures, houses, roads; settled ground hollows; under stockpiles, pickets or stakes in odd places); then mine detectors or probing. Safety before speed; use EOD where possible. Minefield with booby traps: destroy in place with explosives or mechanical means. UXO: disarm by ordnance personnel then remove, or destroy in place. Surface mines/bomblets can be pushed with drag chain or bulldozer. Fill and compact craters with acceptable material using dozers or graders
entries.eq: Mine detectors, probes, drag chain, dozer, grader
entries.wn: Removal method is a command decision

entries.n: Flexible pavement layers and load distribution
entries.desc: Flexible pavement concepts
entries.use: Understand why thicker structures protect weak subgrades
entries.how: Flexible pavements (asphalt/aggregate) are used almost exclusively in the JOA; rigid (cement) generally not. Stress from a wheel load decreases with depth, so thicken subbase/base/surface over weak subgrade. Multiple-wheel assemblies help on thin structures over high-bearing subgrades. High tire pressure mainly stresses surface and base near the top. Layers: surface course, base, subbase/select, subgrade; tack/prime coats as needed. Military engineers classify soil by USCS then test (compaction, CBR, gradation, LL, PI)

entries.n: Evaluate subgrade suitability and set grade line
entries.desc: Subgrade evaluation factors
entries.use: Choose grade line and judge whether subgrade is acceptable
entries.how: Consider soil characteristics, depth to bedrock, depth to water table, achievable compaction, CBR of uncompacted and compacted subgrade, weak/soft/organic layers, frost action or swell. Classify by USCS; set grade line for best subgrade material consistent with design and simple construction

entries.desc: Subgrade compaction rules
entries.use: Reach design density in fills and cuts
entries.how: Cohesive soil: PI less than 5 per Fig 5-4 note (cohesionless PI >= 5 - as printed). Percent compaction is of max density at CE 55. Minimum compacted layer thickness 4 in for road, 6 in for airfield. Cohesionless soils (except silts): compact from surface with heavy rollers or very heavy vibratory compactors. Cohesive soils (including silts) cannot be compacted in thick layers; in cuts remove and replace in 6-in lifts initially, adjust lift thickness to find minimum compactive effort; use penetrating (tamping/sheepsfoot) rollers. Cohesive soils compact at optimum moisture from modified Proctor curve; cohesionless free-draining soils at moisture approaching saturation. Compact to a depth where natural density resists consolidation under traffic
entries.dim: Min compacted layer 4 in (road), 6 in (airfield); initial lift 6 in; CE 55
entries.eq: Tamping/sheepsfoot rollers, heavy or vibratory rollers
entries.wn: Fig 5-4 note as printed defines cohesive as PI < 5 and cohesionless as PI >= 5; verify against figure

entries.n: Treat problem subgrades: strength-losing soils, silts, swelling soils
entries.desc: Special subgrade cases
entries.use: Avoid failures on CH/MH/OH, silt/fine sand, or expansive soils
entries.how: CH, MH, OH soils lose strength when remolded: get CBR undisturbed and disturbed; if undisturbed is higher, do not compact and disturb as little as possible. Silts/very fine sands (ML, SC): good if compacted within moisture range, but with high water table compaction pumps water up and softens; replace with subbase/base or dry soil, or do not disturb subgrade if drainage is not feasible or soil is wet-season saturated. Swelling soils: place at moisture giving no more than 3 percent volume change if wetted later; preswell by compacting at moisture where 3 percent or greater swell has occurred; control moisture
entries.dim: Swell limit 3 percent volume change
entries.wn: Compaction of wet lifts can contaminate upper layers with subgrade fines

entries.n: Select subgrade CBR and stabilize subgrade
entries.desc: Subgrade CBR selection and stabilization
entries.use: Assign a design CBR and decide if stabilization is needed
entries.how: CBR on samples compacted to design density and soaked 4 days, or in-place CBR on undisturbed. Design CBR above 20 only if subgrade also meets subbase gradation and Atterberg limits (Table 5-1). Subgrade CBR 20-50 may need no select/subbase. Stabilize mechanically (granular additions), chemically (lime, Portland cement, fly ash), or by expedient (sand-grid, matting, geosynthetics/geotextiles - reinforce, separate, drain; matting and sand grid for loose sands on unsurfaced roads). Chemical admixture stabilized layers: CBR test not applicable; assign equipment CBR (up to 100)
entries.dim: CBR > 20 requires subbase gradation/Atterberg; stabilized CBR up to 100
entries.eq: Granular material, lime, cement, fly ash, sand grid, matting, geotextile

entries.desc: Frost classification use
entries.use: Avoid frost heave and thaw weakening
entries.how: Use Table 5-2 frost groups (NFS, S1, S2, F1-F4). F3 and F4 are extremely frost-susceptible, especially if water table is less than 5 ft below top of subgrade; silty soils may have CBR below 1 when thawing; thaw weakening may last 1 to 4 weeks, so reduce traffic loads. Select/subbase may lose up to 50 percent strength thawing, especially with over 20 percent fines (No. 200). F1-F4 unsuitable as base or subbase in seasonal frost and permafrost; F1 and F2 may serve as select if plasticity meets Table 5-1. Use NFS or S1/S2 for base in frost areas
entries.dim: Water table < 5 ft below subgrade top; fines > 20%; thaw 1-4 weeks; up to 50% strength loss

entries.desc: Select and subbase requirements
entries.use: Qualify local material as select or subbase
entries.how: Select material: design CBR 20 or less; subbase: CBR over 20. Max size 3 in. Subbase CBR 50: 50% passing No.10, 15% No.200, LL 25, PI 5; CBR 40: 80% / 15% / 25 / 5; CBR 30: 100% / 15% / 25 / 5; Select CBR 20: no No.10 limit, 25% No.200, LL 35, PI 12. If material meets gradation for a higher CBR class but measured CBR is lower, use the measured CBR (e.g., measured 37 meeting CBR 40 limits = CBR 37 subbase); if it fails the higher class use the lower class (CBR 30). Do not mix native or processed materials unless unmixed subgrade meets LL and PI limits. Possible sources: limestone, sandstone, coral, oyster shell, ashes, cinders, caliche, disintegrated granite; stabilize with Portland cement, lime, fly ash or bitumen
entries.dim: See Table 5-1

entries.n: Base course requirements and CBR ratings
entries.desc: Base course quality standards
entries.use: Choose acceptable base material
entries.how: Base is the highest quality structural layer, cohesionless, processed to gradation, dense and uniformly graded. Gradation per Tables 5-4/5-5; rule of thumb: avoid more than 15 percent fines (passing No. 200). LL must not exceed 25 and PI must not exceed 5. Assigned CBR (Table 5-6): graded crushed aggregate, water-bound macadam, dry-bound macadam, central plant hot-mix bituminous base = 100; lime rock, bituminous macadam, mechanically stabilized aggregate, soil cement, sand shell/shell = 80. Do not use stabilized aggregate base for tire pressures over 100 psi
entries.dim: LL <= 25; PI <= 5; fines <= 15% rule; CBR 100 or 80
entries.wn: Do not use mechanically stabilized aggregate for tire pressures above 100 psi

entries.n: Base materials: natural, processed and marginal (coral, caliche, tuff, rubble, bituminous)
entries.desc: Marginal and special base materials
entries.use: Use available local material for base
entries.how: Sand-gravel: blend deposits; uncrushed clean washed gravel lacks fines. Sand-clay riverbed deposits OK with proper proportioning; avoid decomposed rock with mica flakes. Coarse-graded gravel: 50% by weight with two or more fresh fractured faces, each face at least 75% of smallest midsection area. Marginal materials (caliche, lime rock, shells, cinders, coral, iron ore, rubble) judged by service behavior; PI <= 5 generally required. Coral: keep moisture within 1 percent of optimum; salt or seawater sprinkling aids bonding; cure minimum 72 hours. Caliche: air dry 72 hr, LL <= 35 and PI <= 10 (passing No. 40); crushed to 100% passing 2 in, 15-35% passing No. 40, 0-20% passing No. 200; strip surface deposits. Tuff: break oversize, sheepsfoot roll. Rubble: break into 3 in pieces or smaller, remove jagged metal. Bituminous base: lifts no more than 3 1/2 in; binder and leveling courses may be omitted
entries.dim: Rubble <= 3 in; bituminous lift <= 3 1/2 in; coral cure 72 hr; caliche gradation above
entries.tm: Coral cure 72 hr; caliche air dry 72 hr
entries.wn: Rubble may contain mines or booby traps

entries.n: Place, spread, blend and compact base course
entries.desc: Base course construction sequence
entries.use: Build a base course to specification
entries.how: Fine grade subgrade to final grade stakes; compact subgrade first, fix ruts and soft spots. Spread from nearest point to source (haul trucks compact base) or farthest point (compacts subgrade, shows weak spots, avoids segregation). Preferred: self-propelled aggregate spreader; else towed spreaders, scrapers, dump trucks, or windrows spread by grader/dozer/loader. Initial lift about 6 in, then adjust after density tests. Blend with finer material on top, fold with grader blade, mix windrows side to side. Check moisture with nuclear density meter, speedy moisture tester or expedient; add water with truck-mounted distributor (not asphalt distributor) or gravity container. Compact with vibratory or heavy rubber-tired rollers, edges inward, overlap by one-half roller width; use a test strip to find roller and number of passes. Finish crowned and water-shedding, blading edge to middle and back; roll with rubber-tired and steel-wheeled rollers
entries.dim: Lift about 6 in; roller overlap 1/2 width
entries.eq: Spreader, grader, water distributor, vibratory/rubber-tired/sheepsfoot rollers, nuclear density meter or speedy moisture tester
entries.wn: Do not use asphalt distributors for water

entries.desc: Macadam procedure
entries.use: Build water-bound or dry-bound macadam base
entries.how: If subgrade is highly plastic, place blanket of crusher screenings or 3 to 4 in of sand (lightly moistened and rolled) or membrane/geotextile. Spread coarse aggregate in one layer if compacted thickness is 4 in or less; two or more layers if thicker. Roll with steel-wheeled roller from sides to middle on crowned sections or low side to high side on transverse slope, until no creep or wave ahead of the roller. Do not roll on rain-softened subgrade. Then spread screenings thin (hand shovels, spreaders, moving trucks; do not pile), roll continuously, broom, sprinkle with water (no saturation) until a slurry wave forms before roller; allow section to dry completely
entries.dim: Compacted lift <= 4 in per layer; sand blanket 3-4 in
entries.wn: Do not saturate; it softens the subgrade

entries.desc: Straightedge test
entries.use: Verify base grade before paving
entries.how: Use 12-ft straightedge parallel and perpendicular to centerline. Deviation must not exceed 3/4 in for roads and airfields (propeller aircraft) or 1/8 in for jet aircraft. If exceeded, remove material to full depth of the lift, replace and recompact
entries.dim: 12-ft straightedge; 3/4 in (road, prop); 1/8 in (jet)

entries.n: Slush rolling and wet rolling a base
entries.desc: Slush and wet rolling
entries.use: Finish or compact a base when normal compaction fails
entries.how: Slush rolling: only on free-draining, cured base; considerable water; roller carries wave ahead; water rate about 0.5 to 1.0 gal/sq yd for a 6-in lift; roller follows water truck immediately; later hone ridges of fines with sprinkled grader blade and reset with pneumatic roller. Not for high-quality base. Wet rolling: wet upper 1 to 2 in to about 2 percent above minimum moisture, lightly blade to windrow coarse particles, work back with steel-wheeled roller closely following grader; no cure period
entries.dim: 0.5-1.0 gal/sq yd (6-in lift); upper 1-2 in at +2% moisture
entries.eq: Water truck, grader, pneumatic and steel-wheeled rollers
entries.wn: Use slush rolling only when specified or when conventional methods have failed

entries.desc: Asphalt density and traffic-based compaction
entries.use: Specify density and lab method for asphalt base/surface
entries.how: Field density should be 98 to 100 percent of laboratory density. Use Marshall or Gyratory Testing Machine; use 4-in molds (not 6-in) for Marshall. Tire pressure under 100 psi: gyratory 100 psi, 1 degree, 30 revolutions (50 blows Marshall equivalent). 100 to under 230 psi: 200 psi, 1 degree, 30 revolutions (75 blows). 230 psi and over: 240 psi, 1 degree, 60 revolutions; GTM mandatory for Army airfields, preferred for Air Force. If GTM used for design, use for control or correlate Marshall to GTM
entries.dim: 98-100% of lab density; see Table 5-7

entries.n: Soil stabilization method and stabilizer selection
entries.desc: Stabilizer selection criteria
entries.use: Pick a stabilizer and dosage for expedient work
entries.how: Classify soil (sieve analysis + Atterberg limits, gradation triangle Fig 5-6) then Table 5-9 for stabilizer type and Table 5-10 for dosage. Cement: PI under 30, more than 45% passing No. 4 for coarse soils. Lime: PI over 10 and over 25% passing No. 200. Fly ash (with lime): PI not over 25. Bituminous: under 30% passing No. 200 and PI under 10. Higher fines = harder to stabilize; sandy/gravelly soils need cement or emulsion binder; clays may need lime first. Best expedient stabilizer is cement. Polymer emulsions are 45-50% polymer by weight, shelf life up to 2 years, do not dilute with gray or salt water
entries.dim: See Tables 5-9, 5-10

entries.desc: Expedient stabilization procedure
entries.use: Make a quick all-weather surface or platform
entries.how: Dosage Table 5-10: sand/gravel low fines Portland cement 3-5% or emulsion polymer 3-5%, fiber 0.2-0.5%; high fines low PI: Portland cement 5%; clays/silts: lime and cement 5-7% each, or cement 7%. Add polymer emulsion waterproof coat 0.25-1 gal/sq yd (1:2 water dilution). Fibers monofilament polypropylene 3/4 to 2 in (3/4 to 1.5 in good with minimal balling); 0.1 to 0.5 percent by soil weight (above 0.5 lowers density); mixing with reclaimer/stabilizer mandatory; depth 6 in for soils above CBR 8 to 10; one lift only. With Type III cement + fiber, C-130/C-17 loads in 24 hours; large loads in 3 days (Type I may need up to 7 days). Cement water content: +1% over optimum if cement under 5%, +2% if above 5%; compact slightly wet of optimum. Curing doubles for each 20 F drop; below 45 F curing significantly longer; 3% Type III cement = 1 day at 75 F, 2 days at 55 F (or 6% for 1 day at 55 F)
entries.dim: Cement 3-7%; fiber 0.1-0.5%; lift 6 in; emulsion cap 0.25-1 gal/sq yd; fiber 3/4-2 in
entries.eq: Reclaimer/stabilizer, cement, polypropylene fiber, polymer emulsion
entries.tm: Cure 1 day @75 F, 2 days @55 F (3% Type III); 24 h to 7 days to load
entries.wn: Do not use synthetic dust-control fluids on cement-stabilized surfaces. Grading fiber-cement is extremely difficult; grade only within 1-2 hours of compaction. Nuclear density and sand cone give false/large error readings on fiber soils

entries.desc: Weather and frost cutoffs
entries.use: Time stabilization work correctly
entries.how: Asphalt: hot dry weather; thin lifts need air temp 40 F and rising with immediate compaction; cutbacks/emulsions need air and soil temps above freezing. Frost areas: place stabilized soil as single layer directly under surfacing; build early to gain strength before first freeze (7-day cure may not be enough). Lime reactions slow below soil temp 60 F (not rising for a month); cement below 40 F (not rising for a month)
entries.dim: Asphalt thin lift 40 F+; lime 60 F; cement 40 F
entries.wn: Weakly cemented material endures freeze-thaw poorly

entries.n: Dry wet soils chemically with quicklime
entries.desc: Chemical soil drying
entries.use: Dry wet spots when conventional drying is too slow
entries.how: Use quicklime (calcium/magnesium oxides): hydrates with water, exothermic, effective down to freezing temperatures. Only quicklime dries soil; hydrated lime and agricultural lime (calcium carbonate) do not. Portland cement, Class C fly ash, kiln dust with free quicklime can also dry soil; effectiveness depends on free quicklime content
entries.wn: Reaction releases heat; quicklime must be handled with care

entries.desc: Construction drainage measures
entries.use: Prevent delays and subgrade failure during construction
entries.how: Finish drainage before it is needed (too late once storm starts). Recon first for springs/seepage, trees along dry streams, runoff-holding vegetation, level vegetated areas (shallow water table), stream flood marks. Use existing ditches; grade downhill; temporary ditches; drain subgrade excavations and bases; minimize random excavation; sod/seed finished surfaces; retention for turbid water. Fill: roll smooth each day end, crown, no ruts, swales to outlets, temporary culverts. Interceptor ditches on hillsides and foot of slope (make part of final system); roadside ditches at design locations; deep ditches intercept groundwater (or convert to subsurface drainpipe). Swamp ditching: explosives, draglines, timber/steel mats
entries.eq: Existing ditches, temporary culverts, interceptor ditches, mats
entries.wn: Never close natural drainage channels even if dry

entries.n: Clear drainage channels and manage vegetation removal
entries.desc: Clearing for drainage
entries.use: Improve flow and avoid erosion when clearing
entries.how: Clear excess vegetation from streams to increase velocity and flow; widening or cutting meanders increases flow but major realignment can harm other stream parts. Dispose of stripped material away from runoff paths so it does not dam flow. Leave vegetation next to stream/ditch banks or provide a berm with chute. Fill holes and back drag or grade to a slight slope after clearing
entries.wn: Vegetation removal raises runoff and erosion, silting channels

entries.n: Choose design storm frequency and allowable ponding
entries.desc: Design storm criteria
entries.use: Set the storm the drainage must handle
entries.how: Airfields/heliports: minimum 2-year storm, no runoff encroachment on taxiway and runway pavements (incl. paved shoulders); limit ponding at apron inlets to 4 in. Other areas (roads, administrative, industrial, housing): 10-year storm. JOA normal design storm is 2-year (probability 0.5 per year; 75 percent chance of equal or greater storm within 2 years); longer-life construction needs specified storm. Center 50 percent of runways and parallel taxiways and helipad centerline surfaces free from ponding in a 10-year storm. Critical facility parts may use up to 50-year frequency
entries.dim: 2-yr airfield; 10-yr other; apron inlet ponding <= 4 in; center 50% runway free of ponding in 10-yr; up to 50-yr for essential parts

entries.n: Read rainfall intensity from the world isohyetal map
entries.desc: Isohyetal map reading
entries.use: Get 60-minute 2-year rainfall intensity when no local data
entries.how: Find project location on isohyetal map (Fig 6-3). On a line: read that value; between lines: read the larger value; inside an encircling line: read that line. Do not interpolate. Examples (in/hr): S. Australia 1.0; North Dakota 1.5; Washington DC 1.5; Florida 2.5; Vietnam 2.5; Cuba 2.5; New Orleans 2.5. Pinpoint local data (via Air Force staff weather officer) is more accurate
entries.dim: Values in in/hr for 60-min, 2-yr storm
entries.wn: Do not interpolate between isohyets

entries.n: Adjust rainfall intensity to critical duration
entries.desc: Intensity adjustment
entries.use: Convert 60-min intensity to intensity at the basin's time of concentration
entries.how: Use standard intensity-duration curves (Fig 6-4, numbered 1.0-4.0, interpolate between). Enter with duration in minutes, follow vertically to curve matching the 60-min intensity, read intensity. Applies to any frequency. Table 6-1 examples: I60 1.0 at 50 min = 1.2; 1.5 at 30 min = 2.4; 2.0 at 10 min = 5.2 in/hr
entries.dim: See Table 6-1 examples

entries.desc: Watershed delineation steps
entries.use: Find the area contributing runoff to each culvert or ditch
entries.how: 6 steps: locate structures on topo map; mark high points; draw flow arrows perpendicular to contours; continue until they converge at culvert/ditch end (runoff flows parallel to road when intercepted by side ditches); draw delineation lines high point to high point (arrows can't cross except at culverts/ditches); delineate separately by cover/soil type. Crowned road/airfield: divide at centerline; superelevated curve: divide at outside edge of curve
entries.wn: Culverts and ditches must carry water high to low; keep alignment straight and smooth because sharp bends cause erosion

entries.desc: Area measurement methods
entries.use: Get contributing drainage area
entries.how: 1 acre = 43,560 sq ft. Planimeter is accurate. Counting squares: count whole and partial squares on grid, multiply by area per square, convert to acres. Geometric shapes: rectangle A=bh; triangle A=bh/2; trapezoid A=(b1+b2)h/2. Stripper: draw equally spaced lines (1-in stripper width), total lengths, multiply by width and map scale squared, divide by 43,560 (example: L=12.5, scale 175 ft/in: 12.5 x 175^2 = 382,812.5 sq ft = 8.78 acres)
entries.dim: 1 acre = 43,560 sq ft

entries.n: Estimate peak runoff by the rational method (Q = CIA)
entries.desc: Rational method procedure
entries.use: Size ditches and culverts
entries.how: Q (cfs) = C x I (in/hr) x A (acres); factor 1.0083 is ignored. Limits: area not over 1,000 acres, regular shape, homogeneous cover/soil, entire area contributing at peak, uniform rainfall, no active stream (else hasty method). Simple area: one cover/soil over 80 percent: use its C. Complex: area-weighted C = (C1A1 + C2A2 + ...)/(A1 + A2 + ...). Steps: delineate; subareas; acreage; simple/complex; flow paths; split into sheet and ditch flow (about 500 ft +/- 200 ft); slopes; average slope class (<=2%, >2% and <7%, >=7%); C from Table 6-2; travel time per path, longest = TOC; I60 from isohyetal map; adjust to TOC; compute Q. Example: C=0.35, I=4.2 in/hr, A=48.8 ac gives Q = 71.7 cfs
entries.dim: Q=CIA; area <= 1,000 acres; simple area >= 80% one cover; sheet-to-ditch flow at about 500 ft
entries.wn: Check accumulated acreage does not exceed 1,000 acres

entries.desc: Time of concentration method
entries.use: Find the storm duration that produces peak flow
entries.how: Pick representative flow paths (not paths that drain only a small part). Sheet flow: use Fig 6-18 with cover type, slope, length (interpolate between curves, never extrapolate; use limiting curve beyond). Ditch flow: velocity (fpm) from Table 6-4 for slope, time = length / velocity. For multiple covers, sheet-flow curve only for the first segment; later segments use Table 6-4 velocity; add times. Culvert flow assume 5 ft/s (300 ft/min). If path times are within a few minutes, use longest as TOC; otherwise analyze further. Examples (Table 6-3): sparse turf 800 ft 3.0% = 19 min; paved 500 ft 1.5% = 8 min; average turf 600 ft 2.5% = 26 min
entries.dim: Culvert velocity 5 ft/s (300 ft/min); sheet to ditch at ~500 ft
entries.wn: Do not add sheet-flow times from Fig 6-18 for successive covers (laminar flow occurs once)

entries.desc: Successive area procedure
entries.use: Size downstream culverts that receive upstream runoff
entries.how: TOC at downstream outlet X = larger of inlet time X and (TOC of upstream W + ditch time W-X). Ditch time via culvert flow at 300 ft/min if no better data. Compute Q for each subarea with its own C, adjusted I and A, then add: Q_out X = Q_X + Q_W. Peak flows do not simply sum in reality (storage, timing). Keep total area <= 1,000 acres. Example: Q3 = 11.6 cfs, Q4 = 11.6 + 8.4 = 20 cfs
entries.dim: Culvert flow 300 ft/min; 1,000-acre limit

entries.n: Choose ditch type and cross section
entries.desc: Ditch types and shapes
entries.use: Pick interceptor, side or diversion ditch and its shape
entries.how: Interceptor: on hillside above road/cut to intercept runoff. Side ditch: along road to culvert or diversion. Diversion: carries water away from roads/airfields or around the project. Triangular (V) ditch for flows up to 60 cfs (road grader cuts it, in soil not rock); trapezoidal for flows over 60 cfs (wheeled scraper cuts flat bottom, grader dresses slopes). The 60 cfs guideline is flexible: with no scraper, grade an oversized V ditch even for 100 cfs. Segmental shape results from explosives or hand digging
entries.dim: V ditch <= 60 cfs; trapezoidal > 60 cfs
entries.eq: Motor grader, wheeled tractor-scraper; backhoe, dozer, loader, trencher, crane as slow alternatives

entries.desc: Ditch side-slope selection
entries.use: Set safe, stable ditch slopes
entries.how: Roadside ditch (shallow, flat terrain): front slope 3:1, back slope 1:1 (nonsymmetrical). Diversion ditch: symmetrical 1:1. Ditches subject to cross traffic: 3:1 or flatter. Interceptor/diversion ditches usually symmetrical. Recommended side slopes (Table 7-6): firm rock vertical to 1/4:1; concrete-lined stiff clay 1/2:1; fissured rock 1/2:1; firm earth with stone lining 1:1; firm earth large channels 1:1; firm earth small channels 1 1/2:1; loose sandy earth 2:1; sandy porous loam 3:1
entries.dim: See Table 7-6; roadside 3:1 front / 1:1 back
entries.wn: Steep sidewalls invite erosion and clogging and can entrap or overturn vehicles

entries.n: Set cut and fill slope ratios (Tables 7-1 and 7-2)
entries.desc: Slope ratios for cuts and fills
entries.use: Choose stable slopes for earth and rock cuts and fills
entries.how: Homogeneous soils at or above 95% CE 55 density. GW, GP, GMd, SW, SP, SMd: max 1 1/2:1 (not saturated) or 2:1 (saturated), height not critical. GMu, GC, SMu, SC, ML, MH, CL, CH: 2:1 (not saturated) or 3:1 (saturated) for faces under 50 ft. OL, OH, Pt not suitable. Back slopes in loose soil stay near vertical and slough: do not load above the cut. Rock with weak planes (effective dip angle): 0-18 deg = 1:2; 18-35 = 1:1; 35-75 = cut to dip angle; 75-90 or negative = 1:4 to 1:2. Solid rock 1:4 to 1:2 (H:V)
entries.dim: See Tables 7-1, 7-2
entries.wn: Deliberate slope stability analysis required for lower densities

entries.desc: Manning's equation use
entries.use: Compute ditch velocity and flow
entries.how: Q = A x V (cfs = sq ft x ft/s). Manning: V = (1.486/n) R^(2/3) S^(1/2); R = (V n / (1.486 sqrt S))^(3/2); R = A/wetted perimeter. Design assumes steady, continuous, uniform, turbulent flow. Higher slope or Q at fixed area raises velocity; higher n lowers velocity; higher velocity raises erosion. Calculator K method: K = n/(1.486 sqrt S), R = (V K)^1.5

entries.desc: Ditch design procedure with example
entries.use: Size a ditch to carry the design runoff
entries.how: 8 steps: (1) peak runoff by rational method; (2) slope in ft/ft (percent/100); (3) pick n and trial V from Table 7-3, trial V = 1 ft/s below Vmax; (4) compute hydraulic radius Rm; (5) triangular if Q <= 60 cfs, trapezoidal if > 60; (6) find Rt in tables B-1 to B-9 matching Rm (use next smaller Rt), read area and depth; (7) Q = Aw x V must be within 5 percent of design Q (e.g., 44.9 to 49.7 for 47.3): if too high lower V, if too low raise V but not above Vmax, or enlarge section (flatter slopes or wider bottom); (8) add freeboard of at least 0.5 ft to water depth = cutting depth. Peak velocity above 3 ft/s makes ditch self-cleaning. Worked example: 47.3 cfs, S=0.0052, GMd n=0.024, 3:1 V ditch: V=4.2 ft/s, A=10.83 sq ft, depth 1.9 ft, Q=45.5 cfs, cutting depth 2.4 ft
entries.dim: Check within +/-5%; freeboard >= 0.5 ft; V >= 3 ft/s self cleaning
entries.eq: Manning nomograph or calculator; Appendix B tables

entries.n: Control ditch velocity: sediment and erosion
entries.desc: Sediment and erosion control rules
entries.use: Keep ditches clean and non-eroding
entries.how: Sediment settles at 3 ft/s or less; keep peak velocity above 3 ft/s but below Vmax for the soil (Tables 7-3, 7-5). If Vmax < 3 ft/s, line with asphalt or concrete or add freeboard. Reduce velocity by lining with erosion-resistant material, flattening side slopes, widening ditch or bottom (raises wetted perimeter), terracing, check dams. Abrupt changes at transitions, junctions and storm drain outlets cause turbulence and need special design
entries.dim: 3 ft/s self-cleaning threshold; Table 7-3 and 7-5 limits

entries.n: Line a ditch: turf checks, paving, gunite, riprap
entries.desc: Channel lining options
entries.use: Protect ditches on steep grades or where velocity is high
entries.how: Turf: sod strips held by boards/stakes perpendicular to flow at intervals. Paving or gunite required on grades over 5 percent (extend paving downslope until energy absorbed); pavement raises velocity so protect the end with stilling basin or rock. Gunite: cement and sand sprayed 1 to 1 1/2 in thick over steel mesh at mid-thickness. Riprap: hand-place at least two layers, compact each rock; use D50 from Fig 7-12 or 7-13; blanket thickness = longest dimension of max stone or 1.5 x D50, whichever is greater; filter blanket usually 6 in of sand, gravel, crushed rock or cloth; double the thickness at downstream end. Froude F = 0.716 V / sqrt(d)
entries.dim: Paving over 5% grade; gunite 1-1.5 in; riprap thickness >= 1.5 x D50; filter 6 in
entries.eq: Sod, boards/stakes, asphalt/concrete, cement + sand + steel mesh, rock
entries.wn: Riprap fails by stone movement, bed material pulling through, or end undercutting

entries.desc: Gabion assembly, filling, thickness
entries.use: Make erosion protection, headwalls and aprons from wire baskets
entries.how: Box gabion: woven hexagonal galvanized wire mesh with 4- to 8-in openings, divided into cells by diaphragms. Assemble on flat surface, fold to box, lace edges and diaphragms with binding wire. Smooth the ground first; place front-to-front and back-to-back; wire stacked empties tightly to the row below. 3-ft-high gabions: lace about 100 linear ft empty, anchor the first (partially fill with stone) and tension the other end with a come-a-long. Fill with clean, hard, durable stone slightly larger than mesh (4 to 8 in): fill to 1 ft, place a connecting wire each direction looped around two meshes, repeat to full, overfill slightly, lace lid, pack tight. Use plastic-coated wire if soil/water pH < 7 or > 12. Inspect at least once a year. Lining thickness: 12 in for straight channels, side slopes < 35 deg, about 10 ft/s; 18 in for curves with 45 deg side slope; 36 in stepped back for sharper slopes. Manning n 0.025-0.030 (0.012-0.018 grouted). Use filter cloth on erodible soil
entries.dim: Mesh 4-8 in; first fill lift 1 ft; linings 12/18/36 in; n 0.025-0.030
entries.eq: Gabion baskets, binding wire, stone, come-a-long, crowbar, rebar for diaphragm protection
entries.wn: Stack and lace securely; keep taut while filling

entries.n: Protect culvert outlets and size aprons (Table 7-7)
entries.desc: Culvert outlet protection rules
entries.use: Prevent scour at culvert outlets
entries.how: Gabion apron by outlet velocity: under 7 ft/s none (good grass); 7-10 ft/s apron 10 ft long, 12 in thick; 10-15 ft/s apron 13-23 ft long, 18 in thick; over 15 ft/s energy dissipater or stilling basin. Scour starts at ~1.5 ft/s in uniform sand and cohesionless silt, 2.5 well-graded sand, 3.0 silty sand, 4.0 clay, 6.0 gravel. Plain outlets only if outlet channel withstands 1.5 x culvert velocity. Flared wing walls: velocity x flare angle not over 150 degrees (5 ft/s -> 30 deg; 15 ft/s -> 10 deg); paved apron between wing walls unless on stable foundation; riprap at end. JOA stilling basins: riprap or simple concrete
entries.dim: See Table 7-7; flare angle x velocity <= 150

entries.desc: Check dam design
entries.use: Slow water in ditches with 2 to 8 percent slope
entries.how: Use on slopes 2-8 percent (under 2 percent not needed; over 8 percent pave instead). Spacing S = 100H/(A - B) ft, where H = height from channel bottom to lower edge of weir notch (1 ft practical minimum, 3 ft max unless structurally designed), A = original slope %, B = desired slope 2%. S not less than 50 ft. Example: A=5%, B=2%, H=3 ft: S=100 ft. Build weir notch at center sized with Q = 3.39 L H^(3/2) (Table 7-8). Anchor sides and bottom into at least 2 ft of compacted material, apron, riprap at least 4 ft of downstream channel
entries.dim: S = 100H/(A-B); S >= 50 ft; H 1-3 ft; anchor 2 ft; riprap 4 ft
entries.wn: Clogged or small notch causes overtopping and damage worse than having no dam

entries.n: Special drainage channels: gutters, median channels, berms
entries.desc: Special channels
entries.use: Drain wide paved areas and prevent edge erosion
entries.how: Gutters: shallow paved channels for permanent construction; provide enough sump inlets to keep flow depth under 3 in. Median channels: symmetrical wide shallow channels, rational method for flow, solve depth by trial. Berm: raised earth lip at top of channel edge to stop uncontrolled side inflow except at protected inlets; waste spoil banks need frequent openings. Berm on downhill side of interceptor ditches
entries.dim: Gutter flow depth < 3 in

entries.desc: Pipe selection criteria
entries.use: Pick a pipe that survives soil, water and load conditions
entries.how: CMP (galvanized, usually bituminous coated) is the common JOA culvert: nested half sections 2 ft long assembled; diameters 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 60, 72 in; gauges 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 (0.179, 0.135, 0.105, 0.075, 0.0598 in). Minimum diameter 18 in for lengths up to 20 ft, 24 in for longer. Plastic pipe approved for low-volume roads but NOT under airfield pavement (except subsurface water collection). Precast concrete preferred over CMP when available: stronger, less cover, n = 0.013 vs 0.024 for CMP. HDPE: Type C (corrugated in/out), S (smooth interior), D (smooth, spiral); 4 to 72 in ID. Concrete box where full waterway needed or on rock; may need cast-in-place. Avoid concrete where soil pH < 5.5 or fluid pH < 5.5 or > 9.0; Type II or V cement in sulfate soils. Aluminum pipe not in pH < 5 or > 9, OH/OL soils, or contact with other metals
entries.dim: CMP diameters 12-72 in; gauges 8-16; min dia 18 in (<=20 ft) / 24 in (longer); n concrete 0.013, CMP 0.024
entries.eq: Culvert pipe, nuts/bolts, vise grips, ratchet set
entries.wn: Do not install bituminous-coated CMP where solvents enter the pipe

entries.desc: Expedient culvert types
entries.use: Pass water quickly with on-site materials until permanent culverts are built
entries.how: Use logs, oil drums, or sandbags filled with sand-cement mix (Fig 8-1 to 8-3); size using CMP-equivalent end areas for similar slopes
entries.eq: Oil drums, logs, landing mat, sand-cement sandbags

entries.n: Align a culvert and set its slope
entries.desc: Culvert alignment and slope rules
entries.use: Prevent stream from bypassing the culvert and keep it self-cleaning
entries.how: Place culvert in the streambed with inlet and outlet inverts at streambed elevation. If the structure cuts across a meander/bend, cut a new channel and fill and dam the old one with sandbags, logs or riprap. Ditch relief culverts: 5% grade road = 500 ft apart; 8% grade = 300 ft apart. Self-cleaning needs velocity >= 3 ft/s: grade not less than 0.5 percent; keep grade <= 2 percent to limit outlet velocity. Free-falling outlets and slopes over 2% need outlet erosion protection; in JOA it may be better to accept erosion and use a slope over 2% to prevent debris blockage. Reduce slope with drop inlet or by raising the outlet
entries.dim: Slope 0.5% to 2%; velocity >= 3 ft/s; relief culvert spacing 500 ft (5% grade), 300 ft (8% grade)
entries.wn: Never let the stream find another path; it can quickly close the road or airfield

entries.n: Set culvert depth of fill and cover
entries.desc: Cover and fill rules
entries.use: Make sure a culvert is deep enough to be protected and the pipe size fits the fill
entries.how: Depth of fill (invert to shoulder edge/top of fill) must be >= cover + pipe diameter. Road CMP: largest diameter = two-thirds of minimum fill; minimum cover = one-half the diameter or 12 in, whichever is greater. Airfield cover from Tables 8-2 to 8-4 by aircraft culvert weight type, pipe gauge and diameter (interpolate; charts good for 5,000 lb above stated load). Example: C-130E = type 13, 60,000-lb single-tandem, 12-gauge, 36-in pipe = 2.5 ft cover. Rigid-pavement slab cover min 0.5 ft for light loads (25,000-lb single wheel, 40,000-lb twin wheel, 40,000-lb single tandem) else 1.0 ft. Reinforced concrete pipe to 50 ft fill. Add extra cover where heavy construction equipment crosses
entries.dim: Road: cover >= max(D/2, 12 in); D <= 2/3 fill; RCP up to 50 ft fill
entries.wn: Live loads are worse under shallow cover, dead loads under deep cover

entries.n: Bed, backfill and lay a culvert
entries.desc: Culvert installation steps
entries.use: Install a culvert so it does not settle or leak
entries.how: Bedding depth at least 1/10 of pipe diameter, shaped to fit pipe bottom and cambered along centerline for settlement; invert must not rise going downstream. Remove and replace organic, muck, silt or sharp rock; use cradle footings (maybe piles) if soil is inadequate; on rock, trench and backfill with compacted soil bedding. Backfill in well-compacted layers kept level on both sides: 6-in layers with mechanical tampers, 4-in layers if logs used (hand tamp), from bed up to 12 in or half the diameter over the crown, whichever is greater. Concrete pipe: start at downstream end, male ends point downstream, seal joints. CMP: overlap joints so flow passes over joint, seal with caulk/bituminous material; pipe may be asphalt-lined for higher velocity. Length = embankment width; if no downstream headwall extend at least 2 ft beyond toe of fill and riprap
entries.dim: Bedding >= D/10; lifts 6 in (mechanical) or 4 in (logs); backfill to max(12 in, D/2) over crown; 2 ft projection past toe
entries.wn: Poorly sealed joints cause fill voids and collapse

entries.n: Build headwalls, wing walls and aprons
entries.desc: Headwall and outlet protection
entries.use: Guide water, support fill, and prevent outlet scour
entries.how: Headwall always upstream, desirable downstream; mandatory both ends for concrete pipe. Headwall near a road must not protrude above shoulder grade and sits at least 2 ft outside the shoulder. Use wing walls/retaining walls at an angle; reinforced concrete or mortared stone, or expedient lumber, logs, sandbags (soil-cement sandbags best for speed). Culverts discharging to open channels need antiscour protection: gully scour (channel steeper than stable) or scour hole (stable channel); control by lowering velocity (flatter culvert slope may need larger pipe) or by headwalls/wing walls/riprap/linings
entries.dim: Headwall >= 2 ft outside shoulder
entries.eq: Reinforced concrete, mortared stone, sandbags with soil-cement, riprap

entries.n: Compute culvert capacity and hydraulic gradient
entries.desc: Culvert hydraulics
entries.use: Check how much a culvert will pass
entries.how: S = H/L (head over length). Head is: ends elevation difference if inlet and outlet unsubmerged; water surface over inlet to top of outlet if only inlet submerged; water surface at inlet minus water surface at outlet if both submerged. Normal flow = water at crown at inlet with free outlet: use Table 8-7 (n 0.012 clay/concrete; 0.018 CMP paved 50% of dia; 0.024 CMP unpaved). Ponding depth <= 1.2 x diameter: still use Table 8-7; above 1.2 x D with free outlet use Fig 8-17 nomograph and V = Q/A. Above critical slope discharge no longer increases. Box culverts: size by equal area to pipe
entries.dim: Table 8-7; ponding threshold 1.2 x D
entries.wn: Table 8-7 and Fig 8-17 values are graphics not reproduced in extracted text

entries.desc: Submerged inlet design
entries.use: Size pipes where water ponds over the inlet
entries.how: Steps: Q; culvert length; head; size pipes with Fig 8-17 nomograph; compute V = Q/A. Increase pipe size or lower slope if outlet velocity is over outfall limit or if water height above inlet is less than 0.022 V^2 (CMP) or 0.017 V^2 (concrete pipe/box). Example: 210 cfs, L=180 ft: one 42-in concrete pipe about 78 cfs; one 48-in about 92 cfs; use three 48-in pipes
entries.dim: Check H >= 0.022V^2 (CMP) or 0.017V^2 (concrete)

entries.desc: Unsubmerged inlet design
entries.use: Choose pipe size, number and quantity to order
entries.how: Steps: (1) runoff; (2) road or airfield; (3) length in place from cross section (horizontal length + 2 ft if no downstream headwall) and fill critical; (4) largest pipe that fits fill (road D <= 2/3 fill; cover 1/2 D or 12 in min; airfield Table 8-3/8-4); (5) capacity and outlet velocity from Table 8-7; (6) number of pipes = runoff / capacity rounded up; (7) order length = pipes x length in place x 1.15 waste factor, rounded up to 2-ft increments; (8) check outlet velocity against Table 7-3 and protect outlet if higher, use fewest pipes. Example: 32 cfs, 36-in pipe 27.5 cfs at 0.5% = 2 pipes; 2 x 476 x 1.15 = 1,094.8 -> 1,096 ft
entries.dim: Waste factor 1.15; order in 2-ft increments

entries.desc: Ponding area design
entries.use: Store excess runoff to reduce culvert size or protect vital areas
entries.how: Pond edge at least 75 ft from runway/taxiway pavement edge. Drain pond within about 4 hours of storm start. Flatten adjacent fill side slopes. Pond volume V = ((A+B)/2) x contour interval (average end area from contour areas). Example: 62-64 ft = 10,000; 64-66 = 35,000; total 45,000 cu ft; to 68 ft contour total 100,000 cu ft. Compare cumulative runoff curve (volume cu ft = Q cfs at that duration's intensity x time in seconds, Table 8-9) with culvert discharge line; max vertical gap = ponded volume. Example: 30-in CMP at 24 cfs gives 115,000 cu ft ponding (too much); 36-in gives 75,000 cu ft, 95 min (OK within 100,000 cu ft and 4 hr). Ponding most useful with short TOC
entries.dim: Edge >= 75 ft from pavement; <= 4 hr; example safe volume 100,000 cu ft
entries.wn: Do not pond where flooding would affect operations

entries.desc: Drop inlet and grating procedure
entries.use: Collect surface runoff into a culvert or storm drain
entries.how: Always cover drop inlets with grating (expedient: welded reinforcing bars spaced to pass debris). Set grating 0.2 ft below grade. Grate opening is 50 percent of grate area, at least 18 in long, parallel to flow. Size grating by peak runoff and head using Table 8-10 (weir Q = 3LH^1.5 / orifice Q = 5.37 A H^0.5), then multiply area by 1.5 in paved areas or 2.0 in turfed areas. Inspect and clean regularly; cover expedient boxes with bars
entries.dim: Grate set 0.2 ft below grade; safety factor 1.5 paved / 2.0 turf; opening >= 18 in
entries.eq: Steel bars, plate, cast iron, reinforced concrete, brick, timber or CMP
entries.wn: Unmaintained inlets pond and saturate subgrade

entries.n: Decide on and select subsurface drainage type
entries.desc: Subsurface drainage criteria
entries.use: Fix pavements failing from groundwater
entries.how: Three classes: base drainage (pipes along pavement edges with pervious material to base): required where frost action in subgrade, groundwater rises to base bottom, or pavement may be inundated with little drainage into subgrade (Table 8-11: groundwater depth under 8 ft needs K < 1x10^-5 fpm; 8-25 ft K < 1x10^-6; over 25 ft K < 1x10^-7), and at low points of longitudinal grades over 2% where subgrade K < 1x10^-3 fpm. Subgrade drainage: when seasonal groundwater rises to less than 1 ft below bottom of course. Intercepting drainage: when seepage raises groundwater locally to less than 1 ft below base bottom (thin pervious layers, rock cuts, springs). Techniques: raise finished grade at least 5 ft above mean groundwater table (small areas such as narrow swamp crossings), deep V ditches with free outfall, lower natural channels, blind (French) rock-filled drains (not for permanent work; silt up), subsurface pipe, vertical wells (treat bottoms with calcium chloride or hay in freezing areas)
entries.dim: Base drainage K thresholds by water depth; groundwater < 1 ft below base triggers subgrade/intercept drains; finished grade >= 5 ft above mean water table
entries.wn: Subsurface pipe failures give no warning and are very hard to repair. Do not combine surface runoff and subsurface drainage in one pipe system

entries.n: Lay subsurface drain pipe and filter
entries.desc: Subdrain pipe and filter design
entries.use: Install perforated pipe drains with a working filter
entries.how: Slope at least 0.15 ft drop per 100 ft. Manholes at intervals of not more than 1,000 ft, with flushing risers between manholes and at dead ends. Pipe at least 6 in diameter (6 in for drains; 8 in or larger for long intercepting lines or severe groundwater); 6-in pipe generally enough for intercepting lines up to 1,000 ft. Subgrade drain center at least 1 ft below base bottom and not less than 1 ft below groundwater table. Perforated pipe laid with holes down and joints closed. Farm tile not recommended on airfields. Wrap/surround pipe with about 6 in of filter material. Filter criteria: Cu = D60/D10 <= 20; D85(filter)/slot width > 1.2 or /hole diameter > 1.0; D15(filter)/D85(soil) <= 5; D50(filter)/D50(soil) <= 25; D15(filter)/D15(soil) >= 5. Convert hole inches x 25.4 = mm. Use well-graded concrete sand if no analysis available. Geotextile may replace granular filter (nonwoven needle-punch): AOS < 0.6 mm (No. 30 sieve) for soil with <= 50% passing No. 200; AOS < 0.297 mm (No. 50) for > 50%; min grab strength 0.6 kN (130 lb); min puncture strength 0.25 kN (55 lb)
entries.dim: Min slope 0.15 ft/100 ft; pipe >= 6 in; manholes <= 1,000 ft; filter 6 in; Cu <= 20
entries.eq: Perforated pipe, filter sand/gravel or geotextile
entries.wn: Use a simple V ditch if it will do the job instead of buried pipe

entries.desc: Cold-region rainfall and infiltration values
entries.use: Design drainage where permafrost, frost and icing apply
entries.how: Arctic: warmest month mean <= 50 F, annual mean < 32 F. Subarctic: coldest month <= 32 F, warmest >= 50 F, fewer than 4 months above 50 F. Use minimum design rainfall rate 0.2 in/hr; use Alaska design storm index (Fig 9-2) and intensity-duration curves (Fig 9-1); once-in-50-years amount is about 2.2 x the once-in-2-years amount; estimate short-record station value by ratio to nearby long record (example 6/4 x 0.5 = 0.75). Infiltration = zero in permafrost areas; otherwise at most about 0.5 in/hr coarse sand/gravel, as low as 0.1 in/hr for clayey soils. Do not count on ponding above drain inlets in arctic airfield design
entries.dim: Min rain 0.2 in/hr; 50-yr = 2.2 x 2-yr; infiltration 0 (permafrost), 0.5 in/hr max coarse, 0.1 clay
entries.eq: Temporary rain gauge from meteorological agency
entries.wn: Values may deviate widely above 2,500 ft elevation

entries.n: Site and ditch layout in permafrost and icing areas
entries.desc: Cold-weather drainage layout rules
entries.use: Avoid thaw, sloughing and icing problems
entries.how: Don't block natural drainage ways; avoid fine-grained frost-susceptible soils; flowing water thaws permafrost so put ditches as far as possible from runway and road shoulders; make ditches wide and flat for snow equipment, but narrow and deep where flow continues year round (avoids icings); avoid large cuts (thawed zones, water-bearing strata cause icings); preserve and restore vegetation; seal closed-conduit inlets before freeze-up and open before breakup; expect sliding on unprotected ditch slopes over receding frost; avoid ditches over permafrost on steep slopes. Maintenance gear: heavy snow removal equipment and steam boiler with pipes fixed inside culverts for steam thawing. Icing controls: river icing - insulate streambed at critical section; ground icing - frost belt (snow-cleared strip across flow, shift position yearly, optional snow fence on first ice); spring icing - drain or divert, insulated conduit if needed
entries.eq: Steam boiler and pipes for thawing, snow removal equipment
entries.wn: Pavement kept clear of snow is an ideal site for icing to spread

entries.n: Soil-trafficability test set and cone penetrometer
entries.desc: Set contents: canvas case; cone penetrometer with 3/8-in steel shaft, 5/8-in aluminum shaft, 0.5 sq in cone and 0.2 sq in cone; soil sampler; remolding equipment (2 1/2-lb drop hammer, remolding cylinder with base and pin); bag of hand tools. Penetrometer = 30 degree cone, 19-in shaft, proving ring, dial indicator, handle. CI = force per unit cone base area, read on dial inside proving ring. Cannot measure CI in gravels (gravels are considered excellent for 50 passes; judge by eye). The dynamic cone penetrometer (TM 3-34.48-2) is for high-strength subgrade/base, not for trafficability
entries.use: Measure soil strength (CI) to decide whether vehicles can cross an area
entries.how: Carry the 19-lb test set on your back. Use the 3/8-in shaft with the 0.5 sq in cone for most readings; use the 0.2 sq in cone for hard soils and for remolding tests in remoldable sands. Read the dial as CI in psi
entries.dim: Dial 0-300 psi; 0.5 sq in cone loads 0 to 150 lb; set weighs 19 lb; max penetrometer capacity 750 CI
entries.wn: Measurements are valid only for short periods if weather changes

entries.n: Choose the critical layer for a vehicle
entries.desc: Critical layer = layer contributing most to trafficability for that vehicle; depth varies with soil type, strength profile, vehicle type and weight and passes. CI between 10 and 300 in the critical layer is the usable range: below 10 is nontrafficable for nearly all vehicles; above 300 is trafficable to most vehicles for 50 passes. Use this to classify large areas as above or below the critical range without extensive testing
entries.use: Decide which soil depth to measure for a given vehicle
entries.how: Look up the vehicle type in Table 10-1 and read CI and RI for that layer only. For most Army vehicles in fine-grained soil the critical layer is 6-12 in. Coarse-grained soil is 0-6 in. Example: M929 dump truck critical layer is 9-15 in for 1 pass and 50 passes
entries.dim: See Table TM48-T10-1: e.g., tracked vehicles up to 100,000 lb 6-12 in; over 100,000 lb 0-12 in; tracked under 4 psi 3-9 in; wheeled under 2,000 lb wheel load 3-9 in
entries.wn: Low-ground-pressure tracks use the 3-9 in layer even on abnormal profiles

entries.n: Number of penetrometer readings and remolding tests
entries.desc: Average accuracy rises with the number of readings. If tentative route can be chosen in the field, take closely spaced readings to find soft spots. Coarse-grained soils are uniform so fewer penetrations are needed and RI tests are not required
entries.use: Plan how many readings to take in a recon area
entries.how: In soft soil take at least 15 readings spread over a uniform area. If short of time: CI 0-150 take 4-6 sets per location, run remolding tests at enough locations to get the RI range, no remolding if CI under 10. CI 150-200 take 3-4 sets per location; remold at first 2-3 locations, stop if RI is 0.90 or more, else test about 6 locations. CI over 200 take 2 sets per location; remold at first 2-3 locations, stop if RI is 0.80 or more, else about 4 locations
entries.dim: 15 readings minimum for true average in soft soil

entries.n: Average CI by depth and by layer (work sheet method)
entries.desc: Readings are taken at 0-, 6-, 12-, 18- and 24-in depths. For normal profiles measure to 18 in early in recon; if profile is consistently normal only record the critical layer (for a tracked vehicle under 100,000 lb, such as M113A3, only the 6- and 12-in depths)
