entries.use: Turn raw penetrometer readings into a layer CI
entries.how: Average the readings at each depth (0, 6, 12, 18, 24 in), then average top and bottom depth of each 6-in layer. Interpolate 3, 9, 15, 21 in layers by averaging the two adjacent layer values. Always round CI values down. Example: (58+63+65+72+75)/5 = 66.6 = 66; 0-6 in layer = (66+71)/2 = 68; 3-9 in layer = (68+73)/2 = 70.5 = 70; 9-15 in layer = (73+76)/2 = 74.5 = 74
entries.dim: 6-in depth increments; round down

entries.desc: Record in coarse-grained soil an average with a + when several readings exceed 300; do not add a + if fewer than 20% of readings exceed 300
entries.use: Decide how many layers to test and which RCI governs
entries.how: Normal profile: CI stays the same or rises with each depth step; test remolding in the critical layer only. Abnormal profile: at least one CI reading is lower than the one above it; take CI and remolding in the critical layer and the 6-in layer below it, and use the LOWER RCI. Example area B: 6-12 in RCI = 60 x 0.90 = 54, 12-18 in RCI = 40 x 0.90 = 36, so 36 governs. Coarse-grained soil: critical layer 0-6 in; read CI at 3- to 18-in increments or until the 750 CI maximum is reached; no RI tests
entries.wn: Low-ground-pressure tracks: use 3-9 in layer as critical layer

entries.n: Rating cone index (RCI) and go/no-go with VCI
entries.desc: Examples: M1A1 one pass, CI 50 x RI 0.70 = RCI 35 > VCI1 25, passes. M923 50 passes, CI 80 x RI 0.82 = 65 < VCI50 68, fails. Immobilization is likely when RCI is below VCI; it can occur when RCI is only slightly above VCI if surface water causes sinkage or slipperiness. VCI1 and VCI50 listed for military vehicles in TM 3-34.48-2
entries.use: Decide if a vehicle can cross an area for 1 or 50 passes
entries.how: RCI = CI x RI for the critical layer (RI = average of remolding tests, capped at 1.0 even if the average is higher; coarse-grained soils use RI = 1.0). Vehicle goes if RCI is greater than or equal to its VCI. Compare RCI to VCI1 for one pass and to VCI50 for 50 passes. Use the worst-case (highest VCI) vehicle when a mixed convoy crosses. Example M929: RCI 74 vs VCI1 30 and VCI50 68, so go for both
entries.dim: RCI = CI x RI; go if RCI >= VCI
entries.wn: Slippery soil (recent rain on firm soil) degrades performance and the manual's performance relations apply only to nonslippery soils. Chains on rubber-tired vehicles or removal of rubber track pads usually improves mobility

entries.n: Calculate VCI for a new or unlisted vehicle (mobility index method)
entries.desc: Tracked VCI equations: VCI1 = 7.0 + 0.2 MI - [39.2/(MI+5.6)]; VCI50 = 19.27 + 0.43 MI - [125.79/(MI+7.08)]. Wheeled VCI equations: VCI1 = 11.48 + 0.2 MI - [39.2/(MI+3.74)] for MI <= 115, VCI1 = 4.1 MI^0.446 for MI > 115; VCI50 = 28.23 + 0.43 MI - [92.67/(MI+3.67)] for MI <= 100, VCI50 = 9.0 MI^0.446 for MI > 100. Wheeled MI uses weight per tire contact, tire section width/diameter, axle load (breakpoints 2,000 / 13,500 / 20,000 / 31,500 lb) and factors 1.00 or 1.05 (formula symbols are garbled in the extracted text). VCI for wheeled vehicles may vary over 20 percent from tire pressure change alone
entries.use: Estimate VCI when the vehicle is not in TM 3-34.48-2
entries.how: Compute the mobility index (MI) from the eight factors in paras 10-51/10-52, then convert MI to VCI1 and VCI50 with Table 10-3 (tracked) or Table 10-4 (wheeled), or the equations under the tables. Rear-wheel-drive vehicles (nondriven first axle): use all-wheel-drive formulas and multiply the VCI by 1.4. Half-tracked: use all-wheel-drive formulas with notional rear wheels equal in size and load to the front wheels and a grouser factor of 1.1. Central tire inflation system: compute VCI then reduce by 15 percent
entries.dim: Factors: tracked weight factor 1.0 up to 40,000 lb, then rises; track-width and grouser factors (1.0 if grouser under 1.5 in, 1.1 if 1.5 in or more)
entries.wn: Estimates assume equal wheel/track load distribution and nominal highway tire pressure. Do not extend these methods to tractor-trailer combinations

entries.n: Number of vehicles that can pass: VCIn interpolation
entries.desc: Linear approximation: rough estimate only, fair for hand work; actual required RCI changes faster for small n
entries.use: Find how many vehicles can cross when RCI is between VCI1 and VCI50
entries.how: VCIn = (VCI50 - VCI1) x n / 50 + VCI1. Adjust n by trial until VCIn equals RCI. Example M1A1: CI 65 x RI 0.80 = RCI 52; 33 x n/50 + 25: n = 40 gives 51.4, n = 41 gives 52.1, so about 40 tanks. Round VCI estimates up
entries.dim: n = 2 to 49 vehicles
entries.wn: Rough estimate only

entries.desc: Max slope negotiable and max towing force/gross weight are essentially equal for a given RCI. Applies to self-propelled tracked and all-wheel-drive vehicles only
entries.use: Estimate the steepest slope a vehicle can climb
entries.how: Compute RCIx = RCI - VCI1 (one pass) or RCI - VCI50 (50 passes), then read maximum slope percent from Fig 10-8 (one pass) or Fig 10-9 (50 passes) curves. Examples (figure curves not reproduced here): M1A1 one pass RCIx 60 gives 63 percent; M923 in sand one pass RCIx 7 gives 21 percent; M1A1 50 passes RCIx 27 gives 50 percent; M923 50 passes RCIx 25 gives 35 percent
entries.dim: Round slope estimates down
entries.wn: Slipperiness on slopes can make a strong soil impassable

entries.n: Towing a vehicle on level ground or up a slope
entries.desc: Examples: M1A1 tows M923 level, one pass: available 78,750 lb vs required 8,125 lb, yes. M923 tows M1A1 50 passes: available 12,025 lb vs required 22,500 lb, cannot
entries.use: Check if one vehicle can tow another through soft soil
entries.how: Towing vehicle available force T1 = percent (Fig 10-8 one pass, Fig 10-9 50 passes, from RCIx = RCI - VCI) x its gross weight. Towed vehicle required force T2 = percent (Fig 10-10 one pass, Fig 10-11 50 passes) x its weight. Tow is possible if T1 > T2. Slope while towing: Gmax (percent) = (T1 - T2)/(W1 + W2) x 100, round down. Example: M1A1 (125,000 lb) towing M923 (32,500 lb), one pass, RCI 85: T1 = 78,750 lb, T2 = 2,698 lb, Gmax = 48 percent. 50 passes example gives 27 percent; M923 towing M998 (7,500 lb) gives 35 percent
entries.wn: Required towing force may equal or exceed the towed vehicle weight if it drags or bulldozes in soft areas. Do not use these methods for trailers or tractor-trailers

entries.desc: Vegetation on coarse-grained soil indicates stabilized, high-trafficability ground. Girderized tracks (bulldozer type) give higher traction on SP soils than flexible tracks
entries.use: Handle dry sand and beach areas
entries.how: Assume RI = 1.0 and use CI as RCI; no remolding test. Confirm coarse-grained: soil near the penetrometer lightens in color immediately (good internal drainage) or the penetrometer cannot be pushed into a confined sample in the remolding cylinder. Wheeled vehicles: lower tire pressure to mud/sand/snow pressure at least, or emergency pressure if speed is not needed; use all-wheel drive. Tracked vehicles generally cross level coarse-grained soil regardless of strength. The first pass is the most critical; later passes in the same ruts are usually assured
entries.wn: Immobilization can occur easily in dry, loose sand; prepare for recovery. VCI for coarse-grained soil needs NRMM

entries.desc: Fine-grained soil classification example (MH, low topography, high moisture): VCI of 84 or more gives under 50 percent chance of crossing; 56 to under 84 gives 50 to 75 percent; 18 to under 56 gives 75 to 90 percent; under 18 gives 90 percent or more. Stickiness is not mapped
entries.use: Show go/no-go areas for commanders
entries.how: On a gray topographic map print a four-part fraction: soil-type class (A-D), RCI, slope percent, slipperiness (N not slippery, P slippery when wet, S slippery). Color: A dark green passable dry and wet; B light green or green stripes (passable dry, doubtful or impassable wet); C orange or yellow (doubtful dry and wet); D red (impassable); E red stripes (steep slope or rough terrain, soil not evaluated). Use one reference vehicle (e.g., VCI 49) and apply the map to vehicles at or below that VCI. Obstacles circled in red; forests in green pattern; low topography = water table within 4 ft at some time of year

entries.n: Maintenance and repair ground rules and inspections
entries.desc: Inspect more carefully in rainy seasons, spring thaws and after heavy storms. Stockpile sand and gravel, base material and premixed cold patch at convenient places for quick loading
entries.use: Set priorities and inspect roads before they fail
entries.how: Keep traffic moving (work half the surface at a time, night work if needed). Fix the cause before the symptom (surface patch on bad subgrade is wasted). Match original strength, appearance, texture. Prioritize by tactical need, traffic volume and failure hazard. Inspect surface defects and drainage; inspect drainage during or after every storm, in late fall and early spring, and subsurface drains at least twice a year
entries.dim: Subsurface drains: at least 2 inspections per year
entries.wn: Ignore the cause only for temporary combat repairs

entries.n: Maintain drainage: shoulders, ditches, check dams, culverts
entries.desc: Do not use silt, some clays or organic soils (OL, OH, Pt) from ditch cleaning on shoulders; dispose of silt
entries.use: Keep water off the pavement and out of the subgrade
entries.how: Keep shoulders bladed flush with or slightly below the pavement edge and sloping away from it. Keep ditches clear of weeds, brush and sediment and hold line and grade; fix sags and washouts. Keep check dam weir notches and aprons clean and replace washed-out paving. Keep culverts clear (hand cleaning after heavy rain). Make cut-slope interceptor ditches; slope each bench back into the cut and make benches at least as wide as a dozer blade. Line ditches with riprap, asphalt-coated membrane, geosynthetic or concrete where vegetation will not hold. Fill and raise ponding spots; seal joints and cracks
entries.dim: Bench width >= dozer blade width
entries.wn: Avoid unnecessary cutting that destroys ground cover

entries.desc: Improvised road drag: multiple blade drag of iron or iron-shod heavy timber floats mud and water off and prevents washboarding
entries.use: Routine upkeep of dirt roads
entries.how: Light scraping with grader blades and drags; work from the ditches to the center to keep the crown. Blade or drag during or soon after rain because dry loose material will not compact; in dry spells add water or moist subsurface material with rototiller, plow or scarifier first. Compact with the roller type that suits the material at correct moisture. For soft spots (rutting or shoving): find and fix the moisture source, use cobbles on small failures, remove mulch or peat pockets and replace, or add crushed rock or clean gravel as a temporary fix. Control dust with water or bituminous stabilizer. Oiled surfaces: scarify, blade and reshape then re-oil each year; patch with soil and oil mix

entries.desc: Calcium chloride for dust: 1 lb per sq yd in late spring and 1/2 lb per sq yd twice in summer; apply after rain and after blading, or wet the surface first. Quantity depends on rain, traffic and gravel
entries.use: Keep a gravel road smooth and crowned
entries.how: Keep crown at least 1/2 inch per foot. Blade or drag soon after rain until ruts and holes are filled; do not work a dry surface. Keep a slight excess of gravel at edges and blade it over the surface in wet weather; stockpile before fall, winter and wet periods. Potholes: shallow ones blade out when moist; deep ones fill with moistened, compacted new material. Corrugations (waves, ruts up to 4 in deep, 1 1/2 to 3 ft apart): once formed only regrading removes them - scarify, reshape and compact, starting with shoulders and ditches then the whole roadway. Processed rock failures: clean sharp-edged holes to solid subgrade, make sure no silt, mud or water remains, repair subgrade with well-graded aggregate, tamp or roll same-gradation aggregate in place
entries.dim: Crown >= 1/2 in per ft; CaCl 1 lb/sq yd then 0.5 lb/sq yd x 2
entries.wn: Calcium chloride corrodes metal (vehicles, aircraft). Material added in warm dry weather is of little value

entries.n: Repair bituminous, stabilized soil and coral surfaces
entries.desc: Detailed hot-mix, concrete and cratered-runway repair is in UFC 3-270-01, -03, -04 and -07
entries.use: Patch paved and stabilized roads and airfield surfaces
entries.how: Bituminous: trim patches square or oblong with straight vertical sides parallel and perpendicular to the centerline; temporary combat patch with any stable material (good soil, concrete rubble) well compacted and constantly topped up. Stabilized soil potholes: clean, trim rectangular with vertical sides, refill with same-character stabilized mix in thin layers, each compacted. Edge raveling: rebuild shoulder or lower subdrainage first. Coral: use fresh raw coral at proper moisture, repair during or after rain, roll while wet (salt water bonds better than fresh), blade and roll for crown, sprinkle in dry season

entries.desc: Fill with gravel, rock, masonry debris, sandy soil or other stable material, including blown-out material; in an emergency borrow shoulder material and replace later. Alternate layers of sandbags and tamped earth where no equipment or material is available
entries.use: Fix bomb, shell or mine craters in roads and airfields
entries.how: 1) Remove damaged or unbonded surfacing around the edge. 2) Trim surface and base course to a sound vertical edge. 3) Remove water, mud and debris. 4) Fill with successive 6- to 8-inch layers of suitable material up to subgrade level, tamping each layer thoroughly with hand or pneumatic tampers, then compaction equipment. 5) Repair base course and wearing surface
entries.dim: Lifts 6 to 8 in
entries.wn: Explosions can destabilize subgrade over a large area and disrupt drainage; restore subgrade stability

entries.n: Maintenance patrols, repair crews and traffic control
entries.desc: Mark vehicles with red flags or flashing red lights; use speed signs, barricades, flagmen; crew stays out of the traveled way
entries.use: Organize road upkeep and keep traffic moving
entries.how: Patrol plan 1: one squad with dump truck, grader and hand tools covers 5 to 15 miles. Plan 2: one to three people with grader and hand tools handle routine maintenance on 12 miles of average earth, gravel or water-bound macadam road (add truck and repair crew for hauling or patching). Duties: clear drainage, mow, fix minor washouts and potholes, keep surface/shoulders/ditches, inspect, report big jobs. Single-lane traffic: baton method with a flagman at each end. Divert one stream to a stabilized shoulder if possible. Detours/bypasses: recon the shortest route, repair culverts and bridges, stockpile surfacing, sign entrances/turns/hazards, barricade both ends of repair
entries.dim: 5-15 mi per squad patrol; 12 mi per 1-3 person patrol
entries.eq: Dump truck, grader, hand tools, signs
entries.tm: 24-hour patrols in forward or heavy-traffic areas

entries.n: Winter road maintenance: snow fences, plowing, ice control
entries.desc: Spring: open ditch outlets before the thaw; thaw culverts by hand or steamer. Frost boils: bridge soft spots with timber, mats or corduroy, patch with crushed rock, or dig an outlet ditch to one shoulder, bridge with planks and backfill rock/gravel (drain tile optional). Close roads prone to heave/boils during the critical 2- or 3-day period
entries.use: Keep roads open in snow and ice
entries.how: Snow fence on windward side at about 20 x fence height from the road (4-ft fence raised 1 ft: at least 80 ft out; up to 300 ft in extreme cases); one tall fence beats two short; keep fence continuous; bottom about 6 in above ground; install before ground freezes. Plow: 2 1/2- to 5-ton trucks with one-way blades run 15 to 25 mph; 5- to 10-ton trucks with straight or V blades about 15 mph for heavier snow and widening. Start when snow starts. Salt at storm start (sodium or calcium chloride), limit salt on concrete to 1-2 applications a year. Abrasive mix: 40 to 75 lb calcium chloride per cu yd for stockpile plus 25 to 50 lb per cu yd when applied; sodium chloride not recommended below 10 F
entries.dim: Fence spacing 20 x height; 40-75 + 25-50 lb CaCl per cu yd
entries.wn: Salt pits concrete; keep salt bags clear of drain inlets

entries.n: Airfield and heliport maintenance: mud, snow, ice
entries.desc: Mark repairs so they are visible from the air and while taxiing; never leave hazardous equipment on the runway; work at night or in bad weather to avoid stopping flights
entries.use: Keep runways usable in mud and snow
entries.how: Mud: limit taxiway access to service vehicles, clean wheels before taxiing, provide surfaced service roads to hardstands, replace localized soft subgrade. Grader on landing mat: bolt a 4- by 12-inch hardwood moldboard on the cutting edge, extending 2 in below, with optional 1/2-inch rubber belt squeegee extending 1 in; work center to edge overlapping several feet. Snow: wheeled aircraft cannot operate in more than 3 inches of loose snow; ski aircraft use packed snow; start rolling when 3 in has fallen; keep plow blades about 1/2 inch above the runway (runners or castor wheels) and do not straddle the centerline. Ice: urea, coarse sand or cinders; do not use sodium or calcium chloride without approval; abrasives cannot be used where jets operate
entries.dim: Aircraft limit: 3 in loose snow; blade clearance 1/2 in; moldboard 4 x 12 in
entries.eq: Rotary brooms, graders, plows, rollers, blowers
entries.wn: Salts corrode aircraft metal parts

entries.desc: Do not relocate facilities just to meet standard patterns if existing ones serve
entries.use: Bring a damaged enemy airfield into use quickly
entries.how: Assume mines, delayed-action bombs, booby traps, demolished drainage and pavements, debris in runway, plowed turf, flooding, craters and demolished buildings. Priorities: 1) minimum operating strip - clear UXO, mines, booby traps and debris, repair craters on runway and taxiway, repair drainage, give early attention to water and sanitation; 2) remaining runways, taxiways, hardstands, aprons, access roads, fuel and bomb storage; 3) control tower, operations buildings, shelters, communications; 4) camouflage, utilities, bathing/dining, cleanup, seeding and sodding. Combat-heavy engineer battalion usually does the work
entries.wn: Sometimes more effort is needed to restore a field than to build new

entries.desc: Only road Classes B, C and D apply to JOA construction. Design values: see Table TM48-T12-1. Combat zone work is rough and hasty to meet pressing needs; support areas and near airfields, ports and supply installations may need well-surfaced roads
entries.use: Lay out a new military road on a topographic survey
entries.how: Get a topographic survey (minimum 5-ft contour interval). Draw centerline; plot on plan and profile; calculate grades, curve degrees and vertical curve lengths; compare to Table 12-1; shift centerline to cut grades and sharp curves; plot new tangents where limits are exceeded; design horizontal and vertical curves; develop a mass diagram to balance cut and fill; design superelevation and widening; draw typical cross sections; design drainage structures and bridges. Use stage construction to upgrade roads as traffic grows
entries.dim: Contour interval minimum 5 ft
entries.eq: Topographic survey, plan and profile paper or CAD

entries.n: Select road class from traffic volume
entries.desc: Design hourly volume (DHV) in Table 12-1 is total vehicles per hour both directions, about 15 percent of ADT. Values in Table 12-1 assume new roads or roads in good condition; capacity drops as the surface deteriorates. Avoid using the rigid maximum or minimum design values; use the best standard possible in the class
entries.use: Pick Class B, C or D from expected vehicle numbers
entries.how: Estimate vehicles per day: if unknown, take the number of vehicles organic to the using units x 2 (one round trip per vehicle per day). DHV = 0.15 x ADT (rush-hour factor). Class D (1-lane) ADT under 200; Class C 200-935; Class B 935-3,400; Class A 3,400-6,700. Capacity within a class varies with the sight-distance restriction percentage, straight-line on Fig 12-3: more restriction gives lower DHV. Example: 250 vehicles gives ADT 500, DHV 75 (21 veh/hr if spread over 24 hr). Class C works if the sight restriction factor is under 80 percent (the plan gave 62 percent); otherwise build Class B
entries.dim: ADT/DHV by class, Table 12-1

entries.n: Road geometric standards by class (A to D)
entries.desc: See Table TM48-T12-1 for complete values (crown slope, shoulder slope, critical length, curve k values). Widen lanes by the amount a vehicle exceeds 8.5 ft wide. Permanent bridge clearance: traveled way width = lanes + 5 ft (2.5 ft each side); vertical clearance 14.75 ft. Curbs generally not provided in open areas
entries.use: Check lane widths, grades, curves and sight distance against the class
entries.how: Class D: 1 lane, design speed 30 mph, 10-ft lane, 15 ft between curb faces, 4-ft shoulder, max grade 15 percent, max curve 26.7 degrees, stopping sight distance 200 ft, turnouts every 1/4 mile. Class C: 2 lanes, 40 mph, 10-ft lanes, 25 ft curb to curb, 6-ft shoulders, max grade 10 percent, max curve 14.5 degrees, stopping 275 ft, passing 1,500 ft. Class B: 2 lanes, 60 mph, 12-ft lanes, 29 ft curb to curb, 10-ft shoulders, max grade 6 percent, max curve 5.5 degrees, stopping 475 ft, passing 2,100 ft. Class A: 4 lanes, 60 mph, 12-ft lanes, 53 ft curb to curb
entries.dim: Lane 10 ft (C, D) or 12 ft (A, B); shoulder 4/6/10/10 ft; max grade 15/10/6/6 percent

entries.desc: The chord definition (railroads) differs from the arc definition by often less than 1 percent. Make tangents long, curves gentle, and cross other roads and railroads at right angles. Tangent stations: PC = PI - T; PT = PC + L (add curve length, not tangent distance)
entries.use: Compute radius, tangent, length for a simple curve
entries.how: Use the arc definition: D = angle subtended by a 100-ft arc. R = 5,729.58 / D. Tangent distance T = T1deg / D, external E = E1deg / D, middle ordinate M = M1deg / D (1-degree values from the 1-degree curve table in TM 3-34.48-2 for the angle of intersection I). Curve length L = (I / D) x 100. Central angle equals the angle of intersection. The maximum D is set by road class (Table 12-1). Simple curve is the usual JOA choice; spiral transitions only for Class A and B
entries.wn: Increasing D decreases R and T

entries.n: Design a horizontal curve (unrestricted, tangent-limited, external-limited)
entries.desc: If a maximum T or E is the limit, round D up (shorter T and E); if a minimum T is the limit, round D down
entries.use: Find PC, PT and degree of curve for a given PI and angle
entries.how: Unrestricted: choose D (gentle, within class max), R = 5,729.58 / D. Tangent limited: D = T1deg / T(restricted), then round UP to the next half degree. External limited: D = E1deg / E(restricted), round UP to next half degree. Then T = T1deg/D, L = I/D x 100, PC = PI - T, PT = PC + L. Worked: Class C, D = 6 deg, I = 50 deg, PI 14+28: R = 954.93 ft, T = 445.30 ft, L = 833.33 ft, PC 9+82.71, PT 18+16.04. Tangent limit 282 ft with I = 32 deg: D = 1,643/282 = 5.83 deg (5 deg 50 min), use 6 deg, T = 273.82 ft, L = 533.33 ft, PC 23+13.18, PT 28+46.51. External limit E < 85 ft with I = 80 deg: D = 1,749.9/85 = 20.59 deg, use 21 deg, T = 228.94 ft, E = 83.33 ft, L = 380.95 ft, PC 41+03.81, PT 44+84.76
entries.dim: Round D to half degree

entries.n: Stationing equation after a curve is installed
entries.use: Fix the stationing when a curve shortens the centerline
entries.how: Each curve shortens the centerline by 2T - L. When the survey crew designs curves in the field and stations progressively, no adjustment is needed. When curves are designed in the office, write a station equation on the PT stake: PT EQ, BK (correct station back) over AH (correct station ahead), for example BK 12+97 and AH 13+21 (road shortened 24 ft). Duplicate station (BK 13+00, AH 12+00) means the road lengthened by one station. Show equations as a gap in the grade on the profile
entries.dim: Adjustment = 2T - L

entries.n: Lay out a horizontal curve by deflection angles
entries.desc: Other layout methods: arc method (radius under 100 ft, fillets, intersections); external-distance method (short curves, three points, not for precise or long curves). Stake at a minimum of every 100 ft, closer on sharp curves (Table TM48-T12-3). Metric: stake at 20 m maximum and use D20 for deflection angles (Table TM48-T12-4)
entries.use: Stake a circular curve on the ground
entries.how: Deflection angle = half the central angle: 100-ft arc gives D/2. Set the transit on the PC, zero on the PI (or backsight along the tangent), turn the first angle, measure the subarc to the first full station, then turn each next angle (add D/2 per full station) and measure the chord from the previous station. Subarc deflection = (D/2) x (subarc length / 100). Chord for a full 100-ft arc = 2R sin(D/2); for a partial arc = 2R sin[(D/2)(L/100)]. Check: the final deflection to the PT must equal I/2. Example D = 6 deg, R = 954.93: full chords 99.954 ft, first subarc 17.28 ft, last 16.032 ft, final angle 25 deg 00 min = I/2 (I = 50). If a station cannot be sighted, move the transit to the last good station, backsight the PC, and turn the same angle
entries.dim: Staking interval: 100 ft (D 0-3), 50 ft (D >3-8), 25 ft (D >8-16), 10 ft (D >16)

entries.n: Design a vertical curve (crest or sag)
entries.desc: Worked Class D crest: G1 +3.1 percent, G2 -5.75 percent, k = 35, dG = 8.85, L given as 4 stations (400 ft); the check k x dG / 100 = 3.10 stations, so 4 stations exceeds the minimum, PVI 5+00, PVC 3+00 (elev 66.80), PVT 7+00 (61.50), MO = 4.43 ft, offset constant 1.106, high point 140 ft from PVC at 4+40, elevation 68.97 ft. Grade G = V/H x 100; plus sign for rising grades in the direction of increasing stations
entries.use: Smooth the transition between two grade lines
entries.how: Steps: 1) dG = |G1 - G2| (percent). 2) L = k x dG / 100 in 100-ft stations (round up to next full station; check against absolute minimum length in Table 12-1). 3) PVC = PVI - L/2; 4) PVT = PVI + L/2. 5/6) elevations of PVC and PVT from PVI +/- grade x L/2. 7) Maximum offset MO = L x dG / 8 (at PVI). 8) GLE = PVC elev +/- G1 x d; offset = (dG / 2L) x d^2 (d in stations from PVC or PVT, symmetric); crest curve elev = GLE - offset, sag curve elev = GLE + offset. 9) High or low point at d = G x L / dG measured on the flatter grade. 10) Y = -dG x^2/(2L) + G1 x + elev PVC. Stake at every half station (50 ft) or 10 m; closer in rugged terrain. Cut or fill at the stake = ground elevation minus curve elevation
entries.dim: Class k values (crest/sag): A,B 160/105; C 55/55; D 35/28; absolute minimum length 180/180/120/80 ft

entries.n: Vertical curve through a fixed point (e.g., over a culvert)
entries.use: Find the curve length needed to clear a culvert or hit a set elevation
entries.how: Known point at the PVI: L = MO x 8 / dG. Known point at distance A from the PVI: L = 2[A + 2(offset)/dG] + 4 sqrt[A(offset)/dG + (offset/dG)^2] (dG as a decimal; offset = required curve elevation minus grade-line elevation at that point). Worked example: PVI 12+50 elev 73.00; 24-in culvert at 11+00 with invert 85.8 ft; required curve elevation = 85.8 + 2.0 (pipe) + 1.0 (cover) = 88.8 ft; A = 150 ft; dG = 0.165; GLE = 73.0 + 0.081 x 150 = 85.15 ft; offset = 3.65 ft; L = 635.30 ft as printed. Then finish the curve with the normal steps
entries.wn: The L formula as extracted is partly garbled; verify with the original page before relying on the example's final figure

entries.n: Cross section: crown, side slopes, guardrail
entries.desc: Class A example needs 3 ft of shoulder widening for guardrails and guideposts
entries.use: Set road crown and cut/fill slopes
entries.how: Crown 2 percent for asphalt, 4 percent for aggregate surfaces; subgrade has same crown as the finished surface. Shoulders slope 0.0417-0.0625. Embankment front slopes 1V:4H or flatter where practical; 1V:3H is traversable but not recoverable; steeper than 1V:3H overturns most vehicles. Avoid slopes steeper than 1V:2H in erodible clay and silt; loessal soils need special cut-slope design. Vary slope ratios gradually (1 unit of horizontal ratio per 50 ft of road, so 1V:2H to 1V:4H over at least 100 ft). Guardrail not needed on embankment slopes of 1V:3H or flatter; needed on 1V:2H embankments higher than 6 ft. See Table TM48-T12-6
entries.dim: Crown 2% asphalt, 4% aggregate

entries.n: Superelevation and pavement widening on curves
entries.desc: Transitions are desirable but not essential above the heavy line in Table 12-7. Detailed design is in TM 3-34.55. Values for D max by speed: 60 mph 5.5 deg, 40 mph 14.5 deg, 30 mph 28.7 deg (as printed)
entries.use: Bank and widen curves
entries.how: Raise the outer edge to balance overturning force; rate depends on degree of curve and design speed (maximum rate 0.100). Use Table 12-7 for rate E and minimum transition length L (e.g., 60 mph, 5 deg: E 0.099, L 270 ft; 30 mph, 6 deg: E 0.046, L 100 ft). Run two-thirds of the transition on the tangent and one-third on the curve. Widen pavement on curves per Table 12-8 (two-lane, 20-ft tangent pavement): e.g., 30 mph at 6 deg curve +2.5 ft, 40 mph at 6 deg +3.0 ft, at 26-26.7 deg +5.5 ft. NC = normal crown; RC = remove adverse crown and superelevate at normal slope
entries.dim: Max superelevation 0.100; transition 2/3 tangent, 1/3 curve

entries.n: Mountain road design: switchbacks and grade relief
entries.use: Handle steep terrain
entries.how: Break long grades with level or adverse-slope relief sections to prevent truck brake overheating. Switchbacks: minimum centerline radius 60 ft, widen the roadway through the curve, reduce grade through it: maximum 4 percent for 20 mph curve speed, 5 percent for 25 mph
entries.dim: Switchback min radius 60 ft; grade 4% at 20 mph, 5% at 25 mph

entries.n: Mountain road prisms: bench cuts, retaining walls, embankments
entries.desc: Rock embankments: max slope 1V:1.25H placed or keyed riprap (keyed with hydraulic bucket or about 5,000-lb 4 ft x 5 ft flat mass); on rock foundation install dowels 3 to 6 ft apart and grout the bottom layer. Grouted riprap max slope 1V:1H, layers up to 5 ft thick, grout at 35 F or warmer starting at the lowest elevation, 3 days cure between layers, keep moist 3 days, protect from freezing at least 7 days. Cover top of rock embankment with geotextile or choke with smaller rock
entries.use: Build roadbed on side slopes without sliding
entries.how: Sliver bench: sideslope 1V:3H or less - sidecast and compact in lifts; 1V:4H to 1V:3H - plow or step so fill bonds; steeper than 1V:3H - key into slope with 2- to 8-ft high benches at least 12 ft wide (do not just sidecast). Full bench (side slopes over 1V:2H): cut road width plus ditch, haul waste to low spots; costs four to seven times balanced cut and fill. Retaining wall (reinforced concrete, MSE, soil nail, bin) when existing slopes are steeper than 1V:1.5H. Earth embankment: bench the existing slope if 1V:3H or steeper; layers no more than 12 in compacted (24 in if mostly rock); place rock over 24 in individually; reduce rock to under 48 in in largest dimension; prevent nesting; riprap keyway at toe for 1V:1.5H front slopes
entries.dim: Benches 2-8 ft high, 12 ft wide; lifts 12 in (24 in rock)

entries.n: Rock cut slopes and rockfall control
entries.desc: Rockfall options: fallout ditches, barriers, catch fences, draped mesh, rock bolts, dowels, shotcrete, cable lashing, buttresses. Cuts under 20 ft generally need no fallout ditch; slopes higher than 30 ft may need wider ones. Uncontrolled blasting fractures rock tens of feet into the slope
entries.use: Cut stable slopes in rock
entries.how: Use Table 12-9 for maximum cut slope: igneous and massive sedimentary 1V:0.25H massive / 1V:0.50H fractured; interbedded 1V:0.50H / 1V:0.75H; claystone/siltstone 1V:0.75H / 1V:1H; metamorphic 1V:0.25H / 1V:0.50H; slate 1V:0.50H / 1V:0.75H. Use controlled blasting (presplit or cushion/trim) for cuts 1V:0.75H or steeper; cushion blasting in weak rock or rock thickness under 15 ft. Avoid cutting bedrock dipping toward the road. Overburden benches at the top of solid rock with 1V:3H to 1V:2H overburden slope
entries.dim: See Table TM48-T12-9

entries.n: Identify unknown bituminous material in the field
entries.desc: Use grade choice: stiffer asphalt cement in hot climates and heavy traffic. Tar: use emulsified coal tar where petroleum products spill (does not dissolve in them); handle hot tar with care since fumes irritate skin; cutback asphalt may be unavailable or banned, use emulsions. Prime coat/dust control/tack coat product choices are in Table 12-10
entries.use: Tell asphalt, cutback, emulsion and tar apart before use
entries.how: 1) Solubility: drop a sample in kerosene, gasoline, diesel or jet fuel; asphalt dissolves to a dark uniform liquid, tar stays a dark stringy mass. 2) Pour at 77 F: does not pour = asphalt cement; pours and dilutes in water = emulsion; pours with solvent smell = cutback. 3) Rapid cure test: smear on glazed paper; tacky in about 10 minutes = rapid curing; medium cure takes hours; slow cure days. For 800 or 3,000 grades smear for 2+ hours (RC-3000 cures in 3 hr, RC-800 about 6 hr; MC/SC still sticky after 24 hr). 4) Heat in a closed container: strong kerosene odor = medium cure; hot motor oil smell = slow cure. 5) Emulsion: dark brown, wet cloth will not burn, mixes with water; mix 6 to 8 percent by weight with damp sand - rapid-set breaks and gums the spoon, slow/medium set coats sand
entries.eq: Kerosene or diesel, glazed paper, jar, spoon
entries.wn: Tar emissions irritate skin

entries.desc: Angular aggregate needs more binder because it packs less tightly. Los Angeles abrasion (AASHTO T96) is usually not available in the field
entries.use: Decide whether an aggregate is fit for asphalt
entries.how: Want angular, rough, tough and hard, clean and dry, hydrophobic aggregate. Hardness by scratch test (Mohs): fingernail about 2, copper coin 3-4, knife blade, nail, window glass about 5.5; if one of these scratches it, it is soft. Wash dirty aggregate (spread on hard surface and hose, or dry screen, or hand pick). Hot mix needs hot dry aggregate. Stripping test: coat aggregate with bitumen at correct temperature, air-cure 24 hr, put in jar (no more than half full) covered with water, stand 24 hr, shake vigorously 15 min, estimate percent of exposed aggregate. Swell test: sound stone, slag or gravel with limestone filler should swell under 1.5 percent
entries.dim: Swell < 1.5%

entries.desc: Do not let priming run too far ahead of the surfacing or the base gets dirty or fully cured (dead). If too wet, moisture strips the prime; if fully dry, cracks and swelling after rain
entries.use: Seal and bond a soil or aggregate base before surfacing
entries.how: Prepare the base: well graded, shaped, compacted, drained, swept; wet lightly and let it become almost dry before spraying. Prime coat should penetrate about 1/4 in. In moderate and warm climates use MC-30, MC-70, SS-1, SS-1h, CSS-1 or CSS-1h; in cold climates RC-70 or RC-250; skip it in damp cold climates. Wait at least 48 hours before covering. Quantity Qp (gal) = L x (W + 2) x AR x LF / 9. AR = about 0.2 gal/sq yd on dense soil, up to 0.5 on cracked soil; LF = 1.05 to 1.10; the +2 covers 1 ft overspray each side. Example: 1,000 ft x 12 ft, AR 0.2, LF 1.05 = 326.67, about 327 gal
entries.dim: 0.2 to 0.5 gal/sq yd; 48 hr cure

entries.desc: Excess tack bleeds, floods the mix and loses stability. Start-of-run and hand-sprayed areas tend to get heavier application. The manual's worked example prints length 100 ft and result 14 gal for a 1,000 x 12 ft surface at 0.10 and 1.05, but the formula gives 140 gal for 1,000 ft
entries.use: Bond new asphalt to an existing surface
entries.how: Spray existing concrete, brick, bituminous or binder course before overlay. Not needed on a primed base unless the prime has cured and picked up dust. Rate 0.05 to 0.10 gal/sq yd (0.05 smooth dense surface; 0.10 or slightly more worn, rough, cracked). Qt (gal) = L x W x AR x LF / 9 with LF about 1.05. Tack coat should become tacky within a few hours. Apply over the width to be surfaced and use a tack each time a layer is added
entries.dim: 0.05-0.10 gal/sq yd
entries.wn: Check the printed example arithmetic

entries.use: Control dust on soil or aggregate roads
entries.how: Spray a diluted slow-setting asphalt emulsion (up to 5 parts water by volume) or a low-viscosity cutback. Cutback rate 0.1 to 0.5 gal/sq yd. Emulsion treatments usually need several applications. Lay a test strip to find the best rate. Apply with an asphalt distributor or a watering can. Temporary: plan regular inspection and maintenance
entries.dim: Cutback 0.1-0.5 gal/sq yd; emulsion diluted 1:5 water

entries.n: Single and multiple surface treatment (chip seal)
entries.desc: Equipment: distributor spray bar width equals aggregate spread width (one lane); distributor tank sizes 800 to 4,000 gal (maintenance units 400 gal), spray bar minimum 8 ft up to 24 ft, double or triple lap; hopper spreader 4-8 ft wide behind a 5-ton dump truck; pneumatic-tire rollers only (no vibratory); no one on the spreader; control traffic behind a pilot vehicle with red flag
entries.use: Cheap waterproof wearing surface on a base or old pavement
entries.how: Do not build below 50 F; best well above 50 F with low humidity. Surface must be hard, clean, dry. Bitumen by distributor: about 1 gal per 100 lb of aggregate; embed aggregate 1/4 in about 30 percent, 3/8 in about 32 percent, 1/2 in about 35 percent, 3/4 in about 43 percent. Coarse sand with RC-70/RC-250 seals cracks; badly cracked surface 3/4 in max aggregate with RC-800 or RC-3000. Quantities: bitumen Qb (gal) = L x W x ARA x ARB x LF / 9, aggregate QA (tons) = L x W x ARA x LF / (9 x 2,000) with aggregate LF 1.10. Example 1,000 x 12 ft, 3/8 in crushed stone at 100 lb/cu ft: ARA = 28.125 lb/sq yd, Qb = 393.75 (about 394 gal). Multiple treatment: each extra layer uses about half the aggregate size and one-third to one-half the bitumen; sweep loose stone off first layer; roll final layer with pneumatic roller; sweep airfield surfaces (FOD)
entries.dim: Aggregate cover one stone deep, under 1 in; bitumen 1 gal / 100 lb; temperature >= 50 F
entries.wn: Not for tracked vehicles, steel wheels or chains, or heavy high-speed traffic; not recommended on airfields (FOD) except expedient. Do not run the distributor far ahead of the spreader

entries.desc: Production rate = unit of work done / unit of time (e.g., CY per hour, tons per shift, feet of ditch per hour). Time required is the inverse: unit of time / unit of work (e.g., hours per 1,000 CY, hours per acre, days per acre, minutes per foot of ditch)
entries.use: Estimating how fast a machine works or how long a job takes
entries.how: Use the same unit of work and unit of time every time so estimates can be compared
entries.dim: Production rate = work done / time; Time required = time / work done

entries.desc: BCY = 1 cubic yard in natural undisturbed state. LCY = 1 cubic yard after disturbed by excavation. CCY = 1 cubic yard after compaction. Same weight occupies different volumes in each state. Rock needs drilling and blasting; soil is classed by particle size and cohesion (gravel/sand noncohesive, clay cohesive); unclassified is rock plus soil
entries.use: Converting earth volumes between in-place, hauled, and compacted
entries.how: Always get the volume of material and the machine production in the SAME state (BCY, LCY or CCY) before computing time or number of machines. BCY is the standard unit of comparison
entries.dim: BCY / LCY / CCY

entries.desc: Dry clay swells 40%: 1 BCY becomes 1.4 LCY, so load factor = 1/1.4 = 0.72. A scraper carrying 25 LCY of dry clay is carrying 18 BCY (25 x 0.72)
entries.use: Converting loose volume to bank volume
entries.how: LCY x load factor = BCY. Load factor = 1 / (1 + swell)
entries.dim: Dry clay swell 40%; load factor 0.72; 25 LCY x 0.72 = 18 BCY
entries.wn: Averages only; weight and load factor vary with grain size, moisture, compaction. For an exact weight, test a sample of the actual material

entries.desc: Example: a scraper with 25 cubic yard volumetric capacity and 50,000 pound rated load capacity will exceed volume before weight with cinder; with gravel (over 3,000 lb/CY) it exceeds weight capacity first. Soil weight affects how dozers push, graders cast, scrapers load
entries.use: Deciding whether a hauler fills by volume or by weight
entries.how: Light materials (cinders) fill the bowl before reaching rated weight; heavy materials (gravel) hit weight limit before volume limit
entries.dim: 25 CY / 50,000 lb example; gravel > 3,000 lb per CY

entries.n: Zones of operation (power, slow-speed haul, high-speed haul)
entries.desc: Power zone: rough terrain, steep slopes, pioneering, extremely heavy loads; needs crawler tractors with high drawbar pull at slow speed. Slow-speed hauling zone: conditions slightly better, short haul; distances too short for scrapers to reach higher speeds, dozing not economical. High-speed hauling zone: good grade and haul-road surface, haul distance long enough for max travel speed, push tractors available. A mass diagram (TM 3-34.48-1) helps identify zones
entries.use: Choosing equipment type by job conditions
entries.how: Power zone: crawler tractors. Slow-speed haul: dozer and scraper equal speed. High-speed haul: scrapers with pushers once good haul roads exist; get to this condition as soon as possible
entries.wn: Operate equipment at safe speeds to prevent injury or premature failure of major components

entries.desc: Light-class: DEUCE. Medium-class: MCT and D7. Straight blade is fixed perpendicular to travel, tilt and pitch within a 10 degree arc. Angle blades are 1 to 2 ft wider than straight blades, angle up to 25 degrees left or right; can be tilted when angled but not pitched. Rome K/G blade has a fixed angle and a stinger (vertical splitter, triangular web about 2 ft each side) that cuts brush/trees at or a few inches above ground rather than uprooting; split large trees with stinger first, then cut off and push over
entries.use: Selecting a dozer and blade
entries.how: Straight blade for pushing and ditching; angle blade for sidecasting, backfill, sidehill cuts; Rome K/G blade for clearing brush/trees
entries.dim: Straight blade tilt/pitch 10 degree arc; angle blade 25 degrees each side, 1-2 ft wider; Rome K/G web sides about 2 ft
entries.eq: DEUCE (light); MCT, D7 (medium); Rome K/G clearing blade
entries.wn: Keep stinger and cutting edge sharp; requires well-trained operators. Transport dozers on heavy trailers to avoid track wear

entries.n: Clearing and grubbing: quick production rates
entries.desc: Strip-type clearing: increase Table 2-1 values by 60 percent. Rates assume 50 trees per acre; slopes, rocks, soft ground reduce rates significantly. Tactical land clearing is a combat-support function. Plan clearing for disposal of debris in one handling and travel in one direction to avoid damaging trees
entries.use: Estimating clearing time when no tree count is possible
entries.how: Look up hours per acre by tractor size and largest tree size, then divide by efficiency, operator factor and number of dozers
entries.dim: Table 2-1 hrs/acre (bulldozer medium 2.5/5.0/10.0; heavy 1.5/3.0/8.0; shear blade medium 0.4/0.8/1.3; heavy 0.3/0.5/0.8); strip clearing +60%
entries.tm: Total time (hr) = (D x A) / (E x O x N). Well-managed job: 50 min production per hour (E = 0.83)
entries.wn: Address environmental protection before clearing

entries.desc: 500 ft wide x 0.5 mile long = 30.3 acres; 2 medium dozers; largest tree 14 in so 5 hours per acre; operator average daylight 0.75; efficiency 50/60 = 0.83. Total = 5 x 30.3 / (0.83 x 0.75 x 2) = about 122 hours
entries.use: Calculating total clearing time for an area
entries.how: Area acres = width ft x length ft / 43,560. Then T = D x A / (E x O x N)
entries.dim: 1 acre = 43,560 sq ft; 30.3 acres; 122 hours

entries.desc: D (min per acre) = H([A x B] + [M1 x N1] + [M2 x N2] + [M3 x N3] + [I x F]). H hardwood factor: 1.3 if 75-100% hardwoods; 1.0 if 25-75%; 0.7 if 0-25%. A density/vines: 2 if over 600 trees/acre; 1 if 400-600; 0.7 if under 400; 2 if heavy vines; 3 if very heavy vines. B base minutes per acre; M time per tree per diameter range; N trees per acre in range; I sum of diameters (ft increments) of trees over 6 ft at ground level; F min per foot diameter. Total hr = D x A / N (D in hours, A acres, N dozers). Grubbing roots and stumps: add 25 percent to time per acre
entries.use: Detailed clearing estimate after reconnaissance and tree count
entries.how: Use when you can recon and count trees per acre by diameter class; gives better estimate than quick method. No efficiency or operator correction (assumes normal efficiency and average operator)
entries.wn: Times based on reasonably level ground, good footing, average mix of soft and hardwoods

entries.desc: Factors assume good visibility and a 60-minute working hour efficiency
entries.use: Adjusting production for operator skill and light
entries.how: Multiply production by factor: excellent 1.00 day/0.75 night; average 0.75/0.56; poor 0.60/0.45
entries.dim: Excellent 1.00 / 0.75; Average 0.75 / 0.56; Poor 0.60 / 0.45 (day / night)

entries.n: Clear brush and small trees with dozer
entries.desc: A medium tractor with dozer blade can clear and pile about 0.25 acre of brush or small trees per hour
entries.use: Clearing brush and saplings
entries.how: Run blade slightly below ground level; blade cuts, breaks or uproots and bends the rest for removal on the return trip
entries.dim: 0.25 acre per hour (medium tractor)

entries.n: Push over a medium tree (7 to 12 in diameter)
entries.desc: Medium tree 7 to 12 inches diameter
entries.use: Removing medium trees with a dozer
entries.how: Raise blade as high as possible, push slowly; as tree starts to fall back up quickly to avoid rising roots; lower blade and drive forward to lift out roots
entries.dim: 7-12 in diameter; 2 to 9 minutes per tree
entries.tm: 2 to 9 minutes per tree (medium tractor, clear and pile)
entries.wn: Back away fast when tree falls to avoid rising roots

entries.n: Remove a large tree (12 to 30 in) with massive roots
entries.desc: Step 1: start on side opposite proposed direction of fall and cut deep enough to sever large roots, cut like a V-ditch tilted down toward the roots. Step 2: cut side two. Step 3: cut side three. Step 4: build an earth ramp on the same side as the original cut for leverage, push tree over, reverse quickly to avoid rising root mass. Fill the stump hole to prevent water collecting. Roots on the fourth side may also need cutting
entries.use: Removing large trees with deep root systems
entries.how: Probe for dead limbs, find natural lean (best push direction), blade high and centered. For massive roots use the four-step cut method then ramp
entries.dim: Large tree 12-30 in diameter; 5 to 20 min per tree; massive trees often over 20 min each
entries.tm: 5 to 20 minutes per tree (medium tractor, clear and pile)
entries.wn: Probe for dead limbs that could fall

entries.n: Remove roots and small stumps with rake
entries.use: Grubbing roots
entries.how: Mount a rake on the dozer in place of the blade; teeth go below the surface and catch roots and brush while soil passes through

entries.desc: Never operate clearing tractors too close together. Do not follow a tree too closely when pushing; stump and roots may catch under front of dozer. Clean accumulated debris out of the belly pan often to prevent engine-compartment fires
entries.use: Clearing operations
entries.how: Keep dozers apart, do not follow tree closely, clean belly pan
entries.wn: Fire risk from belly-pan debris; stump/roots can catch under dozer front

entries.desc: Start the bench at the highest point of the cut and widen and deepen until desired road profile; start far enough up slope to leave room for inner slope and roadway. Short perpendicular passes give poor blade loads. Keep the inside (hillside) of roadway lower than the outside so the dozer works effectively on the edge and erosion of outer slope is reduced. Hard to change cut slope later, so hold the inside slope; maintain bench slope by moving out from inside slope on each cut. Determine slope ratio by measuring distance moved away and depth of each cut. Cut road cross slope from toe of bench to outside edge. Finish cut with dozer or scraper. Design benches so water runs off without damaging slope
entries.use: Pioneering road cuts along hillsides
entries.how: Angle blade preferred. Start at the top, make a bench several dozer lengths long, then work along the long axis of the project, full blade load, push over the side
entries.eq: Dozer with angle blade; winch for extremely steep slopes
entries.wn: On extremely steep slopes a winch line may be needed to stabilize dozer

entries.desc: Perpendicular: earth falls to lower side of blade and forms windrow; pick it up on later passes to fill holes. Diagonal: start at bottom and work diagonally up; windrow is continually pushed to one side. This is one of few cases a bulldozer is effective pushing uphill
entries.use: Finishing embankment or cut side slopes
entries.how: Two methods: perpendicular to slope (start at top, windrow forms on low side, picked up on next pass) or diagonally up the slope (start at bottom, push windrow to one side filling low spots)
entries.wn: Do not let blade corner dig in too deep or slope will be steeper than specification

entries.desc: Dozers work best on firm ground free of potholes, ridges, rocks. If blade digs in and rear rises, raise blade. If load slows travel, shift lower gear and/or raise blade slightly. Full blade handles easier when finishing. Side-by-side: effective for 50 to 300 ft; under 50 ft maneuver time offsets gain. Slot dozing: use spillage from first passes to make windrows each side of path forming a trench; make parallel cuts leaving a narrow uncut section between slots, then remove it by regular dozing. Downhill: stack loads at top and push all down in one go; go to bottom with each load
entries.use: Increasing dozer output
entries.how: Side-by-side adds 15-25% at 50-300 ft push; slot dozing up to 20% more; push downhill whenever possible
entries.dim: Side-by-side +15 to 25% for 50-300 ft; slot dozing up to +20%

entries.n: Dozing hard, rocky, frozen and wet materials
entries.desc: Tilt blade via blade control, by driving one track onto a ridge, or putting a rock/log under the track; hook only tilted end under material. Boulders: tilt blade, excavate around three sides, lower blade to get under fourth side, raise blade as dozer moves forward for lifting and rolling; if cannot push, lift with blade and have someone put a log under it. Wet: each pass through full depth of wet material for stable base; push mud far enough it does not flow back in cut
entries.use: Working in difficult materials without a ripper
entries.how: Hard material: tilt blade to force one corner in; use turning so grousers break the top layer; frozen: break through at one point. Rocks: rake for small rocks; for boulders excavate around three sides then lift and roll. Wet: push through full depth, use wider shoes, have winch
entries.eq: Dozer; rake; rock shoes/pads; wider track shoes; winch
entries.wn: Rock work increases track wear, use rock shoes or pads. Plan recovery in case dozer gets stuck

entries.desc: Fix humps or holes in a single pass if possible; otherwise use multiple passes
entries.use: Rough or shallow ditches
entries.how: Grader is best for shallow ditches; dozer tilts blade to cut shallow V-ditches. For larger ditches push material perpendicular to centerline, then push along ditch length to smooth sides and bottom

entries.desc: Step 1: first pass push material from excavation to stockpile, no more than 75 ft, cut no deeper than 6 to 8 in, smooth cut. Step 2: begin raising blade one dozer length from stockpile so material forms a ramp as it drifts under the blade. Step 3: successive cuts, working from start point around the work area, overlap cuts by about one-third of blade width to pick up windrows. Step 4: successive cuts as in step 2 to build to desired height
entries.use: Making stockpiles for loader/excavator loading
entries.how: Push first pass max 75 ft from start; cut no deeper than 6-8 in; start raising blade one dozer length from the pile; overlap cuts by one-third blade width; build higher with each pass
entries.dim: Max push 75 ft; cut depth 6-8 in; overlap 1/3 blade width
entries.wn: Check no one endangered before reversing. Keep machine under control; do not shift to neutral to coast; select gear before descending; do not change gears going downhill. Do not stop forward motion or spin tracks while pushing

entries.n: Spread a stockpile with a dozer
entries.desc: Step 1 lower blade to desired height moving forward. Step 2 move into side of pile cutting with only one-third of blade (left side of blade: keep working left; right side: keep working right). Step 3 cut into pile, blade as full as possible without stalling or spinning tracks. Step 4 spread load by continuing forward and slowly raising blade until feathered. Step 5 feather and reverse, raise blade about 12 in off ground, back to the pile and reposition. Repeat
entries.use: Leveling a pile
entries.how: Work large piles from the side with one-third of the blade; feather the load; raise blade about 12 in to back up; do not back blade to level
entries.dim: Cut with 1/3 blade; raise 12 in to back
entries.wn: When spreading material higher than the midpoint of the ROPS, adjust cut height to eliminate danger from collapsing material

entries.desc: Ensure no part of tracks hangs over edge. For soft material or unstable slopes let second bladeful push first over the edge. Keep oversize material out of backfill
entries.use: Backfilling trenches/excavations
entries.how: Angle blade pushes material sideways, moving parallel to excavation. With straight blade approach at a slight angle and turn toward excavation at end of pass
entries.wn: Tracks must not overhang edge

entries.desc: Steps: 1 position dozer uphill side if on slope, about half dozer length before start of area; 2 forward, first gear; 3 lower rippers to depth as dozer begins crossing area; 4 raise rippers out and stop at end of pass; 5 reverse back to start; 6 position to overlap previous pass. Place ripped material on top of unripped formation to cushion machine and give traction. Packed soil, hardpan, shale, cemented gravel: three-shank ripping, as many shanks as possible. Rock with fractures/faults: two shanks in small rock, switch to center shank if machine stalls or tracks spin. Asphalt: raise shank to lift and break. Concrete: one-shank ripping severs rebar/mesh. Solid rock, granite, hard-to-rip or slab-breaking: one shank
entries.use: Breaking hard, packed or rocky material
entries.how: First gear; use center shank when one-shank ripping; add shanks to increase production; rip in same direction scrapers will load; close passes for small final size; cross rip only if needed. Pick shank count by material
entries.dim: First gear; 1 shank hard rock / 2 shanks fractured rock / 3 shanks packed soil, hardpan, shale
entries.wn: Keep straight line while ripping; turning with rippers in ground damages dozer

entries.desc: When moving away from a load use low gear to prevent winch overspeeding. Avoid prolonged winch operation. Suspended loads can drop if engine speed too low even with winch in reel-in
entries.use: Winching and recovery
entries.how: Keep cable straight behind machine; decelerate engine before moving winch lever; low engine speed when stationary
entries.wn: Keep personnel clear of cable; cables can break. Suspended load can exceed engine capacity and drop

entries.n: Dozer production estimate (curves and correction factors)
entries.desc: Chart assumptions: 60-minute hour; power-shift machines with 0.05 min fixed time; cut 50 ft then drift to dump over high wall; soil 2,300 lb per LCY; traction coefficient 0.5 or better crawler, 0.4 wheel; hydraulic blades. Fig 2-13: D6T through D7E straight blade (DEUCE = D5; Marines use D7 for MCT). Fig 2-14: D7R/D8R semi-universal. Weight factor = 2,300 / actual lb per LCY. Efficiency E = working min per hour / 60 (50 min = 0.83). Number of dozers = Q / (P x T). Time = Q / (P x N)
entries.use: Estimating dozer output in LCY/hr
entries.how: Production = max production (from chart) x grade x weight x material-type x operator x technique x efficiency factors. Then convert to needed material state
entries.dim: Std weight 2,300 lb/LCY; Table 2-4 material type: loose stockpile 1.2; hard-to-cut frozen with tilt cylinder 0.8, without tilt 0.7; hard to drift (dead dry noncohesive or very sticky) 0.8; rock ripped/blasted 0.6-0.8. Table 2-5 technique: slot dozing 1.2; side-by-side 1.15-1.25
entries.wn: Charts (figures 2-13 to 2-15) are graphs and not reproduced here

entries.desc: Max 300 LCY/hr x grade 1.15 x weight 0.92 (2300/2500) x material 0.8 x operator 0.75 x technique 1.2 x efficiency 0.83 = 190 LCY/hr. Convert with clay loose to compacted 0.63: 120 CCY/hr. Time for 3,000 CCY with 1 dozer: 3,000 / 120 = 25 h. Dozers to do 3,000 CCY in 7 h: 3,000/(120 x 7) = 3.6, so 4 dozers
entries.use: Example calculation
entries.how: D7 straight blade with tilt, hard-packed clay, 200 ft, 10% downhill grade, slot dozing, 2,500 lb per LCY, average daylight operator, 50 min/hr
entries.dim: 190 LCY/hr = 120 CCY/hr; 25 h; 4 dozers
entries.tm: 25 hours for 3,000 CCY with one dozer
entries.wn: The book's printed example divides by 8 h but states 7 hours; quotient 3.6 corresponds to 7 h

entries.desc: BCY per hour = V / (T x 1.2); V = measured volume in BCY, T = average time in hours. Ripping raises machine maintenance 30-40 percent. Best estimate is a worked test section
entries.use: Estimating ripper output from a test section
entries.how: Time several passes over a measured distance including turnaround; volume = length x width x depth / 27; divide by 1.2 since quick method reads about 20% high
entries.dim: Quick method about 20% high (factor 1.2); 27 cu ft per CY; maintenance +30 to 40%

entries.desc: Chart assumes 100% efficiency; single-shank rippers on power-shift machines; ripping full time, no dozing. Upper limit of band is ideal only; use lower limit for thick or vertical laminations. Tooth penetration is key regardless of seismic velocity (esp. mudstone, claystone, fine caliche). Production = P x E
entries.use: Estimating ripping output for a 300 hp dozer
entries.how: Check ripability on Fig 2-16 by seismic velocity first, then read max production from Fig 2-17 and multiply by efficiency
entries.dim: Example: 9,000 BCY limestone, 4,000 ft/s, thin laminations: 1,700 BCY/hr x 45/60 = 1,275 BCY/hr; 9,000 / (1,275 x 7) = about 1 dozer (1.0)

entries.desc: Never carry personnel on the drawbar. Never turn around on steep slopes; back up or down. Keep low gear when towing heavy load downhill. Always lower attachments when parked. Only one person on the machine while operating
entries.use: General dozer operation
entries.how: Five rules
entries.wn: See description

entries.desc: 621G: single-powered-axle wheel scraper, needs a push tractor. 613B: air-droppable, chain-elevator self-loader (no pusher; pushing damages its elevator). Bowl: lower cutting edge into ground to load, raise to carry, lower to desired lift thickness to dump/spread. Struck capacity = level with sides; heaped = 1:1 repose slope to sides. Elevating scrapers like the 613 have no struck rating
entries.use: Selecting and understanding a scraper
entries.how: Bowl loads/carries, apron opens for loading and spreading (lower for hauling), ejector stays rear when loading/hauling and moves forward to discharge. Best on medium hauls and ripped material/shot rock
entries.dim: 621G: 15.7 CY struck, 22 CY heaped; 613B: 11 CY heaped; EVW 621G 37.5 tons, 613B 15.6 tons; optimum haul 300-3,000 ft (small/medium), larger scrapers effective to 5,000 ft
entries.wn: Do not push-load the 613B (damages loading elevator)

entries.use: Understanding what makes up scraper cycle time
entries.how: Six operations: loading, haul travel, dumping and spreading, turning at dump site, return travel, turning/positioning to load

entries.n: Scraper loading: push assistance and loading methods
entries.desc: Downhill: each 1% favorable grade equals +20 lb per ton of gross scraper weight of loading force. Straddle: make two parallel cuts leaving a ridge no wider than the distance between scraper wheels, then third cut straddling the ridge. Push-loading techniques: Back-track (impractical to load both directions; inefficient due to backing); Chain (long cut, pusher moves to next scraper in adjacent lane without backtracking); Shuttle (short cuts, load both directions; pusher turns and pushes second scraper opposite direction)
entries.use: Loading a 621G
entries.how: Always load in the direction of haul; do not spin wheels to pull away from pusher; downhill loading gives bigger loads faster; straddle loading saves time every third trip
entries.dim: Downhill: 20 lb per ton per 1% grade
entries.wn: Avoid turning while accelerating from loading

entries.desc: Step 1 service brake, first gear. 2 ejector rear. 3 open apron partway. 4 lower bowl after entering cut; push down differential lock pedal and transmission hold button and proceed in second gear when dozer makes contact; cut as deep as possible while moving at constant speed without lugging; reduce depth if scraper/pusher lugs or wheels slip; use router bits on vertical side of bowl to gauge depth and repeat same depth. 5 regulate apron opening to prevent piling at lip or falling out; keep straight with pusher aligned; do not overload; raise/lower bowl rapidly in loose material like sand. 6 raise bowl slowly when full while closing apron. 7 let pusher help out if needed. After cut release hold/diff lock, accelerate quickly, drive short distance before raising bowl to carry position (spreads spillage and keeps following scraper at speed)
entries.use: Loading a scraper in the cut
entries.how: Downshift to first for loading, ejector to rear, apron partway open, lower bowl to efficient depth; second gear with diff lock/transmission hold when pusher contacts
entries.dim: Push tractor waiting about 45 degrees off the lane to be cut
entries.wn: Overloading lowers efficiency and stresses machine. If tires spin before dozer contacts, stop and let dozer assist

entries.n: Scraper loading by material (loam/clay, sand, rock/shale)
entries.desc: Sand tends to run ahead of blade and apron (worse fine and dry). Steps: enter loading area fast to fill rear of bowl using momentum; shift lower gear once momentum is lost and let pusher assist; pump the bowl (drop as rear wheels roll into the depression of previously pumped area, raise as wheels climb out); drop bowl sharply two or three times at end, close apron, raise bowl and exit. Rock/shale: rip first with depth greater than scraper cut depth; leave a loose layer under tires for traction; soft rock/shale may not need ripping; for stratified rock start edge in dirt and catch planes of lamination; pick up loose rock on level ground or slight incline
entries.use: Adjusting loading to soil
entries.how: Loam/clay cut easily (rip very hard clay first). Sand: enter fast, lower bowl slowly, pump bowl, drop sharply 2-3 times to top out. Rock/shale: rip deeper than scraper cut first
entries.wn: Loading rock and shale is hard on equipment (wear and tear)

entries.use: Limiting loading time
entries.how: Aim for push loading in under 1 minute over about 100 ft; about 85% of capacity reached in first 0.5 min; the next 0.5 min adds only about 12%; longer than 1 minute is not worthwhile
entries.dim: <1 min over 100 ft; 85% load at 0.5 min; +12% for next 0.5 min

entries.n: Borrow pit operation and haul roads
entries.desc: Borrow pit needs highly competent personnel; traffic control minimizes waiting and unnecessary travel; proper drainage and maintenance reduces weather downtime. Well-maintained haul roads allow higher speeds, increase safety, reduce operator fatigue and equipment wear. Use grader or dozer to remove ruts and washboard (see ch. 4). Water distributors reduce dust (less wear, better visibility, fewer accidents); keep roads moist but not wet so they pack hard and smooth
entries.use: Managing borrow pit and haul route
entries.how: Use traffic control in pit; maintain drainage; lay out straight haul routes avoiding adverse grades; keep roads damp with water distributors; grade ruts/washboard

entries.desc: Lugging reduces rpm, which reduces hydraulic pressure and can cause loss of steering control. On downgrades slow down, downshift, use transmission hold, use retarder and service brakes; engine speed must not exceed manufacturer's recommended rpm. Use hold also approaching upgrade or rough underfooting
entries.use: Driving loaded scraper on haul road
entries.how: Use highest safe gear; carry bowl about 18 in off ground to lower center of gravity; downshift instead of lugging; never coast downhill
entries.dim: Bowl carry height about 18 in
entries.wn: Never coast on a downgrade; lugging can cause loss of steering control

entries.desc: Dump: 1 move steadily across spreading area; 2 open apron fully at dump start, ejector forward; 3 straight path; 4 close apron when empty and return ejector to rear; 5 raise bowl slowly to clear obstacles (12 to 18 in) on return. Spread: first load at front of fill; later loads travel over previous fill if lifts shallow; start each dump at end of previous fill; finish one full lane before new lane so rollers can start; return to cut as fast as possible; plan egress away from soft ground. Route scrapers to compact fill by overlapping wheel paths. Fill slope: build outside edges high to keep scraper from sliding off; in rain build up low center for drainage or use grader to cut outside edge down creating a crown. Sand: spread as thin as possible. Wet/sticky: do not spread too thin; keep bowl high enough for material to pass; bring ejector forward about 12 in at a time then back about 6 in to break suction; repeat until empty
entries.use: Placing fill in lifts
entries.how: Lower bowl to lift height, open apron at start of dump area, move ejector forward, steady speed in highest gear allowed; return with bowl at 12-18 in clearance
entries.dim: Bowl clearance 12-18 in on return; ejector forward 12 in / back 6 in for sticky material
entries.wn: Do not force wet or sticky material out too fast: it rolls up in front and can damage the hydraulic system

entries.desc: Example: 621G with 20 LCY of dry loam, 2,050 lb/LCY average = 20.5 tons load. Steps apply to other scrapers using their own tables/charts. Consider scraper weight, load weight, average grade and rolling resistance for both haul and return
entries.use: Steps 1 of scraper production estimate
entries.how: Load weight (tons) = load volume (LCY) x unit weight (lb/LCY) / 2,000. GVW = EVW + load weight
entries.dim: 621G EVW 37.5 tons; 613B EVW 15.6 tons; 20 LCY x 2,050 / 2,000 = 20.5 tons

entries.desc: 40 = lb per ton flexing of driving mechanism; 30 = lb per ton per inch to climb out of rut. Tire penetration may differ haul vs return. Example: haul tire penetration 3 in; return 1 in; RR Haul = (40 + 30x3) x 53.8 tons = 7,540 lb (text also shows 6,994 lb in later example); RR Return = (40 + 30x1) x 37.5 tons = 2,625 lb (2,331 lb in later example)
entries.use: Estimating resistance to travel
entries.how: RR (lb) = (40 + [30 x TP]) x vehicle weight in tons, where TP is tire penetration in inches. Use gross weight for haul, empty weight for return
entries.dim: Table 3-2 resistance values 40 to 400 lb per ton by road condition
entries.wn: The text's rolling-resistance examples are not self-consistent between paragraphs 3-26 and 3-28; use the formula

entries.desc: Adverse (uphill) grades positive; favorable (downhill) negative. 20 = lb per ton per percent of slope. Enter grade as a percent not a decimal. Example: -5% grade, GA haul = 20 x -5 x 58 tons GVW = -5,800 lb; GR return = 20 x 5 x 37.5 tons EVW = +3,750 lb. RPR haul = 6,994 - 5,800 = 1,194 lb; RPR return = 2,331 + 3,750 = 6,082 lb
entries.use: Estimating power needed on grades
entries.how: Grade % = rise/run x 100 (1 ft in 20 ft = +5%). GR or GA = 20 x grade(%) x weight (tons). Rimpull required = RR + GA(-) or GR(+); must be less than available rimpull to avoid tire slip
entries.dim: 20 lb per ton per percent grade; example RPR haul 1,194 lb, return 6,082 lb

entries.n: Scraper travel speed and travel time
entries.desc: 88 converts mph to ft per minute. Use correct distance for each leg (routes not always the same). Example: haul 1,194 lb is below chart lowest scale (2,000 lb) so use bottom line: eighth gear, 31 mph. Return 6,082 lb (interpolate 6,000-8,000): sixth gear, 16 mph. Example with SOP cap 25 mph, 800 ft: haul 0.36 min, return 0.57 min? (text lists 0.57 for 25 mph limited leg and 0.36 for 16 mph leg as printed), total 0.9 minute
entries.use: Finding speed and travel time from rimpull chart
entries.how: Find required rimpull on chart, go right to highest gear that gives it, read down to speed. Travel time (min) = distance (ft) / (88 x mph). Total = haul + return. Cap by unit SOP maximum speed
entries.dim: 88 ft/min per mph; 800 ft haul; 621G 8th gear 31 mph; 6th gear 16 mph; total travel 0.9 min
entries.wn: If computed speed exceeds unit SOP maximum, use the SOP speed to compute time

entries.n: Scraper cycle time and trips per hour
entries.desc: Average dump time for scrapers with heaped capacity under 25 CY: 0.3 min. Turning in cut 0.3 min, on fill 0.21 min. Allow 0.81 min for dumping + turning at dump + turning at load for both 613B and 621G. Load time: 621G with D8 or equivalent pusher 0.85 min; with D7 approaching 1 min. Self-loading 613B 0.9 min in good material (loam, loose clay, sand); longer in tight materials. Example: CT = 0.9 + 0.8 + 1 = 2.71 min (as printed); 50/2.71 = 18.5 trips per hour
entries.use: Computing cycle time and trips
entries.how: CT = travel time + turn-and-dump time + load time. Trips per hour = working minutes per hour / CT. Use 50 min/hr on well-managed job; 45 min/hr in confined area (ditch) or narrow bridge header
entries.dim: dump 0.3 min; turn in cut 0.3; turn on fill 0.21; total 0.81 min; load 0.85 (D8) to ~1.0 (D7), 613B 0.9 min; 50 or 45 working min/hr
entries.wn: Time actual equipment for a few cycles to get special-case values

entries.n: Scraper hourly production and total time
entries.desc: Example 621G in loam: 18.5 trips x 20 LCY = 370 LCY/hr x 0.8 = 296 BCY/hr. 19,440 BCY with three scrapers = 19,440 / (296 x 3) = 22 hours
entries.use: Estimating output, duration and scraper count
entries.how: P (LCY/hr) = trips per hour x load (LCY); BCY/hr = LCY/hr x load factor (Table 1-1/1-2). Time = Q / (P x N). Scrapers needed = Q / (P x H)
entries.dim: 370 LCY/hr = 296 BCY/hr; 22 hours for 19,440 BCY with 3 scrapers

entries.n: Push tractors required per scraper fleet
entries.desc: 1.4 = scraper load time and pusher travel between scrapers; 0.25 = pusher positioning. Example: LT 1 min, PT = 1.65 min; N = 2.71/1.65 = 1.64 scrapers. Nine scrapers need 9/1.64 = 6 push tractors. If one pusher feeds two scrapers, pusher cycle controls: P = 50/1.65 x 20 LCY x 0.8 = 485 BCY/hr (the incorrect assumption of pusher handling both gives 590 BCY/hr). Pusher production = working min per hour / PT x load (LCY)
entries.use: Matching pushers to scrapers
entries.how: Scrapers one pusher supports N = scraper CT / pusher PT. PT = (1.4 x LT) + 0.25. Pusher count = scrapers on job / scrapers one pusher supports. Not needed for 613B
entries.dim: PT = 1.4 x LT + 0.25; 1.64 scrapers per pusher; 485 vs 590 BCY/hr; 6 pushers for 9 scrapers

entries.desc: Blade (moldboard) is hydraulically controlled; ends raise/lower together or independently; positioned perpendicular or parallel to travel, shifted side to side. Forward pitch: less cutting, more dragging, rides over material, less chance of catching solid obstruction. Rear pitch: cuts readily, material tends to boil over itself
entries.use: Deciding what a grader can do
entries.how: Graders grade, shape, slope banks, ditch, mix, spread, sidecast, level, crown and maintain roads and runways; they cannot do dozer work. Keep blade pitch near center; forward pitch for light fast cuts and blending, rear pitch cuts readily but material boils over itself
entries.dim: Works slopes as steep as 3:1; cuts ditches to 3 ft deep

entries.desc: Removing teeth for hard material; unbalanced removal or too few teeth can shear the rest
entries.use: Breaking up hard material or asphalt pavement
entries.how: Scarifier has 11 teeth cutting up to 12 in deep. Remove no more than 5 teeth, center one first then alternate. Pitch rear to lift and tear (use for asphalt)
entries.dim: 11 teeth; up to 12 in depth; remove max 5 teeth
entries.wn: Do not remove more than five teeth or the remaining teeth can shear off

entries.desc: Step 1 set up: moldboard high enough off surface; blade pitched halfway; center shift until left lift cylinder (heel) vertical; rotate moldboard so toe just behind outside edge of right front wheel (about 45 degrees to frame); side shift if needed so edge reaches outside of right front wheel; raise left lift cylinder fully; lean front wheels left (ditching position). Step 2 as right front wheel passes the starting point, lower toe to penetrate 3 to 4 in. Step 3 feather material (raise moldboard in 1/2 to 1 in increments, pausing 2-3 seconds each) and raise toe clear at end of marking cut; continue until rear wheels pass off marking cut. Step 4 straighten front wheels, steer right about 45 degrees to ditch. Step 5 back along outside edge of windrow. Step 6 reposition at start. Step 7 lean front wheels left
entries.use: Starting a V-ditch
entries.how: Make a 3-4 in deep marking cut on the first pass at the outer edge of the bank slope (slope stakes), toe of blade in line with outside edge of lead wheel
entries.dim: Marking cut 3-4 in deep; moldboard angle about 45 degrees; feather 1/2-1 in steps, 2-3 s pauses
entries.wn: Frame should be articulated for steps 4 and 7

entries.desc: Start with toe in line with center of lead wheel. Apply as much downward pressure on blade toe as grader will handle; continue along ditch line to finish point and exit using marking-cut exit procedure. Windrows form between blade heel and left rear wheel; move or level them when ditch is at planned depth or when windrow is higher than the grader's road clearance. This material forms the road shoulder
entries.use: Cutting the ditch to depth
entries.how: Second gear, full throttle; cut as deep as possible without stalling or losing control; each successive cut brought in from bank slope edge so toe aligns with ditch bottom on final cut
entries.dim: Second gear, full throttle

entries.desc: Steps: rotate moldboard to 90 degrees to frame, height about 4 to 6 in; center shift fully right; readjust height to about 2 in; side shift fully right; lean front wheels left; circle moldboard counterclockwise until toe 12-15 in from outside edge of front right wheel. Move forward with toe over center of ditch; skim shoulder; continue until material passes under or is windrowed off heel; position to back up and straddle windrow (right-hand general grade position; avoid backing in wide-side reach). Front wheels vertical before backing. Back to start, lean wheels left, lower toe and heel to surface, raise heel 2-3 in with toe just touching so ditch material passes under and off the heel; stay centered on the windrow; skim shoulder with toe and spread windrow to form road surface; feather end of pass; straighten wheels and raise both lift cylinders; reposition at finishing end to cut opposite V-ditch. Excess ditch material: blade into windrow and move to fill elsewhere
entries.use: Finishing ditch shoulder and spreading windrow on road
entries.how: Rotate moldboard 90 degrees; blade 4-6 in above surface then adjust to 2 in; toe 12-15 in from outside edge of right front wheel; skim shoulder, do not cut it. Then back and spread windrow with heel raised 2-3 in
entries.dim: Blade 4-6 in then 2 in; toe 12-15 in from right front wheel; heel raised 2-3 in
entries.wn: Do not adjust moldboard height, especially the left lift cylinder, during step 1. Avoid backing in wide-side reach

entries.n: Grader bank slope, ditch cleaning, shoulder and crown
entries.use: Finishing a road cut
entries.how: Slope bank to prevent sloughing and erosion; cast outer-slope material into ditch bottom, then clean ditch with ditching blade position (casts onto shoulder), move windrow onto road while finishing shoulder, then spread all material to crown or cross slope

entries.n: Leveling and maintaining road surfaces with grader
entries.desc: Steps: 1 moldboard toe on right at 50-60 degrees to frame; 2 pitch halfway; 3 center shift until left lift cylinder vertical; 4 lean front wheels left; 5 lower moldboard until toe and heel slightly touch; 6 as moldboard crosses start line, press heel and toe to penetrate about 1/2 in; 7 straight course; 8 feather end; 9 stop and straighten wheels; 10 raise both lift cylinders; 11 straddle windrow and back to start (do not drive on windrow); 12 stop just outside project boundary. Repeat until leveled
entries.use: Routine earth/gravel road and runway maintenance
entries.how: Blade across surface; in dry weather move eroded edge material toward center; best after rain; moisten with water truck if dry. Penetrate about 1/2 in
entries.dim: Blade angle 50-60 degrees; penetration 1/2 in
entries.wn: Disturbing dry surfaces risks losing binder to traffic or wind

entries.n: Smoothing pitted surfaces and correcting corrugation
entries.desc: Smoothing pits needs binder present and appropriate moisture; spread cut material over smooth base. Rolling after shaping gives better, longer-lasting results than traffic compaction
entries.use: Repairing worn earth/gravel roads
entries.how: Reshape after rain or moisten with water distributor. For washboard: avoid deep cuts (blade chatter); scarify severe corrugation; cut across corrugations to bottom, change blade angle, spread windrows evenly; roll afterward
entries.wn: Deep cuts on washboard cause chatter that emphasizes corrugations

entries.n: Scarifying roads or areas with grader
entries.desc: Steps: 1 position outside area; 2 moldboard high enough for free movement; 3 moldboard perpendicular, 12 in off surface; 4 center shift lift cylinders centered; 5 pitch halfway; 6 front wheels vertical; 7 move forward; 8 lower scarifier at starting point; 9 scarify full length min depth about 6 in; 10 raise scarifier at finish; 11 exit and stop; 12 rotate moldboard to 50 degrees and center shift to straighten heel cylinder; 13 return to start for second pass
entries.use: Breaking up a road surface
entries.how: Moldboard perpendicular and 12 in above surface; scarify entire length to minimum depth of about 6 in; second pass with moldboard at 50 degrees
entries.dim: Min depth about 6 in; moldboard 12 in above surface; 50 degrees on return

entries.use: Clearing snow from pavement or runway
entries.how: Works like a snowplow; raise blade 0.5 to 1 in above uneven pavement or portable runway surface
entries.dim: Blade raised 0.5 to 1 in
