entries.wn: Improper adjustment can damage the grader and gouge the surface

entries.n: Grader asphalt mixing (mixed-in-place and imported aggregate)
entries.desc: Large areas: stake edges of each windrow's spread width; use blue-top hubs for final pavement elevation, typically 20 ft apart in a grid; remove blue tops before rolling. One pass usually flattens the windrow, then spread to each side in increments for uniform thickness and proper lateral/longitudinal slopes
entries.use: Mixing asphalt road surfaces with grader
entries.how: In-place: spread asphalt on road before or after scarifying, then mix with scarifier/windrowing. Imported aggregate: shape and cure base, windrow aggregate (blade to dry if too wet), flatten windrow, apply asphalt, mix by moving windrow side to side (tandem graders OK; continue mixing until dry if rained on), re-windrow before spreading
entries.dim: Blue tops 20 ft apart in grid
entries.wn: A skilled grader operator is essential when spreading large areas. See ch. 12 for asphalt

entries.n: Grader spreading, sidecasting and planing techniques
entries.desc: Spreading: grader has less power/traction than dozer but moves load faster; blade lower and more concave so more rolling action; leveling big windrows may need two or more side cuts. Sidecasting: sharper angle increases speed of side drift so material not carried forward and deeper cuts possible; decrease angle for spreading windrows, increase for hard cuts and ditching. 0 degrees is blade straight across. Planing: on next pass pick up material left at trailing edge; on final pass lift trailing edge so surplus passes under to avoid ridge. Avoid windrows in front of rear wheels (traction and control)
entries.use: Distributing material
entries.how: Spread windrows with side cuts; sidecast with blade angle (25-30 degrees for most road shaping); planing: keep material in front of blade, fill hollows, lighter last pass with trailing edge lifted
entries.dim: Blade angle 25-30 degrees for most road shaping; 0 degrees = perpendicular

entries.n: Grader operating practices (speed, turning, passes, tires, wet ground, haul roads)
entries.desc: Avoid turns on newly laid bituminous road or runway. Number of passes determines efficiency (if job takes four passes, extra passes cost time and money). Overinflated tires reduce contact and traction; unequal rear tire pressures cause slip and bucking; correct pressure is in operator manual. In mud, grader is still best machine (casts surface mud aside). Haul road maintenance: use enough graders to finish one side with a single pass each in tandem, leaving the other side open to traffic
entries.use: Efficient grader operation
entries.how: Full throttle in each gear; drop a gear rather than reduce throttle; back up instead of turning for passes under 1,000 ft; minimize passes; keep tire pressures equal; use tandem graders on haul roads
entries.dim: Back up rather than turn for passes < 1,000 ft

entries.desc: Overlap Lo generally 0.6 m (2.0 ft) so tires stay out of windrow on return pass. Job efficiency 0.70 to 0.85 typical; 0.90 used for long road-maintenance passes (fewer turnabouts). Effective blade length shortens as moldboard angle increases (Table 4-5). Example: Army 120M, 3.66 m (12 ft) moldboard, road maintenance at 13 km/h (8 mph), 30 degrees carry angle: Le = 3.17 m (10.4 ft); A = 13 x (3.17 - 0.6) x 1000 x 0.90 = about 30,069 m2/hr = 3.07 hectares/hr (as printed); English 8 x (10.4 - 2.0) x 5280 x 0.90 = 319,069 ft2/hr (as printed) = 7.33 acres/hr
entries.use: Estimating grader area per hour
entries.how: A = S x (Le - Lo) x 5280 x E (English: ft2/hr, S in mph, Le/Lo in ft). Metric: A = S x (Le - Lo) x 1000 x E (m2/hr, S in km/hr). Divide by 43,560 for acres or 10,000 for hectares
entries.dim: Overlap 0.6 m (2.0 ft); efficiency 0.70-0.85, 0.90 for long passes; 43,560 sq ft = 1 acre; 10,000 m2 = 1 ha; example 7.33 acres/hr
entries.wn: Printed example arithmetic differs slightly from exact results (30,069 m2 is about 3.01 ha); follow the formula

entries.desc: Engage clutch gently (esp. uphill or leaving a ditch); reduce speed before turns or braking; extra care on hillsides (holes, ditches); never use graders to pull stumps or heavy loads; keep blade angled well under machine when not in use; one person only (if buddy seat, max two)
entries.use: Grader operation
entries.how: Red flag or flashing light on staff at least 6 ft above left rear wheel when on road; no riders on blade or rear; low gear on steep slopes
entries.dim: Flag/light at least 6 ft above left rear wheel; max 1 person (2 with buddy seat)
entries.wn: See description

entries.n: Wheel loader description, buckets and attachments
entries.desc: Diesel, rubber-tired, power-shift transmission with torque converter, hydraulic system assists steering. Bucket types: general-purpose (one-piece) or multipurpose (two-piece hinged jaw). Bolt-on replaceable teeth for medium materials. Other attachments: hooks (sling loads), snowplow. Forklift has two movable tines. Uses: loading trucks, stockpiling, digging basements or gun emplacements, backfilling ditches, moving construction materials; rock-type-tread tires for quarries; stripping overburden, charging hoppers, moving forms and large pipe, towing small trailers
entries.use: Choosing loader attachment and use
entries.how: Loader digs best at or above wheel level; buckets 2.5 to 5 CY; multipurpose (clam) bucket can dozer and grab and handles sticky material better; forklift attachment for material handling
entries.dim: Bucket 2.5-5 cubic yards (924H loader)
entries.wn: Loaders excavate soft to medium-hard material well; production drops in medium to hard material

entries.use: Deciding if a loader is the right machine
entries.how: Loader must be able to dump over side of the truck bed; best on flat smooth surface with room to maneuver; use other equipment for poor footing or tight space

entries.use: Filling a loader bucket
entries.how: Bucket parallel to ground to skim and clean the travel surface; at contact go slow and increase power while raising bucket; crowd, roll back to prevent spill; keep bucket up while backing

entries.desc: Steps 1-8 as above; repeat until truck loaded. Best production by keeping angle of turn and travel distance to a minimum
entries.use: Loading trucks from bank/stockpile with a single loader
entries.how: Bucket 1-2 in off ground in low gear to the pile, curl back and raise slightly until full without spinning tires; back away; approach truck at 90 degrees with bucket high enough to clear; do not touch truck with front tires; roll bucket forward slowly; back away lowering boom and leveling
entries.dim: Bucket 1-2 in off ground; approach truck at 90 degrees
entries.wn: Do not touch haul unit with front tires or let bucket hit it

entries.desc: Steps: 1 center front of bucket on middle of the load, open at about 5 ft; 2 forward, 2/3 of open bucket into material; 3 close; 4 load 10-14 in above ground; 5 maneuver to location; 6 open fully; 7 raise to clear dumped material, ensure bucket empty; 8 close; 9 travel position 10-14 in; 10 repeat
entries.use: Handling rocks, timbers, loose stockpiles
entries.how: Open bucket about 5 ft from the load; two-thirds of the opened bucket penetrates the material; close; carry load 10-14 in above ground; to place: open fully, raise to clear previous material, close, return to travel position 10-14 in
entries.dim: Open at ~5 ft; 2/3 penetration; carry 10-14 in
entries.wn: Keep bucket low for balance and visibility; at low speed on rough terrain or terrain that can cause sliding with full bucket, loss of control can cause serious injury or death

entries.n: Excavate basement or gun emplacement with a loader
entries.desc: Steps: 1 choose ramp start point; 2 bucket pitched forward; 3 move forward, penetrate by lowering lift lever (highest gear w/o excessive spin); 4 retract bucket fully; 5 raise lift until bucket clears surroundings; 6 dump on stockpile or haul unit; 7 repeat
entries.use: Digging a pit/emplacement if material is not too hard
entries.how: Build a ramp into the excavation first so the loader works above wheel level and has an exit; bucket pitched forward, high gear without excess spin, use lift lever to regulate cut depth
entries.wn: Difficult material: multipurpose bucket handles sticky material; use clam-type digging; for medium to hard material break or loosen first

entries.n: Backfilling a trench with a loader
entries.desc: Steps: 1 align at 45 degrees with 1/3 of bucket on stockpile (not for large stockpiles: work from edges); 2 lower bucket just off natural ground (open to clam position if multipurpose); 3 forward in highest gear without excess spin; 4 cut and spread along trench; 5 raise bucket 10-14 in before reversing; 6 reverse back to stockpile; 7 repeat
entries.use: Pushing pile into trench
entries.how: Bucket at ground level pushes earth into trench; bucket should be as wide or wider than wheels. Approach pile at 45 degrees so one-third of bucket contacts the pile; raise bucket 10-14 in before reversing
entries.dim: 45 degrees; 1/3 bucket contact; raise 10-14 in
entries.wn: Narrow bucket lets wheels ride up the stockpile and needs more passes

entries.n: Constructing a stockpile with a loader
entries.desc: Steps 1-7: front tires to bank; raise bucket all the way; tilt to dump; tilt back; back away, lower bucket to 10-14 in; back to start; repeat
entries.use: Stockpiling excavated material
entries.how: Drive until front tires contact the bank, raise bucket fully, tilt slowly to dump, tilt back, back away and lower to 10-14 in
entries.dim: Carry height 10-14 in

entries.desc: Fill factor from Table 5-1; cycle time from Table 5-2 (load, maneuver with four reversals, dump; minimum travel). For extra travel add round-trip travel time (e.g., charging aggregate bins): for under 100 ft a wheel loader loaded travels about 80% of max speed in low gear and returns empty at about 60% of max speed in second gear; slightly higher for longer distances. Efficiency factors to judge: work-site dimensions, depth of cut, movement required; surface and weather; equipment condition. Example: 2.5 CY loader in moist loam, average conditions: net 263 LCY/hr; loam at 2,200 lb/LCY = 1.1 tons/LCY, so 263 x 1.1 = 289 tons/hr. For total time and number of loaders use the dozer formulas (time = Q/(P x N); machines = Q/(P x T))
entries.use: Estimating loader output
entries.how: Max production (LCY/hr) = heaped bucket capacity x fill factor x 60 / cycle time (min). Net = max x efficiency (50 min/hr is a good average = 0.83). Tons/hr = net LCY/hr x (lb per LCY / 2,000)
entries.dim: Loader fill factors and cycle times Tables 5-1, 5-2; 263 LCY/hr = 289 tons/hr (example)

entries.desc: Do not extend any body part between cab and lift arms. Block the bucket when working on machine. Use caution removing/replacing lock rings. Do not work between wheels and frame with engine running. Caution at trench edges and under overhangs from digging into banks/stockpiles. Ground bucket and set parking brake before leaving
entries.use: Loader operation
entries.how: Easy to overturn; travel with bucket at or below axle height; no personnel in bucket
entries.dim: Bucket at or below axle height
entries.wn: See description

entries.desc: Extend boom when lifting; retract boom against frame when transporting; use oscillation to pick up loads at an angle. Lower tire pressure in sand or mud (check manual). On ramps/grades carry load on the upgrade end; going downgrade back down with load on upgrade end; tines tipped back. In water: disconnect fan, use four-wheel drive; check manual for servicing after salt water
entries.use: Handling crates and palletized loads
entries.how: Approach square to load and use side shift to align forks; transport with mast tilted back and load raised only 4 to 6 in; change speed gradually; four-wheel steering for normal handling, two-wheel for high-speed runs
entries.dim: Carry height 4 to 6 in
entries.wn: Sudden starts and stops shift the load

entries.n: Forklift safety, capacity and hoisting personnel
entries.desc: Army: capacity and gross weight must be stenciled on the machine in view of operator (Marine Corps does not require). Capacity rating is based on the load center of the fork carriage, not always 24 in from heel of forks. Personnel hoisting only with supervisor approval, skilled personnel only, special personnel pallets with guardrails on all four sides, personnel face away from the mast with hands clear of hoisting mechanism
entries.use: Forklift operation
entries.how: Face direction of travel, load must not block vision, fit steel overhead guards, never exceed load capacity or counterweight, forks flat on ground when parked
entries.dim: Load center not always 24 in
entries.wn: Do not counterweight to increase capacity

entries.desc: Truck cranes (20- and 25-ton): hook block, 0.75 CY clamshell, diesel pile driver 7,000 ft-lb/blow, or dragline; fully extend outriggers and put jacks on base plates so crane is off tires; towing eyes designed to withstand twice dead-weight pull of truck. Crawler (40-ton): hook block, 2 CY clamshell, diesel pile driver 24,000 ft-lb/blow, dragline; normally used for quarry operations; haul by transport truck (slow, track wear). Rough-terrain (22-ton): hook block, 0.75 CY clamshell, 7,000 ft-lb/blow pile driver, dragline; four-wheel drive, two-wheel, four-wheel and crab steering; dual cabs; up to 55 mph on highway; front axle must oscillate; use outriggers to lift and level, place safety wedges on front axle to prevent oscillation; outriggers independent; traverse slopes up to 48 percent if firm and dry
entries.use: Choosing a crane mount
entries.how: Truck: mobile but needs firm level ground and outriggers. Crawler: stable, low ground pressure, best for long-duration jobs. Rough-terrain: larger tires, higher clearance, 55 mph highway
entries.dim: Truck crane 20/25 ton; crawler 40 ton; rough-terrain 22 ton; crawler out-of-level 3 degrees = 30% capacity loss; RT slope 48%; 55 mph highway
entries.eq: 20/25-ton truck crane; 40-ton crawler crane; 22-ton rough-terrain crane
entries.wn: Crawler: 3 degrees out of level can cut hoisting capacity by 30 percent. Do not tow attachment trailer cross-country with RT crane

entries.desc: Do not hoist over front. Ensure the load chart capacity matches the quadrant (side, rear, front)
entries.use: Setting up a truck crane
entries.how: Level the crane, use outriggers, hoist heavy loads over the rear, check base plates, transmission in neutral when operating superstructure
entries.wn: Do not hoist loads over the front

entries.n: Crawler crane on soft ground and in water
entries.desc: Crawler cranes can be secured on barges to operate over water; designed for level ground; can climb slight grades when not lifting
entries.use: Using a crawler crane on soft ground or shallow water
entries.how: Use timber mats on soft or unstable ground; in water, water must not reach the revolving superstructure; check depth and bottom; clean and service after saltwater

entries.desc: Counterweight cast steel at rear of superstructure. Drums: drag/closing-line drums for dragline/clamshell; with hook block called rear or main hoist drum. Lagging diameter affects line speed (smaller lagging gives slower line speed and greater power). Lattice boom: four main chords with lacing, base and upper section joined with bolted butt-plate or pin-and-clevis; offset jib gives greater load radius than same length boom; cranes without jib-boom anchor plates can only use intermediate sections; extend gantry or A-frame when lengthening boom. Hydraulic telescopic boom: two or more telescoping boxes extended with hydraulic cylinders
entries.use: Understanding crane components
entries.how: Counterweight prevents tipping; two independent cable drums plus a third boom-hoist drum on lattice-boom cranes; lattice boom lengthened with intermediate sections or jib; hydraulic telescopic boom only with specific attachments

entries.desc: Boom length, operating radius/boom angle, mount, outriggers, counterweight, hook-block size, hoist position, maintenance. Radius = horizontal distance from axis of rotation to vertical line down from boom-tip sheave outer edge; swing centrifugal force and wind increase effective radius. Tipping limits per PCSA: crawler 75% of max load; truck/rough-terrain 85% on tires or outriggers. Capacity at short radii limited by structure or hydraulics. Do not place tracks/outriggers over underground utilities, recompacted trench backfill, or near excavation edges. Do not add counterweight or anchor to deadman. Hook block and slings count as part of load (tables are gross capacity). Quadrants: crawler over side, drive end, idler end; mobile cranes defined by lines to outriggers; use minimum capacity over the swing path. Maintenance checks: wire rope, hook block, boom structure, engine, clutches and brakes
entries.use: Checking if a crane can lift
entries.how: Capacity falls with longer boom, greater radius, jib use, soft/unlevel ground; assume solid level ground in load chart. Know load weight before lifting
entries.dim: Crawler tipping 75% of max; truck/RT 85%
entries.wn: Adding counterweight or tie-downs risks structural damage

entries.use: Planning a lift
entries.how: Step 1 required clearance (load height, hoisting height, hook-block height, about 2 ft boom-tip to hook-block sheave clearance, sling height); step 2 total weight (load + hook block + slings + stowed jib); step 3 working radius (max over the swing, add effects of swing and wind); step 4 check chart (boom length, angle, tip height, total weight)
entries.dim: Boom-tip sheave to hook-block sheave clearance normally 2 ft

entries.n: Crane operation tips and wind limit
entries.desc: Ensure supporting ground strength; use adequate hoist-line length; organize work for min travel; use power-down device for precision; no excess counterweight or tie-downs. Wind estimated from Table 7-1 (e.g., 25-31 mph strong breeze: large branches move)
entries.use: Routine crane operations
entries.how: Stop work if wind exceeds 30 mph. Level machine, use tag lines, avoid swinging over workers, shortest swing
entries.dim: Cease work if wind > 30 mph
entries.wn: Wind can cause overturning near max capacity

entries.desc: Pile driver parts: adapter plates, leads, catwalk, hammer, pile cap; leads cannot connect to a jib. Drop hammer best for vertical piles (angled piles lose force to friction with leads); heavier hammer with smaller drop preferred. Planning: about 30 min to drive a 12-in diameter pile to 20 ft depth (includes setting pile in leads); only a field test gives true rate. Tips: position crane for minimum travel between piles, parallel to long axis of pile group; place piles near driving locations; high infrequent blows cause pile failure
entries.use: Driving piles with a crane
entries.how: Diesel hammer: self-contained, do not use for pulling piles; may not fire in soft soil, switch to drop hammer. Drop hammer: hammer at least pile weight, ideally twice; shallow continuous blows; 15 ft drop timber, 8 ft concrete; 4-8 blows/min
entries.dim: Drop hammer >= pile weight (ideal 2x); 4-8 blows per min; drop 15 ft timber / 8 ft concrete; 12 in pile x 20 ft = ~30 min
entries.eq: Crane with diesel or drop hammer
entries.tm: About 30 minutes per 12-in pile to 20 ft
entries.wn: Do not use diesel hammer to pull piles

entries.desc: Bucket two hinged scoops; cannot be operated from a jib; needs second hoist line and a tag line with spring winder (prevents twisting; independent of operator). Bucket controlled by holding, closing and tag lines; boom length limits height, drum rope capacity limits depth. Aggregate bins/hoppers: position crane to avoid raising/lowering boom between stockpile and bin. Tips: level ground; digging and dumping at same radius; correct bucket size (large buckets increase cycle time); remove bucket teeth in soft materials
entries.use: Vertical shafts, footings, charging bins
entries.how: Clamshell digs at, above and below ground in loose to medium-stiff soil; crowding only by bucket weight. Keep outside edge of cut lower than center to avoid V-shaped hole; use spotter in deep cuts

entries.desc: Example: 450 LCY aggregate to haul units, 0.75 CY bucket, 40 s cycle, 50-min working hour: working time 50 x 60 = 3,000 s/hr; P = 0.75 x 3,000 / 40 = about 56 LCY/hr; time = 450 / 56 = 8 hours. Loading trucks takes longer than dumping on a spoil pile
entries.use: Estimating clamshell output
entries.how: P (LCY/hr) = bucket size x working seconds per hour / cycle time (sec). Best method is timing the machine on site
entries.dim: 0.75 CY bucket, 40 s cycle = 56 LCY/hr; 450 LCY = 8 hr

entries.desc: Components: drag bucket, fairlead; ropes for drag, hoist and dump. Army usually uses Type II (medium duty) Class S (solid plate) buckets; Type I light, Type III heavy; Class P perforated. Use for trenching, stripping overburden, cleaning and digging roadside ditches, sloping embankments. Do not use with hydraulic cranes
entries.use: Trenching, stripping, ditching, sloping, dredging
entries.how: Long reach for digging and dumping, soft to medium-hard material, good in mud; no positive digging force (only bucket weight), so bucket bounces on hard material
entries.dim: Boom angle not less than 35 degrees from horizontal; throw increases radius up to one-half boom height
entries.wn: Boom angle under 35 degrees increases tipping risk (especially wet sticky material cast to spoil bank). Only experienced operators should do extended casting (cables/boom damage, tipping)

entries.n: Dragline trench, embankment, dredging and loading haul units
entries.desc: Truck bed ideally directly under boom tip with long axes parallel; more commonly at right angle to the boom. Spotting haul units below the dragline in excavation reduces hoist time. Dragline dumps less accurately than rigid excavators
entries.use: Dragline job techniques
entries.how: Trench: in-line approach (carriage on centerline), excavate front while moving backward, start at lower end for drainage. Embankment: parallel approach from top, work bottom to top. Wet digging: keep material as dry as possible, drain, place on levee/spoil bank. Trucks: dry ground, minimal grade, minimize swing
entries.wn: Heavy wet loads are hard to lift

entries.desc: Table 7-2 assumes optimum cutting depth, 90 degree swing, maximum efficiency. Depth ratio = actual depth / optimum depth x 100 (percent of optimum); interpolate Table 7-3 if needed. Example: 3/4 CY crawler dragline, 9 ft cut; optimum depth 7.4 ft so 122% of optimum; efficiency 45/60 = 0.75. Operation tips: position to avoid unnecessary casting/hoisting (bucket can be cast beyond boom length); heavy timber mats on soft ground, kept level and clean
entries.use: Estimating dragline output (BCY/hr)
entries.how: Ideal production (Table 7-2, by bucket size and material) x depth-of-cut/swing-angle factor (Table 7-3) x efficiency (draglines seldom exceed a 45-min working hour = 0.75). Then convert with soil factor if needed
entries.dim: Efficiency 45/60 = 0.75; table values in Tables 7-2, 7-3
entries.wn: Do not guide the dragline bucket by swinging superstructure while digging (side stress can collapse the boom); raise bucket clear of ground before swinging

entries.n: Crane operator responsibilities and hand signals
entries.desc: Operators must understand limits and read load charts, report defects. Signal person must be reliable, qualified, use uniform signals, stay clearly visible. See Figure 7-11 for crane hand signals; see chapter 13 for more crane safety
entries.use: Crane operations
entries.how: Only trained operators; operator can stop operations and refuse loads until safety is assured. Use one qualified signal person when point of operation is not fully visible

entries.desc: Hazards: cables breaking, clutch/brake slipping (radius increases), obstruction of boom/load path, uneven ground, unknown load weight, bent or dented boom chords. Operator errors: dropping/slipping load, no outriggers, no mousing/safety hooks, unfamiliar equipment, not using load chart for different boom lengths, towing with hoist cable (boom is for vertical loads only). Nobody climbs on/off a running crane; only operators (and occasionally examiners, supervisors, trainees, repairers) on the crane. Water: load from under water weighs more (displaced water, water in waterlogged structures); avoid hoisting unknown weights from water
entries.use: Avoiding common crane hazards
entries.how: Boom contact with high-voltage lines is the most hazardous aspect. Know the load weight, use outriggers, use load charts per boom length, use mousing or safety hooks; do not tow with crane hoist cable
entries.wn: Boom contacting high-voltage wires is the most hazardous crane operation hazard

entries.desc: Lower loads slowly, not faster than hoisting speed for the same load; typical hoisting speed of 30-ton motor-operated crane is about 18 ft per minute with rated load; stopping at these speeds over short distance can double stress on slings and crane. Warn workers (bell or siren) if loads must swing over people. Avoid dual lifts unless necessary and under competent supervision (load shift can overload one crane then the other). After repair/alteration affecting capacity or stability, a qualified person must determine and give written safe working load. Test brakes before each new shift and after rain/wet linings; verify heavy-load brakes by stopping hoist a few inches above ground. Equip with fire extinguishers. Never pull pipes or objects out of the ground with a crane
entries.use: Lifting heavy loads
entries.how: Lift slightly first to check sling stress and balance; for near-capacity loads have hoist line vertical and move crane rather than lower boom; never lower hoist line and boom at same time; test brakes each shift
entries.dim: Hoist speed 30-ton crane about 18 ft/min
entries.wn: Dual lifts are extremely dangerous

entries.desc: Never repair diesel or air equipment while operating or under pressure. Inspect air hoses frequently and replace defective hoses. Keep away from power lines (machine does not have to touch to be energized). When not in use hold hammer with cleat or timber at bottom of leads; secure driving heads when moving cribbing. Keep drums and brakes in best condition and sheltered; keep leads well-greased
entries.use: Pile driving operations
entries.how: Level platform and outriggers; safety lashings on all hose connections; tag lines on piles and hammers; closed shackle for steel piles; only pile crew in work area; never stand under unblocked suspended hammer
entries.wn: Never place head or body under suspended hammers not dogged or blocked in the leads

entries.n: Hydraulic excavator and backhoe loader (BHL) description
entries.desc: BHL: pneumatic-tired 2WD/4WD front-end loader and backhoe, diesel, ROPS/FOPS cab, automatic or semi-automatic transmission. Operates in ambient temperatures 25 to 95 degrees F and altitudes up to 10,000 ft. Uses: trench excavation, truck loading, ditch cleaning, concrete breaking, pipe installation, small emplacements. Two excavation types: trenching (linear) and basement (area). Judge length and depth of cut to get a full bucket each pass
entries.use: Selecting a hoe
entries.how: Hydraulic hoe digs below the surface it sits on; stick and bucket cylinders push bucket into material. BHL is good in confined spaces; BHL needs stabilizers; level machine with outriggers
entries.dim: BHL operating range 25-95 degrees F, up to 10,000 ft

entries.desc: Parallel: load haul units or stockpile along trench side for backfill. Perpendicular: more and shorter moves but better bucket digging angles and shorter hoisting distance for upper lifts. Drainage ditches: start at lower end and work upgrade
entries.use: Digging trenches
entries.how: Parallel method: BHL over the trench aligned with centerline, back away as digging continues. Perpendicular method: dig in two or more lifts, first 35-45% of trench depth with boom high, then move forward about half the machine length, lower boom, finish
entries.dim: First lift 35-45% of depth; advance about half machine length
entries.wn: Survey for underground utilities and obstacles first (populated areas)

entries.use: Area excavation
entries.how: First cut is a trench with vertical outside walls; dig all exterior wall faces vertical to reduce hand cleanup; plan the digging sequence so the machine can exit; dig service-pipe trenches last working from basement outward
entries.wn: Use small machines for confined work: close quarters is inefficient

entries.use: Digging hardpan or rock layers
entries.how: Blasting or ripping may be more efficient than the bucket on hardpan and rock; once trench opened, break ledge rock by placing bucket under layers and pulling up; remove top layers first, one or two layers at a time

entries.n: Hoe digging technique and cycle time
entries.desc: Level the hoe, loader bucket flat on ground with front wheels off the surface, gearshift and range-shift to neutral, lower outriggers, level and lift rear wheels slightly, minimal bucket-arm swing. Hoe buckets are rated at an assumed 1:1 repose. Average conditions: cut depth 40-60% of max, swing 30-60 degrees: cycle 14 s for buckets under 1 CY; 15 s for 1 to under 2.5 CY. Greater depth or wider swing increases cycle
entries.use: Digging with bucket and dipper (stick) cylinders
entries.how: Optimum depth of cut is 30 to 60% of max digging depth. Bucket cylinder: pressure on boom to force teeth in, roll bucket to full, raise smoothly to clear spoil/haul unit. Dipper: lower bucket, roll teeth flat on ground, move toward machine until half full with stick cylinder, raise stick and roll until full
entries.dim: Optimum depth 30-60% of max; cycle 14 s (<1 CY) / 15 s (1 to <2.5 CY)

entries.n: Loader bucket (BHL front bucket) digging, leveling, backfilling
entries.desc: If spoil pile is higher than 2 ft or wet, take it in two passes (upper half then cleanup). After the last pass dump remaining bucket load into trench
entries.use: Using the BHL front loader
entries.how: Digging: use bucket cylinders to break ground; flat ramp, drive forward when hauling out (can use steeper ramp forward than in reverse). Level: fill holes, loosen highs, spread by holding bucket near grade tipped forward, finish with bucket dragging in reverse. Backfill: 45 degrees to trench, bucket about 2 in above ground used like dozer blade, keep level (no curl)
entries.dim: Bucket 2 in above ground; 45 degrees to trench; spoil >2 ft = 2 passes

entries.desc: Plan and lay out area; keep working area smooth; raise bucket moving toward truck, lower moving away; shake bucket only when needed to free dirt
entries.use: Efficient hoe truck loading
entries.how: Truck on pit floor saves about 12% of cycle; spot so hoe turns no more than 90 degrees (V-positioning, ch 10); dump over rear of bed not cab
entries.dim: Saves about 12% of cycle; swing max 90 degrees

entries.desc: Average cycle about 15 s (8 to 12 ft cut depth, 30-60 degree swing). Lifting pipe sections: consult specification sheet; position as close to load as possible. Rated for loads up to 15,000 lb at 15 ft swing radius from the side
entries.use: Pipeline trenches, ditches, footings, hasty fortifications
entries.how: Max digging depth about 20 ft, dump height about 22 ft, buckets 1 to 2.5 CY, 3 mph max on site in high range, transport for long moves. Lift capacity is 65 to 70% greater over the front than over the side
entries.dim: Depth ~20 ft; dump height ~22 ft; 1-2.5 CY bucket; 3 mph; 15,000 lb at 15 ft; front lift +65-70%

entries.desc: Factors: width, depth, material, working radius, dumping height. Example: 0.25 CY hoe in hard clay, depth about 50% of max, swing under 60 degrees, 50 min/hr: fill factor 85% (80-90, use average 85); cycle 14 s; ideal = 3,600/14 x 0.25 x 0.85 = 55 LCY/hr; x 50/60 = 45 LCY/hr; x 0.7 (clay loose to bank) = 32 BCY/hr
entries.use: Estimating hoe output (BCY/hr)
entries.how: Ideal LCY/hr = 3,600 s/hr / cycle time (s) x bucket size (CY) x fill factor. Then x efficiency (min/60), then x soil factor to BCY
entries.dim: Example 55 LCY/hr ideal; 45 LCY/hr net; 32 BCY/hr

entries.n: Sizing compressors and number of units
entries.desc: Capacity is free air compressed to specified pressure per minute at standard conditions (14.7 psi absolute at 60 degrees F), in cfm. At higher altitude same gauge pressure gives less air volume (Table 9-1). Example: 1,400 cfm needed = two 750-cfm units. Locate compressors centrally if possible, level and close to air-operated devices
entries.use: Determining compressor capacity for pneumatic tools
entries.how: Add up cfm of tools actually running at the same time (e.g., of ten rock drills only 5-6 run at once), then add 10% for leaks. Altitude reduces output. Add a standby unit if needed
entries.dim: Add 10% for leaks; 1,400 cfm = two 750-cfm units; examples of compressors 260 cfm trailer, 750 cfm wheel-mounted

entries.desc: Protect from excessive dust
entries.use: Daily compressor operation
entries.how: Upwind of work area; drain cocks open after each 8 hours; side panels closed in cold weather; block wheels and set brake; drain receiver when done
entries.dim: Drain condensation every 8 hours

entries.desc: Pneumatic tools use either a reciprocating-percussion motor (free-floating piston, hammering action) or rotary-vane motor (rotation). Pneumatic tools with nonsparking attachments can be used around petroleum or explosives
entries.use: Applications for compressed air
entries.how: Asphalt plants: dryer-burner fuel atomization, cleanup, paving-site tools, dedrumming. Concrete: batch-plant hopper vibrators to prevent bridging, pin drivers and joint-cleaning at paving site

entries.n: Pneumatic tool lubrication and air pressure check
entries.desc: Sluggish or surging tool suggests too little or too much pressure. If compressor gauge consistently reads below 70 psi the unit is overloaded. Heavy vibrating tools cause fatigue; choose physically fit operators
entries.use: Checking tool condition
entries.how: Hold paper at exhaust port: thin oil film = OK; drops or foam = over-lubricated; no oil = check lubricator. Tool pressure must stay between 70 and 100 psi
entries.dim: Never operate tools below 70 psi or above 100 psi at the tool
entries.wn: Excess or insufficient pressure damages tools

entries.desc: Distribution rules: size pipe so pressure drop is not over 10% of initial pressure; outlets close to point of use (short hose); condensate drains along mains. Hose 200 ft long and 3/4 in is the maximum for efficient handheld tool use. Air-line hose 3/4 in ID for hand tools (2 in for crawler-mounted drills), 50 ft lengths with quick fittings; leader hoses (neoprene) 12 or 25 ft long, 1/2 or 3/4 in diameter, between oiler and tool. Air-line oiler installed directly in front of tool; arrow points in airflow direction
entries.use: Distributing compressed air on a job
entries.how: Manifold is large-diameter pipe (Army: 6-in invasion piping) fed by compressors through flexible hoses with one-way check valves; all compressors at 100 psi discharge; do not mix rotary and reciprocating types
entries.dim: Pressure drop max 10%; 6-in manifold pipe; hose max 200 ft x 3/4 in; 50-ft hose lengths
entries.wn: Different compressor types on one manifold can overload one while the other idles

entries.desc: Output: non-reinforced concrete 6 to 8 in deep with moil point: 12 sq ft/hr (narrow cut) to 50 sq ft/hr (large areas); reinforced concrete may drop to 50 sq ft over an 8-hr shift; 15 sq ft/hr of 6-in asphalt with chisel; tamper max lift 8 in; sheeting driver drives wood or up to 2-in thick steel sheeting. Operation: hold down firmly, light pressure; operate breakers in tandem; take small bites 4 to 8 in behind working face; free stuck moil with second breaker or another point
entries.use: Breaking concrete, asphalt, brick; driving sheeting; tamping
entries.how: Weighs 87.5 lb; 65 cfm at 80-100 psi; 3/4-in hose. Attachments: moil point (20 in, 1 1/4 in hex; breaks concrete/stone), chisel point (3-in edge; macadam, frozen/hard earth, marking cut lines in concrete), tamper (5-7 in pad), sheeting driver
entries.dim: Weight 87.5 lb; 65 cfm; 80-100 psi; 12-50 sq ft/hr concrete
entries.tm: 12-50 sq ft per hour (6-8 in concrete)
entries.wn: Double hearing protection and goggles; correct shank size; sharp points; tight nuts, check hose connections; clear work area. Do not drill with moil point or break concrete with chisel point. Turn off after moil breaks through (bounce breaks retainer bolt)

entries.desc: About 12 CY of tough clay loosened per 10-hr shift with spade (1.2 CY/hr). Guide the tool, never ride/lean; not for prying. Do not let tool penetrate beyond the wider part of the clay spade (dirt wears retainer)
entries.use: Spading clay, hardpan, frozen ground; opening drums
entries.how: 25.2 lb; 35 cfm at 80-90 psi; 1/2-in hose. Spade 5 1/2 x 8 in; pick 3 x 8 in; moil 15 in x 1 in; drum-ripping tool Type I (cut drum heads) and Type II (split lengthwise, opens 20 to 30 55-gal drums per hour)
entries.dim: 25.2 lb; 35 cfm; 12 CY tough clay per 10-hr shift; 20-30 drums/hr

entries.desc: Issued with 1/2 in and 3/4 in nail sets and rivet buster. Keep nail set pressed against work; countersinking breaks the retainer spring
entries.use: Driving heavy nails/spikes/drift pins
entries.how: 24 lb; 30 cfm at 90 psi; 1/2-in hose; 250 60-penny (80d in Table 9-2) nails per hour after hand-started; start nails by hand and strike squarely
entries.dim: 24 lb; 30 cfm; 90 psi; 250 nails/hr
entries.wn: Text gives 60-penny in para 9-36 and 80d in Table 9-2

entries.desc: Use correct blade/disc for material; keep material free of nails; never force the saw; if used upside down, keep exhaust port from clogging; keep hands away; air off when idle
entries.use: Cutting lumber (and with abrasive discs, masonry/steel)
entries.how: 32.5 lb; 75 cfm at 80-100 psi; 1/2-in hose; 2,400 rpm governed; 12-in combination blade (wood only); cuts 4x4 in 30 s; max depth at 90 degrees 4 3/8 in; bevel to 45 degrees; depth adjust 2 3/8 to 6 in
entries.dim: 32.5 lb; 75 cfm; 2,400 rpm; 4x4 in 30 seconds

entries.desc: Standard chain 3/4-in pitch, 3/8-in cut; 76-in chain for the 24-in saw (100 in and 124 in for 36- and 48-in saws; 48-in saw needs two operators). Let saw cut at natural speed, do not twist
entries.use: Cutting trees or timber up to 24 in
entries.how: 45 lb; 90 cfm at 80-100 psi; hose 5/8 in (25 ft or less), 3/4 in (26-100 ft), 1 in (over 100 ft). Cuts 12-in hardwood log in 50 s. Chain tension: 1/2 in slack pulled up at center
entries.dim: 45 lb; 90 cfm; 12 in hardwood in 50 s; 1/2 in chain slack
entries.wn: Never operate without the guard bar. Chain too loose can jump the guide; too tight bends and damages sprocket

entries.desc: Reversible. Start slowly until screw set; hold firmly and be ready for torque if bit sticks; keep auger aligned when withdrawing. Use the auger ejector for stuck bits, not a hammer
entries.use: Drilling bolt holes in timber (trestle bridges)
entries.how: 27.5 lb; 60 cfm at 80-100 psi; 3/4-in hose; about 800 rpm at the chuck; auger bits 1 or 3 ft long in 7/16, 3/4, 1 and 2 in diameters; 125 holes 36 in deep per hour with 2-in bit
entries.dim: 27.5 lb; 60 cfm; 800 rpm; 125 holes/hr

entries.desc: Keep inlet strainer clean and pump out of mud; keep exhaust outlet above water; use water-pump grease only; drain when not in use. Silt can stick impeller; water in exhaust port ruins grease seals
entries.use: Dewatering
entries.how: 50 lb; 100 cfm at 80-90 psi; 3/4-in hose; 175 GPM at 25 ft head, 150 GPM at 150 ft head; Class 1 sewage/sludge, Class 2 petroleum; can run submerged with exhaust line; 3-in exhaust
entries.dim: 50 lb; 100 cfm; 175 GPM at 25 ft; 150 GPM at 150 ft

entries.desc: Not reversible. Use cutting oil, center punch, no worn chucks, goggles, clamp work. Excess pressure stalls drill and damages gears
entries.use: Drilling, reaming, tapping metal
entries.how: 27.5 lb; 27 cfm at 90-100 psi; 1/2-in hose; 425 rpm; drills to 1 1/4 in, reams/taps to 1 in; Morse No. 3 taper bits; 30 one-inch holes per hour in steel plate with 1/4-in lead holes
entries.dim: 27.5 lb; 27 cfm; 425 rpm; 30 holes/hr

entries.desc: Do not use bent drill steels. Hold in line with hole, do not feed too fast, firm footing, do not bypass handgrip switch, no loose or torn clothing, check bit flutes
entries.use: Drilling holes in rock
entries.how: 57 lb; 95 cfm at 80-100 psi; 3/4-in hose; rods 2, 4, 6, 8 ft; bits 1 5/8, 1 3/4, 1 7/8, 2 in; designed for vertical drilling (secure for horizontal holes); drills to 10 ft. Output for 1 3/4 in hole per hour: soft rock 15-20 ft, medium 10-15 ft, hard 5-10 ft
entries.dim: 57 lb; 95 cfm; soft 15-20 ft, medium 10-15 ft, hard 5-10 ft (1 3/4 in hole)

entries.n: Compressed air and pneumatic tool safety
entries.desc: Compressors: cool clean intake, no flammables against discharge pipe, working gauges, test safety valves before start, do not exceed rated speed, proper high-flash-point oil in small amounts, clean with soapy water (never benzene or kerosene: vapor explodes when compressed), turn off and lock out and relieve pressure before repair. Tools: protective gear, firm grip, release throttle if out of control, disconnect and bleed line before repairs, secure hose end when blowing out, lay tools down safely, do not lay hose across walkways or between legs, remove leaking hoses. Rock drills: no loose clothing; paving breakers: goggles, roughen slick surfaces with sledgehammer
entries.use: Working with compressed air
entries.how: Compressed air at close range can cause eye damage, ruptured eardrums, skin blisters or death. Shut compressor down if discharge air from any stage exceeds 400 degrees F. Never kink a hose to stop flow; never point hose at people
entries.dim: Shut down above 400 degrees F
entries.wn: Never use compressed air to clean clothing or blow dust off the body

entries.desc: Unit weights range from 1,700 lb/LCY (dry clay) to 3,500 lb/LCY (trap rock). Use spotting markers at hoppers, grizzly ramps, stockpiles and excavators. With excavators place trucks close to bank and within working radius of bucket; with loader form a V between truck and loader to cut loader cycle
entries.use: Hauling earth, rock, aggregate
entries.how: 5-ton FMTV and 20-ton dump trucks rated in tons. Never exceed gravimetric capacity with the volumetric load. Load close to rated capacity but reduce load for poor roads or steep grades. Overload raises fuel use, cuts tire life, increases breakdowns
entries.dim: 1,700 to 3,500 lb per LCY
entries.wn: Overloading causes mechanical failure

entries.n: Dump truck hauling, dumping and body care
entries.desc: Keep bodies clean (rust, dirt, dried concrete, bitumen reduce production). Clean at end of day; spray beds with water before wet concrete and clean ASAP after; coat body walls with diesel fuel or oil to keep plant-mix asphalt from sticking
entries.use: Moving, unloading and cleaning trucks
entries.how: Highest safe speed in proper gear; consistent speed; separate haul roads to and from dump; one-way traffic; use spotters to dump; move forward slowly to spread; set alternate dump spots
entries.wn: Avoid speeding: unsafe and strains equipment

entries.desc: Truck cycle = loaded trip + dump + return + reload. Loader cycle = time to load truck plus wait for truck spotting. Standby trucks: smaller fleets with one loader up to 1 standby per 4 active (1:4); larger jobs need fewer; standby trucks can do lower-priority work. Example: 5-ton FMTV (3 LCY per load), 2 CY loader, haul-unit cycle 20 min excluding loading, loader 0.5 min per bucket. 1 bucket per truck (2 LCY): loading 0.5 min, truck cycle 20.5, trucks = 1 + 20.5/0.5 = 42, production = 2 LCY x 60/0.5 = 240 LCY/hr. 2 buckets per truck: loading 1 min, cycle 21, trucks = 1 + 21/1 = 22, production = 3 LCY x 60/1 = 180 LCY/hr (as printed)
entries.use: Matching trucks to a loader
entries.how: Trucks = 1 + (truck cycle time / loader cycle time). The 1 is a safety factor so one truck is always waiting. Loader controls production
entries.dim: Standby ratio up to 1:4; example 42 trucks = 240 LCY/hr; 22 trucks = 180 LCY/hr
entries.wn: Number of bucket loads per truck must be an integer

entries.desc: Side load where rear loading is restricted (protect trailer bed). Consult unit SOP or technical manual for securing procedures
entries.use: Hauling cranes, dozers, long items
entries.how: Semi-truck required. Load near rated capacity, spotter on trailer to keep machine centered. Use low banks or earth ramps for rear loading. Dozer on ramps: slow, blade raised; at balance point slow/stop, lower blade to let tracks settle on bed. Block, chock and chain; centering marks show load weight positions; unload slowly using ramps
entries.wn: Unload heavy equipment slowly to avoid damage

entries.desc: Water content ratio = weight of water / weight of soil solids. Compacting above or below OMC is very difficult. Each soil has its own OMC for a given compactive effort
entries.use: Deciding if soil needs water added or removed before compaction
entries.how: Compact within about +/- 2 percent of OMC. OMC about 12-25% for fine-grained soils and 7-12% for well-graded granular soils. Finding true OMC needs a lab test
entries.dim: OMC fine-grained 12-25%; well-graded granular 7-12%; acceptable range +/-2% of OMC

entries.n: Calculate water to add per station
entries.desc: Example: 6-in compacted lifts, target dry unit weight 120 lb/cu ft, OMC 12%, borrow 5%, roadway 40 ft wide: volume = 40 x 100 x 0.5 = 2,000 cu ft; gallons = 120 x 0.07 x 2,000 / 8.33 = 2,017 gal per station per lift. Total = gal per lift x number of lifts x stations. Application rate (gal/SY) = gal per station / [(100 ft x width ft) / 9 sq ft per sq yd]
entries.use: Adding water to borrow/fill to reach OMC
entries.how: Gallons per station = dry unit weight (lb/cu ft) x [(target moisture % - existing moisture %)/100] x volume per station (cu ft) / 8.33 lb per gal. Station = 100 ft. Negative answer means water must be removed. Adjust target to OMC + 2 percent (varies with temperature, wind, soil)
entries.dim: 8.33 lb per gallon; 100 ft per station; 2,017 gal per station (example); desert: add up to 6% above OMC

entries.n: Adding water: water distributor, ponding, weather
entries.desc: Weather: cold, rainy, cloudy, calm conditions hold or add water; hot, dry, sunny, windy conditions dry it. Deserts: engineers may add up to 6% above OMC
entries.use: Applying water to soil
entries.how: Typical truck water distributor: 1,000 gal, rear 12-ft folding spray bar adjustable 4 to 24 ft in 1-ft steps; operator sets speed (odometer in fpm), pressure and bar length for required gal/sq yd. Ponding is slow and hard to control (several days). Granular soils: add water at site and mix thoroughly
entries.dim: 1,000 gal tank; spray bar 4-24 ft

entries.desc: Stabilizer mixer: rear-mounted removable-tine rotating tiller with hood forming mixing chamber; handles material under 4 in diameter; tines penetrate up to 12 in; spray bar models add water or stabilizer; works in situ or fill material; open trailing hood edge for drying
entries.use: Drying wet soil and mixing additives
entries.how: Aerate by scarifying with grader teeth or stabilizer mixer or disking; grader blade furrows expose more surface; add stabilizer lime or fly ash for fine-grained soils; high water table needs subsurface drainage. Mix water or drying agent thoroughly and evenly with grader (move material side to side of lane), stabilizer mixer or farm disk
entries.dim: Stabilizer mixer: material < 4 in, tines to 12 in

entries.desc: Compactive effort methods: static weight, kneading, impact, vibration. Compaction differs from consolidation (static, gradual). Handheld vibratory tampers for confined areas, large rollers for extensive work. See Tables 11-1 to 11-3 for roller capabilities, soil classes and requirements
entries.use: Choosing compaction equipment
entries.how: Compaction (dynamic load) raises bearing capacity, cuts settlement and permeability. Choose by soil type, density wanted, lift thickness, job size, equipment available. Tamping-foot for fine-grained cohesive; large steel-drum for gravel/cobble; vibratory for well-graded or gap-graded
entries.eq: Tamping-foot, pneumatic-tired, dual-drum vibratory, smooth-drum vibratory rollers; jay tamper
entries.wn: Use a test strip to see which compactor is more efficient

entries.desc: Loosen any material compacted by wheels during spreading or wetting before compaction. Best for plastic materials and moisture above acceptable range
entries.use: Compacting fine-grained soils
entries.how: Square/angular tapered feet penetrate on first pass and compact bottom to top; walks out when density reached. Max lift 8 in compacted. Not effective for the top 2-3 in or for cohesionless granular material; follow with pneumatic or smooth-drum to finish/seal. Speed up to 8 mph. Aerates wet soil while compacting
entries.dim: Max lift 8 in compacted; top 2-3 in not compacted; up to 8 mph

entries.desc: Sidewalls carry about 10% of load, air about 90%. Example: 50 psi tire with 5,000 lb wheel load has 100 sq in contact area; 10,000 lb gives 200 sq in. Effective contact area = 0.9 x wheel load / tire pressure. Tests used 6-in compacted layers with wheel loads 10,000/20,000/40,000 lb at 65 psi; at shallow depths no extra density from heavier loads, but heavier loads help thicker lifts. Two-row rollers cover in one pass; heavy single-row rollers need two passes; overlap each pass for depth coverage
entries.use: Compacting granular soils and sealing lifts
entries.how: Good for most granular materials; unsuitable for fine-grained clays. Army: towed 13-wheel (about 210 lb contact pressure per inch of rolling width) and self-propelled 9-wheel variable pressure model. Contact pressure set mainly by tire pressure; wheel load drives compaction depth/thicker lifts
entries.dim: 13-wheel towed ~210 lb per inch of width; sidewalls 10% / air 90%
entries.wn: Not for fine-grained clays

entries.n: Dual-drum and smooth-drum vibratory rollers, jay tamper
entries.desc: Vibration amplitude controls depth of penetration; frequency controls number of blows over time
entries.use: Finishing base courses, asphalt, sands and gravels
entries.how: Dual-drum: sand to cobble, preferred for asphalt paving, shallow layers under 4 in, low unit pressure, compacts top-down; avoid excessive crushing of base. Smooth-drum vibratory: best for noncohesive nonplastic sands/gravels; max loose lift 9 in. Jay tamper: small hand-operated gasoline vibratory tamper for trenches around pipes and confined spaces
entries.dim: Dual-drum lifts < 4 in; smooth-drum max loose lift 9 in
entries.eq: Dual-drum vibratory roller; smooth-drum vibratory roller; jay tamper

entries.desc: Information gathered: most effective equipment, optimum lift depth, optimum speed, number of passes, ballast, vibration frequency
entries.use: Determining best roller and procedure
entries.how: Place a test strip next to the site: 6-in (uncompacted) lift, run each machine a set length for typically three passes, density test to pick best roller; then more strips for optimum lift thickness, passes, speed, ballast, vibration/resonant frequency
entries.dim: 6-in uncompacted lift; typically 3 passes

entries.desc: Example: tamping-foot, 5 passes at 4, 4, 5, 8, 9 mph = average 6 mph; width 5 ft, lift 6 in, E 0.83: 16.3 x 5 x 6 x 6 x 0.83 / 5 = 487 CCY/hr. Compactors for 1,500 LCY/hr blasted rock (0.87 loose to compacted): 1,500 x 0.87 / 487 = 2.7, so 3 compactors
entries.use: Estimating CCY/hr and number of compactors
entries.how: Production (CCY/hr) = 16.3 x W x S x L x E / N. W = compacted width per pass (ft), S = speed (mph; use average of all passes), L = compacted lift thickness (in), E = efficiency, N = passes. Day efficiency 50 min/hr; night 45 min/hr. Compactors needed = delivery rate (LCY/hr) x conversion factor / compactor production
entries.dim: 16.3 constant; 487 CCY/hr example; 3 compactors example; Table 11-4 speeds

entries.desc: Subgrade is in-place soil on which road/airfield/heliport is built, to depth that affects structural design or climate effect; up to 10 ft for heavy pavements. Highly organic subgrade may need removal and select replacement
entries.use: Preparing the in-place soil under roads and airfields
entries.how: Heavy pneumatic-tired rollers compact to depths up to 18 in. Scarify top 6 in to adjust moisture, then recompact (scarify and compact in place, SCIP): tamping-foot roller is ideal. Seal top 1-2 in with pneumatic or smooth-drum roller, esp. if rain expected. If a lift was sealed, scarify the top 1-2 in before placing next lift. Sand subgrade: vibratory compactor
entries.dim: Pneumatic roller to 18 in; scarify 6 in; seal 1-2 in
entries.eq: Pneumatic roller; tamping-foot roller; smooth-drum roller

entries.n: Placing, spreading and compacting fill; base course
entries.desc: Spread from farthest point to nearest: hauling units compact subgrade, reveal weak spots, do not hinder spreading. Nearest to farthest: haul equipment travels over new fill and compacts it, reducing compaction effort. Base course thickness depends on subgrade strength
entries.use: Building subbase and base courses
entries.how: Uncompacted lift is 1.5 to 2 times final compacted lift (9-12 in loose for 6 in compacted). Place by scraper or dump truck, spread by dozer or grader. Check moisture first and add water or dry as needed. Base course: well-graded granular, liquid limit < 25%, plastic limit < 6%; compact with smooth-drum vibratory (or dual-drum)
entries.dim: Loose lift 1.5-2x compacted; 9-12 in loose = 6 in compacted; base LL<25, PL<6
entries.eq: Scraper; dump truck; dozer; grader; smooth-drum roller

entries.desc: Gradual turns avoid lift damage and towed roller tongue damage by towing tractor tracks
entries.use: Roller technique
entries.how: Against structures: jay or pneumatic backfill tampers; if rolling, parallel to structure or place fill sloped to axle height. Aerating: highest practical speed. Overlap each pass at least 1 ft. Turn gradually at ends
entries.dim: Overlap at least 1 ft
entries.wn: Take care to avoid damaging existing structure

entries.desc: Chapter covers seal coats, sprayed bituminous with cover aggregate, asphalt emulsions/slurry seals. See TM 3-34.63 for paving and surfacing
entries.use: Choosing a road surface treatment
entries.how: Single: sprayed bitumen then one-stone-thick aggregate cover (wearing surface + waterproofing; minimal equipment, materials, time). Multiple: repeat for denser, stronger layer. Stage construction: add treatments or thicker pavement later as time and materials permit

entries.use: Cleaning base course before asphalt
entries.how: Brooms remove dust and dirt so asphalt bonds to base course/old pavement. Alternatively wet the base and recompact. Before use inspect bristles and broom drives

entries.desc: Maintain heater and pump; calibrate pump tachometer, measuring stick, thermometers, bitumeter; keep spray bars and nozzles clean at correct height
entries.use: Heating and spraying bitumen
entries.how: Army distributor: truck-mounted 1,500-gal insulated tank with low-pressure heating system, hydraulic pump at rear, adjustable spray bar. Two diesel burners fire into two U-shaped fire tubes at the bottom of the tank. Heat only in a well-ventilated area with truck level and fully stopped. See Table 12-1 for spraying temperatures
entries.dim: 1,500-gal tank; keep at least 3 in of asphalt over fire tubes
entries.wn: Exercise extreme caution heating asphalt: possible fires and explosions. Maintain at least 3 in of asphalt cover over fire tubes to prevent overheating

entries.n: Distributor application rate and spray bar setup
entries.desc: Spray bar full-circulating or non-circulating; nozzles same size, clear, bar at correct height or streaking occurs. 4-in nozzle spacing: triple overlap (find height by opening every third nozzle and raising bar until single-layer coverage); double overlap: open every other nozzle. 6-in spacing: only double overlap (triple needs height that wind distorts). End nozzles at 60 degrees are not recommended (thick streak): use a curtain or special end nozzle with all nozzles at the same angle
entries.use: Setting gallons per sq yd
entries.how: Application rate is set by spray bar length (8-24 ft), bitumen pump output (GPM on tachometer) and truck speed (fpm on bitumeter). Look up setting in Table 12-2. 1/8-in nozzles suit most work; 3/16-in nozzles also available
entries.dim: Spray bar 8-24 ft; nozzles 1/8 or 3/16 in; nozzle spacing 4 or 6 in

entries.desc: Keep the bitumeter wheel clean; asphalt buildup causes errors
entries.use: Calibrating distributor speed readout
entries.how: Mark 500-1,000 ft straight level; drive at constant speed with stopwatch; compute fpm and compare to bitumeter; repeat at several speeds bracketing spray speed; tabulate or plot errors
entries.dim: 500 to 1,000 ft test distance

entries.desc: Spread aggregate immediately after asphalt application, before it cools
entries.use: Applying cover aggregate to fresh asphalt
entries.how: Towed spreader with 2.5 CY hopper; push it with dump truck for surface treatments so truck and spreader ride on fresh aggregate; rate (lb/sq yd) set by gate; width 4 to 8 ft in 1-ft steps with blocking plates in hopper
entries.dim: Hopper 2.5 CY; width 4-8 ft

entries.desc: Rollers must start, stop and reverse smoothly
entries.use: Compacting asphalt and surface treatments
entries.how: Rollers need water sprinkling to keep drums/tires wet; drive wheel toward the spreader/paver (otherwise hot mix is pushed into a mound that leaves an unfixable bump). Dual-drum vibratory 7-14 tons for surface treatments after second aggregate layer, moderate amplitude. Pneumatic-tired roller preferred for bituminous surface treatments
entries.dim: Dual-drum vibratory 7-14 tons
entries.wn: Too heavy a roller or too high amplitude damages aggregate

entries.n: In-place mixing of asphalt (grader and stabilizer mixer)
entries.use: Mixing asphalt with aggregate on the road
entries.how: Grader: spread aggregate, apply liquid asphalt with distributor, blade fully forward angled to sidecast the windrow; typically five or six passes after each asphalt application. Stabilizer mixer is faster with better control of asphalt-to-aggregate ratio: loosen in-place material, blend aggregates, distributor feeds mixer pump via flexible metal hose joined with a safety chain, asphalt sprayed from bar under hood while tines rotate
entries.dim: 5 or 6 grader passes per asphalt application
entries.wn: Connect distributor and mixer hose with a safety chain to prevent hose damage

entries.n: Asphalt melter, oil heater, asphalt kettle
entries.use: Handling drummed asphalt and small patching
entries.how: Melter: cut one end off 55-gal drum, place upside down in dedrumming tunnel; hot-oil coils melt asphalt; used with an oil heater (diesel burner, pump circulates hot oil, automatic safety shutdown). Kettle: 165-gal trailer-mounted heater/tank with distillate burner and 2-cylinder gasoline engine pump, handheld spray for patching. Use rough-terrain forklift for asphalt drums and mineral filler; loader for aggregate stockpiles
entries.dim: 55-gal drums; 165-gal kettle
entries.eq: Asphalt melter; oil heater; asphalt kettle; forklift; loader

entries.desc: Post safe load capacities and safe operating speeds (if no governor) at operator position on equipment. Mount ROPS when available; do not modify it. Supervisors may allow exceptions for emergencies, some training, maintenance. Construction equipment other than dump trucks is designed for the operator only. Operators must be tested and licensed (AR 600-55; USMC TM 11275-15/4); apprentices only under direct supervision of a licensed operator. Inspect before use; tag unsafe equipment 'Out of Service, Do Not Use'; check backup alarms and lights. Commander must issue new warnings when hazards are not documented. Reference EM 385-1-1
entries.use: All equipment operations
entries.how: Inspect equipment; qualified, authorized operators only; seat belts; barriers under hoisting loaders; safe speeds; shut down unattended equipment; full stop and park brake before mounting/dismounting; max 10 consecutive hours operation before 8-hour rest; one person on equipment; engine off when refueling
entries.dim: 10 hours max operation then 8-hour rest
entries.wn: Horseplay and practical jokes create hazards

entries.desc: Never remove or disable guards; if temporarily removed, power off first and replace promptly. Equipment must have working warning devices (backup alarms, turn signals). Provide warning device or signal person where moving equipment endangers others; wear reflective orange vest if possible
entries.use: Servicing equipment
entries.how: Lock out controls; position equipment away from project; crib or block suspended items; lower blades, bowls, hooks, buckets and forks to the ground or blocking
entries.wn: Do not work under or between unblocked items

entries.n: Wire rope inspection and removal criteria
entries.desc: Safe load for a single line = (breaking strength / safety factor) x 0.80 (80% fitting efficiency). Table 13-1 breaking strengths of 6x19 wire rope; 13-2 manila and sisal; 13-3 safety factors. New rope under favorable conditions; as rope ages reduce safe load values to one-half
entries.use: Checking rope before hoisting
entries.how: Remove from hoisting service if kinked or has multiple broken wires in any strand: 3 broken wires in one strand of 6x7; 6 in 6x19; 8 in 8x19; 9 in 6x37. Mark defective rope unsuitable and dispose. Wear leather gloves
entries.dim: Broken-wire limits: 6x7 = 3; 6x19 = 6; 8x19 = 8; 6x37 = 9; fitting efficiency 80%
entries.wn: Perform periodic inspections; use within manufacturer safe limits

entries.n: Slings, wire-rope clips, hooks and shackles
entries.desc: Inspect daily; make eye splices with proper thimbles; do not over-torque clips; end-to-end connections add two clips and torque all clips, reverse U-bolts at center. See Table 13-4. Replace bent, twisted or worn fittings. Never clamp the dead end to the live end of wedge socket rope
entries.use: Rigging safely
entries.how: Only qualified rigging personnel attach slings. U-bolt on the dead (short) end; clips minimum 3; spacing 6x rope diameter; tighten after first load and often. Close hooks for human loads or loads over workers. Wedge socket: dead end extends 6-9 rope diameters, clamp to extra short piece of rope
entries.dim: Min 3 clips; spacing = 6 x rope diameter; wedge socket tail 6-9 diameters
entries.eq: Wire rope clips; thimbles; shackles; hooks
entries.wn: Do not use open hooks where tension can be relieved (e.g., lowering in confined space)

entries.n: Equipment loading, transporting, night operations and excavation safety
entries.desc: Excavation exceptions: solid rock, hard shale, hardpan, cemented sand and gravel or similar. Shoring effective to bottom; base design on calculated pressures; extra shoring next to backfilled excavations or when traffic/machinery vibration
entries.use: Moving equipment and digging
entries.how: Truck operator leaves cab when loading by overhead device. Chock and tie down loads; keep load within sides. Oversize: daylight travel, flags/lights, lead and/or follow vehicle. Night: headlights/taillights, illuminated work areas, reflective vests. Excavations over 4 ft deep must be shored, braced or sloped
entries.dim: Shore/brace/slope when deeper than 4 ft

entries.desc: Protect: evacuate, follow MSDS, PPE, extinguish ignition sources, power off if fire risk, ventilate, shower/change clothes after HW contamination. Stop flow: shut valves, turn drums upright. Report to superior, sound alarm, have someone call installation fire department; report any non-petroleum hazardous material spill (any quantity) to unit environmental compliance officer or installation environmental office immediately. Clean: scoop contaminated material into container; mark 'Hazardous Waste, Contaminated Dirt' if spill was on concrete/asphalt cleaned with dirt; check with supply sergeant or DRMS for disposal. Replace: NCOIC accounts for tools/supplies, orders consumables, inventories spill kit before resealing drums. Preoperations checklist: coordinate with staffs, review OPORD/SOP for environmental requirements, land-use permits and range clearances, risk assessment, recon of environmental areas, rehearsals, hazmat/POL labeled with MSDS, trained spill team and spill kits, review prior AARs
entries.use: Planning and responding to fuel/hazmat spills
entries.how: A spill is any petroleum release over 5 gallons, or any amount of hazardous waste (local rules may be stricter). Protect yourself, stop the flow, contain (absorbent, dams; keep out of drains/waterways), report, clean up, replace spill kit
entries.dim: Spill threshold: > 5 gallons petroleum or any hazardous waste
entries.wn: Prevent spills from entering storm or sewer drains or waterways

entries.desc: 120M: minimum shoulder reach 6 ft beyond wheels, lift to min 16 in above ground. MK30 dump truck: 20,000 lb self-recovery winch; 60% gradient; 30% side slope at 15 mph; 40% side slope at 5 mph; 300 mile on-road range; up to 12 passengers with troop seat kit. 260 CFM compressor also powers bridging operations and bulk fuel handling
entries.use: Identifying USMC equipment
entries.how: MCT medium crawler tractor (land clearing, 3-shank ripper, rear winch); D6K dozer with 6-way angle blade; 621G scraper 15.7-22 CY, C-5 transportable; 120M grader 12-ft blade, 6-wheel drive, joystick control; 644 TRAM loader; all-terrain crane 80,000 lb max load with 40-ton slings; BHL 420D/420E over 20 mph, CH-53 transportable; HYEX; 260 CFM compressor at 100 psi; MK29/MK30 7-ton dump truck; vibratory roller compactor
entries.dim: 621G 15.7-22 CY; 120M 12-ft blade; all-terrain crane 80,000 lb; BHL > 20 mph; MK30 60% grade, 30% side slope at 15 mph, 40% at 5 mph, 300 mi; 260 cfm at 100 psi
entries.eq: MCT; D6K; 621G; 120M; 644 TRAM; ATC; BHL 420D/E; HYEX; MK29/MK30; vibratory compactor

entries.n: Water-cement ratio rules for strength and watertightness
entries.desc: Strength is controlled mainly by the ratio of water to cement; durability decreases as W/C rises
entries.use: Selecting mixing water for any concrete job
entries.how: Use as little water as still gives a workable mix: less water gives stronger, more durable, more watertight concrete; too much water makes weak, porous concrete. About 2 1/2 gal of water per sack of cement is needed for hydration. Economical mixes use 4 gal minimum to 7 gal maximum per sack. For watertightness, Corps of Engineers limits: 5.5 gal/sack (W/C 0.48) for fresh-water exposure and 5 gal/sack (W/C 0.44) for saltwater exposure
entries.dim: Hydration water about 2 1/2 gal per sack; economical range 4 to 7 gal per sack; max 5.5 gal/sack (W/C 0.48) fresh water; max 5 gal/sack (W/C 0.44) saltwater; 1 sack = 94 lb = 1 cu ft
entries.eq: Clean water; cement; measuring container for gallons
entries.tm: Hydration is a chemical reaction, not drying; concrete hardens even underwater. Design strength (Type I) reached in 28 days
entries.wn: Too much water (high W/C) reduces strength, durability, and watertightness. Durability should be a strong consideration for structures expected to last longer than 5 years

entries.n: Handling plastic concrete to prevent segregation
entries.desc: Nonsegregation and uniformity rules for plastic concrete
entries.use: Transporting and dropping fresh concrete
entries.how: Keep plastic concrete homogeneous. Do not let it free-fall more than 3 to 5 ft and do not transport it long distances without agitation. Proportion and mix every batch exactly the same for uniformity
entries.dim: Maximum free fall 3 to 5 ft
entries.wn: Segregation weakens the placed mass

entries.desc: Cement type selection by exposure and speed needed
entries.use: Picking the right cement for the job
entries.how: Type I: general purpose (pavements, sidewalks, buildings, bridges, tanks, culverts, masonry units); reaches design strength in 28 days. Type II: moderate sulfate resistance, lower and slower heat; design strength in 45 days. Type III: high early strength, usually design strength in 7 days or less; permits fast form removal and shortens cold-weather protection. Type IV: low heat of hydration for very large structures such as gravity dams; design strength in 90 days. Type V: severe sulfate exposure; design strength in 60 days. IA, IIA, IIIA are air-entraining versions of I, II, III (good for sidewalks, freeze-thaw and deicer scaling)
entries.dim: Type I 28 days; Type II 45 days; Type III 7 days or less; Type IV 90 days; Type V 60 days. Cement is ground to pass No. 200 sieve; sack = 94 lb. Clinkers fused at 2,600 to 3,000 F
entries.tm: Design-strength ages: I 28 d, II 45 d, III <=7 d, IV 90 d, V 60 d
entries.wn: Use Type III cautiously in structures with minimum dimension of 2 1/2 ft or more; high heat of hydration can cause shrinkage cracking. Check local availability of cement types

entries.desc: Cement storage procedure
entries.use: Keeping cement dry in the field
entries.how: Store sacked cement in an airtight warehouse or shed. With no shed, stack sacks on raised wooden platforms, close together (reduces air circulation) and away from exterior walls; cover with tarpaulins so rain cannot reach cement or platforms. Cement must be free-flowing and lump-free when used. Warehouse pack (slightly hardened from tight/high stacking) is cured by rolling sacks on the floor. Hard lumps mean partial hydration; test the cement and do not use it where strength is critical. Store bulk cement in weatherproof bins
entries.dim: Standard sack 94 lb
entries.eq: Raised wooden platforms, tarpaulins, weatherproof bins
entries.tm: Retains quality indefinitely if kept dry
entries.wn: Do not use partially hydrated (hard-lump) cement where strength is critical

entries.desc: Water impurity limits and test method
entries.use: Deciding whether a water source can be used
entries.how: Water must be clean, free of oil, acid, alkali, organic matter. Potable water is usually suitable. Water of unknown quality is acceptable if cylinders made with it have 7- and 28-day strengths of at least 90 percent of control cylinders made with potable water. Algae water is unsuitable. Seawater (up to 35,000 ppm salt) is ok for unreinforced concrete; reduce W/C to offset strength loss; it can corrode reinforcing steel unless cover is 4 in. or more, concrete is watertight, and enough air is entrained
entries.dim: Cylinders >= 90% of control at 7 and 28 days; carbonate/bicarbonate test if >1,000 ppm; NaCl up to 20,000 ppm tolerable (dry service); chloride >550 ppm bad with aluminum embedments; Ca/Mg bicarbonates to 400 ppm ok; Mg sulfate/chloride to 40,000 ppm ok; iron salts to 40,000 ppm ok; acids (HCl, H2SO4) to 10,000 ppm ok; Mn/Sn/Zn/Cu/Pb and Na iodate/phosphate/arsenate/borate salts to 500 ppm ok; sodium sulfide 100 ppm harmful; NaOH over 0.5% by weight of cement reduces strength; KOH to 1.2% little effect; test if pH over 11; industrial waste <4,000 ppm total solids reduces strength no more than 10%; sugar 0.03-0.15% of cement retards, about 0.20% accelerates, about 0.25% cuts strength (test if >500 ppm); silt up to 2,000 ppm ok; mineral oil >2% of cement can cut strength >20%
entries.wn: Unusual water must be tested; impurities can cause efflorescence and rebar corrosion

entries.n: Aggregate quality and fineness modulus of sand
entries.desc: Sand suitability test. Worked example: cumulative % 4.0+17.0+30.0+55.0+82.0+92.0 = 280.0, FM = 2.80
entries.use: Checking sand and gravel before mixing
entries.how: Aggregate (60 to 80 percent of concrete volume) must be clean, hard, strong, durable and free of clay, silt, mica, humus, salts. Washing removes many contaminants. To find fineness modulus: quarter a sand sample of at least 500 g; sieve through Nos. 4, 8, 16, 30, 50, 100; record weight retained on each; add cumulative percent retained and divide by 100. Sand with FM 2.3 to 3.1 is suitable. FM from one source should not vary more than 0.20 between samples
entries.dim: FM 2.3-2.59 fine; 2.6-2.89 medium; 2.9-3.10 coarse. Sample >= 500 g. FM variation <= 0.20. FA: not less than 15% passing No. 50 sieve, 3-4% (not more than 10%) passing No. 100, no more than 5% passing No. 200 (3% if abrasive wear). Normal-weight concrete 135 to 160 lb/cu ft. Limit slivery stones to 15%. Any material retained on No. 4 is CA; passing No. 200 is too fine
entries.wn: Very fine sand is uneconomical; very coarse sand is harsh and unworkable

entries.desc: ACI 318 CA size limits
entries.use: Choosing largest CA that fits the form
entries.how: Use the largest practical CA size. Nominal max size must not exceed 1/5 the narrowest dimension between form sides, 1/3 the depth of slabs, and 3/4 the minimum clear spacing between rebars/bundles/tendons
entries.dim: 1/5 narrowest form dimension; 1/3 slab depth; 3/4 clear rebar spacing. Water for 3-4 in. slump falls as max aggregate size rises
entries.wn: Oversize CA causes honeycomb or voids (first seen when forms are removed)

entries.desc: Aggregate handling and storage
entries.use: Stockpiling sand and gravel in the field
entries.how: Build stockpiles in layers of uniform thickness; do not build high cones or let material run down slopes (segregation). Do not let aggregate free-fall off a conveyor end. Remove from stockpile in horizontal layers. When loading bins let aggregate fall vertically over the outlet; chuting at an angle against bin side segregates it
entries.wn: Damp sand bulks (volume increases from surface moisture) so be careful when proportioning by volume. Keep out contaminants

entries.desc: Total air content for frost-resistant concrete (severe / moderate): 3/8 in. 7.5/6; 1/2 in. 7/5.5; 3/4 in. 6/5; 1 in. 6/4.5; 1 1/2 in. 5.5/4.5; 2 in. 5/4; 3 in. 4.5/3.5 percent. Admixture gives about 9% air in the mortar fraction passing No. 4 sieve
entries.use: Concrete exposed to freeze-thaw or deicers
entries.how: Use air-entraining cement (IA, IIA, IIIA) or an air-entraining admixture added at the mixer (follow manufacturer instructions). Air-entrained concrete resists freeze-thaw, deicers, sulfate, and is more watertight. Always use a machine to mix air-entrained concrete. Make air content tests regularly on plastic samples taken right after discharge (pressure method practical for field; volumetric for lightweight/porous aggregates). Add calcium-chloride solutions separately from air-entraining admixtures
entries.dim: Air content 3.5 to 7.5 percent by max aggregate size and exposure (Table 2-7); up to 8% of volume
entries.eq: Air-entraining cement or admixture, pressure or volumetric air meter
entries.tm: Vibrate no more than needed: even 15 s of vibration reduces air content
entries.wn: Premature finishing brings water to surface and surface zone loses air (scaling). Higher concrete temperature entrains less air. Overloading mixer reduces air

entries.desc: Accelerating admixture limit
entries.use: Speeding set in cold weather
entries.how: Add calcium chloride in solution as part of the mixing water; do not exceed 2 percent by weight of cement
entries.dim: Maximum 2% by weight of cement. Max water-soluble chloride ion in concrete (% by weight of cement): prestressed 0.05; reinforced exposed to chloride 0.15; reinforced dry/protected 1.00; other reinforced 0.30
entries.wn: Do not use calcium chloride or soluble-chloride admixtures in prestressed concrete, concrete with embedded aluminum, in permanent contact with galvanized steel, subject to alkali-aggregate reaction, or exposed to sulfate soils/water

entries.desc: W/C selection procedure
entries.use: Choosing water-cement ratio from exposure and strength
entries.how: Pick W/C from Table 3-1 for exposure and from Table 3-2 for required compressive strength; when both apply use the lower W/C. Flexural-based design (pavement): f'c = R^2 / K, R = modulus of rupture psi, K = constant usually 8 to 10
entries.wn: Chloride admixtures not allowed for S2/S3 sulfate exposure

entries.n: Mixing water and air content by slump and aggregate size
entries.desc: Example: 3/4 in. aggregate, 3-4 in. slump, non-air-entrained = 340 lb water/cu yd; air-entrained = 305 lb water/cu yd. Recommended air for 3/4 in.: mild 3.5, moderate 5.0, severe 6.0 percent
entries.use: Estimating water per cubic yard for trial batches
entries.how: Use Table 3-3 for pounds of water per cu yd by slump and max aggregate size; use air-entrained column when freeze-thaw exposed. Use entrained air in all concrete exposed to freezing/thawing and always in paving concrete
entries.dim: See Table 3-3 (water lb/cu yd, entrapped air %, recommended air %)
entries.wn: Table water values are maximums for reasonably well-shaped angular CA; for aggregate >1 1/2 in. the slump is measured after wet-screening out particles >1 1/2 in

entries.desc: Slump limits by construction type (inches)
entries.use: Specifying workability for the type of construction
entries.how: Use recommended slump (with vibration): reinforced foundation walls and footings max 3 min 1; plain footings, caissons, substructure walls 3/1; beams and reinforced walls 4/1; building columns 4/1; pavements and slabs 3/1; mass concrete 2/1. May increase 1 in. when consolidating by rods and spades. Slump compares batches of the same mix only, not different mixes or aggregate sizes
entries.dim: Max/min slump in.: see practical use. 1 in. = 25 mm
entries.wn: Do not use slump to compare mixes with different proportions or aggregate sizes

entries.desc: Example: retaining wall, fresh water, severe climate, 3,000 psi at 28 d; Table 3-1 W/C 0.50, Table 3-2 about 0.46, use 0.46; CA max 1 1/2 in.; air 5.5 +/- 0.5%; slump 1-3 in. 20 lb cement x 0.46 = 9.2 lb water. Final per cu yd: cement 538 lb; water 247 lb; concrete 144 x 27 = 3,890 lb; aggregates 3,105 lb; FA (32%) 994 lb; CA 2,111 lb. Minimum cement factor 538 lb/cu yd at about 32% FA
entries.use: Developing mix proportions from job materials
entries.how: Make trial batch with 10 to 20 lb cement, machine mixed if possible (always machine-mix air-entrained). 1) Pre-wet aggregate and let it dry to saturated-surface-dry; 2) keep in covered containers; 3) weigh water = cement x W/C; 4) add FA and CA until slump and workability are right; 5) record weights; compute per-bag and per-cu-yd quantities, cement factor, % FA, yield; 6) record slump, air, workability, unit weight; 7) repeat varying FA % to find the minimum cement factor
entries.dim: Batch size 10-20 lb cement; W/C 0.46; unit weight 144 lb/cu ft; 1 cu yd = 27 cu ft
entries.eq: Mixer, scale, slump cone, air meter
entries.wn: Keep W/C, gradation, air, slump about constant across trial batches

entries.desc: Worked example: retaining wall, 3,000 psi, 3/4 in. aggregate, FM 2.70, SG cement 3.15, SGFA 2.66, SGCA 2.61, DRUW CA 104, DRUW FA 103 lb/cu ft, 3 in. slump, Type IA. Air 5%, water 305 lb, W/C 0.46, cement 663 lb/cu yd (7.05 sacks), CA volume 17.0 cu ft (1,768 lb), absolute volumes: cement 3.37, water 4.89, CA 10.86, air 1.35 = 20.47 cu ft; FA 6.53 cu ft = 1,083.9 lb (10.5 cu ft dry); water 36.6 gal
entries.use: Computing a cubic-yard mix from specific gravities
