entries.how: 1) Estimate air (Table 3-3). 2) Estimate water (Table 3-3). 3) Pick the lowest W/C from strength (Table 3-2), durability and watertightness (Table 3-1). 4) Cement lb/cu yd = water / (W/C). 5) CA weight = CA volume per cu yd (Table 3-6 by max size and FA fineness modulus) x CA dry-rodded unit weight. 6) Absolute volume of each = weight / (SG x 62.4); air = % x 27; FA absolute volume = 27 - (cement + water + CA + air); FA weight = vol x SG x 62.4. 7) Convert to dry volumes for first trial batch. 8) Re-trial keeping W/C constant to hit slump and air
entries.dim: Unit weight of water 62.4 lb/cu ft; 8.33 lb/gal; 1 cu yd = 27 cu ft; CA volume for 3/4 in. at FM 2.6/2.7/2.8 = 17.3/17.0/16.7 cu ft/cu yd
entries.eq: Scale, specific gravity and unit weight data, Tables 3-1, 3-2, 3-3, 3-6
entries.wn: Final proportions differ slightly between methods; trial mixes are always needed

entries.use: Slabs and flatwork
entries.how: Use at least the Table 3-7 cement content for flatwork by maximum aggregate size
entries.dim: 470 to 610 lb cement per cu yd (see practical use); 100 lb/cu yd = 60 kg/m3

entries.n: Adjust mix for aggregate surface moisture
entries.desc: Example: 6% FSM on FA and 2% on CA. CA 1,768 x 0.02 = 35.38 lb; FA 1,083 x 0.06 = 64.98 lb; total 100.36 lb = 12 gal. Water 36.6 - 12 = 24.6 gal. CA 1,803.3 lb; FA 1,148 lb. Bulking factor 0.28 (medium sand at 6%): FA 10.5 x 1.28 = 13.44 cu ft. Cement stays 7.05 sacks, CA 17.0 cu ft, air 5%
entries.use: Field batching with wet sand and gravel
entries.how: 1) Squeeze-test FA for free surface moisture (appendix C). 2) Estimate CA moisture (max about 2 percent before dripping). 3) FSM weight = % x aggregate weight per cu yd. 4) Gallons = FSM weight / 8.33 lb/gal; subtract from design water. 5) Batching by weight: add FSM weight to aggregate weights. 6) Batching by volume: V wet = V dry x (1 + BF) using bulking factor from Figure 3-3 (CA does not bulk). Recheck after rain, dry spells, new deliveries
entries.dim: CA FSM max about 2%; 8.33 lb per gal; BF 0.28 at 6% moisture medium sand
entries.wn: Design assumes saturated-surface-dry aggregate, seldom true in field

entries.n: Estimate concrete materials for a job
entries.desc: Example: wall trapezoid 14.75 ft x ((8 in + 12 in)/2 / 12) x 75 ft = 921.9 cu ft plus footing 1.25 x 8.5 x 75 = 796.9 cu ft = 63.7 cu yd; x 1.10 = 70.1 cu yd; cement 7.05 x 70.1 = 495 sacks; CA 123,937 lb = 62 tons; FA 75,918 lb = 38 tons; water 495 x 8 = 3,960 gal
entries.use: Ordering cement, sand, gravel, water
entries.how: 1) Compute total volume in cu yd (split into simple shapes). 2) Add waste: 10 percent if 200 cu yd or less; 5 percent if over 200 cu yd. 3) Multiply per-cu-yd cement, FA, CA by adjusted volume; convert to tons and round up. 4) Water planning factor 8 gal per sack of cement (includes forms, tools, curing)
entries.dim: Waste 10% (<=200 cu yd) or 5% (>200 cu yd); 8 gal water per sack; 27 cu ft per cu yd
entries.wn: Round sacks up to whole numbers

entries.n: Build a wood wall form (parts and rules)
entries.desc: Wood wall form assembly
entries.use: Concrete walls and panels
entries.how: Sheathing (horizontal; tongue-and-groove gives smoothest, most watertight face; plywood or hardboard also ok) is backed by vertical studs (single 2x4 or 2x6). Wales (doubled 2x4 or 2x6, lapped at corners) reinforce studs where they run higher than 4 or 5 ft and tie panels together. Braces: diagonal plus horizontal member nailed to a stake and to a stud or wale, diagonal at 20 to 60 degrees to horizontal; strongbacks behind wales. Spreaders cut to wall thickness hold sheathing apart (friction fit, pull out with a wire before concrete hardens). Tie wires (always double strand) or tie-rods (snap ties) resist lateral pressure
entries.dim: Studs 2x4 or 2x6; wales doubled 2x4 or 2x6; wales needed when studs exceed 4-5 ft; brace angle 20 to 60 degrees; tie wire double strand. Formwork can be up to 1/3 of structure cost
entries.eq: Sheathing, 2x4/2x6 lumber, nails, stakes, wire or snap ties, spreaders
entries.wn: Loose forms lose cement (honeycomb) or water (sand streaking). Tapered/first-pour forms (retaining walls, columns) tend to lift; brace and tie down

entries.n: Choose form material (wood, plywood, metal, earth, fiber)
entries.desc: Form material selection
entries.use: Selecting forming material
entries.how: Soft wood (pine, fir, spruce) that is straight, sound and only partly seasoned is best; kiln-dried lumber swells when wet and can bulge tight forms. Green lumber: allow for shrinkage or keep wet until concrete is in. Surface at least one side and both edges; tongue and groove is most watertight. Waterproof-glue concrete-form plywood warps less and is reused more; 5/8 and 3/4 in. are most economical, 1/4 in. for curves, thinner needs solid backing. Steel forms suit repeat use (sidewalks, curbs, pavement, precast). Earth forms only for stable-soil footings and foundations. Fiber (cardboard tube) forms suit round columns
entries.dim: Plywood thickness 1/4, 3/8, 9/16, 5/8, 3/4 in.; width up to 48 in.; 8-ft length most common
entries.wn: Earth forms give rough finish and need more excavation

entries.desc: Column form parts
entries.use: Square/rectangular concrete columns
entries.how: Run sheathing vertically (fewer cuts); nail corner joints firmly for watertightness. Yokes (rectangular horizontal frames) wrap the column and replace studs; lock with sheathing-, scab-, or bolt-type yoke lock. Battens are strips placed over sheathing joints. No vertical reinforcement is needed for small column dimensions

entries.n: Design a wood panel-wall form (17-step procedure)
entries.desc: Design method for concrete wall forms. Hydrostatic head builds until initial set, usually about 90 minutes (longer in cold)
entries.use: Sizing studs, wales and ties for a wall form
entries.how: Mixer output (cu ft/hr) = mixer yield / batch time (min) x 60. Plan area = L x W. Rate of placing R (ft/hr) = mixer output / plan area; keep R <= 5 ft/hr for economical wood forms. Find max concrete pressure (MCP, psf) from Figure 4-3 using R and placing temperature. Max stud spacing (MSS) from Table 4-1 (boards) or 4-2 (plywood, use strong way), round MCP up. Uniform load on stud ULS = MCP x MSS/12. Max wale spacing (MWS) from Table 4-3 using ULS, round up. ULW = MCP x MWS/12. Tie spacing from Table 4-3/4-4 using ULW, and from tie strength = breaking load x 12 / ULW (round down); use the smaller. Tie at stud/wale intersections (reduce stud or tie spacing to match); tie-rods can be spaced along wales; first tie at half max tie spacing from end. Studs = (length x 12 / MSS) + 1, round up; first and last studs at the ends. Wales per side = height / MWS, round up; first wale half the spacing up from bottom. Placing time = form height / R
entries.dim: R <= 5 ft/hr; Example 1 (40x2x10 ft wall, 1 cu yd per 10 min, 70 F, 1 in. boards, 2x4 studs, double 2x4 wales, No. 9 wire): 162 cu ft/hr, R 2.025 ft/hr, MCP 400 psf, MSS 18 in., ULS 600, MWS 24 in., ULW 800 lb/ft, tie spacing 30 in. by wale vs 21 in. by wire (1,420 lb x 12/800 = 21.3), use 18 in. at studs, 28 studs per side, 5 double wales, about 5 hr to place. Example 2 (1 cu yd per 7 min, 3/4 in. plywood strong way, 3,000 lb snap ties): 231.4 cu ft/hr, R 2.9 ft/hr, MCP 500 psf, MSS 15 in., ULS 625, MWS 22 in., ULW about 917 lb/ft, tie spacing 27 in. (3,000 x 12/917 = 39 in. by strength), 33 studs, 6 wales, about 4 hr
entries.eq: M919 concrete mobile mixer (example), lumber, ties, Tables 4-1 to 4-5, Figure 4-3
entries.tm: Placing time = form height / rate of placing (about 4.93 to 5 hr for 10 ft at ~2 ft/hr)
entries.wn: Pressure depends on rate of placement and temperature; slower cold-weather set means higher pressure

entries.desc: Tie strength values for spacing calculation
entries.use: Choosing ties for wall forms
entries.how: Use minimum breaking loads: double-strand steel wire gage 8 = 1,700 lb; gage 9 = 1,420; gage 10 = 1,170; gage 11 = 930. Barbwire: 12 1/2 = 950; 13 (single strand) = 660; 13 1/2 = 950; 14 = 650; 15 1/2 = 850. Snap ties and pencil rods = 3,000 lb. Tie spacing = breaking load x 12 / ULW
entries.dim: See practical use (lb)

entries.desc: Example: 10-ft wall, 2x6x10 ft brace attached 6 ft up; sin theta = 6/10, theta = 37 degrees; L = 5 ft (mid support); J = 3,710; Smax = 3,710 x 6 x cos37 / (100 x 25) = 7.13 ft, use 7 ft. Formula carries safety factor of 3
entries.use: Bracing a wall form against wind and accidents
entries.how: Assume a horizontal force along the top edge of 12.5 x wall height (ft) lb. Brace angle 20 to 60 degrees (45 best); attach as near the form top as practical. Smax (ft) = J x y x cos(theta) / (h^2 x L^2). Lmax unsupported brace length 6 1/4 ft for 2-in. material, 14 1/2 ft for 4-in.; add a mid-brace support (1x4 or 1x6) if the brace is longer. Supports at least 2 ft apart for 2-in. material and 5 ft apart for 4-in. Connect braces to each other at the center after installing
entries.wn: Reduce Smax for old or green lumber. Braces must be equally strong in tension and compression or placed on both sides. Larger material carries greater load

entries.n: Design overhead slab forms (roofs, culverts, bunkers)
entries.desc: Example: 6 in. slab on 8 ft clear height, 3/4 in. plywood, 4x4 S4S joists/stringers/shores, buggies: DL 75 + LL 75 = TL 150 psf; joist spacing 22 in.; ULJ 275 lb/ft; stringer spacing 55 in.; ULS 687.5 lb/ft; shore spacing 35 in. (stringer strength) vs 54.1 in. (3,100 lb bearing); unsupported shore length 88.25 in.; l/d = 25.21 < 50 so no lateral bracing needed (cross bracing always)
entries.use: Elevated slab formwork
entries.how: Parts: sheathing (plywood or sheet metal best), joists (2-, 3-, 4-in. lumber), stringers (2-in. or thicker; need not be doubled), shores (at least as large as stringer, never smaller than 4x4), lateral bracing (1x6 or larger), cross bracing (always required), wedges, mudsill (2-in. or thicker). Procedure: TL = LL + DL; LL 50 psf (75 psf with powered buggies); DL = 150 lb/cu ft x slab thickness (in) / 12. Joist spacing from Table 4-1/4-2 using TL as pressure. ULJ = TL x joist spacing/12. Stringer spacing from Table 4-3 using ULJ. ULS = TL x stringer spacing/12. Shore spacing = smaller of (a) Table 4-3/4-4 spacing for stringer strength and (b) allowable shore load (lower of Table 4-7 strength and Table 4-8 bearing) x 12 / ULS. Check l/d <= 50 for shores or add lateral and cross bracing
entries.dim: LL 50 psf or 75 psf; concrete 150 lb/cu ft; l/d limit 50; minimum shore 4x4
entries.eq: Plywood/metal sheathing, joists, stringers, shores, mudsill, wedges, bracing
entries.wn: Form failure danger from concrete weight and live load. If compression perpendicular to grain unknown, use lowest value in Table 4-8

entries.desc: Example: shop floor, 7,500 lb wheel, 40 sq in. loaded area, class 5, f'c 4,500 psi: f't = 309; ESL = 9,375 lb; CESL = 9,102 lb; thickness 6.6 in. rounded to 6 3/4 in.; cement 520 lb/cu yd (1 in. aggregate); air 6%
entries.use: Sizing a concrete floor/slab for wheel loads
entries.how: 1) Pick floor class (Table 4-9). 2) Get minimum f'c and slump (Table 4-10). 3) Allowable flexural tensile stress f't = 4.6 x sqrt(f'c). 4) Equivalent static load ESL = 1.25 x static load (25% impact). 5) If f't is not 300 psi, CESL = ESL x 300 / f't. 6) Read slab thickness from Figure 4-6 using CESL and loaded area (sq in.); round up to next 1/4 in. 7) Get minimum cement and air content for freeze-thaw (Table 4-11)
entries.dim: Minimum slab thickness 4 in. for classes 1-3; if loaded area exceeds 80 sq in. consider soil bearing; thicken edge by 50% tapering at not more than 1 in 10 (or use grade beam) where loads reach edges. Unbonded topping (class 7) minimum 2 1/2 in. Heavy-duty topping minimum cement 846 lb/cu yd
entries.wn: Many slabs fail from inadequate thickness; others waste material with excessive thickness

entries.desc: Slab-on-grade rules
entries.use: Preparing subgrade and protecting a slab
entries.how: Always put free-draining (nonfrost-susceptible) gravel or coarse sand under the slab, replacing silts and very fine sand to one-half of the expected frost penetration, with edge drainage. Always include steel reinforcement (welded-wire mesh preferred). Keep slab moist and protected from heat and freezing for the required curing time
entries.dim: Replace frost-susceptible soil to 1/2 of frost penetration depth
entries.eq: Gravel or coarse sand, welded wire mesh

entries.n: Minimum cement and air for slabs by aggregate size
entries.desc: Smaller air percentages can be used for floors not exposed to freeze-thaw or deicing
entries.use: Slab mix floor values
entries.dim: See practical use
entries.wn: Mixtures are for normal-weight aggregate; structural slabs must meet ACI 318

entries.desc: Example: 9-ft column, 36 in. largest dimension: yokes from base spaced 8, 8, 10, 11, 12, 15, 17, 17, and 10 in
entries.use: Spacing yokes on a wood column form
entries.how: Use 2x4 yokes and 1-in. sheathing. Find the column height and largest cross-section dimension (16, 18, 20, 24, 28, 30, 32, 36 in.) in Table 4-12; spacings read from base upward; they are maximums; adjust the last spacing so a yoke sits at the column top. Provide a clean-out hole in the bottom, nail removed pieces to the form, and replace them before placing concrete
entries.dim: Largest dimension 16-36 in.; heights 1-20 ft
entries.wn: Table 4-12 values are not present in the extracted text

entries.desc: Footing form procedure
entries.use: Footing forms
entries.how: Where possible excavate and use earth as the mold, wetting the earth thoroughly. Otherwise build panel forms: pair (a) with vertical 2-in. dressed cleats 2 1/2 in. from each end and on 2-ft centers; pair (b) cleats spaced footing length plus twice sheathing thickness. Drill holes under 1/2 in. beside center cleats and tie opposing panels with No. 8 or 9 black annealed wire; mark footing top with grade nails; for forms 4 ft square or larger drive stakes and nail 1x6 tie braces across the top. Footing less than 1 ft deep and 2 ft square: 1-in. sheathing without cleats. Place a small pier with the footing using 2x4 or 4x4 supports across the footing form. Bearing wall footing: 2-in. lumber sides as wide as footing depth, stakes, spreaders and short braces
entries.dim: Cleats on 2-ft centers; holes <1/2 in.; wire No. 8 or No. 9; 1x6 tie braces; footing < 1 ft deep and < 2 ft square needs no cleats
entries.eq: Forming nails (drive part way), 2-in. dressed lumber, black annealed wire, stakes
entries.wn: Footing pressure is low so strength design is generally unnecessary

entries.n: Install wall form ties and spreaders
entries.desc: Tie wire and tie-rod installation
entries.use: Securing wall forms
entries.how: Tie wires only for low walls or when tie-rods unavailable; No. 8 or 9 black annealed iron wire (barbwire in emergency). Space ties same as stud spacing but never more than 3 ft apart. Place a spreader near each tie. Loop wire around wale on one side, through form, around wale on other. Tighten by twisting with a nail between the strands or with a wedge. Use pull wires through off-center holes in spreaders to remove each as concrete level rises. Use tie-rods if rust stains are unacceptable or exact position needed; after stripping, break off rod at notch and grout holes with mortar mix. Panel-wall units about 10 ft long, sheathing 1-in. (13/16 dressed) tongue-and-groove or 3/4 in. plywood
entries.dim: Max tie spacing 3 ft; wire No. 8 or 9; panel length about 10 ft; sheathing 3/4 in. plywood or 13/16 in. dressed T&G

entries.desc: Stair form for widths up to 3 ft
entries.use: Concrete stairs up to 3 ft wide
entries.how: Make the sloping platform (underside of steps) from 1-in. tongue-and-groove sheathing; extend platform about 12 in. beyond each side of the stairs for stringer bracing blocks. Support back with 4x4 posts, 2x6 cleats on 4-ft centers, posts on wedges. Cut 2x12 side stringers to fit treads and risers; bevel 2x12 risers
entries.dim: Platform extends 12 in. each side; 2x6 cleats on 4-ft centers; 2x12 stringers and risers; 4x4 posts

entries.desc: Steel pavement forms
entries.use: Paving
entries.how: Steel plate sections are 10 ft long, slab thicknesses 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12 in., base plate usually 8 in. wide; locking plates join ends; 3 steel stakes 1 in. diameter per 10-ft section. Drive stakes, set true to line and grade, clamp with splines and wedges. Set ahead of the paver. Oil immediately after setting but wipe the traction edge clean. Leave in place at least 24 hours after placing. Then clean, oil and stack for reuse
entries.dim: 10-ft sections; 6-12 in. depths; 8 in. base; three 1-in. stakes per section; minimum 24 hr in place
entries.eq: Steel forms, stakes, splines, wedges, form oil

entries.desc: Form coating
entries.use: Preventing concrete sticking to forms
entries.how: Treat wood forms with light-bodied petroleum oil; on plywood shellac works better. Oil steel forms with specially compounded oils (synthetic castor oil, some marine engine oils), before erecting column/wall forms and before rebar is placed. Apply by brush, spray or swab; cover evenly, remove excess, keep oil off construction joints and rebar. Do not clean forms with wire brushes. If tannin softens concrete treat with whitewash or limewater first. Fuel oil, asphalt paint, varnish, boiled linseed oil also suitable; mix 1 part petroleum grease to 3 parts fuel oil for warm weather. Wet forms with water only in emergency
entries.dim: Fuel oil mix 1 part grease : 3 parts fuel oil
entries.wn: Oil must not stain/soften concrete or interfere with curing compounds

entries.desc: Safety and failure causes
entries.use: Form erection and stripping
entries.how: Protruding nails are the main source of formwork accidents. Inspect tools; mudsills under shoring on ground; do not raise large panels in gusts; brace all shoring. When stripping only stripping workers in area, do not remove forms until concrete sets, pile forms immediately, take care when cutting wires under tension. Common wall-form failures: not controlling rate of placing with temperature drop, insufficient nailing, ignoring lateral pressure, loose ties, old or undersized material. Overhead failures: no diagonal bracing of shores, unstable soil under mudsills, unplumb shores, unlocked metal shoring, vibration, early support removal, missing reshoring
entries.wn: Formwork can fail from human error even when designed adequately

entries.desc: Control-joint spacing (ft) by slab thickness (in.), for aggregate under 3/4 in. / larger than 3/4 in. / slump under 4 in.: 5 in. 10/13/15; 6 in. 12/15/18; 7 in. 14/18/21; 8 in. 16/20/24; 9 in. 18/23/27; 10 in. 20/25/30. Spacing also applies to distance from control joint to parallel isolation or construction joints
entries.use: Preventing cracks in slabs and walls
entries.how: Isolation joints separate adjacent members (e.g., slab from column), go completely through the member, no load-transfer devices. Control joints create a plane of weakness; run in both directions at right angles; interior slabs cut 1/3 to 1/4 of slab thickness (slabs on grade 3/4 to 1 in. deep) and filled with lead or joint filler; welded-wire fabric may be used for sidewalks and driveways with tooled joints at spacing equal to slab width but not more than 20 ft. Construction joints occur where a pour stops or concrete is cast against hardened concrete; they extend entirely through the element and use keys or dowels for load transfer
entries.dim: Control joint depth 1/3 to 1/4 slab thickness; spacing up to 30 ft; max 20 ft with tooled/temperature steel
entries.eq: Joint tool or saw, joint filler

entries.desc: Anchor bolt placement
entries.use: Anchoring machinery, sills or steel
entries.how: Anchor bolt with pipe sleeve: sleeve diameter at least 1 in. larger than bolt; pack sleeves with grease to keep concrete out. Do not use sleeve when machinery mounts on base 4 or more inches above floor; set bolts in floor extending above base, block machine on scrap steel, level, tighten, then pack base concrete from the sides. Hooked and suspended anchor bolts fasten wood sill to concrete or masonry wall; drill board holes 1/16 in. larger than bolt; do not disturb suspended bolt alignment. Use a templet to hold bolts; set sleeve tops level with finished concrete
entries.dim: Sleeve >= 1 in. larger than bolt; raised base >= 4 in.; sill holes 1/16 in. oversize
entries.eq: Anchor bolts, pipe sleeves, grease, templet

entries.desc: Excavation and layout rules
entries.use: Footing/foundation excavation
entries.how: Use machines for bulk excavation but finish the last 6 in. of the bottom by hand. Excavate beyond exterior wall edges for forms and waterproofing. If over-excavated, place concrete to actual excavation depth (refill needs an elephant-foot tamper). Shore whenever slope stability is questionable; sand and wet earth need more shoring. Stake out the site with batter boards 2 to 6 ft outside each corner with strings between nails
entries.dim: Final 6 in. by hand; batter boards 2-6 ft outside corners. Machine rates (1/2 cu yd, cu yd/hr): power shovel 70/60/45/25, dragline 65/50/40/20, backhoe 55/45/35/25 in sandy loam/common earth/hard clay/wet clay. Hand rates in Table 5-2 (e.g., sand 2.0 cu yd/hr pick to 3 ft)
entries.eq: Power shovel, dragline, backhoe, picks, shovels, shoring, batter boards, string

entries.desc: Form labor rate
entries.use: Estimating form-building time
entries.how: An average carpenter builds and erects about 10 sq ft of wood form per hour. Break large jobs into near-identical units and standardize building, erecting and stripping. Basic tools: claw hammers, pinch bars, hand saws, portable electric saws, table saws, levels, plumb lines, carpenter squares
entries.dim: 10 sq ft of wood forms per carpenter-hour
entries.eq: Hammers, saws, levels, plumb line, squares

entries.desc: Batching tolerances
entries.use: Measuring cement, aggregate, water, admixture
entries.how: Measure each batch within: cement 1%; aggregate 2%; water 1%; admixtures 3%. Check scales periodically and admixture dispensers daily. Use sacked cement in troop construction. Weigh aggregate (most reliable) on platform scales with wheelbarrow runways (same weight per wheelbarrow, not loaded to capacity), or measure by volume with a 1-cu-ft box or 2-3 cu ft wheelbarrow. Simple volumetric 1:2:3 method = 1 part cement : 2 parts sand : 3 parts aggregate by any consistent unit (shovels, cu ft, wheelbarrows). Correct water for aggregate moisture
entries.dim: Tolerances: cement 1%, aggregate 2%, water 1%, admixtures 3%. 1:2:3 = cement:sand:coarse aggregate. Wheelbarrows 2-3 cu ft
entries.eq: Platform scale, 1 cu ft box, wheelbarrow
entries.wn: Over-dosing admixtures causes serious problems

entries.desc: Hand mixing
entries.use: Small batches without a machine
entries.how: Use a clean, even, paved surface or tight-jointed wood platform; moisten it. Spread cement over sand, then CA over cement. Mix with a hoe or square-pointed D-handled shovel; turn dry materials at least 3 times until color is uniform; add water slowly and turn at least 3 more times to proper consistency. One worker can mix 1 cu yd in about 1 hour; for larger batches two workers face each other and work through the pile with shovels close to the platform. Hoe box may also be used
entries.dim: Turn dry mix at least 3 times, wet mix at least 3 times; about 1 cu yd per hour per worker; not economical above 1 cu yd

entries.desc: 16-cu-ft mixer (TOE). Drum 16 cu ft; 2 sacks per batch; 10 cu yd/hr; drum 57 in. dia x 46 in.; 26 hp; 0.5 gal/hr fuel; 26 gal water tank; 158x96x119 in.; 7,150 lb
entries.use: Machine mixing by troops
entries.how: Crew of ten soldiers and one NCO produces about 10 cu yd/hr. Charge skip with aggregate, cement, sand (in that order, sand on top), dump into drum while water runs in; water tank measures water a few seconds before skip dumps. Mixing time starts when water enters; minimum 1 minute per batch up to 1 cu yd, plus 15 seconds for each additional cu yd or fraction. Adjust drum speed: faster for very wet, slower for dry concrete. Clean daily or after each use; coat exterior with form oil first. If shut down more than 1 1/2 hours, put CA equal to half mixer capacity in drum, run about 5 minutes, discharge and flush. Never strike chute, drum or skip. Mixers handle 10% overload; produce a batch about every 3 minutes (10 to 20 batches/hr)
entries.dim: Min mix 1 min; +15 s per added cu yd; clean after >1.5 hr stop with half-capacity CA for 5 min; 10 soldiers + 1 NCO
entries.eq: 16-cu-ft trailer mixer with skip, form oil, hose
entries.tm: About 10 cu yd/hr; batch about every 3 min
entries.wn: Hardened concrete in drum absorbs mixing water and degrades later batches

entries.desc: M919 unit: capacity 8 cu yd; hourly production 16 cu yd; water tank 400 gal; cement bin 63 cu ft; sand bin 128 cu ft; gravel bin 182 cu ft; hi-flow admix tank 42 gal; lo-flow admix tank 12 gal; dry admix tank 2.35 cu ft; L 374 in., W 96 in., H 142 in.; weight empty 37,540 lb
entries.use: On-site mixing of up to 8 cu yd
entries.how: Unit carries enough unmixed material for up to 8 cu yd; mixes meet ACI and AASHTO strength standards; control sand, gravel, water, admixes by dials on rear and sides. Operates intermittently or continuously depending on raw material supply. Settings vary by truck and site
entries.dim: 8 cu yd capacity; 16 cu yd/hr

entries.desc: Remix procedure
entries.use: Concrete left standing before pour
entries.how: Concrete that stiffens before initial set may be reused if remixing makes it plastic enough to compact. Carefully add a small amount of water and remix for at least one-half of the minimum mixing time or number of revolutions; then check that it does not exceed max W/C ratio, max slump, or max mixing/agitating time
entries.dim: Remix at least 1/2 of minimum mixing time or revolutions
entries.wn: Do not add water randomly. Remixed concrete hardens rapidly; fresh concrete placed against it may cause a cold joint

entries.desc: Concrete delivery rules
entries.use: Delivering concrete to the pour
entries.how: Transport requirements: speed, minimum segregation, no delays. Delivery equipment must handle 100% of mixer capacity. Wheelbarrows/buggies for small jobs; runways of 2x10 planks on 4x4 supports at 6-ft centers; 1x6 ledger nailed to wall-form studs; top wale 1 ft below top of concrete; inclined runways for 5-6 ft rise at slope 10:1; hopper and chute where drop is large, chute slope 2:1 or steeper for stiff mixes. Dump trucks: short hauls, slow, smooth road, stiff mix with air-entraining agent. Ready-mix trucks carry 30 to 35% more than transit-mix, but with a more limited radius. 2-cu-yd clamshell buckets with crane are TOE
entries.dim: Runway planks 2x10 on 4x4 at 6-ft centers; ramp 10:1; chute 2:1; bucket 2 cu yd
entries.eq: Wheelbarrows, buggies, planks, chutes, dump trucks, agitator trucks, buckets, crane

entries.desc: 25 hp gasoline pump: 15 to 20 cu yd/hr; double-acting: 50 to 60 cu yd/hr. Mix slump 2 in. or more. Range: 800 ft horizontal, 100 ft vertical, or equivalent; each 90-degree bend cuts 40 ft horizontal; each ft of lift cuts 8 ft horizontal
entries.use: Delivery where space is limited
entries.how: Heavy-duty piston pump through 6-, 7-, or 8-in. pipeline. Lubricate pipeline with light cement grout first; supply an uninterrupted flow of plastic, unsegregated medium-consistency concrete. Max aggregate 3 in. (8-in. pipe), 2 1/2 in. (7-in.), 2 in. (6-in.). Keep line straight with 5-ft-radius bends; cool pipe in hot weather; flush pump and line with water after use
entries.dim: Slump >= 2 in.; max aggregate 2 / 2 1/2 / 3 in. for 6 / 7 / 8 in. pipe
entries.wn: Interrupted flow causes joints. Pumped mix costs more (smaller aggregate, more cement)

entries.n: Prepare subgrade, rock and old concrete before placing
entries.desc: Subgrade and joint preparation
entries.use: Pre-pour preparation
entries.how: Compact and moisten subgrade (or lay vapor barrier). Rock: cut to vertical or horizontal, roughen, clean (stiff brooms, water jets, air, wet sandblast), remove standing water, coat with 3/4-in. mortar of FA only at same W/C as concrete with 6-in. slump, scrubbed in with stiff brush. Clay/fine soils: moisten to 6 in. depth by intermittent sprinkling. Gravel/sand: cover with tar paper (laps not less than 1 in., stapled) or burlap (sewn with wire, wetted); compacted sand left uncovered but moist. Check forms for tightness, cleanliness, bracing and oil; sun-dried forms: saturate to close joints. For new concrete on hardened: level, clean, moist, some aggregate exposed; remove laitance or soft mortar (wet sand-blast best); saturate dried concrete for several hours; no pooled water
entries.dim: Rock mortar 3/4 in. thick, 6 in. slump; clay moisten 6 in. deep; tar paper lap >= 1 in
entries.eq: Brooms, water jets, tar paper, burlap, form oil
entries.tm: Saturate dry old concrete several hours

entries.desc: Placement rules
entries.use: Placing concrete in forms
entries.how: Free fall must be under 5 ft; otherwise use vertical pipes, drop chutes or baffles. Place in even horizontal layers, each consolidated before the next and before initial set of the previous. Layers 15 to 20 in. thick for mass concrete from buckets; 6 to 20 in. for reinforced members. Fill rate not over 5 vertical ft/hr (except columns). Allow at least 4 hr, preferably 24 hr, between placing columns/walls and the slabs, beams or girders they support. Walls/beams: start at the ends and work to center. Wall construction joint lift: overfill about 2 in., remove excess before set, then place 1/2 to 1 in. of sand-cement mortar (same water content as concrete, slump about 6 in.) before the next lift. Port openings about every 10 ft up high wall forms. Slabs: start at the far end, place each batch against the previous; never pile and drag. Slopes: start at the bottom
entries.dim: Drop < 5 ft; layers 6-20 in. (15-20 in. mass); rate <= 5 ft/hr; wait 4 hr min (24 hr preferred); mortar 1/2-1 in. at 6 in. slump; ports every 10 ft
entries.eq: Buckets, chutes, drop pipes, spades, vibrators
entries.wn: Avoid horizontal movement of concrete (paste flows ahead of aggregate)

entries.n: Consolidate with a vibrator or spade
entries.desc: Consolidation procedure. Vibrated concrete slump 5 or 6 in. (as stated in text)
entries.use: Removing rock pockets and air
entries.how: Insert internal vibrator vertically about every 18 in., 5 to 10 seconds in air-entrained and 10 to 15 seconds in non-air-entrained concrete; overlap areas; penetrate several inches into the layer below; withdraw at the same slow rate. Done when a thin mortar line appears near the vibrator, CA disappears into the concrete, or paste just appears at the vibrator head. Vibrators allow stiff mixes with 1-2 in. slump. Do not vibrate easily spaded mixes. Spading: insert spade along inside form face down into the layer below several inches until CA disappears. Do not displace rebar
entries.dim: Insert spacing 18 in.; 5-10 s (air-entrained); 10-15 s (non-air-entrained)
entries.eq: Internal or external vibrator, spades, puddling sticks, tampers
entries.wn: Over-vibrating causes segregation and weak surface

entries.desc: Underwater placement
entries.use: Underwater concrete (tremie, bucket, sack)
entries.how: Use experienced supervision. Do not place in water below 45 F (if so, concrete must be above 60 F but never above 80 F when deposited) or flowing faster than 10 ft/min (tighten cofferdam/forms); no pumping out water while placing or for 24 hours after. Tremie: long funnel pipe with closable gate; keep discharge end buried in the fresh concrete and pipe full; lift slowly to start; if seal lost, raise, close gate, refill and re-lower; do not move horizontally through placed concrete; multiple tremies on 20- to 25-ft centers fed uniformly. Mix: slump about 6 in., 7 sacks cement per cu yd, 50% of total aggregate sand, max CA 1 1/2 to 2 in. Bucket (drop-bottom, canvas flap on one side): fill completely, lower slowly, do not discharge before reaching surface, sound frequently; 7 sacks/cu yd, slightly stiffer. Sack method (emergency): jute sacks about 1 cu ft filled two-thirds, laid in header and stretcher courses at right angles; no compaction
entries.dim: Water > 45 F; velocity <= 10 ft/min; concrete 60-80 F in cold water; wait 24 hr before dewatering; tremie centers 20-25 ft; slump about 6 in.; 7 sacks/cu yd; 50% sand; CA 1 1/2-2 in.; sacks 1 cu ft, 2/3 full
entries.eq: Tremie pipe with gate, crane, drop-bottom bucket with canvas flap, jute sacks

entries.desc: Screeding
entries.use: Strike off flat slabs, walks, pavements
entries.how: Use a screed (straightedge template) in a sawing motion, moving forward along guide forms a short distance each stroke. If it tears air-entrained concrete, slow the advance or cover the lower edge with metal. Hand-screed surfaces up to 30 ft wide (less efficient over 10 ft). Screed a second time to remove the surge
entries.dim: Width up to 30 ft; efficient to 10 ft; 3 workers screed about 200 sq ft/hr (two screed, one pulls excess)

entries.desc: Floating
entries.use: Smoothing after screeding
entries.how: Float immediately after screeding while plastic, with wood or aluminum-magnesium float or machine, to embed aggregate, remove high and low spots and compact surface. Do not overwork or a weak layer of paste and water will scale. For coarse texture float again after partial hardening with long-handled wood float. Start aluminum floating when the water sheen disappears. Do not use cement or water to aid finishing
entries.eq: Wood or aluminum-magnesium float, finishing machine
entries.wn: Overworking plastic concrete brings water and fines up and causes scaling

entries.desc: Steel troweling
entries.use: Dense smooth floors
entries.how: Start troweling after floating when water sheen disappears and concrete is hard enough that fines and water do not rise. Delay as long as possible: too soon causes crazing, too late makes finishing hard. For fine texture not slippery, make a second light circular-motion troweling right after the first, keeping trowel flat. For hard steel-troweled finish, trowel again only when no paste sticks to the trowel and the trowel rings; tilt slightly with heavy pressure. Do not spread dry cement on wet spots; wait until water is absorbed, evaporated or mopped. Close hair cracks before troweling by pounding with a hand float
entries.wn: Overworking causes crazing and hair cracks; rapid drying or cooling worsens them

entries.desc: Brooming
entries.use: Sidewalks, ramps, floors
entries.how: After floating, wait 10-15 minutes, then broom before the concrete hardens thoroughly with a straw broom with fibers at least 4 1/2 in. long. Grooves not deeper than 3/16 in. For light scoring, trowel once smooth then use a hairbrush; for rough scoring use stiff wire or coarse-fiber broom. Score at right angles to traffic
entries.dim: Wait 10-15 min; fibers >= 4 1/2 in.; groove depth <= 3/16 in
entries.eq: Straw broom, hairbrush, or stiff broom

entries.desc: Pavement finishing
entries.use: Pavement strips
entries.how: Machine finish when concrete takes initial set but is still workable: screed, vibrate, screed again; two passes enough with aligned forms and correct workability. Hand floating often does harm. Longitudinal float (wood 6 by 10 in. wide, 12 to 18 ft long, handle each end, two workers on form-riding bridges); 10-ft straightedge from center to form removes laitance. When water sheen disappears belt the surface: drag clean burlap longitudinally, two workers. Round corners with edging tool; clean out expansion joints. After forms removal knock off projections, fill tie-rod holes, repair honeycomb
entries.dim: Float 6 in. x 10 in. wide (as printed) x 12-18 ft long; straightedge 10 ft; 2 passes of finisher
entries.eq: Machine finisher, longitudinal float, burlap, edging tool

entries.desc: Surface cleaning and rubbing
entries.use: Fix color or stains after stripping
entries.how: Mortar method: 1 part portland cement to 1 1/2 to 2 parts fine sand (white cement for light color); brush on after repairs, scour with wood/cork float; remove excess with trowel after 1 or 2 hours; rub with dry burlap after drying; do not leave overnight; finish a whole section without stopping. Burlap alternative: mortar like thick cream on almost dry surface, remove excess with a second clean burlap, set several hours, cure 2 days, sand with No. 2 sandpaper; work in shade on a cool damp day. Sandblast lightly for stains/rust (better than acid). Acid: only after 2 weeks moist curing; wet surface, scrub with stiff brush using 5 to 10 percent muriatic acid, flush immediately with clean water, then 4 more days moist curing. Rubbed finish: coarse carborundum stone when concrete hardens, finer stones after curing, keep damp; keep mortar damp 1 to 2 days
entries.dim: Mortar 1 cement : 1 1/2 to 2 fine sand; acid 5-10% muriatic; 2 weeks moist cure before acid; 4 days after
entries.eq: Brush, wood/cork float, burlap, sandpaper No. 2, muriatic acid, carborundum stones
entries.wn: Wear goggles and protect hands, arms and clothing when handling muriatic acid

entries.desc: Curing methods Table 5-5: sprinkle/wet burlap (excellent if constantly wet; hard on vertical walls); strawing; moist earth (cheap, messy, stains); ponding on flat surfaces (excellent, uniform temperature, labor intensive, bad in freezing weather); curing compounds (inexpensive, easy, need sprayer, film can break, pigment needed against heat); waterproof paper (excellent but costly, bulky rolls); plastic film (light, watertight, must be weighted and patched)
entries.use: Keeping concrete hydrating to design strength
entries.how: Keep concrete moist and near 73 F as practicable. For most structural use, cast-in-place curing is 3 days to 2 weeks (bridge decks and exposed slabs longer). Hydration stops once water is removed and cannot be restarted. Methods adding moisture: continuous sprinkling (do not let dry between), wet burlap, cotton mats, straw, earth laid as soon as the concrete hardens enough not to be marred and kept wet for entire period; flooding horizontal placements with an earth dam. Methods preventing loss: waterproof paper (wet surface first, lap 12 in. or more, weigh edges), plastic film (same rules; may discolor hard-troweled surfaces), curing compounds (sprayed; respray if heavy rain within 3 hours; brush only on formed surfaces; do not use where bond to later concrete is needed), forms left in place if kept wet
entries.dim: Target 73 F; 3 days to 2 weeks typical; paper/plastic laps >= 12 in.; respray within 3 hr of heavy rain
entries.eq: Water, burlap, mats, paper, plastic, curing compound sprayer
entries.tm: 3 days to 2 weeks; design strength (Type I) at 28 days
entries.wn: Hot weather: forms left in place are not adequate; loosen and cover with water

entries.desc: Hot-weather rules. Higher temperature needs more mixing water for same slump, raising W/C and lowering later strength; hot concrete gives higher early but lower later strength; plastic shrinkage cracks
entries.use: Placing above about 70-90 F
entries.how: Limit concrete temperature to less than 90 F. Cool materials: cold mixing water (slush ice in extreme cases); sprinkle CA; insulate or spray/wet-burlap mixer drums; insulate or paint white water lines and tanks; shade materials; work at night; sprinkle forms, rebar and subgrade with cool water before placing. Mixing water is easiest to cool but aggregate (60-80% of weight) governs concrete temperature. Place and finish fast, avoid cold joints, loosen forms early and keep concrete wet by sprinkling or wet burlap
entries.dim: Maximum concrete temperature < 90 F
entries.eq: Ice, shade, sprinklers, wet burlap, white paint
entries.tm: Hardening accelerated; less time to handle/finish
entries.wn: Hot, dry, windy weather on large exposed slabs is worst. Do not rely on forms alone to retain moisture

entries.desc: Cold-weather requirements. Forms retain heat; leave in place as long as practicable. Concrete that freezes shortly after placement is permanently damaged; once-frozen early concrete may recover to nearly normal with favorable curing. Strength cured below 73 F is lower in first 28 days but later overtakes
entries.use: Placing at 40 F or below
entries.how: Do not suspend concreting in winter; protect from freezing at 40 F or lower during placing and early curing. Fresh concrete min temperature as mixed (sections <12 in. / 12-36 / 36-72): above 30 F air 60/55/50 F; 0 to 30 F air 65/60/55; below 0 F air 70/65/60. Min as placed: 55/50/45 F. Max gradual drop in first 24 hr after end of protection: 50/40/30 F. Protection duration (air-entrained): no exposure 2 days normal / 1 day high-early; any exposure 3 days normal / 2 days high-early. No need above 70 F. Heating: aggregate average not over 150 F (pipes or steam, tarp cover); mixing water not over 180 F; when aggregate or water over 100 F combine them first before adding cement. Never place on frozen subgrade (thaw by burning straw, steaming or hot sand). Calcium chloride max 2% by weight of cement; do not use antifreeze; use extra sack of cement per cu yd instead of CaCl for sulfate-resisting concrete. Type III cement helps. Curing aids: live steam, insulation blankets/bats (check corners and edges), heated enclosures (airtight, vented; no CO-producing heaters unless vented for 24 to 36 hr)
entries.dim: See practical use (temperatures F)
entries.eq: Heaters, steam, insulation blankets, tarps, enclosures
entries.wn: Do not use carbon monoxide-producing heaters (salamanders) without ventilation during placing and 24-36 hr of curing

entries.n: Strip forms safely and on time
entries.desc: Form stripping times
entries.use: Form removal
entries.how: Never pry with a metal bar against exposed concrete; use wooden wedges only. Ties may come out as early as 24 hours to loosen forms and let curing water in. Strip away from ornament and work toward it. Withdraw all nails, clean and oil forms for reuse. In cold weather defer stripping or replace forms with insulation blankets. Suspended structures: strip when cylinder strength to design strength ratio is at least dead plus construction load to total design load, with minimum 50% of design strength; one example given is 2,500 psi or two-thirds of design strength. Use job-cured test cylinders. Table 5-8 gives minimum times where no strength basis is provided: walls, columns, beam sides 12-24 hr; pan joist forms 3 days (30 in. or less) or 4 days (over 30 in.); joist/beam/girder soffits 7/14/21 days (live load less than dead load: spans <10 ft, 10-20 ft, >20 ft) or 4/7/14 days; floor slabs 4/7/10 days or 3/4/7 days. Periods count days when air temperature is above 50 F
entries.dim: Walls, columns, beam sides 12-24 hr; pan joist 3 or 4 days; soffits 7/14/21 d (live load < dead) or 4/7/14 d; slabs 4/7/10 d or 3/4/7 d; temp above 50 F; where forms can be removed without disturbing shores use half, min 3 days; min 50% design strength for suspended structures
entries.wn: Do not jerk forms off after wedging at one end (edges break)

entries.desc: New concrete repair
entries.use: Patching honeycomb, bolt holes, ridges
entries.how: Inspect after stripping and repair within 24 hours. Grind off ridges and bulges. Keep surrounding concrete wet several hours, brush on cement-water grout of creamy consistency, then patch; cure at once. Small patches: chip down to solid concrete, edges at right angles or slightly undercut; fill in mortar layers not over 1/2 in. thick, scratch each layer, let mortar stand as long as possible; add white cement to match color (trial mix). Do not skim shallow mortar over honeycomb. Large patches: concrete in forms, reinforced and doweled. Bolt holes: pack very dry mortar; tie-rod holes: fill with mortar using a pressure gun like a grease gun. Flat surfaces: chip at least 1 in. deep with edges square; screed so patch projects slightly; let stiffen before troweling
entries.dim: Repair within 24 hr; mortar layers <= 1/2 in.; flat patch >= 1 in. deep
entries.eq: Chisel, grout, mortar, pressure gun, burlap or curing compound

entries.desc: Old concrete repair
entries.use: Patching deteriorated concrete
entries.how: Remove all questionable concrete (it is better to remove too much). Clean cut faces with air/water; keep area wet several hours, preferably overnight. Large members (walls, piers, curbs, slabs): repair at least 6 in. deep if possible. Leave at least 1 in. clearance around exposed rebar. Use rectangular patches, cut 1 to 2 in. vertically to avoid feather edges. Place low-slump concrete in layers, tamp each, let stand to reduce shrinkage; use forms; reinforce deep patches; start curing immediately
entries.dim: Repair depth >= 6 in. if possible; rebar clearance >= 1 in.; cut edges 1-2 in. deep

entries.desc: Beam reinforcement. Concrete shear strength about 1/3 compressive; tensile strength < 1/2 shear strength and is ignored in design
entries.use: Beam rebar layout
entries.how: Put steel in the tension zone (bottom over the middle of the span; top over supports in continuous beams). Straight and bent-up bars resist bending tension; inclined portion of bent-up bars resists diagonal tension near ends. Add stirrups (U-bars) where bent bars cannot resist all diagonal tension; at least one stirrup must cross every potential diagonal tension crack. Vertical stirrups pass under the bottom bars, are tied with one turn of wire, and anchored by welding, tight hooking, or embedding above midline. Support horizontal steel on bolsters/high chairs so it is not on earth or vapor barrier; skids on vapor barrier or wet subbase; metal chairs for two or more levels or when workers walk on rebar
entries.dim: Stirrup hook dimensions in Table 6-3
entries.eq: Rebar, stirrups, bolsters, chairs, tie wire
entries.wn: Do not omit stirrups where diagonal tension cracks can occur

entries.desc: Column reinforcing
entries.use: Column rebar
entries.how: Columns must always be reinforced. Vertical bars carry load and bending (eight bars around periphery in the square tied column example); lateral ties at close intervals restrain bulging; a second tie system confines intermediate bars. Spiral columns (round) are generally stronger than tied columns; engineer specifies spiral pitch, tie size and bar count. Composite column: steel/cast-iron core thoroughly encased, core area not over 20% of gross area. Combination column: structural steel encased at least 2 1/2 in. thick overall with welded-wire fabric. A vertical member with height less than 3 times its least lateral dimension is a pier or pedestal, not a column. Placement: tie column steel as a unit, erect form around it, tie steel to form at 5-ft intervals; clear spacing between parallel column bars not less than 1 1/2 times bar diameter and compatible with maximum aggregate size
entries.dim: Core <= 20% of gross area; encasement >= 2 1/2 in.; column if height >= 3 x least dimension; clearance >= 1 1/2 bar diameters; tie to form every 5 ft
entries.wn: Aggregate must not lodge between form and steel

entries.desc: Slab and wall steel
entries.use: Slabs and walls
entries.how: Slabs and walls are reinforced both vertically (loads) and laterally with wire mesh (shrinkage/temperature). Lateral steel is usually about one-fifth of 1 percent of the concrete cross-sectional area. Slabs: bolster height set by required cover (or sand-cement mortar spacer blocks); tie intersections frequently with one turn of wire. Walls: erect steel in place (do not preassemble unless using wire mesh), tie bars top to bottom on high walls. Footings: spacer bars hold steel above subgrade. Welded-wire fabric is used mainly to control crack widths
entries.dim: Lateral steel about 0.2% (1/5 of 1%) of concrete cross-section
entries.eq: Welded-wire fabric, rebar, bolsters, spacer blocks

entries.n: Reinforcing bar sizes, grades and minimum cover
entries.desc: Rebar data (Table 6-1) and cover (Table 6-2, from ACI 318-83)
entries.use: Selecting and covering rebar
entries.how: Bars are numbered by eighths of an inch of nominal diameter (No. 3 = 3/8 in.). Minimum yield strengths 40,000, 50,000, 60,000 and 75,000 psi (ASTM A615, A616, A617). Grade marks: continuous line = 60,000 psi; number system 40, 50, 60. Minimum concrete cover (in.): cast against and permanently exposed to earth 3; exposed to earth or weather #6-#18 bars 2, #5/W31/D31 wire and smaller 1 1/2; not exposed: slabs/walls/joists #14 and #18 1 1/2, #11 and smaller 3/4; beams/columns primary reinforcement, ties, stirrups, spirals 1 1/2; exposed to salt water 4. Provide cover at bottom, sides and top
entries.dim: Bar No. 3-18: dia 0.375 to 2.257 in.; weight .376 to 13.60 lb/ft; see table. Yield 40/50/60/75 ksi

entries.desc: Bar bending rules
entries.use: Cold-bending bars on site
entries.how: Cold-bend stirrups and ties under 1/2 in. dia. and bars up to 3/8 in.; heat usually only for bars over 1 1/8 in. Bend around pins at least 6 bar diameters (8 bar diameters for hooks and straight bars over 1 in.). Bars over 3/8 in. are better bent on a bar-bending machine, hickey or bar-bending table, but those bends may be too sharp and weaken the bar. Improvised hickey: 2 x 1 1/2 x 2 in. pipe tee on the end of a 3-ft, 1 1/4-in. pipe lever with a section sawn from one side of the tee. Hook sizes per Table 6-3
entries.dim: Pin diameter >= 6 bar diameters; >= 8 for hooks/straight bars over 1 in.; lever 3 ft of 1 1/4-in. pipe
entries.wn: Sharp bends weaken the bar

entries.desc: Splice overlap in inches (top bars / all others) by bar No. and f'c: see Table 6-4. Example No. 5: 36 / 26 at all f'c; No. 8 at 3,000 psi: 82 / 59
entries.use: Lengthening rebar runs
entries.how: Lap bars; never butt them. Lap length is about 24 to 36 bar diameters; minimum lap for plain bars is twice that for deformed bars. Do not splice without engineer approval except as on plans; never at points of maximum bending; best beyond the beam center; stagger splices. Every bar needs at least two supports with bolsters at about 5-ft spacing. Lap horizontally if aggregate can pass; avoid the simple contact lap in beams, closely spaced bars, where cover is impaired or while form filling
entries.dim: Lap 24-36 bar diameters; supports at about 5 ft
entries.wn: Class C splice, normal-weight concrete; top bar = horizontal bar with 12 in. or more fresh concrete below

entries.desc: Rebar storage and support
entries.use: Rebar care and placement
entries.how: Remove oil, paint, grease, dried mud, weak mortar, and heavy corrosion before outdoor storage; a thin film of rust or mill scale is acceptable; rub loose rust with burlap; cover the steel. Place steel accurately and hold firmly with concrete blocks, metal bolsters and chairs, spacer bars, wires. Never use rocks or wood blocks. Support horizontal bars at 5 to 6 ft minimum intervals; tie with wire not smaller than 18 gage, twisted ends pointing away from the surface. Minimum clearance between parallel bars in beams, footings, walls and slabs: not less than 1 1/3 x largest aggregate, never less than 1 in. Spacer blocks: mortar same consistency as concrete without CA, 1 1/2 in. square or larger, with cast-in tie wire; leave them in
entries.dim: Support spacing 5-6 ft; tie wire >= 18 gage; bar clearance >= 1 1/3 x max aggregate and >= 1 in.; spacer blocks >= 1 1/2 in. square
entries.eq: Burlap, tie wire, bolsters, spacer blocks
entries.wn: Anything that breaks the concrete-steel bond (oil, grease, mud) is a serious problem. Wood blocks rot and let water in

entries.desc: Precast concrete; prestressed concrete is stressed before external loads. Tilt-up: cast wall flat, tilt up. Lift-slab: cast slabs flat then jack up
entries.use: Precasting beams, walls, logs
entries.how: Precast pieces fit like a jigsaw so layout must be accurate. On-site precasting is not recommended without experienced supervision. Prefabrication yard on firm level ground with working space and access. Output about 6,000 sq ft of precast walls per day. Erect with cranes/derricks of enough capacity, spreader bars at the correct pickup points. Haul with adequate support so members are not overstressed. Hollow-core slabs 16 to 96 in. wide, 4 to 12 in. deep; short members 30 ft or less often use ordinary rebar
entries.dim: Team (Table 6-5): reinforcement shop and steel storage 1 NCO + 4 EM; workshop 2 EM; casting/curing/finishing/placing reinforcement/refurbishing forms 2 NCO + 13 EM; mixing and water/cement/aggregate storage 1 NCO + 5 EM; product stockpile loading/distribution 2 EM
entries.tm: About 6,000 sq ft of precast wall per day

entries.desc: Basic tool dimensions
entries.use: Masonry tool selection
entries.how: Trowel: common up to about 11 in. long, 4-8 in. wide (short wide best); pointing/striking trowels 3-6 in. long, 2-3 in. wide. Chisel/bolster 2 1/2 to 4 1/2 in. wide. Mason hammer 1 1/2 to 3 1/2 lb. Jointers (rounded, flat, pointed). Square for right angles. Mason level 42-48 in. (bubble centered in center tube = level; bubbles in two end tubes when vertical = plumb). Straightedge up to 16 ft long, 1 1/8 to 1 1/2 in. thick, middle top edge 6-10 in. wide, to extend a level. Also shovels, mortar hoes, wheelbarrows, chalk lines, plumb bobs, 200-ft ball of mason line. Mortar board 3 to 4 ft square: wet it, mound mortar in center, keep outer edges clean. Clean all tools and mortar boxes daily
entries.dim: See practical use
entries.eq: Trowel, chisel, hammer, jointer, square, level, straightedge, line, mortar box/board
entries.wn: Hardened mortar is difficult to remove

entries.n: Select mortar type (M, S, N, O)
entries.desc: Mortar proportions by volume. Convert to weight: masonry cement per bag weight; portland cement 94 lb/cu ft; hydrated lime 50 lb/cu ft; damp loose sand 85 lb/cu ft
entries.use: Mortar mixes by volume
entries.how: Type M: 1 portland cement : 1/4 hydrated lime (or lime putty) : 3 sand, or 1 portland : 1 Type II masonry cement : 6 sand; general use, best below grade (foundations, retaining walls, walks). Type S: 1 portland : 1/2 lime : 4 1/2 sand, or 1/2 portland : 1 Type II masonry cement : 4 1/2 sand; high resistance to lateral forces. Type N: 1 portland : 1 lime : 6 sand, or 1 Type II masonry cement : 3 sand; above-grade exposed masonry where high strength not needed. Type O: 1 portland : 2 lime : 9 sand, or 1 Type I or II masonry cement : 3 sand; load-bearing solid-unit walls with compressive stress not over 100 psi and no freeze-thaw with lots of moisture. Ordinary service (Table 7-1): 1 unit masonry or portland cement : 1/2 to 1 1/4 lime : 4 1/2 to 6 damp loose sand. Piers under extreme load/wind/quake/frost: 1 masonry cement + 1 portland cement (or 1 portland) : 0 to 1/4 lime : 4 1/2 to 6 sand
entries.dim: M 1:1/4:3; S 1:1/2:4 1/2; N 1:1:6; O 1:2:9. Sand 2 1/4 to 3 times sum of cement + lime volumes (Table 7-1)
entries.eq: Mortar box, hoe, shovel, mortar sand, cement, lime
entries.wn: Use sand in damp loose condition for volume proportions

entries.desc: Mortar mixing
entries.use: Mixing masonry mortar
entries.how: Machine: dry ingredients into drum mixer first, mix 1 minute dry, then add water; mix minimum 3 minutes. Hand: mix all dry materials together in a mortar box first, then add water; keep a steel drum of water near and a second drum to store shovels and hoes. With lime putty: machine, measure putty in a pail and place on top of sand in skip; hand, add sand to lime putty. Use water that meets concrete water standards (no large amounts of dissolved salts: efflorescence). Store mortar materials dry; cover sand and lime
entries.dim: Dry mix 1 min; total mixing minimum 3 min
entries.eq: Drum mixer or mortar box, hoes, shovels, water drum

entries.desc: Mortar working times
entries.use: Mortar working time and cold weather
entries.how: Use mortar within 2 1/2 hours of mixing when air is 80 F or higher, and within 3 1/2 hours when below 80 F; retemper by remixing with water only for mortar stiffened by evaporation; discard anything stiffened by initial set or past these limits. Never use frozen mortar. Do not use antifreeze admixtures. Accelerator: trial mix; calcium chloride not over 2 percent by weight of cement (1 percent for masonry cement); not for steel-reinforced masonry. For repair and tuck-pointing use Table 7-1 mixes and tool joints after partial stiffening
entries.dim: 2 1/2 hr (80 F or higher); 3 1/2 hr (below 80 F); CaCl <= 2% (1% masonry cement)
entries.wn: Freezing destroys mortar bond. Wet brick before laying but never wet concrete masonry units

entries.desc: Scaffold dimensions
entries.use: Working at height on masonry walls
entries.how: Use rough lumber, nail securely, remove lower planks when no longer needed. Trestle scaffold: start when wall is 4-5 ft high; trestles 4 to 4 1/2 ft high; 2x10 planks; trestle at least 3 in. from the wall. Foot scaffold: 2x10 planks on blocks on the trestle scaffold; not over 18 in. high. Putlog scaffold: 4x4 uprights on 2x12x12 bearing plank, on 8-ft centers, 4 1/2 ft from wall; putlogs 3x4 in. lumber, one end in wall (one brick omitted), other on ledger, not fastened; five 2x12 planks on top, not nailed to putlogs; tie with stays (spring stays of two 2x6) or wedge putlog; longitudinal cross bracing. Outrigger scaffold: beam from window sill supporting 2x10 planks (steel beam: threaded U-bolts to formwork). Use prefabricated steel scaffold if available. Materials tower: footing two 2x12x2 ft under each 4x4 post; tower at least 15 ft above highest landing; 6 ft 8 in. clearance for 5-ft platforms; landings of 2x10 or 2x12
entries.dim: See practical use
entries.wn: Lives depend on scaffolds; build with extreme care

entries.desc: Concrete block data
entries.use: Choosing concrete masonry units
entries.how: Standard nominal block 8x8x16 in. (actual 7 5/8 x 7 5/8 x 15 5/8) occupies exactly 8x8x16 with 3/8 in. joints. Solid block: core area not over 25% of gross area; hollow: over 25% (generally 40-50%). Load-bearing grades: N (general use, exterior above/below grade, back-up, interior) and S (above-grade exterior with protective coating, interior); Type I moisture-controlled (arid climates) N-I, S-I; Type II non-moisture-controlled N-II, S-II. Hollow load-bearing 8x8x16: 40-50 lb with heavyweight aggregate (sand, gravel, crushed stone, air-cooled slag); 25-35 lb with lightweight aggregate (cinders, expanded shale, clay, slag, volcanic cinders, pumice)
entries.dim: Nominal 8x8x16; actual 7 5/8 x 7 5/8 x 15 5/8; joint 3/8 in.; solid core <= 25%; hollow 40-50%; weight 40-50 lb heavy, 25-35 lb light

entries.desc: Block making and curing
entries.use: Casting blocks in the field
entries.how: By machine: tamp dry-enough mix in a power-tamping machine, strip mold immediately. By hand: pour fluid concrete into iron molds, strip when hardened (dense, many molds). Weather-exposed blocks: at least 6 sacks cement per cu yd; premix lightweight porous aggregate with water 2 minutes before adding cement. Cure: wet steam at 125 F for 15 hours gives 70 percent of 28-day strength; without steam protect from sun and keep damp for 7 days
entries.dim: >= 6 sacks/cu yd; premix 2 min; steam 125 F for 15 hr = 70% of 28-day strength; damp cure 7 days
entries.eq: Tamping machine or iron molds, steam or damp cover

entries.n: Plan masonry walls on the 4-inch module
entries.desc: Modular planning; Table 8-3: weights/quantities per 100 sq ft of wall (3/8 in. joints; actual wall weight = W x n + 150 x M; mortar quantities include 10% waste)
entries.use: Wall layout to avoid cutting blocks
entries.how: Modular grid is 4 in. Keep horizontal dimensions in multiples of the nominal full-length unit (and 8 in. half-length); vertical dimensions in multiples of 8 in. (4 in. with 8x4x16 blocks). Use full and half units; window/door frames modular. Use Tables 8-1, 8-2 for lengths and heights. Wall length actual = nominal minus 3/8 in. Course height measured center to center of mortar joints. Drawing scale not less than 3/4 in. = 1 ft to show 4-in. grid
entries.dim: 4-in. module; 8-in. course; 3/8-in. joints; 112.5 units/100 sq ft for 8-in. high block; 225 units/100 sq ft for 4-in. high block

entries.n: Footings, drainage and parging for block walls
entries.desc: Foundation block wall details
entries.use: Block wall foundations and basements
entries.how: Footings on firm undisturbed soil below frost, normally twice as wide as the wall thickness (footing thickness equals wall width). Drain tile along exterior footing where groundwater may reach basement floor: fall at least 1/2 in. in 12 ft, roofing felt over joints, cover 12 in. deep with 1 to 1 1/2 in. coarse gravel or crushed stone. Parging: two 1/4-in. coats of portland cement mortar 1:2 1/2 by volume (or joint mortar); fog-dampen in hot dry weather; roughen first coat; wait 24 hr, dampen, apply second coat and keep damp at least 48 hr; very wet soils add two coats of bituminous mastic over primer when dry. Do not backfill until first floor is in place. Support floor beams on solid courses or cores filled with concrete or mortar (with expanded metal lath in bed joint under mortar fill)
entries.dim: Footing width = 2 x wall thickness; drain fall 1/2 in. per 12 ft; gravel 1-1 1/2 in., 12 in. deep; parging 2 x 1/4 in., 1:2 1/2; first coat 24 hr; keep 2nd coat damp 48 hr
entries.eq: Drain tile, felt, gravel, parging mortar, bituminous mastic
entries.tm: Parge coats 24 hr apart; damp-cure 48 hr
entries.wn: Do not backfill before first floor is in place

entries.n: Lay the first course and corners of a block wall
entries.desc: First course and corner leads
entries.use: Concrete block wall start
entries.how: Locate corners; dry-lay the first course without mortar and snap a chalk line. Replace with a full mortar bed, furrowed with the trowel. Position the corner block first; lay the rest thicker end up; butter ends of several blocks on end in one operation; joints 3/8 in. thick; push each block down and against previous block. Check with level after 3-4 blocks; tap with trowel handle to grade and plumb. Corners: build 4-5 courses high, each course stepped back one-half block; mortar only the tops of previous blocks and the vertical joints; check every block with level or straightedge; use a story (course) pole marked every 8 in.; check spacing by placing a level diagonally across the corners
entries.dim: Joint 3/8 in.; corner lead 4-5 courses; course pole marks 8 in
entries.eq: Chalk line, trowel, mason level, story pole
entries.wn: The first course must be aligned, level and plumb or all succeeding courses will be off

entries.n: Lay blocks between corners and set closure blocks
entries.desc: Block wall courses and joints
entries.use: Filling in a block wall
entries.how: Stretch a mason line along the outer block edges from corner to corner each course. Tip the block toward you, set its lower edge on the course below, lay the top outside edge to the line, and tap level with trowel handle. Make adjustments only while mortar is soft; later adjustment breaks the bond and lets water in. Closure block: butter both edges of the opening and all four vertical edges of the block, lower in carefully; if mortar falls out leaving an open joint, remove and redo. Do not spread mortar too far ahead; joint thickness about 3/8 in.; trim excess with trowel and reuse it (not dead mortar from scaffold or floor). Tool joints when thumbprint hard: concave or V tool, vertical joints first, then horizontal with long jointer; trim burrs with trowel, soft brush or burlap
entries.dim: Joint 3/8 in
entries.tm: Tool when mortar is thumbprint hard
entries.wn: Do not rework dead mortar

entries.n: Anchor bolts, control joints and intersections in block walls
entries.desc: Block wall details
entries.use: Wood plates, movement joints, tying walls
entries.how: Plates on hollow block: metal lath in the second mortar joint from top under bolt cores; 1/2-in. dia x 18-in. anchor bolts, max 4 ft apart; insert in cores of top two courses and fill with concrete or mortar; thread projects above wall. Control joints: continuous vertical joints from full and half blocks; rake out stiff mortar about 3/4 in. deep and caulk with a thin flat trowel; or insert building paper/roofing felt in end cores. Intersecting bearing walls: no masonry bond except corners; end one wall at the face of the other with control joint; tie with Z-shaped metal tie bars 1/4 x 1 1/4 x 28 in. with 2-in. right-angle bends, max 4 ft apart vertically, metal lath under cores, filled with mortar/concrete. Nonbearing: metal lath or 1/4-in. mesh galvanized hardware cloth across the joint in alternate courses. Lintels: precast or steel angle with offset; noncorroding metal plate under ends at control joints and full mortar bed. Precast sills after wall; fill end joints with mortar or caulk
entries.dim: Anchor bolt 1/2 in. x 18 in., spacing <= 4 ft; tie bars 1/4 x 1 1/4 x 28 in., 2-in. bends, <= 4 ft apart; control joint rake 3/4 in
entries.eq: Metal lath, anchor bolts, caulk, Z ties, lintels
entries.wn: Do not smear mortar into block face; hardened smears cannot be removed even with acid wash and paint will not cover them. Chip dried droppings with broken block piece or trowel

entries.desc: Rubble stone masonry
entries.use: Random or coursed rubble masonry
entries.how: Use strong durable stones (limestone, sandstone, granite, slate); none larger than two persons can handle easily; varied sizes need less mortar. Mortar per Table 7-1 (use white portland cement to prevent staining). Lay each stone on its broadest face, larger stones low; moisten porous stones; pack tightly and fill voids with small stones and mortar. Random rubble: bed joints horizontal, head joints any direction. Footings use the largest stones, as long as the footing is wide, in a mortar bed about 2 in. deep. Make head joints after laying three or four stones. One bonding stone (through the whole wall) for every 6 to 10 sq ft of wall; offset head joints. Lay out by eye for rough walls; by line with wood corner posts if exact
entries.dim: Bed under footing stones about 2 in.; 1 through-stone per 6-10 sq ft
entries.wn: Do not spread mortar too far ahead. If a stone is removed, lift it clear and reset it

entries.n: Brick sizes, types and field absorption test
entries.desc: Brick facts
entries.use: Choosing and preparing bricks
entries.how: Standard US brick 2 1/4 x 3 3/4 x 8 in.; modular US 2 2/3 x 4 x 8 nominal; English 3 x 4 1/2 x 9; Roman 1 1/2 x 4 x 12; Norman 2 3/4 x 4 x 12. Weight 100-150 lb/cu ft. Solid or cored (cores not over 25%). Types: building (common), face, clinker, pressed, glazed, fire, cored (ten holes), sand-lime. Brick compressive strength 1,600 to over 15,000 psi; cement-lime mortar brick wall working strength normally 500 to 600 psi. Field absorption test: put 20 drops of water in a 1-in. circle (quarter size); if absorbed in under 1 1/2 minutes the brick will suck water from mortar; wet thoroughly and let surfaces air-dry before laying. Wet bricks just before laying in warm weather: better bond, washes dust, even spread, proper cement hydration
entries.dim: Brick sizes as listed; 20 drops / 1 in. circle / 1 1/2 min; 100-150 lb/cu ft

entries.desc: Brick wall performance
entries.use: Fire, weather, expansion and sound
entries.how: Walls up to 200 ft long need no expansion joints; longer walls need one expansion joint per 200 ft. Fire resistance (Table 9-1, cement-lime mortar, at least 1/2 in. of 1:3 sanded gypsum plaster for rating): 4-in. solid clay 1 1/4 hr (no plaster); 8-in. solid clay 5 hr; 12-in. solid clay 10 hr. Good brickwork resists 24-hr rain with 50-60 mph wind. Fill joints solidly (slushing does not), tool concave before setting, caulk around windows and doors. Sound insulation little improved beyond 10-12 in. thickness; cavity walls better. Solid brick gives little thermal insulation; cavity wall or hollow clay tile backing is better
entries.dim: Expansion joint every 200 ft; fire ratings Table 9-1

entries.n: Choose a brick bond and use metal ties
entries.desc: Masonry bonds: structural, mortar, pattern
entries.use: Bond pattern selection
entries.how: Running bond: all stretchers, ties form the structural bond (cavity, veneer). Common/American bond: header course every 5th, 6th or 7th course; three-quarter closure at corner of each header course. Flemish: alternating headers and stretchers per course; Dutch corner starts with three-quarter closure, English corner with 2-in. or quarter closure; blind headers where headers not needed. English bond: alternating courses of headers and stretchers; stretcher joints do not align. English cross/Dutch: like English but stretcher joints align vertically. Stack bond: pattern only; use rigid steel ties or 8-in. stretcher units; pencil rods in horizontal joints for large or load-bearing walls. Use metal ties where there are no header courses
entries.dim: Header course every 5th-7th course (common bond)

entries.desc: Flashing
entries.use: Moisture control in brick walls
entries.how: Flash under sills and copings, at wall-to-horizontal surface intersections (roof, parapet, chimney), above openings, often at floor lines. Flashing extends through the wall face and turns down to form a drip. Provide weep holes every 18 to 24 in. Concealed flashing with tooled joints can trap water and do more harm than good
entries.dim: Weep holes 18-24 in. apart

entries.n: Lay brick: mortar spreading and bed/head joints
entries.desc: Brick joints
entries.use: Bricklaying procedure
entries.how: Mortar joint 1/4 in. is strongest (up to 1/2 in. for irregular brick). Spread bed mortar only 4-5 bricks ahead, about 1 in. thick, make a shallow furrow (deep furrow leaves a gap). Cut off projecting mortar with a smooth stroke. Butter the end of the brick, push it into place so mortar squeezes out of head joint and sides; head joint must be full. To insert a brick in a gap: thick bed, shove until mortar squeezes out of all four joints. Headers: spread bed several bricks ahead, mortar the face of the header. Closure brick: about 1 in. mortar on the side of the existing brick and both sides of closure; lay without disturbing neighbors (relay any disturbed). Slush joints are not acceptable. Pick up mortar for 1 to 5 bricks per trowel load; hold trowel with thumb on top
entries.dim: Joint 1/4 in. best, up to 1/2 in.; bed 1 in. thick before bedding; spread 4-5 bricks ahead
entries.wn: Mortar spread too far dries and bonds poorly; disturbed brick leaves cracks that let moisture in

entries.desc: Brick cutting and joint finishes
entries.use: Cutting and tooling
entries.how: Exact cuts: bolster or brick set, straight side of edge facing the part to save and the bricklayer, one hammer blow; for hard brick rough-cut first. Normal cuts: score a line around the brick with light blows, then a sharp blow to one side splits it; trim with hammer blade. Tool joints before mortar hardens too much: concave (jointer slightly larger than joint, press tight on both sides; very weather tight), flush (trowel nearly parallel, draw point along joint), weather (push down on mortar with top edge of trowel to shed water). Unfinished flush-cut joints crack immediately
entries.eq: Bolster, brick set, brick hammer, jointer

entries.desc: Brick wall footing
entries.use: Brick wall footings
entries.how: Qualified engineer sets footing for high or heavily loaded walls; footing below frost line. Ordinary one-story building with 8-in. wall: footing 16 in. wide and about 8 in. thick, normally concrete leveled on top. Place a mortar bed about 1 in. thick on the prepared subgrade, lay first foundation course on it
entries.dim: 8-in. wall: 16 in. wide x 8 in. thick; mortar bed 1 in

entries.n: Lay out and lay an 8-inch common-bond brick wall
entries.desc: Common-bond wall sequence. Example height calc: 2 1/4 in. brick + 1/2 in. joint = 2 3/4 in./course; sill at 4 ft 4 1/4 in. needs 19 courses
entries.use: Solid 8-in. brick wall
entries.how: Dry-lay bricks without mortar on the foundation, space equally; head joint width = the gap (adjust so a whole or half number of bricks fits). Use course height Tables 9-2 to 9-4 (2 1/4-in. brick with 3/8, 1/2 or 5/8 in. joints). Build corner leads first, 6 or 7 courses or to the next header course. First course is a header course: 1-in. mortar bed; two three-quarter closures with 1/2-in. bed joint, 1-in. head joint; exterior edges flush with foundation face; check level in two positions; 12 header bricks in first course of lead (six each side of the closures). Second course (stretcher): 1-in. bed, shallow furrow, 1/2-in. joint, 7 bricks; plumb the corner. Do not move brick once laid. Build the opposite lead to the same course heights using a 2x2 course pole. Between leads: nails in cross joints, line positioned 1/16 in. outside face and level with brick top, set brick top 1/16 in. behind line (do not crowd). Lay face tier to the second header course (normally five stretcher courses), then backup tier, then header course; raise leads six more courses and repeat. 8-in. wall needs no line for backup brick; 12-in. wall uses two tiers of backup with a line for the inside tier and two overlapping header courses first. Cover tops of walls every night with boards or tarps held by loose bricks. For long walls build a third lead and use a trig to keep the line from sagging
entries.dim: Mortar bed 1 in.; bed joint 1/2 in.; head joint 1 in. on closure; line 1/16 in. off face; header course every 5th-7th course
entries.eq: Trowel, level, line and line pins, nails, trig, 2x2 course pole
entries.wn: Mason level in several places; finish joints before mortar hardens

entries.desc: Openings and lintels
entries.use: Openings in brick walls
entries.how: Find sill height; courses = height / (brick + joint) (e.g., 4 ft 4 1/4 in. / 2 3/4 in. = 19 courses); adjust joint thickness so last course top is no more than 1/4 in. above the window frame top; mark courses on the frame. Rowlock sill course pitched down away from window, takes two courses of height; tool joints watertight. Place frame when mortar sets, brace firmly until masonry about 1/3 of the way up the frame (assumed meaning of printed text), keep braces for several days. Door frames: lay half-closure sized wood blocks in mortar for nails/screws. Lintels: steel, precast reinforced concrete, or wood (avoid wood; not over 3 ft span because it burns out). Lintel rests on the last course, sides bedded in mortar, 1/4-in. angles fit the 1/2-in. joint between face and backing ties. Table 9-5 lintel sizes
entries.dim: Lintel angle 1/4 in. thick; wood lintel span <= 3 ft; joint 1/2 in. (example)
entries.eq: Window/door frames, lintels, wood blocks, braces

entries.desc: Corbeling and arches
entries.use: Projecting courses and arches
entries.how: Corbel: no course projects more than 2 in. beyond the course below; total projection not greater than wall thickness; use headers as much as possible (first projecting course may be a stretcher); fill all joints; consult an engineer for large loads. Arch: full mortar joints, narrower at bottom but never under 1/4 in.; build over a wood template (3/4 in. plywood for spans up to 6 ft, two curved pieces nailed to 2x2 spacers) held on wedges until mortar sets; use an odd number of bricks so the key brick falls at the crown and is laid last; trial-lay bricks around the template and adjust count/joint spacing (not under 1/4 in.)
entries.dim: Corbel step <= 2 in.; arch joint >= 1/4 in.; template plywood 3/4 in. for spans <= 6 ft
entries.wn: Do not let the arch bulge out of position

entries.desc: Waterproofing brick walls
entries.use: Waterproofing brick
entries.how: Water enters through cracks between brick and mortar, mainly head joints. Do not move brick after mortar starts to set; wet high-suction brick in hot weather; tool joints concave; fill all head and bed joints. Parging: plaster the back of the face tier not less than 3/8 in. of rich cement mortar, cutting all joints flush first. Use a membrane where water pressure is high. French drain or tile drain around base; without tile use an 8-in. layer of coarse loose rock. Repair cracks: chip out mortar full width of crack about 2 in. deep, scrub with clean water, coat with thick-liquid cement mortar, fill with prehydrated mortar. Coatings: two coats bituminous mastic on below-grade exterior; sodium silicate solution or other waterproof paints above grade; Type 2 Class A portland-cement paint on walls at least 30 days old after removing efflorescence and dampening
entries.dim: Parge >= 3/8 in.; crack chase depth about 2 in.; French drain 8 in.; cement paint wall age >= 30 days

entries.n: Lay fire brick and silica brick
entries.desc: Fire-resistant brick
entries.use: Furnace and incinerator linings
entries.how: Fire brick standard size 9 x 4 1/2 x 2 1/2 in. Store dry. Mortar = fire clay (from ground used fire brick) and water, thick-cream consistency. Dip the brick in mortar covering all surfaces except the top bed, tap firmly with bricklayer hammer, joints as thin as possible, stagger head joints with one-half-brick lap. Silica brick: lay without mortar, fit so close they fuse at the joints; do not use if alternately heated and cooled; incinerators usually use fire brick
entries.dim: Fire brick 9 x 4 1/2 x 2 1/2 in.; lap 1/2 brick
entries.wn: Heat leaking through cracks damages outer shell

entries.n: Build cavity, rowlock and partition brick walls
entries.desc: Hollow walls
entries.use: Hollow brick walls
entries.how: Cavity wall: two wythes with a 2-in. air space; metal ties every sixth course on 24-in. centers, sloped downward from inner to outer tier; cavity bottom above ground; weep holes (mortar left out of vertical joints) in the first exterior course about 24 in. apart. Rowlock wall: 2-in. cavity; face tier common bond with a full header course every seventh course and backing bricks on edge; all-rowlock: both tiers on edge, header course every fourth course (three rowlock courses per header); less watertight than cavity. Partition: single 4-in. wythe without headers. Erect corner leads first, use a line
entries.dim: Cavity 2 in.; ties every 6th course at 24 in.; weep holes about 24 in.; header every 7th course (rowlock) or 4th (all rowlock)

entries.desc: Manhole
entries.use: Brick manhole walls
entries.how: About 4 ft diameter is satisfactory for small straight-line sewers; circular or oval. Bottom normally concrete, walls brick. 8-in. wall OK for manholes up to 8 ft diameter and under 15 ft deep; engineer must design deeper than 15 ft. 8-in. wall: all headers, no line; check each course level with a level on a straight 2x4 across; 1-in. mortar bed on foundation. Corbel inward to fit frame and cover, no brick more than 2 in. beyond the one below. Wrought-iron steps about every 15 in. vertically in cross joints. Plaster outside at least 3/8 in. thick with the laying mortar. 1-in. mortar bed for the frame
entries.dim: 4 ft diameter; 8 in. wall limit 8 ft dia x 15 ft deep; steps 15 in.; plaster >= 3/8 in

entries.desc: Beam bearing
entries.use: Beam bearing on brick
entries.how: Wood beam: tie to wall, keep mortar away (dry rot if encased), use a beam box, cut the end at an angle so it falls without damaging the wall in a fire; in 8- or 12-in. walls bear on the full inside tier width. Steel beam: steel bearing plate set in mortar under the beam, sized to the beam and load

entries.desc: Tuck-pointing
entries.use: Repairing mortar joints
entries.how: Cut out loose or disintegrated mortar to at least 1/2 in. deep using a chisel with about 1/2-in. cutting edge; brush or water-jet out dust; moisten joints (not needed after water jet). Mortar: prehydrated portland-cement-lime Type S, or prehydrated mix from Type II masonry cement.
