Mix dry ingredients with only enough water to make a damp mass that holds a ball; let stand 1 to 2 hours; remix to stiff but workable. Pack in thin layers about 1/4 in. thick, tool to smooth concave surface, pushing in one direction to avoid air pockets
entries.dim: Cut-out depth >= 1/2 in.; chisel edge about 1/2 in.; stand 1-2 hr; layers 1/4 in
entries.eq: Chisel, pointing trowel and tool, brush or water jet

entries.desc: Brick cleaning
entries.use: Removing stains and efflorescence
entries.how: New brick: remove large mortar with putty knife or chisel; acid solution 1 part commercial muriatic acid to 9 parts water (acid into water, never water into acid); soak masonry first; apply with long-handled stiff-fiber brush to 15-20 sq ft, then wash immediately with clear water; protect frames. Efflorescence: scrub with water and stiff brush, then the acid solution. Old brick: sandblasting (canvas screen; leaves rough surface; may need repointing; waterproof after; never on glazed surfaces); steam cleaning 140-150 psi, about 12 hp boiler per nozzle, nozzle over no more than 3 sq ft at a time then rinse; additives sodium carbonate, sodium bicarbonate or trisodium phosphate. Whitewash/paint coatings: 1 part acid to 5 parts water, scrub while foaming, rinse until acid is gone. Paint removers: 2 lb trisodium phosphate per gal hot water, or 1 1/2 lb caustic soda per gal hot water. Iron stain: 7 parts lime-free glycerin into 1 part sodium citrate in 6 parts lukewarm water, thickened with whiting or kieselguhr. Tobacco: 2 lb trisodium phosphate in 5 qt water mixed with 12 oz chloride of lime paste, clear liquid diluted 1:1, mixed with talc. Smoke: trichlorethylene and powdered talc paste (well ventilated only)
entries.dim: Acid 1:9 (new brick); 1:5 (paint removal); steam 140-150 psi; 15-20 sq ft per acid scrub; 3 sq ft per steam pass
entries.eq: Muriatic acid, stiff brushes, sandblaster, steam boiler
entries.wn: Wear goggles; keep acid off hands, arms and clothing. Acid must be added to water, not water to acid. Trichlorethylene fumes are harmful

entries.desc: Flashing installation
entries.use: Flashing at windows, roofs, chimneys
entries.how: Flashing may be copper (best; stains masonry, use lead-coated copper if staining unacceptable), lead, aluminum or bituminous roofing paper (cheapest, shorter life). Corrugated copper bonds well with mortar and makes interlocking watertight laps. Install at head and sill of windows and at wall-roof intersections, edges turned up; always set in mortar joints. Drainage: 1/4-in. cotton-rope wicks at 18-in. spacing in the joint just above flashing, or dowels removed later to form holes. At chimneys flashing goes completely through the chimney wall and turns up 1 in. against the flue lining. Steps: 1/2-in. mortar bed on brick, press flashing in, another 1/2-in. bed on the flashing, then lay brick or sill. Under steel lintel flashing goes under the face tier, then behind it and over the lintel top. At roof-wall intersection caulk upper end into raggle block groove
entries.dim: Mortar bed 1/2 in.; wicks 1/4 in. at 18 in.; chimney turn-up 1 in
entries.eq: Copper/lead/aluminum flashing, mortar, rope wicks or dowels, caulk

entries.desc: Cold-weather masonry
entries.use: Masonry below 40 F
entries.how: Cover all masonry units and mortar materials with tarps or building paper on plank platforms off the ground. Heat water and sand to no more than 160 F; mortar at use must be 70 to 120 F; steel mortar boxes raised about 1 ft for heating. Never add salt water to mortar. If air is below 40 F, brick must be above 40 F on both sides of the masonry for at least 48 hours (Type M or S mortar) or 72 hours (Type N); with high-early-strength cement 24 and 48 hours. Preheat masonry units to about 40 F when outside temperature is below 18 F. Sprinkle high-suction brick with warm water just before laying below freezing. Never lay on snow- or ice-covered mortar beds. Keep wall tops covered; remove ice and snow with live steam
entries.dim: Heat water/sand <= 160 F; mortar 70-120 F; brick >40 F for 48 h (M/S) or 72 h (N); high-early cement 24/48 h; preheat units to 40 F below 18 F air
entries.eq: Tarps, steel mortar box, heaters, live steam
entries.wn: Frozen mortar loses bond; never use salt water

entries.desc: Brick quantity rates
entries.use: Wall materials takeoff
entries.how: Use Table 9-6 (1/2-in. joint): per 100 sq ft of wall, 4-in. wall 617 bricks / 8 cu ft mortar; 8-in. 1,233 / 20; 12-in. 1,849 / 32; 16-in. 2,465 / 44. Per 1 sq ft: 6.17, 12.33, 18.49, 24.65 bricks. A 3/8-in. joint uses 80% of these quantities; a 5/8-in. joint 120%
entries.dim: See Table 9-6; 3/8-in. joint = 80%; 5/8-in. joint = 120%

entries.desc: Reinforced brick
entries.use: Brick walls, columns, beams, lintels with steel
entries.how: Brick compressive strength at least 2,500 psi; use Type N mortar; tie steel with 18-gage soft-annealed iron wire; avoid high-grade steel. Joints 1/8 in. thicker than bar diameter (1/16 in. mortar around bar). Horizontal bars laid in mortar bed then covered with mortar; Z-shaped stirrups; vertical bars held by drilled wood templates or wired to horizontal bars. Minimum center-to-center bar spacing 1 1/2 x bar diameter. Cover at least 1 1/2 in. of mortar or brick; 3/8-in. hoops or ties at every course in columns. Corner-lead bars extend 15 in.; wall horizontal bars overlap 15 in. Beams: form under the bottom only, cut short 1/4 in. where meeting walls, leave at least 10 days before removing. Beam width = wall thickness (4, 8, 12, 16 in.), depth not over about 3 times width; first course on form with full head joints no bed joint; bed 1/8 in. thicker than bar; lay all brick of a course before the next. Lintels: bars 3/8 in. or smaller to keep 1/2-in. joint, placed in first and fourth mortar joints above opening, extending 15 in. into wall each side. Bars per opening width: 6 ft 2 bars 1/4 in.; 9 ft 3 bars 1/4 in.; 12 ft 3 bars 3/8 in. Footings: first course in mortar bed 1 in. thick; No. 3 bars parallel to wall; dowels tie footing to wall/column
entries.dim: Brick >= 2,500 psi; cover >= 1 1/2 in.; hoops 3/8 in.; lap 15 in.; form stays 10 days; lintel bars Table 9-7
entries.tm: Beam form removal after at least 10 days

entries.desc: Clay tile
entries.use: Hollow clay tile construction
entries.how: Shell at least 3/4 in. thick and web 1/2 in. Side-construction tile has horizontal cells; end-construction has vertical cells. Grades: LB (not exposed, or protected by at least 3 in. of facing) and LBX (exposed). Bed joint end-construction: 1 in. of mortar on the shells only (not webs), spread about 3 ft ahead; head joints plenty of mortar, both hands, joint about 1/2 in.; head joint need not be solid unless weather-exposed. Side-construction: bed 1 in., about 3 ft ahead, no furrow; head joint Method A (mortar on both tile edges) or B (interior shell of bed tile and exterior shell of new unit). 8-in. brick wall with 4-in. tile backing: six stretcher courses between header courses; 4x5x12 tile height = two brick courses + 1/2 in. joint. 8-in. clay tile wall: 8x5x12 tile, half-lap bond, optional 2x5x8 soap at corners. Strength at least 300 psi on cross section; tensile less than 10% of compressive; absorbs up to 16% water for freeze-thaw resistance; weight about 125 lb/cu ft (6-in. wall about 30 lb/sq ft, 12-in. about 45 lb/sq ft); 6-in. partition resists fire 1 hr up to 1,700 F. Use portland-cement-lime or masonry-cement mortar if exposed
entries.dim: Shell >= 3/4 in.; web >= 1/2 in.; joint 1/2 in.; 300 psi min

entries.desc: Selected Appendix A conversions
entries.use: Converting units
entries.how: Inches x 2.54 = cm; feet x 0.305 = m (printed as 0305); yards x 0.914 = m; cu in. x 16.39 = cu cm; cu ft x 0.0283 = cu m; cu yd x 0.765 = cu m; pounds x 0.454 = kg; short tons x 0.907 = metric tons; liters x 0.264 = US gal; cm x 0.0394 = in.; m x 3.28 = ft; kg x 2.20 = lb; sq ft x 0.0929 = sq m; sq in. x 6.45 = sq cm
entries.dim: See practical use

entries.desc: Slump test (Appendix B). Not applicable for aggregates much larger than 2 in
entries.use: Checking concrete consistency
entries.how: Mold: 16-gage galvanized sheet cone 12 in. high, 8 in. diameter base, 4 in. diameter top, open at both ends. Tamping rod 5/8 in. diameter, 24 in. long, bullet-nose tip (radius about 1/4 in.). Sample at mixer or at discharge; scoop repeatedly through the stream; at least five samples from different portions of the pile for paving concrete; remix with shovel. Dampen mold on a flat, moist, nonabsorbent, firm surface; fill in three equal layers, rotating scoops around the rim; tamp each layer 25 strokes spread uniformly, penetrating the underlying layer (bottom layer throughout depth); strike off top with trowel; lift mold straight up without delay and set beside specimen. Place the rod across the top of the mold and measure from the rod to the displaced original center of the top surface = slump. If it shears off to one side, discard and retest; two consecutive shear failures mean the mix lacks plasticity and cohesiveness. Then tap the side gently: a good mix slowly slumps and keeps its shape; a poor mix crumbles and segregates
entries.dim: Cone 12 in. high x 8 in. base x 4 in. top; rod 5/8 in. x 24 in.; 3 layers x 25 strokes; 5 samples
entries.eq: Slump cone, tamping rod, scoop, trowel
entries.wn: Disregard sheared tests
entries.src: TM 3-34.44 Appendix B, B-1 to B-7

entries.desc: Field FSM estimate
entries.use: Estimating free surface moisture for mix adjustment
entries.how: Take a sample 6 to 8 in. below the surface of the pile; squeeze a handful and open the hand. Damp sand (0-2% FSM): falls apart (damper clings more). Wet sand (3-4% FSM): clings together without free water. Very wet sand (5-8% FSM): ball glistens or sparkles and may drip. Percentage approximates water by weight on the sand; reduce added water accordingly
entries.dim: 0-2%, 3-4%, 5-8% FSM categories; sample depth 6-8 in
entries.wn: Estimate is judgmental
entries.src: TM 3-34.44 Appendix C, C-1 to C-3

entries.n: Wall height stack-up for 8-ft platform-framed wall
entries.desc: Western (platform) framing uses a single bottom plate and a double top plate. A precut 2x4x8 stud is 92 5/8 in long; with plates the wall is 97 1/8 in. The extra 1 1/8 in beyond 8 ft lets sheathing be applied to ceiling and walls while leaving a gap at the floor, which keeps sheetrock edges off the floor and stops water wicking into drywall. Best practice for exterior sheathing: align sheet top with top of the first top plate so the sheet extends slightly below the bottom plate (sheds water, seals the sole plate). Walls must be racked and plumb in both directions before fastening top plates; the overlapping plate is normally installed after the wall section is erected
entries.use: Cutting studs/plates so an 8-ft wall takes standard sheathing sheets
entries.how: Use precut studs; no stud cutting needed for most of the wall
entries.dim: 2x4x8 precut stud actual = 1 1/2 in wide x 3 1/2 in deep x 92 5/8 in long; bottom plate 1 1/2 in; double top plate 1 1/2 + 1 1/2 = 3 in; total 92 5/8 + 1 1/2 + 3 = 97 1/8 in

entries.n: Read a floor plan / elevation for door and window locations
entries.desc: Elevations show front/rear/side views, materials, grade and doors/windows; each window/door type is marked and tied to the window schedule (rough-opening sizes are sometimes on the drawing). On floor plans, door and window locations in framed buildings are dimensioned to the CENTER of the opening; in masonry buildings to the EDGE of the opening. Section detail sheets give the framing information; coordinate blocking/ductwork/electrical with electrician, plumber and HVAC technician. Framing plans show size, number and location of members (floor plans give joist/girder/column sizes and spacing; wall plans give studs, plates, sills, bracing; roof plans give rafter size, spacing, slope)
entries.use: Before framing openings
entries.how: Dimensions to openings are measured differently for framed vs masonry walls
entries.dim: Example in text: finished grade minus 2 ft 6 in vs finished floor 0 ft 0 in

entries.desc: Light framing is used in barracks, bathhouses, administration buildings, light shops, hospitals. Heavy framing (timber construction) consists of members at least 6 in in dimension (e.g., 2x6 or 4x12) and is used in heavy roof trusses, timber-trestle bridges and wharves. Main differences are timber size and fastener types
entries.use: Deciding which framing method/fasteners a drawing calls for
entries.how: Heavy framing = members 6 in or more in a dimension
entries.dim: Heavy framing: members at least 6 in in dimension

entries.desc: Determine number/size of alike sections from the drawings first. Build a square, correctly sized template to assemble each section. Cut one piece, use it as a pattern (nail two stop blocks to it, one near each end). Place plate and sole in template with studs and girts between, plus door/window posts; nail girts, sole and plate to studs with 16d or 20d nails. If insulation board/wall sheathing is used, put it on before removing the section from the template (no scaffolds/ladders needed). Erecting party: end section first (may be on graded earth), then sidewall sections kept even, brace temporarily and nail together; then rafters. Works for small buildings up to large warehouses (cranes for heavy sections). Working parties: layout, cutting, assembling (built-in-place only), carrying, erecting (sidewalls), erecting (rafters), sheathing (built-in-place only), roofing, door-and-window, finishing
entries.use: Many similar wall/rafter sections (e.g., base camp); speed and manpower control
entries.how: Build each wall section flat in a template, sheath it, then stand it up
entries.dim: Nails: 16d or 20d for girts/sole/plate to studs
entries.eq: Template, handsaw or power saw, square, tape; crane for heavy sections
entries.wn: When machinery is used, use caution in fastening lifting cable or rope to avoid damaging the section

entries.n: Built-in-place method and order of construction
entries.desc: Each piece is separately erected in its proper place. Parts are built in this order: footings, posts, sills, joists, floor, soles, studs, plates, girts, rafters, bracing, siding, sheathing, roofing, doors, windows, steps, inside finish (if used)
entries.use: Each piece erected separately in place
entries.how: NCOIC splits crew into working parties; idle parties get new tasks

entries.n: Choose lumber grade for the job
entries.desc: Select lumber (Grades A, B, C, D) is for appearance/finish. Common lumber: No. 1 sound, tight-knotted, watertight; No. 2 used for framing, sheathing and structural forms where stress is not too great; No. 3 for rough work such as footing, guardrails, rough flooring; No. 4 for sheathing, subfloors, roof boards in cheaper construction; No. 5 for boxes, crates, dunnage. No. 2 common is used for framing; sheathing and siding lumber are normally No. 2 common softwood with solid knots, no voids. Softwoods are used for wood framing
entries.use: Ordering/selecting lumber
entries.how: Use No. 2 common for framing, sheathing and siding; don't buy a better grade than needed

entries.n: Nominal vs dressed lumber sizes (see Table 2-1)
entries.desc: Quoted (nominal) size is before surfacing; dressed size is smaller because of drying and planing. See Table 2-1 for all sizes. Plywood is usually 4 x 8 ft and 1/8 to 1 in thick
entries.use: Planning/cutting – nominal size is not actual size
entries.how: A 2x4 is really 1 1/2 x 3 1/2 in

entries.desc: 1 board foot = 1 ft x 1 ft x 1 in thick. A board 1 in x 1 ft x 12 ft = 12 board feet. Formula: Board feet = N x T(in) x W(in) x L(ft) / 12, or N x T(in) x W(in) x L(in) / 144, where N = number of pieces, T = thickness, W = width, L = length
entries.use: Ordering lumber (lumber is ordered in board feet)
entries.how: BF = N x T(in) x W(in) x L(ft) / 12
entries.dim: Divide by 12 when L in ft; by 144 when L in inches

entries.n: Choose and drive nails (penny size, length, placement)
entries.desc: Penny size (d) indicates length: 6d = 2 in, 10d = 3 in (common, box, casing, finish nails). Brads and small box nails are given by actual length and gauge. A nail must be at least 3x as long as the thickness of the wood it holds; 2/3 of its length goes into the receiving piece. Drive nails slightly toward each other for holding power; nails driven across the grain hold better than with the grain; a few well-placed nails hold better than many close together. Common nail = rough framing; box nail = toenailing and light work; casing nail = door/window casing and trim; finishing nail and brad = light trim (set with nail set). Annular/spiral (threaded) nails for paneling/plywood flooring; drywall nails are coated; roofing nails are sized by length (3/4 to 2 in) with large heads; double-headed (duplex) nails for forms and scaffolding. See Table 2-2
entries.use: Any nailing
entries.how: Nail at least 3x as long as the thickness of the wood being held
entries.dim: 6d = 2 in; 10d = 3 in; length >= 3 x thickness of piece held; 2/3 of length into anchor piece; roofing nails 3/4 to 2 in
entries.wn: Bend over protruding nails to prevent damage to materials and injury to personnel

entries.desc: From Table 2-2: 16d 3 1/2 in .162 dia large flathead – framing, bridges. 20d 4 in – framing, bridges. 30d 4 1/2, 40d 5, 50d 5 1/2 (heavy/extra-heavy framing, bridges), 60d 6 in (extra heavy framing, bridges). 8d 2 1/2 in .131 large flathead – sheathing, siding, subflooring, light framing; 10d 3 in .148 – sheathing, siding, subflooring, framing; 12d 3 1/4 in. 6d 2 in – casing/finish (small head) or small timber/siding/sheathing (large flathead). 8d extra-large flathead (1 1/4 in listed) – roll roofing, composition shingles
entries.use: Picking nail size for framing, sheathing, siding, finish work
entries.how: Framing = 16d (3 1/2 in); heavy framing/bridges = 20d to 60d; sheathing/subfloor = 8d-10d large flathead
entries.dim: See Table 2-2 for lengths/diameters of 2d-60d

entries.n: Install wood screws (pilot and starter holes)
entries.desc: Screws hold better than nails, draw material together and can be removed without damage but cost more time and money. Wood screws are threaded about 2/3 of their length. Pilot hole = diameter of the screw, bored in the piece to be fastened; starter hole (smaller than thread diameter) bored in the anchor piece to a depth of 1/2 or 2/3 the length of thread to be anchored. Flathead and oval-head screws are countersunk; roundhead are driven flush. See Table 2-4 for drill/bit sizes
entries.use: Where more holding power / removable fastening needed
entries.how: Bore pilot hole in the top piece, smaller starter hole in the anchor piece
entries.dim: Wood screw lengths 1/4 to 6 in: up to 1 in by 1/8 in steps; 1 to 3 in by 1/4 in steps; 3 to 6 in by 1/2 in steps. Starter hole depth 1/2 to 2/3 of thread length

entries.desc: Army name: lag bolt, wood-screw type. Longer and heavier than wood screws with coarser threads running from a gimlet point slightly more than half the length. Combined with expansion anchors, used to frame timbers to existing masonry. See Table 2-5 for sizes
entries.use: Heavy timber connections where wood screws too light and spikes too weak; timber to masonry with expansion anchors
entries.how: Square/hex head, driven with wrench
entries.dim: Sizes per Table 2-5: lengths 1 in to 16 in; diameters 1/4 to 1 in

entries.desc: Use bolts where great strength is needed or the work must be disassembled. Washers between nut/head and the wood avoid marring and allow more torque. Carriage bolts (square, finned, ribbed neck): bore hole to a tight fit for the body, counterbore so head is flush or below surface, drive bolt in with a hammer; use a flat washer under the nut on wood. Machine bolts: threads extend 2 x diameter + 1/4 in (bolts under 6 in long) to 2 x diameter + 1/2 in (bolts over 6 in); hole bored the same diameter as the bolt; externally driven only. Stove bolts are less precise, nearly fully threaded, used with square nuts
entries.use: Wood-to-wood bolted joints (carriage); metal-to-metal close tolerance (machine)
entries.how: Use washers under nuts on wood; counterbore carriage-bolt heads flush
entries.dim: Carriage bolts 1/4 to 1 in dia, 3/4 to 20 in long. Machine bolts 1/4 to 3 in dia, any length. Machine-bolt thread length = 2 x dia + 1/4 in (<6 in long) or + 1/2 in (>6 in long)
entries.eq: Brace and bit or drill, wrench, hammer

entries.desc: Driftpins (driftbolts) are long threadless headed bolts that hold heavy timbers together: make a hole slightly smaller than the pin and drive it; held by wood compression. Expansion bolt uses an expansion shield (lead/plastic) set in a predrilled hole to anchor in substances where threaded fasteners are useless. Corrugated fasteners (18- to 22-gauge) join miter and butt joints, tabletops, and substitute for nails where nails may split lumber; they hold better than nails in small lumber
entries.use: Heavy timber (driftpins); masonry anchorage (expansion shield); joints in small boards (corrugated)
entries.how: Driftpin hole slightly smaller than pin
entries.dim: Driftpins 1/2 to 1 in dia, 18 to 26 in long. Corrugated fasteners 5/8 to 1 1/8 in wide, 1/4 to 3/4 in long, 3 to 6 ridges, ridges 3/16 to 5/16 in center to center

entries.desc: Split rings (low-carbon steel) fit grooves cut half the ring depth into each timber face with a special bit in a drill; for heavy construction. Toothed rings (16-gauge plate, low-carbon steel) are embedded by pressure in contact faces for comparatively light construction. Choose type by joint kind and load
entries.use: Heavy timber joints, timber-to-timber or timber-to-steel
entries.how: Reduce complicated framing and save timber/hardware/time
entries.dim: Split rings: 2 1/2 in and another diameter garbled in source text; toothed rings 16-gauge

entries.desc: List all parts of the building from plans/specs: item, number of pieces, unit length in place, size (nominal), stock length, number per length, quantity. Example (20x40 ft TO building): 15 foundation posts x 3 pieces per footer = 45 footers (2x6, 1 ft 5 in long); cut seven 1 ft 5 in pieces from each 10-ft stock piece, so 45 pieces = seven 2x6x10 (leftovers usable for bridging). Have at least two estimators prepare separate bills and compare for accuracy
entries.use: First step toward a BOM when no BOM comes with the plans
entries.how: Tally every part from the plans, starting at the base and working up
entries.dim: Footers: 45 pc, 1'-5", 2x6 from 10' stock, 7 per length, qty 7 (see Table 3-1)

entries.n: Prepare materials estimate list and waste allowances
entries.desc: Group all pieces of the same size/length (largest size first). Add waste/breakage: 2 percent for flooring, sheathing and other 1-inch material; 10 percent for all materials 2 inches and larger. Add items not on plans (bracing, batter boards, nails, cement, form lumber, tie wire, scaffold). Convert siding/sheathing/flooring to board feet. Nail pounds by formula: 1-inch material uses 4 x (b/100); framing 2 in or more uses 6 x (b/100) (variables are garbled in source text; example uses 8d and 16d nails). The BOM for requisition is a simplified version of this list
entries.use: Convert takeoff into order quantities
entries.how: Add 2% waste to 1-inch stock; 10% to 2-inch and larger
entries.dim: Waste: 2% (1-in material); 10% (2-in and larger). Example list items: 6x6x12 (4+1 waste=5), 2x6x10 (89+8=98), 2x6x8 (15+2+3 temp bracing=20), 1x8x10 (12+2=14), 1x6x8 (9+2+2 batter boards=13), 1x6 RL 800 BF + 160 = 960 BF, 16d nails 36 lb, 8d nails 23 lb

entries.n: Lay out a rectangular building site
entries.desc: From an established line (road or property line AB) parallel to the building, establish the outer perimeter. Measure along side lines from the front line to the required distance and stretch a line tight (this marks the frontage). Measure in from the side lines along that line one-half the difference between the line length and the desired project length to find the front corners. Run lines from the front corners parallel to the side lines for the required depth; join their ends for the rear line. Drive stakes at all four corners; set batter boards at the same time or after. Check dimensions at each step. For irregular outlines, first lay out one large rectangle enclosing the whole building (or most of it), then lay out and prove each small rectangle separately
entries.use: Locating building corners from a road or property line
entries.how: Work from an established base line; drive a stake at each corner
entries.eq: String line, sledgehammer, handsaw, ax/hatchet, hammer, 100-ft tape, chalk line, tracing tape (cotton, about 1 in wide, usually 200 ft), carpenter's level, line level (most accurate halfway between points), plumb bob, framing square, 8d nails for string

entries.desc: Batter boards are temporary framework to locate corners; they survive excavation that disturbs corner stakes. Posts 2x4 or 4x4; corner stakes 2x2; boards 1x4 or 1x6. Erect right-angle boards 3 or 4 ft outside each corner stake and straight boards 3 or 4 ft outside line stakes. Fasten right-angle boards after posts are sunk; set boards at exact height of top of foundation; nail close to perpendicular with a framing square and level with a carpenter's level before securing. Saw cuts or nails in tops hold lines (separate ones for building, foundation, footing and excavation lines). Heavy cord or fine wire stretched between boards marks lines
entries.use: Preserving building lines outside the excavation
entries.how: Right-angle batter boards 3-4 ft outside each corner stake
entries.dim: Posts 2x4 or 4x4; corner stakes 2x2; boards 1x4 or 1x6; set 3 to 4 ft outside corner/line stakes
entries.eq: Sledgehammer, handsaw, hammer, framing square, level

entries.n: Extend and check building lines from batter boards
entries.desc: Step 1: after stakes A and B, erect batter boards 1-4 and stretch line X from board 1 to board 3 over stakes A and B. Step 2: after stake C, erect boards 5 and 6; line Y from board 2 over A and C to board 6. Step 3: after stake D, erect boards 7 and 8; line Z from board 5 to board 7 over C and D. Step 4: line from board 8 to board 4 over D and B. Lines cross at right angle over corner stakes when a plumb bob held over the stake touches the line; check all lines with line level or carpenter's level. Where foundation walls are wider at the bottom than the building, measure out from the building line on each batter board and stretch excavation lines outside the first layout
entries.use: After corner stakes A-D are set
entries.how: Check lines with a plumb bob over each corner stake

entries.n: Square the layout (6-8-10 and diagonal methods)
entries.desc: 6-8-10 method: measure 6 ft along one line (EF) and 8 ft along the other (EG); adjust lines until FG equals 10 ft. Use multiples for large layouts (12-16-20 for a 50 x 100 ft layout). Never start with less than 6 ft. Diagonal method: for a rectangular layout the two diagonals must be equal; if not, move the lines right or left until they are
entries.use: Verifying a building layout is square
entries.how: Measure 6 ft and 8 ft along the lines; the diagonal must read 10 ft
entries.dim: 6-8-10; multiples e.g. 12-16-20; minimum starting measurement 6 ft

entries.n: Choose a foundation: wall vs column (post) foundation
entries.desc: Wall foundations (concrete, rock, brick, cut stone with a footing) are solid for their length, used for heavy loads or low-bearing soil; used in the TO only when other types cannot be used; reinforce concrete walls with steel rod. Rubble masonry (coursed or random) is used when form lumber is not available; use mortar if strength/stability needed; random rubble needs bonding stones through the wall. Column/post foundations save time and labor; spacing based on load, in most cases 6 to 10 ft apart; wood posts are quickest to install; when wood posts extend 3 ft or more above ground, braces are necessary
entries.use: Planning building support
entries.how: Wood posts 6-10 ft apart are quickest; brace posts that rise 3 ft or more above ground
entries.dim: Post spacing usually 6 to 10 ft; braces required if post extends 3 ft or more above ground

entries.desc: Forms must be tight (leaks cause honeycomb and sand-streaking) and braced to stay aligned; watch for concrete lifting forms in first pours and in tapered walls. Lumber straight, strong, only partially seasoned (kiln-dried swells; if green, allow for shrinkage or keep wet). Softwoods (pine, fir, spruce) most economical. Wood touching concrete should be surfaced on the concrete side and both edges (square, shiplap or tongue-and-groove; T&G is most watertight). Plywood: waterproof glue, marked for concrete forms, warp-resistant; thinner plywood needs solid backing; 1/4 in is useful for curves. Fiber forms for round columns
entries.use: Designing/building any wood concrete form
entries.how: Tight, rigid, strong; use waterproof-glue plywood marked for concrete forms
entries.dim: Plywood thicknesses 1/4, 3/8, 1/2, 5/8, 3/4 in; widths up to 48 in; 8-ft lengths most common; the text calls the '6/8- and 3/4-inch' thicknesses most economical (as printed)
entries.wn: Watch for protruding nails (principal cause of accidents on form work); inspect tools; place mud sills under shoring on ground; protect all men on scaffolds and ground; do not raise large panels in heavy gusts; brace all shoring securely

entries.desc: Excavated earth is the mold when possible. For wood forms build four sides in panels: two opposite panels at exact footing width; the other pair has two end cleats on the inside spaced the footing length plus twice the sheathing thickness. Sheathing nailed to vertical cleats on 2-ft centers; use 2-in dressed lumber for cleats. Hold panels with form nails driven only part way from outside until tie wire is installed. Wrap tie wire around center cleats; set rebar before wire. For forms 4 ft square or larger, drive stakes and nail 1x6 boards across the top to prevent spreading. If footings are less than 1 ft deep and 2 ft square, use 1-in sheathing without cleats. For footing plus small pier, nail 2x4 or 4x4 pieces to the top of the lower form to carry the upper form. Wall-footing forms: 2-in lumber sides, stakes, spreaders and a short brace at each stake
entries.use: Forming wall or column footings when excavated earth is not usable as a mold
entries.how: Build four sides in panels; tie wire around the center cleats
entries.dim: Sheathing 1 in; cleats 2-in dressed on 2-ft centers; wire holes < 1 in diameter; 1x6 across top for forms 4 ft square or larger; no cleats if footing < 1 ft deep and < 2 ft square; 2x4 or 4x4 pier-form supports

entries.n: Concrete wall forms (panels, studs, wales, braces, spreaders)
entries.desc: Wall panels: sheathing nailed to studs, built in place or prefabricated (max 10 ft long). Sheathing smooth, normally 1-in (3/4-in dressed) tongue-and-groove lumber or 3/4-in plywood; reinforce against bulging. Studs generally 2x4; reinforce when they extend more than 4 ft. Double wales run horizontally, lapped at corners, tie panels and keep them straight. Braces: horizontal + diagonal member nailed to a stake and to stud/wale, diagonal at 30 degrees to horizontal; strongbacks (vertical members behind wales) add support; braces are not counted as design strength. Shoe plates nailed into foundation/footing hold wall dimensions and alignment; studs tie into shoe plate. Spreaders cut to wall thickness and placed near each tie wire, held by friction (not nailed), with a wire attached so they can be pulled out as concrete rises
entries.use: Building concrete wall forms
entries.how: Panels no more than 10 ft long; double wales; brace at 30 degrees
entries.dim: Panel length max 10 ft; sheathing 1 in (3/4 dressed) T&G or 3/4-in plywood; studs 2x4, reinforce if > 4 ft; brace diagonal 30 degrees

entries.n: Form ties: tie wire and tie rods
entries.desc: Tie wires: always double strands, No. 8 or 9 gauge black annealed iron wire (barbed wire in emergency). Spacing same as stud spacing but never more than 3 ft. Each tie loops a wale, passes through the form and loops the wale on the opposite side; tightened by twisting with a smooth metal rod or spike. Use wire ties only for low walls or when tie rods unavailable. Tie rod and spreader combination is the alternative: break rod off at the notch after stripping and fill holes with mortar if appearance matters. A wood strip wedge is used when curtain walls and columns are poured together; remove wedge first when stripping
entries.use: Holding wall forms against concrete pressure
entries.how: Double strands of No. 8 or 9 wire; spacing same as studs, never more than 3 ft
entries.dim: Wire No. 8 or 9 gauge, double strands; tie spacing = stud spacing, max 3 ft

entries.desc: Column forms: sheathing vertical to save cuts, corner joints firmly nailed, battens over joints; erect after reinforcement is assembled, tie to footing dowels; cleanout hole at bottom, replace the cut-out lumber before pouring. Beam forms: little bursting pressure but must be shored at close intervals; bottom same width as beam in one piece; sides 1-in tongue-and-groove lapping the bottom, nailed to 2x4 struts on 3-ft centers; 1x4 along struts supports floor-panel joists; sides held by continuous strips, crosspieces on top act as spreaders. Beam/girder assembly: beam bottom butts the girder side and rests on a 2x4 nailed to girder; 4x4 posts wedged at bottom or top for easy removal
entries.use: Forming concrete columns, beams, girders
entries.how: Column sheathing runs vertical; include a cleanout hole at bottom
entries.dim: Sides 1-in T&G; struts 2x4 on 3-ft centers; support strip 1x4; ledger 2x4; posts 4x4

entries.desc: Floor panels: 1-in T&G sheathing or 3/4-in plywood nailed to 1x4 cleats on 3-ft centers, supported by 2x6 joists; joist spacing depends on slab thickness and beam span. Stair forms (up to 3 ft wide): underside of steps 1-in T&G sheathing; platform extends 12 in beyond each side of stairs to support stringer bracing blocks; back of panel shored with 4x4; 2x6 cleats nailed to shoring rest on wedges for adjustment/removal; side stringers 2x12 cut for treads and risers; riser face 2-in material, beveled
entries.use: Forming concrete slabs and stairs
entries.how: Floor panel: 1-in T&G or 3/4 plywood on 1x4 cleats 3 ft o.c., supported by 2x6 joists
entries.dim: Slab: 1-in T&G or 3/4 plywood; 1x4 cleats 3 ft o.c.; 2x6 joists. Stairs up to 3 ft wide: 1-in T&G; 12-in platform overhang each side; 4x4 shoring; 2x6 cleats; 2x12 stringers; 2-in beveled risers

entries.desc: Before placing concrete treat forms with oil or other coating (light petroleum oil; shellac is better on plywood; painting preserves reused forms). Wetting with water is an emergency substitute. Use wood wedges to wedge forms from the concrete, not a pinchbar or other metal tool; do not jerk forms off after wedging at one end. Clean and oil reused forms immediately; remove nails as forms are stripped
entries.use: After concrete has set
entries.how: Oil forms before pour; wedge forms off with wood wedges, not pinch bars
entries.wn: Permit only workmen doing the stripping in the immediate area; do not remove forms until concrete has set; pile stripped forms immediately to avoid congestion and exposed nails

entries.n: Types of light framing (western/platform, balloon, braced)
entries.desc: Western (platform) frame: like braced frame but with boxed-sill construction at each floor line; cross bridging between joists and bridging between studs; preferred for one-story structures (bearing and nonbearing walls settle uniformly). Balloon frame: studs run full length from sill to rafters; second-floor joists rest on a 1x4 ribbon set into the studs; less rigid than braced. Braced frame: much more rigid; exterior studs extend only between floors and are topped by girts that form a sill for the next floor's joists; girts, sills and corner posts usually 4x6; knee braces usually 2x4 on each side of corner posts; corner posts run sill to plate. Heavy framing (6 in or larger members) is seldom used in the TO; used for warehouses/shops
entries.use: Selecting the framing system for a light building
entries.how: Platform frame is preferred for one-story TO buildings
entries.dim: Ribbon 1x4; girts 4x6; sills and corner posts 4x6; knee braces 2x4; heavy framing members at least 6 in

entries.desc: Light siding: chicken wire and water-resistant bituminous paper sandwiched for temporary framing in temperate climates. Salvaged framing: corrugated metal or gasoline cans as siding for emergency housing. Local timber: trimmed saplings or bamboo, tied with native vines if necessary. Wood-substitute: adobe (soil, straw, water) for walls, floors, foundations or sun-dried bricks. Excavations: excavation with simple log cribbing covered with sod and drained for shelter. See TM 5-302-1 and 5-302-2
entries.use: When standard lumber is unavailable
entries.how: Poles, bamboo, adobe, sandwiched wire and paper, salvaged sheet metal

entries.desc: Straight butt joint: square end against face; in framing secured with 8d or 10d nails, toenailed. Oblique butt joint (mitered end against face): bracing; strength depends on nailing, don't use too many nails; toenail. Miter butt joint: 45-degree cuts to make 90 degrees; very weak. Plain lap joint: one board over another with nails/screws; as strong as the fasteners and material. Half-lap splice: cut equal-length portions (usually half) from thickness of two boards; saw on waste side of gauge line; relatively strong and easy to make; variations: cross-lap, middle-lap, mitered half-lap
entries.use: Joining two timbers at an angle
entries.how: Lap joint is the strongest; butt joint is the weakest
entries.dim: Straight butt joint: 8d or 10d toenailed; miter = 45 degrees each piece to make 90 degrees

entries.desc: Vertical supports: compression-resistant (butt splice with scabs or fishplates; halved splice). Trusses/braces/joists: tension-resistant (square splice with notched laps; long plain splice as hasty substitute; strengthen with fishplates/scabs). Horizontal beams: bend-resistant – cut oblique complementary laps, square the upper lap, bevel the lower tongue, fasten a scab or fishplate along bottom. Scabs fastened with bolts, screws, nails or corrugated fasteners; nails staggered and driven at an angle away from the splice; too many or too-large nails weaken the splice. Compression splices are worthless for tension or bending
entries.use: Lengthening posts, joists, trusses, girders
entries.how: Match the splice to the stress: compression / tension / bending are different

entries.desc: Sill is the first part set; rests on foundation posts or ground; joined at corners and spliced as needed. Box sills for platform framing (sill plate optional; header at joist ends). T-sills for balloon framing (dry warm vs cold climates). Braced-framing sills: joists notched and nailed to sill and studs. Built-up sills: two or more light timbers such as 2x4s when heavy single timbers are unavailable; joints over posts; plates laid directly on post or (expedient) on graded earth; with earth floors nail studs directly to the sill. Spread thin bed of mortar on top of foundation wall (or fiberglass sill sealer); insulation and termite shield under sill if desired
entries.use: Setting the first member of the superstructure
entries.how: Bed sill in a thin layer of mortar or sill sealer to stop air leakage
entries.dim: Built-up sill: two or more 2x4s

entries.n: Size a girder – load calculation and Table 6-1
entries.desc: Girder carries floor load on each side to the midpoint of the joists resting on it. Dead load allowances per sq ft: 10 lb for average subfloor, finish floor and joists without basement plaster; +10 if basement ceiling plastered; 20 lb for ceiling plaster and joists if attic unfloored (when girders or bearing partitions support first-floor partition); +10 if attic floored for storage. Live load: 30 lb/sq ft for living areas; +20 if attic floored for light storage; local codes govern; snow counts as live load. Load per linear foot = load area width x total lb/sq ft. Example: girder off-center with 14-ft and 10-ft joists: 7 ft + 5 ft = 12 ft load width; 7 ft x 12 ft = 84 sq ft x 70 lb = 5,880 lb on the girder. Table 6-1 gives built-up girder sizes by load per linear foot and span (6-10 ft)
entries.use: Choosing girder size for floor loads
entries.how: Deepen a girder before widening it: doubling depth quadruples safe load
entries.dim: Dead load 10 / +10 / 20 / +10 lb per sq ft; live load 30 / +20 lb per sq ft; Table 6-1 based on Douglas fir, deflection not over 1/360 span, fiber stress 1,600 psi; solid-girder multipliers 1.130 (6 in), 1.150 (8 in), 1.170 (10 in), 1.180 (12 in)
entries.wn: Settling or shrinking can distort the building; take precautions to avoid or counteract it

entries.n: Build and splice a built-up girder
entries.desc: Select lumber as free of knots/defects as possible. Usually three pieces of framing lumber nailed together (nail securely to prevent individual buckling); match end grains per figure 6-13. Nailing pattern: square across the ends of the boards 1 1/2 in from each end, then diagonal every 16 in. Typical two- or three-piece girder of 2-in lumber nailed on both sides with 16d common nails. Lumber long enough that no more than one joint occurs over the span between footings; stagger joints; square each joint and butt tightly. Ends of wood girders bear at least 4 in on posts. Solid beams: half-lap joint (beam on edge, annual rings top to bottom, mark, cut, check with square, nail a temporary strap across, drill 1/16 in larger than bolt and bolt with washer and nut) or strapped butt joint with straps generally 18 in long bolted each side. Girder with ledger board or joist hangers where headroom is limited
entries.use: Making a girder from framing lumber
entries.how: Three pieces of 2x nailed with 16d common on both sides; stagger joints
entries.dim: Nails: 16d common both sides; 1 1/2 in from each end then diagonal every 16 in; bearing on posts at least 4 in; bolt hole 1/16 in larger than bolt; straps 18 in long

entries.desc: Posts may be solid timber or several framing pieces nailed with 16d or 20d common nails; metal columns of heavy pipe, steel angles or I-beams. Column needs a bearing plate at top and bottom; basement posts sit on masonry footings and are fastened at top to the load-bearing member and at bottom to the footing (e.g., metal bearing cap and metal dowel in drilled holes, with asphalt coating at drilled point to prevent rust/rot). Example 24x40 ft building: column B carries half the girder load between wall A and column C, column C half between B and D, column D shares equally with C and wall E
entries.use: Supporting girders under a floor
entries.how: Bearing plate top and bottom; masonry footing for basement posts
entries.dim: Nails 16d or 20d common for built-up wood columns

entries.n: Frame floor joists (spacing, bearing, notching, ledgers)
entries.desc: Joists usually 2 or 3 in thick; spaced 16 or 24 in o.c. (sometimes 12; heavier joists if load requires). 2x6 floor joists are too small for spans over 10 ft but common for ceiling joists. Double joists under concentrated loads or partitions. Joist-over-sill connection is strongest; if notched, never notch to sill and girder over one-third of joist depth. Always place joists crown up; keep them level when framed to girders. On steel girders rest joists on top, or use straps/hangers if headroom is limited. Ledger: 2x4 nailed to face of sill or girder flush with bottom edge using 20d nails 12 in apart (use 2x4 ledgers with 2x6 or 2x8 joists); joists 10 in or deeper may use 2x4 ledgers; joist ties are short 1x4 boards nailed across the joists flush with top and bottom. Overhead joists lap on plates; when two joists lie side by side on a plate nail them together; or butt and connect with a scab. If plans do not give joist sizes use Tables 6-2 and 6-3
entries.use: Building the floor frame
entries.how: Joists 16 or 24 in o.c., crown up; never notch deeper than 1/3
entries.dim: Spacing 12/16/24 in o.c.; 2x6 not for floor spans over 10 ft; notch max 1/3 depth; ledger 2x4 with 20d nails 12 in apart
entries.tm: Appendix C: floor joists/sills 25 man-hours per 1,000 board feet; ceiling joists 25 MH/1,000 BF

entries.desc: Three kinds: solid (horizontal), cross, and compression (metal). Cross bridging is most common: diagonally cut 1x3 or 2x3 between joists, each piece nailed to the top of each joist forming an X with the two pieces touching. Pattern: place a piece of material between joists, mark and saw. Nail the tops (8d; the second nail size is garbled in the source), leave bottoms free until the subfloor is laid, then nail bottoms. One line of bridging on joists more than 8 ft long; two lines on joists more than 16 ft long. Use a power saw if available
entries.use: Stiffening joists and preventing unequal deflection
entries.how: Nail top ends first; leave bottoms free until subfloor is laid
entries.dim: Cross bridging 1x3 or 2x3; one line for joists > 8 ft; two lines for > 16 ft

entries.n: Frame a floor opening (headers and trimmers)
entries.desc: Opening parallel to joists needs two headers and one trimmer; opening at right angles to joists needs one header and two trimmers. Nailing sequence (figure 6-25): headers 1 and 2 nailed to trimmers A and C with three 20d nails; headers 1 and 2 nailed to short joists X and Y with three 20d nails; headers 3 and 4 nailed to headers 1 and 2 with 16d nails 6 in apart; trimmers A and C nailed to headers 3 and 4 with three 20d nails; trimmers B and D nailed to A and C with 16d nails 12 in apart
entries.use: Stairwells, ventilators, chimneys through the floor
entries.how: Headers doubled, at right angles to joists; trimmers are doubled joists
entries.dim: Three 20d per connection; 16d at 6 in o.c. (headers); 16d at 12 in o.c. (trimmers B/D to A/C)

entries.desc: Subfloor laid diagonally on joists, nailed with 8d to 10d nails; boards 8 in wide or more get at least three nails per joist; use larger nails if subfloor is over 1 in thick; normally laid before wall framing so it can be walked on. Finish floor normally 3/4-in square-edged or tongue-and-groove, 3 1/2 to 7 1/2 in wide, nailed with 8d common nails in every joist; building paper between subfloor and finish floor to keep out dampness and insects. Warehouse finish floor: 2-in material, face-nailed with 16d or 20d, not T&G, 4 to 12 in wide, joints on center of joist
entries.use: Laying floors
entries.how: Diagonal subfloor with 8d-10d nails; 3/4-in finish floor with 8d in every joist
entries.dim: Subfloor nails 8d-10d, >= 3 nails per joist for boards >= 8 in wide; finish floor 3/4 in x 3 1/2 to 7 1/2 in, 8d common every joist; warehouse 2-in, 16d or 20d, 4 to 12 in wide
entries.tm: Table C-6: subfloor T&G 24 MH/1,000 sq ft, plywood 16; finish floor softwood 24, hardwood 32 (typical crew 1 leader + 4)

entries.desc: Concrete floors: grade and compact earth, place concrete on ground, reinforce with steel or wire mesh; foundation wall may be built first and floor placed after the building is completed to protect the floor while it sets; provide drainage around footing and floor area; concrete floors tend to be damp unless protected. Miscellaneous floors: earth, adobe brick, duckboard (widely used for shower flooring), rushes/thatch (insulating, must be replaced frequently); used when conventional materials are unavailable or to save time/labor
entries.use: Shops, heavy equipment, aircraft repair, certain warehouses (concrete); expedient floors
entries.how: Grade, compact, reinforce with steel or wire mesh, provide drainage

entries.n: Frame walls and partitions (studs, openings, plates)
entries.desc: Wall frame: studs, diagonal bracing, cripples, trimmers, headers, fire blocks, supported by floor sole plate; top capped by top plate; double top plates tie walls and partitions. Studs usually 2x4, 12/16/24 in o.c. depending on finishes; wider if vertical siding with girts. After sills, plates and braces are in place and openings laid out, nail studs with two 16d or 20d nails through the plates. Bearing partitions support ceiling joists; nonbearing only themselves (one cap/plate); always use a sole plate. Partitions framed like outside walls with corner posts or T-posts for nailing surfaces. Door openings: outside studs first, then short trimmers nailed to the inside face; window sill specified single or double; sill headers toenailed to trimmer; jack stud rests on sole plate
entries.use: Wall frame construction
entries.how: Studs 12, 16 or 24 in o.c.; start studs with two 16d or 20d nails through the plates
entries.dim: Studs 2x4 at 12, 16 or 24 in o.c.; 2 x 16d or 20d through plates
entries.tm: Table C-1: wall frames, plates 45 man-hours per 1,000 board feet

entries.n: Corner posts, T-posts and double T-posts
entries.desc: Corner posts built up from three or more studs; set up, plumbed, temporarily braced. Variants: 4x6 with a 2x4 flush on the board side (for 4-in wall); 4x4 with a 2x4 on each of two adjoining sides; two 2x4s nailed with blocks between and a 2x4 flush with one edge (most common); 2x4 nailed to edge of another 2x4 (used where no inside finish needed). T-posts (where a partition meets another wall): 2x4 centered on face of a 4x6; 2x4 centered on two 4x4s nailed together; two 2x4s with a block between and a 2x4 centered on the wide side; 2x4 centered on face of a 2x6 with horizontal bridging behind. Double T-post where partitions cross: add another 2x4 to the opposite wide side. Wider timber for walls thicker than 4 in
entries.use: Providing nailing surfaces for inside wall finish at corners and partition intersections
entries.how: Most common corner: two 2x4s with blocks between plus a 2x4 flush on one edge
entries.dim: 4x6 + 2x4; 4x4 + two 2x4; 2x4 + 2x4 with blocks + 2x4; T-post on 4x6, 2x(4x4), 2x6

entries.desc: Girts are the same width as studs and flush with stud faces inside and outside. Used when outside walls are covered with vertical siding; studs spaced 2 to 10 ft apart, girts about 4 ft apart running horizontally between them. Vertical siding acts like studs and helps carry roof weight. Used extensively in the TO
entries.use: Hasty TO construction with vertical siding
entries.how: Studs 2-10 ft apart with girts about 4 ft apart
entries.dim: Studs 2 to 10 ft apart; girts about 4 ft apart

entries.desc: Top plate: one or two pieces of framing lumber same size as studs; supports rafter feet. Where doubled, first plate nailed to corner post tops and studs with 16d or 20d nails; after corner braces are in, top part nailed to bottom with 10d nails, over each stud or two nails every 2 ft; stagger all joints; lap the top section edges and corners. If end studs extend to rafters, no plate at the end. Sole plate (2x4 or same thickness as the wall) carries stud bottoms; nail with two 16d or 20d nails at each joist it crosses; if laid lengthwise over a girder or joist, two nails every 2 ft
entries.use: Tying studs together and connecting wall to roof/floor
entries.how: Double top plate: first plate 16d/20d to studs; top plate 10d nails
entries.dim: Top plate: first plate 16d or 20d; second plate 10d nails, one per stud or two per 2 ft; sole: two 16d/20d per joist, or two nails every 2 ft

entries.desc: Horizontal bridging is nailed between studs halfway between sole and top plates, cut to the stud spacing at the bottom; stiffens and straightens studs. Diagonal bridging is nailed at an angle between studs, forming a continuous truss that keeps walls from sagging. Bridge interior partitions and exterior walls alike when possible
entries.use: Stiffening frame walls
entries.how: Diagonal bridging forms a continuous truss and is more effective than horizontal
entries.dim: Horizontal bridging at mid-height between sole and top plates

entries.n: Plumb corner posts and straighten walls
entries.desc: Method 1 (plumb bob): hang bob line over a rule extending 2 in over the post so the line is 2 in from the post; measure at the bottom – it must read 2 in; move post in/out until exactly 2 in, nail temporary brace; repeat from the other outside face. If no plumb bob use a rock, half-brick or small piece of metal. Method 2: plumb-bob string fixed to post top; two identical gauge blocks – tack one near the top between string and post, insert the second between string and post bottom; post is plumb if the whole face of block 2 touches the string. Straightening: plumb and brace all corner posts; chalk line from top of one corner post to the opposite corner post with a 3/4-in block under each end; brace the wall at intervals; nail brace when a 3/4-in block slides between line and plate. Do the full perimeter and inside partitions
entries.use: After posts/studs are nailed to plates or girts and before permanent bracing and rafters
entries.how: Plumb bob 2 in off the post; chalk line with 3/4-in blocks to straighten
entries.dim: Plumb bob 2 in from post; 3/4-in blocks under each end of chalk line
entries.eq: Plumb bob or level, chalk line, rule, temporary braces

entries.desc: Let-in bracing: 1x4 or 1x6 set diagonally into the edges of studs, flush; cut the studs, never the brace; runs top plate to sole plate or between plates and studs. Cut-in bracing: 2x4s cut at an angle and toenailed between studs in diagonal progression from corner posts to sill or plates. Diagonal sheathing is the strongest. If plywood sheathing 5/8 in or more is used, other bracing may be omitted
entries.use: Making frames rigid and square
entries.how: Plywood sheathing 5/8 in or thicker lets you omit other bracing
entries.dim: Let-in 1x4 or 1x6; cut-in 2x4; plywood >= 5/8 in

entries.desc: Wood sheathing: 1 in thick by 6, 8, 10 or 12 in wide No. 1 common (normally 6-12 in wide, 3/4 in thick); square or matched edge; 6- or 8-in boards: two 8d nails per stud crossing, wider boards three 8d; joints over studs; horizontal start at foundation going up, diagonal start at a bottom corner going toward opposite wall (diagonal adds much more strength). Gypsum board: 1/2 in thick, 4x8 ft, T&G long edges, nailed with 1 3/4- or 2-in galvanized roofing nails 7 in o.c.; fireproof, water resistant, windproof, no building paper needed. Plywood (highly recommended; corner bracing can be omitted): minimum 1/4 in for 16-in stud spacing, 3/8 in for 24-in spacing; face grain parallel to studs; 6d common nails for 1/4, 3/8, 1/2-in panels, edges not more than 6 in o.c., elsewhere not more than 12 in o.c. Fiberboard 25/32 in thick, 2 or 4 ft wide by 8, 9, 10 or 12 ft long
entries.use: Covering studs on exterior walls
entries.how: Plywood: 1/4 in min at 16-in studs, 3/8 in min at 24-in; 6d nails at 6/12 in
entries.dim: Wood 1 in x 6-12 in; 8d: 2 nails (6-8 in boards) or 3 nails (wider) per stud; gypsum 1/2 in x 4 x 8 ft, 1 3/4 or 2 in galv roofing nails at 7 in o.c.; plywood 1/4 in (16 in o.c.) / 3/8 in (24 in o.c.), 6d nails 6 in edges / 12 in field
entries.tm: Table C-2: wall sheathing per 1,000 sq ft – building paper 8 MH, T&G 24, plywood 16, fiberboard 16 (crew 1 leader + 8)

entries.n: Apply exterior siding (vertical, beveled, drop, corrugated metal)
entries.desc: Wood siding: decay-resistant, well-seasoned, 1/2 to 3/4 in thick by up to 12 in wide. Vertical: 8d or 10d nails to girts, battens over cracks, optionally tar paper or light roll roofing between siding and sheathing. Beveled siding: thin at top edge, thick at butt, nailed at the butt through the top edge of the board below; frame casings first and butt siding against them. Drop siding: shiplapped or T&G, if used as combined sheathing/siding nail directly to studs with tongue up. Corrugated metal: applied vertically, nailed to girts with nails placed in the ridges; use resin-sized paper behind it, not tar paper (causes rust)
entries.use: Finishing exterior walls
entries.how: Vertical siding nailed to girts with 8d or 10d nails and battens over cracks
entries.dim: Siding 1/2 to 3/4 in thick, up to 12 in wide; 8d or 10d nails
entries.tm: Table C-2: siding per 1,000 sq ft – plywood 16 MH, corrugated asbestos 32, drop siding 32, narrow bevel 48, shingles 40

entries.desc: Rules: nail in center of slots; do not nail tightly; at least 1/4-in clearance at all stops; do not stretch tight; strap and shim uneven walls. Steps: set outside/inside corner trim with bottoms even with the area to weatherproof (level or transit for a constant line); set starter strip level with bottom of corner trim; snap siding bottom onto starter strip, slide tight into corner trim, then out 1/4 in; nail with roofing nails 16 in o.c. in the center of the slot, leaving about 1/16 in between nailhead and sheathing; add further pieces on top, lap tight then pull away 1/4 in; end runs 1/4 in from butt to trim; J-channel where runs break (windows, doors); undersill trim in J-channel on horizontal breaks
entries.use: Low-maintenance wall covering
entries.how: Nail in center of slots, leave loose, keep 1/4-in clearance
entries.dim: Clearance 1/4 in; nails 16 in o.c.; nailhead gap about 1/16 in
entries.eq: Level or transit, chalk line, slotting tool

entries.desc: Resin-sized paper: red/buff (sometimes black), usually 36 in wide rolls of 500 sq ft weighing 18 to 50 lb; normally not waterproof. Coal-tar-saturated heavy paper (sheathing paper): waterproof and insulating. Apply horizontally from the bottom of the wall, nailed with roofing nails at the laps; overlap for runoff; don't tear
entries.use: Protecting walls from dampness/heat/cold under siding, shingles or iron
entries.how: Apply horizontally from the bottom, overlap, nail with roofing nails at laps
entries.dim: Rolls 36 in wide, 500 sq ft, 18-50 lb

entries.desc: Usually lighter than floor joists but strong enough to resist bending and buckling. Installed 16 or 24 in o.c. starting at one side and continuing across, parallel to the rafters; extra joists may be added without changing prime-joist spacing. Nailed to plates and rafters where possible, lapped and nailed over bearing partitions; joists beside rafters on a plate are cut at rafter pitch flush with top of rafter. Crown (camber) up
entries.use: Framing ceilings
entries.how: 16 or 24 in o.c., parallel to rafters, crown up
entries.dim: Spacing 16 or 24 in o.c
entries.tm: Table C-1: ceiling joists 25 man-hours per 1,000 board feet

entries.desc: Locate the hole to avoid studs, braces, plates. Sheathing is cut back in a radius 6 in greater than that of the pipe; safety thimbles or other insulation inside and outside the sheathing (or one outside sheet-metal insulator). Metal flange: mark a circle on the sheet metal 1/2 in larger than the pipe diameter and an inner circle 2 in less in diameter; draw radial lines 1/2 to 3/4 in apart on the outer circumference; cut out the center circle, cut along the lines, bend the strips outward at 45 degrees; force the pipe through
entries.use: Heating-stove pipe through a side wall
entries.how: Cut sheathing back 6 in more than pipe radius; use thimbles/insulation
entries.dim: Sheathing cut back radius pipe + 6 in; outer circle pipe dia + 1/2 in; inner circle 2 in smaller; radial lines 1/2-3/4 in apart; bend 45 degrees
entries.wn: Use safety thimbles or insulation on inside and outside of the sheathing

entries.desc: Condensation most likely in first 6-8 months after construction and in extreme cold with high interior humidity. Upper structure: 1 sq ft of vent per 150 sq ft of floor space without soffit vents; per 300 sq ft with soffit vents; minimum net open area 1/4 sq in per sq ft of ceiling area. Louver frames usually 5 in wide, rabbeted at the back for screen/door; 3/4-in slats spaced about 1 3/4 in apart, sloped to prevent rain driving in; place near the gable top. Crawl spaces: foundation louvers set into foundation as built, copper or bronze screen and adjustable shutters; 1/4 sq in per sq ft of under-floor space
entries.use: Preventing condensation
entries.how: 1 sq ft of vent per 150 sq ft of floor (300 with soffit vents)
entries.dim: 1 sq ft/150 sq ft (no soffit vents); 1 sq ft/300 sq ft (soffit vents); 1/4 sq in net open area per sq ft ceiling or under-floor; louver frame 5 in wide; slats 3/4 in at about 1 3/4 in

entries.desc: Stringers (carriages) 2 to 3 in thick, 8 in or wider; three stringers if stairs are wider than 36 in (both outer edges and center). Frame the floor opening for the stairwell. Steps: mark total rise (lower floor to upper floor incl. joists and flooring) on a story pole; set dividers to 7 in and step off, adjusting until the pole divides evenly (each space = rise of one step); count risers; measure stairwell-opening length for the run; tread width = run divided by (number of risers minus one); lay off on stringer stock with steel square. Ideal rise + run total 17 in. Checks: riser height + tread width between 17 and 19 in; riser height x tread width between 70 and 75 in
entries.use: Building straight stairs between floors
entries.how: Rise about 7 in, tread about 10 in; riser + tread = 17-19 in; riser x tread = 70-75
entries.dim: Stringers 2-3 in thick, >= 8 in wide; third stringer if wider than 36 in; rise about 7 in; tread about 10 in; rise + tread 17-19 in; rise x tread 70-75 in
entries.tm: Table C-4: closed stringer stairs built on job 16 MH per story; prefab 8; open stringer 24

entries.n: Rafter basics and terms (rise, run, pitch, span)
entries.desc: Rafters are the main roof frame: inclined members spaced 16 to 48 in apart; tops fasten to ridge or another rafter; they rest on and are nailed to the top plate (not framed into it); may extend past walls for eaves. Basic right triangle: run (horizontal, normally half the span), rise (vertical), rafter = hypotenuse: rafter length^2 = run^2 + rise^2. Pitch examples: 4, 6 or 8 in of rise per foot of run = pitch 4-12, 6-12, 8-12. Bird's mouth: cutout near the bottom of the rafter (seat on top of plate, heel on side). Types: common, hip, valley, jack (hip jack, valley jack, cripple jack)
entries.use: Framing any roof
entries.how: Pitch = inches of rise per 12 in of run; rafter length^2 = run^2 + rise^2
entries.dim: Rafter spacing 16 to 48 in; unit of run 12 in

entries.desc: Collar tie (beam): 1x4, 1x6, 1x8 or 2x4 fastened horizontally to a pair of rafters between plate and ridge. Most codes require them 5 ft apart or every third rafter, whichever is less. Nail 1-in ties with four 8d nails at each end; 2-in ties with three 16d nails at each end. Long rafters need braces or supports to prevent sagging
entries.use: Small roofs with no ceiling joists to prevent spreading
entries.how: Collar ties every 5 ft or every third rafter, whichever is less
entries.dim: Tie stock 1x4/1x6/1x8/2x4; max 5 ft apart or every 3rd rafter; 1-in tie: four 8d each end; 2-in tie: three 16d each end

entries.n: Lay out a common rafter (scale and step-off methods)
entries.desc: Scale method: find half the span (total run) – e.g., 20-ft-wide building = 10-ft run; lay timber on sawhorses with crown up; hold square (tongue in left hand, blade in right, heel toward you) near the upper end with the rise number on the tongue and 12 on the blade (8 and 12 in the 8-in-rise example) on the top edge; mark along the tongue = plumb cut at ridge; measure the rafter line length from the top of that cut and mark; reposition square for the plumb cut at the seat; measure overhang perpendicular and mark the tail cut (often square across); level cut (seat width) = width of the plate measured perpendicular to the plumb cut. Step-off method: step off the square as many times as there are feet of run; for the remaining inches (e.g., 20 ft 8 in wide = 10 ft plus 4 in run) mark the inch position at the last step; mark along the tongue for line length. After cutting two rafters, place them to check fit before cutting the rest
entries.use: Cutting a pattern rafter
entries.how: Mark plumb cut at ridge, seat cut at plate, tail cut at overhang; test two before cutting all
entries.dim: Unit of run 12 in; example 8-in rise per 12 in run
entries.eq: Framing square, sawhorses, try square, saw
entries.tm: Table C-1: rafters 45 man-hours per 1,000 board feet

entries.desc: Type 1 (face of blade): first line gives common rafter length per foot of run for each rise in inches; e.g., under 16-in mark = 20.00 in (12-in run, 16-in rise); under 13-in mark = 17.69 in. Other table lines (hip/valley/jack/side cuts) are seldom used in the TO. Type 2 (back of blade, some squares): run, rise and pitch for the seven most common pitches; columns: 12 (run), rise, pitch fraction; based on horizontal measurement from center to outside; inch marks may be twelfths of an inch or of a foot. Examples: pitch 1/6, run 12 ft -> 12 ft 7 10/12 in; pitch 1/2, run 12 ft -> 16 ft 11 6/12 in; pitch 1/4 run 23 ft = 25 ft 8 5/12 in and run 4 ft = 4 ft 5 8/12 in, so a 27-ft run = 30 ft 2 1/12 in. Pitch 1/6: rise 4 / run 12; 1/4: rise 6; 1/2: rise 12
entries.use: Finding rafter length quickly
entries.how: Type 1 table on blade face gives length per foot of run; Type 2 gives length by pitch and span
entries.dim: 20.00 in at 16 rise; 17.69 in at 13 rise; examples above

entries.desc: Trusses (Howe and Fink most common) are straight members joined at intersections so stress is along each member's length; web members divide the truss into triangles. Trusses are supported by bearing walls, posts or other trusses; knee braces tie wall to roof. Purlins: support corrugated metal or truss sheathing; in small roofs between rafters, nailed through rafters; in small buildings (barracks, mess halls, small warehouses) 2x4 purlins narrow side up. Layout: get material to a level spot; take all lengths from the prints; cut accurately; lay in position; tack together; mark and recheck hole locations; bore holes to print size perpendicular to the face with brace and bit or compressor wood-borer; dismantle and withdraw nails
entries.use: Building trusses for large spans (shops, hangars) or small rafter-trusses
entries.how: Cut all members accurately, tack, bore holes square to the face
entries.dim: Purlins 2x4 narrow side up (small buildings)
entries.eq: Brace and bit or air woodborer, saws, tape
entries.tm: Table C-1: truss assembly/placement man-hours – 20 ft: 1.5/1; 30 ft: 2.0/8; 40 ft: 12.0/8; 50 ft: 20.0/6*; 60 ft: 24.0/6*; 80 ft: 32.0/6* (*organizational crane). Typical crew 1 leader + 8; minimum 1 leader + 2

entries.n: Assemble a rafter truss with a template (jig)
entries.desc: Rafters are usually made into trusses: two rafters joined at the top with a collar tie well nailed into both; spread rafters at the bottom to building width using a template or tape between seat cuts before nailing ties/chords. Chord: 1x6 or 2x4 nailed across the rafters at the seat cut. Hanger/vertical member of 1x6 nailed to the rafter joint, running to the chord at midpoint. Knee brace (when needed) nailed to the chord at a 45-degree angle with the wall stud; may be omitted until the truss is set. Template layout: baseline A = exact chord length; centerline C at right angles from center of A; hypotenuse B = rafter length; nail 2x4x8 blocks flush with ends of A and C. Assembly: set a rafter in the jig with the plate cut over the baseline block and peak flush with the centerline; nail a holding block outside rafter; lay a 2x4 chord across base blocks; lay two 2x4 rafters over the chord; center a 1x6 hanger under the peak; nail through rafters into the hanger with six 8d; nail rafters to chord ends with 16d; nail bottom of hanger to chord with 8d
entries.use: Repetitive truss production
entries.how: Build a jig from 2x4x8 blocks on a baseline and centerline
entries.dim: Chord 1x6 or 2x4; hanger 1x6; jig blocks 2x4x8; six 8d (rafters to hanger); 16d (rafter to chord); 8d (hanger to chord); knee brace 45 degrees to wall stud

entries.desc: Mark truss positions on the top plate (note face orientation). Rest one end peak-down on a mark on one side, rest the other end on the opposite plate, rotate into position using a pole or rope, line up faces flush with marks, nail with 16d nails. Raise, align and nail the first three assemblies; nail temporary 1x6 braces across them; repeat, checking rafter spacing at peaks as braces are nailed. Braces can serve as a platform for raising trusses where there is no room to rotate. Temporarily brace the end section until sheathing is applied. Knee braces are not needed on every truss
entries.use: Setting trusses on the building
entries.how: Raise by hand, nail with 16d, brace temporarily with 1x6
entries.dim: Nails 16d; temporary braces 1x6
entries.tm: Table C-1 truss placement man-hours (see item TM47-7-05)

entries.desc: Roof openings are framed with double headers at right angles to rafters (rafters set into the headers as joists in floor openings), trimmers are doubled rafters, nailing strips may be added. Roof decking: plywood sheathing is installed like wall sheathing but laid perpendicular to the rafters and trusses
entries.use: Chimneys, vents, skylights, dormers; plywood roof sheathing
entries.how: Double headers and trimmers like floor openings
entries.tm: Table C-2: roof decking per 1,000 sq ft – T&G 32 MH, plywood 20

entries.n: Lay a new asphalt strip-shingle roof
entries.desc: Erect scaffold so eaves are about waist-high. Sweep sheathing clean, inspect for cracks, holes, defects; sheathing must be absolutely dry. Apply roofing felt underlay (usually 3-ft rolls) with 2-in top lap and 4-in side lap. Distribute bundles along the scaffold. First (starter) course at eaves is the inverted first course of shingles or a starter strip of mineral-surfaced roll roofing; begin each following course by stretching a guideline or snapping a chalk line. A 1x3-ft square-butt shingle (three tabs) is laid 5 in to the weather (7 in overlapped by the next higher course). Nails: 1-in copper or hot-dipped galvanized roofing nails, two per tab (six per full strip), about 6 1/2 in from the butt edge so each nail is blind-nailed and passes through two courses. Asbestos-cement shingles laid about the same way. Hips/valleys: cut shingles to match using a 1x6 pattern about 3 ft long made with the square set to the unit run and unit length of a common rafter
entries.use: Pitched-roof covering
entries.how: Strip shingle laid 5 in to the weather; six nails per full strip, two per tab
entries.dim: Shingle 1x3 ft; 5 in to weather; felt laps 2 in top, 4 in side; 27 strips per bundle; 3 bundles per 100 sq ft; nails 1 in, 2 per tab, 6 per strip, 6 1/2 in from butt; 1x6 pattern about 3 ft
entries.eq: Scaffold, chalk line, hammer, roofing nails
entries.tm: Table C-10: asphalt shingles 30 man-hours per 1,000 sq ft (crew 1 leader + 4)

entries.desc: Flashing: galvanized sheet or copper alloy for valleys; felt for hips/ridges. Ridge and hip: strip of felt, then shingle squares (shingles cut into thirds) blind-nailed. Open valley: prefabricated metal (galvanized iron, copper, zinc) with a splash rib down the center and crimps at edges; nail only at edges outside crimps (nails inside crimps leak). Closed valley: roof covering extends across; sheet-metal 'shingle tins' about 18 x 10 in laid under each course along the valley. Side flashing at dormers/chimneys/skylights: tins about 5 x 7 in bent at a right angle; apron flashing along the bottom of the outer wall face; saddle flashing along the bottom of the inner face of a chimney or skylight
entries.use: Making roof intersections and wall junctions watertight
entries.how: Nail valley flashing outside the crimps only
entries.dim: Shingle tins about 18 x 10 in (valley); about 5 x 7 in (side flashing)

entries.desc: Papers: rosin paper, kraft paper, sisal kraft, roofing felt (asbestos or rag felt; 32 to 36 in wide rolls; 15 to 65 lb per square; 15-lb most common). Binder: asphalt (preferred, melting point 350-410 deg F, roofs sloping up to 6 in/ft = 1/4 pitch, cover with slag, gravel or other protection) or coal tar (melting point 300-350 deg F, not recommended above 3 in/ft slope = 1/8 pitch). Aggregate: crushed stone or gravel 1/4 to 5/8 in embedded in a coat of asphalt or tar. Gravel stop on slag/gravel roofs or metal-edge strip on smooth roofs at edges and eaves: flange over last felt ply, nailed to deck, double felt stripped; lip of gravel stop at least 3/4 in above deck; lip of edge strip at most 1/2 in above deck; fasten to fascia board
entries.use: Flat or nearly flat roofs
entries.how: Asphalt up to 6 in/ft slope; tar not above 3 in/ft slope
entries.dim: Felt 32-36 in wide; 15-65 lb/square; asphalt 350-410 F, slope <= 6 in/ft; tar 300-350 F, slope <= 3 in/ft; aggregate 1/4-5/8 in; gravel-stop lip >= 3/4 in; edge-strip lip <= 1/2 in
entries.tm: Table C-8: built-up roofing per 1,000 sq ft – 2 ply 12 MH, 3 ply 20, 4 ply 25, 5 ply 30; flashing 60; insulation 25 (crew 1 leader + 6)

entries.n: Reroof over asphalt roll roofing with asphalt strip shingles
entries.desc: Standard-weight shingles: four-tab, 10 x 36 in, 4-in maximum exposure, about 210 lb per square, 1 1/4- or 1 1/2-in nails with heads at least 3/8 in diameter (zinc-coated best). Thick-butt: three-tab, 1 x 3 ft, 5-in max exposure, about 210 lb/square, 1 1/2- or 1 3/4-in nails, mineral granules over entire surface. Prepare deck: drive in loose/protruding nails; cut out buckles and wrinkles and nail edges down with 3/4- or 1-in roofing nails; if shingles don't match existing roofing apply an 18-in starting strip of mineral-surfaced roll roofing at eaves, nailed at the top about 18 in apart, lower edge bent down and nailed to the sheathing edge (project about 3/4 in as drip edge), nails in sheathing edge 6 in apart. Shingles: first course full shingle, tab bottoms flush with eaves; nails about 3/4 in above each cutout, two nails at every cutout, nail center first then toward ends; second course starts with a half tab cut off, third with one tab cut off, fourth with 1 1/2 tabs, and so on. Hips and ridges: manufacturer shingles, cut strips, or 9-in-wide mineral-surfaced roofing bent equally and nailed on 2-in centers 3/4 in from edges. Almost all problems on Army buildings came from nailing too high
entries.use: Reroofing hospitals/mobilization-type pitched roofs
entries.how: Nail thick-butt shingles about 3/4 in above the cutouts, through the thick part
entries.dim: 4-tab 10x36 in, 4 in exposure, 210 lb/sq, nails 1 1/4-1 1/2 in, head >= 3/8 in; 3-tab thick-butt 1x3 ft, 5 in exposure, nails 1 1/2-1 3/4 in; starter strip 18 in; drip edge about 3/4 in; ridge strip 9 in wide, nails on 2-in centers 3/4 in from edge
entries.tm: Table C-10: asphalt shingles 30 MH per 1,000 sq ft
entries.wn: Nailing shingles too high is the main cause of failures

entries.n: Open and closed valleys with asphalt shingles (reroof)
entries.desc: Open valley: flash with 90-lb, 18-in-wide mineral-surfaced roll roofing, surfaced side down, centered over valley underlayment, lower edge cut flush with eaves flashing; splices overlap 12 in cemented with asphalt plastic cement; a 36-in-wide strip centered surfaced side up and nailed over it. Snap chalk lines starting 3 in from the valley on both sides; clip the upper corner of each end shingle; cement each shingle to the lining; no exposed nails along the valley. Closed valley (strip shingles only; doubles coverage): lining from a 36-in strip of 55-lb or heavier roll roofing centered over underlayment; weave valley shingles over the lining (both surfaces together, or each surface to about 36 in from valley center and weave later); first course extends at least 12 in along the adjoining surface; no nail closer than 6 in to valley centerline; two nails at the end of each terminal strip
entries.use: Valleys on shingle reroof
entries.how: Closed valleys only with strip shingles; no nail within 6 in of valley centerline
entries.dim: Open: 90-lb 18-in strip + 36-in strip, 12-in splice overlap, chalk lines 3 in from valley; Closed: 36-in lining of 55-lb or heavier roofing, 12-in extension, nails >= 6 in from centerline

entries.desc: Cut roll roofing into 18- or 20-ft lengths, stack free of wrinkles in protected piles at at least 50 deg F for 24 hours. Cover roof with 15-lb asphalt-saturated felt, joints lapped 2 in. Starter sheet (plain dry or mineral-surfaced, upside down, flush with eaves) nailed through tin/fiber disks on 12-in staggered centers: one row on 12-in centers not more than 2 in from the lower edge and a second row staggered about 8 in above. Hot asphalt on lower half at 30 lb per 100 sq ft; lay first sheet in the asphalt; two-ply with 2-in head lap; end laps 6 in with underlying edges nailed on 6-in centers; one ply at eaves and edges turned down and secured with a wood member nailed on 8-in centers. Do not apply asphalt more than 3 ft ahead of the roll
entries.use: Low-pitch reroofing
entries.how: Condition the rolls at 50 F or above for 24 hours before laying
entries.dim: Felt 15 lb, 2-in laps; nails on 12-in staggered centers (rows 2 in and about 8 in above lower edge); asphalt 30 lb per 100 sq ft; head lap 2 in; end lap 6 in with nails on 6-in centers; edge member nails 8 in o.c.; keep >= 50 F for 24 h
entries.tm: Table C-9: roll roofing – paper (plain) and felt 7 MH per 1,000 sq ft

entries.desc: Cut into 18- or 20-ft lengths; stack free of wrinkles at at least 50 deg F for 24 hours. Apply single-ply horizontally with at least 4-in side laps and 6-in end laps; nail underlying lap edges through tin or fiber disks on 6-in centers; cement overlying laps with hot asphalt or approved cold-applied sealing compound and step down firmly; double the roofing over the ridge with at least 4-in laps; turn down neatly at eaves and edges; nail roofing on 6-in centers
entries.use: TO roofs
entries.how: Horizontal courses, 4-in side laps and 6-in end laps, nailed on 6-in centers
entries.dim: Side lap >= 4 in; end lap >= 6 in; nails 6 in o.c.; ridge lap >= 4 in

entries.desc: Prepare deck (drive in nails, cut out buckles). Step 1: one layer 15-lb asphalt-saturated felt, laps 3 in horizontally and vertically, nails on 12-in centers at laps and through center of each sheet on 12-in staggered centers, nails penetrate sheathing at least 3/4 in through tin or hard fiber disks. Step 2: mop hot asphalt 25 lb per 100 sq ft. Step 3: two more layers 15-lb 36-in felt, lap each sheet 19 in, end laps at least 6 in, nailed 1 in from back edge on 12-in centers. Step 4: mop each sheet full width of lap with hot asphalt 25 lb/100 sq ft. Step 5: uniform mopping of hot asphalt 30 lb per 100 sq ft. Materials per 100 sq ft: asphalt 80 lb; asphalt-saturated felt 45 lb. Rough deck: remove and use 30-lb felt instead of 15-lb. Slag/gravel finish: step 5 uses 45 lb asphalt with 300 lb roofing slag or 400 lb gravel per 100 sq ft. Lay felt while asphalt is hot, keep wrinkle-free
entries.use: Low-pitch roofs (less than 2 in/ft) previously roofed with roll roofing
entries.how: 15-lb felt; hot asphalt not above 400 F
entries.dim: Felt laps 3 in, 19 in, end laps >= 6 in; nails on 12-in centers, >= 3/4 in into sheathing; asphalt 25/25/30 lb per 100 sq ft (80 total); felt 45 lb; slag 300 lb or gravel 400 lb with 45 lb asphalt
entries.eq: Mop, hot asphalt kettle, tin or hard fiber disks
entries.tm: Table C-8: 3-ply 20 MH per 1,000 sq ft
entries.wn: Do not heat asphalt above 400 deg F

entries.desc: Same sequence as asphalt roof but: one layer 15-lb coal-tar-saturated felt; mop 30 lb pitch per 100 sq ft; two more layers of 15-lb 36-in coal-tar felt lapped 19 in (17 in if 32-in felt), nailed 1 in from back edge on 12-in centers through disks (>= 3/4 in into sheathing), end laps at least 6 in; mop each sheet full width of lap with 25 lb per 100 sq ft; final pour 55 lb per 100 sq ft with 300 lb slag or 400 lb gravel per 100 sq ft.
