Remove rotting dining-facility waste as soon as possible, especially in warm weather; burial, if permitted, must not be near the base camp. POL waste (used oil and POL products, fuels, petroleum derivatives, asphalt) may become hazardous if mixed with water or soil; separate, store in appropriate containers and dispose through contractors or retrograde. Hazardous waste (solvents, paints, cleaners) needs special handling, transportation, disposal and documentation; store in containers, dispose through contractors or retrograde; engineers and preventive medicine give guidance. Medical waste is any health-care waste capable of producing infectious disease; dispose through contractors, or incinerate in certain cases
entries.use: Sorting waste into general, POL, hazardous and medical and deciding who disposes of it
entries.how: Generating units collect and dispose; POL, hazardous and medical waste need contractors, retrograde or special handling

entries.n: Locate and lay out a field latrine
entries.desc: Latrines should be at least 100 yards from the dining facility and 100 feet from the nearest water source to protect food and water. Do not dig below the groundwater table or where they may drain into a water source (find groundwater depth from local inhabitants or by excavating). Build them at least 30 yards from the end of the unit area but within reasonable distance for easy access. Light them at night if the military situation permits; otherwise tie cord or tape to trees or stakes as guides. During wartime commanders must be resourceful; improvised facilities must maintain proper sanitary standards when buildings are unavailable or not used
entries.use: Picking a latrine site and general construction rules (all types except catholes)
entries.how: At least 100 yards from the dining facility, 100 feet from water, above the groundwater table, lighted or cord-marked at night
entries.dim: At least 100 yd from dining facility; at least 100 ft from water source; at least 30 yd from end of unit area

entries.n: Screen, wash, police and close a field latrine
entries.desc: Screen each latrine with canvas or brush or enclose in a tent (heat the shelter in cold climates); dig a drainage ditch around the screen or tent so water cannot run in. Fly control: spray the shelter with insecticide twice a week; if flies persist, spray pit contents and box interior twice a week with a residual insecticide. Install a simple, easy-to-operate hand-washing device with a constant water supply outside each latrine (hands contaminated with fecal material are a common way to spread disease). Police latrines daily with specific personnel assigned. Close a pit when filled to within 1 foot of the surface or when abandoned: remove the latrine box, fill to the surface with successive 3-inch earth layers, packing each; mound 1 foot of dirt over the length of the pit to keep fly pupae from escaping; place a rectangular sign on the mound showing pit type and date closed (include unit designation in nonoperational areas)
entries.use: Day-to-day care of a latrine and shutting it down when full
entries.how: Screen it, hand-wash device outside, police daily, close at 1 ft from surface with 3-in. compacted layers and a 1-ft mound
entries.dim: Close at 1 ft below surface; 3-in. layers; 1-ft mound
entries.eq: Canvas or brush screen or tent, insecticide, hand-washing device, sign

entries.desc: The simplest field human waste disposal device, used by individuals on the march and patrol and where no latrine facilities are available (Figure 1-14). Dig it at least 1 foot wide and 1 foot deep. After use, replace and repack the soil
entries.use: Individuals on the march or on patrol
entries.how: At least 1 ft wide and 1 ft deep; replace and repack the soil after use
entries.dim: At least 1 ft wide x 1 ft deep

entries.desc: The most common latrine for temporary (one to three days) bivouacs (Figure 1-15). Dig 1 foot wide, 2 1/2 feet deep and 4 feet long; it accommodates two people at once. Provide straddle trenches for at least 4 percent of the unit's male strength and 6 percent of the female strength (a unit of 100 men and 100 women needs at least four for the men and six for the women). Place trenches at least 2 feet apart. There are no seats; boards may be placed along both sides for better footing. Put toilet paper on a holder protected from weather by a tin can or other cover. Pile the excavated earth at the end of the trench so each person can cover excreta and paper. Close as in para 1-131
entries.use: Temporary bivouacs of one to three days
entries.how: 1 ft wide, 2 1/2 ft deep, 4 ft long, seats two; provide trenches for 4 percent of male and 6 percent of female strength
entries.dim: 1 ft wide x 2 1/2 ft deep x 4 ft long; trenches at least 2 ft apart; 4 percent of male strength and 6 percent of female strength

entries.desc: Used with a latrine box (Figure 1-16). Standard box has four seats, 8 feet long and 2 1/2 feet wide at the base; a unit of 100 men requires two four-seat boxes. Cover holes with flyproof, self-closing lids; flyproof cracks with strips of wood or tin; put a metal deflector (a flattened can) inside the front of the box to keep urine from soaking into the wood. Dig the pit about 2 feet wide and 7 1/2 feet long to give the box 3 inches of support on all sides. Depth: allow 1 foot for each week of estimated use plus 1 foot for the dirt cover when closed, no deeper than 6 feet (rock or high groundwater may limit depth). Brace sides with planking or similar if the soil may collapse. Pack earth tightly around the bottom edges of the box to seal openings flies could enter. Keep the box clean, lids closed and cracks sealed; maintain fly control; lime or burning does not effectively control flies or odor; scrub the box and seats daily with soap and water. Close per para 1-131
entries.use: Longer-term field latrine with a four-seat box
entries.how: Pit about 2 x 7 1/2 ft, 1 ft deep per week of use plus 1 ft cover, no deeper than 6 ft; two four-seat boxes per 100 men
entries.dim: Box 8 ft long x 2 1/2 ft wide, 4 seats; pit about 2 ft x 7 1/2 ft; depth 1 ft per week + 1 ft; max 6 ft; 3 in. box support
entries.eq: Latrine box, planking, lids, metal deflector

entries.desc: A hole about 18 inches in diameter and 15 to 20 feet deep covered by a one-hole latrine box (Figure 1-17). Actual diameter is not critical; make it as large as available augers permit. Sink a covered metal drum with both ends removed into the ground as the box, with a flyproof seat cover with a self-closing lid fitted to the top of the drum. If no drum is available build a flyproof wooden box 18 inches high. Satisfactory for small units
entries.use: Small units needing a one-hole latrine
entries.how: About 18 in. diameter and 15-20 ft deep, sunk drum or 18-in. wooden box on top
entries.dim: About 18 in. diameter, 15-20 ft deep; wooden box 18 in. high
entries.eq: Auger, metal drum or wooden box, self-closing lid

entries.n: Build a mound latrine where groundwater or rock is shallow
entries.desc: Latrines of the pit type are limited to areas where the water table is deep enough to prevent contamination or standing water and rock is not near the surface; for other locations use alternatives. Mound latrine (Figure 1-18): build an earth mound at least 6 feet wide and 12 feet long that can support a four-hole latrine box and is high enough to meet the pit depth requirement, leaving 1 foot from the base of the pit to water or rock level. Break up or plow the area under the mound to aid seepage of liquids. With timber, build a crib of the desired height to enclose the pit and support the box; build the mound in compacted successive 1-foot layers up to the top of the crib, roughening each layer before adding the next. Without timber, build the mound to height in 1-foot layers and dig the pit into it, bracing walls with wood, sandbags or other material. Flyproof and enclose like a deep-pit latrine. Make the mound base larger if the slope is steep or the soil requires; steps may be needed on a steep slope
entries.use: Deep-pit latrine where the water table is high or rock is near the surface
entries.how: Earth mound at least 6 x 12 ft, built in compacted 1-ft layers, leaving 1 ft from pit base to water or rock
entries.dim: Mound at least 6 ft x 12 ft; 1-ft compacted layers; 1 ft from pit base to water or rock
entries.eq: Timber crib or sandbags, latrine box

entries.n: Build and operate a burn-out latrine
entries.desc: Particularly suitable for jungle areas with high groundwater (Figure 1-19). Burn downwind of the base camp. A unit of 100 men and 100 women needs at least eight men's and eight women's latrines. Place a 55-gallon drum in the ground leaving enough above ground for comfortable sitting height (the drum may be cut in half for two latrines of less capacity). Put a wooden seat with a flyproof self-closing lid on top. Weld handles to the drum sides so two men can carry it, because it must be moved before burning; keep two sets of drums if possible, one in use while the other burns. Encourage male personnel to use a urine disposal facility instead (a liquid content needs more fuel). Burn out daily with enough fuel to incinerate fecal matter; do not use highly volatile fuel because of its explosive nature. A mixture of 1 quart gasoline to 5 quarts diesel is effective but use it with caution. Burn again if contents are not dry and odorless; bury the residual ash
entries.use: Latrines in jungle or other high-groundwater areas
entries.how: 55-gal drum seat with handles, burn out daily with 1 qt gasoline to 5 qt diesel, burn downwind
entries.dim: 55-gal drum; fuel mix 1 qt gasoline : 5 qt diesel; 8 men's and 8 women's latrines per 100 men and 100 women
entries.eq: 55-gal drums, wooden seat and lid, handles, diesel and gasoline
entries.wn: Do not use highly volatile fuel (explosive); use gasoline-diesel mix with caution

entries.desc: Build when a latrine cannot be dug (Figure 1-20). Make a standard latrine box per paragraphs 1-134 to 1-136. Fit hinged doors on the rear, add a floor and put a pail under each seat. If in a building, place the box to form part of the outer wall with the rear opening directly outside. Box must be flyproof and seats and rear doors self-closing. Build the floor of impervious material (concrete if possible) sloped toward the rear for rapid drainage of wash water. In the male latrine install a urinal with a drainpipe to a pail outside, enclosed in a flyproof box. Clean pails at least once daily; bury or burn the contents or dispose of them another sanitary way. Plastic pail liners reduce spill risk; tie filled bags at the top before disposal
entries.use: Populated areas, rocky soil or marshes where a pit cannot be dug
entries.how: Standard latrine box with a floor, a pail under each seat, rear doors opening outside; clean pails daily
entries.dim: Clean pails at least daily
entries.eq: Latrine box, pails, plastic liners, concrete floor

entries.n: Build a urine soakage pit and urinals
entries.desc: Fixed camps normally connect urine facilities to the sewer; in the field separate devices may be needed, collocated in the male latrines to minimize seat fouling; at least one urine disposal facility is required for each male latrine or per 100 personnel. Urine soakage pit (best field device, Figure 1-21): dig 4 feet square and 4 feet deep, fill with aggregate material; lay a border along each edge so each side of the pit's surface is 5 feet long, border 6 inches wide and 4 inches deep of small stones. Optional ventilating shafts with screened openings run from about 8 inches above the pit to within 6 inches of its bottom. Use a soakage trench (para 1-155) where groundwater or rock prevents a pit. Pipe urinals: at least 1 inch in diameter, at an angle near each corner of the pit and, if needed, on the sides halfway between corners, extending at least 8 inches below the pit surface, with a funnel (tar paper, sheet metal or similar) in the top of each pipe, upper rim about 30 inches above ground. Trough urinal (Figure 1-22): U- or V-shaped sheet metal or wood (line wood with heavy tar paper); the four troughs forming the sides no more than 4 1/2 ft long when used with a soakage pit and an apron, each sloped slightly toward a corner where a pipe carries urine to the pit. Urinal (urinoil, Figure 1-23): a 55-gallon drum of oil (vegetable oil preferred; waste POL can be used) set over a recessed soakage pit; urine passes through a screen and sinks through the oil; oil rises in the 3-inch pipe until it reaches the 1 1/2-inch notch on the overflow pipe; the oil seals against odors and flies and the screen lifts out with attached hooks for cleaning
entries.use: Urine disposal in the field
entries.how: 4 ft x 4 ft x 4 ft pit filled with aggregate, 5-ft stone-bordered surface, pipe or trough urinals
entries.dim: Pit 4 x 4 x 4 ft; surface border 5 ft per side, 6 in. wide x 4 in. deep; pipe urinals at least 1 in. diameter, 8 in. into pit, funnel rim about 30 in. above ground; trough sides no more than 4 1/2 ft
entries.eq: Aggregate, pipe, funnels, sheet metal or wood trough, tar paper, 55-gal drum and oil

entries.n: Maintain and close urine disposal facilities
entries.desc: Urinate in the trough or pipe, not directly on the pit surface. Wash funnels and troughs with soap and water daily; replace funnels when necessary. Keep oil or grease out of the pit, which could clog it, and oil leaching through could contaminate groundwater. If the latrine is far from sleeping areas, place a large can or pail as a night urinal; empty into the soakage pit every morning and wash with soap and water before reuse. When a pit is abandoned or clogged, spray it with insecticide, mound over with a 1-foot covering of compacted earth and put a rectangular sign on the mound showing pit type and date closed
entries.use: Keeping urine soakage pits working and shutting them down
entries.how: Urinate in the trough or pipe, wash funnels daily, keep oil out of the pit; spray, mound 1 ft and mark when closed
entries.dim: 1-ft compacted earth mound over closed pit

entries.n: Treat kitchen waste with soakage pits and trenches
entries.desc: Food-service wastewater has food particles, grease and soap, so it requires treatment before disposal. In permanent or semipermanent camps it passes through a grease trap and drains into a wastewater collection system; in temporary camps the soil absorbs it, so install grease traps to keep grease from clogging the soil. Clean traps frequently and, if federal and state regulations permit, burn or bury removed grease; otherwise follow local procedures and unit SOP. Kitchen soakage pit: constructed like a urine soakage pit (para 1-145), normally handles liquid kitchen waste for 200 persons; a grease trap replaces the pipes or troughs. If the camp lasts several weeks build two pits and alternate daily; a rest period prevents clogging. A clogged pit will not accept liquid and must be closed: backfill and compact with soil 1 foot above grade and mark the pit. Soakage trench (Figure 1-24) when groundwater or rock prevents a pit: a pit 2 feet square and 1 foot deep with a trench radiating from each side 6 or more feet, trenches 1 foot wide, depth varying from 1 foot at the center to 1 1/2 feet at outer ends, filled with the same material as a soakage pit. Build two units for every 200 persons fed and alternate daily; use a grease trap and close as for a latrine
entries.use: Disposing of kitchen wastewater at temporary base camps
entries.how: Kitchen soakage pit (built like a urine pit) serves about 200 persons; use two and alternate daily; soakage trench where pit cannot be dug
entries.dim: Pit serves 200 persons; trench center pit 2 ft x 2 ft x 1 ft, trenches 6+ ft long, 1 ft wide, 1 to 1 1/2 ft deep; two units per 200 persons

entries.n: Build a baffle or barrel-filter grease trap
entries.desc: A trap must be large enough that hot, greasy water does not heat the cool water already in it (otherwise grease passes through instead of congealing and rising). Provide a grease trap for each soakage pit except those under showers. Baffle grease trap (Figure 1-25): a 55-gallon drum or box divided vertically into unequal chambers by a wooden baffle extending to within 1 inch of the bottom. Waste is poured through a strainer (a box with openings in the bottom, filled with straw or burlap) into the large chamber, passes under the baffle into the small chamber. The large chamber has a removable lid and the strainer; scrub the strainer frequently with soap and water. Insert a 1-inch pipe 3 to 6 inches below the top of the smaller chamber to carry liquid to the soakage pit. Clean frequently: remove grease, drain, remove bottom sediment; burn or bury grease, sediment and strained material. Barrel-filter grease trap (Figure 1-26): a 30- to 50-gallon barrel or drum with the top removed and a number of large holes bored in the bottom; put 8 inches of gravel or small stones in the bottom, cover with 12 to 18 inches of wood ashes or sand, fasten burlap to the top as a coarse strainer. Place it directly over the soakage pit or on a platform with a trough to the pit (if over the pit, remove the bottom instead of boring holes). Empty every two days: wash the trap, remove and bury the ashes or sand, refill with fresh ashes or sand; wash the burlap daily or replace it
entries.use: Removing grease from kitchen and wash-rack wastewater before soakage
entries.how: Size the trap so hot greasy water does not warm the water in it; baffle trap from a 55-gal drum or box, barrel filter from a 30-50 gal drum with gravel and ashes or sand
entries.dim: Baffle ends 1 in. above bottom; outlet pipe 1 in. dia., 3-6 in. below top of small chamber; barrel filter: 30-50 gal drum, 8 in. gravel, 12-18 in. ashes or sand; empty every 2 days
entries.eq: 55-gal drum or box, baffle, strainer, straw or burlap, gravel, ashes or sand

entries.desc: Use in hot, dry climates or where clay soil prevents standard soakage pits; three-tier beds can be used when acreage is limited (Figures 1-27, 1-28). Beds measure 8 by 10 feet; build enough to allow 3 square feet per person per day for kitchen waste and 2 square feet per person per day for wash and bath waste; space them so waste can be distributed to any bed. Scrape topsoil to the edges to form a small dike; spade the bed to 10 to 15 inches deep; rake into rows with ridges about 6 inches above the depressions, lengthwise or crosswise for best water distribution. Each day flood one bed with liquid waste to the top of the ridges (about 3 inches average depth) and let it evaporate and percolate; after three or four days it is usually dry enough to respade and reform; flood the other beds on successive days in sequence. Rotate, maintain and dose carefully. Kitchen waste must pass through an efficient grease trap first. Used properly, beds create no insect hazard and only slight odor
entries.use: Wastewater disposal in hot, dry climates or clay soil
entries.how: 8 x 10 ft beds, 3 sq ft per person per day for kitchen waste and 2 sq ft for wash and bath waste; flood one bed per day to 3 in
entries.dim: Bed 8 x 10 ft; 3 sq ft/person/day kitchen, 2 sq ft/person/day wash and bath; spade 10-15 in.; ridges about 6 in.; flood to about 3 in.; rest 3-4 days

entries.n: Provide soakage areas and size field wastewater systems
entries.desc: Every device used for washing or drinking needs a soakage area to prevent pools and mud: excavate under and a few inches around hand-washing devices, wash racks and lister bags and fill with small smooth stones. Pass wash-rack wastewater through a grease trap before the pit or trench. Each field shower needs only a soakage pit or trench. The general rules apply to company-sized or smaller elements; for larger camps design to the camp's needs. Wastewater from laundry, bath and kitchen is tied to each facility's water-consumption planning factor: design bath and laundry disposal for 100 percent of the flow and kitchens for 70 percent (part of the water is consumed). Discharge liquid waste into a sewer pipe: for most theater facilities a 6- to 12-inch plastic pipe at a 2 percent slope, buried if possible with minimum cover depending on traffic. In developed countries a waterborne system may connect to the host-nation main; where none exists base-camp design must include treatment and disposal. An underground septic tank with a tile drain field is ideal but may be unfeasible; with no waterborne toilets, soakage pits or evaporation beds usually handle laundry, bath and kitchen effluent
entries.use: Preventing mud and pools at wash points and sizing waste systems for larger camps
entries.how: Stone-filled soakage pit under every hand-washing device and wash rack; size bath/laundry for 100 percent of flow and kitchens for 70 percent
entries.dim: Bath/laundry 100 percent of flow; kitchen 70 percent; sewer pipe 6-12 in. plastic at 2 percent slope
entries.eq: Small smooth stones, grease trap, plastic sewer pipe

entries.n: Run a percolation test for wastewater design and size seepage pits
entries.desc: Steps: 1 Dig one or more holes 1 foot square by 1 foot deep. 2 Fill with water and let it seep into the soil. 3 Refill to at least 6 inches while the bottom is still wet. 4 Measure the depth of water and record the time for all of it to be absorbed. 5 Calculate the time for the water level to drop 1 inch. 6 Use that time to find the application rate from Table 1-8 (surface evaporation beds) or Table 1-9 (seepage or soakage trenches). Table 1-8 (GPD application rate by percolation per inch): 1 min 57,700; 2 min 46,800; 5 min 34,800; 10 min 25,000; 30 min 12,000; 60 min 8,700. A rate over 60 minutes means the soil is unsuited for a seepage pit; over 30 minutes is borderline for soil absorption and other disposal methods should be considered. Seepage pit: size from the percolation test and estimated effluent; 4 to 6 feet deep, square or rectangular; bottom at least 2 feet above groundwater and 5 feet above rock or impermeable soil; effective absorption area is the total wall area (not the bottom); several small pits may be more feasible than one large one, with equal distribution of wastewater; spacing at least twice the pit size; locate outside the base camp and at least 100 feet from the nearest water source
entries.use: Finding the soil's absorption capability before designing wastewater facilities
entries.how: 1-ft hole, 6 in. of water, time the 1-in. drop, then use Table 1-8 (evaporation beds) or 1-9 (seepage trenches); over 60 minutes means unsuited
entries.dim: Test hole 1 ft x 1 ft x 1 ft, refill to 6 in.; seepage pit 4-6 ft deep, bottom 2 ft above groundwater and 5 ft above rock; pits spaced at least twice pit size; at least 100 ft from water

entries.desc: Pits should be no deeper than 6 feet (deeper may need wall shoring). All absorption is assumed to occur in the walls only. Step 1: perform a percolation test twice, initially and again at the full estimated depth. Step 2: get the application rate from Table 1-9 (GPD/sq ft by percolation per inch: 1 min 5.3; 2 min 4.3; 5 min 3.2; 10 min 2.3; 15 min 1.8; 20 min 1.5; 30 min 1.1; 45 min 0.8; 60 min 0.5). Step 3: required absorption area = total estimated effluent / application rate. Step 4: divide by 4 walls. Step 5: divide the per-wall area by pit depth (normally 6 ft) for each wall length; the bottom must be 2 feet above groundwater and 5 feet above any impermeable soil. Step 6: build the pit with walls of that length (several small pits reduce excavation). Step 7: fill with large stones or rubble, pipe wastewater in near the center, and cover with tar paper, plastic or similar to keep rain out
entries.use: Sizing a pit for wastewater absorption
entries.how: Effluent / application rate = wall area needed; divide by 4 walls and by depth (normally 6 ft) for wall length
entries.dim: Depth no more than 6 ft; bottom 2 ft above groundwater and 5 ft above impermeable soil
entries.eq: Large stones or rubble, tar paper or plastic cover

entries.desc: Substitute for a seepage pit if groundwater or a rock stratum is within 6 feet of the surface. A central pit 2 feet square and 1 foot deep with a trench radiating 6 feet or more from each side; trenches 1 foot wide, depth increasing from 1 foot at the pit to 1 1/2 feet at the outer end; fill pit and trenches with gravel or broken rock; length may vary. Design: 1 Percolation test. 2 Application rate from Table 1-9. 3 Required absorption area = total estimated flow / application rate. 4 Divide by 8 (four trenches, two walls each); absorption occurs in the side walls only. 5 Divide wall area by the average depth of 1 1/4 feet to get each trench length. 6 Build four trenches of that length radiating from the central pit
entries.use: Where groundwater or rock lies within 6 ft of the surface
entries.how: Central pit 2 x 2 x 1 ft with four trenches 1 ft wide; area / 8 walls / 1 1/4 ft average depth = trench length
entries.dim: Central pit 2 ft sq x 1 ft deep; trenches 1 ft wide, 1 to 1 1/2 ft deep, 6+ ft long; average depth 1 1/4 ft

entries.desc: Construct enough beds to handle the entire wastewater flow from base camp laundry, kitchen and bath facilities; locate outside the base camp in an open, sunny area; rotate, maintain and dose carefully (no insect problem, slight odor if used properly). An evaporation field is probably the simplest way to dispose of large amounts of shower and laundry wastewater. Steps: 1 Perform a percolation test at 3 or 4 locations over the proposed field. 2 Get the application rate from Table 1-8 (it includes allowances for resting, recovery, maintenance and rainfall). 3 Divide the total daily effluent by the application rate to get the required acreage. 4 Build enough beds to equal that acreage
entries.use: High groundwater or clay soil preventing seepage pits
entries.how: Percolation tests at 3-4 locations; total daily effluent / application rate from Table 1-8 = acreage
entries.dim: Perc tests at 3-4 locations

entries.n: Choose a waterborne sewage treatment for a base camp
entries.desc: Three treatment options for waterborne human waste: cesspools, sewage lagoons, septic tanks with tile drain fields; the septic tank with tile drain field is preferred. Cesspools are no longer used in developed countries (groundwater pollution) but are common in undeveloped ones; check nearby water sources for purity continually; least preferred, last resort. Sewage lagoons (oxidation ponds) work in all regions except arctic, are cheap and easy to build but are not a recommended theater practice; locate at least one-half mile from the population center (odors from anaerobic digestion); longer collection systems and possible lift stations raise material and construction effort; minimize absorption into surrounding soil (Table 1-10 relative absorption: 0-3 min rapid, coarse sand and gravel; 3-5 medium, fine sand or sandy loam; 5-30 slow, clay or loam; 30-60 semi-impervious, dense clay; over 60 impervious, hardpan or rock; the first two soils are not suited for lagoons unless a waterproofing skin is installed). Septic tanks give primary and partial secondary treatment; the preferred installation is a precast or fiberglass unit sized for the expected flow (or build in place); solids settle and digest anaerobically and effluent disperses through a tile drain field of porous underground pipes
entries.use: Rare theater case where a waterborne system for human waste is wanted and no main sewer exists
entries.how: Prefer a septic tank with tile drain field; lagoons only where permitted and far from people; cesspools last resort
entries.dim: Lagoon at least 1/2 mile from population center
entries.eq: Precast or fiberglass septic tank, tile drain field

entries.n: Lay out a tile drain field
entries.desc: Subsurface irrigation is common with septic tanks at small installations, using Table 1-11 application rates (gal/sq ft of trench bottom/day by minutes to drop 1 inch: 1 min 4.0; 2 min 3.2; 5 min 2.4; 10 min 1.7; 30 min 0.8; 60 min 0.6). A tile field is lines of concrete or clay drain tile laid with open joints, or concrete pipe with 1/4- to 3/8-inch perforations in the bottom half, bituminized fiber pipe with holes in the lower portion (2 to 8 in. diameter, 5 to 8 ft long), or perforated plastic pipe (Figures 1-29, 1-30). Needs: groundwater well below the field, soil with satisfactory leaching a few feet down (test the soil on site), subsurface drainage away from the field, adequate area, no risk of polluting drinking-water supplies. Minimum trench width: sand and sandy loam 1 ft; loam 2 ft; sand and clay mixture 2 ft; clay with some gravel 3 ft. Frost line burial not necessary (18 in. depth worked in New England); never lay below groundwater. Use 3- to 6-inch pipe. Lay pipe with 3/8-inch clear openings and cover the top of the space with tar paper to keep gravel out; for bell and spigot pipe break away two-thirds of the bell bottom at the joint and use small wood-block spacers. Slope about 0.5 ft per 100 ft from a septic tank, 0.3 ft per 100 ft with a dosing tank. Bed of 6 in. screened coarse gravel (passes 2 1/2-in. mesh, retained on 3/4-in.) with 3 in. around and over the pipe, then 3 in. medium gravel, then 3 in. fine gravel; keep fill soil out of the voids. Laterals no longer than 75 ft; on slopes lay lines parallel to contours; herringbone or laterals at right angles to the main distributor; lateral spacing three times trench width; trenches 24 in. or wider are most economical. Fence or post the field to keep vehicles off; grass over it is good, shrubs and trees clog tile with roots
entries.use: Dispersing septic tank effluent into the soil
entries.how: Perforated or open-joint pipe on a 6-in. gravel bed, laterals no longer than 75 ft, trench width by soil type, about 18 in. deep
entries.dim: Laterals max 75 ft; lateral spacing = 3 x trench width; trench width 1-3 ft by soil; slope 0.5 ft/100 ft (0.3 with dosing tank); gravel bed 6 in. + 3 in. over
entries.eq: Tile or perforated pipe, graded gravel, tar paper, wood-block spacers, fencing or posts
entries.wn: Subsurface tile must never be laid below groundwater level

entries.n: Build a subsurface filter trench or sand filter and dosing tank
entries.desc: Used where soil is dense and impervious and there is no isolated area for an open filter; underdrains discharge freely to the nearest satisfactory point such as a small stream or dry streambed. Design for filtration not greater than 1 gallon per square foot per day. Filter material: clean coarse sand passing a 1/4-inch mesh with a uniformity coefficient not greater than 4.0, at least 30 inches deep; coarse screened gravel passing a 3 1/2-inch mesh and retained on a 1/4-inch mesh (Figures 1-31, 1-32). Slope of distributors about 0.3 ft per 100 ft with a dosing tank, 0.5 ft per 100 ft without. For more than 800 feet of distributors build the filter in two or more sections with siphons to alternate flow. Distribution lines on 6- to 10-foot centers; underdrains on 5- to 10-foot centers. Provide dosing tanks with automatic sewage siphons when distribution tile exceeds 300 feet; design them to discharge 70 to 80 percent of the volumetric capacity of the distribution piping, usually built as part of the septic tank at the same width (Figure 1-33)
entries.use: Soil too dense for a tile field and no space for an open filter
entries.how: Filtration no more than 1 gal/sq ft/day through at least 30 in. of coarse sand; add a dosing tank when distribution tile exceeds 300 ft
entries.dim: Filtration max 1 gal/sq ft/day; sand 30 in. deep passing 1/4-in. mesh; distributor slope 0.3 ft/100 ft (dosing) or 0.5 ft/100 ft; distributors on 6-10 ft centers; underdrains on 5-10 ft centers; dosing tank when tile over 300 ft; 70-80 percent discharge volume
entries.eq: Clean coarse sand, screened gravel, dosing tank with automatic siphon

entries.desc: Most theater construction: 6- to 12-inch plastic pipe at about a 2 percent slope for gravity flow. Table 1-12: under 300 gpm = 6 in.; 300-700 gpm = 8 in.; 700-1,250 gpm = 10 in.; 1,250-2,200 gpm = 12 in. Minimum cover: pedestrian areas 6 inches; light vehicles 24 inches; heavy vehicles (2 1/2-ton and over) 48 inches. Where freezing occurs, place pipes below the frost line (except subsurface tile systems)
entries.use: Choosing pipe size and cover for wastewater lines to a disposal system
entries.how: 6-12 in. plastic at about 2 percent slope; size from flow (Table 1-12); cover 6 in. pedestrian, 24 in. light vehicles, 48 in. heavy
entries.dim: Slope about 2 percent; cover 6 in. (pedestrian), 24 in. (light vehicles), 48 in. (heavy vehicles); flow to size: <300 gpm 6 in., 300-700 8 in., 700-1,250 10 in., 1,250-2,200 12 in

entries.n: Know the three heating system types
entries.desc: Heating systems carry heat from the point of production to the place of use and are classified by the medium: steam, hot-water and forced-air are the most common. Hot-water heating is used extensively. Forced-air heating is used in most semipermanent construction and most barracks. Appendix B gives plumbing plans including heating symbols used on heating-system plans
entries.use: Choosing between steam, hot-water and forced-air heat
entries.how: Classified by the medium that carries the heat; hot-water is used extensively, forced-air in most semipermanent construction and barracks

entries.n: Read and install a hot-water heating system
entries.desc: A hot-water heating system is a heating unit, pipes and radiators or connectors. Water is heated at a central source, circulated and returned to the heating unit, usually by a pump rather than gravity. It may have its own plan or be combined with hot- and cold-water and sewer lines on the plumbing plan; the plan shows layout of units, pipes, accessories and connections (Figure 2-1 shows boiler, circulating pump and compression tank; one-pipe system with two loops of two radiators, the second radiator in each loop larger). One-pipe system (Figure 2-2): simplest, adequate for very small installations; hot water circulates through one set of pipes through each radiator, so water reaching the last radiator is cooler; to get the same heat from every radiator each must be larger than the one before. Two-pipe system (Figure 2-3): hot water goes from the heating unit to each radiator through the main, connected with Ts and elbows; cooler water leaving the radiators returns to the heater through separate return piping
entries.use: Hot-water (hydronic) heat with one-pipe or two-pipe layout
entries.how: Boiler, circulating pump and compression tank feed radiators; one-pipe needs each radiator larger than the one before; two-pipe has a separate return
entries.eq: Boiler, circulating pump, compression tank, radiators, Ts and elbows

entries.desc: A steam system is a boiler heating water into steam, radiators where steam condenses and gives heat, and connecting pipes carrying steam out and water back to the boiler, with an air valve or other means of removing air. Both one-pipe and two-pipe types are classified as high-pressure (operates above 15-psi gauge), low-pressure (0- to 15-psi gauge), vapor (low-pressure and vacuum conditions) and vacuum (low-pressure and vacuum with a vacuum pump)
entries.use: Choosing and recognizing steam systems
entries.how: Boiler, radiators, pipes and an air valve; classed high-pressure (over 15 psi), low-pressure (0-15 psi), vapor or vacuum
entries.dim: High-pressure above 15 psi gauge; low-pressure 0-15 psi gauge

entries.desc: A one-pipe system uses a single main and riser to carry steam to radiators or other units and to return condensate. Best for small installations where low cost and easy operation matter. Each radiator is equipped with a heat-controlled (thermostatic) air valve (Figure 2-4); larger air valves are installed at the ends of steam mains. These should be the vacuum type with a small check valve to keep air from flowing back into the system when heat input is reduced. The unit connection may have shutoff (angle) valves; because the restricted opening causes repeated banging (water hammer), these valves cannot be partly closed to control heat input
entries.use: Small installations needing low cost and easy operation
entries.how: Single main and riser carries steam and returns condensate; thermostatic air valve on each radiator; do not throttle the angle valves
entries.eq: Thermostatic air valves, vacuum-type end-of-main air valves with check valve, angle valves
entries.wn: Do not partly close angle valves to control heat; the restricted opening causes water hammer

entries.desc: A two-pipe system has two sets of mains and risers: one set distributes steam to the heating unit and the other returns condensate to the boiler (Figure 2-5). It operates under high- or low-pressure, vapor or vacuum conditions, with upflow or downflow distribution. It allows adjusting steam flow to individual heating units and uses smaller pipe than the one-pipe system. A two-pipe upflow vapor system (Figure 2-6) can operate over a range of pressures
entries.use: Steam heat where each unit's flow must be adjustable
entries.how: Separate supply and return mains and risers; can run high- or low-pressure, vapor or vacuum, upflow or downflow; smaller pipe than one-pipe

entries.desc: A forced-air upflow system distributes heated air through ducts, usually from a gas- or oil-fired furnace: furnace, bonnet, warm-air supply ducts and registers, return cold-air registers and ducts, and a fan or blower (Figure 2-7). A downflow furnace uses a crawl space duct system or crawl space plenum system (Figure 2-8). On the plan (Figure 2-9) solid lines are warm-air ducts and dashed lines are cold-air return ducts; duct sizes give the horizontal or width dimension first (depth, the second, is not shown on the plan). Use the plan for the location and size of warm-air registers: ceiling registers (diffusers) show neck dimensions; wall or baseboard registers show face dimensions; the notes give the height of wall registers above the finished floor. Return registers are shown recessed into the wall with face dimensions noted beside the symbol
entries.use: Finding duct and register locations and sizes on a forced-air plan
entries.how: Solid lines are warm-air ducts, dashed lines are cold-air returns; width is given first; ceiling registers by neck size, wall/baseboard by face size

entries.n: Lay out a forced-air system and duct connections
entries.desc: The bonnet above the furnace collects heated air and distributes it through rectangular supply ducts and warm-air registers (ceiling) into rooms; air returns through return (cold-air) registers set in the wall just below the opening, with return ducts in the crawl space. Lay out so warm air is directed at cold exterior walls (in some systems registers are on exterior walls below windows); cold-air returns are normally at baseboard height because cold air moves to the floor. Locate the furnace room centrally to equalize duct lengths (Figure 2-9). Comfort zone is the horizontal band between the top of the average person's head and knees; air blowing from a supply there is uncomfortable, so place registers high on the wall or in the baseboard. Run the main trunk above a central corridor to equalize branch duct lengths. Figure 2-10: a typical warm-air bonnet with two main supply ducts; split T directs airflow on the warm side, straight T may be used on cold-air return; with double-branch connections less air remains in the main duct, so reduce main duct size past the connection; single-branch connections reduce at the connection and reduce depth on the far side; branch connections form a natural air scoop. A boot changes duct shape without changing equivalent cross-section area or restricting flow (Figure 2-11); Table 2-1 gives equivalent lengths of gravity duct fittings (e.g. end boot = 2 ninety-degree elbows, offset boot = 2 1/2)
entries.use: Placing furnace, registers and ducts for even heating
entries.how: Aim warm air at cold exterior walls, returns at baseboard height, central furnace room, main trunk over a central corridor
entries.dim: Table 2-1 equivalent length in 90-degree elbows: 90-degree angle boot 1; end boot 2; offset boot 2 1/2; floor register, second story 3

entries.n: Find and repair a corroded pipe leak
entries.desc: Pipe corrosion is thinning of the pipe wall from electrolysis, rust or acidity; galvanic corrosion occurs where two different metals, e.g. galvanized and copper, are in one system. The first sign may be a leak inside walls or floors; water may show up several levels below. To locate it, use a strip of wood as a resonator: one end against your ear, the other on the pipe, and trace the sound, which gets louder nearer the leak. Galvanized pipe: 1 Shut off the water at the nearest valve below the leak and drain the pipe. 2 If fittings on each side are not readily available, cut out the leaking section; one plumber holds the pipe with a wrench to keep it from turning in the adjoining fitting while the other cuts a thread. 3 Replace the cutout with a coupling, a pipe section of the required length and a union. Copper pipe (resists corrosion except acids): 1 Shut off the water at the nearest valve below the leak and drain. 2 Replace with soldered or compression joints (chapter 6). Allow for the fittings the replacement pipe needs
entries.use: A leak inside walls or floors from pipe corrosion
entries.how: Trace the sound with a wood strip, shut off and drain, cut out the pipe, replace with coupling, pipe and union (galvanized) or soldered/compression joints (copper)
entries.eq: Wood strip, pipe wrench, threading tool, coupling, union, pipe

entries.desc: Two ways: (1) Dielectric unions placed in the cold- and hot-water takeoffs from the tank control galvanic corrosion of tanks; the fiber washer insulates the tank from the rest of the plumbing so no current flows from tank to system. (2) Magnesium rods in some water heaters (e.g. gas-operated) protect against rust and corrosion by acting as electrolytic cells; magnesium goes into solution, flows through the water and deposits on the metal being protected, and the rods dissolve. Maximum rod life is 18 months; then replace them. Check all valves regularly for leaks (most come from leaky washers or bonnets, see chapter 7); faucet repairs are in chapter 7, section II
entries.use: Protecting tanks and water heaters from galvanic corrosion and rust
entries.how: Dielectric unions on tank takeoffs; magnesium rods (replace at 18 months) in water heaters
entries.dim: Magnesium rod life: 18 months maximum

entries.n: Make temporary repairs for small pipe leaks
entries.desc: Before any repair, shut off the water and relieve system pressure. Options: rubber hose or plastic tubing (cut the pipe on each side of the leak with a hacksaw or pipe cutter, remove the damaged section, slip the hose or tubing over the pipe ends and fasten with hose clamps; hose inside diameter must fit the pipe outside diameter); sheet rubber (wrap the leaking area and fasten with two sheet-metal clamps, one on each side, with nuts and bolts); electrician's friction tape (several layers around the hole or crack, extending about 2 inches above and below); wood plugs (drill or ream small holes and drive in a wooden plug; it swells when wet so water pressure cannot blow it out). Make a permanent repair as soon as possible, replacing the weak part (and insulation if used) with a unit of the same size and quality as the original
entries.use: Emergency repair of a small leak until the part can be replaced
entries.how: Shut off water and relieve pressure first; hose and clamps, sheet rubber and clamps, friction tape or a wood plug
entries.dim: Friction tape extends about 2 in. above and below the leak
entries.eq: Hacksaw or pipe cutter, rubber hose or plastic tubing, hose clamps, sheet rubber, sheet-metal clamps, friction tape, wood plugs

entries.desc: Supply lines may freeze below 32 F; bury outside pipes below the frost line (4 feet or more in northern zones); inside pipes may freeze and break at the weakest point if the building falls below freezing. Blowtorch (best method but a fire risk): 1 Open the faucets in the line. 2 Apply heat from one end of the pipe and work along its whole length. 3 Continue until water flows freely. Alternatively wrap the pipe with burlap or other cloth and pour boiling water over the wrapping. If internal freezing is due to heating-plant failure, repair the heating plant and keep the building hot until the pipes thaw
entries.use: Water supply pipes frozen below 32 F
entries.how: Open faucets, work a blowtorch along the pipe from one end, or wrap with cloth and pour boiling water; fix the heat plant if that caused it
entries.eq: Blowtorch, burlap or cloth, boiling water
entries.wn: Do not overheat; solder joints will break loose when the solder melts. Blowtorch use carries fire risk

entries.desc: Steps: 1 Remove the pipe fittings. 2 Place a small thaw pipe or tube into the frozen pipe (Figure 3-1). 3 Add an elbow and a piece of vertical pipe to the outer end of the thaw pipe. 4 Place a bucket under the opening to the frozen pipe. 5 Insert a funnel into the open end of the vertical pipe. 6 Pour boiling water into the funnel; as the ice melts, push the thaw pipe forward. 7 After flow starts, withdraw the pipe quickly and let the flow continue until the thaw pipe is completely withdrawn and cleared of ice. A small pump may clear a piece of pipe, but excessive pump pressure can cause backup, so monitor carefully
entries.use: Water line frozen below grade
entries.how: Push a small thaw pipe into the ice while pouring boiling water through a funnel; withdraw quickly once flow starts
entries.eq: Thaw pipe or tube, elbow, vertical pipe, funnel, bucket, boiling water
entries.wn: Excessive pump pressure can cause a backup

entries.n: Reduce and remove scale and scum
entries.desc: Scale from hard water (calcium and magnesium compounds that prevent lathering) forms scum that slows flow and hardens into scale, sharply reducing flow to fixtures. In very hard water use a water softener, normally containing zeolite that must be recharged regularly by adding sodium chloride (table salt); softeners are programmed to recharge at a set time each day, then the softened water is piped to the distribution system. To remove scum inside a pipe: flush with hot water; use lye, or lye with a small quantity of aluminum shavings (use only cold water with lye); or replace the whole pipe if flow drops sharply. Chemical cleaners should not be used in completely stopped-up pipes because the cleaner must contact the stoppage directly
entries.use: Hard-water scale cutting flow to fixtures
entries.how: Use a zeolite water softener recharged with salt; flush with hot water or use lye with cold water; replace pipe if flow drops sharply
entries.eq: Water softener (zeolite), salt, lye, aluminum shavings
entries.wn: Use only cold water with lye

entries.n: Pick the tool for a waste-system stoppage
entries.desc: A stoppage can occur in a fixture drain, floor drain, branch line or main line; causes include hair, grease and other foreign matter. Use the proper clearing tool (Figure 3-2) for water closets, lavatories and sinks, urinals, bathtubs, shower drains, branch and main waste lines and grease traps
entries.use: Clearing hair, grease or foreign matter in fixture drains, floor drains, branch or main lines
entries.how: Use the clearing tool made for the fixture (Figure 3-2): plunger, snake, closet auger, cleanout

entries.desc: Force-cup plunger: 1 Pump the plunger up and down until the water level drops. 2 Put toilet paper in the bowl and flush to check if cleared. Water closet snake: 1 Push the snake into the bowl and turn the handle clockwise with a push-pull action until the water level drops. 2 Check with toilet paper and a flush as above (Figure 3-3)
entries.use: Clogged toilet
entries.how: Force-cup plunger until the water drops, then test with toilet paper and flush; if it persists use a water closet snake with push-pull and clockwise turning

entries.n: Clear lavatory, sink and urinal stoppages
entries.desc: Plunger: 1 Place a wet rag in the overflow opening; remove the plug if the lavatory has a pop-up plug. 2 Set the plunger over the waste outlet and push up and down until the bowl drains. 3 Remove the rag and replace the pop-up plug if needed. 4 Run water through the drain to confirm. Snake (1/4 to 1/2 in.): 1 Remove the plug if pop-up. 2 Push the snake into the waste outlet as far as it will go. 3 Push-pull and turn until the bowl drains. 4 Remove the snake and replace the plug. A P-trap stoppage can be cleared by disassembling the trap, removing the stoppage, reassembling and flushing to confirm drainage (Figure 3-4). Stoppage beyond the P-trap (Figure 3-5): 1 Place a container under the P-trap and disassemble it. 2 Push the snake into the drain line and turn with push-pull until it moves freely. 3 Remove the snake, replace the P-trap and run water to confirm free flow. Urinals with a water seal or exposed P-trap are cleared the same as lavatories (plunger and 1/4- to 1/2-inch snake)
entries.use: Slow or blocked basin, sink or urinal drain
entries.how: Plunge with a wet rag in the overflow, or snake (1/4 to 1/2 in.); disassemble the P-trap for deep stoppages
entries.dim: Snake 1/4 to 1/2 in
entries.eq: Plunger, wet rag, drain snake, container

entries.n: Clear bathtub, shower and floor drain stoppages
entries.desc: Bathtub P-trap (Figure 3-6): 1 Remove the stopper linkage and overflow cover. 2 Push a 1/4- to 1/2-inch drain snake into the overflow opening until it meets resistance. 3 Turn with a push-pull motion until it turns freely. 4 Remove the snake and run water to check. 5 Replace overflow cover and linkage. A vacuum plunger often works; try it first. Drum trap (Figure 3-7): 1 Remove the drum-top cover and gasket and push the snake into the trap's lower line to search for the stoppage. 2 If found, clear it. 3 If none, withdraw the snake and push it into the upper line. 4 Turn with a push-pull action to clear it; replace gasket and cover. 5 Run water to check. Shower drain (Figure 3-8), hose: 1 Remove the strainer. 2 Hook the water hose to a source and put the other end in the drain. 3 Stuff rags around the hose for a tight seal. 4 Turn water on full, off, and on again; the surge clears the stoppage. 5 Replace the strainer. Snake (1/4 to 1/2 in.): remove the strainer, push the snake in and turn with push-pull until free, remove the snake, replace the strainer. Floor drains are cleared the same way; if the strainer is cemented to the floor, chip the cement away and cement it back after clearing
entries.use: Blocked tub P-trap, tub drum trap, shower or floor drain
entries.how: Try a plunger first, then snake through the overflow or drum trap; for showers and floor drains use a hose surge or a snake
entries.dim: Snake 1/4 to 1/2 in
entries.eq: Vacuum plunger, drain snake, water hose, rags, cement

entries.n: Clear branch, main waste line and grease trap stoppages
entries.desc: Branch lines (Figure 3-9): 1 Remove the closest cleanout plug. 2 Clear with a snake. 3 Replace the plug. 4 Run water to confirm. Main lines: 1 Remove the closest cleanout plug. 2 Clear with a 3/4- to 1-inch heavy-duty snake. 3 Replace the plug. Grease trap (works on the principle that grease is lighter than water and rises): 1 Remove the top cover and dip out the grease with a ladle. 2 Scrape the walls and bottom after the grease is out. 3 Flush with clear water
entries.use: Blockage in building branch or main lines or in a grease trap
entries.how: Open the nearest cleanout and snake it (3/4 to 1 in. heavy-duty snake for mains); grease traps: ladle off grease, scrape, flush
entries.dim: Main-line snake 3/4 to 1 in

entries.n: Size supply pipe for plumbing fixtures
entries.desc: A fixture needs a flow rate that fills it in a reasonable time. Pipe size depends on main pressure (psi), length of piping in the building, number of fixtures and, for water closets, the type of flushing device. Table 4-1 pipe diameter (in.): lavatory 1/2; shower 1/2; bathtub 1/2; kitchen sink 1/2; slop sink 1/2; scullery sink 3/4; laundry tub 1/2; drinking fountain 1/2; water closet tank 1/2; urinal with diaphragm-type flushometer 3/4; water closet flushometer 1
entries.use: Choosing the branch pipe diameter for each fixture
entries.how: Use Table 4-1: most fixtures 1/2 in.; scullery sink and diaphragm urinal 3/4 in.; water closet flushometer 1 in
entries.dim: Table 4-1: scullery sink 3/4 in.; diaphragm-flushometer urinal 3/4 in.; water closet flushometer 1 in.; all others 1/2 in

entries.desc: A water closet carries organic body wastes to the sewer; it is vitreous china, floor-mounted or wall-hung (Figure 4-1). Each bowl has a built-in trap with a water seal based on equal atmospheric pressure on both sides of the trap. Common washdown: least expensive and simplest, trap at the front, small streams from the rim flush it. Washdown with jet: a small hole in the bottom delivers a jet into the upper arm of the trap to start siphoning. Reverse-trap: like washdown but trap at the rear, so a longer bowl that holds more water and is quieter. Siphon-jet: most efficient, quietest and most expensive; looks like reverse-trap but holds more water and is almost completely filled
entries.use: Choosing the bowl for the job
entries.how: Washdown is cheapest and simplest; siphon-jet is most efficient, quietest and most expensive

entries.n: Install a floor-mounted water closet bowl
entries.desc: Installation is the same regardless of flushing action. Need a floor flange, bowl, level, wrench and wax or rubber gasket (Figure 4-2). Steps: 1 Place the floor flange over the closet bend until it rests on the finished floor and make a joint for the type of piping. 2 Put two bowl bolts, threads up, into the flange slots. If the bowl needs four bolts, set the bowl on the flange and mark spots for the two extras and set those. On wood floors use bolts with wood threads on one end and machine threads on the other; on tile or concrete set the machine bolt heads in the holes and fill with cement to floor level. 3 Turn the bowl upside down on protective newspaper or wooden strips and set a wax gasket over the horn. 4 Turn the bowl upright and set it on the flange with the bolts through the holes. 5 Put a washer and nut on each bolt, tightening alternately until the bowl is set. 6 Check level; use thin metal shims if needed. 7 Put a nut cap on each nut and tighten; do not over tighten
entries.use: Setting a toilet on a floor flange
entries.how: Flange on the closet bend, bowl bolts up, wax gasket on the horn, level with shims, tighten nuts alternately and do not overtighten
entries.eq: Floor flange, wax or rubber gasket, bowl bolts, level, wrench, thin metal shims, nut caps
entries.wn: Do not over tighten the nuts

entries.n: Install a wall-hung water closet bowl
entries.desc: Used mainly in commercial buildings, sometimes residential. Install the bowl after the finished wall is up on a carrier mounted between the wall studs (Figure 4-3). Steps: 1 Install the carrier per the manufacturer's instructions. 2 Connect the carrier outlet to the rough-in waste pipe. 3 Place a sealing gasket in the rear opening of the bowl. 4 Place the bowl against the wall with the carrier bolts through the bowl holes. 5 Put a washer and nut on each bolt. 6 Keep the bowl level and tighten the nuts alternately. 7 Put beauty caps over the bolts
entries.use: Hanging a bowl on a carrier between wall studs
entries.how: Install after the finished wall is up; carrier outlet to the rough-in waste, gasket in the bowl's rear opening, tighten nuts alternately keeping it level
entries.eq: Carrier, sealing gasket, washers, nuts, beauty caps

entries.n: Mount a close-coupled or wall-hung water closet tank
entries.desc: Tanks are close-coupled (floor-mounted, attached to a floor-mounted bowl) or wall-hung (attached to the wall above the bowl with fittings to the bowl); the flushing mechanism is the same. Close-coupled (Figure 4-4): 1 Push the cone-shaped gasket over the tank's flush-valve outlet; put the cushion gasket (if included) on the bowl and line up holes. 2 Set the tank on the bowl with bolt holes aligned. 3 Slide a rubber washer on each bolt and push the bolts through the holes from inside the tank. 4 Slide a washer over each bolt under the back lip of the bowl and tighten nuts hand tight. 5 Tighten the nuts alternately to seat the cone gasket and tank. Wall-hung (Figure 4-5): 1 Install a 2- by 4-inch mounting board by notching the wall studs at the manufacturer's recommended height. 2 Install the elbow and spud connection (flange) at the rear of the bowl. 3 Slide the slip nut, ring and washer (in that order) onto the other end of the elbow. 4 Attach the tank to the mounting board with screw bolts, elbow in the tank outlet and tank level. 5 Check elbow alignment and tighten the slip-joint nuts
entries.use: Attaching the tank to the bowl or wall
entries.how: Close-coupled: cone gasket on the flush-valve outlet, bolts through the tank, tighten alternately. Wall-hung: notched 2x4 mounting board, elbow and spud, level
entries.dim: Mounting board 2 x 4 in
entries.eq: Cone gasket, cushion gasket, rubber washers, bolts, 2x4 board, elbow and spud, slip nut and ring

entries.n: Install tank flushing mechanisms and flushometers
entries.desc: Tank flushing mechanisms (Figure 4-6) are mechanically operated; the two most common are the ball cock and float cup. Follow the manufacturer's instructions, then connect the water supply, check operation and adjust to keep the proper tank water level. A flushometer valve delivers a preset amount of water under pressure directly into the bowl; it flushes quickly and shuts off automatically. The most common types are diaphragm and piston. After installing, turn on the water and operate it several times, checking for leaks and proper operation
entries.use: Fitting the flush valve to a water closet
entries.how: Ball cock and float cup are the common tank mechanisms; flushometers are diaphragm or piston types; follow the manufacturer and test
entries.eq: Ball cock or float cup, flushometer valve

entries.n: Connect the water supply to a water closet tank
entries.desc: Steps (Figure 4-7): 1 Slide the chrome cover on the wall pipe against the wall. 2 Coat threads with joint compound or Teflon tape and screw the shutoff valve on, tightened so its other opening is straight. 3 Bend the flexible tube with a spring bender for proper fit (steel-coated flexible supply lines are common). 4 Slide the inlet-coupling nut on with the tubing threads up, attach it to the tank inlet and tighten hand tight. 5 Slide the coupling nut threads and compression ring down onto the tubing and screw the coupling nut onto the valve hand tight. 6 Tighten the inlet-coupling nut and valve-coupling nut. 7 Open the shutoff valve and check for leaks. 8 Adjust the water level to 1 inch below the top of the overflow tube; recheck operation after any adjustment. 9 Put the tank cover on and install the seat
entries.use: Hooking up the supply line, valve and tank inlet
entries.how: Shutoff valve with joint compound or Teflon tape, flexible tube, hand-tight couplings, water level 1 in. below the overflow tube top
entries.dim: Water level 1 in. below top of overflow tube
entries.eq: Shutoff valve, joint compound or Teflon tape, flexible tube, spring bender, coupling nuts, compression ring

entries.n: Repair a flushometer valve and handle
entries.desc: See chapter 3 for water closet stoppages. Diaphragm type (Figure 4-8): 1 Turn off the water and remove the outer cover. 2 Remove the inner core (pry the cover with a screwdriver if stuck). 3 Remove the relief valve. 4 Remove the valve seat. 5 Remove the clogged or worn diaphragm and clean. 6 Install the new diaphragm. 7 Reassemble. 8 Turn on the water and check operation. Piston type: 1 Water off; remove outer cover and gasket. 2 Remove the inner cover and gasket. 3 Remove the brass screws and retaining plate. 4 Remove the clogged or worn rubber cup. 5 Install a new cup. 6 Reassemble. 7 Water on; check. Handle (Figure 4-9) with a water leak: 1 Water off at the angle valve; unscrew the retaining nut. 2 Pull out the handle body with all parts up to the packing nut. 3 Grip the body with one wrench and unscrew the packing nut with another. 4 Replace the worn packing washer. 5 Reassemble (replace the Mylar seal and tighten the retaining nut). 6 Water on; check leaks and operation. Loose or wobbly handle: steps 1-3 as above, then 4 grip the body with a wrench and unscrew the bushing with lock-grip pliers; 5 replace the worn bushing spring or plunger; 6 reassemble; 7 water on; check
entries.use: Valve that will not flush, will not stop flushing, or has a leaky or wobbly handle
entries.how: Water off first; diaphragm type: replace the diaphragm; piston type: replace the rubber cup; handles: new packing washer or worn bushing spring/plunger
entries.eq: Screwdriver, two wrenches, lock-grip pliers, new diaphragm or rubber cup, packing washer, Mylar seal
entries.wn: Turn off the water supply before disassembly

entries.desc: Fixture control devices see heavy wear (Figure 4-10). Water level so high it runs into the overflow pipe: 1 Remove the tank top and unscrew the float ball from the float rod. 2 Shake the ball; if water is inside, replace it. 3 Screw the ball back on. 4 With both hands in the middle of the float rod, carefully bend the ball side down about 1/2 inch. 5 Flush; the level should be about 1 inch below the top of the overflow pipe; replace the tank top. Water running in the closet: 1 Remove the tank top, shut off the water at the shutoff valve. 2 Flush to empty. 3 Unscrew the flush (tank) ball from the lift wire. 4 Check the bottom of the ball for damage or wear. 5 Replace if damaged. 6 Clean the flush outlet valve seat with emery cloth or steel wool. 7 Operate the handle to see the ball sits evenly. 8 Water on, flush to check, replace tank top. Faulty ball cock operation: 1 Remove the tank top; water off. 2 Flush to empty. 3 Remove the float rod with the float ball. 4 Remove the screws or pins at the top of the ball cock assembly. 5 Lift the plunger out. 6 Replace the washer under the plunger and the O-ring around it. 7 Reassemble with the float rod and ball. 8 Water on; check
entries.use: Tank water too high, water running in the closet, or faulty ball cock
entries.how: Check the float ball for water, bend the float rod down 1/2 in.; replace a worn flush ball and clean its seat; or replace the plunger washer and O-ring
entries.dim: Normal level about 1 in. below top of overflow pipe; bend float rod down about 1/2 in
entries.eq: Emery cloth or steel wool, replacement flush ball, washer and O-ring

entries.desc: Water level too high, running into the overflow pipe: 1 Remove the tank top; squeeze the top and bottom of the adjustment clip and move it down the pull rod to lower the float cup. 2 Flush and check the incoming water level, about 1 inch below the top of the overflow pipe. 3 If correct, replace the tank top; if not, repeat steps 1 and 2. Water running in the closet: 1 Remove the tank top, shut off the water at the shutoff valve and flush. 2 Lift the flapper and check the bottom for damage or wear; replace if needed. 3 Clean the outlet valve seat with emery cloth or steel wool. 4 Operate the handle to ensure the flapper sits evenly. 5 Water on; flush to check; replace the tank top
entries.use: High tank water level or running water with a float-cup tank
entries.how: Lower the float cup on the pull rod with the adjustment clip; replace a worn flapper and clean its seat
entries.dim: Level about 1 in. below top of overflow pipe
entries.eq: Emery cloth or steel wool, replacement flapper

entries.n: Install a wall-hung lavatory and its drain
entries.desc: A lavatory washes hands and face; made of vitreous china, enameled cast iron, stainless steel or plastic; hot and cold supply with waste to the sanitary sewer. Types (Figure 4-11): wall-hung (on a wall bracket, with or without legs), vanity (on a cabinet or counter), pedestal (weight on the floor) and trough (commercial plants and certain military facilities). Wall-hung installation (Figure 4-12): 1 Install the mounting board between the studs at the proper height as for a wall-hung flush tank (see manufacturer's specifications for height and elevation). 2 Attach a hanger bracket to the finished wall with wood screws of proper length at the recommended height; the bracket must be level. 3 Place the lavatory on the bracket and push down; check level. Faucets: see chapter 7. Drain (chain or pop-up plug, Figure 4-13; flange installation is the same): 1 Ring of plumber's putty around the drain outlet and set the flange firmly. 2 Connect the flange to the bowl with a washer and locknut. 3 Coat flange threads with pipe-joint compound and screw on the tailpiece. 4 Connect the P-trap between the rough-in waste outlet and the tailpiece (Figure 4-14), with washers and slip nuts for leakproof joints
entries.use: Hanging a lavatory on a hanger bracket and plumbing the drain
entries.how: Mounting board between the studs, level metal bracket, putty and flange, P-trap with washers and slip nuts
entries.eq: Mounting board, hanger bracket, wood screws, plumber's putty, washer and locknut, pipe-joint compound, P-trap, slip nuts

entries.n: Connect lavatory water supply and repair a pop-up plug
entries.desc: After installing lavatory water services (Figure 4-15) turn the water on and check for leaks (P-trap connection, Figure 4-14). Pop-up plug repair when the stopper will not hold water (Figure 4-16): 1 Loosen the clevis screw with pliers. 2 Push the stopper down so it sits snugly on the flange. 3 Tighten the clevis screw. 4 Squeeze the spring clip and pull the pivot rod from the clevis hole; the stopper should now operate easily; put the rod through the next higher or lower clevis hole. 5 Close the stopper and fill the bowl. 6 Check the water level to ensure it holds. If not fixed: 7 Tighten the pivot-ball retaining nut; if it still leaks remove the nut with pliers. 8 Squeeze the spring clip and slide the pivot rod out of the clevis hole. 9 Slide the retaining nut and worn washers off the rod. 10 Slide new washers (plastic or rubber) and the ball nut onto the rod and tighten the pivot ball. 11 Reassemble the pivot rod into the clevis hole. 12 Run water into the lavatory and check for leaks; then confirm the stopper holds water
entries.use: Hot/cold hookup and a stopper that will not hold water
entries.how: Pop-up plug: reseat at the clevis screw, move the pivot rod to another clevis hole, then replace pivot-ball washers if it still leaks

entries.n: Know sink types and connect a kitchen sink
entries.desc: Sinks come in several sizes and shapes (Figure 4-17) of enameled cast iron, enameled pressed steel, galvanized steel or stainless steel (faucets: chapter 7). Scullery sink: large, deep, used in mess-hall-type facilities; needs only faucets installed and connection to waste and water supply lines. Slop sink: for buckets and mops. Kitchen sink: single or double compartment, wall hung or set in a counter top, with a strainer to keep food waste out of the waste system (Figure 4-18); connect the water service the same as for a lavatory (Figure 4-15)
entries.use: Installing scullery, slop and kitchen sinks
entries.how: Scullery sinks need only faucets plus waste and supply connections; kitchen sinks have a strainer and the water service is connected like a lavatory's

entries.n: Install a wall-hung or trough urinal
entries.desc: A urinal carries human liquid waste to the sewer; vitreous china or enameled cast iron; types wall hung, stall and trough (Figure 4-19). Wall hung: built-in water-seal trap or P-trap with washdown or siphon-jet flush; flushing device is a flushometer valve. Stall: set into the floor, beehive strainer on the waste outlet caulked to a P-trap below floor level; washdown flush from a flushometer valve. Trough: wall hung with a flush tank and a perforated pipe across the rear letting water run down the back of the trough. Wall-hung installation (with manufacturer's instructions): 1 Install the mounting board and bracket. 2 Install the urinal on the bracket. 3 Make the waste connection to the rough-in piping. 4 Make the water connection to the rough-in piping including the flushometer valve. 5 Turn on the main water and flush several times to check for leaks. Trough urinal (manufacturer's instructions or military construction drawing): 1 Install the mounting board for trough and tank. 2 Attach the tank to the wall and install the flushing mechanism. 3 Install the hanger for the trough bowl. 4 Attach the bowl to the wall. 5 Install the waste connection to the rough-in piping. 6 Install piping from the tank to the trough bowl. 7 Install a water line between the tank and the rough-in piping. 8 Turn on the main water and flush several times to check for leaks
entries.use: Installing a urinal and checking it
entries.how: Wall-hung urinals use a flushometer valve; trough urinals use a wall tank with perforated pipe across the rear; flush several times and check for leaks
entries.eq: Mounting board, bracket, flushometer valve, flush tank, P-trap

entries.n: Choose and build a shower stall
entries.desc: A shower uses little space and water and is sanitary compared with a tub (Figure 4-20 shows showerheads). Individual showers are tiled or steel-stall; group showers are usually tile or concrete. Tile shower: tile or marble walls on three sides with a waterproof curtain or door; tiled floor sloping to a center (or rear) drain; walls waterproofed by setting tile in waterproof cement; floor generally laid on a lead shower pan (Figure 4-21). Stall shower: prefabricated three sides and a base; thin grooved steel sides with a watertight joint; base usually precast concrete; spray on the thin steel is noisy and metal sides rust rapidly. Complete waterproofing is the most important installation requirement; water standing on tile can seep through, so a shower pan is necessary under the floor. Concrete shower pans with prefabricated steel stalls are easy to install and are often set up after original construction, with the cement base laid directly on the floor. Faucet assembly: chapter 7
entries.use: Setting up a tile or steel-stall shower
entries.how: Waterproofing is the most important requirement: waterproof cement on walls and a shower pan under the floor
entries.eq: Waterproof cement, tile, lead or concrete shower pan

entries.desc: Before installing, a carpenter must rough in the general outline of the stall and lay a solid base of subflooring or plywood; without it the pan is soft and flexible and will sag and leak under the tile's weight. Inspect the rough-in of the trap under the flooring so the outlet is correctly placed. The drain in Figure 4-21 has a proper-length nipple that sets the seepage flange level with the lead pan. Make the pan from a solid sheet of lead 6 to 8 inches larger than the shower floor, bending the edges up at right angles to the desired height. Steps: 1 Cut a hole where the drain is and lower the pan into place, resting firmly on the seepage flange. 2 Coat the inside of the pan with asphalt. 3 Put pipe-joint compound or putty under the top of the flange. 4 Put the upper flange on the lower flange and attach them to make a watertight joint between the shower waste and the pan. 5 Thread the strainer down into the flanges to the desired tile level. 6 Complete by laying cement in the pan and tiling the floor
entries.use: Making the waterproof base under a tiled shower floor
entries.how: Solid subfloor first; lead sheet 6-8 in. larger than the floor; coat with asphalt; flange joint to the drain; then cement and tile
entries.dim: Lead sheet 6 to 8 in. larger than the shower floor on each dimension
entries.eq: Lead sheet, asphalt, pipe-joint compound or putty, strainer, cement, tile

entries.desc: The shower supply may be hidden in the wall or exposed. Exposed (Figure 4-22): hot and cold lines tie into a single line ending in a showerhead; cold line comes in on the right, hot on the left. Unexposed (Figure 4-23) has many faucet and valve combinations: the compression valve provides a tempered water line of chromium-plated tubing ending in a gooseneck and showerhead; in the single-handle mixing valve hot and cold mix in a cast-brass mixing chamber and the handle controls a piston-like valve; turning the handle clockwise supplies warmer water. More showerhead types exist than valve types (Figure 4-20)
entries.use: Hooking up exposed or concealed shower piping
entries.how: Cold on the right, hot on the left for exposed piping; single-handle mixing valve gives warmer water turned clockwise
entries.dim: Exposed: cold on right, hot on left
entries.eq: Compression valve or single-handle mixing valve, showerhead

entries.desc: Built-in tubs are designed to be recessed for corner installation (square, rectangular, angled, tubs with ledge seats), of enameled cast iron or steel, or fiberglass. Modern cast-iron tubs rest on the floor and fit against the wall studs and need no wall support, except steel tubs, whose flanges are supported by 1- by 4-inch boards nailed to the studs. Caulk the joint between the finished wall surface and the tub with waterproofing cement. Mount the over-rim tub filler, with or without a shower diverter, on the wall at one end. The drain may be pull-out or pop-up type. Install a removable service panel in the wall behind the tub for access to the trap and water supply valve
entries.use: Setting a recessed built-in tub
entries.how: Cast-iron tubs rest on the floor against the studs; steel tub flanges sit on 1x4 boards nailed to the studs; add a service panel behind it
entries.dim: Support boards 1 x 4 in. for steel tub flanges
entries.eq: Waterproofing cement, 1x4 boards, tub filler, service panel

entries.desc: Laundry tubs are usually in a basement or utility room; the most common type is concrete with a metal rim; enameled cast-iron or steel and plastic units also exist in single- and double-compartment styles (Figure 4-24). Steps (Figure 4-25): 1 Assemble the metal stand by bolting its sections together. 2 Place the stand in front of the rough-in piping and carefully set the tub on it. 3 Connect the P-trap to the tub. 4 Connect a swing-combination faucet to the hot and cold supply lines; the faucet usually includes a hose bib for a hose (faucet installation: chapter 7)
entries.use: Setting a tub in a basement or utility room
entries.how: Bolt the metal stand, set the tub, connect the P-trap and a swing-combination faucet

entries.desc: Fountains are porcelain-enameled steel, cast iron or stainless steel (Figure 4-26). Types: pedestal (no wall support), wall-hung (bolted to a mounting board on the wall), electrically cooled (refrigerating unit, water supply tubing passes over the cooling coils; needs a nearby electrical outlet). Sanitation is extremely important: water from the drinking outlet should not fall back on the bubbler head; the bubbler head should project at least 3/4 inch above the rim and be located so a person's mouth cannot touch it; the drain should have a good strainer to keep chewing gum and other objects out. Install the bubbler head at a height for the average user, with a sturdy mounting that supports considerable weight in addition to the fixture, and a 1 1/4-inch P-trap below the waste pipe. Follow the manufacturer's instructions
entries.use: Pedestal, wall-hung and electrically cooled fountains
entries.how: Bubbler head at least 3/4 in. above the rim and out of reach of the mouth, strainer in the drain, 1 1/4-in. P-trap, sturdy mounting
entries.dim: Bubbler head at least 3/4 in. above rim; 1 1/4 in. P-trap

entries.n: Know water heater types and safety fittings
entries.desc: Four categories: range boilers, gas, oil-burning, electric. Each should have a temperature- and pressure-relief valve and a sediment drain at the lowest part of the tank. Relief valves are set to blow water into a drain line when temperature exceeds 210 F or pressure exceeds 125 psi. Range boiler: a hot-water storage tank 1 to 5 feet in diameter and 6 to 15 feet long, with a furnace coil, an exterior heating device or both. With a furnace coil (Figure 5-1): usually mounted upright on a stand, drain at the bottom for sediment, relief valve at the top, coil in the furnace firebox; works only when the furnace is heating the building, so impractical in summer. With a heater (Figure 5-2): usually installed horizontally on a stand; heater fired by coal, gas or oil. Side-arm gas heater (Figure 5-3): usually older installations, used mostly in summer to support furnace-oil heaters. Gas heater (Figure 5-4): galvanized-iron, copper or porcelain-lined steel tank in an insulating jacket with a gas burner; automatic thermostat holds any temperature from 110 to 165 F; efficient and inexpensive where gas is available. Oil-fired: like gas but with a vaporizing or pressure oil burner. Electric (Figure 5-5): normally two immersion heating elements, upper higher wattage than lower, thermostat-controlled; needs no flue or smoke pipe and can sit in a closet away from the chimney
entries.use: Choosing between range boiler, gas, oil-fired and electric heaters
entries.how: Every heater needs a temperature-and-pressure relief valve and a sediment drain at the lowest tank point
entries.dim: Relief valve opens at 210 F or 125 psi; gas heater range 110-165 F; range boiler 1-5 ft diameter, 6-15 ft long
entries.eq: Temperature- and pressure-relief valve, sediment drain
entries.src: TM 3-34.70 para ch 5 intro, 5-1 to 5-7; Figures 5-1 to 5-5

entries.n: Build a field vapor burner for water heating
entries.desc: In the field, heating devices maintain health, cleanliness and morale; in some climates the sun takes the chill off shower water (paint containers black to absorb more heat). Two devices for mess-kit washing and showers: the vapor burner and the oil-water flash burner (assembled from a kit). Vapor burner (Figure 5-6) burns diesel oil, kerosene, gasoline or a combination (in cold climates gasoline may be added to thin the oil); needs pipe sections, a valve, fittings and a fuel reservoir; it preheats fuel into vapor before burning. Steps: 1 Assemble the pipe so it doubles under itself; best size 1/2- or 1/4-inch. 2 Drill small holes (1/16 inch or less) in the top of the lower pipe where the water containers will sit. 3 Cap the end so fuel escapes only from the holes. 4 Burn fuel from the lower pipe to heat the fuel in the upper pipe so it vaporizes; vapor pressure forces fuel out the holes as a spray for a better flame. 5 Put the pipes in a fire trench about 1 foot wide and 15 inches deep. 6 Coil iron wire around the lower pipe near the holes and around the upper pipe just above the holes as an automatic relighting device (the wires glow red hot after a few minutes of operation; if the flame goes out they relight the fuel, preventing an explosion from gas collected in the trench). 7 Before lighting, open the control valve to let a small amount of fuel run through the lower pipe. 8 Ignite by heating the upper pipe and starting the fuel-heat-gas pressure cycle
entries.use: Heating water for mess-kit washing and showers in the field
entries.how: Doubled-back 1/2- or 1/4-in. pipe with small holes, in a fire trench, with wire-coil relighting and a control valve
entries.dim: Pipe 1/2 or 1/4 in.; holes 1/16 in. or less; fire trench about 1 ft wide x 15 in. deep
entries.eq: Pipe, control valve, fittings, fuel reservoir, iron wire, diesel/kerosene/gasoline
