entries.wn: Explosion risk if the flame goes out and fuel keeps flowing; the vapor burner is more dangerous than the oil-water flash burner

entries.desc: The oil-water flash burner is assembled and installed from a kit following the manufacturer's instructions. A properly operated burner produces a blue flame. If the blue flame blows itself out, insufficient fuel is getting through the holes: open the valve slightly or enlarge the holes. A yellow flame is incomplete burning from too much fuel escaping the holes: close the valve slightly or decrease the hole size
entries.use: Reading the flame to tune a kit-built burner
entries.how: Blue flame is right; a blue flame that blows out means too little fuel; yellow means too much

entries.desc: Maximum load is the maximum hot water used per person per hour (daily use spread over several hours); it varies with life style and building type. Maximum hourly use per person: schools 2 or 3 gallons; offices 4 or 5; living quarters and barracks 8 to 10. Working load is the percentage of maximum load expected in any hour under normal conditions: school or office 25 percent; residential 35 percent; barracks 40 percent. Example, barracks for 50 soldiers: 50 users x 8 gph = 400 gallons; 400 x 40 percent = 160 gallons. A heater with 100-gallon storage and a 60-gph recovery rate (100 F rise) could be installed
entries.use: Finding the storage and recovery rate a building needs
entries.how: Users x gallons per hour per person x working-load percent
entries.dim: Max hourly use/person: school 2-3 gal; office 4-5 gal; barracks 8-10 gal; working load: school/office 25%, residential 35%, barracks 40%

entries.desc: Carbon monoxide poisoning: colorless, odorless gas from incomplete burning; remove the hazard by proper operation and adequate ventilation. Lead poisoning: from leaded fuel such as ethyl gasoline; breathing the vapors is very dangerous; adequate ventilation is absolutely necessary. Explosion: can occur when a burner is not built or operated properly; if the flame goes out and the fuel is not turned off or relit immediately, gas builds up and can explode if ignited. The vapor burner is more dangerous than the oil-water flash burner, but its automatic relighting device reduces explosion chance
entries.use: Operating field and building heaters safely
entries.how: Ventilate against carbon monoxide and lead (leaded fuel); never leave a burner out with fuel running
entries.wn: Carbon monoxide, lead vapors and explosion hazards

entries.n: Select pipe type for the system
entries.desc: Four basic groups: cast-iron soil pipe and fittings, galvanized-steel/iron pipe and fittings, copper tubing and fittings, plastic pipe. Table 6-1 gives characteristics and uses. Copper tubing types: K (thick wall), L (medium wall), M (thin wall), DWV. Plastic: PB, PE, PVC, CPVC (used for cold- and hot-water systems), ABS. Cast-iron types: hub and spigot, double hub, hubless. See appendix D for pipe capacities and allowance for friction loss
entries.use: Choosing among cast iron, galvanized steel/iron, copper and plastic pipe
entries.how: Use Table 6-1: pipe is rigid or flexible and rated for water and/or waste; appendix D has capacities and friction loss

entries.desc: All joints must be watertight and gastight; each pipe kind has its own material. Oakum: hemp or jute fibers soaked with a bituminous compound, twisted or spun into rope or yarn; used with lead or other materials for caulked joints in hub-and-spigot cast-iron pipe and in vitrified-clay tile or concrete pipe. Lead: melted and poured into the joint, or lead wool/shredded lead packed cold on top of the oakum. Pipe-joint compound (dope): protects threads and eases maintenance. Solder: with solder fittings for copper tubing and brass and copper pipe; a nonacid flux (such as rosin) must be used; a 95 percent tin, 5 percent aluminum compound is used for copper tubing. Solvent cement: with plastic fittings for rigid plastic pipe; different types for each plastic pipe and fitting. Bitumen (asphalt, tar pitch): joints in vitrified-clay tile and concrete pipe. Gaskets (rubber, cork, composition, sheet metal): flange joints. Other: sheet metal, aluminum, lead, copper and galvanized iron for stack flashing and shower pans; cutting oil or lard oil as a thread-cutting lubricant; pipe hangers (perforated iron strap in rolls cut to length, U-shaped wire hangers, iron-ring hangers, Figure 6-1); insulation is in chapter 12
entries.use: Making every pipe joint watertight and gastight
entries.how: Oakum and lead for cast iron, dope on threads, nonacid-flux solder for copper, solvent cement for plastic, bitumen for clay/concrete, gaskets for flanges
entries.dim: Copper tubing solder: 95 percent tin, 5 percent aluminum with nonacid flux
entries.eq: Oakum, lead, pipe-joint compound, solder and flux, solvent cement, bitumen, gaskets, pipe hangers, cutting oil

entries.n: Measure pipe runs: engagement, fitting dimension and face-to-face
entries.desc: Fittings are part of the run length; total length must include pipe engagement (distance the pipe goes into a fitting, set by nominal size, Figure 6-2) and the fitting dimension (center of fitting to its end, Figure 6-3). Measurement methods (Figure 6-4): face-to-face is the distance between the faces of each fitting; pipe length = face-to-face + engagement for each fitting. Center-to-center (fittings on each end): pipe length = center-to-center minus the sum of both fitting dimensions plus the sum of both engagements. End-to-end is the full pipe length including both threads
entries.use: Finding the cut length of pipe between fittings
entries.how: Face-to-face: add each fitting's engagement; center-to-center: subtract both fitting dimensions, add both engagements

entries.n: Calculate an offset around an obstacle
entries.desc: Worked example, 3-in. threaded steel pipe, 45-degree elbows with a fitting dimension of 4 5/8 in., 1-in. engagement (Figure 6-5): 1 Vertical distance A (center to center) = 40 in. 2 Table 6-2 constant for a 45-degree offset = 1.4142. 3 1.4142 x 40 = 56.568 = 56 9/16 in. 4 Two elbows: subtract the sum of both fitting dimensions (4 5/8 + 4 5/8 = 9 1/4 in.) from 56 9/16: 47 5/16 in. 5 Add the engagements (2 x 1 in.) to 47 5/16 = total pipe length for C (49 5/16 in.). Table 6-2 offset constants (A=1,B=; B=1,A=; A=1,C=): 60 deg 0.5773, 1.7320, 1.1547; 45 deg 1.0000, 1.0000, 1.4142; 30 deg 1.7320, 0.5773, 2.0000; 22 1/2 deg 2.4140, 0.4142, 2.6131; 11 1/4 deg 5.0270, 0.1989, 5.1258; 5 3/8 deg 10.1680, 0.0983, 10.2170
entries.use: Running a pipeline around an obstruction
entries.how: Offset travel = center-to-center distance x the constant in Table 6-2 (1.4142 for 45 degrees), then subtract fitting dimensions and add engagements
entries.dim: 45-degree constant 1.4142; example A = 40 in., 3-in. pipe, elbow dimension 4 5/8 in., engagement 1 in

entries.n: Choose cast-iron soil pipe and handle it
entries.desc: Cast iron comes in service weight (SW) and extra-heavy weight (XH). Used for sewers, drains, stacks and vents in a waste system. SW is used in households and is adequate for most military construction; XH is used where liquids may corrode the pipe or where greater strength is needed for tall stacks or under roadways. Types (Figure 6-6): hub and spigot (5-ft lengths, 2 to 15 in. diameter); double hub (2 to 15 in. diameter); hubless (10-ft lengths, 1 1/2 to 8 in.). The pipe is heavy and brittle; store and handle it with care to prevent cracks or breakage
entries.use: Specifying cast-iron pipe for sewers, drains, stacks and vents
entries.how: Service weight (SW) for most military work; extra-heavy (XH) for corrosive liquids, tall stacks or under roadways; heavy and brittle, so handle carefully
entries.dim: Hub-and-spigot 5 ft, 2-15 in.; hubless 10 ft, 1 1/2-8 in
entries.wn: Cast-iron pipe is brittle; handle and store with care

entries.desc: Major fittings: Ts, Y-branches, bends, traps (Figure 6-7 on). Sanitary Ts carry drainage; straight Ts are for vents; use a tapped T (sanitary or straight) to connect threaded branch drains or vents; a test T is used to test a newly installed waste system for leaks; T size is given first by the run (through section) then the outlet. Y-branches join one or more sanitary sewer branches or connect a branch to a main with a smoother flow change; common 45- and 90-degree (Figure 6-8): a 45-degree Y has a side takeoff entering the run at 75 degrees (same or smaller diameter; smaller = reducing Y; also inverted, tapped, tapped inverted); the 90-degree Y (combination Y and 1/8 bend, or T-Y) comes in several shapes: double 90-degree Y used extensively in unit vent installations, box 90-degree Y with a takeoff on each side for a stack in a room corner. Bends change direction, named by fraction: 1/16, 1/8, 1/6, 1/5, 1/4, 1/2 = 22 1/2, 45, 60, 72, 90, 180 degrees; regular, short sweep or long sweep (Figure 6-9). Closet bend connects a soil waste branch for a water closet; plain or tapped; made for different floor flanges (a spigot end for caulking marked for cutting, or a hub end connecting to the floor flange with a sleeve). Traps give a water seal against sewer gas; most common is the P-trap (used in a partition to connect a drain to a waste branch); a running trap goes in the building drain where local code requires it be trapped (Figure 6-10; chapter 9). Other fittings (usable on all pipe types except the tucker coupling, Figure 6-11): offset (regular or 1/8 bend, the 1/8 gives smoother transition); increaser (usually at the top of a stack); cleanout (removable threaded plug); tucker coupling (hub-and-spigot to threaded pipe: hub one end, female threads the other); sewer thimble (building sewer to main sewer)
entries.use: Choosing Ts, Y-branches, bends, traps and special fittings
entries.how: Sanitary Ts for drainage, straight Ts for vents; Y-branches for smoother flow; closet bend for toilets; P-trap in partitions
entries.dim: Bend fractions: 1/16=22 1/2 deg, 1/8=45, 1/6=60, 1/5=72, 1/4=90, 1/2=180; 45-degree Y takeoff enters at 75 degrees

entries.desc: Measure with the methods in para 6-18. Steps (Figure 6-12): 1 Make a chalk or crayon mark completely around the pipe where it will be cut. 2 Cut with a soil-pipe cutter or hammer and cold chisel (Figure 6-13). Soil-pipe cutter: set the pipe in a vise, position the cutting wheels on the mark with the adjusting knob and apply pressure on the handle until cut; use the adjusting knob to keep a good bite. Hammer and cold chisel: place the pipe on a board or mound of dirt at the cut point, put the chisel edge on the mark and tap lightly while rotating completely around the pipe; keep scoring with harder blows until it cuts
entries.use: Cutting soil pipe to length
entries.how: Mark around the pipe, then use a soil-pipe cutter in a vise or score with a hammer and cold chisel
entries.eq: Soil-pipe cutter, vise, hammer, cold chisel, chalk

entries.n: Make a lead and oakum joint in hub-and-spigot pipe
entries.desc: Joint material by pipe size, Table 6-3 (oakum ft / lead lb): 2 in. 3 / 1 1/2; 3 in. 4 1/2 / 2 1/4; 4 in. 5 / 3; 5 in. 6 1/2 / 3 3/4; 6 in. 7 1/2 / 4 1/2. Compression gaskets and neoprene sleeves with stainless clamps are also made. Tools (Figure 6-14) and a lead-melting furnace (Figure 6-15): follow manufacturer's instructions and safety precautions. Horizontal (Figure 6-16): 1 Clean the pipe end and/or fitting end. 2 Center the spigot or cut end in the hub. 3 Pack strands of oakum into the hub all the way around with a packing iron to within 1 inch of the hub's end. 4 Clamp the joint runner around the pipe or fitting. 5 Pour molten lead into the hub in one pour with a plumber's ladle. 6 Remove the runner when the lead hardens. 7 Caulk the lead. Vertical (Figure 6-17): 1 Wipe the hub and spigot or cut end to remove moisture and foreign matter. 2 Center the spigot in the hub. 3 Pack oakum to within 1 inch of the hub end. 4 Pour hot molten lead carefully in one pour with the ladle. 5 Let the lead cool one minute or more. 6 Caulk the lead against the pipe with the inside caulking iron, then against the hub with the outside caulking iron; the joint is leakproof. If hot lead cannot be used, make a cold caulk joint: roll lead wool or shredded lead into strands about 1/2 inch in diameter and 1 to 2 feet long, force the strands into the hub and caulk; for best results arrange strand ends alternately
entries.use: Horizontal or vertical caulked lead joints
entries.how: Center the spigot, pack oakum to within 1 in. of the hub end, pour molten lead in one pour, caulk; use a joint runner on horizontal joints
entries.dim: Table 6-3: 2 in. 3 ft oakum, 1 1/2 lb lead; 3 in. 4 1/2 ft, 2 1/4 lb; 4 in. 5 ft, 3 lb; 5 in. 6 1/2 ft, 3 3/4 lb; 6 in. 7 1/2 ft, 4 1/2 lb; oakum to within 1 in. of hub end; cold strands 1/2 in. diameter x 1-2 ft
entries.eq: Oakum, lead, packing iron, joint runner, plumber's ladle, caulking irons, lead furnace
entries.wn: Always wear protective clothing, gloves, a respirator and goggles when working with molten lead; severe injury and permanent disability may result
entries.src: TM 3-34.70 para 6-39 to 6-42; Table 6-3; Figures 6-14 to 6-17

entries.n: Make a hubless joint and support cast-iron pipe
entries.desc: Steps (Figure 6-18): 1 Remove the neoprene sleeve from the stainless-steel clamp. 2 Slide the sleeve on the end of one pipe or fitting until firmly against the collar inside the sleeve. 3 Slide the clamp on the other pipe. 4 Slide that pipe end into the sleeve until firmly against the collar. 5 Center the clamp over the sleeve and tighten with a screwdriver or wrench. To prevent strain on joints, support cast-iron pipe at various points along runs and fittings, vertically and horizontally, to keep alignment and the proper drainage slope
entries.use: Joining hubless cast-iron pipe with a neoprene sleeve and stainless clamp
entries.how: Sleeve on one pipe against its collar, clamp on the other, slide together and tighten the clamp centered on the sleeve
entries.eq: Neoprene sleeve, stainless steel clamp, screwdriver or wrench

entries.desc: Used for hot- and cold-water supply, certain drainage and vents. Three strengths: standard, extra strong, double extra strong (Schedule 40 and Schedule 80 also describe strengths; Schedule 40 standard is most common in plumbing). Nominal sizes 1/8 to 12 in. (iron-pipe size); 21-ft lengths, threaded or unthreaded (Figure 6-19). Store in a dry place and protect threaded ends. Fittings (Figure 6-20): ordinary (standard) for water service and venting, 3/8 to 6 in.; drainage (recessed) for waste systems, threads at a slight angle so horizontal drain pipe slopes about 1/4 inch per foot, 1 1/4 to 12 in. Ts branch at 90 degrees, sized by run then outlet (Figure 6-21). Elbows (Ls) change direction; common 90 and 45 degrees; standard or reducing; size given larger opening first (Figure 6-22). Couplings join two pipe lengths: standard (same size), reducing and eccentric reducing (different sizes, Figure 6-23). Unions join two pipes that can be turned or disconnected (Figure 6-24): ground union (shoulder piece, thread piece, collar; gastight and watertight), flange union (two female-threaded flanges pulled together with nuts and bolts and a gasket; plain-faced, male-female or tongue-and-groove faces), dielectric (dissimilar-metal supply pipes, e.g. galvanized steel to copper, to prevent electrolysis). Nipples extend from a fitting or join two fittings: 12 in. or less, threaded both ends; close, shoulder and long (Figure 6-25)
entries.use: Specifying pipe for water, drainage and vents
entries.how: Schedule 40 standard is most common; ordinary fittings for water and vents, recessed drainage fittings for waste
entries.dim: Lengths 21 ft; sizes 1/8-12 in.; ordinary fittings 3/8-6 in.; drainage fittings 1 1/4-12 in.; drainage slope about 1/4 in. per foot; nipples 12 in. or less
entries.wn: Store dry; protect threads

entries.desc: Tools: vise, pipe cutter, reamer (Figure 6-26). Steps (Figure 6-27): 1 Determine the length and mark the cut. 2 Lock the pipe tightly in the vise with the mark about 8 inches from the vise. 3 Open the jaws of the single-wheel cutter by turning the handle counterclockwise. 4 Place the cutter around the pipe with the cutting wheel exactly on the mark; the rollers give a straight cut. With a three-wheel cutter, put the movable jaw's wheel on the mark and make sure all three wheels are at right angles to the pipe centerline. 5 Close the jaws lightly against the pipe by turning the handle clockwise. 6 Give the handle a quarter turn clockwise when the wheel and rollers contact the pipe. 7 Apply cutting oil and rotate the cutter completely around the pipe, a quarter turn on the handle each revolution, until cut. 8 Push the reamer into the pipe and turn clockwise in short, even strokes with steady pressure until inside burrs are gone. 9 Remove outside burrs with a file if a three-wheel cutter was used
entries.use: Cutting steel pipe to length without leaving burrs
entries.how: Lock in the vise with the mark about 8 in. from the vise, cut with a pipe cutter and cutting oil, ream inside burrs
entries.dim: Mark about 8 in. from the vise
entries.eq: Vise, pipe cutter, reamer, cutting oil, file

entries.desc: Plumbing and pipefitting threads are NPT and are cut at a taper; identify dies as NPT. A common set has a ratchet, nonadjustable stock with solid dies and guides (Figure 6-28); die and guide must match the pipe size. Follow manufacturer's instructions with these steps: 1 Lock the pipe securely in the vise with enough projecting. 2 Slide the diestock over the pipe end, guide inside; push the die against the pipe with one hand (Figure 6-29). 3 Make three or four short, slow, clockwise strokes until the die starts firmly; apply generous cutting oil. 4 Give the stock a complete clockwise turn then a quarter turn counterclockwise to clear cut metal and burrs; keep oiling. 5 Repeat step 4 until 1/2 to 1/4 inch (or two threads) extends from the diestock; continued threading loses the taper. 6 Turn the diestock counterclockwise until the die is free. 7 Wipe off excess oil with a heavy rag and remove chips with a wire brush. A good rule: cut threads until the pipe extends about 1/4 inch from the base of the dies. Table 6-4 (nominal size: threads/in., approx. thread length in., approx. threads to cut, makeup in.): 1/4 and 3/8: 18, 5/8, 11, 3/8; 1/2: 14, 3/4, 10, 7/16; 3/4: 14, 3/4, 10, 1/2; 1: 11 1/2, 7/8, 10, 9/16; 1 1/4 and 1 1/2: 11 1/2, 1, 11, 9/16; 2: 11 1/2, 1, 11, 5/8; 2 1/2: 8, 1 1/2, 12, 7/8; 3: 8, 1 1/2, 12, 1; 3 1/2 and 4: 8, 1 5/8, 13, 11/16; 5 and 6: 8, 1 3/4, 14, 13/16
entries.use: Cutting NPT threads with a stock and die set
entries.how: Matching die and guide, cutting oil, full clockwise turn then quarter back each time, stop when pipe extends 1/4 to 1/2 in. from the diestock
entries.dim: Table 6-4 thread length; stop when 1/2 to 1/4 in. (two threads) extends from the diestock
entries.eq: Vise, stock and die set (NPT), cutting oil, wire brush, rag

entries.n: Join threaded steel pipe and fittings
entries.desc: Fittings are normally screwed on right after threading while the pipe is still in the vise for a good fit; then the assembly is screwed into place (Figure 6-30). Steps: 1 Check fitting threads for cleanliness and damage; wire-brush or replace. 2 Same for the pipe threads. 3 Apply pipe-joint compound or Teflon tape to the pipe threads only. 4 Screw the fitting on hand tight. 5 Tighten with two pipe wrenches, one on the fitting (backup wrench) and one on the pipe, if no vise is available; the backup wrench keeps the fitting from turning
entries.use: Screwing fittings onto threaded pipe
entries.how: Clean threads, dope or Teflon tape on the pipe threads only, hand tight, then wrench with a backup wrench on the fitting
entries.eq: Pipe wrenches (two), wire brush, pipe-joint compound or Teflon tape

entries.desc: Copper tubing is lightweight, easily joined and corrosion-resistant; rigid or flexible; classified by wall thickness (Figure 6-31); used for hot and cold supply, certain drainage and venting. K: thick-walled, rigid or flexible, 20-ft lengths or 100-ft coils, 1/4 to 12 in. L: medium-walled, rigid or flexible, 20-ft lengths or 100-ft coils, same sizes. M: thin-walled, rigid, 20-ft lengths, same sizes. DWV: 20-ft lengths, 1 1/4 to 8 in. Fittings (Figure 6-32): solder (rigid or flexible; sizes like galvanized fittings), flared (flexible tubing with flared ends, 3/8 to 3 in.), compression, and DWV (like cast-iron fittings, solder type)
entries.use: Specifying K, L, M or DWV copper tubing
entries.how: Lightweight, easily joined, corrosion-resistant; K thick, L medium, M thin rigid, DWV for drainage; solder, flared or compression fittings
entries.dim: K and L 20-ft lengths or 100-ft coils, 1/4-12 in.; M 20 ft; DWV 1 1/4-8 in.; flared fittings 3/8-3 in

entries.desc: Measure per para 6-18. Cut with a tubing cutter or a fine-tooth hacksaw, 32 teeth per inch (Figure 6-33). Steps: 1 Determine the length and mark the cut. 2 Set the cutting wheel on the mark and turn the cutter knob clockwise to get a bite. 3 Hold the tubing firmly with one hand and turn the cutter clockwise around the tubing with the other until cut; with a hacksaw use a miter box or a lumber jig for a square cut. 4 Ream the cut end with the cutter's reamer, or a fine metal file if none
entries.use: Cutting copper tubing square
entries.how: Tubing cutter (bite, turn clockwise) or a 32-tooth/inch hacksaw in a miter box; ream or file the burr
entries.dim: Hacksaw 32 teeth per inch
entries.eq: Tubing cutter or fine-tooth hacksaw, miter box, reamer or fine file

entries.desc: Needs a heating torch, 95-5 (95 percent tin, 5 percent aluminum) nonacid solder, soldering flux and emery cloth or steel wool (Figures 6-34, 6-35). Steps: 1 Check the tubing end is round, burr-free and cut square. 2 Clean the tubing end and the inside of the fitting to a bright shine with emery cloth or fine steel wool. 3 Apply a thin coat of flux to both shined surfaces. 4 Push the fitting onto the tubing and give it a quarter turn to spread the flux. 5 Heat the connection with the torch, flame on the fitting. 6 When the flux bubbles, apply solder; it flows into and around the joint. 7 Clean the joint with a clean rag
entries.use: Joining rigid copper tubing with solder fittings
entries.how: Clean to a bright shine, flux, quarter-turn the fitting on, heat the fitting (not the solder), feed solder when the flux bubbles
entries.dim: 95-5 nonacid solder
entries.eq: Heating torch, solder, flux, emery cloth or steel wool, rag
entries.wn: When the joint is close to wood or other combustibles, put insulation sheet or sheet metal between fitting and combustible before applying the flame. Keep the joint motionless while the solder cools to make a leakproof joint

entries.n: Flare, compress and swage copper tubing
entries.desc: Flared joint (flexible tubing, Figures 6-36 to 6-38): 1 Check the end is burr-free and square. 2 Remove the flange nut from the fitting and slide its unthreaded end on the tubing first. 3 Flare the end: with a flaring tool, loosen the wing nuts, put the tubing in the correct-size hole with the end even with the tool surface, tighten the wing nuts and turn the yoke cone down until the flare fills the beveled pad; with a flanging tool, hold it centered and straight on the end and tap with a hammer until the flare fills the recess in the flanging nut. 4 Slide the flare/compression nut up to the flare, screw on hand tight, then tighten. Mechanical-compression joint (fixture supply tubing to shutoff valves, Figure 6-39): 1 Cut or bend the tubing to length. 2 Slide on the compression nut. 3 Slide on the compression ring. 4 Screw the nut onto the fitting by hand. 5 Tighten; the ring compresses to make a sealed leakproof joint. Swaged joint (two sections of thin-walled tubing with no fitting; swaging-tool set and ball peen hammer, Figures 6-40, 6-41): 1 Check end burr-free and square. 2 Place the correct-size swaging tool in the tubing, centered and straight. 3 Tap firmly with the ball peen hammer to enlarge the end. 4 Join the two sections and solder. Bending: spring benders for flexible copper tubing 1/4- to 7/8-inch outside diameter; slide the correct size over the tubing to the bend and bend spring and tubing together (Figure 6-42). Support copper tubing horizontally and vertically at appropriate points, depending on tubing size and fitting locations
entries.use: Flared, mechanical-compression and swaged copper joints; bending flexible tubing
entries.how: Flare with a flaring or flanging tool; compression ring seals under the nut; swage thin-wall tube and solder; use a spring bender for 1/4-7/8 in. flexible tubing
entries.dim: Spring bender for 1/4 to 7/8 in. OD flexible tubing
entries.eq: Flaring or flanging tool, compression nut and ring, swaging-tool set, ball peen hammer, spring bender

entries.desc: Plastic pipe is lightweight, rigid or flexible, easily joined and corrosion resistant; used for water or waste, hot or cold water, and DWV; classified by material. PVC (cream or white): cold-water lines, sanitary drainage and venting; 10- and 20-ft lengths; 1/2 to 6 in. CPVC (light or cream): hot-water lines, also cold; 10-ft lengths; 1/2 and 3/4 in. ABS (black or gray): above- and below-ground sanitary drainage and venting; 10- and 20-ft lengths; 1 1/4 to 6 in. PB polybutylene (black or dark gray): cold-water lines; coils of 100 ft or more; 3/4 to 2 in.; costly, special fittings, not widely used. PE polyethylene (black): cold-water lines and sprinkler systems; 100-ft coils; 3/4 to 2 in. Fittings (Figure 6-43): sizes like steel and copper, but joined usually with epoxy or plastic sealants instead of threads or solder (check before the project): PVC water and waste; CPVC only for CPVC hot and cold water; ABS only waste and vent; PE insertable type for cold-water and sprinkler piping
entries.use: Choosing PVC, CPVC, ABS, PB or PE
entries.how: PVC cold water/drain/vent; CPVC hot and cold water; ABS drain and vent; PB and PE cold water (PE sprinklers)
entries.dim: PVC 1/2-6 in., 10 or 20 ft; CPVC 1/2 and 3/4 in., 10 ft; ABS 1 1/4-6 in., 10 or 20 ft; PB and PE 3/4-2 in., 100-ft coils

entries.desc: Supports: plastic is less stiff than metal, so support runs more often. Measure per para 6-18. Cutting (Figure 6-44): 1 Determine length and mark. 2 Cut in a miter box or jig with a hacksaw or fine-tooth handsaw for a square cut. 3 Remove burrs inside and out with a pocketknife, or sandpaper. Solvent-cement weld joint (Figure 6-45): solvent cement is plastic filler dissolved in solvents, specific to the pipe type; it melts pipe and fitting to weld them and sets fast. 1 Inspect the pipe end for burrs and the fitting for cracks. 2 Clean the pipe and fitting inside with authorized cleaning primer and a clean rag. 3 Coat the outside of the pipe end and the inside of the fitting with solvent cement. 4 Push the pipe as quickly as possible into the fitting as far as it will go; a small bead of cement shows. 5 Give the fitting a quarter turn to spread the cement. 6 Hold about 30 seconds until solidly set. 7 Wipe off excess cement. Insert fitting joint, flexible pipe (Figure 6-46): 1 Slide a clamp over the pipe. 2 Push the pipe onto the insert fitting to the last serration. 3 Slide the clamp over the pipe and tighten with a screwdriver
entries.use: Solvent-cement welding rigid plastic pipe and clamping insert fittings on flexible pipe
entries.how: Square cut in a miter box, deburr, clean with primer, cement both surfaces, push in fast, quarter turn, hold about 30 seconds
entries.dim: Hold solvent-cement joint about 30 seconds
entries.eq: Miter box, hacksaw or fine-tooth saw, pocketknife or sandpaper, cleaning primer, solvent cement, clamp, screwdriver

entries.desc: Used underground for house-to-sewer and house-to-septic-tank waste lines and storm drainage to dry wells; perforated pipe for septic-tank disposal fields, footing drains and other subsurface drainage; lightweight, easily joined, corrosion-resistant. Plain and perforated, 5- and 8-ft lengths, 2 to 8 in. diameter; plain ends are tapered 2 degrees from a 1/16-inch shoulder (Figure 6-47). Fittings are shaped like cast-iron fittings; an adapter fitting connects to cast-iron, threaded-steel or plastic pipe (Figure 6-48); plain pipe is joined by driving pipe and fitting together; perforated pipe with a snap-collar fitting. Cut with a crosscut or rip handsaw (crosscut shreds less), miter box for squareness. Tapering (Figure 6-49): 1 Make sure the end is cut square. 2 Insert the center guide of the tapering tool until the cutter bracket rests on the pipe end. 3 Expand the guide by turning the expander handle clockwise until tight inside the pipe. 4 Set the cutter against the pipe and tighten the bracket nut. 5 Turn the handle one full turn. 6 Loosen the nut, reset the cutter, retighten. 7 Repeat 5 and 6 until the shoulder at the end of the taper is about 1/16 inch wide. 8 Turn the expander counterclockwise and withdraw the tool. Take thin cuts yielding small flaky bits; do not crush the pipe by over-tightening a vise. Joining (friction joint, Figure 6-50): 1 Check tapers on pipe and fitting for grease or burrs. 2 Fit together; the fitting should slide on easily to within 1/4 to 1/3 inch of the shoulder. 3 Hold a wooden block against the fitting (or pipe end) and have a helper brace the line. 4 Tap the block lightly with a sledge until the fitting butts against the taper shoulder; the driving heat fuses a watertight joint
entries.use: Underground house-to-sewer and septic lines, storm lines to dry wells, perforated drainage
entries.how: Cut square with a crosscut saw, taper the end with a tapering tool to a 1/16-in. shoulder, then drive the fitting on to fuse a friction joint
entries.dim: Lengths 5 and 8 ft; 2-8 in.; taper shoulder about 1/16 in.; fit within 1/4 to 1/3 in. of shoulder before driving
entries.eq: Crosscut saw, miter box, tapering tool, wooden block, sledge
entries.wn: Do not take too big a cut on one turn; do not crush the pipe in a vise

entries.desc: Used underground for sanitary and storm drainage. Made of cement and sand in two grades, nonreinforced and reinforced with wire or steel bars, in various lengths and diameters. Coupling: a cement sleeve and two rubber rings (Figure 6-51); other fittings are like cast-iron soil pipe fittings. Measure as for cast-iron soil pipe, allowing for how far the spigot enters the hub or the tongue enters the groove. Cutting is seldom needed; nonreinforced hub-and-spigot pipe can be cut like vitrified-clay pipe; tongue-and-groove pipe is hard to join once cut; methods for reinforced pipe are not covered. Joints are generally hot-poured bituminous compound and oakum as for clay pipe; follow manufacturer's instructions
entries.use: Underground sanitary and storm drainage lines
entries.how: Nonreinforced or wire/steel-reinforced; sleeve-and-two-rubber-ring coupling; joints with hot bituminous compound and oakum like clay pipe
entries.eq: Sleeve and rubber-ring couplings, bituminous compound, oakum

entries.desc: Also called terra-cotta; hub-and-spigot ends in 2-, 2 1/2- and 3-ft lengths; 4 to 42 in. diameter; fittings like cast-iron soil pipe fittings. Overall length of a section = laying length plus telescoping (1 1/2 in. for 4-in. pipe to 4 in. for 42-in. pipe). Cutting is seldom needed; use a brick chisel and hammer, score lightly around the circumference and repeat, deepening gradually until the pipe breaks cleanly; clay is brittle, so cut with care. Bituminous-compound and cement-mortar joint: 1 Insert the spigot of one pipe or fitting into the hub of another and align. 2 Pack the hub with a 3/4-inch layer of oakum. 3 Fill the joint entirely with bituminous compound and tamp in securely. 4 Finish with a neatly beveled edge around the pipe. 5 Remove surplus mortar or compound. The factory-sealed mechanical-compression plastisol joint (speed seal, permanent PVC) has replaced the cement joint: 1 Spread liquid soap solution on the plastisol joint. 2 Insert the spigot end into the bell or hub. 3 Give the pipe a strong push to lock the spigot into the hub seal. Resilient and rigid joints are the same as for fiber pipe
entries.use: Underground sanitary and storm drainage outside buildings
entries.how: Hub and spigot, 2 to 3 ft long; cut with a brick chisel and hammer wearing safety glasses; oakum plus bituminous compound, or a plastisol mechanical-seal joint
entries.dim: Lengths 2, 2 1/2, 3 ft; diameters 4-42 in.; telescoping 1 1/2 in. (4-in. pipe) to 4 in. (42-in.); oakum layer 3/4 in
entries.eq: Brick chisel, hammer, oakum, bituminous compound, liquid soap
entries.wn: Wear safety glasses when cutting clay pipe to avoid eye injury

entries.desc: Cast-iron pressure pipe, also called corporation, is used for water supply mains; hub-and-spigot pattern or flanged ends for bolting; fittings similar to cast-iron soil pipe fittings are available. It is seldom used today
entries.use: Recognizing old water-main pipe
entries.how: Also called corporation pipe; hub-and-spigot or flanged ends; seldom used today

entries.n: Identify valve types and what they do
entries.desc: A valve (usually bronze) starts, stops and regulates flow of liquid, steam or gas (Figure 7-1; appendix B lists valve symbols). Gate valve: starts or stops flow with a split or solid wedge disk fitting a machined seat; raise the disk to flow, seat it to stop; three models: rising stem outside screw and yoke, rising stem inside screw, nonrising stem inside screw. Globe valve: compression-type; circular disk compressed onto or withdrawn from an annular ring seat; all have a rising stem. Angle valve: a globe valve with inlet and outlet at 90 degrees; recommended for frequent operation, throttling and/or positive shutoff. Check valve: one-way flow, closes automatically against backflow; swing type for low pressure and velocity, lift type for high pressure and velocity. Stop-and-waste (bleeder) valve: plug on the outlet side to drain pipelines. Others: reducing valves (reduce pressure into a building), temperature/pressure-relief valves for water heaters, flushometer valves, foot/check/gate/relief valves on centrifugal pumps (chapter 11)
entries.use: Choosing the right valve for a line
entries.how: Gate = on/off; globe/angle = regulate or throttle; check = one-way; stop-and-waste = drain. Gas and water valves are not interchangeable
entries.wn: Gas and water valves are not interchangeable

entries.desc: Check valves regularly for leaks; most leaks come from worn washers or bonnets. The gate valve part that usually needs attention is the bonnet packing. During disassembly check all parts for wear and replace as needed (Figure 7-2). Leak at the stem and packing nut: 1 Tighten the packing nut; if it still leaks turn the water off. 2 Remove the wheel handle, packing nut and old packing. 3 Install new packing. 4 Replace the packing nut and wheel handle. 5 Turn the water on and check. Will not close to stop flow: 1 Water off; disassemble from the wheel handle to the body. 2 Resurface the disk with a mixture of oil and lapping compound. 3 Reassemble. 4 Water on; check leaks and operation. Unknown malfunction: 1 Water off; disassemble until the fault is found. 2 Replace faulty parts and reassemble. 3 Water on; check
entries.use: Gate valve leaking at the stem, not closing, or unknown fault
entries.how: Tighten the packing nut first; otherwise water off, new packing, or resurface the disk with oil and lapping compound

entries.n: Repair a globe or angle valve
entries.desc: Angle valves are repaired the same as globe valves (Figure 7-3). Leak at stem and packing nut: 1 Tighten the packing nut; if the leak continues turn the water off. 2 Remove the wheel handle, packing nut and old packing. 3 Replace with new packing. 4 Replace the nut and handle. 5 Water on; check. Will not regulate or control flow: 1 Water off. 2 Disassemble from the wheel handle to the body. 3 Composition disk: remove the old disk and install a new one. Plug or conventional disk: remove the disk and insert a washer; then lay the disk to the seat for a snug fit. 4 Reassemble. 5 Water on; check leaks and operation. Unknown malfunction: water off, disassemble until the fault is found, replace faulty parts, reassemble, water on and check
entries.use: Globe or angle valve leaking at the stem or no longer regulating flow
entries.how: Tighten or replace packing; replace a composition disk, or insert a washer and lay in a plug disk to the seat

entries.n: Repair swing and lift check valves
entries.desc: Check all parts for wear during disassembly. Swing check valve (Figure 7-4): Loose disk locknut causing backflow: 1 Water off, remove the cap. 2 Tighten the locknut. 3 Replace the cap. 4 Water on; check. Hinge not closing completely: 1 Water off, remove the cap. 2 Replace the hinge pin and/or the hinge with a hinge pin. 3 Replace the cap. 4 Water on; check. Worn disk face leaking: 1 Water off, remove the cap. 2 Remove the locknut and then the disk. 3 Attach a new disk to the hinge and tighten the locknut. 4 Replace the cap. 5 Water on; check. Lift check valve (Figure 7-5): inspect once a year to avoid repair or replacement: inspect for wear, freedom of motion and alignment; inspect the clapper and body seat rings; remove dirt or foreign matter lodged in the valve; if disk or body seat ring surfaces show wear or corrosion, resurface or replace them
entries.use: Backflow or leaks at a check valve
entries.how: Swing: tighten the disk locknut, replace the hinge pin or hinge, or a worn disk; lift: inspect yearly and resurface or replace worn disk and seat rings
entries.dim: Lift check valve inspection yearly

entries.desc: Compression (washer) faucet: raising the washer off its seat gives flow, compressing it onto the seat stops flow; single (hot or cold) or combination (Figure 7-6). Noncompression (washerless) faucet: a single lever or knob opens and closes ports; three types valve, ball and cartridge, one handle (Figure 7-7). Bathtub faucet: combination compression or single-knob noncompression, mounted in the wall at the drain end of the tub, with or without a shower (Figure 7-8). Install (Figure 7-9): 1 Apply plumber's putty to the bottom of the faucet (not needed if a combination faucet comes with a gasket). 2 Place the faucet on the top rear of the bowl, threaded end through the holes. 3 Put a washer and locknut on each threaded end under the bowl. 4 Tighten each locknut with a basin wrench. 5 Wipe off excess putty
entries.use: Compression (washer) or washerless faucets on lavatories, sinks, tubs and showers
entries.how: Putty on the base (or gasket), through the bowl holes, washer and locknut under the bowl, tighten with a basin wrench
entries.eq: Plumber's putty, washers, locknuts, basin wrench

entries.desc: Before repairing any faucet, drain it by turning the water off at the fixture shutoff valve. Always check the valve seat; if chipped or rough, reface with a refacing tool or replace it. Check parts for wear during disassembly. Leak at the stem and packing (Figure 7-10): 1 Water off at the shutoff valve; remove the cap, screw and handle. 2 Remove the packing nut with a wrench, the old packing material and the washer. 3 Put a new washer on the lower end of the stem and reassemble in order. 4 Water on; check. Leak at the spout: 1 Water off; remove cap, screw and handle. 2 Remove the packing nut and stem from the body. 3 Remove the screw and washer from the stem bottom. 4 Put a new washer on the stem bottom. 5 Check the valve seat inside the body; if chipped or rough reface it with a refacing tool (replace if needed); if even, place the stem into the body. 6 Reassemble in order. 7 Water on; check. Leak at the base of the body: 1 Water off; remove cap, screw and handle. 2 Remove the packing nut with a wrench. 3 Remove the worn washer from the packing nut. 4 Slide a new washer into the packing nut for a snug fit. 5 Reassemble. 6 Water on; check. Combination compression faucets are repaired the same way
entries.use: Leak at the stem, spout or base of a compression faucet
entries.how: Drain at the fixture shutoff valve; replace washers and packing; reface or replace a chipped valve seat
entries.eq: Wrench, refacing tool, new washers and packing

entries.desc: Drain the faucet first (water off at the fixture shutoff valve) and check parts for wear during disassembly (Figure 7-11). Ball faucet (corroded or gouged selector ball, or worn rubber valve seats): 1 Loosen the set screw and remove the handle. 2 Remove the cap and pull out the ball with the cam assembly. 3 Use needle nose pliers to remove the two rubber valve seats and springs. 4 Replace the seats and/or ball. 5 Reassemble so the slot in the ball aligns with the metal protection on the housing; check for leaks. Valve faucet (worn O-ring at the spout base or other worn parts): 1 Remove the spout and lift off the escutcheon; remove the plugs on each side by turning counterclockwise and pull out the gasket, strainer, spring, valve stem and valve seat. 2 Remove the seat with a seat-removal tool or allen wrench. 3 Reassemble and check. Metal cartridge faucet (usually two O-rings in the body): 1 Remove the screw and push a screwdriver down the hole to keep the stem in place while removing the handle and cover. 2 Unscrew the retaining nut and remove the spout to expose the body and O-rings. 3 Replace the O-rings. 4 Reassemble and check. Ceramic-disk cartridge (worn or corroded disk): 1 Press the tile handle all the way back to remove the set screw. 2 Remove the handle and the two set screws under the spout. 3 Disengage the stopper mechanism under the lavatory and remove the ceramic cartridge held by two brass screws. 4 Replace the cartridge. 5 Reassemble and check. If a fault comes from corrosion or wear, follow manufacturer's instructions. Bathtub and shower faucets work the same as sink/lavatory faucets and are repaired similarly (Figures 7-12, 7-13)
entries.use: Leaks in ball, valve, metal-cartridge or ceramic-disk faucets
entries.how: Ball: replace rubber seats or ball; valve: replace worn seat; cartridge: replace the two O-rings; ceramic disk: replace the cartridge
entries.eq: Needle nose pliers, seat-removal tool or allen wrench, screwdriver, O-rings, replacement ball/seats/cartridge

entries.n: Select stack and branch pipe and size the stack
entries.desc: Stacks are the vertical main pipes carrying wastes to the house drain; branches carry fixture discharge to the stack; a soil branch carries water closet waste, a waste branch all other fixtures; most buildings use a single soil-and-waste stack. Stacks and branches may be cast iron, threaded iron, copper or plastic; soil stacks are usually hubless cast iron with neoprene sleeve gaskets or plastic (copper also used); branches are usually threaded galvanized steel with recessed drainage fittings, DWV copper or ABS plastic. Size the stack like the building and house drain: total the DFUs (Table 1-6) and apply to Table 8-1: 3 in. = 60 fixture units; 4 in. = 500; 5 in. = 1,100; 6 in. = 1,900; 8 in. = 3,600; 10 in. = 5,600; 12 in. = 8,400. The 45-DFU example needs a 3-in. stack for cast iron, steel or plastic and 2-in. for copper. Branch sizes are set by DFUs and no branch may be larger than the soil (waste) stack
entries.use: Choosing material and size for the soil-and-waste stack
entries.how: Total the DFUs and read Table 8-1 for stack size; branches are no larger than the stack
entries.dim: Table 8-1 max fixture units per stack: 3 in. 60; 4 in. 500; 5 in. 1,100; 6 in. 1,900; 8 in. 3,600; 10 in. 5,600; 12 in. 8,400

entries.desc: Water closet: no individual waste pipe; short branch to the stack with a closet bend 3 or 4 in. (cast iron, steel, plastic) or 3 in. (copper). Lavatory: use a minimum of fittings and no long horizontal runs; minimum waste 1 1/4 in.; 1 1/2 in. is more satisfactory if not copper. Urinal: equip with an effective strainer; waste 2 in. (cast iron, steel, plastic) or 1 1/2 in. (copper). Shower: single shower 2 in. (or 1 1/2 in. copper); shower room for peak flow 3 or 4 in. Kitchen sink: 1 1/2 in., short and as free from offset as possible. Slop sink: trap-to-floor (stand trap) 3 in.; trap-to-wall 2 in.; copper may be a size smaller. Scullery sink: 2 in. because of grease through the grease trap. Drinking fountain: 1 1/4 in. is ample (clear water)
entries.use: Choosing waste pipe diameter for each fixture
entries.how: Water closet bend 3-4 in.; lavatory 1 1/4 min; urinal 2 in.; shower 2 in.; kitchen sink 1 1/2 in.; scullery 2 in.; drinking fountain 1 1/4 in
entries.dim: Closet bend 3 or 4 in. (3 in. copper); lavatory min 1 1/4 in.; urinal 2 in. (1 1/2 copper); shower 2 in. (1 1/2 copper), shower room 3-4 in.; kitchen sink 1 1/2 in.; slop sink 3 in. floor, 2 in. wall; scullery 2 in.; fountain 1 1/4 in

entries.n: Install a soil stack and vent through the roof
entries.desc: The stack is one continuous run from the house drain up through the roof, its sections named by function (Figure 8-1). From the house drain to the first branch takeoff: 1 Connect the stack to the house drain with a long sweep 1/4 bend to keep pressure to a minimum. 2 Connect a test T to the bend with enough pipe to raise the T's side opening 12 inches above the finished floor. 3 Add pipe up to the desired height of the first branch takeoff. 4 Install a sanitary T or combination Y and 1/8-inch bend there. The main soil-and-waste vent extends above the top branch fitting and is usually connected to the main vent. Vent through the roof (VTR): after the main vent T is installed, run the main soil-and-waste vent through the roof; the VTR pipe must be as large or larger than the stack and extend a minimum of 12 inches above the roof, straight or offset; use roof flashing to make the opening watertight; in freezing climates frost may close the vent outlet, so use pipe a size or two larger than the stack, insulation, high flashing or a frost-proof cover. The main vent T goes in the stack at least 6 inches above the flood level of the highest fixture and joins the main vent to the main soil-and-waste vent
entries.use: Running the stack from the house drain up through the roof
entries.how: Long sweep 1/4 bend at the base, test T 12 in. above the floor, sanitary T or Y at the first branch; VTR as large as the stack and 12 in. above the roof
entries.dim: Test T side opening 12 in. above floor; VTR at least 12 in. above roof and at least stack size; main vent T at least 6 in. above flood level of highest fixture
entries.eq: Long sweep 1/4 bend, test T, sanitary T or Y, roof flashing

entries.desc: Horizontal branches run from stack takeoffs to the fixtures; slope 1/4 inch per foot from the fixture to the stack (check with a carpenter's level). Install a cleanout, same diameter as the waste line, at every change of direction and on each horizontal line 2 feet long or longer. Support stacks and branches so pipe weight does not bear on joints (the weakest points). Cast-iron soil pipe stacks and branches are supported at all joints; the bend at the stack base rests on concrete or masonry (Figure 8-1); vertical stacks can be supported at each floor with special hangers, wood strips under two sides of the hub, or strap iron wrapped at the hub and hung from joists; horizontal cast-iron runs need sturdy iron-ring hangers as close to the caulked joint as possible. Support threaded galvanized iron/steel waste pipe, plastic pipe and copper-tubing drain and vent lines at each floor level
entries.use: Horizontal branches to fixtures and holding pipe weight off the joints
entries.how: Slope 1/4 in. per foot to the stack, cleanout at every direction change and every horizontal run of 2 ft or more, support at all joints
entries.dim: Slope 1/4 in. per foot; cleanout every direction change and every horizontal line 2 ft or longer
entries.eq: Carpenter's level, cleanouts, iron-ring hangers, concrete or masonry base support

entries.n: Test a waste system with water or air
entries.desc: After installing, test to see that all joints are leakproof. Galvanized iron/steel, copper and plastic: choose water or air. Water test: 1 Seal branches and vent lines and place a test plug in the test T. 2 Fill the system with water and watch for a drop in level. 3 If the level drops noticeably, check each joint; satisfactory if the level does not fall more than 4 inches in 30 minutes. 4 Make leaking joints watertight and replace defective material. Air test: needs a special plug through which air is pumped; in a cast-iron soil pipe system close all openings after draining the water. 1 Apply air pressure of about 5 psi by gauge. 2 A drop in the mercury column shows a leaky joint; a satisfactory line holds 5 psi for 15 minutes. 3 Listen for escaping air; if no sound and pressure is falling, apply soap solution to the joints near the leak; bubbles show the leak. Other piping (oakum joints): before the water or air test do a 12-hour test: 1 Seal all branches and vent lines and put a ratchet test plug in the test T at the stack base (Figure 8-2). 2 Fill the system from the top of the main soil-and-waste vent and keep it filled at least 12 hours so oakum in the joints swells and forms a watertight seal. Then do a water or air test
entries.use: Proving all waste joints are leakproof
entries.how: Water test: no more than a 4-in. drop in 30 minutes; air test: hold 5 psi for 15 minutes; do a 12-hour fill first on oakum-jointed pipe
entries.dim: Water test: no more than 4 in. drop in 30 min; air test: 5 psi for 15 min; 12-hour fill for oakum joints
entries.eq: Test plug, ratchet test plug, air pump, pressure gauge, soap solution

entries.desc: A trap is a fitting that, properly vented, forms a water seal that stops sewer gas without affecting drainage flow. Traps are used on some fixtures and floor drains inside buildings; the P-trap connects a drain to a waste branch in a partition; a running trap goes in the building drain line when local code requires the building drain be trapped. Types (Figure 9-1; cast-iron traps Figure 6-10): P-trap (most common; plastic or chromed tubular brass; usual sizes 1 1/4 and 1 1/2 in.; most have a cleanout plug because they stop up), drum trap (mostly bathtubs, also kitchen sinks; holds and discharges a larger volume than a P-trap; 3 or 4 in. diameter, trap screw one size smaller), S-trap and 3/4 S-trap (not used in modern plumbing; if found, remove and replace with a P-trap)
entries.use: Selecting a trap type for a fixture or floor drain
entries.how: P-trap is standard (1 1/4 or 1 1/2 in., with a cleanout plug); drum trap for tubs; replace any S-trap with a P-trap
entries.dim: P-trap 1 1/4 or 1 1/2 in.; drum trap 3 or 4 in

entries.desc: The trap seal is the liquid in the U-shaped part of the trap (Figure 9-2). Loss usually comes from inadequate venting: venting lets the atmosphere enter the discharge side to prevent siphonage; at sea level atmospheric pressure is about 14.7 psi and any pressure difference pushes the seal toward the lower pressure. Direct (self-) siphonage (Figure 9-3): unvented traps on oval-bottom fixtures such as lavatories discharge fast, fill the waste pipe, displace air and lower pressure on the discharge side so the seal is lost; flat-bottom lavatories reseal with the final trickle; showers, laundry tubs, sinks and tubs rarely lose seal this way; manufacturers reduce lavatory outlets to 1 1/4 in. on 1 1/2-in. waste pipe so air keeps atmospheric pressure. Indirect or momentum siphonage (Figure 9-4): a big discharge from a fixture one or more floors above forms a slug in the stack that pulls air from the lower fixture's waste line; no reseal until the lower fixture discharges. Back pressure (Figure 9-5): simultaneous fixture use overtaxes the system so compressed air blows the seal out of the fixture. Capillary action (Figure 9-6): a rag, string, lint or hair lodged in the trap wicks water over the outlet. Evaporation: only when a fixture is unused a long time; faster in warm dry places; ventilation does not help; a deep-seal trap is the best fix (solids may collect in the bottom and clog)
entries.use: A trap that smells or lets sewer gas in
entries.how: Causes: siphonage, back pressure, capillary action (lint, string, hair) and evaporation; fix by venting or a deep-seal trap
entries.dim: Atmospheric pressure about 14.7 psi at sea level

entries.n: Lay out the main vent and fixture vents
entries.desc: The main vent is a vertical pipe connecting fixture vents to the main soil-and-waste vent or directly to the atmosphere; in buildings of three or more stories connect it to the bottom of the soil stack to prevent pressure on the lower branches. Usually within several feet of and parallel to the stack (may be offset for space), with branches (Figure 9-7). Single-fixture (individual, back or continuous) vent: most common, fits all fixtures, prevents direct and indirect siphonage (Figure 9-8). At 1/4 in. per foot drop, Table 9-1 gives the maximum trap-to-vent distance by drain size: 1 1/4 in. = 2 ft 6 in.; 1 1/2 in. = 3 ft 6 in.; 2 in. = 5 ft; 3 in. = 6 ft; 4 in. = 10 ft. Battery of fixture vents: two or more fixtures individually vented, each vent tying into a branch vent pipeline to the main vent (Figure 9-9). Common vent: fixtures side by side or back to back on a wall discharge into a double sanitary T with deflectors (Figure 9-10). Circuit vent: from the main vent to the horizontal soil or waste branch between fixture connections; for batteries of two or more fixtures; maximum eight fixtures per circuit vent; usually between the next-to-last and last fixture; connect into the top of the branch rather than the side to reduce clogging; the last fixture's flow scours the others' vents (Figure 9-11). Wet vent: part of a vent line through which another fixture's liquid waste flows; most common on a small group of bathroom fixtures; tends to foul; size for total DFUs (Figure 9-12)
entries.use: Venting stacks and fixtures so traps hold their seals
entries.how: Main vent parallel to the stack (connected at the stack bottom in 3+ story buildings); individual back vent is the most common; Table 9-1 gives max trap-to-vent distance
entries.dim: Table 9-1 max trap-to-vent distance: 1 1/4 in. 2 ft 6 in.; 1 1/2 in. 3 ft 6 in.; 2 in. 5 ft; 3 in. 6 ft; 4 in. 10 ft; circuit vent max 8 fixtures
entries.src: TM 3-34.70 para 9-16 to 9-22; Table 9-1; Figures 9-7 to 9-12

entries.desc: Never use a pipe smaller than 2 inches in diameter for ventilation. The main vent must be at least one-half the size of the stack, and the main soil-and-waste vent at least as large as the stack. Use Table 9-2 with the DFUs, vent length and stack diameter (maximum permissible developed length of vent in feet by vent diameter). Worked example: 3-in. stack, 59 DFUs, 200-ft vent: 1 Read down the first column to 3. 2 Find 30 in the second column. 3 Go to the next higher number, 60 (59 DFUs). 4 Read across to the figure nearest 200: 240. 5 Read up from 240: main vent is 2 1/2 in. Table 9-3 minimum vent size (in.): lavatory 1 1/4; drinking fountain 1 1/4; sink 1 1/2; shower 1 1/2; bathtub 1 1/2; laundry tub 1 1/2; slop sink 1 1/2; water closet 2; urinal 1 1/2. Table 9-2 lists stack sizes 1 1/2 to 10 in. against DFUs and vent diameters 1 1/2 to 8 in
entries.use: Finding main vent and fixture vent diameters
entries.how: Never smaller than 2 in. for ventilation of a main; main vent at least half the stack size; use Table 9-2 by DFUs and vent length; Table 9-3 for fixtures
entries.dim: Min vent size: lavatory/fountain 1 1/4 in.; sink/shower/tub/laundry/slop/urinal 1 1/2 in.; water closet 2 in.; main vent at least 1/2 stack size

entries.desc: Steam is used for space heating, cooking and laundering; produced in a boiler and passed through headers and branch takeoffs. Most steam pipe is wrought iron or steel with threaded joints; large high-pressure, high-temperature systems use bolted-flange joints. Do not use a supply main smaller than 2 inches; the far end should be no less than half the diameter at the largest part; where mains are smaller than half, use eccentric couplings level with the bottom of the pipes. Expansion: install with atmospheric temperature from 0 to 100 F depending on locality and season; pipe takes the steam temperature and expands (steel about 8 1/2 in. per 100 ft for a 900 F change); insert a flexible connection and use bends and loops to absorb the forces. Pitch: condensed steam must drain back to the boiler, so slope pipes toward the boiler; pitch of the main not less than 1/4 inch per 10 feet; horizontal run-outs to risers and radiators not less than 1/2 inch per foot; where not possible, run-outs over 8 ft long should be one size larger. Faulty piping causes most snapping, cracking and rattling; live steam meeting water in pockets causes water hammer (high boiler water levels, or steam blowing through traps into return lines). Valves: gate valve is the most satisfactory for steam; do not use globe valves with fiber disk washers, which wear fast under high pressure and temperature. Insulation: quality pipe insulation between boiler and appliance, preformed strapped on or cement type mixed with water and molded by hand
entries.use: Piping steam from the boiler to appliances
entries.how: Supply main at least 2 in.; pitch the main 1/4 in. per 10 ft toward the boiler and run-outs 1/2 in. per ft; allow for expansion; gate valves; insulate
entries.dim: Supply main min 2 in.; main pitch min 1/4 in. per 10 ft; run-out pitch min 1/2 in. per ft; run-outs over 8 ft one size larger if not possible; steel expands about 8 1/2 in. per 100 ft over 900 F change
entries.eq: Gate valves, flexible connection, eccentric couplings, pipe insulation

entries.desc: Before maintenance: shut off all the steam lines and remove the pressure; allow lines to cool; insulate all steam lines passing within 6 inches of combustible materials; insulate exposed steam lines within easy reach of personnel; equip all steam boilers with proper pressure- and temperature-relief valves. Steam piping is not interchangeable with gas and air piping
entries.use: Maintenance on steam lines and boilers
entries.how: Shut off and depressurize, let lines cool, insulate lines within 6 in. of combustibles or within reach, boilers need relief valves
entries.dim: Insulate lines within 6 in. of combustibles
entries.wn: Because of high pressures and temperatures, death or physical injury can result from failure to use caution and follow procedures in steam, gas and air piping systems

entries.desc: Fuel gas is manufactured or natural: colorless, odorless, about half the specific gravity of air; odorants are added; natural gas (methane) is not poisonous but can suffocate in a closed space; manufactured gas may contain carbon monoxide; explosive under certain conditions; meet installation standards; generally distributed by steel mains. Piping suitable for water service is suitable for gas. Iron or steel with threaded joints is usual; use galvanized pipe from the meter main to the building and branches can be copper; do not use lead pipe or rubber tubing. Plastic pipe may be used: heat-weld the joints, no glue or cement; do not install plastic above ground in distribution systems over 50 psi or where operating temperature is below -20 F or above 100 F. Install and support as for water piping; fuel gas contains moisture, so slope all pipes; install capped drip legs, check and empty them, never where moisture may freeze; avoid traps; take branches off the top of the service pipe; keep piping exposed with unions and bells visible for inspection. Test: air test the entire gas main and service line under a pressure at least 50 percent of operating pressure, and at least 75 psi
entries.use: Fuel gas service for heating
entries.how: Threaded iron or steel (galvanized meter-to-building, copper branches), sloped with capped drip legs, branches off the top, air test at 50 percent of operating pressure and at least 75 psi
entries.dim: Test pressure at least 50 percent of operating pressure and at least 75 psi; plastic not above ground over 50 psi or outside -20 F to 100 F
entries.wn: Do not use lead pipe or rubber tubing for gas; do not glue plastic gas joints

entries.n: Install air piping and a compressed-air system
entries.desc: Air piping is not used for heating; it is for special purposes such as automotive service stations, machine shops or laundries. Air is compressed in an electric, gasoline or diesel-driven compressor (Figure 10-1) and stored in a tank; air is drawn in, reduced in volume and passed through a check valve into the tank. The pressure control valve and safety valve regulate operation: the compressor shuts off automatically at desired pressure; if the pressure control valve fails the safety valve relieves pressure to prevent an explosion. Air is drawn from the tank through a reducing valve with a gauge on either side, set to give any desired equipment pressure regardless of tank pressure. Installation standards are the same as gas piping, but avoid sharp bends to reduce friction loss
entries.use: Compressed-air lines for service stations, machine shops and laundries
entries.how: Same standards as gas piping; avoid sharp bends; relief valve on the compressor; reducing valve with a gauge on each side
entries.eq: Compressor, storage tank, check valve, pressure control valve, safety valve, reducing valve, gauges

entries.n: Use dresser couplings and observe gas/air safety
entries.desc: Threading reduces pipe wall thickness by about 40 percent, and the pipe is more likely to corrode or be damaged by vibration, so use dresser couplings (leakproof joints without reducing wall thickness) for underground gas and air piping (Figure 10-2). Large-size coupling: seamless body with gaskets and flanges bolted together to form a flexible leakproof joint; gas companies usually install them on large steel gas pipe. Small-size coupling: seamless body with two gaskets, two retainers and two octagonal end nuts; sizes 3/8 to 2 in. Safety: never smoke in an area where gas piping is being installed or repaired; never use matches to test for gas leaks; locate the meter and risers some distance from electric meters, switches, fuses and other equipment; install adequate pressure-relief valves on air compressors; test all lines before use; remove pressure from all lines before working on them; protect pipes from freezing of condensed water in unheated locations
entries.use: Underground gas and air pipe and general safety rules
entries.how: Threading cuts wall thickness about 40 percent, so use dresser couplings underground; no smoking, no matches for leak testing
entries.dim: Threading removes about 40 percent of wall; small dresser couplings 3/8-2 in
entries.wn: No smoking where gas piping is installed or repaired; never use matches to test for leaks; both gas and air piping are explosive under certain conditions

entries.n: Understand how a centrifugal pump works
entries.desc: Pumps deliver water to a distribution or plumbing system, raise pressure, move water from source to storage, or pump wastes into a sewer; this chapter covers centrifugal pumps only (see the manufacturer's manual for specifics). Centrifugal force pushes fluid outward from the center (Figure 11-1); larger pumps can raise a liquid column over 100 feet; capacities 5,000 to 200,000 GPH. Vanes on a rotating impeller sit inside a volute (a snail-shaped channel widening toward the outlet, so speed falls and pressure rises); an intake passage leads liquid to the impeller, a discharge passage away, and a shaft seal keeps liquid in and air out. Head is the force of a fluid column at its lowest point; head capacity is the pressure the pump must produce to overcome it; if head rises at constant speed, discharge falls; beyond the pump's head capacity (shutoff head) no water is pumped and the impeller churns, heating water and pump. The issued general-use pump is self-priming (Figure 11-2): rated 125 gpm at 50 ft head, with a priming chamber (no repriming unless drained), mounted on a frame and driven by a 2-cylinder, 3-hp military standard engine; close-coupled with the impeller on the crankshaft end; self-adjusting mechanical seal; only adjustment is a slight turn of the grease cup nut; works best at 15 ft suction lift and loses capacity and efficiency rapidly beyond. Types: submerged (motor above the water, pump in it, motor near the wellhead with a shaft; used mainly for shallow wells because long shafts vibrate) and submersible (pump and electric motor in one casing, lowered with the motor above the pump, waterproof cable to the ground-level control box; use when suction lift exceeds 25 ft)
entries.use: Choosing and understanding a pump for a water or waste job
entries.how: Impeller whirling in a volute creates pressure; the standard issued pump is a self-priming 125 gpm at 50 ft head; best at 15 ft suction lift
entries.dim: Capacity 5,000-200,000 GPH; issued pump 125 GPM at 50 ft head, 3-hp engine, best at 15 ft suction lift; submersible when lift exceeds 25 ft
entries.src: TM 3-34.70 para ch 11 intro, 11-1 to 11-7; Figures 11-1, 11-2

entries.n: Install and operate a centrifugal pump
entries.desc: Points: set the pump on a firm foundation to avoid vibration; locate it as close to the water supply as possible; make sure the suction hose has no collapsed lining, breaks, cuts or pinholes; tighten hose connections and screw nipples tightly to prevent air leaks, using pipe cement (rigid hose preferred on the discharge side); support the piping so the pump does not carry its weight; reduce friction loss by making all piping, especially suction, short with few elbows; slope the suction pipe up gradually toward the pump (not necessary for a self-priming pump). Install a strainer on the suction line, the strainer net at least four times the size of the net on the suction pipe; inspect and clean it often. To reduce friction loss in long discharge lines use pipe one or more sizes larger than the pump's discharge fitting. A pump lowers intake pressure below atmospheric so atmospheric pressure forces liquid up the suction line; a perfect vacuum would lift water 34 ft, but slippage, valve leaks and friction mean suction lift must never exceed 22 to 25 ft at sea level and less at altitude. Valves: check valve (suction side, prevents loss of priming liquid when idle); foot valve (end of suction pipe, optional, to fill the pipe); gate valve (on discharge and suction lines to cut off flow; never throttle with it because flow corrodes the gate); relief valve (safety valve opening when pump pressure is too high)
entries.use: Setting up a pump so it draws properly
entries.how: Firm foundation, close to the source, short suction piping with few elbows, no air leaks, strainer net 4 times the suction pipe, suction lift never over 22-25 ft
entries.dim: Strainer net at least 4x suction pipe net; suction lift never more than 22-25 ft at sea level; perfect vacuum lifts 34 ft
entries.eq: Strainer, check valve, foot valve, gate valve, relief valve, pipe cement
entries.wn: Never use the gate valve to throttle flow

entries.desc: After installation prime the pump by filling it with water; a self-priming pump needs no repriming unless drained. Steps: 1 Remove the priming plug on top of the casing and fill the case to the top; make sure the valve on the discharge line is wide open. 2 Replace the plug. 3 Start the pump. For shallow suction lifts with little liquid supply, reduce engine speed with the throttle to cut load and fuel consumption
entries.use: First start-up and restart after draining
entries.how: Fill the casing through the priming plug with the discharge valve wide open, replace the plug, start; slow the engine on shallow lifts with little supply

entries.n: Maintain and troubleshoot a centrifugal pump
entries.desc: Shaft seals and packing keep water and air out and in: two rings, one sealed to the rotating shaft and one to the fixed casing, press together; lubricant is grease, oil or the pumped liquid; follow the servicing and replacement instructions. Packing: where a stuffing box replaces a seal use only soft, flexible packing; long fiber tallowed flax is satisfactory for cold water; if tightening the gland does not stop leakage add one ring of packing, and if that fails replace the old rings with new. Bearings: too much grease creates heat and oozes out of the housing; dry bearings thoroughly before replacing; ball bearings need lubrication only two or three times a year; clear the housing once every year or year and a half with carbon tetrachloride, gasoline or kerosene, then relubricate; after draining a pump, run it about a minute to dry the impeller chamber. Trouble sources: pump does not prime; casing not filled; priming hole plugged (clean through the drain plug); pump too slow; air leak at suction line or connections; worn or damaged seal; collapsed suction hose lining; clogged suction line or strainer; clogged, worn or broken impeller; lift too high; not enough water or pressure delivered; engine below rated speed; seal leaking; too much impeller-to-casing clearance from wear; suction hose too long (friction loss)
entries.use: Seals, packing, bearings and finding why a pump will not prime or deliver
entries.how: Follow the shaft seal servicing instructions; soft tallowed flax packing; do not over-grease bearings; check priming, air leaks, strainer and impeller for poor delivery
entries.dim: Ball bearings lubricated 2-3 times a year; clean the housing every 1 to 1 1/2 years
entries.eq: Soft tallowed flax packing, grease, carbon tetrachloride/gasoline/kerosene

entries.desc: Insulation prevents heat loss, freezing of hot and cold pipes, and condensation on cold pipes; protects against fire; reduces noise and vibration and pipe expansion and contraction. Types: unformed blanket (shapes and wraps) or rigid preformed sections (Figure 12-1). Frost proof: cold-water service lines through unheated areas or outside; common supply 3 ft long x 1 1/2 in. thick with canvas cover. Fiberglass: shaped for pipes, tubing, small boilers and water heaters; long life; will not shrink, swell, rot or burn; light. Antisweat: cold-water lines; keeps water colder and prevents sweating if properly installed; nap about 3 in. long extends beyond the joint; canvas jacket on each 3-ft length. Cork pipe covering: ground cork bark molded and finished with plastic asphalt; for brine, ammonia, ice water and cold-water lines; will not rot or burn; coat with waterproof material. Wool felt: matted wool fibers pressure-rolled; cold-water service and hot-water return lines; often with alternate tar paper layers for waterproofing. Flex rubber: tough flexible rubber; good cementing and weather-aging qualities; prevents sweating of cold lines. Magnesia: maximum strength; steam and hot-water lines up to 600 F; canvas jacket; pipes up to 30 in. diameter. Blanket insulation: boilers, furnaces, tanks, drums, driers, ovens, flanges and valves; fiberglass type for small boilers and water heaters; strips, sheets, rolls, blocks; resists vermin and acid; fireproof
entries.use: Preventing heat loss, freezing, sweating and noise
entries.how: Match the insulation to the line: frost-proof outdoors, antisweat or cork on cold lines, magnesia up to 600 F, fiberglass for pipes and small boilers
entries.dim: Frost-proof section 3 ft x 1 1/2 in.; magnesia up to 600 F and 30 in. pipe

entries.n: Install pipe, boiler, tank, valve and fitting insulation
entries.desc: Aboveground pipe: each section is split in half with a canvas cover and flap for quick sealing (cheesecloth may replace canvas but must be glued); use joint collars to cover seams on exposed outdoor piping; hold insulation firmly with metal straps at least 3/4 inch wide placed 18 inches apart. Underground: similar but needs more protection from weather; usually a concrete trench; use molded pipe covering or loose mineral wool or glass wool; protect from ground moisture with coal tar sealer or tar paper or aluminum foil wrap. Boilers and tanks (unjacketed): approved materials include magnesia, mineral wool, calcium silicate and cellular glass at least 2 inches thick; keep it off the metal surface by applying over 1 1/2-in. wire mesh lifted by metal spacers giving an air space of at least 1 inch; fill joints with magnesia, mineral wool or other suitable cement; cover the surface with a thin layer of hard-finished cement reinforced with 1 1/2-inch wire mesh; wire the insulation firmly in place. Valves and fittings: cover with wool felt, magnesia cement or mineral wool cement the same thickness as the pipe covering, molded into shape; for magnesia or mineral wool cement, use cheesecloth to bind and hold it
entries.use: Applying insulation above and below ground
entries.how: Split sections with canvas flap, joint collars outdoors, metal straps at least 3/4 in. wide every 18 in.; boilers get 2 in. insulation over wire mesh with a 1-in. air space
entries.dim: Straps at least 3/4 in. wide, 18 in. apart; boiler insulation at least 2 in. thick over 1 1/2-in. wire mesh with at least 1 in. air space
entries.eq: Insulation sections, metal straps, joint collars, canvas, wire mesh, cheesecloth, coal tar or tar paper

entries.desc: Properly installed insulation needs little maintenance; inspect frequently any insulation exposed to weather or sharp-object damage. If the canvas cover is torn or punctured, patch it with canvas; use only waterproof paste when installing or repairing outside insulation. When repairing a leak in an insulated pipe, remove insulation back far enough to uncover the damaged pipe and reinstall with the same kind of insulation as the rest of the system. If an inspection finds loose straps or loose insulation around valves and fittings, retighten the straps and replace or glue down loose insulation
entries.use: Inspecting torn covers, leak repairs and loose coverings
entries.how: Patch canvas with canvas and waterproof paste; when repairing a leaking pipe use the same insulation as the rest of the system

entries.desc: Table A-1 US to metric (multiply by): feet 0.30480 = meters; inches 2.54000 = centimeters; inches 0.02540 = meters; inches 25.40010 = millimeters; square inches 6.45160 = square centimeters; square feet 0.09290 = square meters; cubic feet 0.02830 = cubic meters; gallons 3.78540 = liters; degrees Fahrenheit: subtract 32, multiply by 5/9 = degrees Celsius. Metric to US: centimeters 0.39370 = inches; millimeters 0.03937 = inches; meters 3.28080 = feet; meters 39.37000 = inches; square centimeters 0.15500 = square inches; square meters 10.76400 = square feet; cubic meters 35.31440 = cubic feet; liters 0.26420 = gallons; degrees Celsius: multiply by 9/5, add 32 = degrees Fahrenheit
entries.use: Converting plumbing measurements
entries.how: Use Table A-1: ft x 0.3048 = m; in. x 25.4 = mm; gal x 3.7854 = L; F: subtract 32, multiply by 5/9 = C

entries.n: Read plumbing plans and detail drawings
entries.desc: An architect prepares a set of prints (a plan) drawn to scale with actual dimensions annotated; the legend lists three sources of more information: a standard detail drawing, a special detail drawing and a BOM. Plumbers use the plan, drawings and BOM to lay out and plan a project (see TM 5-704 for construction prints; heating and plumbing are sometimes on the same plan). Both kinds of detail drawing may show an elevation or plan view; for a small structure use only a plan view with some detail drawings. Standard detail drawings are indicated by a number and letter in a circle, for example 11G. Special detail drawings are indicated by a detail number, such as DETAIL #6. The BOM (specification sheets) details the types and quality of materials (appendix C). Plumbing symbols show the general location of pipes, valves, pumps, water tanks and other items; pipe sizes are also shown, with extra information in the notes and legend. Water supply plan (Figure B-1) is a hospital supply and distribution system. Utility plan (Figure B-2, bathhouse and latrine) shows the water system, waste system and fixtures, from the 4-inch drain in the shower room to the connection with the 4-inch pipe of the sewage system; the plumber decides the exact arrangement and the correct slope; P-traps below drains are specified but not shown; with standard details the plumber must make adjustments for the job. Companion drawings: standard detail of a water closet installation (Figure B-3) and a special detail of control-valve and showerhead-fitting requirements (Figure B-4). Unit construction drawing (Figure B-5): elevation view of a water storage tank and tower giving tower size, steel and dunnage beams and footing dimensions, with a plan view and a float-valve detail. Package units are assembled in the field by the manufacturer's instructions
entries.use: Laying out a plumbing job from a set of prints
entries.how: Use the plan, the detail drawings and the BOM together; standard details are a number and letter in a circle (11G), special details are DETAIL #6
entries.src: TM 3-34.70 para B-1 to B-9; Figures B-1 to B-5

entries.desc: Piping symbols: plans use solid or dashed lines to show piping (Figure B-6), with size marked. Pipe up to 12 inches inside diameter is referred to by nominal size; the exact inside diameter depends on the grade (heavy grades have smaller inside diameters because walls are thicker). Pipe over 12 inches is referred to by actual outside diameter. Fitting symbols (Figure B-7) show size, method of branching and fitting material. Valve symbols (Figure B-8): drawings do not normally specify valve material and size, so use the same size and material as the connected pipes; if valves are on the BOM or takeoff list they are listed by size, type, material and working pressure, e.g. two-inch check valve, brass, 175 pounds working pressure. Fixture symbols (Figure B-9): water closets, sinks or lavatories, urinals and floor drains; fixtures are usually listed on the BOM keyed to the plan. More symbols: heating fittings (Figure B-10), heating fittings and fans (Figure B-11), general purpose fixture symbols (Figure B-12), plumbing symbols (Figure B-13)
entries.use: Identifying pipe, fitting, valve and fixture symbols on a drawing
entries.how: Solid or dashed lines are pipe; up to 12 in. is nominal size; valves are the same size and material as the connected pipe unless the BOM says otherwise
entries.src: TM 3-34.70 para B-10 to B-14; Figures B-6 to B-13

entries.desc: A BOM is a list of all materials required to finish a structure: item number, government stock size and number if required, item name and description, unit of issue, quantity, and weight as applicable. Table C-1 shows part of a BOM for plumbing in a company bathhouse and latrine (complete BOM: TM 5-303): 1 oil-fired water heater, 600 GPH, 1 each (NSN 4410-00-999-5886); 2 single faucet 3/4-in. NPT/M brass with bib, 1; 3 single faucet 3/4-in. NPT/M brass without bib, 8; 4 shower head 1/2 in. chrome, 8; 5 stationary urinal 4-ft trough with tank, 2; 6 water closet without cover, separate, 8; 7 cast-iron floor drain 6-in. square, 2 in. out, 1. The designer or draftsman normally prepares the BOM with the drawings; if none comes with the field prints the plumber must compile it. The takeoff list is an actual count and checkoff of the items shown or specified on the drawings and specifications. The estimate list shows materials not placed on the drawings (nails, cement, lumber, pipe hangers, joint materials, cutting oil), calculated from knowledge of the construction. Use indicated or scaled dimensions of the building or utility layouts to size items (Figure B-2); check, list and record each item by stock number and size.
