Start at the source: trace the cold-water lines and record each item; trace the hot-water lines and record all items; determine quantities listing one material at a time; regroup materials by size, smallest to largest
entries.use: Listing the materials a plumbing job needs
entries.how: Trace cold lines then hot lines from the source, count one material at a time, regroup by size smallest to largest; compile it yourself if none came with the prints
entries.src: TM 3-34.70 para C-1 to C-5; Table C-1; Figure B-2

entries.n: Look up pipe capacity (GPM) by size, pressure and length
entries.desc: Tables D-1 and D-2 give flow capacity in GPM by pipe size (3/8 to 2 in. for galvanized steel/iron; 1/2 to 2 in. for copper tubing and plastic pipe), pressure at source (10 to 80 psi) and length of pipe (20 to 200 ft). Example from Table D-1 (galvanized): 1-in. pipe at 40 psi source carries 80 GPM at 20 ft and 24 GPM at 200 ft; 2-in. pipe at 30 psi carries 300 GPM at 20 ft. Example from Table D-2 (copper/plastic): 3/4-in. at 40 psi source, 20 ft = 30 GPM. Longer pipe or lower pressure lowers capacity. Blank cells mean no listed value. Table D-3 gives equivalent length of pipe in feet for friction loss through valves and threaded fittings by fitting diameter (3/8 to 6 in.): standard 90 elbow, standard 45 elbow, 90 side-T, coupling or straight run of T, gate valve, globe valve and angle valve; e.g. 1-in.: 90 elbow 3.0, 45 elbow 1.8, side T 5.0, straight run T 0.9, gate valve 0.6, globe 25, angle 15 ft. Table D-4 gives head loss as equivalent length of pipe for entrance, sudden enlargement and sudden contraction by pipe size 1/2 to 12 in. Figures D-1 through D-5 are friction-loss charts for pipe of different roughness (fairly smooth, rough, fairly rough, smooth) used with the design procedure in appendix E
entries.use: Choosing a pipe size for a required flow
entries.how: Find the pipe material table (D-1 galvanized, D-2 copper/plastic), pick the source pressure row and length column and read GPM
entries.eq: Tables D-1 to D-4; friction-loss charts D-1 to D-5
entries.src: TM 3-34.70 para D-1, D-2; Tables D-1 to D-4; Figures D-1 to D-5

entries.desc: Water weighs 62.4 lb per cubic foot. Pressure P in psi is the total gravitational force at the base of a 1-in. square column of water of height (head) H in feet: P = (62.4/144) x H = 0.433 H (Figure E-1). Example: 10-ft column, P = 0.433(10) = 4.33 psi. Head is the same force expressed in feet: H = P/0.433, or H = 2.31 P (4.33 psi = 10 ft head). For any other liquid the constant changes with density. Static head is the height of a fluid at rest (Figure E-2). Dynamic head is static head minus the friction loss of a flowing liquid, in feet; also called free-water surface (FWS) elevation (Figure E-3): dynamic head = static head - friction loss
entries.use: Pressure in psi from feet of water, and the reverse
entries.how: P (psi) = 0.433 x H (ft); H (ft) = 2.31 x P (psi); a 10-ft head is 4.33 psi
entries.dim: P = 0.433 H; H = 2.31 P; water 62.4 lb/cu ft
entries.src: TM 3-34.70 para E-1 to E-5; Figures E-1 to E-3

entries.n: Design a water distribution line (9-step procedure)
entries.desc: Terms: Pf allowable = maximum pressure that can be lost to friction without falling below the required service pressure (minimum service-connection pressure in the TO is 20 psi); Pf actual = pressure loss from friction in a segment; PF allowable and PF actual = the same per 100-ft section; Equivalent Length (EL) = a fitting or valve expressed in feet of straight pipe that gives the same friction loss; PSC = actual pressure at the service connection. Steps: 1 Determine flow Q in GPM. 2 Pf allowable = 0.433(E1 - E2) - required pressure (E1 higher, E2 lower elevation, ft). 3 Determine pipe length in feet. 4 PF allowable per 100 ft = (Pf allowable / total system length) x 100 ft; actual velocity should be between 2 and 10 fps; find PF actual from Figures D-1 to D-5. 5 Select pipe size and velocity (intersection of the selected pipe and Q on the chart), using Tables D-3 and D-4 for fittings. 6 Pf actual = (PF actual / 100 ft) x system length. 7 Determine EL for fittings, return to step 4 and recalculate; if the size changes find the new velocity and PF actual; EL is negligible if there is 1,000 ft or more between fittings. 8 FWS = EBT - (2.31 x Pf actual), EBT = elevation at the bottom of the tank. 9 PSC = 0.433(EBT - Esc) - Pf actual, Esc = elevation at the service connection
entries.use: Sizing pipe from a tank to service connections with at least 20 psi
entries.how: Find Q, allowable loss Pf = 0.433(E1-E2) - 20, convert to a 100-ft rate, choose pipe size and velocity (2-10 fps) on the Figure D chart, then check the pressure at the service connection
entries.dim: Min TO service pressure 20 psi; velocity 2-10 fps; 0.433 psi per ft; 2.31 ft per psi
entries.eq: Figures D-1 to D-5, Tables D-3, D-4
entries.src: TM 3-34.70 para E-6 to E-8; Figures D-1 to D-5

entries.desc: Q = 230 GPM tank to A (Figure E-4). Step 2: Pf allowable = 0.433(135 - 70) - 20 = 8.14 psi. Step 3: pipe length 1,300 ft. Step 4: 8.14/1,300 x 100 = 0.63 psi per 100 ft. Step 5: select a 6-in. pipe with velocity 2.6 fps (Figure D-3). Step 6: Pf actual = 0.29/100 x 1,530.5 = 4.44 psi. Step 7: EL is 230.5 ft. Step 8: not applicable. Step 9: pressure at service connection = 0.433(135 - 70) - 4.44 = 23.7 psi, above the 20 psi minimum
entries.use: Check a one-pipe design from a tank to point A
entries.how: Example result: 6-in. pipe, 2.6 fps, 1,300 ft run gives 23.7 psi at the service connection

entries.n: Fixture units and demand flow (Tables E-1, E-2)
entries.desc: Fixture unit (FU) values, Table E-1: water closet (flush valve) 10.0 (one listing shows 5.0 for the smaller type); urinal 1-in. flush valve 10.0; urinal 3/4-in. flush valve 5.0; shower head 4.0; kitchen sink 4.0; lavatory (bathroom) sink 2.0; service (stop) sink 3.0; laundry tub (dishwasher) 3.0; laundry machine 8 lb 3.0; laundry machine 16 lb 4.0; water fountain 0.25. If the water closet type is not specified the TO standard is flush valve (10.0); if the urinal type is not specified the TO standard is a 3/4-in. flush valve (5.0). Table E-2 converts FU load to GPM demand, with one column for supply systems predominantly for flush tanks and one for flushometers; for example flushometer: 30 FU = 41.0 GPM; 140 FU = 77.5 GPM; 100 FU = 67.5 GPM; 1,000 FU = 208 GPM. Use the elevation at the bottom of the tank: it corresponds to the minimum (worst-case) operating pressure
entries.use: Finding GPM demand for a building
entries.how: Add the fixture units for each building, then read demand GPM from Table E-2 (flushometer column for flush-valve fixtures)
entries.dim: Flushometer demand: 30 FU = 41.0 GPM; 100 FU = 67.5 GPM; 300 FU = 110 GPM
entries.src: TM 3-34.70 para E-11; Tables E-1, E-2

entries.desc: Q from the tank to A = QB + QC (Figure E-5). Building B: 1 water closet + 2 urinals = 1(10) + 2(10) = 30 FU, so QB = 41 GPM. Building C: 10(10) + 4(10) = 140 FU, so QC = 77.5 GPM. Q = 41 + 77.5 = 118.5 GPM. Step 2: tank to B 0.433(145 - 85) - 20 = 5.98 psi; tank to C 0.433(145 - 70) - 20 = 12.48 psi. Step 4 per 100 ft: tank to B 5.98/190 x 100 = 3.14 psi; tank to C 12.48/180 x 100 = 6.93 psi; use the smaller (tank to B). Step 5: 3-in. pipe, 5.0 fps (Figure D-4), PF actual 1.7 psi. Tank to A (45 ft): 1.7/100 x 45 = 0.77 psi lost. FWS at A = 145 - (2.31 x 1.7) = 141 ft. Design A to C: Q 77.5 GPM; Pf allowable 0.433(143 - 70) - 20 = 11.6 psi; length 180 - 45 = 135 ft; 11.6/135 x 100 = 8.6 psi; select 2-in. pipe, 7.6 fps; EL 28.4; 11.6/(135 + 28.4) x 100 = 7.09 psi; pressure at C = 0.433(143 - 70) - 8.92 = 22.7 psi; all within limits, no redesign. Design A to B: Q 41 GPM; 0.433(143 - 85) - 20 = 5.1 psi; length 190 - 45 = 145 ft; 5.1/145 x 100 = 3.52 psi; select 2-in., 4.2 fps (Figure D-4); EL 28.4; 5.1/(145 + 28.4) x 100 = 2.94 psi; Pf actual 1.9/100 x 178.4 = 3.39 psi; pressure at B = 0.433(143 - 85) - 3.39 = 21.7 psi, within limits
entries.use: Checking a tank-to-A line that splits to buildings B and C
entries.how: Example result: 118.5 GPM on a 3-in. main, 2-in. branches; both service connections stay above 20 psi (22.7 psi at C, 21.7 psi at B)
entries.src: TM 3-34.70 para E-10 to E-13; Figure E-5; Tables E-1, E-2

entries.n: Know the single- and three-phase systems
entries.desc: Power generators produce single- or three-phase voltage. Single-phase is normally for small lighting and single-phase motor loads. If generated voltage is 120 V a two-wire system is used (Table B-1[A]): one conductor grounded, the other ungrounded (hot). Single-phase 240 V is normally for larger single-phase motors; for lighting loads the 240-V phase is center-tapped to give a three-wire single-phase system (Table B-1[B]); the center tap is the grounded neutral; 120 V from neutral to either ungrounded conductor (half the total) and 240 V between the two ungrounded conductors. Three-phase is the most common: generated EMFs are 120 degrees apart; three or four wires (Table B-1 C, D, E). Delta common phase voltage is 240 V (some systems 480 or 600 V); a delta with grounded center-tap neutral gives half the phase voltage. Y-connected phase voltage equals 1.73 times phase-to-neutral voltage. The most common system in the military is the three-phase, four-wire, 208/120-volt system. Balanced circuit: if load between each of the three phases, or between the two ungrounded conductors and the neutral, is equal, no current flows in the neutral, so three conductors may feed where four are normally required. Lamps in the US generally operate at 100-120 V constant-potential; the three-wire system gives twice the potential between outside wires as between an outside wire and the neutral, so large motors run on 240 V while lamps and small motors run on 120 V. With unbalanced load the neutral carries the difference in current of the two sides; seek balanced load when laying out wiring
entries.use: Identifying the system voltage and wiring a generator or panel will supply
entries.how: Military standard is three-phase, four-wire, 208/120 V; single-phase 120 V is two-wire, 240 V center-tapped is three-wire (120 V each side to neutral)
entries.dim: 120 V single-phase 2-wire; 240/120 V single-phase 3-wire; military common 208/120 V three-phase 4-wire; Y voltage = 1.73 x phase-to-neutral

entries.n: Read electrical drawings and wiring diagrams
entries.desc: An electrician must interpret simple blueprints and make simple sketches for verbal orders (TM 5-704 for engineering drawings). Common wiring symbols and line conventions are in Figures A-1 to A-6. Electrical plans show items to be installed, approximate location, and circuits they connect to. The typical plan (Figure 1-1, post exchange) shows the incoming service of three No. 8 wires and two circuit-breaker panels; an arrow such as B2 means connected to circuit 2 of panel B; three wires to the double home-run arrows B1, B2 are the hot wire to each circuit plus a common neutral. The two hot conductors must connect to different phases so current in the neutral cancels when both circuits are fully loaded; wires run to the panel without additional connections. The wiring diagram is the type used most for construction drawings: single lines show wire locations; two conductors are one line; more than two are shown by short parallel lines through the line; a dot marks connecting wires, no dot where wires cross without connecting. Some drawings omit wiring lines and show only symbols, so the electrician decides the wiring location. Electrical drawings show no actual dimensions or dimension lines; location and spacing come from notes or the installation standards of chapter 3. A list of drawing notes designates special wiring requirements and building conditions that alter standard methods
entries.use: Understanding the construction wiring plan before you pull wire
entries.how: Single line = wire run; short slashes show the number of wires; a dot at an intersection is a connection; no dot when wires cross
entries.src: TM 3-34.46 para 1-6 to 1-11; Figure 1-1; Figures A-1 to A-6

entries.desc: Standard color coding: a grounded (neutral) conductor is identified by an outer color of white or neutral gray for No. 6 wire or smaller; larger conductors may be white or gray or have white markings at the terminals. The ungrounded conductors of a circuit should be insulated black, red and blue, used in that order in two-, three- or four-wire circuits respectively. All circuit conductors of the same color must connect to the same hot feeder conductor throughout the installation. A grounding conductor used solely for grounding should be bare or have a green covering
entries.use: Identifying neutral, hot and ground conductors
entries.how: White or neutral gray = neutral; black, red, blue = hot (in that order for 2-, 3-, 4-wire circuits); bare or green = ground

entries.n: Splice wires with a wire nut or solder
entries.desc: A spliced wire must be as good a conductor as a continuous one. Avoid splices when possible; they are permitted anywhere if inside an electrical box. Best practice (including open wiring) is continuous wires from the service box to outlets. Solderless connectors (Figure 1-2) are used in place of splices: split-bolt connectors for heavy wires; wire nuts for small-gauge and fixture wires (funnel-shaped metal spring insert molded into a plastic shell, or a removable insert with a setscrew). Wire nut steps: 1 Strip about 1 inch of insulation from the ends and twist the stripped ends clockwise at least one and one-half turns. 2 Snip 3/8 to 1/2 inch off the twisted wires so ends are even. 3 Screw the wire nut on clockwise. Soldered splice: without a solderless connector the splice must be soldered; needs a clean iron, a clean joint and nonacid flux (pure rosin or rosin-core solder); apply the iron to the joint until the joint melts the solder by its own heat. Taped splice: plastic tape for temporary or expedient wiring; on a two-conductor cable separate the two legs, secure the tape on one leg, tape it, close the legs together and tape past the end; cover all bare copper; three layers for up to 600 V; half-lap for padded mechanical protection
entries.use: Joining conductors inside an electrical box
entries.how: Strip about 1 in., twist clockwise at least 1 1/2 turns, trim 3/8-1/2 in., screw the nut on clockwise; splices only in boxes
entries.dim: Strip about 1 in.; twist at least 1 1/2 turns; trim 3/8-1/2 in.; three tape layers up to 600 V
entries.eq: Wire nuts, split-bolt connectors, soldering iron, rosin-core solder, plastic tape
entries.wn: Under no conditions pull splices through conduit; put splices in electrical boxes so the hot wire cannot touch the grounding system

entries.n: Strip wire and attach it to a terminal
entries.desc: When attaching a wire to a switch or device, or splicing to another wire, remove the insulation to bare the copper conductor. Cut the insulation at an angle to the conductor to avoid nicking and weakening the wire. After removing insulation, scrape or thoroughly sand the conductor to remove all insulation and oxide. Always insert the wire loop under the terminal screw (Figure 1-3) so that tightening the screw tends to close the loop; correctly inserted, the loop brings the insulation ends close to the terminal
entries.use: Connecting a conductor to a switch, receptacle or other device
entries.how: Cut insulation at an angle, sand the copper bright, and insert the wire loop so tightening the screw closes the loop

entries.n: Follow the interior wiring job sequence
entries.desc: Interior wiring has two major divisions: roughing-in (outlet boxes, cable wire and conduit) and finishing (switches, receptacles, covers, fixtures and completing the service). Other trades use the interval between for plastering, enclosing and finishing walls. Roughing-in: 1 Mount outlet boxes: mark box locations on studs and joists first; some boxes have mounting brackets; concealed boxes must be installed with the forward edge or plaster ring flush with the finished wall. 2 Circuit and install wire, cable or conduit: drill and cut building members for the passage; surface wiring means installing conduit, cable and surface boxes and covers on a finished wall; production-line method: drill holes for all runs at once and then install the wire, cable or conduit. 3 Pull wires in conduit between boxes (may be the first step of finishing); take care not to mar finished wall or floor surfaces. Finishing: 1 Splice joints in outlet and junction boxes and connect the grounding wires; this ensures proper leads to terminals of switches, ceiling and wall outlets and fixtures. 2 Attach devices and cover plates to boxes; connect the service-entrance cable and fusing or circuit-breaker panels and fuse the circuits; fixtures are generally supported by special mounting brackets called fixture studs or hickeys. 3 Test for proper circuiting: test all outlets with a test prod or test lamp, operate all switches and load all circuits
entries.use: Ordering the work: roughing-in, then finishing
entries.how: Rough in boxes and conductors first; finish with splices, devices, covers, panel and testing every outlet, switch and circuit

entries.desc: Pliers (insulated or uninsulated handles): long-nosed for close work in panels or boxes; side-cutter to cut wire and cable; slip-joint to tighten locknuts, small nuts on devices, conduit bushings and fittings; round-nosed for screw loops and limited space. Fuse puller (Figure A-7): removes and replaces cartridge fuses safely, bends fuse clips, adjusts loose cutout clips, handles live parts; a molded-plastic type has an encased circuit like a voltmeter with a neon-glow tube and test probes to show whether voltage is present. Screwdrivers: insulated handles; used to attach devices to boxes and wires to terminals; the screwdriver bit goes in a brace for heavy duty; select a screwdriver that matches the slot and keep tips square and properly tapered. Wrenches: crescent, open-end, closed-end and socket wrenches for hex and square fittings (bolts, nuts, conduit unions); pipe wrenches for pipe and conduit and not where other wrenches can be used (misuse deforms the jaw teeth and mars material). Soldering kit: electric and nonelectric irons; blowtorch (alcohol or propane torch may replace it); spool or solid tin-lead wire solder or flux-core solder; soldering paste; never use acid-core solder in electrical wiring. Hammers: carpenter's claw hammer and machinist's ball-peen hammer. Tape measure and folding rule for cutting conduit and estimating material. Extension light when normal building lighting is not installed or not working. See TM 9-243 for tool usage
entries.use: Choosing the right tool for wiring work
entries.how: Insulated handles help but are not enough protection near hot wires; match screwdriver to slot; use pipe wrenches only for pipe and conduit
entries.wn: Although insulated-handle pliers are always used when working on or near hot wires, they are not sufficient protection alone; take other precautions

entries.n: Drill, saw and cut building members and metal
entries.desc: Drilling: drill holes in building structures for conduit or wire; high-speed drills for sheet-metal cabinets and boxes; carbide drills for tile or concrete; electric power drills. Standard drilling equipment: brace, joist-drilling fixture, extension bit for deep cavities, adjustable wood bit, standard wood bit, and a ship auger used with an electric drill. Masonry drills (usually carbide-tipped) drill brick or concrete to anchor with expansion screws or pass conduit or cable. Woodworking: wood chisels and cross-cut or keyhole saws remove wooden members obstructing a run and notch studs and joists for conduit, cable or box brackets, and build wood-panel mounting brackets; the keyhole saw cuts openings in existing walls for added boxes. Metalworking: cold chisels, center punches; knockout punch makes or enlarges a hole in a steel cabinet or outlet box; hacksaw cuts conduit, cable or wire too large for wire cutters: light steady stroke about 40 to 50 a minute, insert a new blade with teeth pointing away from the handle and tighten the wing nut until rigid; blades have 14, 18, 24 or 32 teeth per inch; 18 is best for general use; 32 is best for thin material. Mill file: file sharp ends of cutoffs to prevent short circuits. Conduit tools: rigid conduit is normally threaded; use the tapered pipe reamer to protect wire; the thin-wall conduit cutter has a tapered blade for reaming ends. Thin-wall impinger: permanently attaches indenter-type couplings and connectors to thin-wall conduit (Figure A-9)
entries.use: Making holes and cuts for conduit, cable and boxes
entries.how: Carbide drills for masonry; hacksaw 18 teeth per inch for general use, 32 for thin material, 40-50 light strokes a minute; file cutoff ends
entries.dim: Hacksaw 18 TPI general, 32 TPI thin material; 40-50 strokes/min
entries.eq: Brace, bits, ship auger, masonry drills, hacksaw, knockout punch, mill file, reamer, impinger

entries.n: Strip, tape, pull and mark wire
entries.desc: Insulation stripping: knives and patented strippers bare wire; scissors cut insulation and tape; the multipurpose tool cuts and skins wires, attaches terminals, gauges wire and cuts small bolts; the cable cutter may replace a hacksaw to remove armor at box entry or cut cable to length. Tapes: friction tape (cotton with insulating adhesive; weather resistance and limited mechanical protection over an insulated splice); rubber or varnished cambric tape (insulator when replacing wire covering); plastic electrical tape (adhesive one face; replaced friction and rubber tape for 120- to 600-V circuits; preferred as it serves a dual purpose on joints). Fish tape: tempered spring steel about 1/4 in. wide, in different lengths; pulls wire through conduit; stiff enough not to bend in normal use but can be pushed or pulled around bends and elbows. Drop chain: small chain links on a lead or iron weight, used with a fish wire between studs in existing buildings, only for vertical wall openings. Wire grip (Figure A-8): pulls wire through conduit and tightens open-wire installations; grips tighter the harder the pull. Splicing clamp: twists wire pairs into a uniform tight joint. Wire code markers: tape with identifying numbers permanently identifies wires and equipment in complicated circuits, panels or junction boxes
entries.use: Insulating and pulling wire and cable
entries.how: Use plastic electrical tape for 120-600 V; fish tape pulls wire through conduit; wire grip tightens as you pull
entries.eq: Plastic tape, fish tape, drop chain, wire grip, splicing clamp, wire markers

entries.n: Test and measure with test lamps and meters
entries.desc: Test lamp or indicating voltmeter: determine system voltage, locate the ground lead and test circuit continuity through the power source; both have a light that glows when voltage is present. Volt probe indicator: tests 120- to 600-V AC circuits and DC polarity. Multimeter (Figure A-10): the clamp-on tester measures current without being hooked into the circuit; for AC amperage clamp only one wire at a time; it measures voltage, current, resistance and continuity. Power: the watt is the basic unit; in AC circuits power is the product of volts, current (amperage) and power factor (percent). A multimeter connected as in Figure 2-1 (current through the stationary field coils; voltage across the armature circuit) automatically includes power factor and gives a true indication of power
entries.use: Checking voltage, current, power and continuity
entries.how: Clamp one wire at a time when measuring AC amps; a test lamp or voltmeter finds system voltage, the ground lead and continuity
entries.eq: Test lamp, volt probe, clamp-on multimeter
entries.src: TM 3-34.46 para 2-28 to 2-32; Figure 2-1; Figure A-10

entries.desc: Single conductor: an individual wire, usually insulated (a ground wire may be bare). AWG numbers indicate only the metal diameter, not insulation. White or gray insulation = neutral, green = ground, all other colors = hot. Copper is best and most common; aluminum and copper-clad aluminum are also used but must be larger than copper to carry the same current. For No. 6 or larger aluminum, smear oxide inhibitor on the conductor end before tightening the terminal, then retighten the next day. Insulation type and gauge classify wire; Table B-2 compares types, temperature rating and recommended use. Wire sizes: AWG; largest gauge size is 4/0; larger wires are sized by circular mil area (one circular mil = a circle 1/1,000 in. across; 0.1 in. = 100 mil = 10,000 circular mils). Common interior sizes: 14, 12, 10 (usually solid). Size decreases as numbers get larger; normal sizes are even numbers; Nos. 8 and 6 (solid or stranded) for heavy-power circuits or service-entrance leads; larger for extremely heavy loads and pole-line distribution. Tables B-3 to B-6 give allowable current capacity for copper and aluminum conductors; Table B-7 gives the percent reduction when more than three conductors are in a cable or raceway; Table B-23 lists characteristics of wire sizes
entries.use: Choosing wire type, gauge and current capacity
entries.how: Smaller AWG number = bigger wire; common interior sizes 14, 12, 10; aluminum must be larger than copper; check Tables B-2 to B-7 for ampacity
entries.dim: Interior sizes 14, 12, 10 AWG; service leads 8 and 6
entries.src: TM 3-34.46 para 2-34 to 2-37; Tables B-2 to B-7, B-23

entries.n: Choose multiconductor cable, cords and flexible cord
entries.desc: Armored cable (Type BX): two- or three-wire with or without lead sheath; twisted wires with a bare bonding wire wrapped in coated paper and self-locking steel armor; without lead sheath for interior dry use; lead sheath required in wet locations and through masonry or concrete partitions. Metal-clad (Type MC) resembles armored cable with an enclosed ground wire, primarily industrial. Nonmetallic-sheathed: Type NM has two or three thermoplastic-insulated wires each with jute-type filler; lightweight, simple, inexpensive; not approved for damp locations. Type NMC is plastic-sheathed with solid copper conductors for outdoors or indoors; no conduit needed; flat gray or ivory; resists moisture, acid and corrosion and can run through masonry, between studs, or in damp locations. Type UF (underground feeder) is like NMC with added water protection and is designed for direct ground contact. Lead-covered cable: two or more rubber-covered conductors in extruded lead sheathing for wet and underground locations; may be immersed in water or used where liquid or gaseous vapors would attack other insulation. Service-entrance cable (Type SEC): normally three wires, two insulated braided conductors laid parallel and wound with a bare conductor, protected by heavy tape or armor and covered with braid; carries power from the service drop to service equipment; may supply electric ranges and water heaters inside at not over 150 V to ground if the outer covering is armor; may feed other buildings on the premises if the bare conductor is the equipment grounding conductor from the main distribution center near the main service switch. Cords: flexible cords for pendant, portable or vibration-type items; lamp, heater or heavy-duty power cords; connect appliances, lamps and portable tools to outlets; never a permanent extension of fixed wiring
entries.use: Picking the right cable for a location (dry, wet, buried, service entrance)
entries.how: NM not for damp locations; NMC indoors or out; UF for direct burial; lead-covered for wet or underground; flexible cord is never a permanent extension of fixed wiring
entries.dim: SEC not over 150 V to ground inside

entries.desc: Outlet boxes join wires and connect to receptacles, switches and fixtures; they bind a conduit or cable system into a continuous grounded system, hold conduit, give space for devices, protect them, and provide space for splices. With appropriate contents and covers the same box can be an outlet, junction or switch box. Boxes come in sheet steel, porcelain, bakelite or fiberglass; round, square, octagonal or rectangular; sectional (gang) or with brackets for studs and joists; some for special cover plates or plastered surfaces. Each box has a volume in cubic inches that limits how many wires of a size it can take; allowable minimum depth is 1 1/2 in. except where building-supporting members would have to be cut, then 1/2 in. Selection: use Tables B-9 and B-10; a conductor running through counts along with each terminating conductor (one through + two terminating = three); tables apply to boxes without devices; each receptacle or switch reduces the allowed number by one. Rigid conduit, thin-wall and armored cable: steel boxes (Figure A-11), zinc or enamel coated (zinc preferred wet); knockouts removed with a small cold chisel or punch; armored-cable boxes have integral screw clamps; covers reduce openings, give mounting lugs or close a junction box; use an antishort bushing between the wires and cut armor. Nonmetallic cable and surface wiring: steel boxes with smooth connectors and clamps (not sharp-edged); nonmetallic boxes of plastic or fiberglass with preformed knockout blanks. Special: boxes with beveled corners and internal clamps for finished walls (Figure A-12). Supports (Figure A-13): wooden cleats nailed between two members; mounting straps for 1- to 5-gang boxes between studs; bar hangers span 16- and 24-in. spacing (offset bar hangers for recessed boxes); patented supports for plastered walls
entries.use: Choosing a box type, size and mounting
entries.how: Minimum box depth 1 1/2 in. (1/2 in. where framing would have to be cut); use Tables B-9 and B-10 for conductor count; each device counts as one conductor
entries.dim: Minimum depth 1 1/2 in. (1/2 in. where framing would be cut); bar hangers span 16 and 24 in
entries.eq: Cold chisel or punch, antishort bushing, cleats, straps, bar hangers
entries.src: TM 3-34.46 para 2-46 to 2-58; Tables B-9, B-10; Figures A-11 to A-13

entries.n: Secure cable and conduit; connectors, straps and staples
entries.desc: Connectors: conductors must be joined with approved splicing devices (Figure A-14) or be brazed, welded or soldered with fusible metal or alloy; splices must be mechanically and electrically secure before soldering; select the connector size for the number and size of wires. Support policy: all conduits and cables must be attached to structural members so they will not sag; cables supported at least every 4 1/2 feet, vertical or horizontal, with a strap or staple (Figure A-15) within 12 inches of every outlet box; conduit spacing varies with size and rigidity (Table B-11 rigid nonmetallic; Table B-17 rigid metal). Cable staples: simple support for armored cable on wood. Insulated staples: bell and signal wires in pairs (12 to 24 V need no conduit or loom) are supported on wood by insulated staples to avoid shorting. Straps: one-hole or two-hole straps formed to the material; attach with nails or screws to wood studs or joists; expanding anchors to cement, brick or plaster surfaces; toggle and molly bolts where the wall is thin and has a concealed air space
entries.use: Supporting wiring without sagging
entries.how: Support cable at least every 4 1/2 ft and within 12 in. of every outlet box; use insulated staples on bell and signal wire
entries.dim: Cable support at least every 4 1/2 ft and within 12 in. of every box
entries.eq: Straps, staples, expanding anchors, toggle or molly bolts
entries.src: TM 3-34.46 para 2-59 to 2-63; Tables B-11, B-17; Figures A-14, A-15

entries.n: Install receptacles, plugs and cord connectors
entries.desc: Receptacles (Figure A-16) are single or duplex. Safety standards require that all receptacles for 15- or 20-amp, 120-V branch circuits be grounding type; earlier-installed receptacles and replacements in the same box may be two-wire; all others three-wire (the third wire grounds the equipment, guarding against leakage and shock). Higher-voltage circuits use special receptacles and matching plugs so a 120-V appliance cannot be plugged into 240 V; receptacles take push or twist-and-turn plugs. Fixtures connect the supply circuit directly to lamps. All receptacles are rated for amperage and voltage; CO/ALR can be used with copper or aluminum wire; unmarked and CU-AL receptacles are for copper wire only. Conduit and cable receptacles have yokes attached to boxes by screws; wire connections are at terminal screws; covers of brass, steel or nonmetallic material close the box. Surface metal raceways (Figure A-17): installed on the wall surface; one-piece type installed like conduit then wires pulled; two-piece: base piece along the run, lay the wiring, hold with clamps, snap on the capping. Multioutlet systems and over-floor raceway handle several tools at once, or telephone, signal, power and lighting wiring in the middle of a floor. Plugs (Figure A-18): male plugs with prongs; a three-prong plug can fit a two-prong receptacle by adapter (connect the adapter lead to the center screw holding the receptacle cover if the outlet has a ground system); twist-lock plugs catch and hold; if no cord grip, tie an Underwriter's knot (Figure 2-2) at the plug entry to relieve tension on terminals. Cord-connector body (female plug) is attached similarly to the cord
entries.use: Wiring outlets and attaching plugs
entries.how: Use grounding-type receptacles on 15/20-A, 120-V circuits; CO/ALR for aluminum; tie an Underwriter's knot when the plug has no cord grip

entries.n: Install switches, entrance switches and service panels
entries.desc: A switch connects and disconnects a circuit from the power source; one-pole or two-pole for ordinary lighting or receptacle circuits (Figure A-19). A one-pole switch must break the hot (ungrounded) conductor; a two-pole switch's hot and ground connections go to either pole on the line side. Three-way and four-way combinations are in chapter 3. Exposed and nonmetallic-sheathed wiring use tumbler type with switch and cover in one piece (also rotary-snap, push-button; generally nonmetallic). Conduit and cable installations use a tumbler switch and two-piece cover plate mounted like box receptacles; foreign installations may still use push-button. Entrance switches (Figure A-20): at every power-line entry to a building a switch-and-fuse combination or circuit-breaker switch must be installed at the service entrance, rated to disconnect the building load at the system voltage; one knife blade per hot wire, enclosed in a sheet-steel cabinet, operated simultaneously by an exterior handle on a common shaft; the neutral is not switched but connected at a neutral terminal in the box; many have integral fuse blocks or breakers; the circuit-breaker type is preferred in field installations because it is easier to reset after the overload is cleared
entries.use: Switching circuits and disconnecting a building
entries.how: A one-pole switch must break the hot conductor; every service entry needs a disconnect; circuit-breaker entrance switches are preferred in field installs
entries.src: TM 3-34.46 para 2-70 to 2-73; Figures A-19, A-20

entries.desc: A fuse (cutout) opens a circuit when current exceeds the safe limit; all circuits and apparatus must be protected from short circuits and overcurrent by correctly rated fuses. Standard: cartridge-type fuses for ratings above 30 amps; plug or screw-type fuses are satisfactory for incandescent lighting or heating-appliance circuits. Special: motors on branch circuits need time-lag fuses (self-compensating elements ride through the momentary heavy starting draw, but cut out on a normal short circuit), e.g. oil burners or air conditioners. Fusing is concentrated at centrally located panels, normally at the service-entrance switch in small buildings or several power centers in large buildings, numbered by connected load. Circuit breakers (Figure A-21) trip in overamperage and can have time-lag features: thermal (bimetallic strip bends with heat and trips the latch), magnetic (increased current pulls an armature; used for motor circuits for closer rating), or thermal-magnetic (thermal covers low overcurrents, magnetic covers short circuits; practically all molded-case lighting panel breakers). Breakers are preferred over fuses because they can be manually reset (fuses must be replaced) and cannot easily be swapped for higher-capacity ones; they combine fuse and switch; on overload all ungrounded conductors of a circuit open together. Each branch circuit must have a fuse or breaker protecting each ungrounded conductor. A main breaker or switch is not required ahead of the branch breakers if less than six hand movements open all the branch breakers; more than six requires a separate main disconnect. Each 120-V circuit requires a single-pole breaker with its own handle; each 240-V circuit requires a double-pole breaker; two single-pole breakers side by side with the handles mechanically tied also qualify; a two-pole breaker needs only one movement of the hand
entries.use: Protecting circuits and motors
entries.how: Cartridge fuses above 30 A; time-lag fuses on motor circuits; 120 V = single-pole breaker, 240 V = double-pole; main breaker needed if more than six hand movements open all branch breakers
entries.dim: Cartridge fuses above 30 A; six hand movements rule

entries.n: Choose lamps, sockets, signals and transformers
entries.desc: Lamp sockets (Figure A-22): screw-base holders for incandescent lamps; fluorescent holders have contacts that engage prongs when rotated; sockets can hang by cord or mount on walls and ceilings; porcelain socket mounting holes fit outlet box ears or a plaster ring with machine screws; in an emergency a socket can serve as a receptacle by screwing in a female plug. Signal equipment (Figure A-23): normally 6, 12, 18 or 24 V, AC or DC; open wiring; interoffice or building-to-building. Reflectors and shades focus light: floodlights flood an area; spotlights concentrate light on a small area; two- or three-light clusters with swivel holders mount on walls, posts or ground spikes. Incandescent lamp: most common general light source; least efficient but preferred for low initial cost, easy maintenance and flexibility; candlepower is proportional to voltage (lower voltage dims); much energy becomes heat; tungsten filament emits more red and yellow than sunlight; built to last 1,000 hours at rated voltage. Fluorescent: bulb for bulb and watt for watt more light; a 40-W tube produces almost six times the light of a 40-W incandescent and lasts about five times longer; needs a ballast (also called a transformer); older fixtures have starters; rapid-start has the starter in the ballast, preheat has a visible starter per tube (starters burn out about as often as bulbs), instant-start has no starter and a single pin on each end. Glow lamps: electric-discharge indicator or pilot lights (neon gives blue); need a series current-limiting resistance in the base; light only above a striking voltage; on AC both electrodes glow alternately, on DC only the negative electrode glows (so it indicates AC versus DC); small, rugged, long life, negligible current. Transformers change AC voltages up for transmission or down for lamps, devices and machines; select by input and output voltage and load current; a doorbell transformer reduces 115 V AC to about 6 to 10 V (two primary leads on the 115-V circuit, two secondary screw terminals)
entries.use: Lighting, signal and low-voltage equipment
entries.how: Incandescent is cheap and easy but least efficient; a 40-W fluorescent gives almost 6 times the light of a 40-W incandescent
entries.dim: Incandescent 1,000 hours; fluorescent about 5x life; doorbell transformer 115 V to 6-10 V
entries.src: TM 3-34.46 para 2-84 to 2-94; Figures A-22, A-23

entries.desc: Pole-line hardware includes bolts, nuts, washers, braces, eyebolts, anchor rods, lag screws, pole steps, guy clamps, guy clips, guy hooks, guy plates, thimble-eyes and steel pins. To increase material life use hardware galvanized according to American Society for Testing Materials (ASTM) specifications. Figures A-24 to A-27 illustrate many items
entries.use: Parts used to build and guy a pole line
entries.how: Use hardware galvanized to ASTM specifications
entries.src: TM 3-34.46 para 2-95; Figures A-24 to A-27

entries.n: Identify the building's service type and voltage
entries.desc: Check voltage and type of distribution at the service entrance of every building you wire, especially when altering or adding circuits. Check voltage with an indicating voltmeter at service-entrance switches or load centers; type of distribution is determined by visually counting the wires entering the building (Table B-1). Two wires: DC or single-phase AC; voltage by indicating voltmeter. Three wires from an AC system: single-phase, three-phase, or two ungrounded conductors and a neutral of a three-phase system (V-phase). Single-phase: two conductors are hot and the third is ground; the reading between the two hot conductors is twice the reading from either hot conductor to neutral or ground. Three-phase: voltage between any two conductors is the same; normally one conductor is grounded as the reference. V-phase is the most common service for TO construction: voltage between the two hot conductors is 1.732 times the voltage from either hot conductor to neutral or ground. Four-wire distribution is three-phase plus neutral: voltages from neutral to each of the three conductors are all the same; voltage between any two of the three should equal the neutral-to-hot voltage x 1.732; common operating voltages are 120 and 208 V, or 277 and 480 V
entries.use: Checking voltage and distribution type at the service entrance before wiring or altering circuits
entries.how: Count the wires: 2 = DC or single-phase; 3 = single-phase, three-phase or V-phase; 4 = three-phase with neutral; V-phase is the most common TO service
entries.dim: Hot-to-hot = 1.732 x hot-to-neutral (V-phase, 4-wire); 120/208 V or 277/480 V

entries.n: Compute the connected load per outlet and per building
entries.desc: Use volt-amperes to find electrical needs (eliminates power factor). Most accurate: the stated value in the blueprints or specifications (incandescent: the lamp wattage). Fluorescent: increase load per outlet about 20 percent for the ballast; example: a two-lamp 40-watt fixture = 80 W plus about 16 W for the ballasts = 96 W. If no specifications, use equipment nameplate wattage; if not available use Table 3-1 average wattage: clock 3; coffeemaker 1,000; fan 8-in. 30, 10-in. 35, 12-in. 50; radiant heater 1,300; griddle 450; grill 600; hot plate 1,250; humidifier 500; iron 1,000; mixer 200; phonograph 40; range 8,000; refrigerator 500; radio 100; soldering iron 200; television 300; toaster 1,200; washing machine 1,200; water heater 4,500 W. Where blueprints list no special loads: heavy-duty outlets or mogul-size lamp holders at 5 amperes each; all other ceiling and wall outlets at 1.5 amperes each. Alternative: watts per square foot x floor area from outside dimensions, with the constants and feeder demand factors in Table B-14 (add large appliance loads over 5 A each). Demand factor = maximum demand / total connected load, as a percent. Example (warehouse, 22,500 W connected): 100 percent of the first 12,500 W = 12,500; 50 percent of the remaining 10,000 W = 5,000; building load = 17,500 W
entries.use: Finding load before sizing circuits
entries.how: Use blueprint wattage; add about 20 percent for fluorescent ballast; if unknown use 1.5 A per ordinary outlet and 5 A per heavy-duty outlet; or watts per square foot from Table B-14
entries.dim: Heavy-duty outlet 5 A; other outlets 1.5 A; fluorescent +20 percent

entries.n: Divide the load into branch circuits
entries.desc: Outlets are divided into branch circuits so one fault does not drop the whole building and so wires stay small enough to connect to devices; circuits are rated in amperes (Table B-15). Total load per circuit should normally not exceed 80 percent of the circuit rating. Small building: breakers or fuses at the service entrance, circuits run from there. Medium building: put the fuse box at the center of the building load to keep branch runs short and minimize voltage drop. Large building or loads concentrated in remote places: a fuse box at each load center, with branch circuits radial from each. Number of circuits = total connected watts / watts allowed per circuit (do not include special heavy loads such as air conditioners, which need separate circuits). Example: 20-A, 120-V circuit allows 80 percent = 16 A; 16 x 120 = 1,920 W; connected load 18,000 W / 1,920 = 9.375, so ten 20-A circuits. This is the basic minimum; for permanent installations add several circuits or use the next larger modular panel; extra circuits reduce outlets per circuit and voltage drop. Industry standards for switches and receptacles may not always be met in TO construction (equipment unavailability, installation time, short occupancy). Large-appliance and motor circuits: see motor switches (rated in horsepower) in a single-motor install, a separate circuit from the panel to the motor with its own fuse or breaker; multiple motors on one branch circuit protected at not more than 20 A at 125 V or less, or 15 A at 600 V or less, if each is 1 hp or less and 6 A full load or less; or any ratings with individual overcurrent protection approved for group installation and branch fusing equal to the largest motor's required rating plus the sum of the full-load ratings of the others
entries.use: Finding how many circuits and where to put the panel
entries.how: Keep each circuit at or under 80 percent of its rating: a 20-A, 120-V circuit carries 1,920 W; divide total watts by 1,920 and round up
entries.dim: Circuit loading 80 percent; 20-A, 120-V = 1,920 W; small motors group: 20 A at 125 V, each 1 hp / 6 A

entries.n: Locate switches and receptacles to standard
entries.desc: SWITCH OUTLETS: wall switches usually on the latch side of doorways, or the traffic side of arches, about 48 inches from the floor. Areas with more than one entrance get a multiple-control switch at each principal entrance unless that puts switches within 10 ft of each other. At least one switch-controlled lighting outlet per dining area combined with another room (over the probable table location). At least one ceiling light in each major room wired for a ceiling fan (run an extra conductor between light and switch). Switched lighting on both sides of mirrors and at least one switched ceiling light in bathrooms and dressing rooms. Kitchens: switch-controlled lights over the sink, range hood, breakfast bar and counter work space. Hallways: a switch at each doorway into the hall, latch side. Stairways: at least one switch-controlled outlet, with switches at each landing that has a doorway. RECEPTACLE OUTLETS: every kitchen, family room, dining room, living room, library, den, bedroom or similar room has receptacles every 6 feet and near wall ends where possible, about 12 inches from the floor unless specified. Kitchen, pantry, breakfast and dining rooms: two or more 20-amp appliance circuits serving all receptacles there (no other room's outlets on them); along counters a receptacle every 4 feet (counter separated by a range top, refrigerator or sink is a separate counter); none face-up in a countertop; any receptacle within 6 feet of a sink must be GFCI protected. Bathrooms: at least one wall receptacle at each basin; all GFCI protected. At least one receptacle on the front and one on the back of each building; all within grade-level access GFCI protected. Laundry: at least one receptacle on its own 20-amp circuit (one more if equipment is in the basement or garage). Hallways 10 ft or longer: at least one receptacle (length measured on the centerline without passing through a doorway)
entries.use: Placing wall switches and outlets in a building
entries.how: Switches about 48 in. above floor on the latch side; receptacles every 6 ft about 12 in. from floor; GFCI within 6 ft of a sink, in bathrooms and outdoors
entries.dim: Switch height ~48 in.; receptacle height ~12 in.; receptacles every 6 ft; counter every 4 ft; GFCI within 6 ft of sink

entries.n: Balance the load across phases and circuits
entries.desc: The ideal system has the same ampere drain on every circuit all the time; since that cannot be achieved, plan circuits to divide the connected load as evenly as possible so each uses about the average for the whole system (Figure 3-2 shows the advantage on a three-wire, single-phase 110/220-V system). AC changes continuously from positive to negative to positive; one cycle usually occurs 60 times a second (60-cycle current): each wire is positive 60 times a second, negative 60 times, with zero voltage 120 times a second. The voltage is never constant; average is about 120 V. The neutral current of a balanced three-wire single-phase system stays at zero. Building loads should also be balanced across the distribution phases: distribution transformers on power-line poles deliver three-wire single-phase 120/240 V and are connected across the phase loads in a balanced arrangement, so building loads must be balanced for maximum transformer efficiency
entries.use: Spreading loads evenly to reduce neutral current
entries.how: Divide the connected load as evenly as possible; a balanced three-wire single-phase system carries zero neutral current

entries.n: Choose wire size and limit voltage drop
entries.desc: Wire sizes No. 14 and larger are rated by maximum allowable current-carrying capacity from their behavior under operating stress and temperature. No. 14 is the smallest wire allowed in interior wiring. Conductor size for feeder and branch circuits depends on allowable current capacity and voltage drop. Branch circuit (the portion of the system beyond the last overcurrent device): voltage drop must not exceed 3 percent to the farthest outlet for power, heating or lighting. Feeders: also 3 percent maximum, provided total feeder plus branch drop does not exceed 5 percent. Table B-16 (3 percent drop) lists wire sizes for distance from supply to load at different amperages for branch circuits from the service entrance; use Table B-15 for proper wire size. The minimum gauge for service-wire installation is No. 8, since service wire must also support its own weight plus ice or branches
entries.use: Selecting conductor size for branch circuits, feeders and service
entries.how: No. 14 is the smallest interior wire; voltage drop at most 3 percent for a branch circuit or feeder and 5 percent total; service wire at least No. 8
entries.dim: No. 14 AWG interior minimum; service No. 8 minimum; drop max 3 percent branch, 3 percent feeder, 5 percent combined
entries.src: TM 3-34.46 para 3-25 to 3-27; Tables B-15, B-16

entries.n: Ground and bond a building electrical system
entries.desc: REQUIREMENT: the neutral conductor must be grounded on all systems if voltage between the hot lead and ground is less than 150 V; systems with voltage to ground not over 300 V should also have a grounded neutral; interior circuits under 50 V need not be grounded if the supply transformer connects to a grounded system. System ground: ground on a neutral conductor, reduces fire and shock by holding one wire at 0 V above ground. Equipment ground: an additional ground on all appliances and machinery to keep them at zero volts; if a short occurs in a hot lead the fuse opens the circuit. METHOD: a No. 6 copper (or No. 4 aluminum) wire between the neutral wire, service box, bonding wire and a grounding electrode at the service entrance (buried water pipe, building metal frame, local underground system or fabricated device); multiple electrodes at least 6 ft apart. Water pipe: underground water piping is always the electrode if available; if it is less than 10 ft deep add supplemental electrodes; interior metallic cold-water piping is always bonded to the electrode(s). Plate electrodes: at least 2 sq ft exposed to the soil; iron or steel at least 1/4 in. thick, nonferrous at least 0.06 in.; bury below the permanent moisture level if possible. Pipe electrodes: clean metallic pipe or conduit at least 3/4-in. trade size, driven at least 8 ft deep (or buried in a horizontal trench at least 8 ft long). Rod electrodes: steel or iron at least 3/8 in. diameter; nonferrous at least 1/2 in.; the standard military ground rod is a 5/8-in. steel rod with three 3-ft sections (Figure 3-3). RESISTANCE: electrodes should have 25 ohms or less to ground; piping and building frames are normally under 25 ohms; fabricated electrodes vary with soil and method; burying below the permanent moisture level normally reduces resistance; test grounding systems with a Megger ground tester (DPW or engineer division). Voltage from neutral to ground (water pipes, frames, rods) should be zero at all times; any voltage indicates faulty wiring. BONDING: a continuous separate circuit between all metallic elements (conduit, boxes) and the service-entrance ground; the neutral is attached to the bonding circuit only at the service entrance, where the neutral and the bonding wire join the grounding electrode; other metal parts connect through conduit, armored cable or flexible metal conduit; nonmetallic conduit or cable must contain a conductor attached to metal boxes or fixtures. All metal-to-metal connections must be tight; use a jumper where continuity is doubtful (e.g., a recessed box where receptacle screws are only adjusting screws: add a wire from the box to the receptacle ground terminal)
entries.use: Installing a grounding electrode and bonding metal parts
entries.how: Neutral grounded if under 150 V to ground; ground resistance 25 ohms or less; ground rod 5/8 in. x three 3-ft sections; multiple electrodes at least 6 ft apart
entries.dim: Rod 5/8 in. x 3 sections of 3 ft; pipe electrode 3/4 in. x 8 ft; plate 2 sq ft; resistance 25 ohms or less; electrodes at least 6 ft apart
entries.eq: Megger ground tester, No. 6 copper wire, ground rod

entries.n: Wire hazardous (Class I, II, III) locations
entries.desc: Special materials and procedures are needed where a spark could cause fire or explosion (hospital operating rooms, acetylene storage or production). Class I: flammable gases or vapors present in explosive quantities. Class II: combustible dust. Class III: easily ignitable fibers or filings not suspended in the air in ignitable amounts. Each class has two divisions: Division 1, hazardous material in free air (dangerous atmosphere); Division 2, hazardous material in containers, dangerous mixtures only through accidents. Get detailed information from theater commands and standard plans. Class I Div 1: threaded rigid metal conduit with explosion-proof fittings or mineral-insulated metal-sheathed (Type MI) cable; Div 2 may have flexible metal fittings, flexible metal conduit or flexible cord approved for hard usage; all equipment (generators, controllers, motors, fuses, breakers) in explosion-proof housings. Class II Div 1: threaded rigid conduit or Type MI cable with flexible metal conduit and threaded fittings where necessary; dustproof cabinets; motors and generators totally enclosed fan-cooled; Div 2 may also use electrical metallic tubing. Class III Div 1: same as Class I Div 1; Div 2: open wiring permitted; motors and generators totally enclosed
entries.use: Operating rooms, acetylene storage, dusty or fiber areas
entries.how: Class I gas/vapor, II dust, III fibers; Division 1 means hazard in free air; Division 1 needs threaded rigid conduit and explosion-proof fittings

entries.n: Install bell, buzzer and signal wiring
entries.desc: Signal equipment may be supplied for 120 V, in which case install it like outlets and sockets of that voltage. Most bells and buzzers are rated 6, 12, 18 or 24 V AC or DC and need minimal circuit insulation as there is no danger of shock or fire from shorts. Wire is insulated with paraffin-impregnated cotton layers or thermoplastic; attach to building members with small insulating staples; thread through members without insulators. Battery operation: old systems used 6-V dry cells in series (two for 12 V; more in series to offset drop over a large area); a poor method as batteries need periodic replacement. Transformer operation: most present systems use a transformer mounted on an outlet box with 120-V primary leads permanently connected to the 120-V circuit and low-voltage secondary leads to the bell circuit (Figure 3-4); more than one buzzer and push button are paralleled with the first (Figure 3-5)
entries.use: Low-voltage doorbell and signal systems
entries.how: Most signals run on 6-24 V from a box-mounted transformer; extra push buttons and buzzers are wired in parallel
entries.dim: Signal systems 6, 12, 18 or 24 V

entries.n: Wire three-way and four-way switches and dimmers
entries.desc: A single-throw switch controls a light or receptacle from one location. For more than one location use a double-throw (three-way) switch, identified by a common terminal normally color-coded darker than the others and located alone at the end of the housing. Figure 3-6: terminals A and A1 are the commons; switch operation connects them to B or C and B1 or C1; either switch opens or closes the circuit. Control from three or more places: two three-way switches plus a four-way switch (Figure 3-7); the four-way unit connects between the two three-way units, with three-wire cable between switches. Dimmers (Figure 3-8): electrical dimmers give a full range from bright to dim for incandescent lighting; special electronic dimmers for fluorescent lighting; a dial sets brightness and a push-knob switches on and off without changing the setting. High-low dimmer: full brilliance at top and about half at the bottom. Variable-control devices also control speed of tools using standard AC or DC motors; some are solid-state
entries.use: Controlling a light from two, three or more places
entries.how: Three-way switches (common terminal darker, alone at the end) for two locations; add a four-way between two three-ways for three or more

entries.desc: Circuit capacity: determine the fused capacity of the building and subtract the present connected load (use average load for outlets without connected loads). If the existing circuits have spare capacity and are near the new outlet, extend them, allowing for the additional voltage drop on the proper wire size. New circuits: if existing outlets cannot take the load and a spare circuit exists in the local fuse or breaker panel, install a new circuit; also when a new circuit is more economical than an extension; a new circuit generally decreases voltage drop on all circuits. New load center: if the panel has no spare circuits or the new circuit is remote from it, the preferred method is a new load center close to the circuit outlets; it must not overload the incoming service and service-entrance switch; if overload is indicated change the service equipment, sometimes by pulling an additional wire from the power line to change a two-wire system into a three-wire 120/240-V service and enlarging the fuse box or breaker panel. Figure 3-9 shows typical arrangements of switches, fixtures and receptacles; before wiring, check with the supervisor for specific equipment requirements
entries.use: Adding outlets: extend a circuit, add a new circuit or add a load center
entries.how: Subtract present load from fused capacity; extend if capacity and distance allow, new circuit if a spare exists, otherwise a new load center near the new outlets

entries.desc: Expedient wiring is temporary wiring for forward-area installations (tactical wiring), TO, field training exercises and civilian disaster relief; complete installations would take too much time and cost. It is typically open wiring exposed on studs, ceilings and joists; military light sets are also used. Wire: select sizes as for normal installations; lay wire over the ceiling joist and fasten with nails driven into the joist and bent over the wire; the nails should grip the wire firmly without damaging the insulation; fasten to joists or studs at least 7 feet above the floor if possible to prevent damage and injury; support as in normal installation. Joints, splices, taps and connections as in chapter 1; use electrical tape as protective covering over the connection and for added protection where nails are bent over the wire. Fixture drops (preferably pigtail splices): tape the leads to the wires and tape the taps; sockets are supported by the tap wires. Cords or nonmetallic-sheathed cable (Figure 3-10): remove the outer rubber or sheathing at the fixture point, tap the fixture leads to the conductor with a Western Union splice, keeping the taps purposely separated, and tape each tap individually
entries.use: Temporary open wiring for forward areas, FTXs and disaster relief
entries.how: Lay wire over ceiling joists, nail-bend supports gripping firmly without cutting insulation, keep it 7 ft or higher, use tape over splices and nail bends
entries.dim: Fasten at least 7 ft above the floor

entries.desc: Armored-cable wiring is permitted for all interior installations except where exposed to saturation by liquid or contact with acid fumes (wet areas require lead-covered cable). Cost is generally higher than Type NM but gives more mechanical protection. Cable: two or three rubber- or thermoplastic-covered wires in flexible steel armor, Type AC (no lead sheath; has a copper or aluminum bonding strip) or Type ACL (lead sheath under the armor). One conductor is always white, so in a switch installation (armored and nonmetallic cable) the white wire can be used as a hot wire connected to a black wire. Support: one- or two-hole straps or staples made for armored cable; at box entry by integral clamps or armored-cable connectors. Installation: run cable through holes centrally drilled in structural members, at least 1/8 in. oversize; avoid notched flush mounting (nails can pierce it and it weakens the member). Support by staples or straps at least every 4 1/2 ft and within 12 in. of each box entry (unless extreme flexibility is needed). Runs across the bottom of ceiling joists and stud faces at least 7 ft above the floor are supported on each joist or stud, or use running boards. On top of ceiling joists or studs in accessible places (attics, temporary buildings) less than 7 ft from the floor, install guard strips at least as high as the cable. Bending: do not damage the armor; inner edge radius of any bend not less than 5 times the cable diameter (Figure 4-1)
entries.use: Wiring interior dry locations with armored cable
entries.how: Not for saturated or acid-fume areas (use lead-covered); holes 1/8 in. oversize, support every 4 1/2 ft and within 12 in. of boxes, bend radius at least 5x cable diameter
entries.dim: Holes at least 1/8 in. oversize; support every 4 1/2 ft and within 12 in.; guard strips under 7 ft; bend radius at least 5 x diameter
entries.eq: Straps, staples, armored-cable connectors, guard strips

entries.n: Cut and connect armored cable to a box
entries.desc: Armored cable may be spliced or connected to devices only in standard junction or outlet boxes, so cut each cable to run box to box. Thread cable through the mounting holes and attach one box; remove slack with just enough force to keep proper bends; keeping tension, cut from the roll and connect (Figure 4-2). Cut cable about 8 inches longer on each end than required for the run; cut the armor about 8 inches from the cable end (longer for fuse boxes and panels). Most electricians use a hacksaw (a cable cutter is made for it): hold the cable end firmly and set the blade at a right angle to the lay of the armor strip, the saw and cable forming two legs of a 60-degree triangle; when the blade has cut almost through, bend the cable end back and forth until it breaks, then twist and pull the loose armor off the leads. Pull the cable tight for a steady cutting surface; from a coil step on the cable end and pull tight; smooth rough ends with a file. Unwrap paper: remove two or three turns of fiber paper from under the armor by jerking it away, so the wires move freely and the bushing fits. Antishort bushing: inner edges of cut armor are sharp and can puncture wire insulation; insert a tough fiber bushing between the armor and the wire. With an armored-cable connector: insert the cable in the connector, tighten the holding screw, insert the connector through the box knockout and secure with the locknut inside the box. With internal clamps (Figure 4-3): remove the knockout, loosen the clamp screw, insert the cable and thread the leads through the clamp, force the armor snugly against the clamp end and retighten. The bonding wire runs the whole cable length and must be bonded to the enclosure at the other end; bend the wire back over the cable before installing the connector or clamp
entries.use: Preparing a BX end: sawing armor, antishort bushing, clamp or connector
entries.how: Cut leads about 8 in. long at a 60-degree hacksaw angle, bend to break the armor, add the antishort bushing, bend the bonding wire back over the cable
entries.dim: Cut ends about 8 in. longer; armor cut 8 in. from end; 60-degree saw angle
entries.eq: Hacksaw or cable cutter, file, antishort bushing, connector or box clamp
entries.wn: Avoid damaging the wire insulation or the metal bonding strip when cutting cable armor

entries.n: Install Type NM / NMC nonmetallic-sheathed cable
entries.desc: Type NM is approved for concealed or exposed dry indoor locations and recommended where a good system ground is not available; inexpensive, lightweight, needs no special tools; not approved for embedding in masonry, concrete, fill or plaster. Type NMC: dual-purpose plastic-sheathed, solid copper conductors, gray or ivory; no conduit; resists moisture, acid and corrosion; can run through masonry and between studs. Type NM cable is rubber- or thermoplastic-covered wires in two- or three-wire combinations with a bare copper bonding wire, each wrapped in spiral paper tape; some local codes also require a bare conductor in NMC; the bare wire attaches to the box with a grounding clip (Figure 4-4). Support with one- or two-hole straps or staples; armored-cable staples are not approved (possible damage). Install on running boards, in holes drilled in the center of joists, or on sides of joists and studs; straps not more than 4 1/2 ft apart and within 12 in. of a box. A run at an angle overhead, supported on the edge of joists, needs running boards; assemblies of two No. 6 or three No. 8 conductors may be secured directly on the bottom of the joist. Damage protection: guard strips at least as high as the cable across the top of a floor or floor joist; in unused places like an attic or crawl space guard strips are only needed within 6 ft of the entrance; avoid concealed cable near baseboards, casings and trim (nails); thermal insulation over cable must be noncorrosive, noncombustible and nonconductive and must not strain the cable. Minimum bend radius is five times the cable diameter. Boxes: metal or nonmetallic with built-in clamps or knockouts; use metal boxes with internal clamps when possible; exposed Type NM may use insulated switches, outlets and lamp holders without boxes if they clamp the cable and fully enclose the stripped section (no splicing; limit to rural areas with few outlets)
entries.use: Dry-location interior wiring where a good system ground is not available
entries.how: NM is for dry indoor locations only; not in masonry, concrete or plaster; no garages, theaters, battery rooms or hoistways; support every 4 1/2 ft and within 12 in. of a box
entries.dim: Support every 4 1/2 ft and within 12 in.; bend radius 5 x diameter; guard strips within 6 ft of attic entrance
entries.eq: Straps, staples, grounding clip, running boards
entries.wn: Do not install Type NM cable in commercial garages, theaters, storage-battery rooms or hoistways, or in humid or wet areas such as ice plants or cold-storage warehouses

entries.n: Strip NM cable and connect it to metal and plastic boxes
entries.desc: Cable runs are continuous outlet to outlet; splices only inside a box. Prepare NM like armored cable but use an electrician's knife: slit the sheathing parallel to the wires (about 8 in. for ordinary boxes, more for panels) without touching the individual insulation, then remove the slit sheathing and the moisture-preventive paper. A cable stripper (Figure 4-5) works on NM, lead-covered cable and portable cords and cannot damage wire insulation. Metal boxes: secure the cable with a built-in clamp or separate connector; leave 6 to 8 in. of cable in the box; a grounding screw or clip takes only one wire; for a switch, self-grounding receptacle or fixture in the last box of a run, attach the cable's grounding wire directly to the box; for a box not at the end or a receptacle that is not self-grounding, make grounding jumpers of wire the same size as the circuit wires; twist all grounding wires and jumpers together and crimp with a compression ring or secure with a wire nut. Nonmetallic boxes: break out a knockout where cable enters; support the cable within 8 in. of the box, sheathing extends into the box at least 1/4 in., and clamp cable to the box (not required to support cable that is fished behind walls, above ceilings or under floors). Nonmetallic boxes need no grounding. Receptacle: at end of a circuit attach the ground wire to the receptacle's grounding screw; in the middle join the cable ground wires with a jumper to the receptacle. Switch: with a grounding terminal treat as a grounded receptacle; in the middle join the ground wires; at the end hold the ground wire between switch bracket and box with the mounting screw. Light fixture: use an octagon box with a metal grounding bar (Figure 4-6); at the end of a circuit attach the cable ground to the bar; in the middle make a jumper from bar to the cable grounds; chain-hung fixtures with a separate ground wire: join it to the circuit ground wire and a jumper
entries.use: Preparing NM cable ends and grounding it in each box type
entries.how: Slit the sheathing ~8 in. with a knife or cable stripper, leave 6-8 in. in the box; ground wire to the box at the end of a run, grounding jumper in the middle
entries.dim: Slit about 8 in.; leave 6-8 in. in box; support within 8 in. of nonmetallic box; sheathing extends in at least 1/4 in
entries.eq: Electrician's knife or cable stripper, grounding clip, wire nuts

entries.n: Add outlets to existing cable wiring (armored and NM)
entries.desc: Analyze whether more circuit capacity is needed (same considerations as other installations). Additions always originate and terminate in electrical boxes; put the junction box close enough to the new outlets that voltage drop stays within limits; the source box needs a neutral and a hot wire of the same circuit; new conductors may connect to existing cable conductors in an outlet box (white to white, black to black) only if the existing conductors trace to the fuse or breaker without interruption. Exposed armored additions follow original rules; changing to another wiring system must be done in a junction box installed for the purpose or in an existing box with enough conductor capacity. Concealed: armored cable is preferred for outlets on completed buildings (armor and bonding strip give continuous ground to metal boxes; flexible enough to feed through small openings from attic or basement); pull cable into a concealed box with a fish tape (feeding from below) or drop chain (feeding from above); put the power-tap junction box in a clear, accessible place; if fishing is difficult the finished wall may have to be opened and replastered. Type NM exposed additions follow original requirements; extending another system with NM requires a junction box (or an existing box with spare conductor capacity). Concealed NM additions are like armored, except insulated receptacles, switches and fixtures may be installed without boxes on wall surfaces, with the cable fished through the wall and fed to the device at the point of entry
entries.use: Extending circuits in finished buildings
entries.how: Additions start and end in boxes; hot and neutral must trace to the fuse or breaker uninterrupted; armored cable is preferred for concealed additions

entries.desc: Fishing gear: fish tapes for long runs; straightened coat hangers or No. 12 wire with a blunt hook for short distances; tool must span the distance plus 2 ft; you need an open space; for more than a foot or so you need a partner (Figure 4-7). Step 1 Make a hole for the box in an open space between studs. Step 2 With a 3/4-inch spade bit, drill up through the sole plate from the basement or down through the top plates from the attic until you hit open space (extension bit may be needed). Step 3 From the basement, run a fish tape through the box hole and down through the drilled hole, attach the cable and draw it into the box hole; verify a clear passage with a flashlight in the box hole while you look into the drilled hole; if the beam isn't visible a fire block is in the way: drill through it with extension shafts, check again; if still blocked move or cut the wall covering and notch the block. Step 4 From the attic, your partner runs a second fish tape or small chain down through the top-plate hole; hook the two together outside the box hole. Step 5 You push the tape up the wall while your partner pulls until he has a secure grip on the tape from the box hole; attach the cable to the tape from the box hole and pull slowly to work it through the wall to the box opening
entries.use: Pulling cable inside a wall from above or below
entries.how: Two-person job: 3/4-in. spade bit through the plate, fish tape up from the box hole, check with a flashlight for fire blocks
entries.dim: 3/4-in. spade bit; tool length = run + 2 ft
entries.eq: 3/4-in. spade bit, extension bit, fish tapes, chain, flashlight

entries.desc: Behind a baseboard: cut the box holes, remove the baseboard between boxes, drill a hole through the wall below each box and cut a channel connecting the holes; fish the cable down one box hole, along the channel and up the other. Adding a light and a switch: mark the fixture box between two ceiling joists and cut the hole; at the ceiling edge between the same joists make a hole in the ceiling and wall where they meet; cut the switch box hole (locate the switch directly below the ceiling hole unless running through notched studs or behind molding); run cable from the source to the switch box; run fish tape down from the top wall hole to the switch-box hole, connect enough cable for the switch loop and pull it up out of the top hole; run the fish tape from the fixture hole to the ceiling hole, connect it to the switch loop cable and pull it out of the fixture hole; notch the top plates to inset the cable and staple it; connect, mount boxes and hook up fixture and switch. Along a wall: cut box holes; cut a straight narrow strip of wall covering exposing all studs between boxes, both ends centered over studs; drill through the center of each stud with a 3/4-in. spade bit and run the cable. Around a doorway: remove the molding around the door frame and baseboard as needed; run the cable between jamb and frame, notching spacers as needed; behind molding: make sure you can get replacements (it may split); pry with a 4-in. or wider putty knife or electrician's chisel; use a 1/16-in. metal plate or thin-wall conduit to protect cable less than 1 1/2 in. from a finished surface; do not nail through the cable when renailing. Back-to-back devices: make the hole for the new box; de-energize the circuit; pull the source device out of its box; remove the knockout from the back of the source box; insert the cable with connector through the new box hole into the source box; connect the cable to the new box and mount it; wire in the new device and the source; turn the circuit back on
entries.use: Running cable in finished walls (baseboard, wall, door, back-to-back device)
entries.how: De-energize first; use 3/4-in. spade bit through stud centers; protect cable within 1 1/2 in. of a surface with a 1/16-in. metal plate or thin-wall conduit
entries.dim: 3/4-in. spade bit; protect cable under 1 1/2 in. from surface with 1/16-in. plate
entries.eq: Spade bit, putty knife, fish tape
entries.wn: De-energize the circuit before working on a source device

entries.n: Mount outlet and ceiling boxes in finished walls
entries.desc: Mount a box: screw a cable connector to the box (or use a box with internal clamps) and thread the cable through; leave 6 to 8 inches of cable sticking out for connections. Plain box with brackets: check fit; adjust ears so the front edge is flush with the finished wall; put a bracket in the wall on either side, pull the tabs snug against the back of the wall, bend the tabs over the box sides and secure with needle-nose pliers. Plain box without brackets: check fit and adjust ears; mark screw placements on the lath at top and bottom of the hole; remove the box and drill pilot holes; screw the box to the stud; on wooden walls screw ears to the wall surface (the faceplate hides them). Cut-in box: one-time mounting; side teeth flare away and the box can't be removed; tightening the rear screw pushes teeth into the wall back; make sure cables are in place and the box fits first (remove the spring ears to test fit). Ceiling box on hanger bar: if no attic access cut out ceiling between two joists and screw the hanger bar to the sides of the joists. Ceiling box with offset hanger: screw the offset bar to the bottom edges of two joists. Ceiling box with flange: cut a rectangle from the ceiling and nail or screw the flange to a joist (Figure 4-8). Pancake box: screw to a joist or beam, positioned to hide the cable hole; no cable junctions in this box
entries.use: Fitting plain, cut-in, hanger-bar, flange and pancake boxes
entries.how: Leave 6-8 in. of cable in the box; the front edge must be flush with the finished wall; cut-in boxes cannot be removed once set
entries.dim: Leave 6-8 in. of cable

entries.n: Wire a new receptacle, switch, light or junction box into the power source
entries.desc: If rewiring adds a new circuit to the service-entrance panel or subpanel, see chapter 3. Figures 4-9, 4-10, 4-11 and 4-12 show wiring a new cable at a receptacle, switch, light and junction box. Table 4-1 checklist for adding a receptacle: de-energize the circuit you will tap; make a hole in the wall for the new box; pull the device that is the power source out of its box; remove the knockout in the source box leading most directly to the new cable route; remove the baseboard between box locations; drill a hole through the wall below each box; cut a channel in the wall between the two holes; cut cable adding 2 feet extra for box and device connections; put the cable connector on one end and fish the cable through the wall hole and knockout up into the source box; connect the cable to the new box and mount it; wire the new device and wire into the source; put faceplates on the boxes and turn the circuit back on
entries.use: Tapping a new cable into an existing circuit
entries.how: Shut off the main breaker or circuit first; use the Table 4-1 checklist (De-energize, new box hole, pull source device, knockout, cable +2 ft, wire in, faceplates, power on)
entries.dim: Cable length = run + 2 ft
entries.wn: Before hooking up the new cable to the power source, shut off the main breaker or disconnect the circuit you are wiring into

entries.n: Choose rigid conduit, fittings and accessories
