entries.desc: Rigid metal conduit (black-enamel or galvanized) is approved for most conditions and locations; enamel-protected conduit and fittings only indoors and where not severely corrosive. Most expensive wiring, but its strength allows installation without running boards, protects against damage, carries more conductors in one run than any other system and needs fewer supports; the size chosen usually allows more conductors later. Sizes use water-pipe designations and are given by inside diameter. Conduit smaller than 1/2 in. is only for finished buildings where extensions go under plaster (5/16-inch conduit or tubing permitted). Standard interior sizes: 1/2, 3/4, 1, 1 1/4, 1 1/2, 2, 2 1/2 in.; up to 6 in. for commercial and factory use. Unlike water pipe, conduit is softer (bends easily), smooth inside to protect wires, rust-resistant. Black-enamel for dry indoor; galvanized for outside moisture protection; aluminum, copper-alloy or plastic-jacketed for corrosive atmospheres. Conductors: rubber-covered Types R and RH in most interior work; thermoplastic Types T and TW gaining favor for better insulation; underground or wet installations need lead-covered cables in galvanized conduit. Supports: conduit straps (chapter 2), spacings per Table B-17. Fittings: standard outlet boxes Type F for exposed installations housing receptacles or switches; condulets provide pull-through points in long runs or junctions for concealed work: Type SE (service entrance), Type L (elbow), Type C (through), Type T (through with 90-degree take-off). Boxes: steel or cast-iron with knockouts and bushings and locknuts (Figure 5-1); wet or hazardous locations need threaded hubs. Couplings: threaded couplings come with each length; threadless couplings may be used if installed tightly. Elbows for 90-degree bends. Conduit unions permit opening a conduit at any point without sawing; runs can start from two outlets and join anywhere
entries.use: Selecting conduit type, size, boxes and couplings
entries.how: Black-enamel for dry indoor, galvanized outdoors; sizes are inside diameter; use unions to open a run without cutting
entries.src: TM 3-34.46 para 5-1 to 5-13; Figure 5-1; Table B-17

entries.n: Bend, cut, ream and thread rigid conduit
entries.desc: Bends: do not collapse the wall or reduce the internal diameter. Field bend inner radius at least six times the internal diameter for rubber-, braid- or thermoplastic-covered conductors and at least 10 times for lead-covered (Table B-18); a maximum of four quarter bends between two openings, and no more than three quarter bends in a 10-ft length. Factory bends are optional but rarely used (extra cutting, threading, couplings). Conduit up to 3/4 in. is usually bent with a hand bender called a hickey (Figure 5-2); bending forms on pipe-vise stands exist; or use leverage between two fixed posts. Right-angle bend in 1/2-in. conduit at 20 in. from the end: mark 20 in.; place the hickey 2 in. in front of the mark and bend about 25 degrees; move to the 20-in. mark and bring to 45 degrees; move 1 in. behind the mark and bring to 70 degrees; move 2 in. behind the mark and bring to 90 degrees. Draw the bend contour in chalk on the floor for accuracy. Use a hydraulic bender for conduit over 1 in. Cutting: hacksaw (hold in a vise, cut square) or pipe cutter; a power hacksaw for large amounts; hacksaw recommended because a pipe cutter leaves a burr that takes time to remove; always use cutting oil. Reaming: remove the sharp inside edge with a pipe reamer or file before installing. Threading: conduit has the same dimensions as gas, water or steam pipe so standard threads, tools and dies apply; small sizes with dies cutting a thread each turn; 1 1/2 in. and over with a ratchet-type cutter; motor-driven machines for large jobs; inspect each threaded piece for foreign matter inside and for thread condition (rethread if damaged, painted or dirty); always use cutting oil
entries.use: Fabricating conduit runs in the field
entries.how: Inner bend radius at least 6 x inside diameter (10 x for lead-covered conductors); at most four quarter bends between openings; ream every cut; cutting oil when threading
entries.dim: Inner radius >= 6 x ID (10 x lead-covered); max 4 quarter bends between openings; 3 per 10 ft
entries.eq: Hickey, hydraulic bender, hacksaw, reamer, die, cutting oil
entries.src: TM 3-34.46 para 5-14 to 5-21; Figure 5-2; Table B-18

entries.n: Install rigid conduit and connect it to boxes
entries.desc: Run conduit as straight and direct as possible; erect parallel adjacent conduits simultaneously. Support on surfaces with straps or hangers: wood: nails or wood screws; brick or concrete: drill holes with a star or carbide drill, install expansion anchors and use machine screws; tile or hollow material: toggle bolts; metal: drill, tap and use machine screws; number of supports per Table B-17. Cut conduit between boxes to length, thread, ream and bend to suit the building; attach the ends to the boxes; in concealed installations notch building members sufficiently to place conduit behind the wall surface but avoid undue weakening. Threaded-hub boxes: screw conduit ends into the hubs and connect the run at midpoint with a coupling. Knockout-type boxes: Step 1 place boxes loosely on studs and joists. Step 2 screw a bowed locknut, teeth adjacent to the box, onto the run-end threads. Step 3 insert the conduit ends into the knockout openings. Step 4 screw bushings (smooth inside) tightly onto the conduit ends inside the boxes. Step 5 tighten locknuts against the boxes so the teeth dig into the metal, driving a drive punch against a locknut lug. Step 6 fasten the box securely to the building after making all box connections
entries.use: Running and securing conduit between boxes
entries.how: Run straight and direct; erect parallel runs together; strap anchors by surface type; bowed locknut with teeth against the box
entries.eq: Straps, expansion anchors, toggle bolts, locknuts, bushings, drive punch

entries.desc: After installing boxes and conduit, pull the conductors. For short runs with few wires, pair conductors and push them through box to box. For runs with several bends and more than two conductors, use a fish tape: bare the conductor ends, connect them to the fish tape and tape the junction to the tape (protects conduit interior and conductors already in place, and compacts and strengthens the joint) (Figure 5-3). Wire pulling is generally a two-man job: one pulls, the other feeds, keeping the wires in the same relative position throughout the run to avoid insulation injury. Wire lubricant such as powdered soapstone may be rubbed on or blown into the conduit. In intricate runs pull in sections between boxes (extra splicing and time). Preferred: pull from the source through to the last box; make loops extending about 8 inches from the box openings for each conductor that is to be tapped or connected; if not tapped, pull through the box directly to the connection. Splices in conduit installations are not under tension, so a carefully made pigtail splice is fine; do not make any splice that will be concealed inside the conduit runs (reduces pulling area, source of failure)
entries.use: Pulling conductors with a fish tape
entries.how: Two-person job: one feeds, one pulls; tape wires to the fish tape; lubricate with powdered soapstone; no splices inside the conduit; leave 8 in. loops at boxes
entries.dim: 8-in. loops at boxes

entries.desc: Layout and circuiting follow chapter 3. One conduit can carry many conductors where cable would need several runs, so plan conduit layouts to use the minimum conduit and keep conductor runs short to maintain a low voltage drop. Color coding: no exceptions to the standard code. Every load device (fixtures, receptacles) operating at line-to-neutral voltage in a grounded neutral system connects to both a white and a black (or substitute color) wire. White is always the grounded neutral. Black wires are hot leads that are fused and switched. Red, blue and orange may substitute for black when wire combinations are combined in a conduit or circuit. Never connect a white wire to a black or substitute-color wire. Do not fuse or switch the white wire except in a multipole device that opens all conductors of the circuit simultaneously. Green insulation denotes an auxiliary equipment ground. Expedient: paint the ends of the insulation or use wire code markers when colored insulation is not available. Induced current: a conductor that changes position or reverses current induces current in an iron or steel conduit around it, heating it and wasting power; in AC both wires of a circuit are enclosed in one conduit so the induced currents cancel; therefore both wires of a circuit must travel in the same conduit
entries.use: Applying the white/black/green code in conduit
entries.how: White is always the grounded neutral; black (or red, blue, orange) is hot; green is equipment ground; both wires of an AC circuit go in the same conduit

entries.desc: Conduit can accommodate several conductors in one run. Table B-19 lists the maximum number of conductors of a gauge in each conduit size used in interior wiring; e.g., six No. 14 wires require 3/4-inch conduit. For more than one wire size in a run, the combined cross-sectional area must not exceed the allowable percent of conduit area (Table B-20). Table B-21 lists the percent of conduit cross-section in square inches available for conductors. Example: three No. 10 Type R and four No. 8 Type R conductors: combined area from Table B-22 = 0.4420 sq in. (3 x 0.0460 + 4 x 0.0760). In Table B-21 column 7, 0.4420 lies between 0.34 sq in. (1-inch conduit) and 0.60 sq in. (1 1/4-inch conduit); 1-inch is too small; use 1 1/4-inch conduit
entries.use: How many wires fit in a conduit
entries.how: Table B-19 gives the count for one wire size (six No. 14 = 3/4 in.); for mixed sizes add cross-section areas (Table B-22) and pick the conduit from Table B-21
entries.dim: Six No. 14 = 3/4-in. conduit; three No. 10 R + four No. 8 R = 0.4420 sq in. = 1 1/4-in. conduit
entries.src: TM 3-34.46 para 5-29, 5-30; Tables B-19 to B-22

entries.n: Add or upgrade circuits in existing conduit wiring
entries.desc: Increase of circuit amperage: a 1/2-inch conduit generally carries two No. 14 conductors (15 A); from Table B-19 it can also take two No. 12 (20 A). To raise the load on an existing circuit, replace the No. 14 with No. 12 wires; when every wire in the circuit is replaced, increase the fuse or breaker in the central panel from 15 to 20 A. Addition of a new circuit: when circuit analysis shows the need, use existing conduit for most of the distance: pull an additional wire (red) from the panel to the existing outlet and add the new outlet box beyond; connect the new load to the additional circuit; check Table B-19 for room for another wire; the added box and conduit follow the earlier rules; use a common grounded-neutral wire
entries.use: Raising amperage or adding a circuit through existing conduit
entries.how: Replace two No. 14 (15 A) with two No. 12 (20 A) in 1/2-in. conduit, then raise the breaker to 20 A; a new circuit can use a red wire pulled through existing conduit

entries.desc: EMT (thin-wall conduit) can be exposed or concealed but only in dry interior locations (thin plating rusts in weather or humidity). Cheaper and easier than rigid, ends are not threaded, bending takes less effort; ranks behind rigid conduit but ahead of other wiring in quality; most generally specified in home building. Install like rigid conduit but with pressure-type couplings and connectors. Same interior diameter and area as rigid; sizes 3/8 to 2 in. (3/8 in. only for under-plaster extensions); enameled inside; couplings and box connections are threadless clamp or compression type (Figure 5-4); some fittings are sleeves secured with an impinger tool that pinches a circular indentation; others have threaded bushings that force a tapered sleeve against the tubing. Same conductor types, capacities and maximum numbers as rigid (Tables B-17 to B-21). Bends: avoid kinking or reducing the inside area; inner radius at least 6 x internal diameter with thermoplastic-covered conductors, 10 x with lead-covered (Table B-18). Bender (Figure 5-5): cast-steel head on a steel pipe handle about 4 ft long, makes standard and offset bends; one bender per conduit size; the foot step steadies the bender; numbers on the shaft are inches for offset depth. 90-degree bend: place conduit on a level surface, hook the bender under the stub end, bending groove over the conduit; push down on the handle and step on the foot step with steady continuous force; for 45 degrees move until the handle is vertical. For an accurate stub, place the bender at the stub dimension minus the take-up height: 5 in. for 1/2-in., 6 in. for 3/4-in., 8 in. for 1-in. conduit. Cut with a hacksaw or thin-wall cutter and ream. Support like rigid. With no positive link between couplings, connectors and conduit, make each joint electrically and mechanically secure: insert ends until they touch the inner limiting edges and tighten firmly
entries.use: Dry interior exposed or concealed runs with unthreaded conduit
entries.how: Dry interior only; threadless clamp or compression fittings; bender take-up height 5 in. (1/2 in.), 6 in. (3/4 in.), 8 in. (1 in.); inner bend radius 6 x ID
entries.dim: Sizes 3/8-2 in.; take-up height 1/2 in. = 5 in., 3/4 in. = 6 in., 1 in. = 8 in.; bender handle ~4 ft
entries.wn: Do not loosen conduit from fittings: a loose joint can cause a short circuit, an electrical fire and loss of ground continuity
entries.src: TM 3-34.46 para 5-34 to 5-40; Figures 5-4, 5-5; Table B-18

entries.desc: Flexible metal conduit (Greenfield) resembles armored cable but wires of various sizes and numbers can be pulled in after installation. Use plastic-covered Greenfield where conductors are exposed to oil, gasoline or materials that deteriorate insulation (thermoplastic outer sheath like Type T wire, Table B-2). Figure 5-6 shows fittings. Install like thin-wall conduit but support more often. Because of high cost, use it for connections between rigid wiring and movable or vibrating equipment (motors, fans), or where a conduit bend is difficult or impossible. Ground most flexible conduit systems with a separate grounding wire run with the circuit conductors. Runs between boxes and fittings must not bend more than four quarter turns; support with a strap within 12 in. of every box or fitting and at intervals no longer than 4 1/2 ft
entries.use: Final connections to motors, fans and vibrating equipment
entries.how: Strap within 12 in. of every box or fitting and at intervals of no more than 4 1/2 ft; no more than four quarter turns between fittings; run a separate ground wire
entries.dim: Strap within 12 in. of fittings and every 4 1/2 ft; max four quarter turns

entries.desc: Schedule 40 polyvinyl chloride (PVC) is the most-used nonmetallic conduit: rigid, heavy-walled, flame-retardant, heat- and sunlight-resistant; wet or dry locations, in walls, ceilings, above or below ground. Do not substitute PVC irrigation pipe; look for the insignia of an electrical materials testing laboratory. Use with metal or nonmetallic boxes (not the same as boxes used with Type NMC cable). Nonmetallic conduit is not a grounded system, so run a separate grounding wire with the circuit conductors. After cutting, trim the ends inside and out with a pocketknife to remove rough edges. Bending: heat in a special infrared heater until soft; do not use a torch (it chars the conduit); design runs so no piece between fittings bends more than four quarter turns. Joining: 10-ft lengths each with a coupling; glue with gray conduit cement, not water-pipe cement; male and female adapters for transitions to other conduit and boxes
entries.use: Wet, dry, buried or in-wall runs with schedule 40 PVC
entries.how: Schedule 40 PVC with a lab insignia (not irrigation pipe); separate ground wire; heat bends in an infrared heater (not a torch); glue with gray conduit cement
entries.dim: 10-ft lengths; max four quarter turns
entries.eq: Infrared heater, gray conduit cement, pocketknife

entries.n: Handle foreign voltage, frequency and wiring differences
entries.desc: Most foreign wiring is not installed to prescribed standards (material shortages) and generally resembles open wiring, with other types in urban areas. Nominal US single-phase low-voltage is 120 to 240 V at 60 cycles; many countries use other voltages, so equipment must be converted, modified or operated inefficiently (FM 5-422 has voltage and frequency charts). Foreign frequencies include 25, 40, 42, 100 and commonly 50 cycles. Wire: AWG is peculiar to the US; most foreign wire differs in size and usage; Table B-23 gives standard and metric diameters of AWG sizes. Receptacles, switches and plugs are peculiar to each area and normally cannot mate with US ones. When the Army commandeers a foreign installation, the electrician or commander decides based on supplies and time; components are not interchangeable; compare installing foreign equipment to modifying US items to meet local standards. If time is short, use standard US items with modified plugs or connections; efficiency drops but adaptability and supply usually outweigh it. Operate all equipment at its rated voltage where possible. Voltage effects: fluorescent lamps at higher voltage shorten lamp and ballast life; below the minimum of the operating ranges (110 to 240, 199 to 216, or 220 to 250 V) cause uncertain starting, short lamp life and reduced efficiency. Incandescent lamps above 115/120/125 V rating have shortened life and increased output; below standard, life increases and efficiency drops about 3 percent for each 1 percent drop in rated voltage. Motors and fans usually tolerate 10 percent voltage variation (combined voltage and frequency variation also 10 percent); higher voltage gives more torque, efficiency and starting temperature; lower voltage gives less torque and efficiency and more running temperature; beyond 10 percent only in extreme emergency (damage). Frequency effects: resistance heaters, hot plates and stoves work at all frequencies; fluorescent lights rated 60 cycle can run at 50 cycles with shorter ballast life; below that, visible flicker, avoid; incandescent works at all; motors should not be connected to frequencies varying more than 5 percent from rating; shaft speed is proportional to frequency (1,800 rpm at 60 cycles becomes 1,500 at 50); special larger-frame motors are needed for the same power at lower frequency; radio and other transformer-equipped gear will not work satisfactorily off its rated frequency (emergency only). Material differences: never use dissimilar metals together except in an emergency expedient installation (galvanic corrosion, especially aluminum with copper); special connectors marked for copper/aluminum exist; if only aluminum is used, apply joint compound to all connections because aluminum oxide adds high contact resistance
entries.use: Using or modifying equipment on host-nation or commandeered electrical systems
entries.how: Operate equipment at rated voltage; 50-Hz power shortens ballast life and slows motors (1,800 rpm becomes 1,500); avoid mixing aluminum and copper
entries.dim: Motor tolerance 10 percent voltage; motors within 5 percent of rated frequency; incandescent lumen loss ~3 percent per 1 percent voltage drop; 1,800 rpm at 60 cycles = 1,500 at 50
entries.wn: Operation more than 10 percent off rated voltage may damage or destroy equipment; use only in extreme emergency

entries.n: Use and maintain disconnect and bypass switches
entries.desc: Manual and automatic switches open and close circuits; they must carry rated current continuously without overheating and have clearances and insulation for the circuit voltage. Fuses and circuit breakers give simple, inexpensive overcurrent protection and show where breakdowns happen. Disconnect switches are generally used in primary circuits where opening is under voltage with little or no load current; they interrupt only charging or exciting current; used to disconnect branch lines, off circuit breakers and transformers. Open-type (Figure 7-1) is used at switch structures and on the line and can be operated from the ground with a long-handled switch stick if mounting height allows; enclosed line-sectionalizing types (Figure 7-2) mount on crossarms of the primary circuit and are operated by a switch stick fastened to the lineman's belt. Bypass switches at booster and regulator installations take apparatus in and out of service without de-energizing feeder circuits and prevent winding burnouts from open-circuit windings. Gang-operated disconnects open more than one phase simultaneously; most common is the air-brake type in 200-, 300- and 400-ampere ratings in all voltage classes from 5,000 V up, used at substations, switching structures and on lines to energize and de-energize transformer banks and for sectionalizing; handle-operated (or motor-operated) from the ground, often restoring service without pole climbing. Maintenance: contacts smooth and covered with a thin film of nonoxide grease; bearings well lubricated; blades move freely yet rigid for alignment; find and replace broken or defective insulators immediately; keep bolts and nuts tight
entries.use: Opening primary circuits and taking apparatus in and out of service
entries.how: Disconnects open circuits with little or no load; ground the handle to the counterpoise or ground plate; keep contacts smooth with a thin film of nonoxide grease
entries.dim: Gang-operated air-brake disconnects 200, 300, 400 A, 5,000 V and up
entries.wn: Always ground the switch handle by connecting it to the counterpoise or ground plate, below the topsoil, directly beneath the operating handle

entries.n: Operate and understand oil circuit breakers and reclosers
entries.desc: Oil circuit breakers open a circuit automatically under load; designed for one or more automatic reclosings to restore service quickly when a fault clears; generally in substations or switching stations needing high interrupting capacity or high-grade service. Pole-mounted oil circuit breakers (reclosers, sectionalizing oil circuit breakers, interrupters) suit the low side of step-down substations, branch circuits tied to important feeders, protecting important loads and isolating line trouble. Reclosers: up to 50 A and 15,000 V; the 50-A breaker interrupts about 1,200 A. The recloser is connected in the line, normally closed; the trip coil is in series with the contacts and takes energy from fault current. On a fault the circuit promptly opens and recloses automatically in about three seconds; if the fault isn't cleared the recloser opens a second and possibly third time; if cleared on the second or third interruption the mechanism resets automatically; if the fault persists after the third, it opens a fourth time and locks open and must be reset manually. Internals: one pair of contacts (lower stationary at bottom; upper movable connected to the trip coil); on a short circuit the movable contact rises rapidly drawing an arc in oil; heat forms a gas bubble that pressurizes the oil-blast chamber, forcing a blast of cool air between the contacts so the arc cannot restrike after an early current zero; butt-type contacts compensate for burning and can be replaced. Figure 7-3 shows a single-phase installation with bypass switch and lightning arrester (bypass optional; some breakers have internal lightning protection)
entries.use: Automatic protection on substations and distribution lines
entries.how: A recloser reopens after a fault, recloses in about 3 seconds, and locks open on the fourth trip until reset by hand
entries.dim: Recloser up to 50 A, 15,000 V; recloses in ~3 s; locks open after 4th trip

entries.n: Know oil fuse cutouts and circuit-reclosing fuse cutouts
entries.desc: Oil fuse cutouts: most common on underground systems; also overhead systems up to 7,500 V needing intermediate interrupting capacity where automatic restoration is not essential. Circuit-reclosing (multiple-shot) fuse cutouts are porcelain-housed (50- and 10-A ratings, 5,000- and 500-V classes) or open (higher voltage classes, pin-and-cap or post-type insulators; up to 100 A in classes up to 46 kV; up to 200 A limited to 7,500- and 15,000-V ratings). They permit quick restoration where temporary faults come from lightning or high wind; open type more common; both fit feeder or branch circuits; confine use to remote, unattended substations or remote points on distribution circuits. Operation: when the fuse link blows, the first holder drops out; dropping of the holder or cartridge (by pressure or spring) closes the circuit through the next cartridge; a three-shot repeats this; three faults blow all three fuses, all three barrels in the dropout indicating position; cartridges can be replaced in any sequence without momentary service interruption. Distribution fuses: some have the element in a tube filled with powder or granular material to absorb vaporized metal and extinguish the arc; others have the element in a tube with a dielectric extinguishing the arc; high initial and replacement cost so usually limited to circuits of 13,200 V or more (Figures 7-4, 7-5)
entries.use: Fusing distribution lines and restoring service after transient faults
entries.how: Multiple-shot cutouts drop out one barrel at a time; three faults blow all three fuses and all three barrels hang in the dropout position
entries.dim: Oil fuse cutouts to 7,500 V overhead

entries.n: Identify mobile generator sets (AC, DC, sizes)
entries.desc: A mobile generator set uses an engine to drive a generator with an internal fuel supply (Figure 8-1 shows a power-generating site). Table 8-1 lists models with kW, frequency and voltage output; Table 8-2 groups them by engine type, application and TM. Gasoline- or diesel-driven; produce AC or DC. Match set characteristics to the connected equipment. AC: most lighting and power loads use AC; 60 cycle common, some loads (radar, fire-control sets, communication controls, guided-missile systems) need 400 cycle. A set producing 60 kW can be moved in a 2 1/2-ton truck; over 60 kW needs a 5-ton truck; units parallel several 60-kW sets for large loads. Several small sets near their loads may replace a large one but need more operators and maintenance. Small: gasoline-engine 0.5 or 1.5 kW, 120 or 240 V single-phase, 60 cycle (0.5 kW also 400 cycle); the 1.5-kW 60-cycle set is the most versatile and widely used small set. Medium: gasoline or diesel, 3 to 10 kW, 60 or 400 cycle; a reconnection switch selects single-phase two-wire 120 V; single-phase two-wire 240 V; three-phase three-wire 120 V; three-phase four-wire 120/208 V (printed as 210/208 V). The 10-kW 60-cycle set is the most versatile (small maintenance shops); usually skid-mounted. Large: diesel, 15 to 500 kW, 50/60 or 400 cycle, three-phase four-wire 120/208 or 240/416 V; output at 50 cycles is 82 percent of rated power, at 60 cycles 100 percent; standard-frequency sets are 50/60 cycles and high-frequency 400 cycles; supply lighting and power over a wide area. DC sets (MEP-024A 28 V 17 A; MEP-025A 28 V 53 A; MEP-026A 28 V 103 A) charge batteries and power communications and some missile equipment; they are basic AC generators with rectifiers. Table 8-1 examples: MEP-016A 3 kW 60 Hz; MEP-017A 5 kW; MEP-018A 10 kW; MEP-004A/103A 15 kW; MEP-005A/104A 30 kW; MEP-006A/105A 60 kW; MEP-007A/B/106A 100 kW; MEP-009A/108A 200 kW; MEP-029A 500 kW; MEP-404B 60 kW 400 Hz turbine. Data plates: alternator data plate (50-, 60-, 400-cycle ratings, serial number, kW, DC excitation requirement, date, volt and amp outputs, power factors, model, rpm; on the main generator housing); equipment identification plate (model, serial number, horsepower, date, cylinders and firing order, NSN, contract number, sometimes the TM; Figure 8-2); starting and stopping instruction plate (also called paralleling and synchronizing plate; inside the main control-panel cover; may show dark-lamp synchronizing procedures)
entries.use: Knowing which MEP set is small, medium or large, gas or diesel, 60/400 Hz
entries.how: Small gas 0.5/1.5 kW; medium 3-10 kW (60 or 400 cycle, reconnectable); large diesel 15-500 kW (50/60 or 400 cycle, 3-phase 4-wire 120/208 or 240/416 V)
entries.dim: 60 kW max for 2 1/2-ton truck; 50 Hz = 82 percent of rated power; DC sets 28 V

entries.n: Connect the right distribution system to a generator
entries.desc: A distribution system carries power from generator to loads and is identified by phases, wires and voltage between wires. Check equipment data plates before connecting a distribution system to a load. Single-phase two-wire (Figure 8-3): one wire is the neutral (grounded wire or grounded circuit conductor), the other the live (ungrounded) wire; usually 120 V between them; lights, portable tools and most low-power equipment. Single-phase three-wire (Figure 8-4): one grounded wire and two live wires; usually 120 V from either live wire to ground and 240 V between the live wires; small loads such as barracks lighting. Three-phase three-wire (Figure 8-5): all three wires are live; a 120-V three-phase load connects to all three; single magnitude of voltage so all loads must need the same voltage; for structures where three-phase power load exceeds the single-phase lighting load (lighting from a separate single-phase service or a step-down transformer). Three-phase four-wire (Figure 8-6): can produce single- or three-phase voltages (e.g., 120 and 208 V, or 240 and 416 V; 240/416 common on 15-500 kW sets); flexible; shops, hospitals. The ratio of line voltage to phase voltage is fixed (1.73 x phase voltage = line voltage). From it you can feed: single-phase two-wire 120 V (any live wire and grounded wire); single-phase two-wire 208 V (between any two live wires); single-phase three-wire 120/208 V (two live wires and grounded wire); three-phase three-wire 240 V (reposition the tap change board and connect to the three live wires); three-phase four-wire 120/208 V (all four wires)
entries.use: Wiring single- and three-phase distribution from a set
entries.how: Check data plates first; 120 V: live to grounded wire; 208 V between two live wires on 120/208; line voltage = 1.73 x phase voltage
entries.dim: Line voltage = 1.73 x phase voltage; 120/208 V or 240/416 V
entries.wn: Any attempt to operate equipment at other than its rated frequency will damage it

entries.n: Compute the load for a field site (demand, diversity, voltage drop)
entries.desc: Prerequisites to selecting generators: compute the load, compute cable size, balance the load. Steps: 1 Map the field unit: locate and mark all structures needing power (Figure 8-7). 2 Determine the electrical load for each area (amperes, kW or kVA; the total fluctuates as equipment starts and stops). 3 Connected load per structure (kW-amps): total wattage of all lights and devices plus the horsepower of all motors. 4 Demand load = connected load x demand factor (demand load never exceeds connected load, but may equal it if all equipment must run at once). Table 8-3 demand factors: housing 9; aircraft maintenance 7; operation facilities 8; administrative 8; shops 7; warehouses 5; medical 8; theaters 5; navigational aids 7; laundry, ice plants and bakeries 10; all others 9 (factors are printed as whole numbers, i.e. tenths). 5 Diversity factor (at the point of supply): ratio of the sum of the maximum demands of the parts of a system to the maximum demand of the whole system; example: three sites of 30 kW max each = 90 kW potential, but because the maxima don't coincide the generator load is only 60 kW (Figure 8-8); a dining facility may contribute about 25 percent of its actual load to the system peak. 6 Power factor = true power (watts) / apparent power (volt-amperes); noninductive loads (lights, heaters, soldering irons) PF 1.0; inductive loads (partly loaded transformers, induction motors) below 1.0; DC watts = volts x amps (no reactance). 7 Voltage drop (line loss) = difference between input and output voltage, expressed as a percent of the receiving-end voltage (usual); example: generated 231 V, receiving 220 V, drop 11 V = 11/220 = 5 percent (4.8 percent of sending voltage) (Figure 8-9). Maximum allowable for lighting and power is 5 percent: no more than 3 percent in branch lines and 2 percent in main and feeder lines. To raise receiving-end voltage raise the generator output but never above the set's rating; monitor voltage periodically; resistive heat varies with voltage: 10 percent below rated voltage gives 19 percent less heat. 8 Allow growth: at least 50 percent of the initial load; circuits must carry at least 50 percent more than actual connected loads
entries.use: Estimating the power a field unit needs before choosing generators
entries.how: Demand load = connected load x demand factor; keep total voltage drop to 5 percent (3 percent branch, 2 percent feeder); allow at least 50 percent growth
entries.dim: Max voltage drop 5 percent (3 branch + 2 feeder); growth allowance at least 50 percent; demand factors in Table 8-3

entries.n: Size the cable from generator to load
entries.desc: Cable size affects generator efficiency; undersized cable loses power along the line, may overheat and burn the insulation, and melting wires break the circuit; resistance depends on the distance between set and load. Steps: 1 Use Table 3-1 and Tables 8-4 (load conversion factors) and 8-5 (full-load currents of motors) to compute total current demand per phase. 2 Use Table 8-6 (allowable current capacities, three or fewer conductors in a raceway or cable; AWG 14 to 4/0 by insulation type) to find the wire size that carries the current. If that size is not available use parallel runs of smaller wires or the next larger size; substitute sizes by Table 8-7 (e.g., for 1/0 AWG, 125 A: two No. 4, three No. 6, four No. 8, five No. 10); substitutions must not cause excessive voltage drop; monitor receiving-end voltage. 3 Use Table 8-8 (physical and electrical properties of conductors; resistance of bare and tinned copper per 1,000 ft at 77 F) to find total cable resistance between generator set and load. Ampacity is the current-carrying capacity in amperes. High current and short wire: ampacity needs a larger wire; low power and long line: voltage drop needs a larger wire; the criterion giving the larger wire governs. Table 8-6 sample (Types R/RW, column A): No. 14 = 15 A; 12 = 20; 10 = 30; 8 = 40; 6 = 55; 4 = 70; 3 = 80; 2 = 95; 1 = 110; 1/0 = 125; 2/0 = 145; 3/0 = 165; 4/0 = 195 A. Overhead cable: minimum No. 8 AWG, meeting voltage drop and strong enough for its own weight plus branches, ice or snow
entries.use: Choosing conductor size for a generator-to-load run
entries.how: Compute amps per phase (Tables 3-1, 8-4, 8-5), read wire size from Table 8-6; the larger of the ampacity size and the voltage-drop size governs; overhead min No. 8
entries.dim: Overhead cable minimum No. 8 AWG

entries.desc: Balance the load among phases before selecting sets: each phase carries an equal share. A load between a live wire and the ground wire pulls the unbalanced current through the ground wire; a load between two or more live wires splits equally among them. A three-phase four-wire set can feed a single-phase load on each of the three phases; the generator supplies the total load on each phase; connect loads so each phase receives an equal current. Unbalance has two bad effects: high voltage on the lightly loaded phase and low voltage on the others (poor regulation system-wide); a long-term unbalanced load damages the generating equipment. Single-phase two-wire 120 V cannot be unbalanced (Figure 8-10). Single-phase three-wire 120/240 V (Figure 8-11): two live wires and a ground; can supply two single-phase 120-V loads and one single-phase 208/220-V load group. Three-phase three-wire 208 V (Figure 8-12): three live wires; three single-phase 208-V loads or one three-phase 208-V load; for single-phase divide the load equally across the three. Three-phase four-wire 120/208 V (Figure 8-13): three live wires and a ground; single-phase 120 V, three-phase 208 V and single-phase 208 V loads. When the total load is balanced, mark the voltage and phases needed on a site diagram (markings are on most AC and DC motors)
entries.use: Spreading loads equally so the generator isn't damaged
entries.how: Give each phase an equal share; an unbalanced load gives high voltage on the lightly loaded phase and low voltage on the others and eventually damages the set

entries.desc: After designing distribution and balancing the load, select sets. Active field-unit electrical systems run day and night; annual load factor of a well-operated, active unit is 50 percent or more of generator capacity, and annual load power factor is 80 percent or more of average. Criteria: electrical loads to be supplied, kW rating, operating voltages, number of phases, frequency. Also consider fuel availability, expected life of the unit, skilled maintenance personnel, probable load deviation. Layout: load more than a few hundred feet from the set may need a high-voltage distribution system; if the plant serves a primary distribution system, rate the set at that voltage (no transformer at the sending end); most loads can be divided and balanced so most medium and large sets are three-phase. Most US loads need 60 cycles; most equipment tolerates drift of about 5 cycles above or below 60; teletypewriters and clocks are sensitive. If no time to build a central station, install a set at each work site (small single-phase set for a headquarters with lights and single-phase motors; a three-phase set for a maintenance shop with single- and three-phase loads). Coordinate with maintenance and supply: skills, tools and spare parts must be available. Power: a 1.5-kW, 120-V two-wire set supplies 120-V single-phase equipment under 1.5 kW combined; a 5-kW AC set supplies equipment needing 1.5 to 4.5 kW. If motors are in the load increase capacity to cover reduced terminal voltage and frequency surges on starting; remove the existing load when starting a large motor and re-add small loads after it reaches speed. Loads with 115 V and 230 V equipment need a single-phase three-wire 120/240 V output. Sets run 0.5 to 500 kW. Guides: single-phase for small lighting, AC and DC motors, arc welders, some furnace loads; three-phase for almost everything except small loads (balance each phase at the set when taking single-phase from it); lighting is rated 120 V (single-phase 120/240 V or three-phase 120/208 V); small motors under 5 hp use DC or single-phase 120 V; large three-phase motors (5 hp or more) work between 200 and 240 V; DC sets for specific tasks, mainly battery charging (Figure 8-14); a single generator set is the least desirable for continuous power (use only when isolated and failure won't hurt the mission). Engines: gasoline sets resemble small automotive engines (easier to fix); diesels run longer under more strain and need less maintenance (no ignition system); fuel availability may limit the choice. Load classification: a generator supports its full kVA rating if the load is mostly inductive; a purely resistive load (PF 1.0) can only reach 80 percent of kVA: MEP-017A rated 6.25 kVA supports only 5 kW (6.25 x 0.80); a 0.8-PF set can't support its kVA on a resistive load. Many sets allow multiple voltages with ampere rating changing; Table 8-9 (MEP-018A, 5 kW class): single-phase 120 V = 104 A; 240 V = 52 A; three-phase 120 V = 34.7 A per phase; 208 V = 17.3 A per phase. Ratings are on the alternator data plate and in the TM
entries.use: Choosing the type, size, voltage and fuel of a set for a unit
entries.how: Selection criteria: load, kW, voltage, phases, frequency; add capacity for motor starting; a 6.25 kVA MEP-017A supports only 5 kW of purely resistive load
entries.dim: Resistive load = 80 percent of kVA; Table 8-9: 120 V 1-ph 104 A, 240 V 1-ph 52 A, 120 V 3-ph 34.7 A, 208 V 3-ph 17.3 A

entries.desc: Paralleling gives a combined kW equal to the sum of the sets (Figure 8-15) and keeps power continuous while one set is shut down for service (e.g., surgical hospitals). Synchronize before connecting to the load. Steps: 1 Close the main circuit breaker on the base set. 2 Ensure the meter shows the frequency required for the load (base set may be loaded or unloaded). 3 Open the circuit breaker on the incoming set. 4 Ensure its voltage and frequency match the base set. 5 Place the paralleling switch on the control panels of the base and incoming sets ON; the two paralleling lamps on the incoming set's panel blink; they should blink on and off together if connected properly (if not in unison, turn all power off before reconnecting). If the base set is under load, watch its kW (percent-of-power) meter; at the incoming set adjust the throttle (utility sets) or frequency adjust rheostat (precise sets) until the lamps go on and off at 3- to 5-second intervals; when the lights are completely dark, close the main circuit breaker on the incoming set; adjust the incoming set's frequency rheostat until the kW meter shows one-half of the base set's power; adjust voltage rheostats on both sets as needed to eliminate crosscurrents. When the lamps blink in unison the sets operate in parallel as one. 6 Repeat 3-5 for each additional set (third set's meter should show one-third of the load). 7 When all are in parallel divide the load equally by adjusting voltage and frequency outputs of each set
entries.use: Running two or more sets together for more power or continuous service
entries.how: Close the base set breaker, match voltage and frequency on the incoming set, turn both paralleling switches ON, adjust until lamps blink together every 3-5 s, close the incoming breaker when lamps are dark
entries.dim: Lamps on/off every 3-5 s
entries.wn: If the current meter on either set shows excessive current and the voltage rheostat will not balance it, do not operate the generators in parallel; refer to the next higher level of maintenance

entries.desc: Power-generating equipment must be grounded (Figure 3-3). Rod: standard military rod is 5/8-in. rod in three 3-ft sections; drive at least 8 ft into the soil below the moisture level; if not possible replace with an 8-ft electrode in a horizontal trench at least 2 1/2 ft deep, below the moisture level. A network of three or more rods about 6 ft apart (straight line or triangle for three; more than three in a straight line) with the grounding cable from the set to each rod in series. Pipe: clean metallic pipe, 3/4-in. trade size or larger, iron or steel galvanized or coated; drive at least 8 ft; or an 8-ft electrode in a horizontal trench at least 2 ft deep below moisture. Plate: buried at least 36 x 36 in. (9 sq ft); an iron or steel plate at least 1/4 in. thick and coated may substitute; below moisture level. Attach with No. 6 AWG or larger cable from the set's grounding terminal (tighten the nut per the TM) to the electrode with a special grounding clamp. Soil (Table 8-10): fine granules with high moisture = very good; clay, loam, shale = good; mixed with gravel or sand = poor; gravel, sand, stone = very poor. Topsoil (1 to 6 in.) is dry and loose and conducts poorly; subsoil is tight, retains moisture and grounds best; wet soil conducts better. Poor ground: mix 5 pounds of table salt in 5 gallons of water; dig a hole about 1 ft deep and 3 ft wide; pour in the solution, install the rod and strap, backfill; keep soil moist. Frozen soil (below 32 F) is a poor conductor: place the ground near a heat source (generator or vehicle exhaust), or connect to something already grounded (metal building, underground pipe) with a clamp or bolt; or drive several stakes as deep as possible in a network, using drilled/dug/blasted holes and salt; a temporary ground can be a spike driven deep into a large tree. Locations: deserts (very poor; use salt solution, keep moist; near an oasis or subterranean water); mountains (site selection; near a streambed); packed, rocky or frozen soil (slip hammer, Figure 8-16); tropics (good ground; fast corrosion: apply waterproof tape at the strap connection and keep rod clean and dry). Checks: remove paint, oil and grease from rods, straps and connections; keep them clean; keep rods straight with sharp points; proper strap and cable lengths; proper clamps; tighten terminal and clamp screws
entries.use: Establishing a field ground for a generator (rod, pipe, plate, salt solution)
entries.how: Drive the rod at least 8 ft below the moisture level; use a No. 6 AWG or larger cable and grounding clamp; salt solution for poor soil
entries.dim: Rod 5/8 in. x 3 ft x 3 sections, driven 8 ft; pipe 3/4 in. x 8 ft; plate 36 x 36 in.; cable No. 6 AWG+; salt 5 lb in 5 gal
entries.eq: Ground rod, slip hammer, grounding clamp, No. 6 cable, table salt
entries.wn: If electrical power-generating equipment is not grounded, stray current in the set or distribution system can injure or kill the operator and damage the equipment
entries.src: TM 3-34.46 para 8-57 to 8-69; Figure 3-3; Figure 8-16; Table 8-10

entries.n: Select and prepare a generator site
entries.desc: Place generator sets near the largest loads (plot all demands on a map first, including sets for parallel operation); this reduces cable size and line voltage loss. Provide shelter from weather and enemy fire; a revetment also controls noise (for air-cooled sets of 0.5 to 10 kW); ventilation must remove heat and exhaust; sets in a closed structure need exhaust piped outside, as short as possible with no more than one 90-degree bend, combustibles at least 6 in. away, wrap with insulation if people can touch it. Site guides: clearance for maintenance; away from noise-sensitive areas; clean, level, dry, well-ventilated, well-drained ground; planks, timbers, logs or ammo boxes under skids; keep level, preferably within 5 degrees, never tilt over 15 degrees in any direction (lubrication); cargo trucks or two-wheeled trailers (a set on a trailer is a power unit, Figure 8-17); surface must support the weight; supply of clean fuel for the life of the installation (underground tanks for long term); auxiliary tanks for sets under 10 kW as near the shelter as possible with tank bottoms less than 4 ft below the fuel pump; for sets of 15 kW or more tanks less than 12 ft below the fuel transfer pumps; run line from the auxiliary tank to the fuel selector valve and keep dirt and water out; above-ground tanks roped off with engineer tape; No Smoking signs at each entrance to the fuel area, at least 50 feet from the fuel supply and set; shelter from rain and sun; fire point with a Class A extinguisher, shovel and pickax. Long-term: noncombustible shelter if possible (4 to 6 ft clearance if combustible); lean-to, shack or shed acceptable; bolt to a foundation to cut vibration; do not use portable, totally enclosed, winterized sets in a permanent indoor installation
entries.use: Siting, shelter, fuel and exhaust for a generator set
entries.how: Place near the largest loads; level within 5 degrees (never over 15); fuel NO SMOKING signs 50 ft away; keep combustibles 6 in. from exhaust; never run gasoline sets indoors without ventilating exhaust
entries.dim: Level within 5 degrees; max tilt 15; fuel tank bottom < 4 ft (under 10 kW) or < 12 ft (15 kW+) below pump; no smoking 50 ft
entries.eq: Engineer tape, signs, Class A extinguisher

entries.desc: Only for air-cooled engine-driven sets, designed to operate in the open with unrestricted ventilation; one set per revetment; no other heat-generating equipment inside (Figure 8-18). Minimum inside dimensions for 1.5 to 10 kW sets: 7 1/2 ft long, 5 1/2 ft wide, 4 ft high (3-ft walls plus 1-ft openings around the top); entrance 2 ft wide; sill 1 ft or less; also suitable for 0.5 kW sets (economy: 4 x 5 ft). Dimensions are for engine cooling and ventilation only, minimum servicing space. Foundation: a shipping pallet if attached; otherwise planks, timbers, logs or ammo boxes; foundation less than 6 in. high. Drainage: runoff away from the set and out of the revetment; all drain holes at inside ground level; sump and drainage trench outside for each hole if water doesn't drain naturally. Walls: sandbags, ammunition boxes filled with sand or dirt, or any material. Roof: at least 1 ft above the wall, as much open space as possible for ventilation; usually two 4 x 4 in. lumber or 4-in. logs about 10 ft long plus cross pieces about 8 ft long (lumber, logs or steel planking); roof thickness by protection needed (be sure it supports the weight; sandbags in Figure 8-18). Fuel storage compartment outside the revetment (heat hazard); do not use integral fuel tanks inside a revetment. Exhaust may or may not be ducted outside (commander's decision); a flexible pipe chimney is preferred (ducts gases away and cuts noise). Doorway shield: wall 3 ft high and 7 1/2 ft long preventing projectiles and fragments entering directly. Align so the door faces the prevailing wind and the set's long axis is parallel with the revetment's; center it; Table 8-11 orientation: 1.5 kW generator end toward door; 3.0 kW engine end toward door; 4.0 and 10.0 kW generator end toward door
entries.use: Protecting an air-cooled set from weather and attack
entries.how: One air-cooled set per revetment, minimum inside 7 1/2 x 5 1/2 x 4 ft; 3-ft walls with 1-ft ventilation gap; door faces the prevailing wind; fuel stored outside
entries.dim: Inside 7 1/2 x 5 1/2 x 4 ft; walls 3 ft; entrance 2 ft; sill <= 1 ft; foundation < 6 in.; door shield 3 x 7 1/2 ft
entries.wn: Never operate an air-cooled, gasoline-engine generator set inside a closed building unless forced ventilation can remove engine heat and exhaust (carbon monoxide: poisonous, odorless, colorless)

entries.n: Know the generator engine controls and safety shutdowns
entries.desc: Controls are on a control panel (Figure 9-1; numbers in parentheses are callouts). DC circuit breaker (20): protects DC circuits against shorts and emergency stops. Start-run-stop switch (32): in START completes the battery circuit to the starter; released, it returns to RUN after start and stays until set to STOP. Manual speed control (21): regulates engine speed. Heater controls (Figure 9-2): circuit breaker, heater-on press-to-test light, on-off switch; the light is on when the heater is operating. Three-way fuel valve (Figure 9-3): directs fuel to the pump; positions auxiliary fuel tank, set fuel tank, off. Safety controls (Figure 9-4): relays, overspeed safety devices, pressure-temperature controls; the set shuts down when a safety device actuates (stops the engine or trips the breaker) for overspeed, low fuel, low oil pressure or high coolant temperature. Indicators: low oil-pressure (8), coolant high-temperature (9), overspeed (10, when speed exceeds rated rpm and the overspeed device actuates, Figure 9-5), no-fuel (11). Battle-short switch (22): emergency operation; a four-pole on-off switch that keeps the generator able to start after a safety device actuates by locking out the starter circuit; bypasses all protective device circuits except overspeed and short circuits; OFF during normal operations. Engine instruments: oil-pressure gauge (37); coolant-temperature gauge (38); fuel-level gauge (36); battery-charge ammeter (35); hour (time-totalizing) meter (34)
entries.use: Reading the control panel: start switch, fuel valve, safety lights, battle-short
entries.how: Safety devices shut the set down for overspeed, low fuel, low oil pressure or high coolant temperature; the battle-short switch bypasses all but overspeed and short circuit protection

entries.n: Read the AC generator controls and meters
entries.desc: AC controls: volts-amps selector switch (5): current and voltage for each phase (a meter on each phase; usually six positions). Phase-selector switch (Figure 9-6): matches generator output to load voltage and phase; rotary on sets up to 10 kW; changeover boards on sets of 15 kW or more. Parallel-lights switch (26): closes the synchronizing-lights circuit to parallel units (two-position). Voltage-adjust rheostat (24): small variable resistor adjusting output voltage. Circuit-breaker switch (30): connects and disconnects load lines, acts as main switch and overload protection; automatically disconnects on overload, short circuit or ground on the load lines or in the powered equipment. Meters: AC ammeter (6) current output (usually percent of rated load); AC voltmeter (7) output terminal voltage; frequency (hertz) meter (3) line frequency for 50-, 60- and 400-cycle sets; kilowatt meter (4) output in percent of kilowatts, which must not exceed the rated capacity of the power plant; reduce the load if it does. Convenience outlet: 120-V AC for lights around the set, protected by fuses or a circuit breaker
entries.use: Monitoring output voltage, current, frequency and load
entries.how: Keep the kilowatt meter at or below rated capacity; reduce load if it exceeds; the convenience outlet is fused 120 V AC
entries.dim: Kilowatt meter must not exceed rated capacity

entries.n: Inspect and service a newly received generator set
entries.desc: A set shipped from a supply or maintenance point has had fluids drained and is not operational-ready. Inspect all incoming equipment: identification plate matches the equipment; check for damage and document it on DA Form 2404 (Equipment Inspection and Maintenance Worksheet), submitting to the next echelon; compare with the packing list for missing or unserviceable items; check for loose and missing hardware (tighten or replace); turn the engine over by hand so all moving parts in the engine and generator move freely; remove all tags, tape, cloth and barrier materials. Service: perform daily PMCS after inspection; lubricate the engine per the current lubrication order; correct what deficiencies you can and report the rest to organizational maintenance
entries.use: Receiving a set from supply or maintenance (fluids drained)
entries.how: Check ID plate vs. equipment, packing list, hardware; turn the engine over by hand; write damage on DA Form 2404; do PMCS and lubrication

entries.n: Install and maintain the generator fuel supply
entries.desc: Gasoline, diesel or JP-4 may power a set. Plan by duration, security, fire and safety hazards, and contamination sources. Duration: long term, install tanks underground with proper fittings per manufacturer, in a convenient location (limits contamination, vapor lock, fire); short term, tanks or drums above ground as far from the equipment as the auxiliary line allows (metal pipeline: about 25 ft from the set); keep the auxiliary fuel line as straight as possible. Security: follow the unit SOP. Fire/safety: mark the whole area NO SMOKING and OPEN FLAME; dig an open trench 4 ft wide and 6 in. deep around it to contain leaks, mound the earth around the trench, put crushed rock or sand in the trench to absorb spills; cover small spills immediately with dry sand or earth; prohibit trash burning within 200 ft; no electrical wires above or near tanks; direct hot exhaust away; bury or cover fuel lines from sun and damage; avoid rubber hose except temporary: clamp a light flexible copper wire to the end fittings, twist a ground wire around the hose, attach one grounding wire to the auxiliary tank and another to the generator set (static electricity builds in long non-conductive hose); fire point with shovel, pickax, extinguisher, and sand buckets if available. Contamination: storage at least 50 ft from work areas and equipment that doesn't use fuel and from heavily traveled roads but accessible to fuel trucks; leaks must flow away from equipment, work areas and housing; shelter or cover the fuel as needed. Maintain: match type and grade to specifications; never mix fuels; label each tank with type and grade; before changing grade or type, clean the tank thoroughly, drain old fuel, remove sediment and condensation; when draining an engine-mounted tank don't spill on engine parts (use a flexible hose from the petcock to the container)
entries.use: Setting up safe fuel storage for a field generator
entries.how: Long term: tanks underground. Short term: tanks/drums above ground ~25 ft from the set; 4-ft wide x 6-in. trench around the area; fuel storage at least 50 ft from work areas and roads
entries.dim: Trench 4 ft wide x 6 in. deep; metal pipeline tanks ~25 ft from set; no trash burning within 200 ft; storage 50 ft from work areas and roads
entries.eq: Ground wires, sand, fire extinguisher, shovel, pickax

entries.n: Do before-operation PMCS on a generator set
entries.desc: Refer to the set's manual for required PMCS. Check fuel lines for leaks, fuel level (refill), winterization heater leaks (some heaters use main-tank diesel), auxiliary tank levels; drain condensation and clean fuel filters before operating. Gas-turbine sets: inspect the plenum drain fitting (clear, no fuel accumulated), use only clean fuel, drain sediment from the filter into a small container and dispose, check fuel control valve positions. Coolant: check radiator level (allow room for expansion in a cold radiator); in cold weather add antifreeze per Table 10-1 (ethylene glycol compound, issued full strength and ready mixed; do not dilute with water; pints of inhibited glycol per gallon of coolant for lowest expected temperature: +20 F 1 3/4; +10 F 2; 0 F 2 3/4; -10 F 3 1/4; -20 F 3 3/4; -30 F 4; -40 F 4 1/4; arctic antifreeze preferred at -50 F and below; maximum protection at 68 percent by volume = 5.4 pints per gallon; test with an accurate hydrometer; fasten a tag near the radiator cap showing antifreeze type). Verify tools, TMs and basic issue items (auxiliary fuel hose, grounding rods and cables, fire extinguisher, paralleling cable, load-terminal wrench, grounding-wire clamps). Batteries: electrolyte about 3/8 in. above the plates; add distilled water as necessary; never from a metal container (TM 9-6140-200-14). Engine oil: check and add; lubricate per the lubrication order. Check the fuel tank, radiator, oil covers and oil pan and all lines for leaks. Instruments securely mounted, connected, undamaged; check gauges while operating. Inspect for cracks, breaks, loose or missing hardware; wires and terminals; gas-turbine air-inlet screen (remove obstructions); the changeover board (Figure 10-1) and phase selector switch for correct link connections/positioning for the desired voltage; set the frequency selector for the desired output on 50/60 cycle precise Class 1 sets; place the circuit breaker (main switch) OPEN (off); connect the output service cable to the load-panel terminals. Ensure the grounding connections and ground rod are tight with No. 6 AWG or larger wire
entries.use: Pre-start checks of fuel, coolant, oil, batteries, wiring, breaker and ground
entries.how: Circuit breaker open (off) before start; batteries 3/8 in. above plates, distilled water only, never from a metal container; ground with No. 6 AWG or larger wire
entries.dim: Battery electrolyte 3/8 in. above plates; antifreeze per Table 10-1; ground wire No. 6 AWG+
entries.wn: Never attempt to start a generator set with the circuit breaker closed (on): a power surge will damage the equipment

entries.n: Lay the distribution cable (overhead, buried, ground)
entries.desc: Distribution cable is supplied in predetermined lengths and sizes with quick-disconnect connector plugs, or as building wire in rolls. Overhead: utility poles are seldom available; use 6 x 6 in. wood long enough to be set rigidly with safe wire clearance; trees as last resort with proper weatherproof cable. Minimum height 20 ft for vehicle clearance over roads; space poles so quick-disconnect joints are supported by the pole (Figure 10-2); tie cable together with quick-disconnects; align the male and female plugs on multiphase cable to prevent a reverse-power condition (marks are countersunk circular or triangular depressions or raised buttons; each receptacle usually has one pin and one jack larger than the others, which represent the grounding (neutral) conductor; match large pin to large jack if unmarked; if marking in the field paint a color code on the receptacle). Underground: trench at least 18 in. deep; moistureproof cable only, on a cushion of sand (or loosen the trench base and remove rocks); moistureproof any quick-disconnect joints; separate cables uniformly with at least 6 in. between centers; cover with rock-free earth. On the ground: lay planks or logs on both sides of the cable so vehicles don't drive on it; where it has the least interference with operations; install warning signs; moistureproof cable that withstands weather. Connecting: direct line from the set when the load is few items with steady phase; a load-terminal board when there are many scattered loads with different phase and voltage requirements; always balance the load across phases. All AC sets have a load-terminal board (Figure 10-3) with four terminals L0, L1, L2, L3. When no single set is large enough, parallel two or more sets and distribute through a bus-bar distribution center (Figure 10-4), also used when widely scattered loads need two or more branch feeder lines. Before connecting: equipment securely mounted, supported and insulated; wire sized from Tables 8-7 and 8-8; fuse/trip element ratings adequate for overloads and shorts on branch feeders (circuit breaker contact points or fused-knife switch blades must carry the rated current and voltage); protect switch gear and bus bar with a weatherproof canopy. Typical layout (Figure 10-5): shielded cables connect loads in four central areas; shielding grounded at one end; three-conductor stranded copper cable; three-phase 120 to 208 V
entries.use: Running power cable from the generator to the load
entries.how: Overhead 20 ft over roads on 6x6 poles with quick-disconnects supported at poles; buried at least 18 in. deep on sand with 6 in. between cables; ground lay protected by planks or logs
entries.dim: Overhead clearance 20 ft over roads; trench >= 18 in.; cable centers >= 6 in.; poles 6x6 in
entries.eq: Planks or logs, warning signs, bus-bar center, load-terminal board
entries.wn: Equipment damaged by rain or snow can injure personnel who touch electrical distribution devices

entries.n: Operate a generator in cold, heat, dust, rain, salt or altitude
entries.desc: EXTREME COLD: sets start and run to -25 F without a winterization kit; colder needs preheating (blowtorch for most air-cooled engines; liquid-cooled engines usually have a winterization kit with preheater; see the set manual). Checks: antifreeze protects to the lowest expected temperature (Table 10-1); coolant at proper level; frequent leak checks; watch the water temperature gauge; shutters, controls, thermostats work; shutters and baffle rods on air-cooled systems positioned for cold weather; report uncorrectable faults. Electrical: batteries fully charged to avoid freezing; electrolyte daily, 3/8 in. above plates; keep batteries clean, free of ice, moisture, corrosion; connections clean, lightly greased, tight; vent holes open; inspect insulation for cracks, frays and breaks; tighten loose connections; disturb wiring as little as possible (insulation gets brittle). Water added to a battery may freeze unless immediately mixed by charging: do not add water unless the engine will run at least 1 hour. Fuel: keep the tank as full as possible to reduce condensation; right fuel grade for temperature; service filters more often; keep cap and filler neck free of ice and snow; drain contaminated fuel and sediment daily. Lubricate per cold-weather lubrication order; remove ice, snow and moisture before each run. Warm the set to operating temperature before applying load (some are damaged at low rpm). EXTREME HEAT: maximum ventilation; keep engine shrouds, cooling fins, generator blower cover and air passages clear; shutters and baffle rods in position; check coolant often with clean coolant; approved rust inhibitor and regular flush; no alkaline or salt water; radiator fins and screens clear; fan V-belt tension; if automatic shutter control fails operate shutter manually and report; electrolyte daily; check terminals for corrosion (heat swells and softens insulation; chafing is more frequent); ample air circulation in a shelter; ventilation screen and louvers clear; watch instruments for overload; don't fill the fuel tank completely (expansion); run without load to cool the engine before shutdown. DUSTY/SANDY: wind shield (natural barriers; windward side of dusty areas); clean frequently with approved solvent; wet the surrounding terrain when water is plentiful; keep generator free of grease and oil; blow dust from electrical components with low-pressure dry compressed air; check cooling system, radiator cap closed; drain and flush more often; keep lubricant containers sealed; service oil, oil filter and air cleaner more often; clean points before lubricating; inspect the fuel filter after each operating period and clean filters and strainers more often; check the air cleaner. RAINY/HUMID: keep doors and panels closed when not in use and open in dry weather; keep electrical equipment dry; inspect wiring; keep the area dry (use insulating materials around the set if damp); keep fuel tanks full; no water in the fuel; drain contaminated fuel. SALTWATER: never let electrical equipment contact salt water (if so, wash with fresh water and dry thoroughly); cover idle outdoor sets with canvas; salt-free coolant with approved rust inhibitor; paint exposed unpolished surfaces and coat polished steel/ferrous parts with rust-proofing or a light grease. HIGH ALTITUDE: sets are rated at sea level; rating may drop with altitude; see data plate and TM
entries.use: Weather and terrain PMCS for field generators
entries.how: Cold: preheat below -25 F, keep batteries charged and fuel tank full, warm up before loading. Heat: maximum ventilation and run unloaded before shutdown. Dust: shield and clean filters more often. Wet: keep the area dry and insulated
entries.dim: Operate to -25 F without kit; battery electrolyte 3/8 in
entries.eq: Approved rust inhibitor, low-pressure compressed air
entries.wn: Do not use salt water in the cooling system except in an emergency (damages equipment); keep the area dry; use insulating material around sets in damp conditions

entries.n: Reduce generator noise, heat and visibility in a combat area
entries.desc: Generator sets are noisy and hot, making it hard to avoid detection and to hear enemy activity (signature-suppressed sets are being studied). Noise comes from exhaust, air-intake cooling fan and vibrating metal. 0.5 to 10 kW: install in a revetment; connect an auxiliary exhaust line from the engine to the revetment chimney (Figure 10-6); an empty 55-gal drum can replace a sandbag chimney: punch holes in the bottom with area equal to or larger than the engine exhaust area, lay it on its side, and insert the auxiliary exhaust line into the large hole (Figure 10-7); use flexible or rigid metal pipe larger in diameter than the muffler outlet; reduce mechanical and fan noise by placing the set behind a barrier (hill, dense woods, large vehicle, plywood wall). 15 to 500 kW diesel, liquid-cooled: very loud at the radiator end (fan and exhaust, Figure 10-8); long-term units can build underground muffler systems (fan noise remains); put a barrier (van, plywood sheets, convex containers) in the noise path or use a natural barrier between the radiator and the direction needing quiet; do not restrict air flow out of the radiator. Visibility: camouflage equipment and revetments. Infrared: generators have a thermal signature detectable by infrared sensors; no way to eliminate it. Ice fog (exhaust at -25 F and below): put a tube on the exhaust pipes and cover it with a tarpaulin to diffuse the exhaust in the snow
entries.use: Concealing and quieting a generator set
entries.how: Small sets in a revetment with an auxiliary exhaust line to a sandbag or 55-gal drum chimney; large sets need a barrier at the radiator end; do not restrict air flow; infrared signature cannot be eliminated
entries.dim: 55-gal drum chimney: hole area >= exhaust area
entries.wn: 1) Do not overload a generator set: heavy loads produce excessive noise, dangerous sparks and hot exhaust gases. 2) Do not restrict air flow around the engine; an air-cooled engine in a confined space like a foxhole can overheat severely in hot weather

entries.n: Run a service drop to a building
entries.desc: All electrical energy to a building passes through service-entrance equipment where it is metered, protected and distributed to branch circuits; power from military generators or the local utility enters via overhead or underground lead-in conductors. Service wire from the pole to the building is usually two, three or four conductors on separate insulators at pole and building, or two- or three-conductor concentric service cable; use insulated conductors; if an overhead drop is impractical, run underground services from a transformer installation. Length: keep service drops under 100 ft for No. 8, 6, 4 or 2 wire; for No. 0 or larger do not exceed 75-ft spans unless properly anchored and supported; guy long or large services at the line pole. Size: No. 6 wire recommended for overhead service cable but size by maximum demand load of each building; Table 11-1 (copper AWG / aluminum or copper-clad AWG / ampere rating): 4/2/100 A; 3/1/110; 2/1/0/125; 1/2/0/150; 1/0 / 3/0 / 175; 2/0 / 4/0 / 200; 3/0 / 250 MCM / 225; 4/0 / 300 MCM / 250; 250 MCM / 350 MCM / 300; 350 / 500 / 350; 400 / 600 / 400 A. These calculations ignore motor-starting current, so check separately for objectionable flicker. Two-wire service limit: two circuits in general-service buildings and four circuits or a 3-kW connected load in barracks; three-wire services for greater loads; three- or four-wire service to supply more than one service switch. Attachment: attach where outlet wires can be tapped in without trailing along the building, at least 10 ft above ground or 18 ft above a roadway; if the building isn't high enough, use a riser or pole for clearance. Figure 11-1 shows a correct open-wire service installation; Figures 11-2 to 11-13 show insulator attachment for different constructions (wood siding, brick veneer, solid masonry, hollow tile, shingles, tension over 900 lb on wood); Figures 11-14 to 11-16 show attaching services to structures
entries.use: Bringing power from the pole to a building service entrance
entries.how: No. 6 recommended; drops under 100 ft for No. 8-2 (75 ft for No. 0+); attach at least 10 ft above ground or 18 ft above a roadway; two-wire service limited to 2 circuits (4 circuits / 3 kW in barracks)
entries.dim: Drop < 100 ft (No. 8, 6, 4, 2); <= 75 ft (No. 0+); attach >= 10 ft above ground or 18 ft above roadway
entries.src: TM 3-34.46 para 11-1 to 11-4; Table 11-1; Figures 11-1 to 11-16

entries.n: Inspect the pole and climbing gear before climbing
entries.desc: Inspect the pole before and during the climb for rake (lean), shell rot, cracks, breaks, knots, woodpecker holes and foreign attachments. Heart rot: sound the pole with a hammer (solid sound = safe). Butt rot on an old pole: dig about 6 inches at the base and drill a hole partway into the base; the shavings show rot; plug the hole afterward. Remove rocks and objects within 10 feet of the pole to reduce injury if you fall. Lineman's equipment has five main parts: climbers, body belt, safety strap, hard hat and leather gloves; inspect before climbing (chapter 13 and TM 9-243)
entries.use: Pre-climb check for rot, cracks and unsafe conditions
entries.how: Sound the pole with a hammer for heart rot; dig 6 in. and drill for butt rot; clear rocks within 10 ft; gear is climbers, body belt, safety strap, hard hat, leather gloves
entries.dim: Clear 10 ft around pole; dig 6 in. for butt-rot check
entries.eq: Hammer, drill, climbers, body belt, safety strap, hard hat, leather gloves

entries.n: Belt in and unbelt on a pole
entries.desc: Carry the safety strap correctly: a right-handed person carries it in the left D-ring with the double (looped) end snapped so the keeper faces outward nearest the body, and the single end and keeper face inward away from the body (prevents twisting); left-handed uses the right D-ring. Adjust the strap at the base: belted in with feet at equal height, place your elbow against your stomach and raise your fist to the pole; there should be 1 to 2 inches between fist and pole; with fingers extended, if they don't touch the pole the strap is too long. Belting in: both gaffs firmly set; right-handed: left leg low and locked, right leg about 6 in. above in a comfortable position; knees and hips away from the pole; unsnap the single end with the left hand while holding the pole with the right; pass it around the pole to the right hand; grasp the pole with the left hand and snap the keeper into the right D-ring; both keeper snaps face outward and the strap lies flat (Figure 12-1); then put weight on the strap. Left-handed reverses. Unbelting is the reverse: left leg low and locked, right 6 in. above; grasp the pole with the left hand and pull up the left leg keeping the right gaff angle; unsnap the hook from the right D-ring with the right hand; pass the strap to the left hand; grasp the pole with the right hand and snap the strap to the left D-ring
entries.use: Securing yourself at the work position
entries.how: Strap fit: with elbow against stomach, fist 1-2 in. from the pole and fingers touching; both snaps face outward; left leg low and locked (right-handed)
entries.dim: Fist-to-pole gap 1-2 in.; right leg ~6 in. above left
entries.wn: Always ensure the snaps are secured and properly engaged

entries.n: Ascend and descend a pole (gaff technique)
entries.desc: Ascending: climb the high side if possible; arms and body relaxed; hips, shoulders and knees a comfortable distance from the pole; steps about 8 to 10 inches; hands at about shoulder level on the pole (higher tempts you to pull up; do not overlap hands on the back side); aim gaffs at the heart of the pole with toes pointed up (Figure 12-2). Feet turned out and apart so the gaff, not the foot side, hits the pole; gaffs belong on adjacent quarter points (A and B, B and C, C and D, D and A) never opposite sides (D and B or A and C), horizontally about 4 to 6 inches apart (Figure 12-3). Coordination is opposite of walking: left foot up with left arm up. Weight shifts to the lower foot and the knee locks each step; adjust step length to avoid knots, nuts and holes; always look where you're going. Gaff comes above the point and drops back down into it at about a 30-degree angle (keep about 8 inches between knee and pole) = inverted-J method (Figure 12-4). Never sneak (ease up lightly setting gaffs) or slap (kick horizontally); set gaffs firmly; let legs do the work; don't pull up with the hands (Figure 12-5). Descending: reverse; keep the proper climbing position; look down between your feet; right hand with right foot and left with left; gaffs break out when you roll your knee to the outside with an outward and lowering movement; break out the upper gaff, keep it aimed at the heart, relax, straighten and lock the leg, then drop the gaff in with weight behind it; steps about twice as long as ascending but not excessive; don't coast or slide; last step to the ground 6 inches or less to avoid gaffing yourself (Figure 12-6)
entries.use: Climbing with climbers
entries.how: Short natural steps (8-10 in.), hands at shoulder level for balance only, gaffs aimed at the pole center set at about 30 degrees, never sneak or slap
entries.dim: Step 8-10 in. up; gaff spread 4-6 in.; gaff angle ~30 degrees; knee-pole ~8 in.; last step <= 6 in
entries.wn: If the gaffs are positioned on opposite sides of the pole they point away from the center and can cause you to cut out (fall)

entries.n: Hitchhike, circle and position on a pole; hoist tools
entries.desc: Hitchhiking: after belting in, move up or down without unbelting. Climb to the work height (for a crossarm work only to eye level with the lag screw on the crossarm brace, belt in, then hitchhike). Up: slide the strap up the pole by moving the hips slightly toward the pole and moving the strap with your hands; with the strap angled up, take one or two small steps (smaller than normal), locking the leg back; repeat. Down: slide the strap down slightly, hips in; belt falls naturally when pressure is removed; one or two small steps; use your weight to drive the gaff into the pole; unbelt before stepping off if close to the ground. Circling left: left foot about 6 in. lower than the right with left knee locked; right gaff close to left foot about 6 in. higher; shorten the left strap by rotating the hips slightly clockwise; step up on the right foot and lock the right knee (left gaff comes out and body swings left); keep the left knee locked and gaff aimed at the heart; swing the left foot 3 to 4 inches left, unlock the right knee and drop onto the left gaff; steps no more than 3 to 4 inches apart horizontally; repeat to stay at the same height; reverse to circle right. Work positions: to work to the right keep the right leg low and locked, lengthen the strap slightly to the right, twist slightly in the belt to face the work, all weight on the right foot; left reverses. Hoisting: tie items to a lineman's rope with a lineman's knot (Figure 12-7)
entries.use: Moving at the work position without unbelting
entries.how: Hitchhike: slide the strap, take one or two small steps; circle: left leg low and locked, 3-4 in. swings; hoist with a lineman's knot on a lineman's rope
entries.dim: Circle steps <= 3-4 in
entries.wn: Working in the incorrect position could cause back injuries

entries.desc: Reasons: electrical shock, heart attack, heat stroke, physical injury, equipment failure. Equipment on all line trucks: climbing gear (hooks, body belts, safety straps), a 1/2-inch rescue rope twice the height of the highest crossarm plus 10 feet, a knife, rubber protective equipment (if victim or pole is energized). Four steps: evaluate, protect yourself, climb to the rescue position, lower. Evaluate: call to the man; if no response or he seems dazed, go; time is critical; check whether the pole or crossarm is split, cracked or burning, whether the victim contacts a live conductor, whether rubber goods or hot sticks are needed; see the whole scene. Protect yourself: tools and rubber goods in good condition; hot-line tools ready; survey the pole for damaged conductors and equipment, fire, splits; do not take chances. Climb to the rescue position: slightly above the victim and to one side (Figure 12-8); clear hazards. Assess: conscious: first aid, tie off, lower, further first aid, call for help. Unconscious, breathing: try to revive; if not, tie off, lower, first aid, call for help. Unconscious, not breathing: tie off, lower, give first aid (mouth-to-mouth or CPR), call for help. Tie the rescue rope: position the line over the crossarm or structure (Figure 12-9) 2 to 3 ft from the pole; wrap the short end around the fall line twice, then around the victim's chest and tie three half hitches with the knot in front near one armpit and high on the chest. Lower: pull the slack out of the hand line; firm grip on the fall line with one hand; cut the victim's safety strap on the side opposite the desired swing with the other; control descent by tightening and loosening the two twists in the rope with one hand while guiding the victim past lower obstructions with the other
