entries.use: Rescuing a lineman who cannot get down (shock, heart attack, heat stroke, injury)
entries.how: Evaluate, protect yourself, climb to slightly above and to one side, tie rescue rope (two wraps on fall line, three half hitches at chest), cut the victim's strap, lower under control
entries.dim: Rescue rope 1/2 in. dia., length 2 x highest crossarm height + 10 ft; line 2-3 ft from pole
entries.eq: Rescue rope, knife, rubber protective equipment, hot-line tools
entries.wn: Do not accidentally cut your own safety strap when cutting the victim's safety strap

entries.n: Follow basic electrical shop safety rules
entries.desc: Keep the work area clear of grease, oil, water and debris (slip/trip hazards). Warn fellow workers who get into dangerous positions. Avoid horseplay and unnecessary conversation on duty. Clothing: no clothing with uncovered zippers or metal fasteners; sleeves rolled down; no loose flapping clothes or flammable items (celluloid visors); no thin-soled, heel-plated or hobnailed shoes (high-cut sewn-sole shoes preferred); suitable gloves and approved goggles or head shields when welding; leather gloves (linemen and groundmen); remove all jewelry (rings, metal wrist bands, watch chains); inspect personal gear (climbing gear, hard hats, rubber gloves) before use. Report unusual conditions that may affect continuity of service or endanger life or property to the installation engineer and take protective steps immediately. Fire prevention: don't block approaches to fire apparatus; flammable waste in self-closing waste cans, removed daily; flammable liquids in approved safety cans with self-closing covers, no more than 1 gallon per can inside a building; never use flammable liquids to start a fire in a salamander or rubbish pile; no gasoline as a cleaner (low-hazard, preferably nonflammable solvent); no gasoline furnace or blowtorch where flammable vapors are present; train all personnel on extinguishers: Class A (paper, wood, textiles): water-type; Class B (oil, gasoline): foam, carbon-tetrachloride or carbon-dioxide, dry compound, or sand; Class C (electrical equipment): carbon-tetrachloride or carbon-dioxide; notify the fire department when an extinguisher is used so it is recharged or replaced. First aid (FM 21-11): stocked first-aid kits in the shop and each truck; treat minor cuts, get medical attention for serious ones; report all accidents to the foreman; train everyone in prone-pressure and pole-top artificial respiration with monthly practice by every member of the electrical section
entries.use: Daily working practices, clothing, fire prevention, first aid
entries.how: No exposed metal fasteners or jewelry, sleeves down, remove rings and watches; no more than 1 gal of flammables in a safety can inside; know extinguisher classes A, B, C
entries.dim: Max 1 gal flammable per safety can indoors
entries.wn: When using a carbon-tetrachloride or carbon-dioxide extinguisher (especially in unventilated spaces) try not to breathe the vapors or gases

entries.n: Tag out and switch circuits safely
entries.desc: Wire stripping: direct the cutting force away from your body and others. Soldering: keep furnaces away from manhole openings; never put a cold or wet ladle or object in molten solder or hot compound (spatter); attach the pot with a hook and steady line when hoisting molten solder/compound, people clear below; work from above or the side; wear goggles for large joints and when tinning lugs or T connectors. Circuit testing: never modify or repair an existing circuit until tested (chapter 14); do not test with fingers or any tool but a test lamp or voltmeter. Switching and tagging: the installation engineer must notify the serving utility's system operator before any switching that may affect its system; the electrical foreman does switching with great care and ensures each worker knows exactly which equipment is energized. When any line, feeder circuit or apparatus is taken out of service, put a tag on all main or control switches; the equipment stays de-energized until released by the person who removed it from service. The tag must say: DANGER. Do not remove this tag or energize the circuit; the name of the individual who removed the item from service; and the date and hour (Figure 13-1; purchased or made from a manila folder). When work is complete the person who installed the tag removes it and restores service. Tools: keep in good condition and replace if broken; never use malfunctioning equipment; periodically check handle fit, keep handles tight and insulated when possible; keep cutting tools sharp; cover bench surfaces and floor with rubber insulation
entries.use: Lockout/tagout, switching, soldering and circuit testing precautions
entries.how: Tag every main or control switch with DANGER, name, date and hour; only the person who tagged it removes it; test circuits only with a test lamp or voltmeter

entries.n: Use hand tools, goggles, scaffolds and ladders safely
entries.desc: Hand tools: insulated handles are an extra precaution only; select the right tool (no makeshift); sharp keen-edge tools stored properly; skinning knives without sharp points and shanks not through the handle; anchor work when using a draw knife; sharp pipe-wrench jaws; right-size wrench, adjustable wrench jaws facing the direction of pull; don't hammer highly tempered tools (drills, files); tape plier handles (ends) to avoid dropping; never use tools with cracked or broken handles or heads; never use a wrench on a running motor; never use a tool such that you could be injured if it slips; flashlights in basements, vaults and manholes; never carry open flames there. Goggles: wash before another person wears them; required when tinning/soldering lugs or large joints; chipping, breaking or drilling concrete, brick or stone; tree trimming; installing or removing fuses or jumpers from live distribution busses (approved colored lenses); electric arc welding (ASA-approved electric arc goggles; acetylene goggles can't be used). Scaffolds: for large or complex inaccessible installations use scaffolds rather than ladders; sturdy, securely anchored, cross-braced; planking free of knots, checks and cross-grain; load-test planks periodically up to three times the working load. Ladders: good condition, safely constructed, unpainted; anchor with rope or chain or against a projection, or have an assistant at the base; foot-to-wall distance approximately one-quarter the ladder length; inspect often; remove dirt that could hide defects; use a safety strap when both hands are needed (Figure 13-2); not in strong wind; not as a guy, brace, skid or scaffold member; never metal ladders on electrical work; no cleat-on-single-rail makeshift ladders; approved anti-slip devices; with traffic nearby a partner at the bottom with a red flag (day) or light (night); don't reach out; move the ladder. Placing: never on slanting or slippery footing unless tied or held; stepladders fully open; extension ladders standing with hooks caught on rungs; ladder jacks not above the third rung from the top of a 24- or 36-ft extension ladder or the fourth rung of a 46-ft. Use: face the ladder; one person at a time; free use of both hands; no higher than the third rung from the top on straight/extension ladders or the second on stepladders; never slide down
entries.use: Tool selection, eye protection, elevated work
entries.how: Insulated handles are not full shock protection; goggles for soldering, chipping masonry and live bus work; ladder foot at one-quarter its length from the wall; never a metal ladder near electrical equipment
entries.dim: Ladder base distance = 1/4 ladder length; planks tested to 3 x working load

entries.n: Handle tools, materials and rope safely on exterior work
entries.desc: Work area: don't throw tools or materials between levels (hand lines, canvas bags or buckets); stand clear of raised/lowered loads; keep tools and materials from touching wires; avoid working at the base of a structure or pole that others are working on, except in an emergency. Materials: pick up insulators by the top (the petticoat can cut gloves); don't screw insulators down too tight (the top may break off); lift heavy material with bent knees and straight back, use mechanical devices or enough help; use ropes or tackle on inclines and keep workers off the downhill side; use approved hoisting apparatus, rope off areas under the load, display warning signs and guard the area; lash transformers and oil drums to prevent sliding or tipping. Rope: free of metal strands near live conductors; replace frayed rope; keep clean (solder particles cut hands and rubber gloves); hands at a safe distance from a rope passing through a block; no tape, string or marlin to repair defects; never loop rope over hand or arm; never leave uncoiled wire, rope or material unguarded on streets/roadways/alleys; never hang safety lines, ropes or wires from a pole. Vehicles: never hang coils of wire or rope outside a truck; danger flag (day) or red lantern (night) on materials extending 4 ft or more behind a truck; red lantern or taillight on towed equipment at night
entries.use: Lifting, hoisting and rope care at the job site
entries.how: Never throw tools up or down: use hand lines and canvas bags; no rope with metal strands near live conductors; keep all but the lift crew out from under loads
entries.dim: Flag loads extending 4 ft or more behind truck
entries.eq: Hand line, canvas bag, danger flag, red lantern

entries.n: Inspect body belts, safety straps, climbers and gaffs
entries.desc: The foreman inspects all body belts and safety straps during regular tool inspections; repair or replace at once if: leather is worn or crushed (D-ring loops not worn enough to weaken; straps usable to not less than 1/8 in. thick except in the doubled part); hard and dry; burnt (dry outside, cracks when bent, small pieces come off with a fingernail); cracks, cuts, nicks or tears (especially across or at edges); loose or broken rivets (D-ring loops); broken plier pouch; broken or defective buckle or snaps; broken or badly worn steel-reinforcing strap; torn or oversized buckle hole (tongue must work freely without side play and close securely under spring tension); grain worn so fibers or red stitching show (cut up and discard). See TM 9-243. Gaffs: never sharpen on the underside except to make the shoulder (changes the angle); keep the underside straight when removing metal for the shoulder; don't use a grindstone or emery wheel; put the climber in a vise gaff up (Figure 13-4); sharpen the two outer surfaces with a file using long strokes from heel to point, removing only enough for a good point; never needlepoint; leave a shoulder about 1/8 inch back from the point; distance across the gaff at the shoulder about 5/32 inch. Climbers: do not use after gaffs are worn shorter than 1 1/4 inches on the underside; remove climbers when moving job to job, working on the ground, working on a ladder, standing on a rubber blanket, or riding in a vehicle
entries.use: Deciding whether climbing equipment is safe to use
entries.how: Replace belts/straps with worn, hard, burnt, cracked or torn leather, loose rivets or defective buckles/snaps; do not use climbers when gaffs are worn shorter than 1 1/4 in
entries.dim: Strap leather >= 1/8 in.; gaff min length 1 1/4 in.; shoulder 1/8 in. back from point; width at shoulder ~5/32 in

entries.n: Inspect, use and care for rubber protective equipment
entries.desc: Inspection: before work on or near live conductors/equipment between 300 and 5,000 V each worker personally tests rubber gloves and visually inspects for holes and thin spots; tag and turn in suspect gear immediately; semiannual electrical test of gloves, annual for other rubber protective equipment (arranged with the serving utility). Use: wear rubber gloves on or within reach of energized conductors/equipment at 300-5,000 V; leather protector gloves over rubber ones; use approved live-line tools without rubber gloves above 5,000 V; wear rubber gloves while cutting supposedly dead cables and testing supposedly burned-out transformers on both primary and secondary; don't remove them until entirely out of reach of energized equipment; don't work with the gauntlet rolled down; wear them when tending reels while wire is strung or removed near other wires energized 300-5,000 V and when working near someone near such conductors; raise or lower in a canvas tool bag or bucket with a hand line (Figure 13-3). Care: gloves issued to each lineman as personal items; store in a canvas bag; air test each day and after any event that may damage them; wash with warm water and mild detergent; don't work over energized conductors while applying/removing; dry before storing (or dry soon after); do not carry in truck compartments or tool bags with tools; roll (never fold) rubber blankets; lay hoods and hoses flat in truck compartments
entries.use: Rubber gloves, blankets, hoods, hose for work near 300-5,000 V
entries.how: Visually inspect and air-test gloves daily; wear leather protectors over rubber gloves; electrical tests semiannually (gloves) and annually (other items); store in a canvas bag, roll blankets
entries.dim: Gloves: semiannual electrical test; other rubber goods annual; 300-5,000 V range
entries.eq: Rubber gloves, leather protectors, canvas bag

entries.n: Observe hot-line tool, pole and excavation safety rules
entries.desc: Hot-line tools: no hot-line work when rain or snow threatens or with heavy dew, fog or excess moisture (exceptions: switching, fusing, clearing damaged equipment hazardous to public/troops); if weather turns, finish quickly to allow safe temporary operation; foreman judges conditions; do it in daylight if possible (artificial light OK if conductors and equipment are clearly visible); do not wear rubber gloves with hot-line tools (hides brush discharges); avoid holding outer braces or metal attachments; avoid unnecessary conversation; cooperate; treat wooden pole structures like steel towers (don't rely on wood insulation); cover distribution primaries on the same pole as high-tension lines with rubber protective gear before climbing or working above; look around and inform others before changing position; never use hands to hold a live line clear of a lineman—secure it with live-line tools and lock in a clamp; stay below the live wire when moving it; special care on poles with guy lines; no rope on conductors above 5,000 V unless isolated by an insulated tension link stick. Excavation: barriers, red flags and warning signs (red lights/flares at night) near highways; signs 100 to 300 feet from the outside edge of the work area; shoring and bracing per EM 385-1-1; MEN AT WORK sign for brief manhole openings; report obstructions found while digging. Manholes: gas check before opening if possible; remove covers with cover hooks; don't enter until a gas check (mine safety lamp or chemical detector, several times a day; careful near gasoline tanks); ventilate with a power blower if gas exists; only gasproof lights if explosive gas is suspected; someone with a red flag or lantern to warn traffic (day) and mark open manholes at night (Figure 13-5); ensure the safety of workers who can't be seen from the surface. Potheads: open the neutral pothead last and close it first; don't stand on concrete or ground when operating potheads in manholes or vaults (insulated stool, crossarm or dry lumber); cover grounded framework; keep clear of grounded equipment. Poles: warn nearby persons when moving a pole (flagman); report poles that look unsafe for climbing (untreated pine deteriorates quickly); don't remove wires or guy lines until the butt condition is checked; support unsound poles with pike poles or guys before digging or removing wires; clear equipment around a pole before removing it; climb by the safest path; don't use pins, braces or guys as handholds; never carry tools or material in your hands while climbing; repair rusted hardware, defective guys, braces and arms immediately; when two people climb, the first reaches working position or ground before the second moves. Climbing: avoid damaging another worker's safety strap with gaffs when passing; don't let the strap catch on pole steps; when not in the working position snap both strap ends in the same D-ring; never both snaps in one D-ring in working position (one in each D-ring); avoid pressure on the tongue snap when leaning against arms, pins, braces and wires
entries.use: Working on live lines, in manholes and around poles
entries.how: No hot-line work in rain, snow, fog or heavy dew (except emergencies); do not wear rubber gloves with hot-line tools; gas-check manholes before entering; keep signs 100-300 ft from excavations
entries.dim: Signs 100-300 ft from work area
entries.eq: Cover hooks, power blower, gas detector, flags

entries.n: Observe electrical safety by voltage level (low, intermediate, high)
entries.desc: LOW (300 V or less): work on energized conductors only if all adjacent energized or grounded conductors and equipment are covered with insulating material or approved rubber protective equipment; tape or cover all bare places on one conductor before exposing another; open switches and remove fuses when working on building wiring, motors, belting, shafting, blowers and machinery, and attach hold cards; don't touch steam or water pipes when handling portable tools or light cords; never leave joints or loose ends untaped; never turn on current in a building after a fire until the fire department or a safety inspector has inspected (heat/water/extinguisher fluid damage may short and rekindle). INTERMEDIATE (300-5,000 V): de-energize ground lines and equipment before work (exception: overhead lines, wearing rubber gloves); work on energized lines except in emergency only by work order. Consider conductors in this range energized until positively proven otherwise; if no visual proof use an approved voltage detector, first checking it on a known energized conductor, then rechecking on a known live conductor after testing a dead one (or use two detectors as a cross-check). Within reach of energized/grounded parts cover with rubber line hose, insulator hoods, line protectors (pigs) or blankets, or isolate with barriers; re-cover when you change position. Precautions: de-energize by opening sectionalizing switches and ground the section; treat line wires being installed on poles already carrying energized conductors as energized, pull with rope; remove wire from the underside of reels; ground the truck when using a pay-out reel near energized wires; the reel tender wears rubber gloves and stands on dry lumber or insulating material; brake the reel rim opposite the pull direction (a crossarm or sidearm may brake); hold loose ends of jumpers clear; keep tie wire coiled; test for voltage before removing a primary or secondary wire and have the foreman recheck; treat spans to be removed as energized, rope each end and lower one at a time; make all possible connections to dead wires with only the final connection to the energized conductor; never open the ground connection at a ground pipe or bus bar unless first disconnected at the equipment; make the ground pipe connection first when connecting a ground wire on a pole; treat coil wires in a take-up reel as energized (rope on far end; rubber gloves); the person in charge ensures correct phase rotation when restoring three-phase service; identify cable in the manhole against the working print and exploring coil before cutting; remove a 3-in. strip of lead and test with two voltage detectors at two or more points and at the center of the insulation; place a hacksaw on the cable insulation touching the grounded lead sheet when cutting; open the switch before working on an oil circuit breaker with a bus feed switch; treat series circuits and devices as energized unless opened by disconnects; never open a series circuit at the work point—bridge it with a jumper. HIGH (5,000 V or more): de-energize and ground before work, except overhead lines worked with live-line tools, energized lines only on an authorized work order (except emergency); work on only one conductor at a time with live-line tools; keep tools dry and clean (dry and test after damp weather); protect tools on trucks (waterproof canvas bags, padded hooks or bins); keep minimum body clearance (Table 13-1: 5 to 7.5 kV 1 ft; 7.5 to 12 kV 2 ft; 12 to 33 kV 3 ft; 33 to 66 kV 4 ft; 66 to 132 kV 5 ft; 132 to 220 kV 8 ft); work on de-energized circuits between two sets of grounds (first pole toward source and pole nearest load); feel out a supposedly dead circuit for static discharge with a switch pole before grounding; net off energized substation equipment and install barriers/signs; remove substation apparatus from service for cleaning/repair and place hold cards (red light if hard to see); don't work on any apparatus until the foreman has proved it dead; don't touch reactors unless disconnected from all live lines and grounded; don't raise, move or lower cables energized up to 12 kV more than 18 in.; do not move cables over 12 kV; discharge electrolytic and oxide-film lightning arresters by grounding and shorting the horn gaps before touching
entries.use: Working on or near energized conductors
entries.how: 300 V or less: cover adjacent conductors; 300-5,000 V: de-energize and ground, rubber goods; 5,000 V+: de-energized and grounded except live-line work on overhead lines, with Table 13-1 clearances
entries.dim: Table 13-1 min clearance: 5-7.5 kV 1 ft; 7.5-12 kV 2 ft; 12-33 kV 3 ft; 33-66 kV 4 ft; 66-132 kV 5 ft; 132-220 kV 8 ft
entries.eq: Voltage detectors, line hose, blankets, hold cards

entries.n: Work on de-energized or hot circuits and protect with fuses
entries.desc: De-energized: do all installation work dead if possible; most electricians pull the main service-entrance switch, remove the fuses, and tag the switch with name, date and time; if not possible, remove the branch fuses or trip the branch breaker to OFF. Hot circuits are not recommended except in emergencies, by experienced, cautioned personnel only. AC voltages as low as 67 V and DC as low as 110 V have caused death by electrocution. Procedures: insulate yourself so your body is not a conductor path; work on only one side of the circuit at a time; insulating gloves at all times, stand on nonconducting material; keep equipment, tools and clothing dry. Protection: fuses/breakers protect against overload and short circuit; choose ampere rating at the maximum allowable for the smallest conductor or equipment in the circuit; e.g., a device with a 15-A fusible rating on a circuit of No. 12 (20 A) gets 15 A fusing. Tables B-12 and B-13 give motor current requirements. Overload: frequently blown fuses or tripped breakers mean short circuit, ground or overload; do not install larger fuses (fire risk); find the cause and rewire overloaded circuits with larger wire or divide the load into more circuits. Bypassed: do not use jumpers to bypass fuses or remove circuit-breaker protection
entries.use: Normal procedure to isolate a circuit; hot-line emergency rules; fuse sizing
entries.how: Pull the main switch, remove fuses and tag it; AC as low as 67 V and DC as low as 110 V have killed; fuse to the smallest conductor or device rating; never up-size fuses or bypass protection
entries.dim: AC death at 67 V, DC at 110 V; fuse to smallest conductor/device

entries.n: Work safely on transformers and switchgear
entries.desc: Oil-filled transformers: keep moisture out when removing covers; keep tools, bolts and nuts from dropping in (tie with twine; empty pockets of knives, keys, watches); wipe oil from covers, floor and scaffold. Blow gaseous vapor out of large transformer cases with an air blower before working; if you feel gas effects, sound the alarm and get to fresh air. Stay away from the base of the pole while transformers are raised or lowered; work above or well clear while transformers are raised or supported with blocks. Ground the secondary before energizing (except as part of an ungrounded delta bank). Test the secondary voltage of each transformer before connecting to secondary mains; on three-transformer Y-delta banks bring in the primary neutral and keep it connected until secondary connections are complete. Taking a paralleled transformer out of service: disconnect secondary-phase leads before opening primary cutouts; don't disconnect secondary neutral or ground until the primary cutouts are open. Don't stand on energized transformers unless absolutely necessary, with foreman permission, a rubber blanket protected with a rubbish bag over the cover, and no climbers. Treat the grounded case of a connected transformer as a grounded conductor and an ungrounded case as energized. Oil circuit breaker: make sure it cannot open or close automatically and is open or blocked; de-energize metal-clad switching equipment before working. Regulators: off automatic and in neutral before switching a regulated feeder; don't break the charging current of a regulator or large substation transformer by opening disconnect switches (dangerous arc; use oil- or air-brake switches unless authorized otherwise); operate outdoor disconnects only with the disconnect pole; confirm all contacts are actually open with safe clearance on all three phases each time an air-brake switch opens (don't trust the handle); no switch operation without authority and thorough familiarity; remove potential-transformer fuses with wooden tongs, wearing rubber gloves and leather overgloves; never open disconnect switches under load—open the series oil circuit breaker first, open disconnects slowly and reclose immediately if an arc is drawn. Wire markers are only a guide: check each conductor with a test lamp or voltmeter before working
entries.use: Transformer, oil circuit breaker, disconnect and regulator precautions
entries.how: Tie tools with twine, test secondary voltage before connecting, ground the secondary (except ungrounded delta), open breakers before disconnect switches, use the disconnect pole, never trust the handle position
entries.eq: Twine, wooden tongs, disconnect pole, air blower

entries.desc: Shock results from equipment failure, human failure, or a combination; human failure is prevalent: failing to observe precautions (not testing that equipment is de-energized; careless contact with known energized equipment), making unauthorized modifications or using unauthorized equipment, failing to adequately repair equipment that has already caused non-fatal shocks, and failing to test insulation resistance and the ground connection after repair. Safety codes require every 120-V circuit to have a grounding system; it does nothing in normal operation but protects in a malfunction. Grounding keeps all metal parts you might touch at zero volts by connecting them directly to earth. Example: a metal pull-chain light fixture whose hot wire comes loose and touches the metal canopy is hot; touching the chain or fixture makes you the path to ground and you are shocked. The same can happen with power tools and appliances with metal housings, metal switch, junction and outlet boxes and metal faceplates. A grounding wire from the neutral bus bar to the fixture's metal housing gives an auxiliary path, carries the fault current back to the distribution center and ensures the fuse or breaker opens and shuts off current
entries.use: Why shocks happen and why 120-V circuits need a ground
entries.how: Shock comes from failing to test, unauthorized modification, unrepaired equipment and untested insulation/ground after repair; a ground wire carries fault current so the fuse or breaker opens

entries.n: Do preventive maintenance on a wiring system
entries.desc: Maintenance is routine periodic inspection, cleaning, testing, tightening, adjusting and lubricating, in that order, with duties delegated to specific personnel. Insulation: include periodic tests and checks; tape, repair or replace frayed wire and damaged protective devices; maintain and replace field-installed shielding (antishort bushings, damage protection); inspect conductors and supports routinely and replace damaged parts immediately. Loose fittings: periodically spot-check conduit couplings, connectors and box-entry devices for looseness or separation; tighten or reclamp. Capacitors: a static capacitor stays charged after disconnection; do not inspect or work on it until fully discharged. Wait 5 minutes after the circuit is opened before short-circuiting the capacitor terminals (lets the discharge device drain most residual charge), then short between terminals and stay clear of the discharge arc. Conductor connections: check solder splices, wire taps and terminal connections; loose, partly contacting or partly broken connections can cause short circuits, arcing and burning, radio interference, rapid oxidation, or a dangerous short against grounded metal; the added resistance increases voltage drop (inefficient operation) and heat that can start a fire. Devices: inspect all operating devices for defects, normal operation and operation under rated load; replace or repair those that fail, are broken or loose in mountings; if breakage repeats in a location replace with more durable devices or relocate outlets and switches. Housekeeping: rotating equipment is rated in degrees above ambient (e.g., rated 30 F above ambient in an 80 F area = 110 F maximum); keep clean and dry because dust and moisture insulate and keep heat in; poor housekeeping raises short-circuit risk. Lighting: dirt on reflectors, lamps, walls and ceilings cuts light (planned drop 10-15 percent; neglect can cut output 50 percent); clean fixtures and lamps at least every 3 months, more often if dirty. Storage: store electrical materials and tools on shelves, racks or cabinets to avoid insulation damage. Tools: keep in good operating condition. Lubrication: follow lubrication orders; do not overlubricate (overheating, leakage, grease deteriorates insulation, collects dust). Pole-line hardware: salvage surplus hardware; discard hardware weakened by corrosion; replace a bolt when the head is rusted over (worst corrosion is hidden)
entries.use: Periodic checks of insulation, fittings, capacitors, connections and devices
entries.how: Order of maintenance: inspect, clean, test, tighten, adjust, lubricate. Discharge capacitors: wait 5 minutes, then short the terminals and stay clear of the arc
entries.dim: Cleaning interval: lamps and fixtures every 3 months
entries.wn: Wait 5 minutes after opening the circuit before short-circuiting capacitor terminals; stay clear of the discharge arc

entries.n: Test circuits for shorts, grounds and opens
entries.desc: Even after pulling the main switch, removing a fuse or tripping a local switch, recheck with a test lamp or voltmeter before work. The test lamp voltage rating should be twice the estimated circuit voltage (or a series of lamps each at the estimated voltage); touch the prods to hot and neutral at the fuse, breaker panel, device or box. Short circuit: two bare conductors of different potential touching (damaged insulation, a staple through the cable, wrong wiring); contact with a metal part such as a motor frame or conduit is a ground. Types: solid (full voltage across the terminals of a blown fuse with the load disconnected; very low resistance and high current, fuse/breaker trips immediately); partial (resistance lowered but still too high to blow the fuse; dim lights while others are normal); floating (varying resistance; repeated phase-side fuse blows while tests show no defect; trouble may reappear after days). Open circuits: usually an incorrect, loose or missing connection at a box; spotted after devices are installed and power is on; check conduit bonding continuity if conduit will be covered (touch the neutral wire and the box to the tester ends; light/bell on = OK). When: test at rough-in with splices made so the circuit is continuous to the last box; retest after walls, ceilings and floors are in (a nail may have penetrated). Continuity testers: purchased (battery and light, or buzzer or bell) or homemade (doorbell and a 6-V dry cell; connect one battery terminal to one bell terminal, a 2-ft wire to the other bell terminal; touching the wire to the free battery terminal should ring the bell) (Figure 14-1). Example (new light fixture): no bulb in the fixture; tester between the breaker end of the hot wire and ground; clip on the neutral bus bar, touch the probe to the hot wire end; switch on and off—no light/ring means no short; put the bulb in and repeat—tester on with switch on and off with switch off = circuit working; then connect the hot wire to the breaker terminal and energize; a continuity tester also tests cartridge fuses. How: first visually check, starting at the distribution center and tracing each circuit. Shorts: temporarily join the hot wires at each switch to simulate ON; at the service panel clip to the neutral bus bar and touch each circuit's hot wire in turn—should be open (no light/ring); at a subpanel run the test twice: clip on neutral bus bar (hot/neutral) then on the grounding-wire terminal (fault-current circuits). Finding a short: make sure free-device wires at each box aren't touching each other or the metal box; if not found or already covered, undo splices at the next-to-last box and retest at the distribution center, moving toward the source each time until the circuit tests open; the short is between that box and the previous one. Cause: most shorts are in flexible cords, plugs or appliances; look for black smudge marks on faceplates or frayed or charred cords on a dead circuit; replace the damaged cord or plug before installing a new fuse or resetting the breaker (Figure 14-2)
entries.use: Verifying a circuit before energizing and finding a short
entries.how: Re-check any 'dead' circuit with a test lamp rated at twice the circuit voltage; use a continuity tester only with the breaker off; test at rough-in and after walls are closed
entries.dim: Test lamp rating = 2 x estimated circuit voltage; homemade tester 6-V dry cell + doorbell + 2-ft wire
entries.wn: Turn off the breaker or pull the fuse before using a continuity tester

entries.n: Troubleshoot a generator set (engine and electrical faults)
entries.desc: Table 14-1 symptom / probable cause / solution (selected): Engine hard to start or fails: tank empty (fill); fuel filters clogged (replace); fuel-pump screen clogged (clean); foreign material in fuel (drain, refill with clean fuel); air cleaner clogged (clean/replace element); overspeed switch tripped (reset); battery circuit fuze blown (replace); batteries discharged (charge/replace). Engine stops suddenly: empty tank, clogged filters/screen/auxiliary fuel hose (clean); safety device tripped (inspect oil and coolant levels, reset overspeed switch, operate at proper speed); low oil (add); low coolant (add); overheating (ventilate); cooling system clogged (flush); fan-drive V-belt inoperative (tighten); shutter control inoperative (operate shutter manually, report). Low oil pressure: adjust pressure, add oil, replace filter, change diluted oil. Excessive exhaust smoke: insufficient warm-up (warm up before load); defective shutter (operate manually, report); oil too high (drain to level); air cleaner clogged; wrong fuel grade (drain, correct grade). Lacks power: air cleaner, fuel filters, water in fuel, pump screen, wrong fuel grade. Knocks/noisy: low oil (add); stop the engine immediately if it knocks at proper oil level—report to organizational maintenance. Starter fails to crank: blown fuze (replace), tripped breaker (reset), loose/corroded cables (tighten/clean), discharged batteries. Generator fails to build voltage: frequency/voltage too low (adjust), defective wiring (report). Voltage too high: adjust voltage/frequency. Generator overheats: ventilation doors closed (open), screens obstructed (remove), overloaded (reduce load). Main breaker keeps tripping: output voltage too low (increase), defective wiring (report), overloaded (reduce load or report). Frequency drops after load increase: speed droop wrong (adjust). Frequency fluctuates: air cleaner, fuel filters, air in fuel system (prime), governor (report). Main generator noisy: object in screen (remove); stop immediately for unusual noises (part failure). Instruments: adjust controls per manual; stuck needle: tap gauge lightly. Winterization heater won't ignite: blown fuze, dirty fuel-pump screen/filters, empty main tank. 120-V AC receptacle dead: replace fuze or reset breaker; 24-V DC receptacle dead: replace fuze. Fluorescent lamp: won't light (burned-out tube, tube installed wrong, fuze/breaker, burned-out starter, dirty tube (rapid-start), broken holder, fixture too cold—raise to at least 50 F, oxide on pins—rotate tube once or twice); flickers (poor tube contact, wrong install, worn tube, oxide buildup, too cold); discolored ends (nearly worn out tube; defective starter; temperamental tube: turn end for end; darkened bands about 2 in. from the ends are normal; new tubes may flicker briefly); ends glow but center not (defective starter or ballast); fixture hums (ballast installed wrong, wrong type, or defective). If the suggested solution fails, report to the next higher level of maintenance
entries.use: Using symptom, cause, fix tables for hard starting, stalling, overheating, tripping breakers and lamps
entries.how: Hard start: check fuel level, filters, pump screen, air cleaner, overspeed switch, battery fuze/charge; engine knocks with correct oil: stop and report; unusual generator noise: stop and report
entries.dim: Fluorescent fixtures need at least 50 F
entries.wn: Stop the engine immediately if it knocks at proper oil level; stop the generator immediately for unusual noises (part failure) and report

entries.n: Perform generator PMCS and load-bank testing
entries.desc: Perform regular PMCS (Table 14-2); operators identify and write down all faults and shortcomings and stop operating immediately if a deficiency could endanger personnel or damage equipment; operators repair most faults; otherwise record the problem or defective part numbers on DA Form 2404 and submit it to organizational maintenance (DA Pamphlet 738-750). Table 14-2 items: lubrication system (crankcase leaks and oil level; breather; oil filter hardware, oil lines, service per lubrication order); cooling system (radiator, grille, shutter leaks/mounting/obstructions; lines and connections; hoses; record antifreeze freezing point; drain, flush and refill if contaminated; manual shutter control; water pump, fan and guard; fan-drive V-belt wear, alignment and tension; thermostat housing cracks); fuel system (pump, primary/secondary filters, enough clean fuel for the planned period, tank leaks/sediment/cap/strainer/gasket, lines and fittings); electrical system (batteries cracks, leaks, dirt, corroded cables, electrolyte level; generator/starter commutator and brushes; lights, wiring, switches; regulator; gauges, meters; fault-indicator panel lights; rheostats; speed-control governor; main generator, blow out dust with low-pressure dry air; control-panel meters). Testing: test before operation, periodically during operation and after repair/replacement; keeping the load on reduces carbon buildup in the engine. Test with the equipment it powers or with a load bank (preferred: operator sets and controls the load; use for sets that often run with little or no load). A load bank is a self-contained cabinet unit that generates no power, operates through the system being tested, connects with cables, may be automatic or manual to hold a minimum load; load tests add increments of resistive or reactive load to simulate any load in its rating (single-phase 2-wire 120/240 V; 3-phase 3-wire 240 V; 3-phase 4-wire 120/208 or 240/416 V) at 50 to 1,000 cycles per second. Fluorescent lamp repair: tubes—double-pin: twist a quarter turn and pull out; install by pushing into holders and twisting a quarter turn; single-pin: push against the spring-loaded holder until the other end comes out; starters—remove the tube, twist a quarter turn counterclockwise, pull; new starter in, quarter turn clockwise; tube holders—take the old one to buy a matching one; disconnect wires (loosen terminal screws; push-in connectors: insert a small screwdriver or nail in the slot next to the wire), remove mounting screw (may need to take off the end bracket), reverse to install; ballasts—shut off all current, disassemble to the ballast (table lamp: in the base; ceiling/wall: in the metal enclosure); a replacement ballast is pre-wired with about 5 in. of each wire; cut the old ballast wires about 5 in. from the ballast, remove screws, mount the new one, strip 1/2 in. of insulation from each wire, use a medium wire nut for every two wires, match colors (red to red, blue to blue) and check the diagram printed on the ballast
entries.use: Scheduled checks and testing a set under load
entries.how: Write down every fault on DA Form 2404; a load bank is preferred for testing and keeps sets from running with little or no load; never use water on an electrical fire—use carbon dioxide
entries.dim: Strip ballast leads 1/2 in.; cut old leads 5 in. from ballast
entries.wn: Store and use the load bank upright only, never upside down or on end; ground the frame; turn the load bank off for excessive vibration or unusual noise; shut down the power source before touching or connecting leads; disconnect at once if the motor or components overheat; NEVER use water on an electrical fire—ALWAYS use carbon dioxide

entries.desc: Engineering capabilities and activities that directly support maneuver of land combat forces requiring close, integrated support. Enhances friendly mobility and denies enemy mobility by shaping the physical environment
entries.use: Close support to maneuver of land combat forces; only discipline trained and equipped to support movement and maneuver in close combat
entries.how: Combat engineers mainly do mobility, countermobility and survivability (M/CM/S); with tools/training they can also do some general engineering (e.g., improve culverts and fords, repair command posts)
entries.eq: Trained and equipped for close combat; small arms/crew-served weapons (general & geospatial have limited small arms for self-defense)

entries.desc: Most diverse of the three disciplines; may use all engineer MOSs. One of the Army logistics elements: establishes and maintains infrastructure to conduct and sustain operations
entries.use: Provide infrastructure and modify, maintain or protect the physical environment; construction support across all levels of warfare and every operation type
entries.how: Common tasks: restore damaged areas; build/maintain LOCs; establish base camps; assess/repair infrastructure; environmental surveys/reports; hazmat/waste infrastructure; master facility/design support; electrical power generation/distribution; real estate acquisition/disposal

entries.desc: Supports all warfighting functions through terrain analysis and visualization via the Army Geospatial Enterprise (AGE); data held in Theater Geospatial Database (TGD), ASCC geospatial planning cells, Army Geospatial Center
entries.use: Provide geospatial information and services (GI&S) so commanders/staffs understand the physical environment; supports running estimates and decisions
entries.how: Four primary functions: generate, manage, analyze, disseminate (GMAD). Support from ASCC to BCT includes terrain analysis, 3-D terrain visualization, tailored map products (cross-country mobility, view shed, zone of entry, hydrology), SSGF data for the COP, and TGD maintenance

entries.desc: Orchestrates combat, general and geospatial engineering in combination
entries.use: Gain/maintain a position of advantage (mobility) and deny the enemy freedom of action (countermobility); supports movement and maneuver, incl. special operations forces
entries.how: Achieved through the assured mobility framework (ATP 3-90.4). Normally organic combat engineers; general engineers may be task-organized. Does not include nontactical movement of personnel/material for logistics

entries.desc: Combination of the three disciplines supporting force preservation
entries.use: Preserve the force so commanders can apply maximum combat power
entries.how: Largely survivability operations, but can include selected mobility (e.g., perimeter roads), countermobility (protective obstacles) and explosive-hazards tasks (area clearance)

entries.n: Line of Support: Enable Force Projection and Logistics
entries.desc: Often performed by engineer units or contract construction (e.g., USACE) and may combine joint units, contractors, HN or multinational engineers
entries.use: Enhance theater strategic-to-tactical movements; executed mainly by general engineering
entries.how: Tasks free combat engineers for maneuver, build/maintain infrastructure for follow-on forces, sustain operations during/after hostile action, recommend site selection for facilities, joint fires and protection

entries.n: Line of Support: Build Partner Capacity and Develop Infrastructure
entries.desc: Primarily general engineering; also uses geospatial engineers and USACE experts for technical advice and data exchange
entries.use: Stability and counterinsurgency tasks; building/repairing infrastructure, essential services, and co-developing HN capability
entries.how: Purpose differs from logistics: e.g., a road for the local economy may prioritize local labor/ coordination/ training HN managers over speed. USACE FFE units advise HN capacity building; BCT engineers may provide training or reconstruction teams

entries.desc: Combat engineers usually at tactical level in support of maneuver; general engineers typically at operational level. Road/bridge/airfield repair is usually general engineering
entries.use: Mitigate effects of natural and man-made obstacles so friendly forces can move and maneuver freely
entries.how: Five primary tasks: combined arms breaching; clearing (areas and routes); gap crossing; construct/maintain combat roads and trails; construct/maintain forward airfields and landing zones. Also bypass, reduce or clear obstacles and mark lanes and trails

entries.desc: Combat engineers play prominent tactical role; general engineers may support operational/strategic effects or deception. In stability, may support traffic/population control
entries.use: Use or enhance natural/man-made obstacles to prevent enemy freedom of movement and maneuver; shape enemy movement; isolate objectives in the offense
entries.how: Tasks: siting obstacles; constructing, emplacing or detonating obstacles; marking, reporting and recording obstacles; maintaining obstacle integration. Engineer advises commander on integration, coordinates obstacle emplacement authority, establishes obstacle control, supervises employment, tracks status; plans to clear obstacles at end of hostilities
entries.wn: As of 1 Jan 2010 U.S. forces may not employ persistent, undetectable land mines; self-destructing/self-deactivating (scatterable) mines and networked munitions are used. Follow current U.S. land mine policy

entries.desc: Geospatial engineers work as staff members supporting the orders process and the COP
entries.use: Help combat/general engineers visualize the operational environment for mobility tasks
entries.how: Products: 3-D fly-throughs; mobility corridor and combined obstacle overlays; fields-of-fire/line-of-sight analysis; urban tactical planners; hydrologic/bathymetric/gravimetric analysis; LOC analysis and overlays

entries.desc: Equipment and personnel to conduct underwater operations (see ATP 3-34.84, TM 3-34.84). Integrate into early-entry operations and port opening
entries.use: Underwater operations; river-crossing support and force protection dives
entries.how: Provides near-shore/far-shore recon; hydrographic surveys of bottom composition; underwater/surface recon of bridges for structural integrity; repair/reinforce bridge structures; emplace, mark or reduce underwater obstacles; check ships, docks, piers, intakes for enemy tampering; identify/remove underwater explosive hazards
entries.eq: Diving detachment equipment and personnel (details in ATP 3-34.84 / TM 3-34.84, not in this source)

entries.desc: Formed by combat engineer units. See ATP 3-34.81
entries.use: Classify routes, locate obstacles, recommend bypass or reduction; recon proposed obstacle locations
entries.how: Normally supports BCTs, cavalry squadrons or scout platoons; can operate independently. Submit all terrain, obstacle and recon data to geospatial engineers to update the COP and TGD. Teams are ad hoc, so building them from organic resources drains platoons/squads
entries.wn: Ad hoc formations; commanders must understand the risk of drawing from organic platoons and squads (para 2-106)

entries.desc: Limited to ordnance in the EOCA guide or supplemental EOCA ordnance list
entries.use: Limited disposal of authorized explosive ordnance in support of mobility; advise on protective measures
entries.how: Combat engineers with extra training; advise on-scene commander on personnel/equipment protective measures; isolate blast and fragmentation danger areas; may assist EOD
entries.wn: Only authorized ordnance on EOCA list; EOD assist as directed by theater

entries.desc: Tactical level: usually combat engineers in support of maneuver; operational level: general engineers. Protective positions and hardened facilities also support protection against nuclear blast and improve shielding in CBRN environments; engineers support decontamination sites and scrape roads/surfaces to reduce contamination
entries.use: Alter the physical environment to provide or improve cover, concealment and camouflage when terrain is insufficient
entries.how: Four areas: fighting positions, protective positions, hardened facilities, camouflage and concealment. Tasks are equipment-intensive; use equipment timelines to manage low-density critical equipment. See ATP 3-37.34 for details
entries.eq: Dig assets and other engineer equipment (not itemized)

entries.desc: See ATP 3-34.20
entries.use: Mitigate effects of explosive hazards at all echelons
entries.how: Includes area and route clearance; specialized searches using engineer mine detection dogs and patrol explosive detection dogs; collection, analysis, dissemination of explosive hazard information. Where tactical situation permits, area clearance can be a USACE-contracted capability
entries.eq: Mine detection dogs, patrol explosive detection dogs
entries.wn: Area clearance is not demining; 10 USC 401 Chapter 20 restricts armed forces from demining unless supporting a U.S. military operation

entries.n: Protective Obstacles and Entry Control Points (perimeter protection)
entries.desc: See ADP 3-37
entries.use: Protect bases and base camps
entries.how: Examples: construct a trail for use as a perimeter road to secure a base; provide protective obstacles or entry control points

entries.desc: Limited-asset teams
entries.use: Fire prevention and protection (limited assets)
entries.how: Fire prevention inspections/investigations, fire suppression, search and rescue, hazmat response, medical response/assistance to victims, technical oversight of nonfirefighting personnel supporting firefighting

entries.desc: See ATP 3-34.5, AR 200-1
entries.use: Identify, prevent and mitigate hazards to the environment, personnel and mission before force projection and site occupation
entries.how: Embedded engineers conduct environmental baseline surveys, analyze site conditions, identify resources/hazards, recommend actions. Records during contingency location life cycle: Environmental Baseline Survey Checklists and Reports, Environmental Conditions Reports, inspection reports, Environmental Site Closure Surveys and Reports. Example site problems: poor drainage, contaminated soil, poor water/air quality, erosion, flooding, over-stacked/leaking hazmat containers, improper waste

entries.n: Route Reconnaissance and Clearance for Force Projection
entries.desc: See ATP 3-34.81
entries.use: Determine trafficability and route classification; clear hazards for freedom of movement along LOC, APOD or SPOD
entries.how: Combat engineers conduct route recon; detect/mark explosive hazards; clear hazards within capability

entries.use: Port facilities unavailable, damaged or denied
entries.how: Engineers augment sustainment units; prepare access routes to/from beach; prepare landing sites and staging areas

entries.n: General Engineering Task List (construction and sustainment)
entries.desc: See ATP 3-34.40
entries.use: Primarily not under close-combat conditions
entries.how: Construct/maintain strategic and operational LOCs, airfields, seaports, railroads, bases/base camps, pipelines, bulk and distribution storage facilities, standard and nonstandard bridges; facilities engineer support; electrical power generation/distribution; utilities and waste; real estate; firefighting; battle damage repair; environmental surveys/reports; improving fighting/protective positions and hardening facilities; Corps real estate teams; engineer divers; neutralize water-borne obstacles in ports/channels; repair/reinforce subsurface structures (port facilities, dams, bridges); search and recovery of submerged equipment; JLOTS support

entries.n: Well Drilling and Water Source Mapping
entries.use: Long-term water restoration issues
entries.how: Specialized units can locate and map water sources; well-drilling teams are limited assets

entries.use: Describe the OE with eight operational variables: political, military, economic, social, information, infrastructure, physical environment, time
entries.how: Engineer view adds items such as port access, enemy explosive hazards, availability of materials, laborers and local engineer resources, power considerations, infrastructure deficiencies, urban/complex terrain, and base camp permanence vs duration

entries.desc: Early identification of essential engineer tasks lets the maneuver commander request augmentation early
entries.use: Mission analysis for a specific operation
entries.how: Mission; Enemy (disposition, enemy engineering capabilities, obstacle intelligence, recon, explosive hazard reporting); Terrain and weather (five military aspects: observation and fields of fire, avenues of approach, key terrain, obstacles, cover and concealment); Troops and support available; Time available; Civil considerations; (Informational considerations)

entries.desc: Special operations forces support: engineer LNO integrated into SOF HQ; contingency/crisis action planning; speed and resource ingenuity
entries.use: Link tactical actions to national objectives
entries.how: National strategic (policy); theater strategic (force planning, GI&S, TGD, SPOD/APOD, LOCs, basing, joint targeting, foreign humanitarian assistance, environmental, explosive hazard mitigation); operational (base camp site selection, supply routes, waste programs, Class IV procurement, environment); tactical (task-organize engineers at lowest level, survivability and infrastructure; geospatial engineers validate recon data and submit to TGD)

entries.use: Small UASs make suppression/obscuration for breach or gap crossing harder, and can observe survivability work and pinpoint battle positions
entries.how: Commanders account for enemy capabilities and implement counter-small-UAS techniques based on organic and attached capabilities; Soldiers must be trained and equipped (see ATP 3-01.81)

entries.n: Engineer support across strategic contexts (competition, crisis, armed conflict)
entries.use: Engineer demand remains high from competition through armed conflict
entries.how: Competition: geospatial and general engineering tasks, theater setting, partner capacity. Crisis: real estate/basing, opening ports of debarkation, LOCs, hardening facilities, AAs/battle positions; reserve component mobilization time matters (about three-fourths of Army engineer units are in the reserve component). Armed conflict: support to ground combat and sustainment

entries.desc: Supporting orgs: theater engineer command (TEC) and USACE. See ATP 3-37.10 (base camps), ATP 3-37.34
entries.use: Establish favorable conditions for rapid execution of operations for a specific OPLAN
entries.how: Infrastructure improvement; bases and base camp planning; APOD/SPOD hardening; surveys of assembly areas, LOC capacity, gap-crossing sites; real estate; environmental services. Manage Class IV (barrier/construction) and Class V (explosives) supply separately

entries.use: Evaluate whether infrastructure meets operational needs
entries.how: Questions: meets needs over campaign phases (quantity, quality, location, force protection)? meets coalition/HN needs? repair/upgrade/maintain/new construction? defense/protection needs? is it on the critical, defended or protection prioritization list? FEST-A provides infrastructure assessment

entries.desc: Defense demands the greatest survivability effort (HQ, artillery, air and missile defense, critical equipment/supplies, individual/crew-served and defilade vehicle positions). Use engineer work timelines; digging assets are intensively managed
entries.use: Defeat enemy attack, gain time, develop conditions for offense/stability
entries.how: Engineer focus: combined-arms obstacle integration (countermobility), survivability of defending force, and assured mobility for repositioning/counterattacking forces. Combat engineers: construct field fortifications and fighting positions, combat roads, FACE, obstacles, demolitions, place mines/munitions, recon, fight as engineers/infantry. General: harden facilities, horizontal construction, support CM/S, mitigate hazards, protect water supplies, environmental. Geospatial: terrain analysis of EAs, SSGF for COP
entries.eq: Digging assets, barrier materials, munitions, construction equipment (not itemized)
entries.wn: Countermobility efforts compete with survivability resources and assets; commander must give clear priorities (note after para 2-62)

entries.desc: Link obstacles to restrictive/natural terrain. See ATP 3-90.8
entries.use: Mass effects to contain and destroy an enemy force
entries.how: Seven steps: identify likely enemy AAs; identify most likely enemy COA; determine where to kill the enemy; *position subordinate forces and weapons; *plan and integrate obstacles; *plan and integrate fires; rehearse (*simultaneous). Obstacle siting is a support rehearsal: walk the terrain with the supported maneuver unit to ensure fires cover the EA. Obstacle options: networked munitions, scatterable mines, demolition obstacles (road craters), constructed obstacles, field expedient obstacles

entries.desc: Mobile defense generally needs less engineer effort than area defense
entries.use: Destroy enemy through decisive attack by striking force/mobile reserve
entries.how: Use obstacles to defeat enemy maneuver; give mobility to striking force; situational obstacles advantageous; primary and alternate hull-defilade positions in primary and subsequent battle positions; protective obstacles concentrated at final subsequent positions; obstacle control measures so brigade obstacles do not limit the reserve; dedicated engineer support to the mobile reserve

entries.desc: Area defense generally requires more robust engineer effort due to higher survivability requirement
entries.use: Deny enemy access to terrain for a specific time; retain terrain
entries.how: Variations: defense of a linear obstacle, perimeter defense, reverse slope defense. Brigades may need primary, alternate and supplementary turret-defilade positions; heavier protective obstacles; coordinate adjacent brigade obstacle efforts; scatterable mines allow less risk

entries.use: Organized movement away from the enemy (delay, withdrawal, retirement)
entries.how: Maintain mobility of force (disengagement of force in contact) and protect the force; normally under limited visibility; hinder enemy mobility with obstacles, fires, and terrain optimization

entries.use: Authority to emplace reinforcing obstacles
entries.how: Delegated: theater commanders -> corps commanders -> division commanders; division commanders retain unless higher commander withholds/restricts

entries.desc: Position engineers well forward; keep task organization changes minimal (time/event-based triggers). Fighting/protective position development is minimal in offense; CPs and key assets need improved survivability on halts
entries.use: Defeat/destroy enemy forces and gain control of terrain, resources, population centers
entries.how: Priority: mobility. Combat: breach obstacles, demolitions, clear explosive hazards, field fortifications, assault bridging, combat roads, FACE, recon. General: port construction, horizontal construction, quarry aggregate, asphalt, concrete, underwater construction, firefighting. Geospatial: terrain analysis of assembly areas and objectives. Prefer bypass; mark bypasses and hand off to follow-on engineers; LOC bridging replaces assault bridging

entries.n: Engineer considerations by offensive operation type
entries.use: Movement to contact, attack, exploitation, pursuit
entries.how: See Table 2-3

entries.desc: See ATP 3-90.4
entries.use: Allow maneuver through an obstacle covered by enemy fire
entries.how: Synchronized combined arms activity under maneuver commander control; breaching tenets: intelligence, breaching fundamentals, breaching organization, mass, synchronization; rehearse breach, assault and support forces; engineers reduce, mark and guide units through obstacles; corps units expand lanes and breach bypassed obstacles

entries.use: Eliminate enemy obstacle effects or residual obstacles affecting a route or area
entries.how: Clearance teams task-organized and rehearsed; area clearance organized so sustainment assets can echelon forward

entries.use: Project combat power across a wet or dry gap
entries.how: Fundamentals: surprise; extensive preparation (less for hasty); flexible planning; traffic management; organization; speed. Requires specialized crossing resources and a force to secure the bridgehead. Corps bridging provides assault float bridging and LOC bridging

entries.n: Construct and Maintain Combat Roads and Trails
entries.use: Move personnel/equipment/supplies through untrafficable areas and bypass obstacles or sensitive areas
entries.how: Combat engineering mission in close support; general engineers also build them. Corps units upgrade combat roads and trails

entries.use: Hasty construction/repair of landing strips, landing zones, forward arming and refueling points
entries.how: Shortens distance to objective areas, reduces turnaround times, improves sustainment for fixed-, rotary-, tilt-wing aircraft (manned/unmanned)

entries.use: Improve trafficability and movement
entries.how: Repair and clear roads; traffic pattern studies; design/install permanent traffic control devices (technical expertise)

entries.desc: Technical expertise often through reachback or forward USACE contingency element
entries.use: Secure environment, essential services, emergency reconstruction, humanitarian relief
entries.how: Six primary stability tasks; essential services: food and water, emergency shelter, basic sanitation. General engineering: harden facilities, horizontal/vertical construction, LOC construction and repair, infrastructure, waste, well drilling, quarry, asphalt, concrete, power, utilities, survey and design, construction management, firefighting. Early on-ground assessment tailors force. Contract capabilities (LOGCAP, AFCAP, NAVFAC GCCC) take over as AO matures

entries.use: Make operational success enduring
entries.how: Assess civil infrastructure; area clearance; recon LOCs/roads/bridges; improve force protection for critical infrastructure; improve combat roads and replace tactical bridging with LOC bridging; contract Class IV and equipment/labor; assess/document environmental conditions; construct base camps

entries.use: Transitions can be chaotic and increase risk
entries.how: Anticipate and plan deliberately; consolidate gains facilitates transition

entries.use: Urban operations and sharing GD&I
entries.how: ATP 3-06 urban framework: understand, shape, engage, consolidate, transition. Geospatial engineers partner with local authorities to share GD&I; support SSGF; GEOINT cells

entries.use: Many threats/non-state actors do not mark mines doctrinally
entries.how: Learn local marking methods (readily available materials); consult local authorities about natural, cultural, historic resources and sensitive populations

entries.desc: Smaller multifunctional elements
entries.use: Engineer support at company, platoon, squad or Soldier level
entries.how: GI&S, infrastructure development, facility construction/maintenance, training indigenous populations to construct protective obstacles, mobile electric power, facility hardening

entries.n: Support to Cyberspace Operations and Electromagnetic Warfare
entries.use: Protect cyber-dependent operations
entries.how: Harden facilities; construct protective obstacles; provide uninterrupted medium-voltage power; clean/secure power supply and grid systems to mitigate electromagnetic disruption

entries.n: Host-Nation Support and Engineer Support Plan (ESP)
entries.desc: Wartime HN support agreements exist in Europe and Korea
entries.use: Reduce early lift requirements for RSOI
entries.how: JCMS planning module identifies construction requirements; USACE Centers of Standardization site-adapt drawings; analyses produce the ESP (see para 6-28). HN may provide geospatial data, land, facilities, construction support, manpower, equipment, materials, services, waste disposal. Pre-position equipment regionally; HN local contractors and materials (cement, asphalt, aggregate, lumber, steel)

entries.use: Unity of effort with joint, multinational, interagency, NGOs
entries.how: Provide engineer LNOs (linguist, communications, transport); request HN geospatial data; use ATP 3-34 / ATP-3.12.1 for allied engineers; establish liaison with civil-military operations center; NGOs may be Class IV source

entries.n: Engineer Support at Echelon (Theater Army, Corps, Division, BCT)
entries.use: Understand who does what by echelon
entries.how: Theater army: infrastructure assessment, basing, set the theater, RSOI. Corps: base camp planning, geospatial products, recon, joint fires and survivability recommendations; corps normally has an engineer brigade HQ. Division: up to five BCTs; division engineers integrate combat, general and geospatial support. BCT: divisionally aligned engineer battalion/BEB provides baseline combat capability; BCT HQ has geospatial engineers in the intelligence section

entries.n: Engineer Support Across the Six Warfighting Functions
entries.desc: Six warfighting functions: C2, movement and maneuver, intelligence, fires, sustainment, protection. Engineer disciplines are organized by discipline and synchronized through these functions (Figure 3-1)
entries.use: Linking engineer disciplines to the warfighting functions so engineer capability is applied as combat power
entries.how: Know which discipline mainly feeds which function: combat engineering -> movement and maneuver + protection; general engineering -> sustainment (secondary: protection); geospatial -> C2 (liaison to intelligence); survivability links to fires + protection
entries.eq: Combat, general and geospatial engineer units

entries.n: Engineer C2 Support (Command and Control WFF)
entries.desc: Engineer units integrate the operations process activities with the supported unit (through assigned engineer staff or staff counterparts). Engineer headquarters control ongoing engineer operations: monitoring engineer forces/assets, mitigating explosive hazards, coordinating engineer reconnaissance, and providing geospatial support through GI&S
entries.use: Engineer units integrate with the supported unit's operations process; prioritizing scarce engineer capability
entries.how: Prioritize carefully because there are usually not enough engineer capabilities; expect to shift capabilities within the AO as mission changes; use mission command approach

entries.desc: A graphic control measure: a coordinated boundary or phase line used to compartmentalize an AO and designate areas of work responsibility for subordinate engineer organizations
entries.use: Designate which engineer unit has primary responsibility for engineer effort in part of the AO
entries.how: Used at division level to separate an AO supported by division engineer assets from an AO supported by direct/general support corps engineer units
entries.eq: Graphic control measure on operations graphics

entries.desc: Engineers support movement and maneuver through geospatial engineering, engineer reconnaissance, and M/CM/S. Combat engineer support is focused on assured mobility
entries.use: Combat engineers support forces in close combat; shape the battlefield for early-entry operations
entries.how: Support assured mobility; BCT organic and divisionally aligned engineers use mobility and countermobility tasks to enable and expand lodgments
entries.eq: BCT organic and divisionally aligned engineer units

entries.desc: Combat engineers can perform as general engineers (and vice versa) only with additional equipment, training and augmented technical expertise. General engineer units tasked in support of maneuver forces are closer to the front than usual; without maneuver security they must self-secure, which pulls personnel from the task and extends time on site
entries.use: Close combat support to maneuver forces
entries.how: Integrate and coordinate with fire and movement of combat forces. Combat engineer units are organized like infantry squads/platoons with extra medical personnel, specific weapons and vehicles, trained with supported forces
entries.eq: Combat engineer units; general engineers need augmentation/security
entries.wn: General engineers lack the same weapon types as combat engineers, increasing risk to personnel and equipment (para 3-15)

entries.desc: Close-combat engineer tasks: neutralize explosive hazards (locate, assess, render incapable of interfering; except render-safe); enhance mobility (route and obstacle reconnaissance, obstacle reduction, assault gap crossing, combat roads and trails, forward aviation combat engineering); deny enemy movement (land mines, network munitions, demolition and constructed obstacles); enhance protection through survivability (fighting and protective positions, hardening, camouflage and concealment)
entries.use: Combat engineers engage in close combat to accomplish engineer missions
entries.how: Be prepared to fight and integrate with fire and maneuver; the enemy tries to detect and engage engineers quickly regardless of location
entries.eq: Land mines, network munitions, demolitions, constructed obstacles (as listed)

entries.desc: A combat engineer organization can execute infantry tasks or task-organize to fight as infantry. The combat engineer unit commander has authority to reorganize unless reserved; must weigh gain in infantry strength against loss of engineer support
entries.use: Rare: engineer unit designated to fight as infantry
entries.how: Requires added fire support and medical positions; decision normally made at operational-level command and coordinated with higher HQ. An immediate need may only require engineers to engage in close combat without reorganizing
entries.eq: Extensive equipment and training specific to reorganization
entries.wn: Reorganization requires resources, time and training; employing engineers merely means short-term use (para 3-18)

entries.n: General Engineer Support to Movement and Maneuver
entries.desc: General engineer support is typically applied through sustainment but crosses over to movement and maneuver
entries.use: Tasks exceeding combat engineer capability; major upgrades or new construction of LOCs and base camps
entries.how: Examples listed: roads/trails beyond combat engineer capability, runway repair, airfield surveys, firefighting and aircraft rescue, marking airfield surfaces, field-expedient landing strips, standard and nonstandard bridging, theater access (LOCs, MSRs, ports, airfields, base camps)

entries.n: Intelligence WFF Support / Engineer IPOE Support
entries.desc: Engineers play a major role in IPOE supporting G-2/S-2 and G-3/S-3 analysis. Geospatial engineering improves terrain visualization and provides SSGF to GEOINT
entries.use: Adds to commander's situational understanding of terrain, weather, civil considerations
entries.how: Provide digitized mapping and terrain analysis; predictive and deductive analysis of enemy engineering capabilities; civil infrastructure considerations (PMESII-PT); support information collection through engineer reconnaissance

entries.desc: A deliberate process. Engineer information requirements are determined by engineer staffs at division, corps, theater army and in-theater engineer HQs in coordination with the G-2
entries.use: Determine feasibility of areas for use; assess AO before and during deployment
entries.how: Collect remotely or physically; may include conditions/capacities supporting mobility, sources of construction materials, local construction standards, key industrial sites, cultural heritage sites, geotechnical data (soils, geology, hydrography). Feed the COP continuously
entries.eq: Engineer staffs; remote or physical collection means

entries.desc: Engineer disciplines provide a menu of reconnaissance capabilities. Units do not have dedicated reconnaissance elements (except the armored BCT). See ATP 3-34.81
entries.use: Answer commander's critical information requirements; support the lines of engineer support
entries.how: Reconnaissance is inherent in all three disciplines; information may be tactical or technical. Commanders task-organize combat and general engineers with other disciplines based on mission
entries.eq: Mix of engineer specialties and equipment

entries.desc: Engineer reconnaissance teams are composed of combat engineers
entries.use: Collect tactical and technical information for M/CM/S: division's freedom of maneuver and survivability of friendly forces and facilities
entries.how: Engineer company commanders form and train ad hoc teams for tactical reconnaissance that collect technical information and perform limited analysis

entries.desc: Engineers complete EBS to record detailed environmental conditions. See ATP 3-34.5
entries.use: Record and analyze environmental conditions to judge whether areas are feasible for use
entries.how: Records hazardous materials, spills/contamination, disease vectors and pests, poor drainage and erosion, natural resources, cultural and historic resources. DD Form 2993 (EBS Checklist) is used to verify and record technical information

entries.desc: GI&S is collection, information extraction, storage, dissemination and exploitation of geodetic, geomagnetic, imagery, gravimetric, aeronautical, topographic, hydrographic, littoral, cultural and toponymic data referenced to a precise location
entries.use: Terrain visualization and understanding for planning, training and operations
entries.how: Common applications: planning, training, terrain visualization, navigation, mission planning, mission rehearsal, modeling, simulation, targeting. AGC reachback provides instruction, training and guidance on using geospatial data
entries.eq: Geospatial engineering teams; Army Geospatial Enterprise (AGE); AGC

entries.desc: At division and above, engineer targets enter the Army targeting process/joint targeting cycle; shift terrain-shaping obstacle systems during dynamic targeting (ATP 3-60.1). Staff planners also protect infrastructure from friendly targeting for future use
entries.use: Facilitate targeting and artillery displacement
entries.how: Geospatial engineers: templated observer and firing points from line-of-sight and slope; mobility/suitability analysis of targets and EAs. Combat engineers: emplace obstacles that enhance fires, construct survivability positions for fires units, support mobility during displacement
entries.wn: Damage to enemy critical infrastructure (airfields, roads, bridges, intersections, yards) may need significant engineer effort to restore for friendly use (para 3-29)

entries.desc: Sustainment elements: logistics, financial management, personnel services, health service support. Engineers support through mobility and survivability tasks
entries.use: Base camps, ammunition holding areas, revetments/hardening of distribution facilities, clearing and repairing LOCs
entries.how: In stability and DSCA, general engineering effort (incl. USACE) is very high at onset then decreases; may transfer to external support contracts (LOGCAP, AFCAP, NAVFAC global contingency construction contract). Operational contract support: general engineers give subject-matter expertise to oversee contracted services and materials

entries.desc: Tasks: vehicle, crew-served and individual fighting positions; protective earth walls, berms, revetments, protective positions for vehicles, information systems, equipment and material; hardening of structures with overhead cover, pre-detonation screens, shielding barriers; bridge protective devices (against waterborne demolition teams, floating mines, debris); install/remove protective obstacles; protective equipment (vehicle crash barriers, entry control points, security fences); environmental baseline surveys
entries.use: Protect the force from enemy action in the AO; hardening and field fortification
entries.how: Combat engineers typically provide basic hardening and field fortification; general engineers focus on long-term survivability, pollution/hazmat control, and facility hardening. See ATP 3-37.34
entries.eq: Engineer equipment and personnel; barriers, fences, bridge protective devices (as listed)

entries.n: CBRN Contamination Control and Firefighting (Protection Tasks)
entries.desc: Listed as engineer protection tasks
entries.use: Control CBRN contamination; fire protection
entries.how: Engineers identify, prevent and mitigate hazards to environment, personnel and mission; see ATP 3-11.33 (CBRN) and TM 3-34.30 (firefighting)

entries.desc: Engineer operations contribute lethal and nonlethal combat power. Corps, divisions and BCTs are task organized with engineer capabilities based on mission variables: platoon, company, battalion or brigade HQ
entries.use: Understanding how engineers contribute to combat power
entries.how: Five dynamics: leadership, firepower, information, mobility, survivability. Survivability is how hard a formation is to kill; includes avoiding detection and deceiving the enemy

entries.n: Lethal and Nonlethal Actions / Shift to Stability
entries.desc: Lethal and nonlethal actions complement each other and create dilemmas for the opponent; nonlethal action denies the enemy a propaganda tool where lethal force is counterproductive
entries.use: Choosing mix of lethal/nonlethal action; stability operations focus
entries.how: In stability operations, building partner capacity and developing infrastructure become the primary line of engineer support: build/repair/maintain infrastructure, provide essential services, codevelop HN capabilities

entries.n: Engineer Regiment and Operating-Force Engineer Categories
entries.desc: Regiment = Regular Army, ARNG, USAR engineer organizations; USACE; DOD Civilians; affiliated contractors/agencies.
