Engineer Army School training listed: Joint Engineer Operations Course, Combat Engineer Heavy Track Course, Engineer EOCA Course, Mine Detection Dog Course, Crane Course, Sapper Leader Course
entries.use: Know where engineer capability sits (active/ARNG/USAR) and how it is organized
entries.how: Five categories: three in the EAD force pool (engineer headquarters, baseline units, specialized units), divisionally aligned units, and BCT organic engineers. About three-fourths of Army engineer units are in the reserve components

entries.n: Engineer Headquarters: TEC, Engineer Brigade, Engineer Battalion
entries.desc: Three echelons of engineer HQ (TEC, brigade, battalion). Multifunctional HQ such as the MEB may also command engineers (FM 3-81)
entries.use: C2 of engineer units at theater, corps/division and battalion level
entries.how: TEC: theater infrastructure development, ASCC synchronization, prioritizes theater distribution of construction material, bridging and equipment; main CP + two contingency CPs; can form core of a joint forces engineer component command. Engineer brigade: C2 up to five engineer battalions; deliberate gap crossing; one contingency CP; SPOD/APOD support in early entry. Engineer battalion: HHC + forward support company, up to five engineer companies; can serve as breach force command or crossing-site command

entries.desc: Combat units may construct tactical obstacles, defensive positions, fixed and float bridges; repair CPs, tactical routes, culverts, fords; support gap crossing; assist assault of fortified positions; breach. General units construct, rehabilitate, repair, maintain and modify CPs, LOCs, supply installations, buildings, bridges; repair railroads, water and waste facilities. Augmentation enables quarrying and crushing, pipeline support, dive support, major horizontal construction (highways, storage, airfields)
entries.use: Company-size building blocks of engineer battalions; augment BCT engineers
entries.how: Baseline combat: combat engineer company and sapper company. Baseline general: horizontal and vertical construction, engineer support, bridging (multirole bridge), mobility augmentation, clearance companies. Airborne/air assault units can employ air-droppable rapid runway repair kits
entries.eq: Per Table 4-1 company types; augmentation tools/equipment/training

entries.desc: Support operational to strategic level, some tactical
entries.use: Technical, often low-density capabilities for construction support
entries.how: Listed: asphalt detachment, concrete section, construction management team, engineer facility detachment, engineer utilities detachment, FEST-A, FEST-M, quarry platoon, well-drilling teams

entries.n: Specialized Engineer Units — Infrastructure Support (Prime Power, Facility Detachment, Firefighting)
entries.desc: See ATP 3-34.40 and TM 3-34.56 (waste management)
entries.use: Power generation, base camp development, fire protection
entries.how: Prime power: generate electrical power, advise on electrical power and distribution, electrical surveys, operate/maintain/minor-repair power equipment including HN fixed plants (limited design/analysis). Facility detachments: theater opening/closing, base camp development, construction management, contract technical oversight, base camp operations incl. waste management, master planning. Firefighting teams: base and base camp fire protection, search and rescue
entries.eq: Prime power, facility detachment, firefighting teams

entries.use: Underwater/maritime engineering support
entries.how: Scuba and surface diving to a depth of 190 feet in support of combat, general and geospatial engineering. Tasks: reconnaissance, river-crossing, hydrographic survey, demolition, port construction and rehabilitation, harbor clearance, ship husbandry, salvage, joint logistics-over-the-shore, hyperbaric life support
entries.dim: Diving depth: 190 feet

entries.n: Explosive Hazards Support (Tracking, Detection, Neutralization, Proofing)
entries.desc: Specialized capabilities integrated to counter explosive hazards
entries.use: Counter the explosive hazards threat
entries.how: Link to Army EOD (Ordnance Branch) and Navy/Air Force EOD. Engineer squad (canine) mine dog teams help locate firearms, ammunition and explosives in rural and urban environments and augment route and area clearance in the clearance company
entries.eq: Mine dog teams; clearance company assets

entries.desc: Provides geospatial support to deployed units requiring augmentation
entries.use: Theater geospatial engineering asset to generate, manage and disseminate the Theater Geospatial Database (TGD)
entries.how: Capabilities: analysis, collection, generation, management, finishing, printing. Supports ASCC HQ and GCCs; manages TGD; explains military significance of terrain to the commander (ATP 3-34.80)

entries.desc: See also EBS DD Form 2993
entries.use: Mission-tailored teams collecting engineer-specific tactical and technical information
entries.how: Route classifications and assessments; surveys of bridges, engineer resources, infrastructure, environmental conditions, airfields. Critical source for IPOE (ATP 3-34.81)

entries.desc: Intentional flexibility lets division commanders apply command and support relationships
entries.use: Engineer units pre-aligned to divisions to meet baseline engineer requirements
entries.how: Division engineer brigade commander is senior engineer in the division, advising on integration across three disciplines; brigade supervises contract construction, labor, indigenous personnel, terrain analysis, geospatial operations. Battalions: engineer battalion, engineer battalion (wheel), engineer battalion (airborne), each with HHC and field service company, up to five companies. Relationships may change with mission

entries.desc: Organization: HQ section; two combat engineer platoons (HQ + three combat engineer squads each); assault and obstacle platoon (countermobility squad, HQ section, two construction sections, bridging section, breach section) (Figure 4-1)
entries.use: M/CM/S support to armored division; engineer battalion
entries.how: Plans, supervises, executes M/CM/S tasks; C2 for up to five platoons with assault, obstacle, route clearance, area clearance, bridging or general construction capability

entries.desc: Organization: HQ section; three combat engineer platoons (HQ + three squads each); assault and obstacle platoon (obstacle squad, mobility and survivability squad, HQ section, bridging section) (Figure 4-2)
entries.use: M/CM/S support to infantry division (engineer battalion (wheel))
entries.how: Same C2 and capabilities statement as CEC–A (up to five platoons)

entries.desc: Organization identical to CEC–S text: HQ section; three combat engineer platoons; assault and obstacle platoon (obstacle squad, MOB/SURV squad, HQ section, bridging section) (Figure 4-3)
entries.use: M/CM/S support to infantry division (engineer battalion (wheel))
entries.how: Same C2 and capabilities statement (up to five platoons)

entries.desc: Organization: HQ section; three combat engineer platoons; assault and obstacle platoon (obstacle squad, MOB/SURV squad, HQ section, bridging section) (Figure 4-4)
entries.use: M/CM/S support to airborne infantry division (engineer battalion (ABN))
entries.how: Same C2 and capabilities statement (up to five platoons)

entries.desc: Can C2 task-organized engineer organizations, signal and military intelligence companies, and a CBRN reconnaissance platoon (in HHC) (Figure 4-5)
entries.use: Organic engineer planning and execution capability for the BCT; BEB commander is the brigade engineer
entries.how: Integrates engineers into brigade planning; responsible for all engineer units assigned/attached to or working in brigade AO. Maneuver support for bridging, breaching, route clearance, explosive hazards identification, horizontal construction. Administrative, logistical, training and protection support of subordinate units. BCT commander directs command/support relationships
entries.eq: Engineer companies, signal and MI companies, CBRN recon platoon

entries.desc: Located in BEB HHC
entries.use: CBRN hazard reconnaissance and surveillance to protect the force
entries.how: May be detached to give early warning in deep operations or CBRN route reconnaissance and site assessment support to the BEB; gets admin/sustainment from BEB; technical advice to BEB (FM 3-11)

entries.n: BCT Engineer Companies A and B
entries.desc: Route clearance platoon detects/neutralizes explosive hazards and reduces obstacles along routes; sustains LOCs as part of a combined arms team or autonomously in low-threat environment
entries.use: Minimum BCT capability for offense/defense: breach and cross obstacles, assist assault on fortified positions, emplace obstacles, construct/enhance survivability positions, route reconnaissance and information collection, identify and neutralize explosive hazards
entries.how: Company A: HQ, two combat engineer platoons, one engineer support platoon (horizontal squad + breach squad); Stryker BCT has a bridge section instead of the support platoon and its breach squad is limited to mine-clearing line charges and proofing equipment. Company B: one combat engineer platoon, one route clearance platoon, one engineer support platoon; armored and Stryker breach section = bridging, infantry BCT breach section = mine-clearing line charges. Infantry BCT (non-airborne) has no bridging and needs EAD augmentation
entries.eq: Mine-clearing line charges, bridging, horizontal squad equipment, route clearance assets

entries.desc: Provide support to the assigned echelon and lower
entries.use: Geospatial support to brigades and BCTs
entries.how: Two types: geospatial engineer team (supports functional and multifunctional brigades: aviation, engineer, sustainment, division artillery, MI, fires, maneuver enhancement, security force assistance) and GEOINT team (supports BCTs, divisions, corps under G-2 guidance)

entries.desc: Supports SFAB and CCDR objectives
entries.use: Engineer technical and tactical advisory support to HN/coalition partners
entries.how: Provides C2 of attached/assigned units to train, advise and assist foreign security forces; advising team sizes/numbers adjust to mission; company and battalion HQ support dispersed teams

entries.n: Army Geospatial Enterprise (AGE) and Standard Shareable Geospatial Foundation (SSGF)
entries.desc: AGE is cross-cutting across all warfighting functions and phases and supports shared situational awareness with coalition partners
entries.use: Common geospatial foundation for the COP and MDMP
entries.how: SSGF has four basic data types: georeferenced imagery, elevation matrices (raster), geospatial features (vector), military standard maps. Overlay GD&I, analysis products, operational graphics, current ops, demographic/cultural/economic/industrial/infrastructure data and running-estimate information

entries.desc: Reachback management team
entries.use: Technical engineering RFIs from deployed forces, including environmental
entries.how: Submit RFIs through the UROC; it is one door to USACE, ERDC labs, Base Development Teams and Centers of Expertise. Completed requests available through the Reachback Engineer Data Integration portal. See chapter 5
entries.eq: RFI submission to UROC; REDI portal

entries.desc: Theater army commander recommends force mix and deployment sequence. Tailoring is not task organizing; commanders task-organize tailored units for missions. Units are normally employed in modules, units or companies under an engineer battalion HQ. Early activation affects Army force generation; surge possible short term only
entries.use: Determine right mix and sequence of engineer forces for a JFC
entries.how: Think beyond garrison structures; consider augmentation and which requirements can be met through reachback and geospatial products rather than a larger footprint; combat engineers need reinforcement for general engineering in stability operations. Actual requirements typically exceed planning figures

entries.n: Interagency and Echelon Force Tailoring Coordination
entries.desc: Most agreements made at CCMD JTF level and normally put legal restrictions on use of military personnel and equipment
entries.use: Coordination with other nation forces, U.S. agencies, NGOs, UN agencies, HN agencies; theater-level planning
entries.how: Authority for direct coordination must exist; agreements written as MOUs or terms of reference; liaison with the civil-military operations center (or J-9 at JTF level). Consider USACE/NAVFAC contract construction, HN military and civilian resources, and unified action partners; theater planners need clarity on SPOD/APOD upgrades and GLOC construction
entries.eq: MOU / terms of reference; engineer liaison

entries.n: USACE Support to Theater Army (Technical Engineering & Construction)
entries.desc: USACE provides technical engineering reconnaissance, planning and design, construction services, execution of contract construction, acquisition of real estate, and environmental services through regionally aligned divisions and districts in a GCC AOR. Districts have reimbursable support agreements with the ASCC; contingency districts can be added if workload outgrows the district
entries.use: Theater army HQ/ASCC needs engineering recon, design, construction, contract construction, real estate and environmental services
entries.how: Request through the theater Army Engineer; the TEC and/or USACE LNO gives direct access to USACE resources. Regionally aligned USACE divisions/districts are the 'one door to the corps'
entries.eq: Regionally aligned USACE division/district; contingency district (requirements-only TDA); TEC and/or USACE LNO

entries.n: USACE Division / District Alignment to Combatant Commands
entries.desc: Divisions handle C2, regional relationships, program management and QA for the AOR; districts execute construction projects, operate projects and deliver services. See Table 5-1 for alignments
entries.use: Identify which USACE division and district supports a given combatant command
entries.how: Look up the supported command in Table 5-1 to find the executing division and district

entries.n: USACE Set-the-Theater and Real Estate / Flood-Plain Support
entries.desc: Set-the-theater engineering tasks to receive and enable onward movement of U.S. forces. Real estate acquisition follows SOFA/HN agreements (rent-free facilities per HN agreements). Environmental baseline surveys are done on terrain U.S. forces occupy
entries.use: Crisis and onset of armed conflict; receiving and moving deploying forces; acquiring land and facilities
entries.how: USACE can recon SPODs/APODs, roads and bridges; do site assessments for staging; real estate personnel deploy early; GIS specialists with water-resource engineers provide flood-plain analysis so staging areas and basecamps are not placed in flood plains
entries.eq: USACE real estate, environmental and GIS specialists

entries.n: USACE Support to Competition, Capacity Building and Stability Operations
entries.desc: Supports theater security cooperation and assistance projects (humanitarian assistance to building partner capacity), water management SME support, interagency technical/project support, cooperative R&D, and ESP-integrated construction programs in stability operations
entries.use: Competition below armed conflict, security cooperation, stability operations and transitions to civil authority
entries.how: USACE districts build HN military facilities (foreign military sales construction), repair HN infrastructure, advise HN ministries and clear munitions/UXO from HN land
entries.eq: USACE districts; Ordnance and Explosives Directorate

entries.n: Engineer Research and Development Center (ERDC) Labs
entries.desc: ERDC is the premier USACE R&D center. Labs: Coastal and Hydraulics; Cold Regions Research and Engineering; Construction and Engineering Research; Environmental; Information Technology; Geospatial Research; Geotechnical and Structures
entries.use: Technical solutions such as flood-plain analysis, dam break analysis, tunnel detection, hardening and gap-crossing techniques
entries.how: Reach ERDC through UROC for technical answers; ERDC capabilities include siting basecamps, hardening facilities for force protection and expeditionary gap crossing

entries.desc: Manages projects in five portfolios: medical, facilities and base operations, energy, operational technology, and environmental. Programs and centers of expertise are listed in Table 5-2
entries.use: Electrical safety inspections, HN UXO cleanup, expedient medical facility designs
entries.how: Request for electrical safety (TF SAFE) or UXO/medical design support

entries.desc: AGC collects, analyzes, manages and delivers geospatial data and products. Functions: system engineering, terrain, imagery, acquisition support, acquisition program lifecycle management, and high resolution 3-D (HR3D) data shareable with interagency and international partners
entries.use: Need geospatial data, terrain products, imagery or acquisition support at any echelon
entries.how: Use AGC reachback for terrain reasoning, 2D/3D visualization, imagery (aerial, LIDAR, bathymetry) and HR3D data

entries.n: Institute for Water Resources (IWR) / Risk Management Center
entries.desc: IWR provides water resource trend analysis, planning and hydrologic methods, and national data management for civil works. Core missions include dam/levee data management, safety training, risk management and policy. Has seven subordinate organizations including the Risk Management Center
entries.use: Dam and levee safety, water resources planning
entries.how: Source of dam and levee risk assessment and analysis (example: technical oversight of Mosul Dam grouting)

entries.desc: Provides commercial level power to military units and federal relief organizations. Platoons install, operate and maintain complete medium voltage power generation and distribution systems worldwide. USACE can also establish a TF SAFE for electrical safety in occupied facilities. (See ATP 3-34.45.)
entries.use: Semi-permanent electrical power generation and distribution when tactical generators are impractical or utility power is unstable or unavailable; contingency and civil disaster response
entries.how: Request through theater army or JTF commander. Services include power requirement assessment, production, transformer test, plant/substation repair, breaker/relay maintenance, IR surveys, base closure support and medium voltage contractor oversight
entries.eq: Prime Power platoons; medium voltage generation and distribution systems

entries.desc: FFE is the application of Army engineering capabilities from the three disciplines through reachback and forward presence. USACE is the primary organizing agent. Deployable FFE capabilities also reside in USAR, National Guard and Joint engineers. USACE LNOs embed in GCCs and SOCOM to support RFF/RFA development
entries.use: Application of combat, general and geospatial engineering through reachback plus forward presence when forward capacity is limited
entries.how: Engineer commander or theater engineer decides the mix of Soldier, USACE civilian and contractor capabilities. FFE relies on reachback and satellite TeleEngineering when in-theater networks are down
entries.eq: USACE deployable teams; TeleEngineering communications; reachback network

entries.desc: Conducts infrastructure assessment, engineer planning and design, environmental, geospatial and other technical support. Active component team: military plus DA Civilians (civil, mechanical, structural, environmental, electrical engineers and a GIS specialist). USAR FEST-A is all military. With a JTF HQ may include real estate, environmental and prime power planners
entries.use: Persistent embedded technical engineer support to theater army through division engineer staffs
entries.how: Request by formal request for forces. Needs sustainment and security from the supported unit
entries.eq: Team augments engineer staff; sustainment and security from supported unit

entries.desc: Provides technical engineering recon, environmental considerations, planning and design, geospatial, construction services and contract construction below MILCON threshold; can provide technical oversight of other deployed FFE teams; may operate as a discrete HQ element
entries.use: Oversight of general engineering for a theater army or JTF, including construction below the MILCON threshold
entries.how: Needs contracting augmentation or local contracting command to execute projects below MILCON threshold. Requested by RFF. Resides in USAR and National Guard
entries.eq: Sustainment and security from supported unit; contracting augmentation

entries.desc: Deployable USACE element of DOD Civilians acting under delegated authority (10 USC chapter 159). Typically tailored to an Army component HQ
entries.use: Acquire, manage and dispose of real estate outside the U.S. for U.S. forces
entries.how: Request by RFF or as a reimbursable service through the aligned USACE district. Works with ENVST on suitability of HN facilities
entries.eq: Sustainment and security from supported unit

entries.desc: USACE DA Civilian environmental experts integrating environmental considerations into site planning, sustainment and closure; pollution prevention and hazardous substances management programs; collaborate with operational public health
entries.use: Environmental studies, surveys and reports for base camp development, closure and repurposing; HN facility suitability
entries.how: Request via RFF; may be paid as a reimbursable service through USACE division. Can deploy early and stay for closure remediation
entries.eq: Sustainment and security from supported unit

entries.n: Contingency Engineer District and USACE Augmentation Cell
entries.desc: The augmentation cell augments theater engineer staff, participates in infrastructure construction requirements, engages HN and interagency, supports construction acceptance decisions, provides programmatic oversight, communicates construction effects and implements USACE business processes in theater
entries.use: Emerging contingency exceeds capacity of the aligned USACE district; TEC or engineer brigade needs headquarters/staff augmentation
entries.how: Both are requirements-only TDA structures staffed with contingency construction program funding

entries.desc: UROC provides TeleEngineering communications equipment, expeditionary environmental tool kits, reconnaissance and infrastructure assessment tools, software and training. REDi is a COP database for RFIs, project details and site assessment data
entries.use: Technical engineering requests for information (RFI) across contingency and natural disaster operations
entries.how: Submit RFIs to UROC ('one door'); UROC uses ERDC labs and centers of expertise. Tracks via REDi database

entries.desc: Teams of architect/master planners, CAD technicians, and geotechnical, civil, electrical, environmental, mechanical, structural and cost engineers
entries.use: Master planning and facility design for intermediate staging bases, base camps, FOBs and dislocated civilian camps
entries.how: Uses JCMS to turn designs around in 24 to 36 hours. Ten district-based teams managed by ERDC

entries.desc: Designated USACE organizations with demonstrated capability in a specialized area; improve capability, eliminate redundancy and speed emergency response
entries.use: Specialized technical expertise (for example Protective Design Center, Hydrologic Engineering Center, Concrete Technology)
entries.how: Use via USACE reachback; see Table 5-3 for the full list

entries.desc: Suite of tools with over 900 unified facility criteria compliant standardized designs, from site preparation and defensive positions to logistics bases (initial and temporary level construction)
entries.use: Plan contingency locations from design through construction
entries.how: Identify potential sites, adapt standardized base camp designs, produce bills of material, cost, labor and equipment estimates. Desktop version works in limited-communication environments; online repository also available; latest designs via JCMS or REDi
entries.eq: Desktop application or online network repository

entries.n: Theater Army Engineer Staff Planning and Running Estimate
entries.desc: Examines mobilization, deployment, employment and sustainment requirements including RSOI, environmental considerations, construction and real estate. Collaboration points: understand intent, analyze environment, know systems and time, identify risk and use reachback, consider AO depth, integrate environment, plan sustainment, account for logistics
entries.use: Translate the operational approach into a feasible concept of engineer employment at theater army echelon
entries.how: Build a running estimate by discipline and warfighting function; keep updating as assessments, priorities and feedback arrive. Collaborate with subordinate engineers (see listed collaboration points)

entries.desc: TEC commander is senior engineer in theater. TEC plans for RSOI, operational mobility/countermobility, general engineering, power, area damage control, MILCON, geospatial, design, construction material, environment and real property. Can deploy scalable staff specialty capabilities and provides technical oversight of contracted construction
entries.use: Operational C2 of engineer forces at echelons above corps
entries.how: Large-scale combat usually needs early or phased deployment of the full TEC HQ; stability and DSCA may need the supporting TEC or its contingency CP

entries.desc: Provides reduced capability compared with the TEC. Collective tasks it may cover (typically a MEB role, if augmented): terrain management, information collection, movement control, area security, base defense, area damage control, stability. Taking a multifunctional role risks its functional capacity
entries.use: Fill C2 gap in division and corps support areas; complex missions such as wet-gap crossings, deliberate defenses and city-wide reconstruction
entries.how: Engineer brigade may be task-organized under theater functional commands, under the TEC, or directly under theater army. Division-level wet-gap crossing exceeds the divisional engineer battalion/BEB span and needs a brigade-level HQ

entries.n: Joint and Multinational Engineer Force Tailoring
entries.desc: Planners organize by discipline, link requirements to warfighting functions, analyze construction requirements that exceed Army unit capabilities, and use FFE/reachback for specialized requirements
entries.use: Build a tailored engineer force that includes Navy, Air Force, multinational and contract capabilities
entries.how: Navy and Air Force engineers have strong technical skills but limited ground combat capability and may not be able to move to and secure a work site: use for in-base requirements

entries.desc: Erect temporary shelters and clinics; emergency power; remove debris; temporary construction to reinforce weakened structures; reestablish transportation rights-of-way; construct protective structures; build levees; flood prediction models; mitigate environmental damage; fight fire
entries.use: Relieve or reduce the results of natural or man-made disasters
entries.how: Engineer response options listed in source

entries.n: Theater Development-Level Comparison (Lesser vs Highly Developed)
entries.desc: Lesser developed theaters generate more operational-level engineer effort earlier
entries.use: Estimating engineer effort based on how developed the theater is
entries.how: Use Table 5-4 to anticipate SPOD/APOD, geospatial data, real estate, environmental baseline, bases, roads, obstacles and infrastructure needs

entries.n: Engineer Support Across Offense, Defense, Stability and DSCA (Theater Level)
entries.desc: Operational frameworks have less impact on technical engineering tasks (for example a road upgrade supports attack, counterattack and civil security). DSCA is governed by the National Response Framework with 15 Emergency Support Functions
entries.use: Planning engineer force posture for each type of operation
entries.how: Offense: tailored force pushed to subordinates under support relationships. Defense: construction capability is short, so recommend priorities for countermobility and survivability. Stability: broadest requirements, construction exceeds Army unit capacity. DSCA: local/state lead, federal in support; USACE leads ESF #3 Public Works and Engineering

entries.n: Command and Support Relationships for Engineers
entries.desc: Table 6-1 compares Army command relationships and Table 6-2 compares Army support relationships. Relationships can change when tasks end, for example after a breach
entries.use: Decide how engineers are task-organized to a maneuver commander
entries.how: Command relationship (attach/OPCON/TACON) gives the maneuver commander direct authority and fits offense/fluid fights. Support relationship (DS, R, GSR, GS) leaves command, admin and logistics with the parent unit

entries.n: Engineer Planning Considerations (Speed, Economy, Flexibility, Decentralization, Priorities)
entries.desc: Engineer tasks are resource-intensive in time, materials, manpower and equipment
entries.use: Planning engineer tasks at any level
entries.how: Use existing facilities, standardization, simple design, modular and prefabricated components, phased construction; conserve resources; use adjustable standard plans; decentralize authority; set priorities and accept risk on low priority tasks

entries.n: Engineer Staff Integration and Engineer Staff Officer Duties
entries.desc: Every echelon down to BCT has an organic engineer planner. Only one engineer officer is designated the engineer staff officer; at task force and company level the senior supporting engineer typically acts as the task force engineer (ATP 3-34.22)
entries.use: Integrate engineer considerations into the supported unit's staff
entries.how: Engineer staff officer: determines engineer information requirements, writes the engineer annex, plans forward supply points for Class IV/V and engineer equipment parks, identifies haul assets and medevac needs, estimates Class III/IV/V needs, tracks supplies, coordinates MSR clearing and EOD, and integrates the environmental program

entries.desc: Geospatial planning cells (GPCs) are the only units with a dedicated geospatial data generation capability and manage the TGD. AGC provides reachback; NGA produces digital terrain and feature data (analysts may attach at division and above); DLA distributes maps
entries.use: Geospatial support at each echelon
entries.how: Theater/CCMD: data generation, analysis, management, quality control. Corps/division: database management, mission planning, IPOE. Below division: current operations and updating the SSGF for the COP. Geospatial teams need classified tactical network access to update and push data

entries.n: Joint Engineer Staff Organization and Responsibilities
entries.desc: Joint engineer responsibilities and key functions cover planning theater support, recommending missions and standards, construction/real estate priorities, Class IV, joint boards, the ESP, contract support, and environmental considerations
entries.use: Organize engineers on a joint force staff
entries.how: Place engineers as a cell in J-3 (movement/maneuver, fires, protection focus), J-4 (sustainment focus) or as a separate staff reporting to the JFC (preferred when engineering is a key element or split between combat and general)

entries.desc: Process used to meet force projection requirements
entries.use: Request engineer forces, units or individual augmentees
entries.how: Engineer staffs at the GCC and theater army are primary contacts; subordinates forward requests to theater army, then CCDR, then the Joint Staff for sourcing (JP 1-0)

entries.n: Plans and Orders for Engineer Operations
entries.desc: Plans and orders convey mission, intent and concept; task-organize, allocate resources and assign tasks. Annexes carry detail
entries.use: Direct engineer operations through supported-unit and engineer-unit orders
entries.how: All follow the five-paragraph format: situation, mission, execution, sustainment, signal. Plan types include OPLAN, CONPLAN, OPORD, service support order, warning order, FRAGORD

entries.desc: The ESP follows a broad order outline but is not a format guide for OPORDs/OPLANs
entries.use: Joint planning to identify essential engineering capabilities, locations and times
entries.how: Produced by joint engineer staff as the most critical engineering appendix to a joint OPLAN; format in CJCSM 3122.05

entries.desc: Sustainment functions: supply, field services, transportation, maintenance, health service, HR, finance, legal, religious, band. Leaders must submit accurate, timely personnel and logistics reports
entries.use: Keep engineer units supplied and maintained
entries.how: Engineer units depend on the Forward Support Company for fuel, supplemental transport of Class IV/V and limited field maintenance. Above BCT, the sustainment brigade (general support) and CSSB support EAD units. The supported unit provides Class IV and V construction and obstacle materials regardless of command/support relationship

entries.n: Command and Control of Engineer Forces (Including Degraded Communications)
entries.desc: C2 has two functions: command of engineer forces and staff control of assets and activities
entries.use: Control engineer forces and assets critical to the mission, including during communication breakdowns
entries.how: To maintain C2 when comms are degraded, train to: employ all C2 systems, operate dispersed CPs, maintain an other-than-digital COP, manage information with analog processes, monitor channels and crosstalk, keep manual running estimates, run CP battle drills

entries.desc: Outputs feed boards such as Protection Working Group, Joint Facility Utilization Board and Joint Targeting and Coordination Board. Geospatial units may form the GEOINT cell
entries.use: Coordinate functional or multifunctional activities
entries.how: Working groups prepare material at action-officer level; boards set policy, priorities and oversight; cells integrate functions. Engineer staff may chair construction-related groups. Bring analysis of why data matters, not just data

entries.n: Planning Processes (Army Design, MDMP, Troop Leading Procedures)
entries.desc: Value lies in the result, not the process
entries.use: Select a planning method for the mission and time available
entries.how: Do in detail if time permits or abbreviate when time-constrained. Engineers also use the running estimate, framework of assured mobility and development of essential M/CM/S tasks

entries.desc: A running estimate assesses friendly capabilities, enemy capabilities, civil considerations and OE effects, and is continuously updated
entries.use: Early integration of engineer considerations into combined arms planning
entries.how: Mission analysis steps for engineers: analyze higher HQ orders (intent, mission, concept, timeline, AO); IPOE and terrain/weather; enemy and friendly M/CM/S capabilities; specified/implied/essential tasks, assets, limitations, risk, time; risk assessment (safety, environment); obstacle intelligence; recommend CCIR; integrate engineer recon. COA development: develop scheme of engineer operations, refine essential M/CM/S tasks, allocate forces, set priority of effort

entries.desc: Expedient/rapid construction techniques are selectively employed to meet mission timelines
entries.use: Facility shortfalls that cannot be sourced from existing assets
entries.how: Plan expeditious construction of shortfalls; Service/HN/alliance/coalition should build during peacetime where possible; operational contract support augments. If time prevents new construction, seek alternatives; consider expedient construction such as prefabricated buildings or clamshell structures (minimum time, cost, risk)
entries.eq: Prefabricated buildings; clamshell structures; operational contract support

entries.desc: Funding requirements include facility construction, associated contract administration services, and real estate acquisition and disposal services. The commander articulates funding requirements
entries.use: Funding early engineer reconnaissance and facility acquisition
entries.how: Adequate funding must be available for early reconnaissance and acquisition by construction or lease. Do facility construction planning routinely so mission-essential facilities are identified in advance and on-the-shelf designs are ready. For construction funding see JP 3-34

entries.n: Construction Standards and Unified Facilities Criteria (UFC)
entries.desc: UFC are jointly developed and managed by USACE, NAVFAC and the Air Force Civil Engineer Center; they are effective upon issuance and may be compulsory for contingency/enduring general engineering tasks. CCDR/ASCC base camp standards consider regional troop living conditions; standards in OPORDs/FRAGORDs may take precedence over guidebooks. See ATP 3-34.40 and JP 3-34
entries.use: Choosing the standard a facility is built to
entries.how: CCDR specifies construction standards in theater; the Joint Facilities Utilization Board periodically revalidates them. Standards are guidelines; CCDR determines exact construction type. Differences between nonpermanent and permanent construction can be marked. UFC cover pavement design, water supply, military airfields, concrete design and repair, plumbing and electrical, and are distributed only electronically (UFC Index, UFC Library, NAVFAC Engineering Criteria and Programs Office, Construction Criteria Base Index)

entries.desc: Process described in TM 3-34.42. General engineering missions can arrive via OPORD, FRAGORD, warning order or verbally
entries.use: Running an engineer construction project from directive to turnover
entries.how: Project management has three parts: preliminary planning, detailed planning, project execution. Begins at unit level with the construction directive (who, what, when, where, why; plans, specifications). Analyze a construction directive like a fragmentary order. Products usually generated with JCMS: design, activities list, logic network, critical path method or Gantt chart, bill of materials. Reachback tools/organizations: US Army Engineer School, UROC, Air Force Civil Engineer Support Agency, NAVFAC, Army Facilities Components System
entries.eq: JCMS; Army Facilities Components System; reachback organizations

entries.desc: Combat engineering: conduct mobility, countermobility, survivability. General engineering: restore damaged areas and essential services; construct and maintain sustainment LOCs; engineer construction support; mobile electric power; facilities engineer support; environmental compliance; waste and distribution facilities. Geospatial engineering: generate, manage, analyze and disseminate geospatial information
entries.use: Tailoring the engineer force to requirements
entries.how: Assess requirements in terms of the three disciplines to tailor the force

entries.n: Engineer Task Organization and C2 Headquarters
entries.desc: Theater Engineer Command: C2 for task-organized Army engineer brigades and other units for the joint force/land component/Army commander; main CP and two CCPs; augmentable with USACE FFE. Preferred organization for operational command of engineers above corps. Engineer Brigade: controls up to five mission-tailored engineer battalions across all three disciplines; not designed to control terrain; one or more required in a division or corps when brigade-level C2 is needed. Engineer Battalion: controls any mix of up to five mission-tailored companies; typically in the engineer brigade, MEB, or supporting a BCT
entries.use: Choosing the engineer HQ that commands engineer forces
entries.how: Task organization allocates assets and sets command/support relationships. Engineer forces may be task-organized to non-engineer HQs (e.g., Sapper company attached to a BCT; clearance company OPCON to a MEB). An engineer brigade or battalion HQ usually provides longer-term C2
entries.dim: Engineer brigade: up to 5 battalions; Engineer battalion: up to 5 companies; TEC: main CP + 2 CCPs

entries.n: Engineer Functional Control and Control Mechanisms
entries.desc: Engineer work line: a coordinated boundary or phase line used to compartmentalize an AO to indicate where specific engineer units have primary responsibility for the engineer effort
entries.use: Exercising control over engineers
entries.how: Operators use maneuver graphics; engineers use standards, priorities, engineer work lines and obstacle free zones. Establish policies and construction standards, assign priorities, delegate authority (e.g., employing scatterable mines), set relationships with USACE, assign missions, write engineer portions of plans and set graphic control measures including engineer work lines. Use routine reports, supporting engineer cells, running estimate and supporting unit CPs

entries.desc: Risk management is the process of identifying, assessing and controlling hazards that arise from operational factors and balancing those risks with mission benefits
entries.use: Identifying, assessing and controlling hazards during all operations process activities
entries.how: Balance risk against mission benefit. See ATP 5-19 for the process

entries.n: Principles of Sustainment Applied by Engineers
entries.desc: Engineer resources are not easily resupplied and may present a tempting target. Engineers usually lack lulls for sustainment since many missions occur during lulls, so plan continuous support
entries.use: Applying the eight sustainment principles to engineer support
entries.how: Principles: integration, anticipation, responsiveness, simplicity, economy, survivability, continuity, improvisation. Integrate: sustainment is not an afterthought. Anticipate: forecast Class IV and V early; anticipate financial/contract management, fuel, maintenance needs; use HN assets. Respond: reconnoiter local materials, preconfigured loads, pre-positioned supplies. Simplify: mission-type orders, standardized procedures, preconfigured loads. Economy: improvise within shortfalls. Survivability: protect Class IV/V with camouflage, concealment and overhead cover. Continuity: plan continuous, routine and emergency logistics. Improvise: know local resources and train on improvised methods

entries.desc: Materials and products need proper transportation, handling, storage and disposal
entries.use: Making sustainment means survivable
entries.how: Construct sustainment bases and clear LOCs; build ammunition holding areas; provide revetments or other hardening for POL products. Manage wastewater, medical, hazardous and solid waste with integrated waste management programs

entries.desc: Supported unit provides fortification, barrier and construction materials, mines and demolitions needed for tasks assigned to supporting engineers, regardless of command/support relationship (para 7-15)
entries.use: Planning and tracking engineer logistics at each echelon
entries.how: Write engineer annex/appendixes (distribution of command-regulated supply classes and special equipment); plan locations of the engineer forward supply point (Class IV/V engineer-configured loads) and engineer equipment parks (e.g., tactical bridging) in coordination with the S-4/G-4; identify haul assets (including HN); identify MEDEVAC coverage; identify critical equipment shortages; give S-4/G-4 initial estimates of Class III (construction), Class IV and V (countermobility, survivability) and Class IV (construction); track Class IV/V flow; coordinate route and area clearance with the explosive hazard coordination cell; coordinate EOD; advise on environmental policy and site surveys

entries.desc: Commander provides insight during the supported unit's planning
entries.use: Keeping an engineer unit supplied and mission capable
entries.how: Coordinate external support; track push packages; set unit resupply points; monitor equipment location, maintenance status, fuel consumption; update Class IV/V needs after site reconnaissance; consolidate and forward logistics, personnel, casualty reports; supervise casualty/detainee/damaged equipment evacuation; orient replacements; conduct sustainment rehearsals; supply field sanitation; integrate EOD; oversee environmental compliance

entries.desc: In BCTs, track essential sustainment tasks for all supporting engineer units and integrate augmenting EAD engineers' supply needs into brigade sustainment plans
entries.use: Starting when the supported unit gets a warning order
entries.how: Focus on the upcoming mission and sustainment of all organic and task-organized engineer units. Essential elements: Class I, II, III, IV, V and IX supplies and personnel losses. Use the running estimate to compare requirements with reported unit status, then coordinate with the supporting sustainment unit/forward support element. Input goes to base OPORD and paragraph 4 of the engineer annex. Consider a field maintenance team per engineer unit, preconfigured barrier loads, and OCS integration (ESP)

entries.desc: Form referenced: DD Form 2993 Environmental Baseline Survey (EBS) Checklist (References)
entries.use: Environmental risk and waste management during sustainment
entries.how: Complete environmental risk assessments; integrate environmental considerations into each MDMP step; survey and record environmental conditions throughout the life cycle of an occupied site; follow policies, mitigate impacts, manage waste storage/collection/disposal. See ATP 3-34.5 and TM 3-34.56/MCRP 3-40B.7

entries.desc: Contracted support differs from military support: authorized contractor personnel are neither combatants nor noncombatants; they are not in the chain of command and are managed through contracts and a unit contracting officer representative; they perform only tasks specified in the contract. Most engineer units lack dedicated contingency contracting teams; support comes from the operational contract support brigade, joint command or USACE district
entries.use: Anticipating problems unique to engineer support
entries.how: Heavy equipment needs low-density haul assets and often exceeds size/weight restrictions; low-density equipment makes maintenance and Class IX parts hard and mechanics scarce; high fuel use and difficult refueling (travel to fuel points cuts productivity; fuel trucks at scattered sites are at risk); construction materials need long lead times and may be dictated to local procurement; frequent moves and task-organization changes ripple through sustainment; demand exceeds capacity, tempting delayed preventive maintenance and local procurement; waste management burden, plan for population surges
entries.wn: Contractors perform only tasks in their contract; not in the chain of command

entries.n: Defense Support of Civil Authorities (DSCA) - Engineer Tasks
entries.desc: DSCA is conducted in support of local, state and federal agencies; U.S. law limits military actions (particularly Regular Army). Army National Guard often responds first for state authorities. USACE keeps a constant response capability. Four primary tasks: domestic disasters, domestic CBRN incidents, civil law enforcement support, other designated support
entries.use: Responding to natural/man-made disasters, accidents and incidents in the U.S. and territories when events exceed civilian capacity
entries.how: Engineer DSCA tasks: construct/repair rudimentary surface transportation, basic sanitation and public facilities and utilities; detect/assess water sources and drill wells; construct feeding centers; environmental reconnaissance and technical advice; waste treatment and disposal facilities; base camp construction; electrical power generation and distribution; infrastructure reconnaissance, technical assistance and damage assessments; emergency demolitions; debris/route clearing. Primary focus is restoring essential services. Engineer equipment suits rubble/debris removal for rescue and access; likely needs include temporary shelters, water and sanitation
entries.eq: Engineer equipment (rubble/debris removal), water well drilling, temporary shelters, power generation
entries.wn: U.S. law carefully limits actions military forces may conduct in the U.S. and territories
entries.src: FM 3-34 paras A-1 to A-4, A-6

entries.n: Notional Engineer Support to DSCA by Discipline
entries.desc: Also A-5: combat engineer route clearance may be critical; general engineering missions include base camp, sanitation, power; debris/route clearing; road construction/repair; FACE (repair of paved, asphalt, concrete runways/airfields); expedient landing strips for manned/unmanned aviation; installing FOD-prevention assets for rotary-wing aircraft; temporary bridges; port/airfield/RSOI upgrades
entries.use: Matching engineer disciplines to DSCA missions
entries.how: General: horizontal and vertical construction, LOC construction and repair/maintenance, infrastructure reconnaissance, electrical power, utilities, sanitation, survey and design, manage construction, engineer advice, firefighting. Combat: reconnaissance, assault bridging, combat roads, FACE. Geospatial: generate/collect geospatial data, manage map data, analyze terrain, partner with local authorities, advise commander on terrain, answer terrain questions, manage SSGF for COP, disseminate hard/soft terrain products, digital services

entries.n: Urban Search and Rescue (Engineer) in DSCA
entries.desc: Training covers rescues involving rope, confined spaces, vehicles and machinery, trenches, and structural collapse
entries.use: Rescue during DSCA
entries.how: Engineer units tasked for urban search and rescue (rescuer or extraction) must be qualified through formal training as level one or level two rescuer
entries.wn: Formal qualification required

entries.desc: USACE and institutional general engineering have the preponderance of the roles
entries.use: Planning domestic disaster support
entries.how: Planning differs from offense/defense/stability because hazard is unpredictable. Geospatial engineers produce predictive analysis of potentially impacted and support areas. Local and state lead; federal supports under the National Response Framework. Army commanders support designated agencies; engineers plan geospatial products for life-support areas and may provide manpower or unique capabilities (water well drilling, temporary shelter, power, firefighting). Environmental compliance is tasked to domestic agencies such as EPA or Fish and Wildlife Service

entries.desc: Four levels of estimates: (1) Order of magnitude (preliminary) - limited info, rough costs for budget and to program labor; method: adjusted historical data. (2) Budget/planning - engineering parameters from historical databases; method: square foot, cubic foot, means, parametric. (3) Definitive - automated software, used to award contract work. (4) Detailed - most accurate, most time to complete, done manually using the materiel/quantity takeoff method by the engineer unit
entries.use: Deciding which kind of estimate fits the planning stage
entries.how: Know that unit-level crew estimates are the 'detailed' (manual takeoff) level; budget/order-of-magnitude are done by higher HQ, USACE, NAVFAC
entries.dim: Cognizant org: Preliminary planning = USACE/NAVFAC (order of magnitude); Budget/planning = engineer unit higher HQ; Definitive = estimating software; Detailed planning = engineer unit (manual materiel/quantity takeoff)
entries.wn: Chapter 5 data is designed for detailed estimates; it is not intended to set production standards

entries.n: Break a project down for estimating (master activity, construction activity, work element)
entries.desc: Master activities = MasterFormat divisions (e.g., 03 Concrete, 31 Earthwork). Construction activities = subsets with clear cut-off points. Construction work elements (work items) = single trade/skill definable item expressed by a work rate (time per unit of measure). Example work element: placing a concrete grade beam direct from chute at 0.480 man-hours per cubic yard
entries.use: Structuring a project before takeoff
entries.how: Break project into master activities (MasterFormat divisions), then construction activities, then construction work elements; estimate each work element separately and summarize
entries.dim: Work element number is 12 digits: first two = master activity/division (Level 1); next two pairs = Level 2 and Level 3; optional Level 4 pair after decimal; last four digits after a dash = user-assigned sequence number. Master activities: 00 Procurement/contracting, 01 General req, 02 Existing conditions, 03 Concrete, 04 Masonry, 05 Metals, 06 Wood/plastics/composites, 07 Thermal/moisture, 08 Openings, 09 Finishes, 10 Specialties, 11 Equipment, 12 Furnishings, 13 Special construction, 14 Conveying, 21 Fire suppression, 22 Plumbing, 23 HVAC, 25 Integrated automation, 26 Electrical, 27 Communications, 28 Electronic safety/security, 31 Earthwork, 32 Exterior improvements, 33 Utilities, 34 Transportation, 35 Waterway/marine, 41 Materiel processing/handling equip, 46 Water treatment equip
entries.wn: Work element number is for estimating data organization only - not used for scheduling

entries.n: Know what the estimator must be given before starting
entries.desc: Key items to be provided: (1) drawings and specifications; (2) master and construction activity listing plus narrative scope; (3) project materiels and methods or assumptions noted; (4) amount and types of construction equipment available; (5) location, local materiels, quarries, gravel pits, borrow pits, spoil areas, soil types, haul roads and distances, foundation conditions, expected weather, time allotted; (6) availability of labor. Estimates assume normal/ideal conditions unless limits are known; record assumptions and limitations so the crew can adjust
entries.use: Starting a detailed estimate
entries.how: Do not start the takeoff until you have the six key inputs; note assumptions
entries.wn: Carelessly made estimates can jeopardize the project, waste personnel/materiel/time/equipment and jeopardize a tactical or strategic situation

entries.desc: Private industry focuses on unit prices; military engineers focus on man-day quantity to determine labor. Estimate is split into materiel (Ch 2), equipment (Ch 3), labor (Ch 4)
entries.use: Understanding what the labor estimate is for
entries.how: Military estimates man-days, not unit prices; man-days stand in for labor cost
entries.wn: Project estimate is not arranged for managing the job; it identifies minimum required resources

entries.desc: Builder (bricklayer, carpenter, concrete finisher, mason, painter, plasterer, roofer); Electrician (generators/power production, power distribution, interior wiring, motors/controls, telephone); Engineering services (draftsman, surveyor, QA/materiel testing tech); Equipment operator (vehicles/trucks, MHE, pile-driving/drilling/blasting, dozers/loaders/excavators/graders, cranes, rollers/graders/asphalt paving); Steelworker (rigging, placing/fitting/welding/cutting/bolting reinforcing and shapes, sheet metal); Utilitiesman (HVAC/refrigeration, compressed air, water treatment/distribution)
entries.use: Labeling labor in crew/labor estimates
entries.how: Use these six broad trade categories when listing labor by skill

entries.desc: Steps: (1) determine construction work elements from plans/specs and state assumptions; (2) determine materiels by materiel takeoff; (3) scale/count/calculate quantity of each item and record on estimating worksheet; (4) determine waste allowance and add to net quantity to get total (gross) materiel; (5) consolidate/tabulate/summarize like items by work activity into the materiel estimate; (6) supervisors use it to create the BOM or compare to an existing BOM. Net quantity = before waste; gross quantity = after waste is added
entries.use: Producing the materiel estimate / bill of materials input
entries.how: Follow the six steps: define work elements, take off materiels, record on worksheet, add waste, consolidate, give to supervisor for BOM
entries.dim: Rounding to two decimal places is sufficient for most quantity takeoff purposes
entries.tm: Best practice: two independent takeoffs by different estimators, compared as a check
entries.wn: Mistakes in the takeoff carry into equipment and labor estimates. If method of construction differs from the one assumed, crewleader must adjust the materiel estimate

entries.desc: Work items require labor but have no materiel directly tied to the labor (e.g., final grading, finishing concrete) and may not appear on plans. Materiel items have a materiel requirement or value. Decide English vs metric based on the design plans and materiel source (if procuring overseas in metric, estimate in metric)
entries.use: Making sure labor-only tasks are not missed
entries.how: List labor-only work items (final grading, finishing concrete) and give them a unit of measure; use 'lump sum' if no standard unit applies

entries.desc: Rules: read all notes/details (a note may say a component is symmetrical); use specs with drawings (when drawings and specs disagree, specs are normally followed; when plans/elevations/details disagree, the detail drawing is normally followed); identify items by sheet and detail number; use DOD standard unit of issue; work in field-construction order (foundation to roof or clockwise); use a project checklist; confirm drawing scale and check for photocopy reduction; prefer printed dimensions to scaling but verify them; always list dimensions length, width, depth/height; use decimals (feet and tenths) not fractions; keep English/metric consistent; round to two decimals; mark plans as items are taken off; have an independent second estimator check
entries.use: Doing a takeoff from drawings
entries.how: Follow these rules to avoid omissions and errors
entries.dim: Dimension order: length, width, depth/height. Round to 2 decimals
entries.wn: Example error: reading 300 ft as 30 ft on a 100 ft slab gives 3,000 SF instead of 30,000 SF - one error flows into cement, sand, rebar, equipment and manpower

entries.n: Apply waste and loss allowance (net to gross)
entries.desc: Waste and loss arise from shipping, handling, storage, cutting and final fitting (e.g., lumber, conduit, pipe issued in standard lengths longer than needed with unusable remnants). Waste factor should reflect site conditions, intended use of materiel, and skill level of troops. Gross quantity = net quantity + waste allowance
entries.use: Ordering materiel
entries.how: Add waste only after total net requirement is known; use Chapter 5 waste factors by materiel
entries.wn: Failure to make proper allowance gives incorrect estimates. Do NOT carry waste into equipment/labor work-rate quantities (see TM41-3-03 and TM41-4-01)

entries.desc: Long lead items: not readily available in normal supply system, cannot be delivered to the job site in fewer than 60 days from order date, or need special attention. Examples: steam boilers, special doors and window frames, items larger than standard issue, electrical transformers for power distribution; anything not commercial off-the-shelf or not available in the project area
entries.use: Avoiding delivery delays
entries.how: Identify and order early any item not readily in supply or taking 60+ days
entries.dim: 60 days

entries.desc: BOM is developed from materiel, equipment and labor estimates; official record of line items ordered (costs, vendors, NSNs) arranged by category (structural, electrical, mechanical). Includes construction materiels, rental equipment, special tools and safety items not in the unit's organic TE, and technical assistance/contracted services (e.g., fire alarm certification). Project supervisors work with the unit's materiel liaison officer and logistics officer
entries.use: Turning estimates into procurement
entries.how: BOM includes more than construction materiel

entries.desc: Steps: (1) list work elements needing CESE; (2) worksheet per activity; (3) list available resources and methods; (4) take task quantity from materiel estimate (excluding waste); (5) pick work rate per piece of CESE; (6) divide quantity of work by production per day = days of operation; (7) compare to scheduled time and add equipment/groups to finish on time; (8) sum activity estimates for total CESE requirement. Grouped equipment: one loader plus five trucks for 10 days is shown as that group for 10 days, not 10 loader-days plus 50 truck-days
entries.use: Determining CESE needs and days of operation
entries.how: Work quantity / production per day = days of equipment operation; show grouped equipment as group-days
entries.dim: Days of operation = quantity of work / production per day
entries.wn: Sample worksheet: 36,000 CYD at 100 CYD/hr = 360 hr / 8 = 45 eight-hour days

entries.n: Haul-cycle truck requirement worked example (loader and dump trucks)
entries.desc: Example: loader 100 CYD/hr; 10 CYD trucks => 10 truckloads loaded/hr => 6 min loading time per truck. Haul 2.5 mi each way = 5 mi round trip; at 15 mph = 20 min haul; dump 4 min. Round trip = 4 + 6 + 20 = 30 min => 2 loads/hr per truck. Trucks required = 10 / 2 = 5. Output = 100 CYD/hr x 8 hr = 800 CYD/day. To finish 36,000 CYD in 15 working days: 2,400 CYD/day = 3x => 3 loaders, 15 trucks (add 1-2 extra trucks), 2 compactors (tractor + tandem sheepfoot, 1,200 CYD/day each), 2 dozers to spread (1,400 CYD/day each), 1 grader, 1 water distributor, 1 rubber-tired roller on standby
entries.use: Sizing the truck fleet to keep a loader at capacity
entries.how: Trucks needed = loads per hour from loader / loads per hour one truck can make
entries.dim: Loader 100 CYD/hr; dozer spread 1,400 CYD/day; sheepfoot compaction 1,200 CYD/day; 3 days lost per 17 working days to rain assumed (15 working days available); 36,000 CYD / 15 days = 2,400 CYD/day; 2,400/800 = 3. Trips: round-trip miles / mph x 60 = haul minutes
entries.eq: Front-end loader (2.5 CYD), 10 CYD dump trucks, bulldozer, grader, tractor with tandem sheepfoot roller, water distributor, rubber-tired roller
entries.tm: 45 days with 1 loader/5 trucks reduced to 15 days with tripled spread
entries.wn: Add one or two extra trucks so a truck is always waiting to be loaded and to cover breakdowns

entries.n: Use net quantity for equipment/labor rates (backfill example)
entries.desc: Materiel estimate usually includes waste, but when applying a work rate only the required quantity is used. Example: backfill given in linear feet of trench - extra fill ordered as waste is omitted; the amount is determined by trench length and width
entries.use: Applying a work rate to the right quantity
entries.how: Apply work rates to quantity actually worked, not ordered including waste

entries.desc: Considerations: operator experience/training; age and condition of equipment (downtime; loader breakdown stops all trucks, spreaders, compactors); deadlines and space (smaller crews on two or more shifts are more efficient; adjust maintenance cycle if CESE runs two or more shifts); materiel type (wet sticky clay is slow; consider weight, load factor, swell, moisture, compactability); haul distance and speed limits; site conditions and safety limits; climate/weather
entries.use: Adjusting equipment production estimates
entries.how: Adjust rates for operator, equipment age, schedule, materiel, haul speed, site/safety, weather
entries.dim: Average equipment haul speed is usually 40 to 65 percent of speed limit (depends on road condition, intersections, traffic, haul length; long hauls give higher averages). Safety limit example: crane rated 40 tons at 70-ft boom, 45 degrees limited to 85 percent of rating = 34 tons
entries.wn: Do not use the speed limit as the average speed. Production rates in the publication apply to any make/model but get specific data from the operation and maintenance manuals; see FM 5-434/MCRP 3-40D.9 for earthmoving

entries.desc: Mobilization includes loading at origin; transport to site including permits; unloading; assembly and testing; standby. Highway-capable trucks are usually driven and may carry minor items. If equipment location is undetermined, base distance on a circular area around the site. Demobilization is based on the portion returned to origin (may be a percentage of mobilization) plus cleaning/prepping to arrival condition. Plant equipment mob/demob = delivered cost + erection and dismantling - salvage value at end of project; maintenance and repair are operating costs spread across the work
entries.use: Including equipment move-in/move-out in the estimate
entries.how: Include loading, transport, permits, unloading, assembly, testing, standby; demob can be a percentage of mobilization

entries.desc: Standard effort (man-days) = (quantity of work / unit of issue size) x work rate (man-hours per unit) / 8 man-hours per man-day x multiplier. Steps: break into tasks and crews; worksheet per activity; take quantity from materiel/equipment estimates (normally without waste); pick work rate from Ch 5 (man-hours per unit of issue, based on unit of one, e.g., 0.007 man-hours/SF) and convert other forms to match; divide man-hours by 8; apply a multiplier per work element (not one for the whole job); sum all activities
entries.use: Computing man-days for a work element
entries.how: Quantity / unit size x work rate / 8 x multiplier = man-days
entries.dim: 1 man-day = 8 man-hours. Initial estimate multiplier normally 1.0. Multiplier > 1 = less efficient (more hours); < 1 = more efficient (fewer hours)
entries.wn: A single multiplier cannot be applied to the entire job; apply per construction activity/work element. Work rate data are not production standards

entries.n: Man-day definition and types of labor
entries.desc: Man-day = one person's work in 8 hours (standard, does not change; workday hours may). Direct labor = man-days expended directly on a construction task in field or shops, excluding administrative time. Indirect labor = supports construction but does not contribute directly (e.g., construction management, coordinating crews, maintaining tools). Overhead labor = non-productive labor done regardless of mission (e.g., administrative)
entries.use: Counting direct labor correctly
entries.how: A man-day is always 8 hours regardless of workday length; only direct labor goes in the estimate
entries.dim: 1 man-day = 8 hours

entries.desc: See Figure 4-2 for minute equivalents of fractional man-hours (0.017 hr = 1 min ... 1.000 hr = 60 min). See Figure 4-3 for fractional man-day to hours (0.1 man-day = 0 h 48 min ... 1.0 = 8 h)
entries.use: Converting decimal man-hours to minutes
entries.how: Multiply decimal hours by 60 (see table)
entries.dim: 0.1 man-day = 48 min; 0.5 man-day = 4 h; 1.0 man-day = 8 h
entries.wn: Figure 4-2 as printed lists 41 minutes as 0.183 / 0.383; the correct value is about 0.683

entries.n: Factors that affect labor production rate
entries.desc: Considerations: workload/schedule (long hours or no days off sharply reduce hourly production; sometimes add workers or shifts); project site area (maneuver, storage, access; hard-to-reach site causes delays); labor skill/size of crew/training; supervision; job conditions (low-quality finish allows higher efficiency, temporary work average, high-visibility work low efficiency; heavy wet clay harder than sandy loam; bulky materiel needs more time); weather (cold/damp or hot/humid reduce output; rain delays and adds repair/dewatering; heat/protection in cold climates); equipment available; operational environment/location (expeditionary more labor intensive; remote site low productivity)
entries.use: Choosing multipliers for labor estimates
entries.how: Apply multipliers only if you know the specific conditions; otherwise use 1.0

entries.n: Convert civilian (commercial) production rates to military rates
entries.desc: Materiel weights/measures and equipment production figures from commercial publications may be applied directly. Labor hours from commercial publications need a multiplier of 1.33 through 2.00 depending on complexity of the task relative to the skill and training of military engineers. Chapter 5 data is primarily RSMeans building construction cost data modified by military SMEs using historical military data. Labor rates are man-hours per unit of work (one unit, e.g., 1 SF or 1 ft), converted to man-days at 8 hours
entries.use: Using RSMeans or other civilian estimating guides
entries.how: Multiply civilian labor production figures by 1.33 to 2.00 based on task complexity vs troop skill
entries.dim: Multiplier 1.33 to 2.00 (labor only)
entries.wn: Equipment production and materiel weights/measures from commercial sources do not need this multiplier

entries.n: Crew size and trade classifications in Chapter 5
entries.desc: Crew data is primarily from RSMeans and suggests minimum personnel and skill types to safely and efficiently do the task. Two labor categories: Skilled (specific trade e.g., builder, electrician, welder) and Laborer (unskilled in the specialty; general laborers/helpers). Modify for personnel availability, experience, training and operational situation
entries.use: Using minimum crew data
entries.how: Crew sizes in the figures are minimums, not rigid standards
entries.wn: Data covers general engineering; combat engineering data is outside scope (see Appendix A)

entries.n: Project mobilization, scaffolding and general-conditions labor rates (Div 01)
entries.desc: Man-hours per unit: floodlight set (4-light telescoping, trailer mounted) 0.5 each; jobsite portolet 0.5 each; erect and dismantle tubular scaffold (including planks and leveling) 0.040 per SF of wall surface; CESE mobilization or demobilization 3.0 each; tool kit inventory 2.0 per kit; project sign 16.0 each
entries.use: Estimating overhead tasks such as scaffolding, signs, CESE mobilization
entries.how: Use Figure 5-A-1 rates
entries.dim: Scaffold crew: three or four laborers; increase crew size for multiple tiers
entries.wn: The first tier of scaffolding takes more time due to leveling and alignment

entries.n: Temporary construction rates (roads, barricades, fencing, walkways)
entries.desc: Man-hours per unit: gravel road no surfacing 4-in depth 0.090/SY; 8-in depth 0.104/SY; ramp 3/4-in plywood on 2x6 joists 16 in OC 0.070/SF; on 2x10 joists 0.077/SF; fill and place sandbags 0.0280 each; barricade 5 ft high 3 rail 2x8 fixed 1.0640/LF; movable 0.7090/LF; wooden guardrail 3 ft 1x6 on 2x4 posts 0.1060/LF; chain link 11 ga 5 ft high 0.053/LF; 6 ft high 0.070/LF; plywood painted 2x4 frame 4 ft high 0.237/LF; wire mesh on 4x4 posts 4 ft high 0.213/LF; protective walkways 2x12 planks (two uses) 0.031/SF; exterior plywood 1/2-in 0.015/SF; 3/4-in 0.017/SF
entries.use: Estimating temporary site items
entries.how: Use Figure 5-A-2 rates
entries.dim: Protective walkway crew: two to four laborers

entries.desc: Man-hours per unit: topographic survey level area 0.003/SY; hilly 0.012/SY; per acre 10.90 min to 80.00 max; lot location and lines large quantities per acre 18.00 min, 28.80 average, 48.00 max small quantities (3.750 each); property lines perimeter cleared land 0.036/LF; stake out clearing limits (roads/runways) 0.005/LF; layout baseline with offset hubs at 100-ft intervals level 0.005/ft, hilly 0.008/ft; set blue top at 25-ft interval 0.009/ft; layout building bounds 4.50 each; layout and grade pipe/culvert 4.50 each
entries.use: Estimating surveying and layout time
entries.how: Use rates per acre/SY/LF; crew is chief of party, instrument person, 1-2 rodman/chainman
entries.dim: 1 acre = 43,560 SF

entries.n: Site demolition labor rates (pavement, curb, guiderail, fencing)
entries.desc: Man-hours per unit: bituminous road pavement removal 4-6 in 0.1260/SY; concrete to 6 in thick with hydraulic hammer, mesh reinforced 0.2090/SY; rod reinforced 0.2660/SY; concrete 7-24 in thick rod reinforced 2.2170/CYD; concrete curb plain 0.0890/LF; reinforced 0.1160/LF; bituminous curb 0.0600/LF; corrugated steel guiderail remove only 0.320/LF, remove and reset 0.800/LF; precast median barrier remove and store 0.150/LF, remove and reset 0.164/LF; railroad track and ties removal 0.230/LF; ballast 0.128/CYD; remove and reinstall track 1.277/LF; bituminous sidewalk 2.5 in thick removal 0.098/SY; plain concrete 4 in thick 0.200/SY; mesh reinforced 0.213/SY. Fencing: barbed wire 3-strand 0.049/ft; 5-strand 0.076/LF; chain link 8-10 ft high remove only 0.072/LF, remove and reset 0.456/LF. Snow fence on steel posts 10 ft OC, 4 ft high 0.064/LF
entries.use: Estimating demolition of pavement, curbs, sidewalks, fences, guiderail
entries.how: Look up man-hours per unit; crew sizes follow safety and scope

entries.desc: Man-hours per unit: concrete foundations 5.000/CYD; concrete walls 6.000/CYD; slabs on grade no reinforcing 4.000/CYD; with wire mesh 4.000/CYD; with rebar and mesh 6.000/CYD. Selective cutout: sheetrock or suspended acoustic ceilings 0.024/SF; wood door and frame 3x7 ft 0.550 each; steel door and frame 3x7 ft 0.730 each; ceramic/quarry tile 0.050/SF; resilient tile 0.040/SF; wood floor finish 0.060/SF; wood subfloor 0.030/SF; steel framing 0.240/LF of wall; wood framing 0.072/LF of wall; gypsum or plywood wallboard 0.030/SF; corrugated roofing 0.030/SF; 5-ply buildup roofing 0.030/SF; metal windows 0.096/SF; wood windows 0.100/SF. Rubbish: 18-in steel chute 0.798/LF; 30-in chute 1.064/LF; dust partition 6-mil poly 2x4 frame (two builders) 1.064/SF; rubbish disposal up to 5 miles 1.500/CYD. Torch cutting: 1-in plate 0.030/LF; 1-in diameter bar 0.050 each; oxygen lance reinforced concrete wall 12-16 in thick 1.064/LF
entries.use: Estimating building demolition and selective cut-out
entries.how: Use for tear-out of foundations, finishes, doors, windows, framing
entries.dim: Concrete demolition crew: average two tool operators and three to five laborers (pneumatic tools)
entries.eq: Pneumatic tools, torch / oxygen lance, rubbish chutes
entries.wn: Crew sizes dictated by safety, scope, weight and bulk of materiel. Work includes removal and stacking onsite at ground level; upper-story work includes dumping into rubbish chutes; includes salvage (cleaning, pulling nails)

entries.n: Concrete estimating tips - what each labor item includes
entries.desc: Forming labor = fabrication, handling, erection/oiling, ties, tie wire, struts, chamfer, screed guides, bracing/shoring, runways/scaffold, checking during pour; stripping = removing, cleaning, reconditioning. Forming measured in SF of contact surface (or LF of form); screed guides = equivalent edge form length. Reinforcing steel is computed in tons of bars; mesh in SF; labor includes handling, tying, supporting, site cutting. Mixing labor = loading, measuring, wheeling, dumping aggregate and cement, bringing water, operating mixer. Placing = hoisting, spreading, vibrating, screeding to grade. Finishing = floating, troweling, tooling, filling voids; pointing and patching = tie holes and fins. Curing = compound, sand, paper, tarps, burlap, straw, keeping wet. Fine grading = fill/remove, spread, level, compact, sprinkle. Vapor barrier = handle, cut, smooth, seal joints. Cold weather protection = cover with sand/straw/paper, heat water and aggregate, enclosures, heaters
entries.use: Knowing what labor is in the Division 03 rates
entries.how: Check that your scope matches what the rate includes (forming, rebar, mixing, placing, finishing, curing)
entries.wn: Review all drawing categories for concrete use and keep specs aligned with drawings

entries.desc: If drawings/specs give no guidance: splice = 32 times bar diameter, minimum 24 inches per splice, whichever is greater. Bar number = number of eighths of an inch of nominal diameter. Nominal dimensions of a deformed bar equal those of a plain round bar of the same weight per foot
entries.use: Estimating rebar when drawings give no splice detail
entries.how: Splice = 32 x bar diameter, but not less than 24 inches
entries.dim: Splice = 32 x diameter, min 24 in

entries.use: Converting rebar length to weight (tons)
entries.how: Look up pounds per foot by bar number

entries.desc: Max permissible water-cement ratio by weight, non-air-entrained / air-entrained: 2,500 psi 0.67/0.54; 3,000 psi 0.58/0.46; 3,500 psi 0.51/0.40; 4,000 psi 0.44/0.35; 4,500 psi 0.38/see note. Above 4,500 psi non-air-entrained (and above 4,000 psi air-entrained) use trial-batch method (TM 3-34.44)
entries.use: Selecting maximum water per bag of cement
entries.how: Look up max water-cement ratio by weight for 28-day strength
entries.dim: Strength achieved at 28 days; ratios give averages above specified strength
entries.wn: Water-cement ratio is the most important factor controlling strength; determine sand/stone moisture before adding water

entries.n: Concrete mix materiel quantities and the Rule of 42
entries.desc: Rule of 42: add the mix numbers (1:2:4 -> 1+2+4 = 7); 42/7 = 6; cement 1x6 = 6 CF (6 sacks); sand 2x6 = 12 CF = 0.45 CYD; stone 4x6 = 24 CF = 0.89 CYD; total dry mix 42 CF makes 1 CYD concrete. Use Rule of 42 when coarse aggregate not over 2 1/2 in; Rule of 41 when not over 1 in. Waste factor: add 5 percent for jobs of 200 or more CYD of concrete, 10 percent for smaller jobs. Per 1 CYD of concrete: Mix 1 (1:1:1-3/4) 10 sacks, 0.37 CYD sand, 0.63 CYD stone; Mix 2 (1:2:2-1/4) 7.75 sacks, 0.56 sand, 0.65 stone; Mix 3 (1:2-1/4:3) 6.25 sacks, 0.52 sand, 0.70 stone; Mix 4 (1:3:4) 5 sacks, 0.56 sand, 0.74 stone. Sack = 94 lb
entries.use: Estimating cement, sand, stone per cubic yard of concrete
entries.how: Sum mix numbers, divide 42 by the sum, multiply each part; add 5 or 10 percent waste
entries.dim: 42 CF dry mix = 1 CYD; waste 5% (>=200 CYD) or 10% (smaller)
entries.wn: Printed note says 'CDs' of concrete; context is cubic yards

entries.desc: Slab thickness (in) -> CF per SF -> SF coverage per CYD: 2 in 0.167, 162; 3 in 0.250, 108; 4 in 0.333, 81; 5 in 0.417, 65; 6 in 0.500, 54. Per 100 SF: 4 in 33.3 CF (1.24 CYD); 6 in 50.0 CF (1.85 CYD); 8 in 66.7 CF (2.47 CYD); 10 in 83.3 CF; 12 in 100.0 CF (3.70 CYD)
entries.use: Finding concrete needed for a slab by thickness

entries.desc: Source documents for engineer estimates: USCENTCOM Reg 415-1 (The Sand Book); ATP 3-34.40/FM 3-34.400/MCWP 3-17.7 General Engineering (Appendix E base camp estimating); FM 3-05.230 Special Forces Tactical Facilities; TM 3-34.85/MCRP 3-34.1 Engineer Field Data; FM 5-430.00.1 (road design) and FM 5-430.00.2 (airfield/heliport design); GTA 90-01-011 Deployed Forces Protection Handbook (JFOB); MSTP Pamphlet 5-0.3 MAGTF Planner's Reference Manual; UFC guidance. Reachback: USACE Reachback Operations Center (UROC) UROC@usace.army.mil, tel (601) 634-2439/3485, DSN (312) 446-2439/3485; Navy NAVFAC (NAVFACLANT (757) 322-8302; NAVFACPAC (808) 472-1162)
entries.use: Short-fused contingency missions needing data beyond this manual
entries.how: Where to get more data or expert help

entries.desc: JCMS gives access to Army Facilities Components System (AFCS) design, logistics and planning data for initial, temporary and semipermanent construction. Rolls up facilities, BOMs and construction man-hours per mission. Provides over 600 standardized initial and temporary facility designs, over 80 component designs, nearly 5,000 national stock numbers and over 2,800 construction activities. Features: planning, design, management, reporting/communication. Available on request to all U.S. military engineer units (portal: AFCS REDi, 1-877-ARMY-ENG).
