Supervisor may assign a tool custodian: inventory all project tools (usually biweekly), maintain tools and resolve discrepancies, provide secure storage, set accountability (authorize tool kit custody to crew members, usually the senior in a trade; check tools in and out daily), and record lost/damaged tools for replacement (submit paperwork quickly, usually every 2 weeks at tool kit inventories). Lost tools are charged to the individual who last had custody
entries.dim: Inventory usually biweekly; daily check-in/out
entries.wn: Lost tools are charged to the individual who last had custody

entries.desc: Example from the manual: a $45,000 project completed ahead of schedule and under budget is no success if $35,800 of equipment repair and replacement results from negligence
entries.use: Take ownership of equipment, the costliest and most dangerous resource
entries.how: Consider: jobsite access, visitor parking, equipment staging, traffic flow, POL environmental protection; preventive maintenance schedule and its effect on construction schedule (coordinate with field maintenance crews instead of returning equipment to the shop; give rental equipment the same oversight); licensed and trained operators; operator accountable to the project supervisor if equipment comes with an operator; determine if equipment stays for an extended period; who checks out/turns in daily trip tickets; assign someone accountable for each piece; physical security and weekly inventory; accountability of equipment, vehicle and fuel keys and documents, including after hours. Operators use equipment for intended purpose, report abuse/neglect, and document (with photographs) any damage immediately; perform daily prestart inspections and first echelon maintenance (engine oil and coolant checks, washing, lubricating) and promptly report discrepancies. An equipment custodian may be assigned
entries.dim: Weekly equipment inventory; daily prestart

entries.use: Present the project professionally to official and unofficial visitors
entries.how: Keep the site in order, brief the crew for scheduled visits, and have visitor safety items (hard hats, ear plugs, eye protection) on hand. Meet and greet on arrival, introduce leaders, project title/number and crew; guide visitors, no one walks unescorted (except QC or safety inspectors on daily inspections); crew members find a safe breaking point before addressing visitors; get back to visitors with answers you do not know. Notify the client, PW/BOS and contracting office before visits by non-unit personnel E-8 and above. Briefing in the field office: project scope (activities, time in MDs, manpower, material, equipment), client and expectations, budget, civilian subcontractors, project management (top three QC and safety concerns, safety posture and safety rep, major hazards such as trenching, scaffolding, electrical, confined spaces, concerns, delay factors/RFIs), and progress photos
entries.dim: Notify team before visits by non-unit personnel E-8 and above
entries.eq: Hard hats, ear plugs, eye protection for visitors
entries.wn: Do not blame problems on 'they'; do not place blame on another unit. Render courtesies but never at the expense of safely stopping the work

entries.desc: Delays affect the client's plans and may affect the follow-on engineering unit schedule
entries.use: Compare scheduled to actual progress and report it to HHQ
entries.how: Monitoring uses: situation reports (SITREPs) required by supported HHQ (format per unit SOP); labor reporting and timecards; data computations for SITREP input; controlling procedures and corrective actions. HHQ conducts an in-process review at or about the 30-day mark when the operations officer and project managers set a firm schedule committing the unit to the scheduled completion date. Supervisor informs the project manager as soon as the scheduled completion date is no longer achievable; if company leadership cannot regain the schedule they inform the operations officer
entries.dim: In-process review at about 30 days

entries.use: Document construction milestones for HHQ
entries.how: Provide digital pictures of each active project on a regular basis, coordinated with SITREP comments. Use the same point of reference and broadest view over time to show sequence of progress. Also take pictures of working crews and major evolutions for historical/public affairs purposes
entries.wn: Supervisor ensures photos reflect professionalism and do not show safety violations

entries.desc: Labor accounting data feeds construction management and statistics. See appendix F
entries.use: Report labor hours in standardized categories
entries.how: Timecards use three categories: direct labor (construction activity numbers), indirect labor (codes below), and readiness and training. Indirect labor codes: XO1 Equipment, Repair, and Records; XO2 Project and Camp Maintenance Support; XO3 Project Management; XO4 Location Moving; XO5 Project Travel; XO6 Material Support; XO7 Tools; XO8 Administration and Personnel; XO9 Lost Time; XO10 Other
entries.dim: 10 indirect labor codes (XO1-XO10)

entries.desc: Labor is recorded to the nearest whole man-hour. If more than one labor category applies to a man-hour, use the dominant category
entries.use: Record actual man-hours daily and roll them into SITREP feeder data
entries.how: Prepare daily timecards of actual man-hours by all personnel assigned (rows = crew members; columns = direct labor by construction activity number, indirect codes, training; totals). Support element crew leader uses the same timecard marked support element, completes it in duplicate, and both the project supervisor and support crew leader sign; supervisor keeps a copy and turns it in with the lead element card. Record all timecard data daily on a two-week labor summary before submitting timecards through the chain of command; it feeds SITREP feeders, actual MDs per activity, and crew availability
entries.dim: Nearest whole man-hour; two-week labor summary
entries.wn: Fill out timecards honestly and accurately; timecards are the most accurate record of actual man-hours

entries.desc: Example: MA 03 Concrete completed activities total 60 percent; activity 031050 (Set Forms Beam and Canopy) is 50 percent complete and represents 18 percent of the MA, so it adds 9 percent: 60 + 9 = 69 percent. Example: MA 31 weighted 10 x 55 percent = 5.5. Example project overall 38.5 percent. Example: a 20-MD activity 25 percent complete has .75 x 20 = 15 MDs remaining. MDs remaining reflects work left to do, not MDs expended. MDs actual is not part of the SITREP to HHQ
entries.use: Calculate actual percent complete per master activity and for the project
entries.how: SITREP feeder columns: [a] MD estimate (tasked baseline), [b] weighted percent = a / total project MD estimate, [c] MA percent complete (WIP), [d] project percent complete = b x c, [e] earned MDs = a x c, [f] MDs remaining = a - e, [g] MDs actual (from timecards). Overall project percent complete = sum of column d. Compare actual WIP to scheduled percent complete (from the Level II Gantt) to find percent deviation. For each MA in progress complete a Master Activity Percent Complete worksheet: weighted percent = CA MD estimate / total MA MD estimate; total work and work complete (linear feet, square feet, cubic yards...); CA percent complete = work complete / total work; MA percent complete contribution = weighted percent x CA percent complete; MDs remaining = percent of work remaining x MD estimate. WIP is 0 for MAs not started and 100 for completed MAs. Add a comments line describing work since last SITREP; if actual WIP is less than scheduled WIP, explain the delay and give the recovery plan
entries.dim: d = b x c; e = a x c; f = a - e; Weighted % = a / total MD estimate; MDs remaining = (1 - % complete) x MD estimate
entries.wn: If actual WIP falls behind scheduled WIP by more than the HHQ-allowed percent deviation, the unit must advise HHQ, include a plan to get back on schedule, and request approval for any needed changes to the Level I or Level II Gantt chart

entries.n: Man-Days Earned Method for Percent Complete
entries.desc: Example: activity 031050 at 50 percent of 25 MDs = 12.5 or 13 MDs earned; MA 03: 97 / 140 = .69 = 69 percent; project 179 / 454 = .394 = 39.4 percent. Results differ slightly from the WIP method because of rounding to whole MDs
entries.use: Alternative way to calculate project percent complete
entries.how: For each construction activity: man-days earned = MD estimate x percent complete (WIP): complete = full estimate, not started = 0, in progress = estimate x percent. MA percent complete = total MDs earned / total MD estimate. Project percent complete = total MDs earned / total project MD estimate. Either method is acceptable; ask the chain of command which to use
entries.dim: MDs earned = MD estimate x % complete; % complete = MDs earned / MD estimate

entries.n: Level II Gantt Chart - Actual Progress
entries.desc: Hand-drawn and software charts may differ slightly because of rounding and significant figures
entries.use: Plot actual progress against the scheduled progress curve each SITREP period
entries.how: Level II is the primary tool showing actual vs scheduled progress; update it every unit SITREP period (typically two weeks) with percent complete from the SITREP feeder, plotted against the percentages on the chart. Connect the plotted dots to make the actual progress curve: above the planned curve = ahead of schedule; below = behind. A large variation indicates a problem. Level II data is the baseline until the HHQ in-process review, when MD tasking may be renegotiated and the new data becomes the baseline

entries.desc: Contracting office and/or client representatives hold regular progress meetings; use them to give notice of potential schedule problems and to seek technical or coordination help
entries.use: Respond early when a project is falling behind
entries.how: Avoid any delay. Instill a sense of mission and urgency, especially on critical-path activities. Monitoring systems show that a project is in trouble but not why: the project manager must get on the job, observe, and work with the supervisor and crew on corrective actions, and ensure execution is within planning numbers (crew size, crew availability, length of workday). Prefer challenging, realistic schedules over inflated estimates

entries.use: Save man-days by changing method or equipment on upcoming activities
entries.how: Review CAS sheets for upcoming activities where a change of method could increase production efficiency, consult others for MD-saving alternatives. Example: rent a trencher rather than using the unit's backhoe on an underground pipe job. Funding availability affects the choice

entries.use: Compress the schedule by overlapping activities
entries.how: Because logic diagrams are typically finish-to-start (which stretches duration and reduces crew size), compress by working several activities at the same time: split the crew so some start the next activity, or replan with start-to-start or finish-to-finish relationships. Real gains probably need additional people; present the recovery plan to the chain of command, who may assign temporary crew members

entries.n: Regain Schedule: Apply More Resources and Increase Availability
entries.desc: Planning AF is site-specific between 0.75 and 0.85 (0.90 for contingencies). Increasing availability by 10 percent has the same effect as adding another member to the crew
entries.use: Add people, hours, equipment, or raise actual availability
entries.how: First consider getting more productive man-hours from the same people by increasing actual availability. Compute actual AF = MD Actual / (CS x WD x ME), where CS = crew assigned, MD Actual = MDs expended, WD = available workdays (not calendar) in the period, ME = hours worked per day on the job divided by 8. If actual availability is low (below 0.75) consider permanent changes to the crew's daily routine (haircuts, leave, medical appointments, watch standing). If average, raise it temporarily and work with the chain of command to coordinate dental/medical and administrative issues
entries.dim: AF = MD Actual / (CS x WD x ME); planning AF 0.75-0.85 (0.90 contingency); low actual AF < 0.75
entries.wn: Working longer hours changes ME and needs HHQ approval (see para 3.3.4)

entries.n: Level I Gantt Chart - Actual Progress
entries.use: Show unit-wide tasking progress against plan
entries.how: Level I (developed in preconstruction planning) is the primary tool showing actual progress of unit tasking vs scheduled; update every SITREP period (typically two weeks). Baseline remains until the HHQ in-process review, where project managers negotiate MD tasking on documented need and the new data becomes the baseline

entries.desc: Beneficial occupancy date is when the facility is ready to fulfill its intended purpose, available for occupancy, and accepted by the client
entries.use: Move from finished construction to client acceptance
entries.how: (1) Project supervisor requests the pre-final inspection using the Pre-final Inspection Request and Checklist via unit QC staff to the contracting office. (2) Pre-final inspection by unit project manager, supervisor and crew leaders; unit ops officer and/or QC; contracting office; PW/BOS/BCE; client/user representative. Contracting office issues the official punch list; unit completes items (except possibly minor cosmetic work) before setting the final inspection date. (3) Supervisor requests final inspection after punch list items are done. (4) Final inspection outcomes: no discrepancies or minor discrepancies = client accepts, beneficial occupancy date established, one-year warranty begins (minor discrepancies get an official punch list completed expeditiously); discrepancies = client does not accept, punch list issued, repeat until accepted. (5) Operations prepares a transfer letter with two sets of as-built drawings, O&M manuals/parts catalogs/technical service manuals, and statement of actual material cost, labor cost and actual man-days. (6) Contracting office issues an acceptance letter; project files are closed and retained onsite for 2 years
entries.dim: One-year warranty; 2 sets as-built drawings; project files retained 2 years
entries.wn: An excessive punch list indicates the project was not ready to transfer. In most cases the project will not transfer until all punch list items are complete. Do not schedule closeout while significant work remains

entries.use: Prepare the project for the pre-final inspection
entries.how: Supervisor completes and forwards the checklist to QC a minimum of 2 working days before the requested inspection date; it is a guide and not limited to listed items. Items (initialed by supervisor): sitework (final grading/grassing, trash disposal, sidewalks, curbs and paving, light); mechanical (piping/fixtures/equipment, insulation and hangers, water system sterilization, shop drawings, water supply test, gas and oil piping, heating/cooling units, ductwork, thermostats, registers, exhaust fans/hoods, manufacturer catalogs, boiler working test); electrical (catalogs, test all lights, test fire alarms, telephone hook-up, main panel all breakers labeled); concrete and masonry (joints, cracks); structural steel touch-up paint; hardware; doors and windows (clean, fit); finishes (acoustic tile, ceramic/quarry tile, floor covering, painting, plastering); furnishings; general (project package current, as-builts completed, site clean, excess material turned in)
entries.dim: Submit to QC at least 2 working days before inspection

entries.use: Return everything cleaned, inventoried and accounted for
entries.how: Clean, inventory and return all tools, excess material and equipment to the proper outlet. NAVSUP Form 1250-1 Single Line Item Consumption/Requisition Document for missing or broken items accompanies tools and tool kits returned to custodians. Line item requisition forms in red ink with BOM line item numbers accompany all material turned in to MLO. Offer all material, tools and equipment bought with project funds to the customer before considering them excess

entries.use: Record the project as actually built
entries.how: Keep drawings updated during construction to reflect as-built condition; at closeout turn in two sets of as-built (red-line) drawings to the contracting office, reflecting all DCDs and approved FARs
entries.dim: 2 sets

entries.n: Closeout Project Package and DD Form 1354
entries.desc: DD Form 1354 is the legally established method for transferring ownership of Government real property and lets the host base real property office add the facility to its records
entries.use: Complete final documentation and real-property transfer
entries.how: Provide a current and complete project package (including computer-generated data) and the final acceptance letter, forwarded to HHQ via the unit QC staff; completed files remain in the deployed location operations files for the warranty period. Project managers may need to submit DD Form 1354 (Transfer and Acceptance of DOD Real Property) or provide the data to complete it; it is required after constructing a new facility, adding to an existing one, or renovating/upgrading an existing system. Follow service guidance and UFC 1-300-08

entries.n: QC vs QA and the Two Levels of QC Plan
entries.desc: Military engineers must turn concern for quality into an institutional and personal ethic and incorporate it proactively
entries.use: Understand who owns quality and which plan is whose
entries.how: Construction quality management = QA + QC. QA is the contracting office's system to monitor the unit's QC. QC is the engineering unit's system in execution to manage, control and document compliance with plans and specs. Two QC levels: Project QC Plan (project managers and supervisors) and Unit QC Plan (unit QC manager and QC specialists). The unit's QC plan must be accepted by the contracting office before construction starts. Refer to UFGS 01-45-00.00-10; ER 1180-1-6; COMFIRSTNCDINST 4355.1
entries.wn: The unit's QC plan must be accepted by the contracting office prior to the start of construction

entries.use: Know what goes into a project QC plan
entries.how: Project supervisor tailors the plan to project QC requirements approved by the unit QC manager. Cover sheet items - planning phase (1-14): project scope sheet; QC requirements list by spec number; definable features of work submittal list; required skills and training; special licenses; activity hazard analysis (feeds safety plan); QC plan summary/QC inspection plan; testing plan and log; testing equipment required; PPE for testing; submittal procedures and status log; RFI and status log; FAR and status log; DCD file. Execution phase (15-19): preparatory phase checklist file; initial phase checklist file; daily QC inspection reports (including follow-up phase checklist); rework items procedure and list; completion/turnover inspection roles and procedures. Level of QC is commensurate with size, complexity, cost and risk (a sidewalk needs less than a project with many types of construction/materials); operations officer, with project manager and QC manager, directs the amount of QC effort
entries.dim: Items 1-14 planning; items 15-19 execution

entries.desc: Example for reinforcing steel: size, placement, anchoring, lap distance. Reinforcing steel must be at least 1 1/2 inches from inside of forming; reinforcing steel must be lapped 24 inches at splices
entries.use: Capture what must be checked, by spec reference, in plain language
entries.how: Supervisor and crew leaders annotate plans and specs while building the estimate. List the spec/drawing reference number, the QC requirement, and control measure/remarks (the QC plan summary form can serve). Each QC requirement must be specific; measurable or seen in the field; and listed in plain language on the CAS sheet. Cited references must be valid for use by a military service organization (Whole Building Design Guide site or unit SOP)
entries.dim: Rebar clear from inside of forms: at least 1 1/2 in.; rebar lap at splices: 24 in. (manual's example)

entries.use: Break work into separately controlled tasks for QC
entries.how: A DFOW is a task separate and distinct from other tasks, with separate control requirements; may be identified by different trades or disciplines, or the same trade in a different environment; a spec section may contain more than one. Four steps: (1) supervisors and crew leaders make an initial list (Definable Features of Work Submittal form) while numbering activities/work elements; QC manager/specialist validates it when the initial Level III schedule is finalized; (2) place each DFOW on the proper CAS sheet and analyze QC requirements for materials, skills, equipment and testing; (3) the DFOW submittal list becomes the scheduling tool to monitor preparatory and initial phase checklist controls; (4) supervisor monitors the list and flags the two-week schedule to notify the project manager and QA representative of preparatory/initial phase meetings

entries.n: QC Skills, Training, Equipment, Licenses and Activity Hazard Analysis
entries.use: Identify what QC actions need in people, gear, and hazard review
entries.how: Identify skills, training and equipment needed for QC actions, plus contractor/special equipment not on the TOA to be funded on the BOM. Ensure requested training meets QC requirements; if available training gives an equivalent certification but not the exact spec requirement, submit a FAR to the contracting office to change the spec to allow the equivalent. Identify special licenses and submit via the project manager to the unit training officer. Conduct an activity hazard analysis of each definable feature of work; it feeds the project safety plan

entries.n: QC Plan Summary and Independent QC Inspection Plan
entries.use: Consolidate QC requirements and have them independently validated
entries.how: Supervisor and crew leaders create the project QC plan by summarizing QC requirements by activity number from each CAS sheet (Figure 9-2 form). The QC specialist validates it against an independently developed QC inspection plan (what the specialist will use to verify each QC element). The reconciled plan is the source for the preparatory and initial phase checklists and the specialist's daily QC inspections and follow-up phase checklist

entries.n: QC Testing Plan and Log, Testing Equipment and PPE
entries.desc: Examples of agreeing on method: asphalt laid 2 inches thick - measured with a poker device or string line and tape measure? Block required within 1/4-in plumb within 10 feet - string line, level, or other method?
entries.use: Plan and schedule required tests (soil compaction, concrete, etc.)
entries.how: Identify on-site testing requirements and the unit's testing capabilities from each CAS sheet; consolidate by activity number into the QC testing plan and log (Figure 9-4). QC specialist validates with an independent testing plan. Supervisor flags the two-week schedule to notify the project manager, QC manager and QA representative of the test schedule and ensures testing service requests are submitted well in advance; also annotate tests on the Level III Gantt. QC manager/specialist keeps the official test log. If the unit lacks the capability, the QC manager coordinates with other agencies. Agree in advance with the QC specialist and QA representative on exactly how tests are measured. Submit testing equipment requirements through the project manager to the QC manager on the tool requirement summary form and PPE for testing on the equipment requirement summary form; confirm items are on the TOA and available or on the BOM, with remarks on how each item will be used
entries.dim: Examples: asphalt 2 in. thick; block 1/4 in. plumb within 10 ft

entries.use: Handle manufacturer data, shop drawings and samples correctly
entries.how: The design agent generates a submittal register (materials, equipment, systems needing submittals and the approving authority), typically with the plans; project documents usually include UFGS 01-33-00 Submittal Procedures. Supervisor provides submittals as directed by the project manager and QC manager. The Government or authorized representative and the unit QC manager are the only two submittal approval authorities. QC manager maintains the submittal status log

entries.use: Formally ask and track questions about plans and specifications
entries.how: Supervisor submits questions on the RFI form (description, reason, drawing and sheet numbers) and keeps an RFI log. Project manager ensures the RFI is fully researched before forwarding to the QC manager. Route: lead element, QC manager, engineering, operations officer, contracting office. All returned RFIs go in the project package. May be submitted anytime from planning through construction. An RFI should receive a written response within seven working days; faster requests are expedited by exception
entries.dim: Written response expected within 7 working days
entries.wn: An RFI response is not authority to proceed with a changed condition; if the supervisor considers it a changed condition, a FAR is required

entries.use: Formally request a change to plans/specs because of changed conditions
entries.how: Use when site conditions differ from the plans or there are print/design defects. Supervisor researches and submits the FAR form (include drawing and sheet numbers; estimated additional cost and man-days) and keeps a FAR log. Project manager ensures it is fully researched and warrants approval before forwarding to the QC manager. Route original and three copies to the contracting office; contracting office returns original and two copies. The contracting officer or authorized representative is the only approval authority. All returned FARs, approved or not, go in the project package. Check unit SOP for approval limits on labor and material cost of changes
entries.dim: Submit original + 3 copies; contracting office returns original + 2 copies
entries.wn: Only approved FARs and DCDs authorize changes to the plans/specs

entries.use: Record changes directed to plans/specs
entries.how: A DCD is a formal procedure to record changes to plans or specifications approved by the contracting office as directed by the design agent, customer or HHQ. All received DCDs become part of the project package and may arrive anytime from planning through construction

entries.n: Three Phases of QC Control (Preparatory, Initial, Follow-up)
entries.use: Prevent defects and verify work for each definable feature of work
entries.how: Control is preventive, ongoing planning to avoid discrepancies; inspection is after-the-fact examination of ongoing and completed work. Discrepancies found by the QC specialist represent failures in execution of the supervisor's QC plan. Each DFOW goes through three phases: preparatory, initial, follow-up. Project supervisor is primarily responsible for quality of work and production

entries.use: Make sure everything is ready before starting a feature of work
entries.how: Supervisor and responsible crew leader prepare the checklist ahead of the meeting; items must correlate with the QC plan. Attendees: project supervisor, designated crew leader, QC manager/specialist, QA representative. Covers: approvals of submittals/shop drawings, test reports and mix designs; all materials on hand and match approved submittals; storage; tools on hand and working; review each spec paragraph and procedure; preliminary work correct and permits on file; testing (what, frequency, by whom, when, where, test facility approved); safety (activity hazard analysis approved, review EM 385-1-1). Physically check material onsite against submittal approvals and contract requirements, and do safety checks of equipment, to find trade conflicts in time to correct
entries.dim: Notify attendees at least 3 workdays in advance

entries.use: Verify the first segment of work meets quality and safety before continuing
entries.how: Held when the crew is ready to start. Actions: establish required workmanship quality (per QC plan and preparatory meeting); resolve conflicts; ensure required testing is performed; check procedures against the safety plan and activity hazard analysis; document initial phase checklists (lead and support element crew leaders) for the QC specialist's daily QC inspection report. QC manager/specialist and supervisor observe the initial segment to confirm the crew understands and can do the work, check safety, and correct workmanship discrepancies immediately. Decide whether a sample panel is required or the initial work will be kept as the sample. Phase ends when the QC manager or specialist signs the checklist
entries.dim: Notify attendees at least 3 workdays in advance
entries.wn: The initial phase must be repeated for each new crew working onsite or when work does not meet the specified quality

entries.n: Follow-up Phase and Daily QC Inspection Report
entries.desc: See ER 1180-1-6 and NTRP 4-04.2.7 for service-specific formats
entries.use: Document ongoing control and compliance every day
entries.how: QC manager/specialist owns the daily QC inspection report. It documents: required checks, tests and inspections performed; whether work completed or in progress conforms to the QC plan and specs; actions on all three control phases and rework items. Specialist signs (QC manager certifies compliance except as noted); project supervisor signs acknowledging content and posts a copy on the jobsite information board. Follow-up phase starts after the initial phase meeting and ends when the QC manager/specialist signs off the completed work. Supervisors and crew leaders also inspect subordinates' work daily and record findings in the logbook

entries.use: Track and correct nonconforming work
entries.how: Supervisors and crew leaders avoid or correct deficiencies from the start; require rework on nonconforming work. If a deficiency is not corrected that same day, note it on the daily QC inspection report and track on the rework items list (date identified, description, contract requirement, action taken, resolution, date corrected). Supervisor keeps a list at the jobsite; QC specialist keeps an independent list. QC manager has authority to correct any deficiency even if it stops work on a segment and notifies the project manager if the deficiency will significantly impact schedule or cost
entries.dim: Rework over 50 MDs or $500 in materials needs HHQ approval
entries.wn: QC should not allow adding to, building upon, or enclosing nonconforming work. Any rework estimated to require more than 50 MDs or $500 in materials requires approval of HHQ

entries.desc: QA representatives do not fill the same role as QC managers
entries.use: Know what the contracting office QA representative does and whom they talk to
entries.how: QA representative is the primary jobsite POC among project manager, supervisor, QC manager, client, user and contracting office; the QC manager is their primary POC on quality and workmanship. QA tasks include: attend the preconstruction conference and weekly/bi-weekly QC meetings; check certifications of delivered materials and equipment; check as-built status; conduct pre-final and final inspections; site visits and spot-check workmanship; evaluate the unit QC system; observe safety enforcement and testing; prepare noncompliance notices; review/approve the QC plan; comment on schedules; review submittal register, rework list, testing plan and log; review daily QC reports; coordinate utility outages; verify and decide changed conditions (FARs, DCDs). Include the QA representative in all communications affecting execution of the work

entries.n: As-Built Record Drawings and Record of Materials Used
entries.use: Keep red-line drawings and a material record current
entries.how: Supervisor keeps a full-size as-built (red-line) set on site, updated daily with all deviations (approved FARs, DCDs), including buried or enclosed utilities and conditions found during construction. Project manager and QC manager review them every 2 weeks; QA representative checks monthly. QC manager keeps a full-size set, initials each revision, and furnishes a certificate of accuracy before submission. Submit two sets to the contracting office. Supervisor also keeps an accurate record of materials incorporated into the project (project manager ensures it; QC periodically inspects); submitted to the contracting office in the final completion package
entries.dim: 2 sets of as-builts; review every 2 weeks; QA check monthly

entries.use: Know who is responsible for safety and that anyone can stop unsafe work
entries.how: Engineering units have an appointed safety officer, assistant safety officer and safety supervisor; each subordinate component and project site assigns a safety supervisor as a collateral duty who reports to the project supervisor. Each military engineer must learn safe-construction procedures and is empowered to identify and stop an unsafe situation. Operational risk management (ORM) is part of the daily safety routine per DODI 6055.1 and is an inherent part of every safety plan element, not a standalone element

entries.n: Project Safety Plan (Accident Prevention Plan) Contents
entries.use: Know the 17 parts of a project safety plan and that it must be approved before work starts
entries.how: Planning-phase items (1-11): project organization sheet; project scope sheet; definable features of work submittal list; activity hazard analysis sheets; required skills and training; special licenses and permits; safety inspection plan summary; administrative controls; safety equipment required (tools and materials); PPE required; special safety plans. Execution-phase items (12-17): emergency phone number form; daily safety lecture log; daily safety inspection reports; safety hazard/deficiency list; report of unsafe or unhealthy working conditions; completion/turnover inspection roles and procedures. Cover sheet signed by project supervisor, project manager, and safety officer (approve/disapprove)
entries.dim: Items 1-11 planning; 12-17 execution
entries.wn: The project safety plan must be approved before work at the project site can start

entries.desc: A competent person can identify existing and predictable hazards in the surroundings or working conditions that are dangerous to personnel and has authorization to take prompt corrective measures. A qualified person, by recognized degree, certificate, professional standing, or extensive knowledge, training and experience, has demonstrated the ability to solve problems related to the subject matter, work or project
entries.use: Identify hazards and controls for each definable feature of work before starting it
entries.how: Do one for each DFOW; ideally the workers doing the activity develop it (they know the process and hazards); use it as a training tool and review it before work begins. Prepare before any activity with hazards not previously experienced on the project or when a new work crew or support element crew performs the work. Define the activity; identify work sequences, anticipated hazards, site conditions, equipment, materials, and the control measures to eliminate or reduce each hazard to an acceptable level of risk. Name the competent/qualified person(s) for activities such as excavations, scaffolding, fall protection (per 29 CFR 1910, 29 CFR 1926, EM 385-1-1) and submit proof to the safety office before the activity starts. Assign a risk assessment code (RAC) per activity using the risk assessment matrix and ORM process. Review and modify for changing site conditions, operations or competent/qualified persons; adding a person to the list is administrative but the new person must acknowledge in writing that they reviewed the AHA and know current site safety issues
entries.wn: Work does not begin until the AHA is accepted by the safety officer and discussed with everyone engaged in the activity (lead element, support elements, unit safety representatives) at preparatory and initial control phase meetings

entries.use: Identify safety training and permits during hazard analysis
entries.how: Identify skills and training needed during each AHA; a safety supervisor is designated on each project crew and needs required minimum training (get the up-to-date list from the unit safety officer). If special training is not unit-funded, add it to the BOM. Identify special license and permit requirements; submit via the project manager to the unit training officer; coordinate permit requests with the unit QC manager (see para 6.3.8.2)

entries.n: Safety Inspection Plan Summary, Administrative Controls, Safety Equipment and PPE Lists
entries.use: Consolidate controls and gear needed for safety
entries.how: Safety inspection plan summary: consolidate safety requirements by activity number from each CAS sheet and AHA; unit safety officer reviews before the lead element project manager resource-levels and approves. Administrative controls: get the safety officer's list of standard safety actions, policies, procedures and SOPs first. Safety equipment and PPE lists: get the safety officer's standard lists, confirm items are on the TOA and available or on the BOM; list quantity required, quantity onsite, and proper use

entries.use: Know which hazards require their own written plan
entries.how: Specific plans are required for: fall protection; scaffolding; excavation; demolition; confined space; traffic control. Risk assessment from AHAs and mandatory OSHA compliance programs may require additional plans. Use EM 385-1-1 and/or 29 CFR 1926 as a guide and contact the unit safety officer
entries.dim: 6 special plan areas

entries.use: Make sure crews know how to respond to a mishap at this site
entries.how: Tailor the unit's emergency response plan to the project location. Crew members must know the location of the nearest telephone or means of communication, have access to a map or know the nearest medical facility, and know how to report mishaps. Hold rehearsals, especially on first arrival at a new location and when a new support element crew is onsite. Submit to the project manager for approval via the unit safety officer
entries.tm: Rehearse on arrival and with each new support crew

entries.n: Daily Safety Lecture and Daily Safety Inspection
entries.use: Raise hazard awareness for each day's tasks and document control measures
entries.how: Daily safety lectures are coordinated with the schedule and focus on hazards of that day's production tasks; crew leaders must be trained and motivated to properly use protective equipment and follow any specific procedures every time. Safety officer/assistant safety officer produces the daily safety report documenting that required hazard controls are in use; safety inspector signs, project supervisor and project safety supervisor sign acknowledging, and a copy is posted on the jobsite information board

entries.use: Track and close out safety deficiencies
entries.how: Address hazards immediately. Deficiencies not corrected immediately go on the daily safety report and the safety hazard and deficiency list (date identified, description, contract requirement, action taken, resolution, date corrected). Supervisor keeps a list at the jobsite; the safety officer keeps an independent list. Project manager monitors corrective action and resource allocation and must be notified of all mishaps and near mishaps per unit safety SOP. Repeated hazards/deficiencies get command attention if not corrected within several days
entries.dim: Repeat deficiencies escalate if not corrected within several days
entries.wn: Do not allow unsafe work practices to continue. Each crew member has the authority to stop unsafe acts

entries.n: Report of Unsafe or Unhealthy Working Conditions
entries.use: Give every worker a direct path to the safety office
entries.how: Any person may submit a report directly to the safety office. Supervisor posts the proper form on the jobsite information board and briefs crew members on its use. Get current forms and procedures from the unit safety officer

entries.use: Include safety in completion and turnover
entries.how: The project manager, supervisor, safety supervisor and safety officer play a significant role in completion or turnover inspections; use the unit safety officer's SOP for joint facility and site inspection criteria. All received documents become part of the project package

entries.desc: Guidance: FM 3-34.5/MCRP 4-11B, NWP 4-11, AFI 91-301
entries.use: Know the project environmental plan requirement and who approves it
entries.how: Every project needs an approved plan. The contracting office must accept the unit environmental plan before construction starts (UFGS 01-45-20.00-10). Two levels: project plan (project manager and supervisor) and unit plan (unit environmental manager). Supervisor must keep the project plan current and onsite. Project manager engages base public works early to forestall problems and meets with the contracting officer before plan submittal to discuss implementation, later revisions and reporting. Plan contents - planning items 1-10: project organization sheet; scope sheet (general site info, preconstruction site description, photos); DFOW list; activity hazard analyses; skills and training (each crew has a designated HM/HW representative); licenses and permits; environmental protection plan summary; administrative controls; environmental equipment; PPE. Execution items 11-15/16: HM inventory; authorized user list; MSDS file; project environmental inspection checklists; spill response plan; other plans and considerations. Cover sheet approved by the environmental manager
entries.dim: Items 1-10 planning; 11-15 execution (cover sheet also lists 16)

entries.n: Environmental Plan Development (Summary, Controls, Equipment, PPE)
entries.use: Build the environmental plan from CAS sheets and AHAs
entries.how: Environmental protection plan summary: consolidate environmental requirements by activity number from each CAS sheet and AHA; unit environmental manager reviews before the lead element project manager resource-levels and approves. Administrative controls: start from the environmental manager's list of standard actions, policies, procedures and SOPs. Environmental equipment and PPE: get standard lists from the environmental manager, confirm on TOA/available or on BOM; list per activity number the quantity required, quantity onsite and proper use. Permits and licenses go via the project manager to the unit environmental manager and are coordinated with the QC manager. If special training is not unit-funded, add it to the BOM

entries.n: Hazardous Material / Hazardous Waste Management, Authorized User List, and MSDS
entries.desc: Federal law requires the supervisor to inform crew members of the risks and precautions for any HM on the jobsite and ensure the crew knows the MSDS location and use (can be done at the daily safety lecture)
entries.use: Handle, store, and document HM/HW correctly
entries.how: Supervisor and crew leaders identify all HM and understand storage, use and disposal; HM/HW representative keeps an accurate site inventory. Leaders: train subordinates on the HM they handle; keep an up-to-date list of all HM/HW in the area; label, tag or mark containers to identify the material and warn of hazards; keep an MSDS for every HM on site; train personnel to recognize, understand and use MSDS and labels; ensure proper procedures and PPE. The authorized user list is the list of HM authorized for unit use; if an item is not on it, the unit cannot obtain it. Identify HM during planning and have the environmental manager add any missing item. An MSDS summarizes identity, health and physical hazards, exposure limits, precautions, safe handling, PPE, storage, and first aid; one must be on site for each HM, and MSDSs for HM in use are posted on the jobsite information board
entries.wn: If an HM is not on the authorized user list, the unit cannot obtain it. Do not accept materials without an MSDS; MSDS travel with the material

entries.use: Verify environmental protection measures daily
entries.how: Supervisor, a crew leader, the project safety supervisor or HM/HW representative inspects the jobsite daily; inspector signs and files in the jobsite project file. Checklist sections: administration (oil/hazardous substance spill checklist posted in a high-visibility area; emergency phone numbers by field office phones; ignitable/reactive waste separated from ignition sources; smoking and open flames confined to designated area; NO SMOKING signs; MSDS available and workers know how to use them); HM containers/pallets/covers (DOT-approved containers; environmental pallets/covers; drip pans/absorbent; ignitable containers grounded with 6-in freeboard; sealed; not leaking, damaged or overfilled; containers 50 inches from the facility; no heat generation from incompatible waste mixing; marked and labeled; none overdue; oily rags in containers marked OILY RAGS ONLY); safety equipment (warning signs; gloves, face shields, protective aprons); emergency response (stocked spill kit; personnel briefed on response/cleanup, hazards, HW management training); fugitive dust (visible plume extending more than 50 yards from point of origin?); cleaning paving equipment (solvent such as diesel fuel runoff contained); CFC use (Freon recycling equipment; operators certified to service air conditioners)
entries.dim: Containers: 6-in freeboard for ignitable; 50 in. from facility; dust plume: 50 yards
entries.eq: Spill kit, gloves, face shields, protective aprons, drip pans/absorbent
entries.wn: Do not accept materials without an MSDS

entries.use: Be ready for HM/HW spills at every site
entries.how: Required for all construction sites. Covers site-specific response procedures and spill response equipment for each major HM/HW operation. Project manager ensures an approved plan exists; supervisor executes it and ensures crew members are trained. Get up-to-date information, checklists and procedures from the unit environmental manager; see FM 3-34.5/MCRP 4-11B
entries.eq: Spill kits at satellite HM storage areas

entries.use: Include environmental actions in completion and turnover
entries.how: Project manager, supervisor, HM/HW representative and environmental manager have significant roles; follow the unit environmental manager's SOP for turnover/completion actions. All received documents become part of the project package

entries.use: Handle demolition/renovation of older structures safely
entries.how: State environmental regulatory departments closely scrutinize demolition of older structures. Many contain asbestos and lead-based paint, both known health hazards. Installations are required to notify the State before beginning demolition or renovation. If asbestos is suspected, immediately stop work and contact the unit environmental manager. All asbestos-containing materials and lead-based paint must be removed by trained personnel
entries.wn: Immediately stop work and contact the unit environmental manager if asbestos is suspected. Only trained personnel may remove asbestos-containing materials and lead-based paint

entries.use: Minimize airborne dust from construction
entries.how: Address: is a dust permit required; does the project have the proper dust control permit; does it have a dust mitigation plan. Take reasonable precautions whenever an activity produces fugitive dust: conditions agreed in the project permit; sprinkling; compacting; enclosure; chemical or asphalt sealing; cleaning up; sweeping; other measures the project manager specifies
entries.dim: Dust mitigation 24 hours a day, 7 days a week regardless of construction status; plume extending > 50 yards on checklist
entries.wn: Dust mitigation must occur 24 hours a day 7 days a week regardless of construction status

entries.n: Storm Water, Waste Disposal/Recycling, and Wetlands
entries.use: Protect waterways and follow base waste policy
entries.how: Storm water: many projects need a specific plan and permit; consult the host base environmental representative (many bases have a template and can help write the permit). If not required, still follow best management practices to protect storm sewers and waterways. Waste: dispose per base policy, use recycling/reuse programs, and look for ways to reduce project waste. Wetlands: if the project is in a wetlands area, start working early with the base environmental representative on all possible issues

entries.desc: In contingency operations some forms may be waived or vary in format per command/HHQ guidance. Forms may be computer-generated but must have the same content; check source documents for changes
entries.use: Know what goes in the project folder and where
entries.how: Section 1 General Information and Correspondence (messages, tasking letter, deployment calendar, pre-beneficial occupancy inspection request, preconstruction conference summary, predeployment site visit summary, project organization, sign-off sheet, planning milestones, scope sheet, turnover memorandum). Section 2 Activities and Network (Level II Gantt, precedence diagram, master activity listing and summary sheets, two-week schedules, CAS sheets, Level III Gantt, SITREP feeders/photo SITREPs, two-week labor summaries). Section 3 Resources (30/60/90-day list, BOM, equipment and tool requirement summaries, submittal status log, add-on/reorder forms, BOM/MTO comparison, borrow log, long lead list, MTO worksheets, transfer requests). Section 4 Plans (4A QC plan; 4B safety plan; 4B environmental protection plan with all supporting forms and logs). Section 5 Drawings and Specifications (plans, highlighted specs, slab layouts, forming plans, rebar bending schedule, shop drawings, site layout, technical data)
entries.dim: 5 sections

entries.desc: RED HORSE units normally use a design-build process during their training cycle
entries.use: Know the USAF project folder layout
entries.how: Operations holds the official folder; an on-site folder is kept during the project then turned over. Design engineer creates the folder with programming, evaluation and design information; the project engineer/manager maintains it after design until closeout documentation is added. Sections: 1 Approval Documentation (DD 1391/1391c, AF 332 work request or AF 327 work order, AF 813, RED HORSE 1391c cost evaluation, customer notification letter); 2 Design Diary; 3 Funding Documentation (including BOM, receipts); 4 Temporary Duty/Weekly Reports (project OPORD, team roster, TDY orders, weekly SITREPs/cost reports); 5 Construction Diary (blue book, AF 103 work clearance request, reduced-size drawings, project schedule, lab results, problems/site adaptations, minutes); 6 Project Summary (closeout checklist, DD 1354, after action report, photographs)
entries.dim: 6-part folder

entries.n: Alternate CPM: Determine Activity Relationships (Preceded Immediately By)
entries.desc: Manual example: 40-ft by 40-ft by 8-in concrete pad plus a 12-ft wide, 1,000-yard gravel road; activities A-K (clear pad site, clear roadway, acquire gravel, prepare pad foundation, prepare subgrade/subbase, lay gravel, prepare forms, place forms, mix and place concrete, cure concrete, remove forms)
entries.use: Build the logic diagram from an activity list (USA/USMC method)
entries.how: For each activity ask: Start (can it start at project beginning?), Precedence (which must finish before it begins?), Concurrence (which can start/finish at the same time?), Succession (which cannot begin until it finishes?), Lag/Lead (which may start when part of another is done?). Add a 'Preceded Immediately By' column listing only immediate predecessors (enter 'None' if it can start at the project start). Use activity-on-the-node (precedence diagramming): nodes (parallelograms) hold number, duration, resources, ES/EF/LS/LF; start and finish milestones have no duration; arrows show sequence; an activity cannot begin until all activities sending arrows to it are complete. Build the diagram by trial and error: start activities from the Start node, connect followers, connect dangling activities to the Finish node, then check logic. Node numbers must be unique and the number at the arrow head must be greater than at the tail; increment by 5 or 10 to allow insertions
entries.dim: Node numbers increase by 5 or 10; head number > tail number
entries.wn: Only mark immediate predecessors (e.g., B precedes F but does not immediately precede it)
entries.src: TM 3-34.42 App C paras C.2 - C.2.4 / Figures C-1 to C-3

entries.n: Alternate CPM: Time Analysis, Float and ES Schedule
entries.desc: Event times represent the end of a time period (day 5 = end of fifth day)
entries.use: Compute project duration, critical path and float using the node method; build an early-start schedule
entries.how: Put duration and resources in each node from the CAS sheet. Forward pass: ES of first activities = 0; ES + DUR = EF; the largest EF among incoming arrows sets the next ES; the largest EF into Finish is project duration (example 14 days). Backward pass: last activities' LF = project duration; LF - DUR = LS; smallest LS among outgoing arrows sets the LF of the preceding activity. Critical if ES = LS, EF = LF, and ES/LS + DUR = EF/LF. TF = LS - ES = LF - EF; TF = IF + FF; interfering float IF = LF - (ES of following activity, using the smallest); FF = TF - IF. Example: node 25 TF = 7, IF = 6, FF = 1. Early start schedule: list activities in numerical order with followers in parentheses, e.g., 15 (30, 45); bracket the time span from ES+1 to LF; schedule resources flush left from ES; mark an 'X' for each day of interfering float from the right bracket leftward; remaining blanks are free float; noncritical activities leading directly to Finish have all FF. Multiple-resource schedules list each resource on a separate row with separate daily sums
entries.dim: TF = LS - ES = LF - EF; TF = IF + FF; IF = LF - ES(following); FF = TF - IF
entries.src: TM 3-34.42 App C paras C.3 - C.6 / Figures C-4 to C-11

entries.desc: Lag factor example: paving can start after 25 percent of compaction of a 10-km road; adding a 25-percent lag factor reduces duration from 24 to 15 time periods. Another example: soldiers with hand tools start digging a fighting position while waiting for the SEE excavator. Forward pass with lag: (DUR of activity x percent lag) + ES = ES of following activity. Backward pass: [DUR of previous activity x (1 - percent lag)] + LS = LF of previous activity
entries.use: Shorten a schedule that exceeds HHQ's completion date
entries.how: Examine the critical path for activities whose durations can be shortened; shortening a noncritical activity does not shorten the project. Options: add resources to critical activities (more equipment/personnel or longer hours; a moderately extended workday is usually the most economical and productive; double shifts or weekends possible); commit more materials (e.g., more forms for concrete slabs rather than reusing, or own transportation to expedite deliveries); redefine logic (do sequential activities concurrently, or add a lag factor so a following activity can start after part of the first is done). After shortening a critical activity by one time unit, re-check whether other paths became critical. Compute cost of each possible reduction and choose successive reductions at least additional cost
entries.dim: ES(next) = DUR x % lag + ES; LF(prev) = DUR(prev) x (1 - % lag) + LS; example 25% lag: 24 to 15 periods
entries.wn: Crashing always costs money if the original network used the most efficient methods. Expediting can create safety concerns and loss of efficiency (nights, weekends, extended continuous operations); watch equipment maintenance during extended use
entries.src: TM 3-34.42 App C para C.7 / Figure C-12

entries.desc: Variations if the result is unacceptable: split an activity already started into two; delay an activity that starts earlier by more than one period (needs plenty of float); delay several activities with plenty of float rather than one critical or near-critical one. Sample problem: 14 squads reduced to 11 because 3 squads are needed for post cleanup; two resource delays and one logic delay; project duration unchanged and three more activities (15, 20, 35) became critical
entries.use: Fit an early-start schedule to limited resources with minimum project delay
entries.how: Three tasks: resource-constrain the ES schedule, update the logic network, update the ES schedule. Step 1: working chronologically left to right, find the first period where requirements exceed available resources. Step 2: choose an activity to delay by priority: (1) an activity that starts that period (do not stop one already under way); (2) one that frees enough resources to solve the problem (or a combination); (3) the one with the most total float; (4) the one with the most free float; (5) the one with the shortest duration. Step 3: delay it one period and follow the delay through follow-on activities (those whose ES precedes the new EF move to the next period). Step 4: re-sum resources. Step 5: repeat for next period. Step 6: mark 'R' to the right of the LF bracket for resource delay, 'L' for logic-only delay (R takes precedence). Step 7: draw resource flow arrows from the activity releasing the resource (EF one period before) to the resource-delayed activity, counting mothballed (unused) resources. Step 8: add a resource dummy arrow to the logic network for each flow arrow. Step 9: redo the time analysis (new forward/backward pass; critical path may change). Steps 10-12: list new follow-on activity numbers, re-mark timeframes (ES and LF brackets), recompute interfering float and update Xs
entries.dim: Priority order: starts this period > enough resources freed > most TF > most FF > shortest duration
entries.wn: The manager ultimately decides which activities to delay; must understand the techniques. Do not delay an activity already under way if avoidable
entries.src: TM 3-34.42 App D paras D.1 - D.5 / Figures D-1 to D-8

entries.desc: Aim for positive acknowledgement of preparedness and ownership: know the project, show ownership, appear confident rather than defensive. A hard question usually means the evaluator has firsthand knowledge of a problem area
entries.use: Prepare the brief to the commander/HHQ representative
entries.how: Use a modified five-paragraph order. 1 Situation: managers, team, organization; supported operation and basis for tasking. 2 Mission: project title, scope, name, customer, location, budget and dates, and the order of presentation (plans overview, crew makeup, walk through Level II, specific requirements and concerns, summary of plan of attack). 3 Execution: use key drawings; crew number/rate makeup/experience and surge plan; walk the Level II and precedence network chronologically, pointing out high-interest areas (do not talk to every activity and duration; do not wing it or bluff; MA list sanity check). 4 Administration and logistics: CAS sheets (a well-prepared one lets someone with basic construction experience start working; troubleshoot variable planning factors actually varying, QC items measurable and understandable, safety section with references and equipment); QC plan (more than cut-and-paste of CAS QC checks; reviewed with QC SME); safety plan (through safety department, ORM applied to every high-risk activity, equipment available, contracting office approval); materials (LL items tracked with MLO; inspect on arrival to allow returns/reorders); equipment (CESE and tools available, alternate plans B, C, D); training; customer issues (historical, cultural, environmental, high-visibility, flag interest). 5 Command and signal: at minimum, reporting requirements

entries.n: Labor Accounting System (Direct, Indirect, Readiness and Training)
entries.desc: System is the NCF system (COMFIRSTNCDINST 5312.1A) and may be adopted by all services unless HHQ or unit SOP directs another
entries.use: Charge man-hours to the right category on timecards
entries.how: Direct labor: labor directly on assigned construction tasks in the field or shop, reported under the project number; includes project and site surveying, shop prefabrication, camp maintenance done as direct labor tasking, mineral products operations, and construction equipment operation on a tasked project. Indirect labor (reported under codes, not project number): XO1 equipment/tool maintenance and repair, spare parts, related recordkeeping; XO2 planning, estimating, MTOs, trouble desk, project planning and scheduling; XO3 supervising project/shop work, arranging equipment and tools, scheduling utility outages, coordinating with crews, inspections, meetings, turnover; XO4 mobilization/demobilization of equipment, tools, field offices, motor pool, taxi drivers, road master; XO5 travel to and from project sites; XO6 receipt, storage, inventory, issue, delivery of materials, records, ordering and follow-up; XO7 tool maintenance, inventory control, ordering parts and rental equipment; XO8 administration and personnel (legal, counseling, education, medical and dental, leave and liberty, security, timekeeping, etc.); XO9 lost time (inclement weather, awaiting transportation, shortage of tools or material, unauthorized absence and confinement); XO10 other indirect. Readiness and training: military exercises, disaster preparedness, mobility, technical training, service schools, safety training, any organized unit training
entries.dim: Direct, indirect (XO1-XO10), readiness and training

entries.n: Choose the survey precision the job needs
entries.desc: The officer or NCO in charge usually sets the degree of accuracy. The surveyor picks methods and procedures by considering allowable time, the tactical situation, construction-force capabilities and current conditions. Results cannot be more accurate than the least precise measurement used, so angular and linear precision must be kept comparable. Watch for cumulative or systematic errors (instrument maladjustment/calibration, error-producing habits)
entries.use: Deciding how accurate a survey has to be before you start
entries.how: Run the survey only as precise as the job requires, in the least time. Location surveys need more accuracy than recon; erecting structural steel needs more than initial roadbed grading
entries.dim: Results are no more accurate than the least precise measurement involved
entries.wn: Systematic errors from maladjusted or uncalibrated equipment accumulate. Machinery foundations and angular limits of fire on training ranges are examples that can demand high precision

entries.desc: Rules: use a sharp hard pencil (4H preferred); do not crowd data (use more pages); keep sketches plain and uncluttered; record values to the precision measured; use explanatory notes (usually right-hand page, same line as the data they explain); follow basic note-keeping rules in TM 5-232. Office entries such as computed or corrected values should be clearly distinguishable from original material, often red ink
entries.use: Recording any survey measurement in the field notebook
entries.how: Write notes so they can only be read one way. Pencil only, uncrowded, plain sketches; keep office-computed values distinguishable (red ink)
entries.dim: Rod readings to nearest 0.01 ft are written 5.30 ft, not 5.3 ft
entries.wn: Poor or ambiguous notes defeat the instrument work

entries.desc: Determine distances, areas and angles; establish horizontal and vertical reference points; set stakes marking lines, grades and principal points; determine ground profiles on centerline/cross-section lines for cut, fill and earthwork volumes; prepare large-scale topographic maps by plane table or transit-stadia for drainage and site design; lay out structures, culverts and bridge lines; determine vertical and horizontal placement of utilities
entries.use: Knowing what a construction survey section is expected to do
entries.how: Checklist of what the surveyor supports: distances/areas/angles, control points, stakes, profiles, topo maps, structure/culvert/bridge layout, utilities

entries.desc: The military surveyor may work from metric data or convert data into metric equivalents. Tables A-13 and A-14 give the conversions. Values read from Table A-5 can be converted to metric by multiplying by 0.3048
entries.use: Working from metric data or converting to metric
entries.how: Convert meters to feet and feet to meters with the Appendix A tables when data is in a different system
entries.dim: x 0.3048 for feet to meters (Table A-5 note)

entries.n: Reconnaissance survey for a road or airfield
entries.desc: An extensive study of an entire area that might be used for a road or airfield, to eliminate impractical routes/sites and identify promising ones. Include all possible routes. Report summarizes collected information, a description of each route/site, a conclusion on economy of use, and maps/aerial photos where possible. Typical data: sketches of all routes; clearing and grubbing data; number of stream crossings with bridge spans over 20 ft (6 m); approximate number of culverts and spans under 20 ft (6 m); marsh areas and obstacles; unusual grade/alignment problems; effects of landslides, snowmelt and rainfall; soil, stream and substrata conditions at bridge sites; map/photo discrepancies; availability of local materials, equipment, transport and labor; photos/sketches of reference points, control points, structure sites and obstacles
entries.use: First look at an area to pick the best route or site
entries.how: Study all possible routes/sites with maps and aerial photos, rule out impractical ones, and write up the promising ones with sketches and data
entries.dim: Bridge spans exceeding 20 ft (6 m) counted separately from culverts/spans less than 20 ft (6 m)

entries.n: Site a new road: location guidelines
entries.desc: Guides: locate along or over existing roads, railroads or trails; use high-bearing-strength, stable, easily drained soil, avoid swamps, marshes and organic soil; run along ridges and streamlines to minimize drainage structures and keep the grade well above the high waterline beside a stream; stay near material sources and along contour lines to avoid unnecessary earthwork; use the sunny side of hills/canyons and the canyon wall side where strata inclination supports the road; in forward combat zones conceal and protect the road (may conflict with engineering considerations); conserve engineer assets, avoiding rockwork and excessive clearing; avoid sharp curves and bridging. Keep in mind future operations may need an expanded road net
entries.use: Selecting where a new road goes when specs/plans are not available
entries.how: Follow existing roads/ridges/streamlines on firm, drained, sunny ground; avoid swamps, rockwork, sharp curves and bridging; conceal roads in forward combat zones
entries.wn: Concealment from enemy fire may conflict with engineering considerations

entries.desc: Study the engineering specifications of the road. If unavailable, use Table 2-1 (see tm55_tables.json)
entries.use: Laying out or checking a road when the specifications are unavailable
entries.how: Quick reference for minimum widths, grades, curve radii, sight distance, slopes, drainage and traffic values
entries.dim: One-way 11.5 ft (3.5 m) min; two-way 23 ft (7.0 m) min; shoulders 4 ft (1.5 m) min each side; clearing 6 ft (2 m) each side; normal max grade 10%; desired max <6% (<4% on sharp curves); min radius desired 150 ft (46 m), absolute 80 ft (25 m); sight distance nonpassing 200 ft (60 m), passing 350 ft (110 m); vertical curve min 125 ft (40 m) per 4% summit, 100 ft (30 m) per 4% hollow; paved crown 1/4 to 1/2 in/ft (2-4%), gravel/dirt crown 1/2 to 3/4 in/ft (4-6%); shoulder slope 3/4 in/ft (6%); cut and fill normally about 1 1/2 to 1; grade at least 5 ft (1.6 m) above groundwater table; overhead clearance 14 ft (4.3 m) min; turnouts single lane every 1/4 mile (0.4 km)

entries.desc: Procure and use all existing maps including up-to-date aerial photos; large-scale topographic maps are best. Maps with overlays serve as worksheets for plotting trial alignments and approximate grades/distances. Mark limiting boundaries and specified terminals; observe existing routes, ridge lines, water courses and mountain gaps; look for moderate grades, simple alignment and balance between cut and fill. Classify routes, lower the classification as disadvantages appear, mark routes for field recon with different colored pencils by priority, determine grades, estimate clearing per route, and mark stream crossings and marsh areas for fords, bridges or culverts
entries.use: Pre-selecting routes on maps and aerial photos before field recon
entries.how: Mark limits and terminals, look for moderate grades and cut/fill balance, rank routes with colored pencils, and flag stream and marsh crossings
entries.eq: Maps, aerial photographs, overlays, colored pencils

entries.n: Preliminary survey (traverse, level and topographic parties)
entries.desc: Runs a traverse along the proposed route, establishes levels, records topography and plots results. Traverse party: sets and references control points, measures distances, numbers stations, establishes PIs, ties to existing control (or assigns a starting value later tied to geodetic control). Level party: establishes benchmarks and elevations along the route; takes rod readings and records elevations to the nearest 0.01 ft or 0.001 m; sets benchmarks well outside the construction area, marked to last the whole project; with no vertical control, assign an arbitrary elevation large enough to avoid negative elevations. Topographic party: gets enough relief and planimetric detail to locate obstacles and prepare rough profiles/cross sections; transit-stadia party works in open country with long clear sights; plane-table party works where terrain is irregular, with fieldwork and map drawing done simultaneously
entries.use: Detailed study of a tentatively selected route
entries.how: Run a traverse along the route, set benchmarks, take topography, plot a map, and determine the final location from the plot
entries.dim: Elevations to nearest 0.01 ft or 0.001 m
entries.eq: Transit-stadia or plane table, level, rod, tape
entries.tm: Parties are normally separate efforts but may be combined to use personnel and equipment efficiently
entries.wn: Benchmarks set inside the construction area will be lost

entries.n: Run and station the final centerline
entries.desc: The final centerline determines all construction lines; do not make changes from the paper location without authority of the officer-in-charge. Centerline starts at station 0+00. Number stations consecutively, set at full 100-ft or 30-m stations; also stake important points (culvert locations, road intersections, beginnings and ends of curves, breaks in the grade). In feet, plus stations are numbered from the last full station; station 4+44.75 is 44.75 ft past 4+00 and 444.75 ft from the project beginning. In metric, the station is simply the distance from the project start (e.g., 135.56)
entries.use: Staking the final road centerline
entries.how: Start at station 0+00, stake every full station, and add stakes at culverts, intersections, curve ends and grade breaks
entries.dim: Full station 100 ft or 30 m
entries.wn: Do not change the location from the paper survey without authority of the officer-in-charge

entries.desc: The control points established by the location survey determine the construction layout, so they must be carefully referenced (procedure in TM 5-232). Set control point references far enough from the construction to avoid disturbance
entries.use: Protecting control stations from construction damage
entries.how: Set reference stakes for control points well outside the work area so you can re-find them after clearing and grading
entries.wn: References too close to construction get destroyed

entries.desc: After centerline and horizontal curves are staked, determine elevations along the centerline and laterally across the road. Interval usually matches the station interval, shorter where terrain changes abruptly. Centerline elevations plotted give the profile (design engineer sets road grade from it); cross-section elevations plotted give views across the road that determine earthwork volume. Set cross-section lines at regular stations, any plus station and intermediate ground breaks; lay out short crosslines by eye and long crosslines at 90 degrees to the centerline with an instrument. Measure elevations at abrupt ground breaks with rod and level and distances from centerline with a tape. In rough country, use a hand level for cross sections if centerline elevations were run with the engineer level
entries.use: Getting centerline and lateral ground elevations after the centerline is staked
entries.how: Level the centerline (profile) and across it (cross sections); sketch short cross lines by eye, long ones at 90 degrees with an instrument
entries.dim: Cross lines at 90 degrees to centerline
entries.eq: Engineer level, rod, tape, hand level

entries.n: Keep surveyors ahead of road construction
entries.desc: The construction layout is an instrument survey giving alignment, grades and locations for clearing, grubbing, stripping, drainage, rough grading, finish grading and surfacing. The command must keep surveyors far enough ahead in time and distance to guarantee uninterrupted progress. A hasty alignment (flags and rods) can guide clearing and grubbing; a deliberate centerline is needed for final grading and surfacing. Mark curves and minor structures with the centerline; major structures (tunnels, bridges) need a site survey and the site layout is a separate survey
entries.use: Scheduling construction layout so crews are never waiting
entries.how: Hold the centerline 1,500 ft ahead of clearing, slope stakes 1,000 ft ahead of grading, and exact-grade stakes 500 ft ahead of finish work
entries.dim: Centerline 1,500 ft (450 m) ahead of clearing and grubbing; rough grade and slope stakes 1,000 ft (300 m) ahead of stripping and rough grading; stakes to exact grade 500 ft (150 m) ahead of finish grading and surfacing

entries.desc: Determine cut or fill at the centerline station: cut/fill = grade rod - ground rod. Grade rod = height of instrument (HI) - subgrade elevation. Ground rod = foresight reading at the station. Positive result = cut, negative = fill. Example: HI 115.5, subgrade 108.6, ground rod 3.1: grade rod = 115.5 - 108.6 = +6.9; cut = 6.9 - 3.1 = +3.8 ft, marked C38 on the back of the stake. To help the earthmoving crew, mark stakes to nearest whole or half foot (cut 3.8: measure up 0.2 ft; fill 3.8: measure up 0.3 ft). The number under the cut/fill is the stake's distance from the centerline. Set offset stakes along the traveled way, roadbed and ditches so grading does not destroy them; if the road is superelevated or in rough terrain, the survey crew provides stakes for all grade lines (centerline, edge of traveled way, edges of roadbed, possibly ditch centerlines)
entries.use: Telling the earthmoving crew how much to cut or fill at a station
entries.how: Grade rod = HI - subgrade elevation; cut/fill = grade rod - ground rod. Positive is cut, negative is fill. Write it on the stake as C or F plus the value
entries.dim: Rod readings and computations normally to nearest 0.1 ft or 0.01 m
entries.wn: The construction foreman, not the surveyor, decides how many grade stakes are needed and where. Where stakes cannot be driven (hard coral, rock), mark grade on the rock with chisel or lumber crayon

entries.desc: After rough grading, determine the final grade elevation and compute the grade rod reading. Set that reading on the rod with a rod target, hold the rod on top of the stake, and drive the stake until the horizontal crosshair bisects the target and the stake top is at final grade. Mark the top with blue lumber crayon. Provide blue tops on all grade lines; the construction foreman makes the final decision on which stakes are required
entries.use: Marking exact finished grade after rough grading
entries.how: Set the grade rod on the rod target, hold the rod on the stake top, and drive the stake until the crosshair bisects the target. Paint the top blue
entries.dim: Rod readings and computations to 0.01 ft or 0.001 m
entries.eq: Level, rod with target, blue lumber crayon, stakes

entries.n: Locate slope stakes on level ground
entries.desc: On level ground transversely, cut or fill at the slope stake equals the center value (plus the crown). Fill: distance from center stake to slope stake = center fill x slope ratio (horizontal : vertical) + one half roadbed width. Cut: distance = slope ratio x center cut + distance from centerline to outside edge of ditch. Right and left stakes are equidistant on level ground; on superelevated sections add the widening factor, which differs for each side
entries.use: Marking where the cut or fill slope meets natural ground when the ground is level across the road
entries.how: Distance to slope stake = (center cut or fill x slope ratio) + half roadbed width (fill) or + distance from centerline to outside edge of ditch (cut)
entries.dim: Fill: d = fill x ratio + 1/2 roadbed width. Cut: d = cut x ratio + centerline-to-outside-ditch-edge
entries.wn: On superelevated sections right and left slope stakes will not be equidistant from the centerline

entries.n: Set slope stakes on sloping ground (trial and error)
entries.desc: Use trial and error. Example (cut): HI 388.3, subgrade 372.5 at centerline for a 23-ft roadbed, 1.5:1 side slopes, 4-ft shoulders, 7-ft ditches. Grade rod = 388.3 - 372.5 = +15.8. Ground rod at center = 6.3, center cut = 15.8 - 6.3 = +9.5. Trial distance = 9.5 x 1.5 + 22.5 = 36.8 ft. Rod at 36.8 ft (right angles to centerline, point A) reads 9.1 so cut = 6.7; computed distance for that cut = 6.7 x 1.5 + 22.5 = 32.6 ft (the text words this as 'one half the roadbed width' but the arithmetic uses 22.5), so A is too far out. Move to 32.6 ft: reading 8.9, cut = 15.8 - 8.9 = +6.9, computed 6.9 x 1.5 + 22.5 = 32.8, measured 32.8 ft, so that is the slope stake, marked C69. Moving the rod 0.1-0.2 ft would not materially change the reading. Mark cut/fill as the numerator of a fraction over the distance out from the centerline, facing the center of the road; the back shows station and slope ratio. The instrumentman verifies by computation. Fill with HI above grade: grade rod is less than ground readings (example 2.8 - 6.5 = -3.7 center fill). Fill with HI below grade: grade rod is negative; add the negative ground rod (example -2.40 + -2.35 = -4.75 m)
entries.use: Finding the slope stake position when ground is not level across the road
entries.how: Estimate a trial distance, read the rod there, recompute the distance from the actual cut, and move until measured and computed distances agree. Usually 2-3 trials
entries.dim: Number of trials generally 2 or 3; cut distance = cut x slope ratio + centerline-to-ditch-edge (22.5 in example); fill distance = fill x slope ratio + 1/2 roadbed width
entries.tm: Approximating the position becomes quick with practice; usually two or three trials
entries.wn: Moving the rod at right angles to the centerline; verify the figures by computation

entries.desc: Locate the intersection of the roadway centerline and a line defining the culvert direction; culverts generally follow natural drainage lines.
