Stake inlet and outlet points and mark any cut or fill. Follow the construction plans; set alignment and grade stakes on the centerlines beyond the work area so disturbed stakes can be replaced. Set a benchmark near the site but outside the work area to re-establish grades. Location and construction surveys may be run simultaneously
entries.use: Staking a culvert where a road crosses drainage
entries.how: Find where the roadway centerline meets the culvert line, stake inlet and outlet, mark cut/fill on stakes, and set line/grade stakes beyond the work area plus a benchmark

entries.desc: The surveyor must anticipate drainage problems and gather enough field data to indicate the best design and location for drainage structures (see TM 5-330). Proper drainage is of primary importance for operational requirements and useful life; temporary drainage during construction prevents delays from standing water or saturated work areas. Poor drainage results in mud, washouts and heaves
entries.use: Gathering the field data needed to design drainage
entries.how: Collect enough field data so drainage structures can be designed and located; inadequate drainage causes most road and airfield failures
entries.wn: Inadequate drainage causes most road and airfield failures

entries.desc: Number stations forward from the beginning of the project; 0+00 is the start. A full station is 100 ft or 30 m (15+00 and 16+00). A plus station is a point between full stations (15+52.96). In metric the plus system is not used; the station number is the distance from the project start
entries.use: Numbering points along a route
entries.how: Stations count forward from the project start; 15+52.96 is 1,552.96 ft out. Metric work uses plain distance
entries.dim: Full station 100 ft or 30 m

entries.n: Locate short-radius curves with a tape
entries.desc: For short radius (usually less than one tape length) hold one end of the tape at the center of the circle and swing it in an arc, marking points. For longer radius/length, use measured angles and straight-line distances to locate stations on the circumference
entries.use: Staking a curve of radius under about one tape length
entries.how: Hold one end of the tape at the circle center and swing an arc, marking as many points as needed
entries.dim: Radius usually less than one tape length

entries.n: Know the elements of a simple curve
entries.desc: PI: where back and forward tangents intersect (a preliminary traverse station). I: intersecting (deflection) angle at the PI, computed from preliminary traverse station angles or measured. R: radius. PC: where the circular curve begins. PT: end of curve. L: distance from PC to PT along the curve. T: tangent distance PI to PC or PT (equal on a simple curve). Central angle: angle at center between radii to PC and PT, equal to I. LC: chord from PC to PT. E: external distance PI to curve midpoint, bisects the PI interior angle. M: middle ordinate, curve midpoint to long-chord midpoint; its extension bisects the central angle. D: degree of curve. Simple, compound, reverse or spiral are the horizontal curve types; the simple curve is an arc of a circle and the most common; larger radius means a flatter curve. Reverse curves should not be used unless absolutely necessary (safety)
entries.use: Identifying and defining curve parts before computing
entries.how: PI, I, R, PC, PT, L, T, central angle, LC, E, M, D: what each means and which equal each other
entries.dim: Central angle = I; T equal at PC and PT
entries.wn: Avoid reverse curves unless absolutely necessary

entries.n: Degree of curve and radius (arc and chord definitions)
entries.desc: Arc definition: D is the angle at the center subtended by a 100 ft (30.48 m) arc; D and R are inversely proportional (as D increases R decreases); used primarily by civilian highway engineers. 1 degree curve R = 5,729.58 ft or 1,746.38 m. Chord definition: D is the angle at the center subtended by a 100 ft (30.48 m) chord; R = 50 ft / sin(D/2) or 15.24 m / sin(D/2); R and D are not inversely proportional; used primarily on railroads in civilian practice and by the military for both roads and railroads. 1 degree: R = 5,729.65 ft or 1,746.40 m. One definition is no better than the other, but the two give different radii and so different elements for the same D. Some engineers use 5,730 ft for a 1-degree radius (arc method); this differs from 5,729.58 by less than 1 part in 10,000. Table A-5 is based on 5,730
entries.use: Converting between degree of curve and radius
entries.how: Arc definition: R = 5,729.58 / D. Chord definition: R = 50 / sin(D/2). The Army uses the chord definition for roads and railroads
entries.wn: Be sure all crews use the same definition; misunderstandings between surveyors are common

entries.n: Select chord length for staking a curve
entries.desc: Stake long-radius curves by locating the ends of a series of chords. Recommended chord lengths keep the arc-to-chord discrepancy within the allowable taping error (0.02 ft per 100 ft on most construction surveys); the surveyor may use shorter or longer chords depending on terrain and foreman needs. The surveyor customarily places the first stake after the PC at a plus station divisible by the chord length and stakes the centerline between curves at 10, 25, 50 or 100 ft intervals so the level party is not confused
entries.use: Choosing how long the chords are when staking a curve
entries.how: Sharper curve, shorter chord: 100 ft for 1-3 degree curves down to 10 ft over 16 degrees
entries.dim: D 1-3: 100 ft / 30 m; D 3-8: 50 ft / 15 m; D 8-16: 25 ft / 7.5 m; D over 16: 10 ft / 3 m (radii in table); allowable taping error 0.02 ft per 100 ft

entries.desc: Formulas apply to both definitions except as noted. T = R tan 1/2 I. L = (I/D) 100 ft or (I/D) 30.48 m (arc length for the arc definition, distance along the chords for the chord definition). PC = PI - T. PT = PC + L. E = R(1/cos 1/2 I - 1) or E = T tan 1/4 I. M = R(1 - cos 1/2 I). LC = 2R sin 1/2 I. Deflection to a point: d = (D/2)(C/100 ft) degrees or (D/2)(C/30.48 m) (exact for the arc definition, approximate for the chord definition); in minutes d = 0.3 C D (English)
entries.use: Computing tangent, length, external, middle ordinate, long chord
entries.how: T = R tan(I/2); L = (I/D) x 100 ft; PC = PI - T; PT = PC + L; E = R(1/cos(I/2) - 1); M = R(1 - cos(I/2)); LC = 2R sin(I/2)
entries.dim: T = R tan(I/2); L = (I/D)100 ft (or 30.48 m); PC = PI - T; PT = PC + L; E = R(sec(I/2) - 1) = T tan(I/4); M = R(1 - cos(I/2)); LC = 2R sin(I/2); d = (D/2)(C/100) degrees = 0.3 C D minutes
entries.wn: Must know three elements first: PI station, I angle, and D (from specs or a terrain-limited element)

entries.n: Solve a simple curve (worked example, chord definition)
entries.desc: Given PI = 18+00, I = 45, D = 15 degrees (chord definition, feet): R = 50/0.130526 = 383.07 ft; T = 383.07 x 0.414214 = 158.67 ft; L = 45/15 x 100 = 300.00 ft; PC = 1,800 - 158.67 = 1,641.33 (16+41.33); PT = 1,641.33 + 300 = 1,941.33 (19+41.33); E = 31.56 ft; M = 29.16 ft; LC = 293.19 ft. D = 15 degrees so chord length is 25 ft; first stake after PC at 16+50 so first subchord C1 = 8.67 ft; last subchord C2 = 16.33 ft (station 19+25 to the PT). Number of full chords = (19+25 - 16+50) / 25 = 11
entries.use: Working a full curve solution from PI, I, D
entries.how: Example PI 18+00, I 45 degrees, D 15 degrees gives R 383.07, T 158.67, L 300.00, PC 16+41.33, PT 19+41.33
entries.wn: Calculator results may vary slightly from six-place table results

entries.n: Compute deflection angles for a curve
entries.desc: Deflections are measured at the PC from the tangent to each chord end. Sum of deflections is always one half of I; if it is not, a mistake was made. Example (D = 15, 25 ft chords): d_std = 0.3 x 25 x 15 = 112.5' (1 deg 52.5'); d1 = 0.3 x 8.67 x 15 = 0 deg 39.015'; d2 = 0.3 x 16.33 x 15 = 1 deg 13.485'. Sum: 11 x 1 deg 52.5' = 20 deg 37.5'; plus d1 and d2 = 22 deg 30.000' = I/2. Round each station's deflection to the smallest reading of the field instrument (one-minute instrument in the example), e.g., 0 deg 39', 2 deg 32', 4 deg 24', ... 22 deg 30' at the PT. Formulas for the arc definition may be used for the chord definition when a one-minute instrument is used
entries.use: Getting the angles to turn at the PC for each station
entries.how: d = 0.3' x C x D. The sum of all deflections must equal I/2. Round to the smallest reading of the instrument
entries.dim: d = 0.3 x C x D minutes; total of deflections = I/2
entries.wn: If the sum does not equal I/2 there is a computation mistake

entries.n: Curves with angles in degrees and minutes
entries.desc: When I and D include minutes, convert each to a decimal part of a degree (to five decimal places) or convert I and D to minutes for the length formula. Example: I = 42 deg 15' = 2,535 minutes, D = 5 deg 37' = 337 minutes; L = 2,535/337 x 100 = 752.23 ft (exact). When I has an odd number of minutes and a one-minute instrument is used, compute to the nearest 0.5 minute; if total deflection checks to the nearest minute in the field it can be considered correct (the surveyor normally stakes the PT first so total deflection checks the PT). Table A-3 converts minutes/seconds to decimals of a degree
entries.use: Working a curve when I or D include minutes
entries.how: Convert minutes to decimal degrees to five decimal places, or convert both to minutes before dividing for length
entries.dim: Five decimal places; L = 2,535/337 x 100 = 752.23 ft
entries.wn: Do not truncate the decimal conversion

entries.n: Use curve tables A-5 and A-6
entries.desc: Table A-5 lists long chords, middle ordinates, externals and tangents for a 1-degree curve (radius 5,730 ft) for various I angles. Arc definition: divide the tabular value by the degree of curve. Example: I = 75 deg, table T = 4,396.7 ft and E = 1,492.5 ft; divide by D = 15: T = 293.11 ft, E = 99.50 ft. Chord definition: add Table A-6 corrections (0.83 ft to T and 0.29 ft to E in the example) giving T = 293.94 ft and E = 99.79 ft. A second example (D = 18 deg 20', I = 9 deg 46'): T = 489.56/18.333 = 26.70 + 0.12 = 26.82 ft; E = 20.88/18.333 = 1.139 + 0.005 = 1.14 ft. Compute the remainder of the curve afterwards. Multiply table values by 0.3048 for metric
entries.use: Shortcut for tangent and external distances without trig
entries.how: Look up LC, M, E, T for a 1-degree curve at I, divide by D (arc definition); add the A-6 correction for the chord definition
entries.dim: Arc: value = table value / D. Chord: add Table A-6 correction. 75 deg example T 293.11 to 293.94, E 99.50 to 99.79
entries.wn: Tabular values are for a 5,730 ft radius curve
entries.src: TM 3-34.55 para 3-51 to 3-55; Tables A-5, A-6

entries.desc: With the instrument at the PI, sight the preceding PI and keep the head tapeman on line while the tangent distance is measured; set a stake marked with PC and station. Then point on the forward PI and measure the tangent distance to set the PT stake
entries.use: First step of staking a simple curve
entries.how: From the PI, sight the adjacent PI and measure the tangent distance to set the PC; repeat on the forward PI for the PT
entries.dim: Distance = T

entries.n: Lay out a curve from the PC (deflection method)
entries.desc: Set up at the PC with 0 deg 00' on the PI. Right curve: measure the angle to the PT if visible (should equal I/2); set d1 (e.g., 0 deg 39') and measure C1 (8.67 ft) to set station 16+50; then set d1 + d_std (2 deg 32') and measure the standard chord (25 ft) from the previous station keeping the head tapeman on line; continue; last deflection should point at the PT and last distance be the subchord C2 (16.33 ft). Left curve: angle to PT subtracted from 360 should equal I/2; subtract d1 from 360 and set on the circle; continue subtracting deflections from 360 and measure chords from the previous station. The last station before the PT should be C2 from the PT and its deflection equals the measured angle plus the last deflection d2
entries.use: Staking the curve stations with a one-minute instrument
entries.how: Zero on the PI, turn each deflection, measure the chord from the previous station. Left curves: subtract deflection from 360 degrees
entries.dim: Left curves: circle reading = 360 deg - deflection; check angle to PT = I/2
entries.eq: One-minute transit/theodolite (circle reading to the right), tape, stakes

entries.n: Stake a curve from an intermediate setup
entries.desc: Stake as many stations from the PC as possible. Move forward to any station on the curve. Pick another station already in place and set that station's deflection angle on the horizontal circle; sight it with the telescope reversed. Plunge the telescope and set the remaining stations as if the instrument were over the PC
entries.use: Continuing a curve when you cannot see the rest of it from the PC
entries.how: Move to a staked station, sight a known station with the telescope reversed using its deflection, plunge, and continue as if still on the PC

entries.n: Back in the curve from the PT
entries.desc: Occupy the PT. Right curve: sight the PI with I/2 on the horizontal circle; the instrument then reads 0 deg 00' on the PC. Left curve: sight the PI with 360 deg minus I/2. Set remaining stations using their deflections and chords from the PC or in reverse order from the PT. Widely used even when no obstruction exists: set about half the stations from the PC and the remainder from the PT
entries.use: Finishing a curve when obstructions block the PC setup; also to push error to the middle
entries.how: Stake about half the stations from the PC and the rest from the PT; any error lands in the middle where it is least noticeable
entries.dim: Right: PI sighted at I/2; Left: PI sighted at 360 deg - I/2

entries.desc: To remove the discrepancy between chord and arc lengths, correct chords using values from the nomography in Table A-11 (curve computed by arc definition) or Table A-10 (curve computed by chord definition). Example: 100 ft chord from 18+00 to 19+00 with nominal 50 ft subchords; placing a stake at 18+50 requires a 0.19 ft correction so each subchord is 50.19 ft
entries.use: Laying out a curve more precisely than the standard chord lengths allow
entries.how: Use Table A-10 (chord definition) or A-11 (arc definition) to correct intermediate-stake subchords so main stations stay the right distance apart
entries.dim: Example: 50 ft nominal subchord corrected to 50.19 ft
entries.wn: Tables A-10 and A-11 are graphics not reproduced in the extracted text

entries.n: Locate curve with an inaccessible PI
entries.desc: Mark two intervisible points A and B, one on each tangent, so line AB clears the obstruction; measure angles a and b at A and B and measure AB. I = a + b; K = 180 - I; AV = AB sin b / sin K; BV = AB sin a / sin K (the text prints sin b for both; by the sine rule BV uses the angle at A); PI = Sta A + AV. Determine T from the degree of curve (or other limiting factor). Locate the PC at distance T - AV from A and the PT at T - BV from B, then compute and lay out the curve
entries.use: PI cannot be occupied (water, building, etc.)
entries.how: Mark A and B on the tangents, measure angles a and b and distance AB, compute AV and BV by sine rule, then set PC and PT at T minus AV and T minus BV
entries.dim: I = a + b; K = 180 - I; PI = Sta A + AV; PC at T - AV from A; PT at T - BV from B
entries.wn: The manual's printed BV formula repeats sin b; confirm angle assignment on the sketch before using

entries.n: Locate curve with an inaccessible PC
entries.desc: Place the instrument on the PT and back the curve in as far as possible. Select station P so line PQ, parallel to tangent AV, clears the obstacle. Compute PW = R(1 - cos dp) where dp is the part of the central angle subtended by AP (two times the deflection of P); W lies on the tangent with PW perpendicular. Set the instrument at the PI, lay off angle V (V = 180 - I) to sight along the tangent, and swing a tape of length PW to set W. Measure VW. Set up at P, backsight W, turn 90 degrees, measure to Q beyond the obstacle, record PQ. At Q backsight P, turn 90 degrees, measure QS = PW and set S; station S = PI - (VW + PQ). Set an offset PC at Y by measuring from Q toward P a distance equal to station PC minus station S. After the obstacle is removed, set up at Y, backsight Q, turn 90 degrees and measure from Y to the PC a distance equal to PW and QS. Carefully reference Q, S, Y, W
entries.use: PC is blocked but PI and PT are accessible
entries.how: Back the curve in from the PT, offset a line parallel to the tangent clear of the obstacle, and reference points Q, S, Y, W to set the PC later
entries.dim: PW = R(1 - cos dp); V = 180 - I; Sta S = PI - (VW + PQ); QS = PW
entries.wn: Reference points Q, S, Y and W carefully so they survive clearing and construction

entries.n: Locate curve with an inaccessible PT
entries.desc: Use the inaccessible-PC method with these exceptions: letter the curve so point A is at the PT; lay the curve in as far as possible from the PC instead of the PT; angle dp is the angle at the center between P and the PT, equal to two times the difference between the deflection at P and one half of I; set PQ and QS as before. Station at S = computed PT station + YQ. Use station S to number the stations of the alignment ahead
entries.use: PT is blocked but PI and PC are accessible
entries.how: Same offset method as an inaccessible PC, mirrored: letter the curve so A is at the PT and lay the curve in from the PC
entries.dim: dp = 2 x (deflection at P - I/2); Sta S = Sta PT + YQ

entries.n: Bypass an obstacle on a curve
entries.desc: Set the instrument over the PC at 0 deg 00' sighting the PI; check I/2 to the PT if possible; set as many stations as possible before the obstacle (point b). Set over the PT with the plates at I/2 sighting the PI; back in as many stations as possible beyond the obstacle (point e). Set obstructed stations (c, d) after removal. Do not waste much time on preliminary work
entries.use: A few curve stations are hidden by an obstacle
entries.how: Stake what you can from the PC, back in the rest from the PT, and set the hidden stations after the obstacle is removed

entries.n: Fit a curve through a fixed point
entries.desc: With the PI and I known, set up at the PI and measure angle d between the fixed point and the tangent on the same side; measure y, the PI-to-point distance. c = 90 - (d + I/2); sin e = sin c / cos(I/2); b = 180 - e; a = 180 - (b + c); R = y sin c / sin a. D (arc) = 5,729.58 ft / R or 1,746.385 m / R; D (chord): sin D = 2(50 ft / R) or 2(15.24 m / R) as printed. Compute D to five decimal places, then the remaining elements and deflections and stake
entries.use: Curve must pass through or avoid a given point and join two tangents
entries.how: Measure angle d and distance y from the PI to the fixed point, solve the triangle for R, then get D
entries.dim: c = 90 - (d + I/2); sin e = sin c / cos(I/2); b = 180 - e; a = 180 - (b + c); R = y sin c / sin a; D to five decimals

entries.n: Curve with a limiting tangent, external or middle ordinate
entries.desc: Given a limiting factor, first compute R: tangent R = T/tan 1/2 I; external R = E/[(1/cos 1/2 I) - 1]; middle ordinate R = M/(1 - cos 1/2 I). If the factor is stated as an exact value, compute D to five decimal places and finish the curve. If the limit is written so the recomputed E must be equal to or greater than the given value (example E 50 ft), round D down to the nearest 1/2 degree, recompute E (new E equal to or greater than 50 ft) and the rest of the curve; if the recomputed M must be equal to or less than the given value (example M 45 ft), round D up to the nearest 1/2 degree and recompute (new M equal to or less than 45 ft). Table values may be used (the text cites 'table B-5', apparently Table A-5): divide the tabulated 1-degree T, E or M by the limiting value (example: I = 20 deg 20', T 1,027.6/45.00 = 22.836 deg, rounded up to 23 deg)
entries.use: Terrain fixes T, E or M and you must pick D
entries.how: R = T / tan(I/2), E / (sec(I/2) - 1), or M / (1 - cos(I/2)); then round D to the nearest half degree in the safe direction and recompute
entries.dim: R = T/tan(I/2); R = E/(sec(I/2) - 1); R = M/(1 - cos(I/2)); round D to nearest 1/2 degree
entries.wn: The inequality symbols in this paragraph were lost in extraction; confirm which direction rounds up or down against the original

entries.desc: A compound curve is two or more simple curves with different centers, bending the same direction on the same side of the common tangent; the PT of the first equals the PC of the second (PCC). It fits topography well but is more hazardous than a simple curve; never use where a simple curve will do. Steps: get PI of the first curve (A); get I1, I2 and distance AB; determine D1 (limiting factor, scaled from road plan or project engineer); R1; T1 = R1 tan 1/2 I; T2 = AB - T1; R2 = T2 / tan 1/2 I2; D2 carried to five decimals since T2 must be held exact; compare D1 and D2; compute first-curve data and deflections; PI2 = PT1 + T2; compute second-curve data and deflections and lay in the curves
entries.use: Two curves in the same direction joined to fit rugged terrain
entries.how: Fix D1, find T1 and T2 = AB - T1, then R2 and D2 (five decimals). D1 and D2 should not differ by more than 3 degrees
entries.dim: T1 = R1 tan(I1/2); T2 = AB - T1; R2 = T2/tan(I2/2); |D1 - D2| not more than 3 degrees; PI2 = PT1 + T2
entries.wn: If D1 and D2 differ by more than 3 degrees consider changing the curve configuration. Do not use where a simple curve will do

entries.desc: Determine PI and I from field data; determine I1 and AB (field measurement or scaling from the plan and profile sheet). C = 180 - I; I2 = 180 - (I1 + C); AC = AB sin I2 / sin C; BC = AB sin I1 / sin C; PI1 = PI - AC; determine D1, R1, T1; compute T2, R2, D2; PC1 = PI - (AC + T1); compute first-curve data and deflections; PI2 = PT1 + T2; compute second curve and stake
entries.use: Fitting a compound curve into a given tangent pair
entries.how: From I and I1 and the distance AB, solve the triangle for AC and BC, then position PI1 and PI2
entries.dim: C = 180 - I; I2 = 180 - (I1 + C); AC = AB sin I2 / sin C; BC = AB sin I1 / sin C; PC1 = PI - (AC + T1)

entries.n: Stake a compound curve in the field
entries.desc: Between successive PIs: stake the first curve normally; verify PCC and PT2 by placing the instrument at the PCC, sighting PI2 and laying off I2/2 (the line of sight should intercept PT2); stake the second curve the same way. Between successive tangents: set up at the PI, sight back tangent, lay out AC and set PI1; continue along back tangent a distance T1 to set PC1; sight the forward tangent and lay out BC to set PI2; continue distance T2 to set PT2; check PI1 and PI2 by measuring the distance between them against computed AB or by setting up at PI1, sighting the PI and laying off I1 (line of sight should intercept PI2); then stake the curves
entries.use: Setting a compound curve and verifying the PCC and PIs
entries.how: Stake curve 1 normally, then verify PCC/PT2 by sighting PI2 and laying off I2/2
entries.dim: Check angle at PCC = I2/2 to PT2; check PI1-PI2 against AB

entries.n: Reverse curves: when to use and how to set up
entries.desc: A reverse curve is two or more simple curves turning in opposite directions; their PIs lie at opposite ends of a common tangent and the PT of the first coincides with the PC of the second (PRC). Useful for pipelines, flumes and levees; may be used on low-speed roads and railroads; not on high-speed roads or railroads because they cannot be properly superelevated at the PRC; used on canals only with extreme caution (hard to navigate, contributes to erosion). Three problems: between successive PIs (computed like a compound curve between successive PIs), connecting parallel tangents, connecting diverging tangents
entries.use: Pipelines, flumes, levees, low-speed roads where direction must flip
entries.how: Two simple curves in opposite directions meeting at the PRC. Not for high-speed roads or railroads (cannot be superelevated at the PRC)
entries.wn: Safety: use only when absolutely necessary; cannot be superelevated at the PRC

entries.desc: Measure p, the perpendicular distance between the tangents; locate the PRC and measure m1 and m2 (if the PRC is at midpoint both arcs are identical); determine R1; cos I1 = (R1 - m1)/R1; L1 = R1 sin I1; R2, I2, L2 the same way; stake each arc as a simple curve; locate PC and PT by measuring L1 and L2. Example: equal arcs, D = 5 degrees, p = 225.00 ft: R1 = R2 = 50/0.043619 = 1,146.29 ft; cos I1 = 1,033.79/1,146.29 = 0.901857; I1 = 25 deg 36'; L1 = 495.30 ft
entries.use: Joining two parallel tangents with two arcs
entries.how: Measure the offset p, locate the PRC (midpoint gives equal arcs), compute I1 from cos I1 = (R1 - m1)/R1 and L1 = R1 sin I1
entries.dim: cos I1 = (R1 - m1)/R1; L1 = R1 sin I1; example R 1,146.29 ft, I1 25 deg 36', L1 495.30 ft
entries.wn: Example arithmetic in the text uses R = 1,146.29 in one line and 1,145.29 in another; recompute with a consistent R

entries.desc: Measure I at the PI; measure Ts to locate the PT; determine R1 and R2 (make equal if practical). Angle s = 90 - I; m = Ts tan I; L = Ts / cos I; angles e and f = I1 (similar triangles); I2 = I + I1; n = (R2 - m) sin e; p = (R2 - m) cos e; cos I1 = (R1 + p)/(R1 + R2); g = (R1 + R2) sin I1; TL = g + n + L. Measure TL from the PI to locate the PC, stake arc 1 to the PRC from the PC, set up at the PT and verify the PRC (invert telescope, sight PI, plunge, turn I2/2), stake arc 2 to the PRC from the PT. Example (D = 5 each, I = 41 deg, Ts = 550 ft): R1 = R2 = 1,146.29; m = 478.11; L = 728.76; n = 438.37; p = 504.28; cos I1 = 0.719962; I1 = 43 deg 57'; g = 1,591.12; TL = 2,758.25 ft
entries.use: Reverse curve when one simple curve will not fit
entries.how: Measure I and Ts, pick R1 and R2, solve for I1, g, n and L, and measure TL from the PI to find the PC
entries.dim: TL = g + n + L; example TL = 2,758.25 ft
entries.wn: Some symbols in the printed example are inconsistent (e.g., angle I used for s); follow the step order

entries.desc: A transition curve (spiral) of varying radius is inserted between a circular curve and its tangent to reduce skidding and steering difficulty and to allow adequate superelevation of the outer pavement edge. Curvature increases uniformly: zero at the TS where it leaves the tangent, and equal to the degree of the circular curve it joins at the SC. The A.R.E.A. 10-chord spiral measures the spiral by 10 equal chords to match field practice; it coincides with the cubic spiral up to Delta = 15 degrees, and the exact formulas apply when Delta does not exceed 45 degrees. Points: TS (tangent to spiral), SC (spiral to circular curve), CS (circular curve to spiral), ST (spiral to tangent), SS (one spiral to another). PC/PT, TS/ST and SC/CS swap when the direction of stationing reverses
entries.use: Adding a spiral between a tangent and a circular curve
entries.how: A spiral eases a vehicle or train from straight to curve and lets superelevation build up uniformly. Know TS, SC, CS, ST
entries.dim: Exact 10-chord formulas valid for Delta up to 45 degrees; empirical field formulas for Delta up to 15 degrees; Ls = 10 equal chords

entries.desc: Exact (10-chord spiral, Delta <= 45 deg): d = k s = kL/100; D = k S = k Ls/100; delta = k s^2 / 2 = d^2 / 2k = k L^2 / 20,000 = dL/200; A = (Delta/3) - 0.00297 Delta^3 seconds; B = Delta - A; C = Ls (cos 0.3 Delta + 0.004 exsec 3/4 Delta); X = C cos A; Y = C sin A; U = C (sin B / sin Delta); V = C (sin A / sin Delta); R = 50 ft / sin 1/2 D (chord definition); Z = X - (R sin Delta); o = Y - (R vers Delta); Ts = (R + o) tan 1/2 I + Z; Es = (R + o) exsec 1/2 I + o; vers = 1 - cos; exsec = sec - 1. Empirical field formulas (Delta <= 15 deg): a = delta/3 degrees; A = Delta/3 degrees; a = 10 k s^2 minutes; A = 10 k S^2 minutes
entries.use: Computing spiral elements for a transition curve
entries.how: Deflection grows with the square of distance; use A = Delta/3 and a = 10 k s^2 (minutes) in the field when Delta is 15 degrees or less
entries.dim: Delta up to 45 deg exact; up to 15 deg empirical; a = 10 k s^2 minutes; Ts = (R + o) tan(I/2) + Z
entries.wn: The worked example writes Z = X - R sin A in one place and Z = X - R sin Delta in the formula list; the example uses sin 5 deg = Delta

entries.desc: Highway: Ls = 1.6 V^3 / R, Ls minimum spiral length in feet, V design speed in mph, R radius of the simple curve (approximation from observation and road tests, not mathematically exact). Table 3-1 gives recommended superelevation and minimum Ls for multiples of 50 ft. For a spiral between the arcs of a compound curve use Ls = 1.6 V^3 / Ra, where Ra is the radius of a curve whose degree equals the difference in the degrees of curvature of the circular arcs. Railroad: Ls must allow an increase in superelevation not exceeding 1 1/4 inches per second at maximum train speed; Ls = 1.17 E V, E full theoretical superelevation in inches, V speed in mph, Ls in feet; for compound arcs E is the difference between the superelevations of the two arcs
entries.use: Choosing Ls for a highway or railroad spiral
entries.how: Highway: Ls = 1.6 V^3 / R. Railroad: Ls = 1.17 E V. Table 3-1 gives highway values in multiples of 50 ft
entries.dim: Highway Ls = 1.6V^3/R; Railroad Ls = 1.17EV; superelevation rise not over 1 1/4 in per second

entries.use: Working the full spiral problem from D, V, PI station and I

entries.desc: a : A = L^2 : Ls^2, so a1 = A/100, a2 = 4a1, a3 = 9a1, ... a9 = 81a1, a10 = 100a1 = A. k = D(100)/Ls = 4(100)/250 = 1.6; a = 10 k s^2 minutes. Example results: a1 0 deg 01', a2 0 deg 04', a3 0 deg 09', a4 0 deg 16', a5 0 deg 25', a6 0 deg 36', a7 0 deg 49', a8 1 deg 04', a9 1 deg 21', a10 (SC) 1 deg 40' = Delta/3. Circular arc from the SC: d1 = 0.3 c1 D = 0 deg 24.4' (c1 = 20.34 ft to station 41+00); d2 = d1 + D/2 = 2 deg 24.4'; d3 4 deg 24.4'; d4 6 deg 24.4'; d5 at the CS = (I - 2 Delta)/2 = 7 deg 05'. The second spiral uses the same angles in reverse order from the ST
entries.use: Computing the angles to each spiral chord point
entries.how: Deflections vary as the square of the distance: a1, 4a1, 9a1 ... 100a1 = A. Circular arc part uses 0.3 C D as usual
entries.dim: a_n = n^2 a1; a10 = A = Delta/3; k = 100 D / Ls

entries.n: Lay out a spiral curve (TS to SC, arc, ST to CS)
entries.desc: Set TS and ST: at the PI sight along the back tangent and measure Ts; mark TS; sight the forward tangent, measure Ts, mark ST. First spiral: set up at TS with 0 deg 00' on the PI; check the angle to the ST (should equal I/2); subtract a1 (0 deg 01') from 360 and set; measure the standard spiral chord (25 ft) from the TS and set the first station (38+54.66); continue by subtracting each deflection from 360 and measuring 25 ft from the previous station. Circular arc: set up at the SC with Delta minus A = 5 deg 00' - 1 deg 40' = 3 deg 20' on the circle, sight the TS with the telescope reversed, plunge and turn to 0 deg 00' (now on the tangent to the arc at the SC); subtract d1 (0 deg 24') from 360, measure c1 = 20.34 ft to set station 41+00; continue subtracting deflections and measuring chords from the previous station. Second spiral: set up at the ST on the PI with 0 deg 00'; check the angle to the CS (should be 1 deg 40'); set stations using deflections in reverse order and 25-ft chords. Correct any error by adjusting the circular arc chords from the SC to the CS
entries.use: Staking a spiral-circular-spiral curve with a one-minute instrument
entries.how: Set TS and ST from the PI, run spiral 1 by subtracting deflections from 360 degrees, run the arc from the SC with a backsight on the TS, and run spiral 2 from the ST
entries.dim: Standard spiral chord 25 ft in example; angle ST to CS check 1 deg 40' (= A); angle TS to ST = I/2

entries.desc: Unlike a circular curve, the TS deflections cannot be used from another point. Stake the first five points normally; check point 5 by repetition. Table 3-2: with the instrument at any chord point, the coefficients times a1 give the deflections to the other points. At point 5, coefficients for points 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 are 16, 34, 54, 76, 100, giving a6 0 deg 16', a7 0 deg 34', a8 0 deg 54', a9 1 deg 16', a10 1 deg 40'. The angle from point 5 back to the TS is 50 a1 = 0 deg 50'. Set up over point 5, set that angle on the circle, invert the telescope and sight the TS, plunge, and stake points 6-10 by subtracting the deflections from 360 degrees
entries.use: Moving the instrument onto a spiral station
entries.how: Deflections from the TS cannot be reused; use the Table 3-2 coefficients times a1 for the new setup and the backsight to the TS
entries.dim: Point 5 coefficients: to 6 = 16, 7 = 34, 8 = 54, 9 = 76, 10 = 100; back to TS = 50

entries.desc: Two intersecting grade lines are rounded off with a parabolic vertical curve. A sag (invert) curve connects a descending grade with an ascending grade or a less sharply descending one; a summit (overt) curve connects an ascending grade followed by a descending grade or a less sharply ascending one. Grades G1 and G2 are percent rise per 100 ft, plus ascending and minus descending in the direction of survey. L is the horizontal distance in 100-ft stations from PVC to PVT; the curve extends L/2 stations on each side of the PVI. Minimum L in stations = algebraic difference of grades (Delta G) / rate of change r (design criteria). If r is not given: Summit L = 125 ft (G2 - G1)/4 or 38.10 m (G2 - G1)/4; Sag L = 100 ft (G2 - G1)/4 or 38.10 m (G2 - G1)/4 (metric figures as printed). If L is not a whole number of stations extend it to the nearest whole number (this reduces the rate of change) and recompute r = Delta G / L (e.g., 4.8 stations extended to 5)
entries.use: Rounding a grade change with a parabolic vertical curve
entries.how: L (stations) = algebraic difference in grades / rate of change r. If r is not given: summit L = 125 ft x (G2-G1)/4; sag L = 100 ft x (G2-G1)/4
entries.dim: L = Delta G / r; summit 125 ft per 4%; sag 100 ft per 4%; extend L up to a whole station
entries.wn: These formulas are for road design only; railroad and airfield design use different formulas. The metric sag value is printed as 38.10 m (same as summit); verify

entries.n: Vertical curve: stations and tangent elevations
entries.desc: Select a station interval (SI): rougher terrain means smaller SI, and the interval must place a station at the center of the curve with equal numbers of stations on both sides (a 300-ft curve cannot be staked at 100-ft intervals but can be at 10, 25, 30, 50 or 75 ft; usual intervals 10, 25, 50, 100 ft). PVI is the only fixed station: PVC = PVI - L/2; PVT = PVI + L/2; other stations from the PVI adding the SI until the PVT. Tangent elevations: Elev PVC = Elev PVI + (-1 x L/2 x G1); Elev PVT = Elev PVI + (L/2 x G2); back tangent station elev = Elev PVC + (distance from PVC x G1); forward tangent station elev = Elev PVI + (distance from PVI x G2)
entries.use: Setting PVC, PVT and station elevations on the tangents
entries.how: PVC = PVI - L/2, PVT = PVI + L/2; elevations from the PVI by grade x distance. Pick a station interval that puts a station at the curve center
entries.dim: PVC = PVI - L/2; PVT = PVI + L/2; Elev PVC = Elev PVI - (L/2)G1; Elev PVT = Elev PVI + (L/2)G2

entries.n: Vertical curve: offsets, curve elevations and checks
entries.desc: Vertical maximum Vm = (L/8)(G2 - G1) (L in 100-ft stations) or Vm = 1/2 [ (Elev PVC + Elev PVT)/2 - Elev PVI ]; compute both ways as a check on Vm, Elev PVC and Elev PVT. Vertical offset = (distance)^2 x Vm; it varies as the square of distance from the PVC or PVT; the curve is a mirror image so offsets are the same on both sides. Curve elevation = tangent elevation plus or minus the offset (plus for a sag curve, minus for a summit). First differences = elevation difference between successive stations; second differences = differences of the first differences; they should be all equal, may vary by one or two in the last decimal place from rounding (they should then form a pattern); if they vary too much or form no pattern, there is an error. Observe and record the algebraic sign. Example: G1 = -10, G2 = +5, r = 2.5: L = 15/2.5 = 6 stations; Vm = (15)(6)/8 = 11.25 ft
entries.use: Getting finished grade at each station on a vertical curve
entries.how: Vm = (L/8)(G2 - G1); offset = distance squared x Vm; curve elevation = tangent elevation +/- offset (plus for sag, minus for summit); second differences should be equal
entries.dim: Vm = L(G2 - G1)/8; offset = d^2 x Vm; example L = 6 stations, Vm = 11.25 ft
entries.wn: Carefully observe and record the sign of the first and second differences

entries.n: Vertical curve: high or low point
entries.desc: Use the high/low point to determine direction and amount of runoff on summit curves and to locate the low point for drainage. Equal tangent grades: at the center of the curve. Both grades plus: low point at the PVC, high at the PVT. Both minus: high at the PVC, low at the PVT. Unequal plus and minus grades: the point falls on the side with the flatter gradient. Distance from PVC or PVT in stations x = G L / (G2 - G1), where G is the flatter gradient and L is the number of curve stations. Elevation difference y = -(G2 - G1)/(2L) x^2 + G x. Example (G1 = +3.2%, G2 = -1.6%, L = 4): x = 1.3333 sta = 133.33 ft from the PVT; station of high point = (16+00) - 133.33 = 14+66.67; y = 1.07; elev = 128.00 + 1.07 = 129.07
entries.use: Finding the summit or sag low point for runoff and drainage
entries.how: x = G L / (G2 - G1) from the PVC or PVT; y = -(G2-G1)/(2L) x^2 + G x
entries.dim: x = G L/(G2 - G1) stations; y = -(G2 - G1) x^2/(2L) + G x; example x = 133.33 ft, y = 1.07 ft

entries.n: Plot cross sections and handle scale
entries.desc: Earthwork cross sections are vertical sections perpendicular to the centerline at full and plus stations showing boundaries of cut or fill. Plot on cross-section paper, normally same vertical and horizontal scale (standard 1 inch = 10 feet); an exaggerated vertical scale may be used when cut/fill is small compared with width. Take care to get the proper area: 1 in = 10 ft both ways gives 100 sq ft per square inch, but 1 in = 10 ft horizontal and 1 in = 2 ft vertical gives only 20 sq ft. Side slopes are horizontal : vertical (1 1/2:1 means 1 1/2 ft horizontal per ft rise/fall; also 3:1, 2:1, 1:1) set from design specs based on soil stability; cut slopes may be flattened to produce fill material for a nearby fill rather than operating a borrow pit
entries.use: Preparing cross sections for earthwork volume
entries.how: Plot on cross-section paper at 1 in = 10 ft; if you exaggerate the vertical scale, correct the area for it
entries.dim: Standard scale 1 in = 10 ft; 1 in = 10 ft x 1 in = 2 ft gives 20 sq ft per sq in
entries.wn: Compute areas with the proper scale factors

entries.desc: Hasty approximation: count the squares enclosed by the boundary lines and multiply by the square feet per square. Example: about 350 tenth-inch squares (3.5 one-inch squares); a tenth-inch square represents 1 ft horizontally and 6 in vertically = 1/2 sq ft, so 350/2 = 175 sq ft; or 3.5 x 50 = 175 sq ft with the 1-inch square (10 ft x 5 ft)
entries.use: Quick approximate area from a plotted cross section
entries.how: Count the squares inside the boundary and multiply by the area each square represents
entries.dim: Example 350 squares = 175 sq ft
entries.wn: Gives approximate results only. Determine cut and fill areas of a section separately

entries.desc: Subdivide the area into simple figures (no set rule; pick subdivisions giving the most direct and accurate result), compute each, and total. Triangle A = bh/2; trapezoid A = h (b1 + b2)/2, where h is the perpendicular distance between parallel bases (trapezoid) or base to vertex (triangle). Add all products first (double areas) and divide the total by 2. Example five-level section: double areas 22.8 + 60.8 + 87.4 + 133.5 + 29.8 + 6.8 = 341.1; area = 170.5 sq ft
entries.use: Accurate cross-section area by splitting into triangles and trapezoids
entries.how: Triangle A = bh/2, trapezoid A = h(b1 + b2)/2; add the double areas and divide by 2
entries.dim: A = bh/2; A = h(b1 + b2)/2; example 341.1 / 2 = 170.5 sq ft
entries.wn: As accurate as the field data permits. Cut and fill areas must be determined separately when both occur

entries.desc: Subdivide the plotted section by vertical lines at regular intervals (3, 5 or 10 ft, depending on ground roughness). Cumulatively mark the length of each line along the edge of a stripper (paper or plastic). Example stripper 5 squares wide by 60 squares long with zero index at the ground/side-slope intersection: move 5 squares at a time, bringing the previous top reading to the bottom line (readings 2.5, 6.0, ... final 53.0). Multiply the final reading (53.0) by the strip width (5) = 265.0 squares; multiply by the square feet per square for the area. Consider the horizontal and vertical scales
entries.use: Fast area measure from a plotted section using a paper or plastic strip
entries.how: Divide into vertical strips (3, 5 or 10 ft), accumulate the strip lengths on a stripper, and multiply the total by the strip width
entries.dim: Strip widths 3, 5 or 10 ft; example 53.0 x 5 = 265.0 squares
entries.wn: Gives approximate results

entries.desc: More precise than the stripper method but more effort and time; needs the elevations (latitudes) and distances from the centerline (departures) of all points. Procedure: compute and record all latitudes and departures; start at the far left station as the first point to avoid negative areas; DMD of the first course = its departure (4.0 in the example); DMD of any other course = DMD of preceding course + departure of preceding course + departure of the course itself (4.0 + 4.0 + 30.0 = 38.0; then 38.0 + 30.0 + 30.0 = 98.0); the last course's DMD equals its departure with the opposite sign (+14.0); multiply each DMD by its latitude, positive products under north double areas and negative under south; sum of north double areas minus sum of south double areas, disregarding signs, equals twice the area; divide by 2
entries.use: Most precise cross-section area when full point coordinates are known
entries.how: Compute latitudes (elevation) and departures (distance from centerline), DMD each course, multiply by latitude, and take half the difference of north and south double areas
entries.dim: DMD(n) = DMD(n-1) + dep(n-1) + dep(n); area = (sum N double areas - sum S double areas)/2
entries.tm: More effort and time than stripper or counting squares

entries.n: Measure area with a polar planimeter
entries.desc: Touch points: anchor point (B), tracing point (A), drum (C), support wheel (G); the adjustable tracing arm (E) is set to the plot scale using scale screws F1-F3 (settings come with the instrument; if the area reads too large increase the scale reading and vice versa). Read the disk for thousands, then the drum for hundreds and tens, then the vernier for ones. Rules: measure cut and fill separately; check consistency by tracing 1 square inch with the arm at a 1:1 ratio (disk, drum and vernier should read 1.000); set the arm by the chart in the case and verify by tracing a known area (such as five large squares); set the anchor outside the area, place the tracing point on a perimeter point, take an initial reading, trace clockwise exactly on the line, and read again when the tracing point closes; the difference is proportional to the area; make two independent measurements, the second from a point on the opposite side, and take the mean; divide plots larger than the instrument's capacity into sections
entries.use: Measuring a plotted cross section or irregular area
entries.how: Test the instrument on a 1 sq in area (reads 1.000), set the arm to the plot scale, trace the outline clockwise twice from opposite starting points and average
entries.dim: 1 sq in test area reads 1.000 at 1:1 ratio; two traces with opposite start points, take mean
entries.wn: A fixed-scale planimeter cannot be adjusted to a 1:1 ratio

entries.desc: Classifying material is not a survey function, but the surveyor must differentiate so excavation records match the construction work; record the three classes separately. Common excavation: earth or earth with detached boulders less than one-half cubic yard. Loose-rock excavation: consolidated material loosened without blasting using picks, bars or simple air and mechanical devices. Solid-rock excavation: rock from solid beds or boulders of 1 cubic yard or more broken up by explosives
entries.use: Keeping excavation quantity records separate by material class
entries.how: Record common excavation, loose rock and solid rock separately in the field notes
entries.dim: Boulders under 1/2 cu yd = common; 1 cu yd or more = solid rock (by explosives)

entries.n: Survey a borrow pit or waste area (grid method)
entries.desc: Needed when buying fill dirt or paying for excavation. Establish a grid over the area at any convenient interval (10, 25, 50 or 100 ft squares) and level the elevation of each grid corner. Volume removed at any time = (average elevation of the grid corners before excavation - average elevation after excavation) x number of square feet in the grid square(s), after re-establishing the corners and re-leveling. Lay out two baselines parallel to two adjacent grid sides, far enough outside the excavation to avoid destruction but close enough to be convenient, for re-establishing the grid. Treat waste areas or dumps the same way, measuring the volume deposited
entries.use: Measuring how much earth was removed from or deposited in a pit
entries.how: Stake a grid, level every corner before and after, and multiply the average elevation change by the square area
entries.dim: Grid intervals 10, 25, 50 or 100 ft; volume = (avg elev before - avg elev after) x area
entries.wn: Place baselines outside the excavation so they are not destroyed

entries.desc: Bridge surveying locates the site, gets design information and furnishes lines and grades; recon at all possible sites, preliminary survey at the best site (horizontal and vertical control), location survey to lay out the bridge, then additional lines/grades during construction. Precision ranges from hand-level and sketchboard work for a tactical bridge to precise measurements for a prefabricated steel bridge. Recon items: access roads (overlay sketches of approach roads); bridge length by tape, electronic measuring device or stadia; banks (vegetation, slope, height, composition, dikes; tentative abutment positions; usable abutments or piers); character of flow (stream velocity by timing a floating object over a measured course; high-water levels from drift, marks on vegetation or piers, local inhabitants, tide tables and flood records); river bottom character (intermediate supports; anchor holding power for floating bridges); streambed or gap profile by horizontal tape or cable or instrument-stadia (floating bridges need profiles only for trestles near shores); estimate local materials (timber, sand and gravel, cement, water, lumber)
entries.use: Selecting and evaluating tentative bridge sites
entries.how: Tactics fix the general area, technical factors fix the exact spot. Report access roads, length, banks, flow, bottom, profile and local materials
entries.eq: Tape, electronic distance measuring device, stadia, hand level

entries.n: Take soundings for a bridge site
entries.desc: Determine the relief of the stream bottom along the centerline and on lines each side; each sounding depth is related to the vertical control datum, and each sounding location is referenced to onshore control stations. The design engineer specifies offsets from the centerline and sounding intervals; unless specified use 25 ft for a fairly uniform streambed and 10 ft for an irregular streambed. For more accurate locations use the intersection method (instruments on the ends of an onshore baseline reading simultaneous angles). Method: set up over C and sight F; the sounding boat travels range line CF from the far shore toward the near shore; the instrumentman signals the crew into line at the proper distance by tape or stadia; the crew takes readings at the specified intervals; in shallow water take direct rod readings with the instrument near the river's edge; in deeper water measure depth from the boat with a suitable device. For profiles on each side, set stakes at specified distances from the centerline (B, D, E, G) and repeat from B and D, sighting E and G
entries.use: Mapping the streambed relief along and beside the bridge centerline
entries.how: Run the sounding boat along a range line, space soundings 25 ft (uniform bed) or 10 ft (irregular bed), and fix each position by an instrument on shore
entries.dim: Intervals 25 ft (uniform) or 10 ft (irregular) unless specified
entries.eq: Transit/theodolite, tape or stadia, sounding boat, rod

entries.desc: Subsurface investigations use borings, test pits, trenches and field tests to determine bearing capacities and substructure design. The surveyor references boreholes and test pits to nearby instrument stations and records elevations of strata encountered; the data are used to prepare a profile of subsurface conditions
entries.use: Supporting borings and test pits at a bridge site
entries.how: Reference every boring and test pit to a nearby instrument station and record strata elevations for a subsurface profile

entries.desc: Plans show pile-bent or crib-bent abutments. Check the layout after excavation and before any concrete is poured; check abutment elevations and establish lines for setting forms (concrete). Stake abutments per plans; distance between abutments must be within steel fabrication limits, especially for prefabricated sections; tie abutment stakes to a horizontal control system. Procedure (Figure 5-2): set the instrument at H (station 40+97.5), sight J, invert and tape to locate F; turn 90-degree angles and tape to locate C and D; move to F (station 41+37.5), sight H and turn 90-degree angles to locate A and B; locate E and G in line with A and B as horizontal control points
entries.use: Laying out abutment faces at right angles to the bridge centerline
entries.how: Set up on the centerline, tape to the face point, turn 90 degrees for the corners, and set offset control points in line with the faces. Check layout after excavation and before concrete
entries.dim: 90-degree angles to the bridge centerline
entries.wn: Distance between abutments must be within steel fabrication limits

entries.desc: An extension of abutment layout. Set the instrument at B, sight G and turn the wing angle; set L and M at any convenient distance along that line. Set up at A and locate N and O. Since A and B may be lost, two points on each wing wall's front line of sight are set. To relocate A, set up at O and sight through N, or set up on N, sight O and invert
entries.use: Laying out oblique wing walls from an abutment
entries.how: Turn the wing angle from the abutment corner and set two reference points on each wing-wall line so a lost corner can be re-found

entries.desc: After the bridge centerline is established, locate piers by taping; if impractical, triangulate. Set centerline stakes C and E on each side; lay out baselines CD and EF approximately at right angles; for well-proportioned triangles baseline length should be at least one-half CE. Steps: establish and reference baselines CD and EF; measure each baseline commensurate with required precision of CE; measure all angles of triangles CDE and EFC; compute CE from each triangle and check, difference within the prescribed limits of error; compute angles BDC, ADC, BFE and AFE (A and B are located by construction plans); draw a triangulation diagram; turn computed angles; set targets DA, DB on the far shore and FB, FA on the near shore, carefully referenced so intersecting lines can be reestablished without turning angles. Two instruments occupying F and D simultaneously locate crib piers at the intersection of sights FA and DA
entries.use: Locating piers across water when taping is impractical
entries.how: Tape if possible; otherwise triangulate from two baselines at about right angles to the centerline, each at least half of CE long
entries.dim: Baseline length at least 1/2 CE
entries.tm: Two instruments needed to locate crib piers

entries.n: Position piles and record driving data
entries.desc: Position piles, record pile-driving data and mark piles for cutoff per plans. Example: reference line AB 10 ft from the bridge centerline with a wire rope stretched and tape or cable clips marking pile-bent positions; locate upstream pile 1 by an offset (4 ft) from AB; float a template (3 ft pile spacing in the example) nailed to pile 1 into position and place the rest of the piles with it. If a cable cannot reach the far shore, set up an instrument at a convenient distance from the centerline and position the template by sighting a mark at the same distance from the template centerline; find template distance from shore by angle measuring or taping. Record: location and number of piles; dimensions; kind of wood; total penetration; average drop of hammer; average penetration under last five blows; penetration under last blow; amount of cutoff. Mark elevations on the two end piles and nail two 3- by 12-inch planks to guide the saw for cutting piles to height
entries.use: Placing pile bents and logging driving information
entries.how: Stretch a wire rope 10 ft off the centerline, offset to pile 1, space the rest with a template, and log driving data
entries.dim: Reference line 10 ft off centerline; first pile offset 4 ft; spacing 3 ft (example); guide planks 3 x 12 in

entries.desc: Objective: lay out the structure per plans and mark controlling points so they are most useful to construction forces (stakes, batter boards with string lines, drill holes, cut-and-fill notations). Plans give controlling dimensions (overall length and width, distances to road centerlines and other structures, interior measurements). Steps (Figure 6-1): establish baseline AB and locate CD by measurement; at C turn 90 degrees from B and locate corner stakes E and F by measurement; locate H and G from D the same way; check diagonals EH and FG using c = sqrt(a^2 + b^2); install batter boards; establish line and grade. Typically preceded by reconnaissance, site selection, control (horizontal and vertical) and topography (plane table or transit stadia)
entries.use: Staking building corners from plans
entries.how: Run a baseline, turn 90 degrees to set the corner stakes, check both diagonals with c = sqrt(a^2 + b^2), then install batter boards and set line and grade
entries.dim: 90-degree corners; diagonal check c = sqrt(a^2 + b^2)

entries.desc: Batter boards preserve outline and grade after corner stakes are disturbed. Each is two 2- by 4-inch stakes with a 1- by 6-inch crosspiece nailed to each pair. Drive stakes about 3 to 4 feet away from the building line (straddling the line, not disturbed by construction). Outside corners use three stakes, one a common post for two directions. Procedure: after laying out corner stakes, drive the 2x4 stakes 3-4 ft outside each corner chosen to bring all crosspieces to the same elevation; mark stakes at the grade of the top of the foundation or a whole number of inches/feet above or below; use a level to mark the same grade on all stakes; nail 1x6 boards with the top edge flush with the grade marks; mark the distance in crayon; locate the prolongation of the building lines on the boards with an instrument, or with a cord and plumb bobs over undisturbed corner stakes (move the cord until it just touches both plumb strings); drive nails into the top edges to mark the building line. A cord held against the nails defines building line and grade elevation. All batter boards for one structure are set to the same grade
entries.use: Preserving building lines and grade outside the excavation
entries.how: Drive 2x4 stakes 3-4 ft outside each corner, mark all to the same grade, nail 1x6 crosspieces flush with the marks, and nail the building line on top
entries.dim: Stakes 2 x 4 in, 3-4 ft outside the building line; crosspiece 1 x 6 in
entries.eq: Level, instrument or plumb bobs and cord, nails, 2x4 stakes, 1x6 boards, lumber crayon

entries.n: Transfer line and grade into a building
entries.desc: Line: set instrument stations outside to establish a line that, extended, intersects the building at a window or doorway; set up on the station farthest from the building, sight the nearest point, and transfer the line by sighting a plumb bob held in an upper-story window; extend inside by setting up on that point with outside stations as backsight, prolonging by double centering; with short sights, set an angle to clear an obstruction and measure by repetition. Grade: use direct leveling if possible; for an upper floor suspend a steel tape with a weight on the zero end approximately equal to the normal tension of the fully supported tape minus one half the weight of the suspended portion of the tape; read the tape with the level on the first floor, read again with the level on the upper floor to compute the HI, then hold a rod on an upper-floor point to establish a benchmark; an inverted rod can mark elevations on a wall
entries.use: Carrying lines and elevations inside and to upper floors
entries.how: Traverse and level; transfer elevation upstairs with a hanging steel tape and an appropriately weighted zero end
entries.dim: Tape weight = normal tension - 1/2 weight of suspended tape portion
entries.eq: Level, rod, steel tape, weight, plumb bob, transit

entries.n: Lay out a sewer line (batter boards, battens, invert grade)
entries.desc: Design: sewer lines are located on paper from the topographic map; the ditch centerline is staked and profile levels run; profile and grade lines are plotted and cut stakes set. After the trench is dug, set batter boards (usually every 10 to 25 ft, on edge across the trench) for pipe alignment and manhole or drop inlet placement; determine batter board interval, station and sewer grade elevation at each. Sewer grade = invert grade = pipe grade = flow line = grade line elevation, the elevation of the low point on the inside circumference of the pipe; all grade marks on the batter boards between two successive manholes are set the same distance above invert grade. Battens (small pieces of wood) nailed vertically on the same side of each batter board with the same edge over the sewer centerline indicate alignment; check them frequently by sighting past the edges
entries.use: Aligning pipe and setting manholes in a trench
entries.how: After the trench is dug set batter boards every 10-25 ft across it; all grade marks between two manholes sit the same distance above the invert grade
entries.dim: Batter boards every 10 to 25 ft
entries.eq: Level, rod, batter boards, battens, nails, string

entries.n: Transfer sewer line and grade with sighting cord and grade pole
entries.desc: After computing the invert elevation, add an even number of feet to get the cord elevation at each batter board; mark it on the centerline edge of each batten with a nail; fasten the sighting cord to the nails (centerline directly below the cord; invert grade at the chosen distance below it). Grade pole: a rod or stick with a mark at a distance from the foot piece equal to the cord-to-invert distance. Place the foot piece on the pipe invert, hold the pole plumb, raise or lower the pipe end until the mark is level with the cord. Hold a plumb line lightly against the cord and shift the pipe sideways until its crown is directly below the plumb bob point. Place the grade pole again, hold plumb, and recheck the mark against the cord
entries.use: Laying pipe to line and grade in the trench
entries.how: Stretch a sighting cord a fixed whole-foot distance above invert grade; use a grade pole with a mark at that distance to set the pipe height, and a plumb line to center the pipe
entries.dim: Cord height above invert = a whole number of feet
entries.eq: Sighting cord, grade pole, plumb bob, level

entries.desc: A traverse is a series of straight traverse legs connecting traverse stations (TS); distances and angles give the relative positions of the stations on a coordinate system. Open traverse: starts at a station, ends at a station whose relative position is not previously known; least desirable since it gives no check on fieldwork or starting data; plan for closure; close traverses in all cases where time permits. Closed on the starting point (loop traverse): starts at a point, proceeds to its destination and returns without crossing itself; used for tract/parcel boundary control and area computation, and where there is little or no control and only relative position is needed; can use assumed coordinates and azimuth; gives some check on fieldwork and computations but not on starting data or all systematic errors. Closed on a second known point: begins and ends on points of known coordinates; preferred because it checks fieldwork, computations and starting data and gives a basis for judging overall accuracy
entries.use: Deciding whether to run an open, loop or two-point closed traverse
entries.how: Always close the traverse if time permits. Best is closing on a second known point; a loop gives some checks; an open traverse gives none
entries.wn: An open traverse gives no check on fieldwork or starting data

entries.n: Establish starting control for a traverse
entries.desc: A traverse needs starting data: coordinates of a starting point and an azimuth to an azimuth mark. Known control: published trig list stations, or stations established by higher headquarters; get azimuth from the trig list or compute from known coordinates. Maps available (no control): assume the starting coordinate as close to correct as possible, scaled from the map (scaled data are considered assumed data), and scale the starting direction from the map. No maps: assume the starting coordinate; determine starting direction by the most accurate means available
entries.use: Getting coordinates and starting azimuth
entries.how: Use the best data available: known control, scaled map data (treated as assumed), or an assumed coordinate with the best starting direction you can get

entries.desc: Three stations matter: rear station (just left, or a station with a known azimuth), occupied station (instrument set up over it) and forward station (next). Always measure horizontal angles at the occupied station by sighting the rear station and measuring clockwise to the forward station, pointing on the lowest visible point of the target marking each station. Measure the distance in a straight line between the occupied and forward stations using horizontal taping procedures or electronic distance measuring equipment. With a one-minute instrument turn each horizontal angle once direct and once reverse
entries.use: Taking angles and distances at each traverse station
entries.how: At the occupied station sight the rear station and turn clockwise to the forward station; sight the lowest visible point of the targets; measure the leg by taping or EDM
entries.dim: Clockwise angles from rear to forward station; one direct and one reverse position (one-minute instrument)
entries.eq: Transit/theodolite, tape or EDM, range poles

entries.n: Select, mark and signal traverse stations
entries.desc: Select sites as the traverse progresses so both rear and forward stations are visible from each; for taping the line between stations must be free of obstacles. Keep the number of stations to a minimum to reduce accumulation of instrumental errors and computing; short legs mean more stations and may cause excessive azimuth error because small errors in centering, station marking and pointing are magnified. Markers: usually 2- by 2-inch wooden stakes at least 6 inches long (hubs) driven flush, center of the top marked with a surveyor's tack or an X. Reference (witness) stake driven sloping toward the station with identification on it (lumber crayon, china marking pencil or tag); signal cloth may be tied to it. Signals: most commonly a range pole, tapered point on the station mark, made vertical with a rod level, checked by confirming the bubble stays centered at other points on the pole; keep it vertical during observation by tripod or by holding; place a range pole vertical only on a survey station to avoid angles to the wrong point
entries.use: Placing traverse stations in the field
entries.how: Pick stations so rear and forward stations are visible, keep the number of legs minimal, use 2x2 hubs flush with a tack or X, add a sloped witness stake, and signal with a vertical range pole
entries.dim: Hubs 2 x 2 in, at least 6 in long
entries.eq: 2x2 hubs, tack, witness stakes, lumber crayon/china pencil, signal cloth, range pole, rod level
entries.wn: Short traverse legs magnify centering and pointing errors into azimuth closure

entries.desc: Organization depends on the unit TOE and SOP. Chief of party: selects and marks station locations, supervises, assists with recon and planning. Instrument operator: measures horizontal angles at each station. Recorder: keeps the field notes (appendix B), records angles, distances and other data; usually the member who checks taped distances by pacing. Two tapemen: measure distance station to station. Rodman: assists the chief marking stations, removes the target from the rear station when signaled and moves it forward. Party size may be reduced by combining chief, operator and recorder; a tapeman may double as rodman, but it is best to have two tapemen and a separate rodman
entries.use: Assigning jobs for a traverse crew
entries.how: Chief, instrument operator, recorder, two tapemen and a rodman; you can combine chief/operator/recorder but keep two tapemen and a separate rodman
entries.dim: Minimum recommended: two tapemen plus a separate rodman
entries.tm: Roles: chief, instrument operator, recorder, 2 tapemen, rodman

entries.desc: Azimuth is the horizontal angle measured clockwise from a base direction (grid north; in extreme cases magnetic) to the line; determine an azimuth for each leg. Each succeeding leg azimuth = azimuth from the occupied station to the rear station (back azimuth of preceding leg) + the measured angle at the occupied station; subtract 360 if the sum exceeds 360; back azimuth = azimuth +/- 180. Example: Az A to azimuth mark 120 deg 00'; angle Az mark-A-B 310 deg 15': 120 deg 00' + 310 deg 15' = 430 deg 00' - 360 = Az A-B 70 deg 15'; back Az 250 deg 15' + angle A-B-C 270 deg 57' = 521 deg 12' - 360 = Az B-C 161 deg 12'; back Az 341 deg 12' + angle B-C-A 313 deg 28' = 654 deg 40' - 360 = Az C-A 294 deg 40'; back Az 114 deg 40' + angle C-A-Az mark 5 deg 19' = 119 deg 59', a 1' error against the known 120 deg 00'
entries.use: Getting the azimuth of every traverse leg
entries.how: At each station: back azimuth of the previous leg + the measured angle (subtract 360 if over). Finish by computing the azimuth back to the azimuth mark as a check
entries.dim: Az(next) = back Az(previous) + angle at occupied station (-360 if > 360); back Az = Az +/- 180
entries.wn: The manual prints the back azimuth of B-C as 314 deg 12'; the correct value is 341 deg 12' (161 deg 12' + 180 deg) and the later arithmetic uses 341 deg 12'

entries.n: Check and adjust angular closure (azimuth adjustment)
entries.desc: Determine the need for adjustment before final coordinate computation. Allowable angular error AE = 1' sqrt(N) or 20 seconds per station, whichever is less (N = number of traverse stations). Example N = 3: 1' sqrt(3) = 1.73' = 104"; 20" x 3 = 60"; allowable is 60 seconds. If azimuth error is not within allowable the station angles must be reobserved in the field. Azimuth error = computed closing azimuth - known closing azimuth (example 119 deg 59' - 120 deg 00' = -01'); correction = reverse sign (+01'). Because errors are assumed to accumulate gradually and systematically, divide the correction equally among the angles with any remainder going to the larger angles (4 angles: +01' / 4 = +15" each). Then compute adjusted azimuths of each leg from the starting azimuth and adjusted angles and check against the correct closing azimuth before further computation
entries.use: Distributing a small angle error before computing coordinates
entries.how: Allowable angular error is 1' x sqrt(n) or 20" per station, whichever is less. If within limits, change the correction's sign and divide it equally among all angles; if not, reobserve the angles
entries.dim: AE = 1' sqrt(N) or 20" per station, whichever is less; example 60"; correction per angle = total correction / number of angles
entries.wn: If the error exceeds the allowable, reobserve the angles in the field

entries.desc: If a calculator with angular functions is available use the azimuth directly; otherwise use bearings with tables. Bearing = the acute angle between the line and the north-south line through the occupied point. First quadrant (0-90 deg): bearing = azimuth. Second (90-180): bearing = 180 - azimuth. Third (180-270): bearing = azimuth - 180. Fourth (270-360): bearing = 360 - azimuth. Since values repeat, label the quadrant (N or S and E or W). Example: azimuth 341 deg 12' 30" is in the fourth (northwest) quadrant, bearing N 18 deg 47' 30" W
entries.use: Using tables of trig functions that list only 0-90 degrees
entries.how: Bearing is the acute angle from the N-S line; by quadrant: Q1 bearing = Az; Q2 = 180 - Az; Q3 = Az - 180; Q4 = 360 - Az. Label N/S and E/W

entries.desc: If the coordinates of a point and the azimuth and distance to a second point are known, compute the second point's coordinates. dN = cos Azimuth x Distance; dE = sin Azimuth x Distance; add dN and dE (with sign) to the northing and easting of the first point. With a trig calculator entering the azimuth directly gives the correct sign; with tables, assign signs by inspection: lines going north have positive dN, south negative; lines going east have positive dE, west negative. Examples: Az 70 deg 15' 15", 568.78: dN = +0.337848 x 568.78 = +192.16; dE = +0.941200 x 568.78 = +535.34. Az 161 deg 12' 30", 548.74 (SE quadrant): dN -519.49; dE +176.76. Az 294 deg 40' 45", 783.74 (NW): dN +327.24; dE -712.15
entries.use: Getting the northing and easting of the next station
entries.how: dN = cos(azimuth) x distance; dE = sin(azimuth) x distance. North and east are positive
entries.dim: dN = cos Az x D; dE = sin Az x D

entries.n: Check traverse acceptability (linear error and accuracy ratio)
entries.desc: Construction surveying normally seeks an accuracy ratio of 1:5,000; horizontal distances accurate to at least 0.02 ft per 100 ft; with a one-minute instrument turn angles once direct and once reverse with angular closure of 20 seconds per station or 1' sqrt(stations), whichever is less. Loop traverse: the algebraic sum of dNs (and of dEs) should equal zero; the discrepancy is the linear error in dN (eN) and dE (eE) (example eN 0.09, eE 0.05). eL = sqrt(eN^2 + eE^2) = sqrt(0.0106) = 0.1029. Allowable error AE = (1/5,000) x length of traverse (or 1/3,000 as appropriate) = 1,901.26/5,000 = 0.3802. If AE is greater than eL the traverse is good and can be adjusted; if not, rerun it. Accuracy ratio = eL / total length reduced to 1/x and rounded down: 1,901.26 / 0.1029 = 18,476.77 or 1:18,000 (the text prints 118,476.77). If the ratio is outside limits rerun; distances may be correct and the error due to large compensating angular errors
entries.use: Deciding if a traverse is good enough or must be rerun
entries.how: Linear error eL = sqrt(eN^2 + eE^2); allowable = traverse length / 5,000 (or /3,000). If AE > eL the traverse is good. Ratio = eL : length, rounded down
entries.dim: Ratio 1:5,000 normal (1/3,000 also referenced); taping 0.02 ft per 100 ft; example eL 0.1029, AE 0.3802, ratio 1:18,000
entries.wn: The text prints 118,476.77 for the ratio quotient; 1,901.26/0.1029 = 18,476.77

entries.n: Adjust coordinates with the compass rule
entries.desc: Compass rule: for any leg, the correction to dN or dE is to the total correction as the leg length is to the total traverse length; total correction equals the error (eN or eE) with opposite sign. dN correction = (total dN correction / length of traverse) x distance to station; same for dE. Example: first leg 568.78 of 1,901.26: dN correction = +0.09/1,901.26 x 568.78 = +0.03; dE correction = +0.05/1,901.26 x 568.78 = +0.01. Loop traverse: apply corrections to the dNs and dEs before computing coordinates; total corrections must equal the total error; if rounding leaves a difference of one, reduce the correction on the shortest line or increase the longest line; if greater than one arbitrarily adjust until total correction equals total error. Next station = previous coordinate +/- dN/dE +/- correction. Traverse starting and ending on two different stations: compute coordinates first, then apply cumulative corrections directly to coordinates (after leg 1: correction 1; after leg 2: correction 1 + 2; ... last must equal total correction)
entries.use: Distributing the linear misclosure among the legs
entries.how: Correction to each leg = (total correction) x (leg length / traverse length), opposite sign of the error. Apply to dN/dE before coordinates for a loop; accumulate on coordinates for a two-point traverse
entries.dim: Correction = (total correction / traverse length) x cumulative or leg distance; example +0.03 and +0.01 on first leg

entries.n: Solve right and oblique triangles (Table A-4 formulas)
entries.desc: Right triangle: sin A = a/c = cos B; cos A = b/c = sin B; tan A = a/b = cot B; cot A = b/a = tan B; sec A = c/b; csc A = c/a; vers A = (c-b)/c; a = c sin A = b tan A; b = c cos A = a cot A; a = sqrt((c+b)(c-b)). Oblique: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C; law of cosines a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos A (and cyclic); given A, B, a: b = a sin B / sin A, c = a sin(A+B) / sin A as printed; given C, a, b: tan 1/2(A-B) = [(a-b)/(a+b)] tan 1/2(A+B); given a, b, c with s = 1/2(a+b+c): sin 1/2 A = sqrt[(s-b)(s-c)/bc], cos 1/2 A = sqrt[s(s-a)/bc], area = sqrt[s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)]; area = 1/2 a b sin C. Other identities: sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1; sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A; cos 2A = 2cos^2 A - 1; 1 radian = 57.2957790 deg; pi = 3.141592654; circle area = pi r^2; sector area = 1/2 L r
entries.use: Solving distances and angles for inaccessible points or curve problems
entries.how: Right triangle: sin A = a/c, cos A = b/c, tan A = a/b. Oblique: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C; c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab cos C
entries.dim: See formulas in description
entries.wn: Where the printed sine-rule line for c (given A, B, a) reads sin(A+B), the correct third angle is 180 deg - (A+B) with sin(180-x) = sin x, so the two are equal

entries.desc: Table A-2 gives, for vertical angles 0 to 30 degrees in 2-minute steps, the horizontal distance and difference in elevation per 100 units of stadia intercept (adequate for feet and meters). Table values follow horizontal distance = 100 cos^2 V and difference in elevation = 50 sin 2V
entries.use: Getting horizontal distance and elevation difference from a stadia rod intercept
entries.how: For vertical angle V and rod intercept 1.00 ft, Table A-2 gives horizontal distance per 100 and difference in elevation; multiply by RI
entries.dim: Hor. dist. = 100 cos^2 V; diff. elev. = 50 sin 2V (per 1.00 rod intercept x 100)

entries.desc: Curvature of the Earth's surface is about 0.7 foot in 1 mile; curvature in feet = 0.667 (distance in miles)^2. The difference between arc and chord length is 0.02 foot in 11 1/2 miles
entries.use: Judging whether curvature matters over a long sight
entries.how: Curvature = 0.667 x (distance in miles)^2 feet; about 0.7 ft in 1 mile
entries.dim: Curvature = 0.667 x miles^2 ft; 0.7 ft per mile; arc-chord 0.02 ft in 11 1/2 miles

entries.n: Differential leveling notes: closure check and adjustment
entries.desc: Backsight (BS) and foresight (FS) distances determined by stadia should be balanced. Make a page check (PC) for each page; page checks verify the arithmetic, not the accuracy of the survey. Error of closure (EC) = computed elevation - starting or fixed elevation. Total correction (TC) = EC with sign changed. Allowable error (AE) may be given in the project specifications; if BS and FS distances are balanced as near as possible: normal construction work AE = +/- 0.1 ft sqrt(miles) or +/- 24 mm sqrt(kilometers); third order AE = +/- 0.05 ft sqrt(miles) or +/- 12 mm sqrt(kilometers) (square-root signs lost in the extracted text; standard form). Adjust fixed-point elevations by dividing TC by total distance and multiplying by the distance from the beginning station to the station being adjusted, then add algebraically to the station's computed elevation
entries.use: Recording and checking a level line
entries.how: Balance backsight and foresight stadia distances; do page checks (they check math only). Error of closure = computed - fixed elevation; allowable +/-0.1 ft x sqrt(miles) for construction, +/-0.05 ft x sqrt(miles) third order
entries.dim: Normal: +/-0.1 ft sqrt(mi) or +/-24 mm sqrt(km); third order: +/-0.05 ft sqrt(mi) or +/-12 mm sqrt(km)
entries.wn: A page check proves the arithmetic only

entries.n: Horizontal taping notes: forward and backward check
entries.desc: Tape each line in both forward (FWD) and backward (BKWD) directions. The difference between forward and backward totals is the error of closure (EC). Allowable error AE = mean distance (MEAN) / 5,000, not rounded up; this gives accuracy ratio 1 in 5,000 or third order accuracy. AE must equal or exceed EC for the taping to be acceptable
entries.use: Taping a line twice and testing acceptability
entries.how: Tape forward and back; difference is the error of closure; allowable error = mean distance / 5,000 (do not round up). Must be equal or greater than the error
entries.dim: AE = MEAN distance / 5,000; ratio 1:5,000
entries.wn: Do not round the allowable error up

entries.n: Measure station angles direct and reverse
entries.desc: Measure the angle first with the telescope direct (D), then double it by measuring again in reverse (R); mean (MEAN) = R value divided by 2; mean must be within +/-30 seconds of the D value. Total of mean angles should equal (N-2) 180 degrees, N being the number of station angles in the loop traverse. For a one-minute instrument an error of +/-30 seconds per station angle is acceptable. To close the horizon, also measure and mean the explement angle; if the explement D value exceeds 180 degrees, add 360 degrees to the R value and divide by 2 to get the mean; both mean angles at a station must total 360 degrees within +/-30 seconds, and each mean must be within +/-30 seconds of its D value
entries.use: Taking a one-minute-instrument angle and checking it
entries.how: Measure with the telescope direct, then double it by measuring reverse; the mean must be within +/-30 seconds of the direct value. A loop's mean angles must total (N-2) x 180
entries.dim: +/-30" between mean and D value; sum of loop angles = (N-2) x 180; explement pair = 360 deg +/-30"

entries.n: Record deflection angles in the notes
entries.desc: When the direct (D) value for direction exceeds 180 degrees the deflection angle = 360 - D and is a left deflection preceded by L; mean deflection = (360 - R)/2, also preceded by L. When D is less than 180 degrees the deflection equals D, preceded by R (right), and the mean = R/2, preceded by R. Deflection angles never exceed 180 degrees.
